title: Musical masterpiece, but a disappointing performance
text:
"Neither" is a very unique "opera" and an important work in the history of modern music. The result of a near-failed collaboration between two uncompromising artists, Feldman and Beckett, "Neither" is a masterpiece. The music has a compelling ethereal beauty, while surprising the listener through the use of unusual orchestration, rhythms, and musical forms.
However, this particular recording of the work is disappointing. The soprano, Sarah Leonard, sounds strained from the first note to the last, and fails to remain perfectly on pitch throughout the performance. It makes the work painful to listen to.
The version by Petra Hoffmann and the Symphony Orchestra of Bayerischen Rundfunks directed by Kwame Ryan is far superior, and is the most definitive version of this piece thus far, in my opinion. Petra Hoffmann blends nicely with the rest of the orchestra, and the changes in the atmosphere from one part to the next are more marked by the artful directing of Ryan. The Kwame Ryan/Petra Hoffmann version is understandably the version chosen by the Ballett am Rhein to accompany Schläpfer's choreography of the piece.

title: This Hybrid SACD is better Sounding than the Red Book DSD.
text:
This review will be concerned primarily with the sound.
I just finished listening to these performances twice. The first time I listened to the disc [number 17] in the Living Stereo box Volume 1 remastered to DSD, as was everything in the box, by Soundmirror. I thought and probably still think they did a fine job of remastering the red book layer of the CD.. Indeed, some of the best upgrades I've heard; so fine that I intended to sell this Hybrid SACD that I also have. First I checked that it was in resale condition. Perfect. Then, just out of curiosity I put the SACD in the same SACD/CD player. The sound that I heard actually startled me; it was that much better. Most noticeable was the soundstage which opened up considerably; also, the instruments tonal quality sounded more like the real thing.
My advice: If you now have any of the Living Stereo Hybrids don't get rid of them thinking that the sound on the discs in the big box is the same. Even if you have both now and can't hear the difference, hesitate. If you someday upgrade your equipment you will!
I have all the hybrids and will be doing a close listening comparison between them and the discs in the Living Stereo box. If it should turn out that what I hear doesn't confirm the comparison herein I'll amend this review.
One final note: Unlike the USA the Japanese have not given up on SACD. They are so convinced that SACD sounds better that they are now releasing remastered discs in SACD only. The theory, as I understand it, is that the SACD tracks are easier to read whenn they don't have to go through the red book CD tracks first. HiRez DSD downloads might sound as good or better, but unless you have plenty of time to wait for the great performances of the past to appear and become available in that form you might miss out on a lot of great performances in very good sound.

title: A Latin American specialist sleepwalking
text:
Once again, another pianist comes along on the heels of the Lecuona revival started by the re-release of Lecuona playing his own works on BMG/RCA, and Tirino's monumental, comprehensive and incomparable series on BIS records, and once again, this one fails miserably. Seems like so many pianists are trying to get on the Lecuona bandwagon these days.
Polly Ferman, a wonderful pianist who has done much for Latin American music in performance on and off disk wonderfully, unfortunately, like many other pianists, really misses it here with the music of Cuba's Ernesto Lecuona. It is unfortunate, because one would expect greater insights and interpretations from this pianist, who, sounds at times asleep at the piano.
The tempi are SO slow. No concept of contrast and/or what a danza Cubana is. The malaguena lacks every bit of fire needed, as well as technical panache. The other works lack insights, color variation, and style or understanding of the various works. The music is relegated to a salon like feel, at its worst.
Once again, as a Cuban, in my humble opinion-go get the Tirino BIS series of Complete Piano music of Lecuona. There's really no other game in town, and no competition.

title: Jim Reeves Radio Show Available Again
text: For years unavailable, these five cds present the great Jim Reeves hosting his own radio show.  Fortunately for us fans, VoiceMasters has made these performances available again; as a limited edition.  You get to hear Mr. Reeves sing songs that he didn’t record commercially – pop songs along with some of the songs that he did record commercially.  And there is also the wonderful “Amen Corner”, where Mr. Reeves presents clever and funny sayings and stories.  One of the things I enjoy about these shows is you get to hear Jim Reeves interacting with the other performers.  You get to hear him speak and laugh.  You also get to hear a very funny boo boo that he made.  And the Christmas show is not to be missed.  All the songs are backed by the Owen Bradley Orchestra.  Owen Bradley certainly needs no introduction to any fan of Country Music.  He produced Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn, Brenda Lee and many other well-known stars.  In addition to Mr. Reeves, there are performances by the Bradley Orchestra, Dolores Watson and Buddy Hall, resulting in 165 tracks and 5 hours.  I was very pleased at the fantastic sound quality.  When I got my set, I was amazed to see there are 5 hours of music on this set.  Considering that, this set is a bargain in my humble opinion. title: music to chase hares down holes to - quelques chansons brillantes
text:
This is one of my favorite albums of all time. Ces mecs sont pure seventies. Imagine the Beatles mixed with a touch of Crosby Stills Nash & Young and Jefferson Airplane cut with someone like Leo Kottke- but in Quebecois French.

The entire album is mostly mellow acoustic- guitar driven 70's folk rock. They're aptly named, because the harmonies & melodies here will catch you. The lyrics are really exquisite, too, I think. Pretty sure quite a bit of chemical inspiration went into the writing of these songs. Par example, from the title song, Harmonium:

Imaginez qu'un homme musicien vienne voir si je suis vivant, chargé par ses milles instruments. y'en avait un pour moi, justement. il est entré sans rien me dire, l'encre s'est mise à couler dans ma tete et sur un vieux papier.. il m'a dit de vous dire qu'il n'y a plus rien a dire, il m'a dit de vous dire d'ecouter.

Roughly: Imagine, a music man come to see if I'm alive, bearing his thousands of instruments. He had one for me, only one. He came in without saying anything.. Ink has begun to flow in my head onto an old paper.. He told me to tell you that there's nothing more to say, he told me to tell you to listen.

It's more poetic in French, but you get the semantic thrust. Anyway, can't be sure, but I think someone dropped a couple tabs, there. It must have been fun. The result is quite nice & trippy, anyway.

This album is a very good tool to improve your French with, btw, having very clear enunciation - excepting that there's a bit of l'argot quebecois here, but that to me only adds to their allure.

Highly recommended. Seek it out if you like French music at all.

title: Believe it!
text: A Mahler symphony performed by high school students? Hard to believe. A Mahler symphony performed with sure technical command and idiomatic fluency by high school students? Unbelievable. But one listen to this live recording by Rudolf Barshai and the Junge Deutsche Philharmonie, and you'll become a believer. While Barshai is probably best known as a Shostakovich conductor (he premiered the composer's Fourteenth Symphony in 1969), on the evidence of this CD he's a natural Mahlerian as well. Arguably the most difficult of Mahler's symphonies to put over convincingly, the Fifth here is a model of architectural strength and contrapuntal clarity, which flows beautifully and even effortlessly. Barshai refuses to indulge in self-conscious phrasing or sensational effects, yet the climaxes are as shattering as the composer would want, while the sinuous (and sinewy) Adagietto comes off as the love song to future-wife Alma that Mahler intended. This is something very special; the same recording is also available on Brilliant Classics coupled with Barshai's own orchestration of the unfinished Tenth Symphony.

title: As always, the Ronettes rock, and perfection is the expectation.
text:
The CD arrived as promised with a nice personal thank-you from the sellers - a nice touch! I'm a Ronettes freak, so this review may be a bit more critical than some others would be. The original stereo LP (it wasn't easy to find back in the day, as the US release was mono) remains as the "bomb" in my personal view, - as it has decent stereo separation, good echo and reproduction of the girl's voices. Although I love the "Wall of Sound," I could do without Phil's mono fetish.

This CD is nicely executed, but at this point on my small office stereo sounds like re-engineered mono, but comes across with stunning echo (I love it!) and nice reproduction of Ronnie's voice. The Estelle and Nedra sound somewhat distant, as do the smaller percussion instruments, - a negative in my view. I'm not yet sure about the bass. This is really petty on my part as I don't know what the engineers had to work with - but I'd like just a bit more of the mid-range. All in all, I'd rate this CD as just short of excellent. I may revise the rating upward (it won't go down, no way) after I play it in my car's larger system, or on the big (and old) 100w Sansui system in the living room. If you like the Ronettes, buy this CD. It's worth every penny.

title: The use of the word "summer" is questionable................
text:
A word of warning for those interested in buying British compilation albums with the word "summer" in the title. In my record buying experience, the word "summer" usually refers to when it was released, and not because the tracks featured relate to "summer" songs. This is a prime example of what I mean. "Ultimate Summer Party Megamix", endorsed by Chris Tarrant - the host of the UK's version of 'Who Wants To Be A Millionaire' - is basically a collection of the biggest selling songs appearing in the UK charts from January-July 1999. There's a couple of other well-known songs that have become karoke classic over the years, plus several bona-fide "summer songs". But really, this is a megamix version of "Now That's What I Call Music" - and it's released by the same people too. So if it's a genuine "summer" album you're after, check the track listings carefully.
Jon.

title: Fine performance, poor transfer source
text:
This review is of the Arkadia CD, # GA2027, of the 18 January 1941 Metropolitan Opera broadcast of Verdi's OTELLO, with Giovanni Martinelli, Stella Roman and Lawrence Tibbett, conducted by Ettore Panizza, Amazon's ASIN: B00004UECD, which I include since these reviews are mixed with those of other editions and performances. While for vocal quality not the best of Martinelli's four broadcasts of the work, it is still compelling, and has Stella Roman as Desdemona, a popular artist at the Met in the 1940s. But Arkadia's source was seriously flawed with digital mistracking noise, especially in the last act, which is why I rate it down to 2-stars.

This is certainly an exciting performance, energetically led by Ettore Panizza. Martinelli may be having more vocal trouble than in his earlier broadcasts, but it remains a dramatically committed portrayal. Tibbett's vocal problems were well known; he had cancelled all performances for several months after suffering some damage due to a "throat infection," returning to the Met only a couple weeks before this broadcast. While lacking the ease he once had in the more-dramatic passages, his voice retains its characteristic resonance, and he is fine in more-lyrical parts like "Era la notte." Stella Roman sings some beautiful high notes, and does a few strange things at other times, but as usual with sopranos singing Desdemona, she is at her best in the last-act arias. And for once the effect of the string basses at Otello's entrance is not ruined; the audience refrains from applauding after the "Ave Maria."

Sound quality from the original transcriptions is fairly good with reasonably wide frequency range and little surface noise, though the tape transfer introduced a few dropouts and small glitches where splices were made to eliminate noise or join transcription sides. Unfortunately, the immediate source used for this edition had a problem that didn't exist in 1941, digital data loss that sounds like CD mistracking, periodic racket at the rotational speed of the disc, and mostly at higher volume levels. About four or five crunches per second are heard when this happens. While the copy I got was "new" and factory sealed, the deteriorating plastic disc holder in the case showed it had been sitting around for many years. I thought it might have been the old CD "bronzing" problem, but saw no corrosion of the reflective layer. To be sure, I found a used copy (cheap!) and the "mistracking noise" is in exactly the same places. There's a small amount on the first disc near the end of Act II, from "Era la notte" through most of "Si, pel ciel" but it goes away a minute or so before the end of the act. The second disc has more of the trouble; it starts about 25 minutes into Act III, right before the big ensemble, and gets continually worse through Act IV.

The problem doesn't seem unique to Arkadia's edition; one of the 1-star reviews for the Pearl CD (ASIN: B005Z50Q54) mentions what is likely the same issue, if poorly described. I decided to get a version unlikely to have have any "digital noise," the LP set from Robin Hood Records (see https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00FGAQBEI/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_search_asin_title?ie=UTF8&psc=1 since the ASIN number alone fails to bring it up) which despite the minor clicks and pops of old vinyl pressings was decidedly more satisfactory than Arkadia's CD. But I don't know of a CD release of this performance without the noise problem.

Martinelli and Tibbett were in better vocal shape in their earlier OTELLO broadcasts, including those from 12 February 1938 found on Naxos (ASIN: B0009SQC5U) and from 24 February 1940 in the "Verdi at the Met" collection (ASIN: B00DWOUY3Y). The sound quality of this one from 1941 is preferable in some respects, if distant microphone placement still kept "Esultate!" from having the impact it should. The dramatic intensity makes this performance worth hearing, though with the transfer issues of Arkadia's edition I'd suggest looking for a copy at a low price.

title: Under rated release from Wings
text: As McCartney began his solo career, he released "McCartney" and "Ram," two of the best albums of his career, and two of the best home produced records of all time. Its no wonder then, that when this album was released, fans and critics were dumbfounded. Often hailed as one of Macca's worst records, "Wild Life" is odd, built on jams and riffs, and contains trite lyrics. But it is important to remember: McCartney wanted to form a gold-old-fashioned touring band. Here it sounds like the members of that band got together in a living room or garage, drank a few beers, and started playing. Only "Tomorrow" and "Dear Friend" really sound calculated, and this record is just fun- Its great to but on in the background one day, or while your driving, but certainly not to sit around and listen to like you would with a Beatles record- this isn't close to a Beatles record. So it is possible to call this a bad record, or to call it what it is: a fun, folky, enjoyable relaxed record which hints at what Wings would accomplish.

title: Knott this mess!
text:
This is one Michael Knott release that, the less said about it, perhaps the better. NO ONE SHOULD START THEIR JOURNEY WITH KNOTT AT THIS POINT! This is a compilation album covering LSU history from “Shaded Pain” through “Cash In Chaos—World Tour”. It’s not trying to pick the most popular LSU songs as illustrative; it throws in some odd ducks, a few new cuts (which is the only real reason to get this one), some head scratching and horrendous “remixes”, and several live tracks. This mish mash seriously hurts the presentation of LSU’s work. One reviewer pointed out the craziness of Knott and that’s true, but his craziness made sense and was artful in much of his studio albums. Here it just turns everything into a huge glob of mess and makes these songs lack cohesion. The live cuts might be of interest to Knott fans but they uniformly fail to deliver the goods of the actual studio songs. The remixes sport scratchy distortion, a drowning of the original sounds, and a telephone ring that might literally drive you crazy. They are infuriating!

I’ll get to the three new cuts in a moment but before that I wanted to note that there was apparently a cassette release with four additional tracks, three untouched tracks (There’s A Time; Shaded Pain; and G.G.G.) plus one track that may have contained a sample of every LSU song. I haven’t heard it but that must have been one messy track. As for the new tracks contained (to the best of my knowledge) only on this release they are: Funky Space Cat; Baby Flies A Comet; and It Fits Inside. “Funky Space Cat” is a fun and funky song true enough to its title. “Baby Flies A Comet” is very repetitive and could have been a rejected Aunt Bettys song. “It Fits Inside” is a quiet acoustic solo guitar number, very introspective.

Unless you’re a Knotthead looking to complete your collection I’d beg you off this disc in a hurry. If you think that I’m being too unfair or harsh regarding this release that’s cool but I’d encourage you to balance your judgment against my reviews of other Knott related releases. I love the dude and most of his offerings, but most definitely Knott this mess!

title: I wanted to kill myself after seeing this film
text:
This film should be used in film schools, in comparison to Star Wars and Empire, to illustrate what exactly makes a bad film bad and a good film good. What made Star Wars great? Genius imagination. Fresh, interesting, unique, memorable characters. Fantastic music. Masterful attention to detail. Suspense. Surprises. A blend of sweet and strange, disgusting and spectacular. Good and evil were represented in human terms, authentic and rich with mythic resonance.
What makes this film so awful? Zero imagination. I suppose there were some interesting digital elements, but clever digital rendering is not a substitute for real storytelling. Characters? Who, the third rate Romeo and Juliet? R2D2 with a different number? All the nondescript aliens with flaccid tenticles hanging off their heads (what is up with that?)? Music, whatever, I guess there must have been music. Those little touches like the appropriate funkiness and unreliability of the Millenium Falcon or Luke's landspeeder are gone - replaced with spankin' new artifacts of Godlike perfection for all. In this visionless anti-story "goodness" is equated with perfect skin and flying puppets while evil is merely an alternate set of pompous and pretentious elites, a Pepsi vs. Coke cosmology.
Truly this film demonstrates all that is wrong with what Western Civilization has become. Stop the madness!

title: Jazz Guitar and Jazz Adventure
text:
The album, Days, makes it clear that jazz guitarist Gabriel Vicéns is someone to pay attention to.   The Puerto Rico native serves up progressive Latin jazz characterized by fluid improvisation, exciting melodic explorations and a sense of musical adventure.   Tracks on Days include “El Teatro,” which features lively syncopation and a smooth, rising-falling melody on which Vicéns and other soloists take turns exploring the different altitudes.  
The song “Days” features greater conversational interplay among Vicéns and his bandmates that culminates in joyful cacophony.   The tracks “Morph” and “Prelude to Amintiri” put Vicéns more at the center of the musical action where he shows great range as a single-line soloist and with inventive chordal play.   "Breaking through Shadows” was my personal favorite – a high energy showcase for Vicéns and the other soloists with a super-catchy bridge.   Days is an ambitious album featuring many musical ideas and an outstanding supporting cast. I look forward to his next project.

title: Ornette for the masses
text:
This actually surprised me as if managed to get Metheny into a more passionate mode. Ornette, as always, astonished.
I also wanted to correct some errors of fact that occurred in one review and try to set the record straight.
Miles Davis did indeed say at one point that Ornette sounded all screwed up inside based on Coleman's music; this was reported in the book by A.B. Spellman, BLACK MUSIC; FOUR LIVES. However, Spellman and others reported that David later retracted that statement and even apologized for it. When Coleman first came to New York, lots of celebrities came to see him (including Leonard Bernstein, who was so taken that he was seen with his ear next to Charlie Haden's bass to hear how Haden was using microtonal variations to match the music. Ornette was actually a pioneer in pitch manipulation at pitch level- and his drummers in the 1960s-especially Ed Blackwell.
Ornette influenced people as diverse as Coltrane, Miles Davis Cream, Jerry Garcia and Lou Reed. Davis, at Tony Williams' recommendation, hired Boston-based multi-instrumentalist Sam Rivers and Davis actually incorporated many of Coleman's ideas into his 60's work, including Bitches Brew, Live-Evil, In A Silent Way. Before, Ornette, Miles wasn't incorporating the "telepathic" communication" or interplay for which the 1960s groups became famous. That came from Ornette, who influenced John Coltrane, Eric Dolphy and many others. No Ornette, by implication, no fusion movement. Also, Ornette didn't copy Miles' two drummers approach. Ornette had two drummers as far back as Free Jazz in 1962. He also took a journeys into electric instruments through the electric violin and Charlie Haden (by everyone's account, one of the finest bass players in jazz) employed double bass through a wah wah pedal! Ornette's original background was in Rhythm and Blues and this showed up repeatedly throughout his career, culminating in an effective fusion of free and funk with his group Prime Time in the mid 1970's. He also wrote string quartets, symphonies, choral works, and was one of the pioneers in the world music movement. In 2006, Coleman won a Pulitzer Prize for music (only the second jazz musician to receive that honor, and the first strictly jazz album to receive that honor. By the way, to show how fully ensconced Ornette is now, Wynton Marsalis is now doing Ornette Coleman tributes.
One of the unfortunate things about jazz post 1990 was that a reactionary trend set in. Academics and bad actors with an agenda (Stanley Crouch and Marsalis, for example) gained influence and the truly interesting changes that pushed jazz forward in the 1960s and 1970s were ridiculously disrespected. (King Crimson, Soft Machine, the Mothers, etc.were all influenced by the free jazz movement that Ornette spearheaded-only shrieking saxophones could compete with shrieking guitars for attention, after all!). So, you get documentaties like Ken Burns' Jazz which state that nothing much happened after Ornette appeared or (worse!) Miles went electric. Burns himself said he didn't know much about music! So he let Crouch and Marsalis make the assessment-both of whom, from personal experience of rejection by that community, hated free jazz.
Metheny is a skilled but pretty tonally boring player. He is to be admired for hiring Ornette for this album. It is the most beautiful and exciting thing I have ever heard Metheny play and actually shows his considerable chops in an exciting context.
Kudos to Metheny for honoring one of the most important musicians of the past 70 years, Ornette Coleman!

title: A Wild Thyme with Jo Grant
text:
Elixir of Doom finds Iris Wildthyme and Jo travelling back in time to the Golden Age of Hollywood where they find that many of the movie monsters are real and famed Hollywood starlet Vita Monet.

There are two things that are absolutely great about this story. First is Katy Manning. As in Find and Replace, she plays an older Jo and she plays Iris. She also plays Vita Monet as a real character with a very good American Hollywood accent. She also shows her ability to somehow manage to capture the essence of yet another Doctor with whom she hadn't appeared.

The sound design is superb. It captures the feel of the Golden Age of Hollywood, particularly during the Party. This has that beautiful feel of so many of the later Companion Chronicles which transcended the idea of "talking books" to become great experiences.

The story itself was typical Paul Magrs fare, not quite on the level of , "Find and Replace" but a quirky and fun story that plays around with ideas, language, and settings. Jo comes off as nice, though maybe a bit naive for her age.

On the downside, the Doctor that appears on the cover isn't the Doctor that appears in the story. Some fans may be bothered by Iris statement that she can't regenerate and isn't a Time Lord given that we saw a future regeneration of her in, "The Wormery." But with Iris it's hard to tell when she's lying or when she's merely shading the truth. At any rate, fans will have to work out how they feel about that "twist" for themselves.

text:
Do any of these reviews correspond to the recording described? the MET production from the early 50's...with Milanov and Stiedry conducting? Well, this one does.

One overriding feature makes this production next to worthless. In order to perform it as a three act opera, the stupid MET cut the entire and dramatically pivotal first act inn scene. Thus the action goes from the dark opening scene to the equally dark scene outside the monastery. Possibly the most ridiculous and damaging single cut in MET history. The old RCA recording with Milanov is still available and clearly the one to get. It probably still contains the standard cuts that riddle and subvert most recordings of Verdi...cuts that would NEVER be tolerated in Wagner...but no entire scenes are removed.

title: TimeLife AM GOLD CD Music Series - Great Sound, Great Music, & Great Memories
text:
I LUV LUV music...after spending years as a nightclub/radio DJ and still spinning around town...I wanted to share how delightful this Out-of Print TimeLife music series is. The series is titled AM GOLD. There are 40 cd's in the series. The cds can still be found in abundance here on amazon, on eBay and in used music stores. The recording's appear to be remastered and sound terrific. The music ranges from the early 1960's to the late 1970's. They'll bring back incredible memories!

It's VERY IMPORTANT TO NOTE THE FOLLOWING: TimeLife issued a similar series through the Warner Brother's Label in Europe under the title "Good Time Gold" but, these CD's WILL NOT DOWNLOAD into iTunes without distortion. They will play fine in audio cd players, but when downloaded/ripped there is an intolerable distortion. Some folks refer to this as "defective by design." While it appears WB's has never commented on this publicly they were not the only label to do this. These and other cd's during the initial years of the digital era were sometimes label as not PC compatible. I own a number of WB Classical CD's during this period and the same is true for them as well...so I do not buy any WB CD's new or used that have a release date between 1998-2004, although the dates might not actually fit that period its what I use so I don't waste my money.

P.s. most of the cd's reasonably to moderately price, but the later years especially the 1978, 1979, Smash Hits of the 70s, Mellow Hits of the 70s and Perfect Harmony cd's are priced as if they are made out of real gold!.UGH! Some folks are asking ridiculous prices for these cds so be patience and you'll get the ones you want at a decent price. Also don't be afraid to contact the sellers and see if they will work out a better price for you.

ENJOY THE MEMORIES!

title: This is really an amazing record - but the mastering is crazy
text: Altogether an amazing experimental pop/no wave/protest record, absolutely of it's time but still fascinating.  A few of these songs are both riveting lyrically and super cool and listenable enough to put them into my 5,000 desert island songs...but wait!  The mastering on this is so thin as to require the listener to ignore the screechy guitar at the high end in order to hear what's going on.  My theory is that this is a mastering job gone wrong.  Maybe the band wanted a crunchy guitar and thought the end result was how an album with crunchy guitars had to sound...or whoever was in charge of this reissue never asked anyone whether a different mastering job would serve the music better...or something!  There's gotta be an explanation for how bad this sounds!!  My suspicions are reinforced by examining where the screeching lies -- I found that there is one thin frequency band that is clearly boosted - the guitar occupies a few bands of frequency while this boosted frequency is just one thin part of the guitar sound, suggesting to me that something went wrong.  I experimented with attenuating that band and boosting the midrange and lower midrange and you are really left with a really great record that is also pretty listenable.  Please, please, whoever owns these masters, remaster this album so the world can hear how great it is!

title: Competent playing (mostly), but often plodding and uninspired
text:
I wanted to love this set -- I really did. After all, I love Scott Joplin's music. I have all of the "complete" sets (Hyman, Zimmerman, Arpin, Kirby, Parker, Nielsen, Dowling). I have many, many more Joplin albums on CD and LP. I've read Ed Berlin's masterful Joplin biography cover-to-cover several times. I play many of Joplin's rags myself. Yes: I'm a Joplin nerd. No one really *needs* that much Joplin, but I find it endlessly fascinating to hear how various performers interpret his music. Even if he wasn't the "inventor" of ragtime, Joplin was certainly the finest ragtime composer of his day -- or any day since! Joplin crafted such delightful melodies, embedding many "hidden" counter-melodies along the way. He was a thoughtful, deliberate composer who clearly intended his works to be played as written. While I'm no purist -- I love to hear performers embellish and improvise on Joplin's themes -- his works are so well constructed that often the best interpretations are those that stick close to the score -- and that also bring the scores to life. William Appling succeeds on the first count, but falls short on the second.

The best thing I can say about this set is that Appling's performances sound like what I've always imagined Joplin himself sounded like at the piano. That's not exactly meant to be a great compliment. Based on testimony from those who knew Scott Joplin and heard him play, he was never an especially skilled pianist. Debra Harder's own notes to this CD set quote one of Joplin's pupils, William Sullivan, who said that Joplin's playing was "very slow and methodical." That's exactly what we get from William Appling. Very slow and methodical. Plodding even. While it is true that Scott Joplin famously advised that "it is never right to play ragtime fast," that doesn't mean s-l-o-w. Anyone familiar with popular piano playing of the early 20th century will know that the vaudeville and Tin Pan Alley type of ragtime was often played at breakneck speed. Pianists like Mike Bernard and Willie Eckstein sought to impress and dazzle their audiences with playing that was fast and flashy. Rags by composers like Charles L. Johnson and George Botsford (with lots of 3-against-2 rhythms) were well-suited to such fast playing. But not Joplin. His rags are more densely scored, with lilting melodies and carefully considered harmonies. To play them very fast and flashy would ruin the "weird and intoxicating" effect Joplin sought to achieve. But played too slow, they lose all life and "snap." Ragtime -- even Joplin's ragtime -- was at its heart dance music, and at dirge-like tempos, the "fire" goes out and we are left with... musical mush.

There are a few selections where Appling turns in sensitive, enjoyable readings. His rendition of "Solace" is actually quite lovely, and "Augustan Club Waltzes," though lacking in finesse, has a quaint "parlor piano" charm (despite the horrendous edits). I also rather liked Appling's atmospheric "Binks' Waltz." I must also admit that "Maple Leaf Rag" -- surprisingly -- sounds pretty decent at Appling's sedate tempo.

According to the booklet that comes with these CDs, Appling came to Joplin's music late in life, after an illustrious career as a pianist and choral director. He may have been a fine conductor of classical choral works, but he does not seem to have had much of a feel for the ragtime idiom. On these recordings, he sounds like a competent amateur classical pianist sight-reading Joplin. Not only are the performances often unbearably slow, but they are often devoid of nuance -- unless you consider the odd misplaced accent or self-indulgent rubato to be "nuance." Appling gets the right notes and the right rhythms most of the time, but dynamics are generally limited to the mezzo-forte to forte range, and there is little attempt to bring out Joplin's lovely counter melodies. It doesn't help that Appling's illness at the time of these recordings prohibited him from working the pedals much. In the dry acoustic of his home studio (where the recording was made), Appling's pedal-less performances have an unpleasant, angular, "choppy" sound. Appling also has the bad habit of grunting, humming, or "singing" along with his playing at times in a way that I find both irritating and distracting. (I suppose some will find it "charming.") If you want a sample of his vocalizing, check out "Euphonic Sounds."

Appling's performances aside, the recording and editing of this CD set is sub-par. Many of Appling's herky-jerky accents over-saturate the recording, leading to moments of harsh distortion. Adding insult to injury, the rather clumsy editing has left many, many audible splices that mar the performances. Some performances seem to have been stitched together from multiple takes where the microphones were repositioned between takes, leading to a piano that moves around the soundstage without warning. And if only the producers had carried some WD-40 to the recording sessions! Apparently, Appling *could* work the pedals in some cases. When he uses them, the pedals squeak like crazy!

The booklet features two essays: one by Debra Lew Harder that tells us about William Appling and tries to make the case that his performances are "definitive" because Scott Joplin was African-American and William Appling was African-American too. Somehow, she claims, Appling's race gives him a "profound understanding of Joplin's music." That's skating on thin ice, and I don't buy it. The other essay, by Patricia Oldham, summarizes the injustices African-Americans faced in the post-Civil War South, making shaky inferences about what the Joplin family experienced in the 1860s and 1870s, and providing little of substance that directly relates to Joplin's career as a ragtime composer in the early 1900s. The booklet is illustrated with pictures of the choirs that Appling conducted, a few portraits of him and Joplin, and a heavily pixilated color reproduction of the Scott Joplin mural in Sedalia, Missouri.

As a side note, this set claims to present Scott Joplin's "complete rags, waltzes, & marches," but all of the Joplin collaborations are missing. Thus, no "Heliotrope Bouquet." No "Swipesy Cakewalk" or "Something Doing." No "Kismet" or "Felicity Rag." No "Sun Flower Slow Drag." These works are part of the Joplin oeuvre too, and their omission is regrettable.

It seems that Appling was a genuinely good guy, and I think his heart was in the right place. I am delighted that he discovered Scott Joplin's music, and he obviously took great joy in it. It's just too bad that he doesn't seem to have been up to the task of playing Joplin's works at "full steam" when these recordings were made. Had he come to Joplin earlier in life, and had he had more time to study and develop a feel for ragtime, perhaps he would have played Joplin's rags with a bit more elan. I realize that these recordings were made when Appling was ill -- and I was tempted to give an extra star out of "pity." This CD was put together in the years following Appling's 2008 death by people who knew Appling and obviously held him in high esteem. I can imagine that this CD will be a treasure to those who knew Appling -- a wonderful keepsake of a teacher, friend, and colleague. Joplin completists like myself will want to have it, but for the Joplin newcomer or someone wanting a single good "definitive" performance, I'd suggest looking elsewhere.

title: if you enjoy plainchant...
text:
Had I known what this recording actually was – I wouldn’t have bought it. I was exploring the Gimell catalog and the recordings of the Tallis Scholars, a great British a cappella vocal ensemble, and chanced on this one, from 1988 and the early days of the CD. I guess I was expecting something like Hildegard von Bingen, or the Chants of the Sybil ([[ASIN:B0000264IM El Cant de la Sibil-la I]]), mystical chants, or maybe early polyphony in the style of Leonin and Perotin.

Not so. This is plainchant. The “Sarum rite” is the Roman Catholic liturgy as it was exercised in the 13th century at the Church of Salisbury, one of the major churches and rites of Medieval England. “The music recorded here is from the First Mass of Christmas according to the Salisbury Rite. It would have been celebrated after midnight on Christmas Eve, and was known as the Missa in gallicantu – the Mass at Cockcrow”. The Chant was taken from 16th century Missals and Graduals.

So, okay, this is plainchant: monophonic, square and simple rhythms modeled on spoken language, limited melodic intervals – maybe great for the rite, but, truly, the degree zero of music. 55 minutes of it.

If you like plainchant and Gregorian chant, you may enjoy this recording more than I did. At least my copy was cheap – that’s why I bought it, in fact. Well, you can’t win every time. Now I'll return to Hildegard and Perotin.

title: For the Rootsheads Only. . .
text:
Should you ever find yourself seeking a really really mellow reggae vibe, eight times out of ten I'll probably recommend that you seek out the latest Luciano release. Those other two times I'll suggest you take the route that I've been doing for the past year or so and check out a Batch release. Batch is one of the preeminent producers and ever developing artists coming out of the Virgin Island reggae scene and briefly being based in the States (in the very reggae heavy Virginia I believe, to my knowledge he has since returned operations to St. Croix) Batch continues to spread his heavy, yet very smooth blend of reggae music through his label Sound Vizion Records. Having originally made his name as a virtual utility musician, playing a variety of instruments for a variety of very well known artists including some Jamaica's finest roots and dancehall talents, Batch is now very known and respected for not only his own music, but having done production work for some of the finest talents in the Virgin Islands (and I'm just waiting until an artist from Jamaica, especially Lutan Fyah, makes his way to Batch's studio). Batch has even done production work for the Midnite band (on the He is Jah album), the dominant name of the Virgin Island reggae scene and has pushed his name alongside the most respected production and musician names of the genre such as Tuff Lion, Laurent `Tippy' Alfred, Ronnie Benjamin and Dean Pond. All the big producers have definitely their own style; while often times the VI reggae sound is categorized by many (including myself sometimes) to be like the old school Jamaican sound just before the digital dominance began, it isn't always a fair comparison on categorization as the genre continues to develop nearly daily. The brilliant Tuff Lion for instance (and check his debut album, Utterance, as well) is most noted for his guitar works and thus his productions (which occurs largely with Laurent Alfred) reflects that; while with Alfred himself, he seems to take his compositions in a variety of directions, encompassing both that ultra heavy, old school vibe as well as, at times, that large anthem sound of today's roots for his label, I-Grade Records; Dean Pond, most noted for working with veteran St. Croix singer Army and doing lead production for the debut of Pressure Busspipe, The Pressure is On, but also having a basis which began with Midnite production as well as works for other artists, almost exclusively has that large sound of `neo-roots' reggae. Ronnie Benjamin's production style is almost completely the very heavy and mellow old school sound which blends perfectly with the style of ultra roots music his band, Midnite, makes. Batch's style is closer to Benjamin's style with a touch of Dean Pond and others. Could you take somehow take Batch back to 1960's-1970's Jamaica, today he would probably be a household name in reggae music.

His own works have lead to the creation of his label which most notably has served as a launching pad for one of the future (and arguably current) superstars of the genre, Ras Attitude. The connection between the two artists has proven to be quite successful, Batch's Sound Vizion has, to date, released two albums (his debut Happiness and the very solid Love Life) from Attitude, and as his base has also pushed him into very successful ventures with other producers all over the world (I recently saw a video for a Ras Attitude song played here in Jamaica!). Credit goes to Attitude definitely for encouraging the previously almost exclusive studio and instrumental performing Batch to take the front stage more and more and actually produce for himself. The result has been a very respectable run of now five albums (the fifth is I-Ver Strong which I'm currently listing to), four of which were produced by Batch (the new one was not) and three of which saw their exclusive release on his own Sound Vizion label. I'm anticipating that someday the two will actually be releasing an album together, that album will undoubtedly be one of the most substantial pieces for the genre to date. Batch has also done production work on his label for Mada Nile, a very nice chanter from out of St. Croix as well (check out her new album on Sound Vizion, Many Roads), his `secret weapon' the developing Ahfyah and others such Masta Chang, Shepard, fellow producer Ras L and even Ima, Batch's wife (who plays a very prominent role on this album, as a background singer, although wonderfully credited as a `front ground` vocalist). I've always maintained that Batch's production work is undoubtedly where his true success lies, I hope someday Sound Vizion grows to the size of Alfred's I-Grade label thus giving Batch the opportunity the opportunity to work with nearly every sensational young roots talent from out of the VI scene, but his talents on the mic are definitely not to be overlooked. While Ras Attitude often times comes off as the supremely talented wordsmith capable of adopting almost any style while still seemingly (at least these days) being entirely more comfortable as a singer, Batch, on the other hand is almost a pure chanter. His style of chanting, however does involve a great deal of singing and he basically veers between the two styles at such a rate that they both, combined, actually BECOME his style. I liken him to an overall more vocally talented version of Vaughn Benjamin, lead singer of Midnite (although certainly not as talented with the word as that lyrics machine, but very respectable still) and perhaps even more closely related vocally to a lite version of Bambu Station lead singer Jalani Horton (minus the occasional volcanic outbursts which make Horton's style so very unique to him). And the good thing about Batch, the artist, is that he obviously continues to grow, on one of his most recent albums, To the Root, he displayed a much more melodically nice vibe which wasn't present on his previous work, Jah Guidance (although that album STILL stands as musically, in my opinion, his greatest piece to date).

Besides To the Root, I-ver Strong and Jah Guidance, his three most recent pieces, there was the beginning with Who You Are, which really got the international buzz going about him as an artist, becoming one of the most popular underground pieces in the brief history of the VI reggae genre and then Keep the Faith. Keep the Faith didn't exactly attract much of the same attention as Who You Are (which I took an extraordinarily long and dumb time in picking up) but purely from a musical standpoint stands in very fine comparison to that album just a year before.

Checking in at a very healthy seventeen tracks and featuring no official combinations, Keep the Faith is an excellent showcase of Batch's overall musical game. It is, for the most part a heavier vibe (which he himself attributes to having had more experience at the point) and an album which definitely requires a several listens to truly appreciate. Keep the Faith is just, in its simplest form, knowledge, you can literally learn something about yourself listening to it, and its all delivered in that typical laid back, Batch style which is just doing wonders or me these days. The album opens with Leave Out of Babylon a very solid repatriation anthem which Batch is very good at writing (also is devastatingly proficient at the herbalist tune as well). The song isn't too dissimilar lyrically to a track which appeared on the To the Root album, Carry Beyond. Batch can write a repatriation vibe that just makes you want to pack up everything, get your family and head Black to Afrika at that MINUTE, all done in a very mellow style, just a nice inspiring vibes. The aforementioned herbalist tune (which is also a nice penchant Luciano) comes in the form of early track Tree of Life. Batch's method of writing these types of tune is almost a praising vibe where you almost personify or in some cases even deify the herb itself, focusing more on the positive aspects of it (which is his style with almost everything), rather than taking the road used by so many in defending it. Tree of Life is no different and it stands as one of the more interesting songs on Keep the Faith and if you are an enjoyer of the herb, definitely a song you would be interested in hearing. Sons & Daughters is just a compete praise His Imperial Majesty and HIS followers from all walks of life and one of the best tracks you will probably hear Batch voice (my two favorite Batch tunes remain Ah Rulah from the Who You Are album and Hail the King from the To the Root album). Later on in Keep the Faith is a very interesting song Reaching. Reaching speaks on many of the trivial and inconsequential things which have arisen to divide Afrikan people. While definitely not his greatest creation musically (its built over a riddim which is pretty much all over the place), you definitely need to hear the lyrical vibe poured into the message on Reaching , definitely a must hear for fans of Batch and others as well. Check Justice. Justice is a quietly aggressive of all the struggles Afrikan men and women face in the world and its just a lovely done song over a riddim done so minimally but one which certainly is one of the most powerful on the album altogether.

My absolute favorite tune on Keep the Faith is the title track (I don't think that happens very often at all). Keep the Faith, the song, is an excellently done challenge to those in the struggle to maintain and `keep the faith' for the reward for doing such will be great. While not an official combination, his wife, Ima, compliments her husband very well adding vocals throughout and while she appears on several tracks (and on some in slightly more prominent roles)(check Jah Run Things) Keep the Faith is undoubtedly her highlight as she voices the wonderful twenty five second long intro to the track and continues to hold a high vibe throughout. Another tune here which stands out to a very high case is the wicked wicked Sane Cry. While you could never describe Batch's musical style as even bordering near anywhere dancehall, Sane Cry is about as close as he gets to that vibe, even almost getting to something which gives a semblance of a DJ style on the tune. Sane Cry is Keep the Faith's changeup, a nice mix of the vibes and what you're used to from Batch into something different which is definitely worth listening to. One of the other real standouts on Keep the Faith (there are four altogether) is the tune When. When is an admonishment to those in society who have lost their way and not living in a positive way or in a selfish way. Its done over one of the best riddims you'll hear out of the Sound Vizion camp, I recognized it almost immediately as the tune which backed Ras Attitude brilliant War to Win, from the Love Life album, the riddim is such a heavy heavy one drop which absolutely serves perfectly as a showcase for Batch's talents as a producer and simultaneously, an excellent backdrop for one of his finer tunes as a vocalist. The final truly big track on Keep the Faith is the closer, the To the East instrumental. To the East is the name of the riddim which backs the aforementioned tune When and its almost a reward to the fans. You hear that wonderful riddim and its almost not even a matter of opinion, but a matter of fact: The To the East is a beautiful riddim. The decision to include it as the final track on Keep the Faith was a wonderful idea and one that truly strengthens the album overall.

Another nice spot of tracks I have to mention on Keep the Faith comes just before the very solid ending tracks. Check Zion Kingdom Come which is a lovely song speaking not only the wonders of Zion itself, but the wonders of seeking Zion as well; check the song for the Empresses, the lovely Good Virtues, very nice track for the Black Queens and men who treat their Queens like such; and lastly I'll mention Full Circle which sounds like something snatched out of 1960's Jamaica, I was expecting to hear Alton Ellis chime in after the very nice beginning, but Batch does a very respectable job with the vibe.

Overall, I'm recommending taking undoubtedly long road it would take to find this very hard to find gem (although, shockingly, you can RIGHT NOW purchase it on Amazon) to the more experienced and initiated roots fans. Newer fans, I think you may find Batch's newer and extremely more accessible (both musically and actually finding the albums) material. When considering that along with recording and producing this massive album, he was also recording and producing Ras Attitude's Love Life album as well as Mada Nile's debut album, Rise Today simultaneously. While all the productions were definitely similar, they shared very little in the way of actual production and riddims. Batch is to be commended for that along. Also commend him for the very nice album that is Keep the Faith, a very nice and mature roots album for the well versed and experienced roots fan.

title: The Dead Years
text:
Between 1980 -1987 there were no studio releases from the Grateful Dead. The songs just kept on coming forth and the band was on the road more than ever before. Spring Tour 1984 began in Hampton Coliseum on Friday the 13th of April and again on the 14th. I attended both shows and brought some newbies along to two of them. Jerry had a couple of good nights in Virginia and his vocals are much better than what you will hear on the Philadelphia shows a week later. Brent, shined on a really soulful "Don't Need Love" that was amazing to hear on the second night and I do wish they had released Hampton over Philly but that's how the wheels turn in Deadville.

Dave's Picks has avoided 1984 like it was a killer virus and at long last here is Dave's #35 and love it or don't we have (at last) an 84 show to enjoy. Fresh outta the gates with "Feel Like A Stranger" "Cold Rain & Snow" and "Beat It On Down The Line" is a good one-two-three punch of thrust and the band is playing solid and even if Jerry's vocals are a bit off for this run it shows that Brent is right in there making every thing better with his harmonies making Jerry a bit thicker in the mix. The first set is good example of old favorites with a bit of the new mixed in ("My Brother Esau") that appeared on a studio record from the band a few years down the road.

The second and third discs spotlight the second set with seven selections from the 19th added on to make it even better. "Scarlett>Fire" at almost 30 minutes in length is a monster. "Morning Dew" into the two Chuck Berry rockers close out a hot set of playing. "Keep Your Day Job" wasn't a big favorite of Deadheads but it's the encore at the end of show. With the (at long last) official release of "Day Job" on an official GD recording you now cab be your own judge to decide if this one passes muster or not.

The 7 selections from the 19th are very well selected. "The Wheel" "Wharf Rat" and "Sugar Magnolia" are on the end of disc two. The final disc features "China Cat>Rider" "Estimated Prophet" and "Terrapin Station" and (for me) the tunes from the 19th are the stars of the second and third discs they all add to the overall quality of this collection. It sure is nice to hear something from the 1980's included in the "Dave's Picks" series and I sure do hope we don't have to wait to much longer for a crispy 1985 show to be introduced for the faithful.
Four Stars!

This is album #9 from Canada's self-proclaimed "Metal Queen", and represents a drastic departure in style and sound texture from her previous albums.
"Emotional Rain", her previous album, displayed more subdued rock and better polished melodies than its predecessors, but this present album switches gears into what I call the "nowhere rock" genre.
I like LA's singing, and "LA&2P" demonstrates her talents. But everything around that is a great disappointment. From the opening notes of the first track, in which the vocals seemed to have been recorded in a large underground garage (maybe it was), I was afraid this album would be a musical catastrophe: the instrumentation is basic, poorly recorded, but mostly pointless: it's music without melody or purpose, and even though some of the arrangements are at times (but rarely) adequate, you won't be captivated by any of it.
This album was a 1-off: her latest, "Slick Chick", is a tribute to swing: talk about lack of constant direction!
Perhaps this will be enjoyable to people ignorant of Lee's previous albums, since they'll have nothing to compare it with. But if you're somewhat familiar with albums like "Powerline", "Bodyrock" or "Metal Queen", be careful this time: try to borrow a copy from someone else first, or listen to some song samples: this is no "traditional" Lee Aaron...

title: From the forgotten dusty corners of artsy Krautrock comes...
text:
I've always enjoyed this Cd a little bit more than the other reviewer, apparently. A couple of the songs sound a bit trite for the Artrock genre, i admit. For example on "LOOKING IN THE PAST", you have long instrumental passages, arpeggios on keyboards, and female guest vocals sung by Gabi Rossmanith, who sounds a LOT like Renate from Amon Duul II. However, TANZ IM SCHNEE (Dance in the Snow) is much more fun, even tho the artrock standard acrouitments remain in place. TIMES OF DELIGHT has some interesting electric lead guitar work, that meshes well with the keyboard player. The lyrics, tho indecipherable, at least are sung by guys in the band. The next track is WEIT WEG, a very long composistion, starting out with acoustic guitar leads over heavy synth beds, with abrupt changes in time signiture--all well performed, no doubt thanks to a solid drummer. Also, there's a beautifully delicate flute passage doubled by the violin, over a guitar arpeggio. THe song makes a blitzkrieg change, with a totally unexpected instrumental color... TUBA! YUP, now that's what i call teutonic, TUBA! (and the song moves into waltz time, as if you walked into a beerhall on acid.) WHen the song flows into the vocal section, you'll hear a HUGE surprise for krautrock from the 1970s....GERMAN LYRICS! After some pretty violin/flute, the dynamics change again into two heavy electric guitars in call and response, then back to soft keyboard arpeggios draped with lead electric guitar. Overall, WEIT WEG's sound is psychedelic, tho probibly ecclectic would be a better discription. Instead of sitars, you got tubas, and instead of moogs, you have violins. The unusual instrumentation provides the saving grace of SIDDHARTHA's "WELTSCHMERZ". The CD concludes with GIFT OF THE FOOL-- violin figuring prominantly once again. Overall, SIDDHARTHA is one of those mildly trippy, krautrock/artrock bands, with tight, focused changes, long melodic passages, utilizing occasional unexpected instrumentation for a rock record. SIDDHARTHA unfortunately only recorded this one album, breaking up after 4 years.
If you are into early ELOY, or bits of AMON DUUL II, RUFUS ZUFALL, LIGHTSHINE, or maybe FRAME, then you'd probibly enjoy this album, as an occasional sonic treat.

title: Amazing, disturbing...ermmm...music?
text:
I love the game of "Silent Hill". It scared me to death and is still better than all the sequels. The chance to get the soundtrack was too good to miss, and I soon found out that it was filled with the same kind of nightmarish atmosphere as the game.

So why only 2 stars? Because as I found out, this is not music that you can actually sit down and listen to. When the CD starts up you are treated to the dreamy and mysterious scratchy guitar-backed opening theme which is absolutely stunning. It's very reminiscent of David Lynch's soundtrack music, "Twin Peaks" in particular springs to mind. Little wonder it makes the game's CGI movie intro so effective, and why it was also featured in all the trailers and demo discs when the game first came out. But once I had finished enjoying this theme, the rest of the tracks on the CD soon had me reaching for the fast-forward button. Transplanting the disturbing ambient noises of the game onto an audio CD leaves you with something like aural wallpaper to a nightmare, with metallic scrapings, hollow clanging, distant rumblings and industrial grinding noises all featuring prominently. Now, this may add up to a pretty horrific atmosphere in the game, but music it ain't, and I don't think I have ever let the entire CD play through in one sitting without jumping through most of the middle section. There must be some situations that would call for for an ambient soundtrack like this, but I can't think of many, and that's why I have only given the CD two stars, as only a fraction of it is bearable under normal listening conditions. Don't get me wrong - I was not freaked out or scared by the sounds, just bored.

Stick around to the end, though and you get the more melodic closing themes and the vocal song "Esperandote", plus the bonus track of the music to the "out-takes" if you wait long enough. My biggest gripe - and something that spoiled the whole CD for me - is that the music for Lisa's death scene is not included!! This sorrowful guitar piece was played out at length in the game, but fades out after barely 30 seconds of intro on the CD to make way for yet another industrial noise track. Unforgiveable....what with the distinct lack of real music on the whole album anyway, and they decided to deprive listeners of the most beautiful track of the lot!

Let me just re-affirm: I love the game, I love the musical compostions featured in it. I even love the creepy CD packaging, and the mysterious sounding tracklisting just add to the appeal. (As an aside, I have the European CD release of this which features a picture of the doll-like Cheryl on the cover rather than Lisa, which is possibly even more disconcerting!)

But I don't like 75% of what's on this disc. Its exactly as heard in the game (apart from Lisa's Death - curses!!), so I can't say it's unfair. I just don't enjoy it.

I normally keep an open mind to the music I encounter. I received this CD for free at a music festival, so I gave it a try. That is what prompted my first-ever Amazon review.

The music portion doesn't sound so bad, but it is really just a backdrop for the words. This isn't something you can dance or even tap your foot to. The singing is poor, to say the least. The lyrics are carefully-chosen, adjective-laden, and pretty much sheer nonsense for a musical setting.

For more info on the lyrics, read some of the 100+ reviews of his book by the same name ([[ASIN:B000HWYQX8 Wild Animus: A Novel]]). He must have a lot of money to get the book published and to cover all the production and marketing for the CDs. I'm not sure any publishing company would have ever accepted this.

I suppose some may say that you can't judge art, or that it will grow on you. I understand what they mean, but I feel this isn't even up to that level.

What about my copy? I just tossed it in the trash. First time I ever did that. Its pungent scent did sting my nostrils and lurid sounds pierced my very eardrums.

Please don't consider paying money for this unless you've listened to samples of it first and read some of the book reviews. Your ears will quite possibly thank me.

Obscure band from Texas and usually not my cup of tea but like anything in life there will always be exception to ones rules if enough effort is made.
Well here you have a quartet of musicians who where probably well tuned into 80s new wave and pop rock where the echoes of Sting's Police and early U2 is surely a medium this bands channeled for the release. From the opening track you can hear the chiming echoes guitar ala Andy Summers, tight dynamic drumming and the vocals which are very much in the Sting/Jim Kerr aka Simple Minds style of singing.
Another thing that really threw me off the cliff is that these lads are religious and dont hide it in the tracks titles and lyrics however the music doesnt come off as preachy or pretentious this is really good 80s influenced alt rock without the negativity of grunge toxicity. What you get here is well composed upbeat rock sounds done with good intent and artistic merit.

title: What happened between 1983 and 1999?
text:
What a waste of a perfectly good saga! I'm sorry, but I would rather have watched every single 'Never-ending story' movie than this horrid excuse of a film!
1) This "movie" has absolutely no Star Wars feel to it at all. It's just a bunch of flashy spaceships and robots (all CGI, of course!) flying around shooting bright red and green lasers at each other with a bunch of familiar characters thrown into
the middle of it all.
2) There's no freakin' plot for goodness sake! Wow, Obi-Wan goes hunting for some clones, and Anakin falls in love with Padme. Whoa, George! Slow down! You lost me way back when Jar-Jar was given some more screen time, what's going on again? Oh, yeah. Nothing worth remembering more than the 2 hours of torture the audience has to endure while the movie is still playing.
3) Count Dooku (whoa, George did u think of that name when watching Sesame Street or something? What kind of evil, villain name is that?) was not the menacing bad guy in the background of the plot making things harder for our heroes that every Star Wars movie so desperately needs! He just shows up half way through the movie and talks to Obi-Wan for a few seconds and chops off Anakin's arm at the end. If you're going to make a bad guy, George, give him some more life, and more things to do to disrupt the progress of the good guys!
4) George, when are you going to realize, you don't need 10 billion CGI shots in a movie to make it look real? I mean, the original dewbacks who couldn't move at all in the original Star Wars looked more real than those 'creatures' in the arena at the end of the movie!
5) The lines in this movie are quickly forgotten. Don't even get me started on the Anakin and Padme 'attraction' because there wasn't any accept in the director's head. Even the "skills" of the actors couldn't make the lines on the script more heartfelt. They were just horrible! Or how about when Anakin's mom dies?! PLEASE! Has there ever been a worse on-screen death in movie history? "Oh, you've grown so much, I'm so proud of you, I love..., I love..., uggggh"! I would rather have to memorize every single meaning of every word in the dictionary than watch this scene ever again!
6) To be completely honest, the only character I felt any sort of connection to was Watto when he had his brief 30-seconds of spotlight. He was a corny, delightful addition to the movie, and I don't really know why. He's not a hero, he's not a villain, he's a middle man. You feel this sense of pity on him since he can no longer even fix a simple droid any more. It's sad to see how memorable and well-written the characters in the first trilogy were and how the second one has only supplied me with one character I actually enjoyed seeing on-screen.
7) The only good thing about this movie was the score. I admit, John Williams did a good job in conveying the real feelings of what the characters should have portrayed on the screen. I really enjoy the "Across The Stars" song, and all the music for every action sequence was well-written! That's at least one thing I can find enjoyable about this movie. Frankly because George Lucas had little-to-no say in what the music sounded like. Cudos, John for a wonderful score. Maybe George will make a script to go along with it next time.
I'll be honest, I was truly a die-hard fan of Star Wars 'till Episode 1 hit theatres. I'm sorry to say it, but George, you've ruined a perfectly good saga and replaced it with two consecutive hyped-up, big money, all talk, no walk movies. I hope for the sake of the fans that you take a hint from your critics instead of your yes-men for once! Maybe you will still be able to salvage what dignity and respect is left in the Star Wars universe and put together a decent film for those of us who have been let down by the last two!

title: It's not the flowers of paradise that Pelecis is gardening but cheap plastic avatars
text:
Having already heard Nevertheless, Pelecis’ Double Concerto for violin and piano, in Kremer’s previous recording on Teldec, [[ASIN:B000005823 From My Home]], I guess I knew what to expect: sentimental and sweet film music. Not that I’m attracted to that kind of music, it’s out of an interest for the label, the Belgian Megadisc Classics, really, that I bought the CD. Launched in 1992, Megadisc did great service by bringing to the attention of music lovers a whole array of composers from the, by then, ex-Soviet empire: some that had already had some recorded exposure in the West, like Silvestrov, but mostly some that didn’t, or not much – and, for the most of them, still don’t: Alexander Knaifel, Vladimir Tarnopolski (see my review of [[ASIN:B00004WHA4 Introduction to the Music of Vladimir Tarnopolski]]), Tigran Mansurian, Faradj Karajev, Alexander Wustin, Nikolai Korndorf, Alexander Rabinovitch, Avet Terterian, Alexander Rastakov, Rytis Mazulis, husband and wife Elena Firsova ([[ASIN:B0002ZL19C Firsova: Mandelstam Cantatas]]) and Dmitri Smirnov ([[ASIN:B00006J9MG An Introduction to Dmitri Smirnov]]) – and Pelecis, then. In particular, Megadisc was the first really to unearth the music of Shostakovich’s maverick student Galina Ustvolskaya, and if only for that it deserves eternal gratitude.

And in truth, I had forgotten about the Pelecis being featured on the competing Teldec disc, but by an extraordinary coincidence it was brought back to my memory by a comment posted under my none too enthusiastic review there, exactly when I had pulled this one out of my shelves to listen to it.

But, still, with all that, I didn’t expect Pelecis to write the same kind of music as Michael Nyman or Philip Glass: repetitive, fresh, propulsive, jubilant. Yet it’s what he does in Revelation. Also tonal, easy, sounding almost like joyous rap music, or like music for a kids choir, something like Pelecis’ version of The Little Sweep. The music could easily pass for absolutely corny, but it is so unabashedly so that I feel like a perverse attraction to it (and I like the music of Nyman also, sometimes). I like also what sounds to me as a total contradiction between the mood of the music – jubilant and facile, music for your kids’ show at the end of the year of elementary school - and what the piece is about. In the composer's own words, “Revelation presents three soloists – a countertenor, a pianist and a trumpet-player – refusing to accept the familiar dreadful prophesies, preferring the promises of a realm of light and joy, in the New Jerusalem. The theme is divided into three parts: the last lines of he Revelation of Saint John, Gloria in Exelsis Deo and Hallelujah in Paradise”. Do I read a subtext here, Pelecis talking about his refusal of “ugly” contemporary music, preferring the promises of a realm of light and joy in music in the style of Michael Nyman?

The rest is a it was expected to be: Nevertheless sweet, pretty and sentimental music, at times derivations of Chopin in the style of Richard Clayderman (that thing returns a lot in the double concerto), music for Elton John ballads, for a sentimental Hollywood romance (the moment of dreamy nostalgia, memories, hazy image, slow motion, gauze skirts rustling under the breeze), music that Yann Tiersen could have written, folk dances, moments that may hark back to late 19th and early 20th century English pastoralism – like Elgar, or Vaughan Williams’ The Lark Ascending. Sometimes the solo violin line even seems to want to reproduce that of Brahms’ Violin Concerto. In fact, just read what the composer says about it, and you can guess what’s in store: “this double concerto… reveals the importance of the psychological dimension in music. At the beginning of this piece, the piano plays in a minor key, in a state of permanent melancholy. The violin on the other hand, almost always in a major key swims in happiness and wants to convince his partner to join him there. For a long time he doesn’t manage it, and it is only after three violin solos, three passionate cadences, that the piano finally says “yes”. Because true happiness is happiness shared!”. Am I incredibly cynical or is this incredibly corny? Probably both. Always, when I have multiple versions of a same work, I’ll do some comparative listening. Here, sorry, but I cringe. Anyway, given the underlying program of the concerto, I’m in no doubt that Kremer plays it with more conviction with his partner Latia Skanavi here than he did with Vadim Sacharov in 1993.

Pelecis’ combined homage to Piazzola and Oskar Stork, track 3, is a mixture of symphonic tango (that’s the Piazzola part) and of more sentimental and crooning music with syrupy violins (Oskar Strock must be something like the Latvian Piazzola). 5 minutes of it might have been fun, nearly 20 seemed aimless. "The Last Song", the last piece on the CD, a solo for violin and strings, is 5 minutes-long, and although it is in the same sentimental, brooding, nostalgic, melancholy vein as the double concerto, with the same echoes of early 20th century English pastoralism (Vaughan Williams’ Tallis Fantasia comes to mind), it’s a piece that can hold its own in the neo-simplistic trend illustrated by Pärt’s Fratres.

At least, and to his credit (I guess), Pelecis is entirely unabashed about his aesthetic stance. He writes, in the liner notes (awkwardly translated to English, presumably from the German, by someone who obviously had only a vague understanding of German. When necessary I substitue my own): “I invite my listeners to be aware that the evolution of music has not only been a progression, but also a long sequence of losses. These losses are a painful memory to me and I cannot break away from them. I try to save and re-establish as much as I can. For the average listener, as indeed for me, the scope of classical music (from Monteverdi to Mahler) is a paradise that invites us into the most sumptuous realms that the mind of a composer can imagine. The imagination of a composer contemplates and rejoices in a certain ideal, that of sonic perfection in all its dimensions. Who then has chased composers from this Garden of Eden? I’m afraid that they’ve done it by their own decision [the liner notes’ translation of the German “auf eigene Faust” here is: “I rather fear that they have often escaped from their own master” This is senseless]. But I won’t let myself be chased away. So I remain there and I feel good. I see myself almost as a gardener, part guardian and part creator of pretty things in the musical paradise that belongs to all of us”.

So this is music for those who equate paradise and sentimental film music. De gustibus… But I'm afraid it's not the flowers of paradise that Pelecis is gardening, but cheap plastic avatars salvaged from dumps. TT 67 minutes, no complaint there – at least for those interested in that kind of music.

title: A Gift Never Opened
text:
Barney GreenE was a great pianist, who in spite of childhood poverty and no access to a piano in youth, managed to overcome obstacles and become a phenomenon at the piano. As an adult he joined a big band. He later formed his own big band but was drafted into the army and forced to give up his band, his dream. When he returned to civilian life, he performed in hotels and fine night clubs. And made a record, Piano by Starlight.

The record does not begin to reflect the mastery of his keyboard skills. According to my father, the producer insisted that the record reflect dinner or mood music. My Dad relinquished his technical wizardry for what was popular at the time, the excessively bland, souless, mood music. And he was forced to play with a bass player and a percussionist, when he was strictly a soloist. He fought against the trio but he had no artistic decision-making powers. He was confined to the rules of a producer that resulted in artistic rigidity.

He was a magnificent pianist but it will forever remain a secret. This is his only album. He was so disenchanted with its outcome, the product off a producer who stifled him in the pursuit of profit. Such an irony. Given full reign, my father's record could have made a profit. It didn't.

He never cut another album.

But he didn't need an album. He had a multitude of followers who loved his unfettered talent.

Listen to an album and imagine the potential of a man who exhibits, on occasion, the glimmers of mastery.

title: Excellent movie for middle-agers and old-timers alike
text:
A local radio station (WTOP, Wasington D.C.) said while the movie was good, David Strathairn didn't look like Edward R. Murrow but people who remember him wouldn't watch the film, and it didn't do enough to explain why communism was a big deal, so people that don't remember Murrow wouldn't appreciate the gravity of the conflict. I would like to disagree with both points.

Although I can't speak to what Edward R. Murrow looked like, (I'm 37, so WTOP was right about that), half the theater was full of people that looked like they were plenty old enough to remember him. Secondly, they were also right that I never fully understood why the fear of communism was such a big deal, I feel the movie was perfectly accessible to me. The way I see it, this movie is exceptionally important to people my age, given politically events over the last few years. It makes you wonder how life might be different if a highly repected Murrow of today took on the powers that be a few years ago, how things might been different.

This movie is a tribute to integrity and placing beliefs and values ahead of careers and the corporate bottom line while paradoxically maintaining the highest level of professionalism.

There was applause at the end of the movie, and a majority stayed put while the credits ran. I recommend it highly.

title: Much improved from 1986
text: I never liked the score for Star Trek IV.  I thought it was too short and didn't seem to "fit" with other Treks.  Well, I may have been too hasty.  This has more cues than the original release.  It's been cleaned up so the sound is excellent.  There are a number of alternate tracks, etc.  I absolutely adore the original main title and can't believe I've never heard this arrangement of the Alexander Courage theme.  If Leonard Nimoy wanted to change the main title with the end title, then he should have played this fantastic version over the end credits!  Although STIV is not my favorite film, it has some of the greatest Trek moments, especially the reveal of Enterprise-A.  I get chills every time!  And I had a huge lump in my throat when I saw it in 1986.  I think the other extended versions of Treks 1-5 are better than this one.  But this is a very enjoyable CD and for me that alternate main title alone is so worth it.  As always, great liner notes by Jeff Bond.  I hope they move on to The Undiscovered Country soon.  I loved that one.  I am glad there are fans of Trek music out there to keep it alive.  I always thought that in addition to Shatner/Nimoy/Kelley and great writing, the music was an integral and overlooked part of Trek's success.  I see myself appreciating this CD more and more with repeated listenings.  Very good overall.
