title: Vivaldi for the nostalgics of the 1960s
text:
Vanguard 08 2006 71, European edition, bringing back an LP published at the end of 1964, Vanguard/The Bach Guild BG 665 (mono) / Stereolab BGS (stereo) 70665, “Concertos for diverse instruments”, all performed by I Solisti di Zagreb under Antonio Janigro. Contents are:

- Concerto for 2 Mandolins RV 532 with Anton Ganocki and Ferdo Pavlinek
- Concerto for Flute “La Notte” op. 10-2 RV 104 with Julius Baker (flute) and Karl Hoffmann (bassoon)
- Concerto for strings RV 158
- Concerto for Bassoon RV 495 with Rudolf Klepack
- Concerto for Violin & double string orchestra “Per la Ss Assunzione di Maria Vergine” RV 581 with Jelka Stanic.

The Concertos weren’t attributed any catalog number back then, but the presence of the solo bassoon in “La Notte” makes it unmistably the Chamber Concerto version of that work, RV 104, and not the Concerto version, RV 439. Note that the continuo harpsichordist is Herbert Tachezi, better known as the harpsichordist of Harnoncourt and his Concentus Musicus Wien.

This is Vivaldi from the mid-1960s; then. Back then, in the realm of Vivaldi interpretation, reigned ensembles like I Musici, Renato Fasano's I Virtuosi di Roma, Angelo Ephrikian and his Orchestra della Scuola Veneziana. Many among the older generation of music lovers grew up with that, but in the 1970s new groups appeared who became great Vivaldi champions, like Claudio Scimone’s I Solisti Veneti and Neville Marriner and his Academy of St. Martin-in-the-Fields (and I Musici continued), and they were superseded by the first period instrument ensembles in the early 1980s, Trevor Pinnock’s English Concert, Christopher Hogwood’s Academy of Ancient Music, Nikolaus Harnoncourt’s Vienna Concentus Musicus, and even they were the springboard to new generations of Vivaldi interperters that emerged in the 1990s, many of them from Italy, like Il Giardino Armonico or Fabio Biondi’s L’Europa Galante.

So, other than the nostalgia effect on those older generations, how does Janigro’s Vivaldi hold up today? Not too well I'm afraid. It sounds like Vivaldi in the 1960s.

Heard on its own, without any references, this kind of Vivaldi playing may, at its best, seem convincing. After all the music is beautiful, sunny, buoyant, colorful. But as soon as you start comparing, it appears, even at its best, as a bit too thick, a bit too ponderous, a bit too proper and solemn and lacking true jubilation, a bit too overtly sentimental in the slow movements: and Concerto for strings RV 158 is very typical: there’s so much life and dynamism with Concerto Köln ([[ASIN:B000001WM0 Antonio Vivaldi: Concerti For Wind And Strings / Concerto Koln]]) (and Tachezi’s loud and clanging harpsichord doesn’t help either in the saccharine Andante). Julius Baker in “La Notte” (CD 1 tracks 4-7) is not to blame but - to limit myself to recordings of the chamber concerto version, RV 104 - Camerata Köln in 1988 ([[ASIN:B00000E6VA Vivaldi: Flute Concerti Op. 10 - Camerata Köln [Deutsche Harmonia Mundi]]]), and even more Il Giardino Armonico in 1990 ([[ASIN:B000000SEM Antonio Vivaldi: Concerti da Camera, Vol. 1 (Concerti, Op. 10) - Giovanni Antonini / Il Giardino Armonico]]) have brought so much more expression, imagination and drama in that work - and revealed how much the work gains being played one to a part: Vanguard’s La Notte is pretty, theirs takes my breath away (and don’t miss, on You Tube, flautist Sebastian Marq and Jean-Christophe Spinosi live on Mezzo in the "full concerto" version, RV 439, played one to a part: this is not “classical music” anymore, it’s rock & roll!). Compared to Klaus Thunemann with I Musici in 1994, [[ASIN:B00000133A Vivaldi: 7 Bassoon Concertos]], Rudolf Klepac and I Solisti di Zagreb sound positively trudging. Klepac’s tone is fine enough, but Thunemann ornaments profusely and imaginatively, and it sounds great.

The Concerto for 2 mandolins RV 532 (tracks 1-3) sounds again colorful, but pedestrian in the outer movements, too grand and heavy in its orchestral textures and too loud, verging dangerously on the solemn at the expense of the jubilant, Vivaldi in St. Marco rather than at Ospedale della Pietà. But the middle Andante – a beautiful “raindrop” movement – is still today entirely valid, despite the higher pitch and hence more crystalline sounds of the two mandolins compared to the one is accustomed of hearing now, and the Finale of the same concerto is taken with a drive and enthusiasm that leaves even modern period-instrument ensembles behind and that I’ve seen emulated only by Il Giardino Armonico. The two mandolinists, Anton Ganocki and Ferdo Pavlinek, are superb, and wouldn’t disgrace a period-instrument ensemble of today.

But sometimes, you don’t even need to compare to anything else to sense that something is wrong, as in the Violin Concerto with two antiphonal orchestras RV 581 (tracks 14-16): thick textures, heavy and trudging basses. This feels like, “ouch”. And go to Fabio Biondi – one of his first recordings, not with his Europa Galante ensemble but with counter-tenor Gerard Lesne’s Seminario Musicale, [[ASIN:B00000DNW5 Vivaldi - Salve Regina / Biondi · Il Seminario musical · Lesne]] – and hear not a big, juicy romantic tone like Jelka Stanic’s, much leaner, but hear also imaginative violin playing, going way beyond the written notes, adding wild improvisation at the cadential points in the first movement… and letting you fantasize what it might have been with Vivaldi himself played it. Giuliano Carmignola, [[ASIN:B0000245ZI Antonio Vivaldi Vivaldi: Violin Concertos / Concerto for Strings]], is much more score-bound than Biondi in the outer movements, but his violin playing is still way more interesting than Stanic’s; but his middle Largo is even wilder than Biondi, a long and ornate improvisation over Vivaldi’s melodic line. But, to be entirely fair, there is something to be said also in favor of Stanic’s simplicity there, just playing the notes as written. But the few individual moments or movements that still hold up today aren't enough to make this style of Vivaldi interpretation still valid today.

So, ultimately, who is this for? Nostalgics of the 1960s, people who grew up with that style of interpretation, learned their Vivaldi that way and want to stay there. But sometimes "before" is not better, and, in matters of Vivadli interpretation at least, I'm personnally glad to be "today".

title: Short book with a very small audience
text:
If you are not currently employed, this ebook will not help you beyond the value of obvious suggestions throughout its 17 pages (dress well, be relaxed, don't use your current employer's fax machine to fax resumes, and customize your resume to the position you are seeking). Hopefully, you're already aware of the more obvious requirements for successful interviewing - but if not, there are more useful books than this one.
The ebook is very light on the "how to" of what the author suggests as well. One of the author's suggestions was to cold-call people listed on the website of a company you're interested in to arrange for an informational interview. Knowing how difficult it is to create an email or letter catchy enough to warrant a response, I was surprised the author failed to make a single detailed (and therefore, useful) suggestion.
The author addresses the currently-employed with this document, and even there she falls short in describing the logistics of finding a new job while employed. She describes the search process at a very high level, give some suggestions without specifics of how to accomplish what is fairly obvious to begin with, and then fails to provide the reader with what could have been very valuable - the why and how of getting hired in tough times like these.

title: FILM MUSIC BY MAX STEINER - ENOUGH SAID!
text: With more than 300 scores, Max Steiner was one of the greatest film composers of all time. Primarily based at Warner Bros. after a stint at RKO, Steiner was a pioneer in the film music genre, particularly with such noteworthy scores as the ones for King Kong, She, Gone with the Wind, and a slew of Bette Davis movies. In his last years, he was still writing superb scores for such films as The Last Command, A Summer Place, Parrish, and Helen of Troy. His career spanned 5 decades and BYU now houses the Max Steiner Archives. This 2-disc collection is heralded as "The Dark Side of Max Steiner" with suites from Key Largo, Flamingo Road, Caged, The Unfaithful, Backfire, The Breaking Point, and Lightning Strikes Twice. It is only because my personal taste runs more to the more romantic and "lighter side" of Max Steiner that I did not give this collection 5 stars. Others may feel differently. Regardless, this is a worthwhile and interesting selection to add to anyone's personal collection. Four stars for Max Steiner is like six stars for most other film composers.

text: This is a very attractive program blending history, literature, and theology; much has been written on the value for homeschool and allows for unique dialog and interaction in a homeschool environment - or in a brick & mortar school (private "Classical Christian" schools often use the Omnibus program).  While the structure and relational blending of historical topics is well-done and engaging; most courses (1-6) do subtly promote a socio-political outlook of the editors.  Omnibus 3, covering the modern era, may be the most notorious in this regard - as recurring themes strongly promote a specific angle of Reformed theology promoted by Idaho pastor Douglas Wilson.  However, this particular course presents highly controversial lessons and assignments the present southern slavery as a "mutual affection" between races, which I find extremely abhorrent, and completely inaccurate.  The account of 19th and 20th century history is politically motivated well outside mainstreams at best, and a deviously twisted, intellectually dishonest, rhetorical work of propaganda to some.  The format is used to create a systematic "worldview" that justifies historical interpretation and literary expression with alleged biblical doctrine - within a curriculum structure that does not include specific or isolated study of Biblical Scripture - rather uses the Christian Bible as a "lens."  While sounding mature in intellect at the outset - if you are keen to the progression of "worldview development," you may find this program to not be a fit at all for an objective Christian Education program, because it will place the doctrine and political motivation of the publisher over a historical study of the Christian Faith and it's scriptural revelation.  Because of this subjectivity, I cannot give it a high score as a safe option for homeschool or institutional Christian Education.  Please, in all cases - do your own research on the publishers (including Douglas Wilson and the organizations he's founded in Idaho) to understand what this curriculum is, and the intended conclusions and "worldview" that it is designed to result in.  (Full disclosure - I am a school board member of a private Christian K-12 school who has had to evaluate this program after it had been implemented for 3-4 years; I do hold a BRE degree in Religious Education with a graduate degree in Biblical Studies)

title: A Staple of Low Comedy
text:
Wagner was the George Lucas of his day, cribbing bits and pieces of authentic legends into a confused mish-mash of, in his case, fantasy opera, as Lucas later did in space opera. Wagner was the apotheosis of the Central European late-Romantic tradition's devolution into pure bombastic excess. As music could not develop further in this direction, in the 20th Century composers turned their backs on Wagner's overblown emptiness, freeing themselves to explore serialism, atonality, minimalism, ambient sound, and other previously unthinkable techniques.

The "Ring" cycle has since become a staple of low comedy, with the large, screaming blonde women in horned helmets, and the expression "it ain't over until the fat lady sings" (what impatient spectators were told while sitting through interminable "Ring" performances). In "What is Art," Tolstoy gives an outstanding review of an early "Ring" production that may be the funniest piece he ever wrote. His insight is remarkable - it's easy to make fun of Wagner today, but at the time Tolstoy saw it, the "Ring" was considered to be the highest art imaginable. My idea of the ideal "Ring" would have all of the characters dressed as clowns, with Larry David as Seigfried, Rosie O'Donnell as Brünnhilde (lip-syching to vocals by Yoko Ono), and Justin Bieber as Alberich. There should be plenty of pie throwing, banana peels, and eye poking á la The Three Stooges. With the special effects available today, it should also be possible to show someone skiing through a chain-link fence and turning into a pile of ice cubes on the other side.

Suffering through the marathon of an entire "Ring" performance can be of value only to specialists in the history of music or obsessed completists. Castorf's recent production at Bayreuth in honor of Wagner's 200th birthday was roundly booed by the audience.

title: It presents most of the material in edited and unnecessarily fragmented form
text:
CAVEAT EMPTOR! This is the most sloppily assembled CD I have ever heard. The main source material for this borderline bootleg is a tape of a live jam recorded at the Scene Club in NYC in 1968 with the Jimi Hendrix Experience along with Buddy Miles, a second guitarist (possibly Rick Derringer), and Jim Morrison. It's historically important as the only time Hendrix and Morrison appeared on stage together, but unfortunately Morrison was obnoxiously drunk (The biographical liner notes make no mention of this live performance). However, Jimi's guitar playing is dazzling, and there are unedited versions of this jam that are worth hearing, but this CD isn't one of them. It presents most of the material in edited and unnecessarily fragmented form. The 8-minute uptempo version of "Red House" was originally 11 minutes, but is faded out 3 minutes early. The 7-minute "Peoples,Peoples" is a fragment of the 12:29 "Bleeding Heart". "Whoa Eeh" is a 3-minute fragment of a 5-minute jam on "Tomorrow Never Knows." "Lime Lime" medley" is a 6-minute fragment of a 10-minute jam on "Outside Woman Blues" and "Sunshine of Your Love". The misleading track listing lists "Lime Lime Medley" as track 9, "Outside Woman Blues" as track 10, and "Sunshine" as track 11. not only are there only 9 tracks, but the jam is faded out BEFORE "Sunshine of Your Love", so it isn't even on this disc. In an act of blatant carelessness (or perhaps a deliberate cheat), although the 8-minute title track is included in its entirety, the disc also has a 6-minute fragment of the same track entitled "Blues,Blues." Also, "Urnaus Rock" and
Whoa Eeh" contain about 2 minutes worth of overlap (where Morrison falls down on stage and Jimi says "For those who don't know what's going on, we've got...Jim Morrison here..."). You can hear Morrison's drunken moans on both tracks, and he also sings a verse of "Peoples". Also included on the disc are 2 studio recordings. "Voices" is a song sung by Lonnie Youngblood with Hendrix on guitar recorded in 1965 and "Gonna Take a Lot" is sung by an uncredited female singer( Gloria Barnes according to some sources, and according to some of those same sources, Hendrix does not even appear on this track). Both songs are actually pretty good, but they sound out of place interspersed with these live jams. The only Scene Club selection not included here in any form is "Morrison's Lament" which consists of the band riffing behind Jim Morrison's drunkenly shouted obscenities. If you want a CD of the Scene Club jam (a must for Hendrix completists although it was never meant to be released) and you don't mind Morrison's foul mouth on one track, there are other CDs that have the whole jam unedited. Some of them are also titled Woke Up This Morning..., while others have titles like Live at the Scene Club and Bleeding Heart. Go with one of those, but avoid this hatchet job. I generously gave it 2 stars for pretty good sound quality and Hendrix's amazing chops, but the material here can be heard in much better context elsewhere.

title: Audiobook is ABRIDGED version
text:
I bought this as a used book on CDs from a private Amazon seller. The author was new to me, and I chose the book partly because I have Mennonite ancestry (though not Mennonite upbringing). I was surprised at the matter-of-fact adolescent cynicism of the story line, but not greatly put off by it. Yet the story seemed strangely choppy. I was well into it when I finally grew suspicious --- the writing was too good not to be better than it was, if you see what I mean. I closely examined the cover and found in the small print and partly obscured that it was an abridged version. I never knowingly buy an abridgement; bad writers' books are not improved and good writers are often injured. (And there was evidence of corrupt intent: somebody had put a tiny sticker over the word so you couldn't tell whether it said Abridged or Unabridged --- INSIDE the jewel case; this was deliberate.)
So I hold judgement about Miriam Toews, but warn off from the audiobook!

title: Look elsewhere for an exciting Fantastique
text:
Sadly, this recording is another unexciting miss in a whole series of unexciting misses issued by DG in their Boulez series.

The playing of the orchestra is impeccable, but the interpretation itself just sort of sits there. There's no forward momentum, nothing eerie, spooky or - well - fanatastic about the proceedings.

Textual notes: Boulez omits the cornet part in the second movement and observes the unwritten DC al segno repeat at the double bar in the 4th movement.

Skip this and pick up the Maazel/Cleveland/Sony version instead. A absolute overlooked gem of a recording that is everything this Boulez recording is not, and in much better recorded sound.

title: BEAUTIFULLY CRAFTED HISTORICAL FICTION...
text:
This gifted author weaves a mesmerizing tale around Dutch artist Johannes Vermeer's most famous painting, creating an incandescent and luminous work of her own. His painting is a simple, though enigmatic, portrait of a girl with a pearl earring, about which little is known. The author, however, a born storyteller, creates a living, breathing story around it, using a singular, first person narrative. Told in spare, elegant prose, the author leaps into literary renown with this book.

The events in the book are viewed through the eyes of Griet, a sixteen year old Dutch girl, whose changed family circumstances force her into taking a position as a maid in the home of a renowned painter, the taciturn Johannes Vermeer. There, the painter resides with his tempestuous wife, Catharina, their brood of unruly children, his commanding and shrewd mother-in-law, Maria Thins, and their loyal housekeeper and cook, Tanneke. The author lovingly details seventeenth century life in the Dutch city of Delft. It is here that Griet's story unfolds.

Sensitive and perceptive, Griet is attuned to the under currents in the Vermeer household and, at first, takes care not to draw attention to herself. Still, she, the daughter of a tile painter, is curious about Vermeer's artistry and is drawn to his work and his methods. Vermeer, sensing a kindred artistic spirit in Griet, draws her into his world of paint, color, light, and beauty, creating an intimacy of the spirit between the two.

Still, Griet, a girl on the brink of becoming a woman, finds herself confused and breathlessly desiring more than she may have. Her longing for more than a communion of the spirit with Vermeer is palpable. It is, therefore, not surprising that the undercurrents in the Vermeer household should come bubbling to the surface and engulf Griet, much to her consternation.

This is a stunning literary work that fully realizes the promise that the author showed in her debut novel, "The Virgin Blue". She is an author that understands the less is often more, and she makes every word count. Deliberate and spare, her prose is lyrical in its simplicity, weaving a tale that will keep the reader spellbound. This is historical fiction at its finest. Bravo!

title: Life goes on, so where's Gerry?
text:
It has been about five years since Rafferty's last release "Another World," so this treading-water mishmash of re-issues from several earlier recordings, re-edits of some earlier tracks, and a few other songs that were available as free downloads from his now-defunct website comes as rather a disappointment.

The re-issues are fine, but real fans will already have them. The re-edits don't change the orignal songs to any great extent, although "The Waters of Forgetfulness" has an evocative, eastern-sounding intro that was not on the original recording (from 1994's "Over My Head") which improves the song's atmosphere but hardly merits a re-release. The other re-edits have different running times, but even though I am very familiar with the original versions, I would be hard-pressed to determine what changes have been made. They're all fine songs, but we've heard them.

This leaves the tracks that were originally free downloads from the late, lamented website. There are, as I make it out, six of these. "Kyrie Elieson" and "Adeste Fidelis" are multi-multi-tracked Gerry producing the effect of a choir of Gregorian chanters. "Because," the Beatles tune, is also given the multi-multi-track treatment, and it's gorgeous, fully a match to the original recording. "Your Heart's Desire" is a fine song, one of his strongest from the late 80s, when it was recorded for but not released on "North and South." If you liked that recording, you'll love this song dating from those sessions. "The Maid of Culmore" is a traditional Scottish song, and Rafferty's recording makes me wish he had followed through on plans to do an all-traditional recording.

A few of the web downloads are inexplicably not included here. I'd rather that they would see the light of day than the straight, unchanged re-issues that take up too much of this CD. He had a new "film noir" version of "Keep it to Yourself" from the second Humblebums album, released in 1971, another traditional song--"She Moved Through the Fair"--that was a modal, mystical folk club staple in the 1960s and beyond, and a version of "Fever" that almost outdoes Peggy Lee's definitive version, with a slinky, jazzy cool feel that is immensely appealing. There was also a forgettable instrumental, remnent of a plan for an all-instrumental project.

Sorry to go on so much about what's not on here, but if a place-holder release was all that Rafferty was able to come up with, even that could have been a bit better than this disappointment. I hope this is a deck-clearing maneuver to make way for the kind of tastey and tunefuliscious pop music that has been his hallmark for decades now. He doesn't release recordings very often, and it's too bad this one is something of a miss.

If you are a fanatic, you will want this. If not, try "Another World," "North and South" or even "City to City," which holds up beautifully after all these years.

title: Road to Wellville-- Audio CD, Cassette, "Voyager Company Expanded Book"
text:
I love this novel. It is one of my "keepers" and I pull it out to read every couple of years. (I enjoy the movie too in spite of liberties that were taken with the story; the casting was very appropriate and the "laughing exercises" sequence that it opens with, is hilarious.)

I am also a very big fan of UNABRIDGED audio books, and ever since I discovered that Books on Tape had put out an unabridged audio version on cassette in the mid-90s, I have tried to get my hands on it, or on an unabridged mp3 or CD version. At this point I do not think any unabridged version was ever published on mp3 and CD.

The "One Star" on this review pertains ENTIRELY to the "Expanded Book" (Voyager Company) version.

Lately I just ordered and returned an edition of THE ROAD TO WELLVILLE that was falsely listed as "audio CD"-- "The Voyager Company Expanded Book". I was unable to find enough information (on Amazon, Worldcat, or anywhere else) to determine whether this format was unabridged or not, and the seller did not answer my query before I ordered the item. I decided to risk it after speaking with Amazon customer service about buyer protection (so it has been fully refunded as I write this). I also took documentary photos of the front and back of the package, as I did not need to open it, to find out it could not be any kind of audio CD.

I am writing this review not to praise the book, since many have and I can but repeat them, but to put information online about this particular format in case it ever surfaces again, or for that matter, if other "Voyager Company Expanded Book/s" get put on the market as audio CDs.

This was an edition put out in the mid-90s by The Voyager Company, back when all digital media were still a novelty. There is no way this can be an audio book of any kind. It contains one single floppy disc with only 1.4 MB of data, which is only enough to hold a text-only document. No form of compression can make an unabridged audio book that small. Even the smallest mp3 abridgments are over 50 MB in size, generally.

Other clues: there is no reader listed. There is a synopsis of the book and reviews, below which is this copy, which I assume was printed on every "Expanded Book":

"Just as computers have changed the way you write, they are beginning to transform the way you read. Electronic text is a dynamic medium that enables you to become a more active reader.

With Voyager's Expanded Books, you can:
*Instantly access every occurrence of an word
*Add margin comments and end notes
*Locate any word or phrase in the text and in your notes
*Highlight text and mark pages in 2 different ways"

Also listed:

"SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Designed especially for Macintosh PowerBooks, or any Mac with hard drive and large display (640 x 400 or greater). System 6.0.7 and Hypercard 2.1 for later versions. Shipped on 1.4 MB high density floppy."

No reference to a reader or recording date, printed on an obsolete medium, all text referring to word processing attributes only. it's pretty obvious why The Voyager Company went out of business, isn't it? If you are looking for audio, this is not audio. And to be honest, electronic versions of this book are also readily available.

Let's start with the basics: THE JEDI. In "Empire" Yoda tells us that the Force unites us, binds us, and what luminous beings we are. Well, in Episode II the Jedi seem to have forgotten this. They're police officers with lightsabers. Nothing more. The "religious" aspect is erased as if it never were.
The mythology is also gone. I guess Joseph Campbell's teachings were lost on Lucas when writing this. It's just a series of random event after random event. Anakin getting his arm stapled to a conveyer belt.. WHY?
But let's get to the juicy details, shall we?
DIALOGUE: Whoever said the dialogue in this movie sounds like Shakespeare should be slapped silly. It's HORRIBLE! Tacking on "m'lady" at the end of a horrible sentence maketh not Shakespeare! The fact that most lines are delivered with no emotion and gives you a recipe for corny atrocities and a lot of painful watching. The classic lines such as "Your thoughts betray you" and "Be mindful of your feelings" are delivered over and over and OVER again.
ROMANCE: This movie has romance? It's more like Al Gore and Michael Dukhakis reading bad poetry. NO emotion whatsoever. I'll grant Hayden that he tries so hard to make these horrible lines work. "I've been dying every day since you came here." *YAWN* "My heart is a black hole of torture with foul robots kicking me in the ..." Yea, George, great dialogue. Atrocious.
ANAKIN: I was hoping we would see his descent into madness with this film. Do we? NO. We see him whine. Again and again. "You're holding me back!" "I want my mommy!" "It's all your fault!" on and on and on.
PACING: Is this movie paced? I would have never known from watching it. The first hour or so is pure drama, and the last half is one nonstop torture session in how ridiculous things get. Episode I had pacing. The finale, for example. Excellently switching between the Maul fight and the space battle. Episode II just pours it on, and the result is so horrible.
Let's look at some really bad action sequences:
R2 with Jets. WHY? He doesn't have them in Episodes 4-6. Why did Lucas think it would be so cool to have them now?
The big fight. Is it just me, or do all the Jedi forget how to use the Force? and I'm supposed to believe that the dumb droids from Episode I can kill Jedi in a tight circle formation? No wonder Palpatine wants them dead. They stink!
The vehicles completely lack heart, and the big ship fighting sequence is so emotionally empty I was actually BORED. I went to this film pumped up in my Darth Vader garb, and I was actually BORED! and Lucas's attempt to keep my attention by having Natalie bare her tummy was a feeble mind trick that didn't make me forget the movie stunk.
YODA: He went from Ghandi-esque Guru to ... Matrix spinoff character. His big scene is so absurd I was laughing AT it, not with it. Episode V's Yoda is NOT the Yoda we see now.
Conclusion: Ewan, Ian, and Shaft do an admirable job trying to salvage this movie from George's insanity, but ultimately fail. Spiderman and Fellowship of the Ring are two films that blow this one away in terms of completeness... They prove a movie can have heart, action, romance, comedy, and special effects. Star Wars has 1 or 2 of these at most. And if you don't believe me, watch Spider-man right after you see Clones. You'll realize Episode II is a clone, alright. Just not of Star Wars.

title: Weird science?
text:
I was initially intrigued by Lipton's comments, especially his long discourse on how genes and proteins work. However, about 5 minutes from the end of the audio book, he mentions "Jesus" at least twice in the context of our ability to create miracles, or the "miracles of Jesus', with our mind. I was not sure where he was going with the book since almost all of it is discussion of cell biology, or at least cell biology as described by Lipton. The author goes through a lengthy explanation of cell biology only to end up asserting we can change our gene expression, or biology, through our thoughts. As other reviewers have noted, he does not go into how we can change our biology, simply referencing some techniques. The book is really just a "scientific" argument to lay the groundwork for something else, namely another new age theory of how mind energy can control matter. I bought this book on iTunes and only after hitting the "Buy" button did I think to run Lipton through a quack detector. There is little out there but I did find some discussion on a forum for readers of Richard Dawkins; I would give the link to the forum, but Amazon keeps deleting it in my review. Some of the other reviewers have done an excellent job of pointing out the problems with Lipton's theory.

I agree that we really do not know all that much about the universe, why we are here, how our brains work and so on. We have a lot to learn and we may very well discover someday that our thoughts can have a substantial impact on our gene expression, cure us of disease and perform an infinite number of miracles. However, the evidence for this is sketchy and almost all experiments to prove the existence of psi, or other mysterious mind energy or control, have shown that nothing like this exists, or at least we cannot measure it yet. I am skeptical and need evidence - Lipton's book provides none. The book is just rambling weird science and I cannot recommend it because it does not do a good job of addressing epigenetics (this is a real area of science) and seems to be the foundation for Lipton's new age philosophy and business. Also, Lipton's mention of Jesus at the end of the book is incongruous; faith is not science because you cannot observe, measure, prove or disprove mythological beliefs and their consequences. By resorting to religious fervor at the end of the book, Lipton completely undermines his credibility as a scientist, and all his material up to that point gets called into question. Look elsewhere for learning about epigenetics - this book goes onto the shelf with the new age hucksters.

title: The Very Best Indeed
text:
Valery Kipelov had been the lead singer of Russian heavy metal band Aria for seventeen years until, in 2002, he left them and formed his own band, Kipelov. The music of Kipelov is similar to that of earlier Aria; their lyrics, written by professional poets, are meaningful and flowing; and Mr. Kipelov's voice, which seems to be getting better with age, never ceases to impress me and to stir my heart.

The album is divided into two discs that feature fourteen and fifteen Kipelov's best songs, respectively. It is rather difficult for me to closely follow the band's work from so far away, but, to the best of my knowledge, twenty-eight of the songs have been previously released, and they represent--not equally, but justly, in my opinion--all but one of Kipelov's albums to date. The vast majority of the songs--twenty of them, to be exact--are from the band's three albums: 2003's The Way Up (seven songs), 2005's Rivers of Time (eight songs), and 2011's To Live in Defiance (five songs). All these remakes sound very similar to the originals, clean and very clear, as if they've been filtered through crystal. The only noticeable exception (in instrumentation, not in sound quality) is the sixth track on disc one, I Am Here. It is quite different from the original: the added piano and strings are great, I can hear the guitars better, and they even have a slight Flamenco tone, especially the solo. I have to admit that I have never before heard this version, and although I like the original, I love this one much more.

Every song on the album is remarkably good. If I were hard-pressed to choose my second favorite song from the collection, I would probably be lost, for I can easily name at least five songs that fit the bill. However, my absolutely favorite one is, without a doubt, Rivers of Time. It is a melodic song that tells the story of Alexander the Great and his ambitious attempt to conquer the world. The music is incredible, the lyrics are smart, the vocals are impassioned, and the fact that I find King Alexander of Macedon to be fascinating also helps:

Prisoner of your own words, you have brought others with you
In silence, you have sacrificed all that you kept in your heart
Driven by your thirst of fame, you realized too late that you were alone

The weight of passed victories suffocates you like a noose
There's no need to keep on living if you know everything about the world
Blinded by a dream, you stood still on the edge of Earth

Brilliant, isn't it? Of course, the lyrics rhyme in Russian.

I have two complaints about this compilation. The first one is that it is a mix of live and studio versions. Unless I am at a concert, I don't like live performances. In the comfort of my home, I prefer to listen to flawlessly recorded music on a great stereo, and without distracting sounds of people screaming, chanting, or singing along, and the band's members talking. Unfortunately for me, the last seven tracks on disc two are live versions--these are the seven songs from The Way Up, Kipelov's concert album which consists mainly of old Aria songs. Although they don't sound like they've been recorded through a pillow, the sound quality is a bit different from that of the rest of the album, and I found myself skipping these songs most of the time on the CD. But since I have studio versions of them on my iPod, it is not a big deal to me.

The second complaint is that Castlevania is not on the album, and I think it should have made the cut.

Other than those minor issues, which really are both a matter of my personal preferences and taste, I truly did, and do, enjoy this thrilling album. I'm giving it 4.5 stars and rounding the number up to five.

My favorite English-singing heavy metal bands are Avenged Sevenfold, Metallica, Sabaton, and Iron Maiden. If you have similar tastes in music and like these, chances are you'll enjoy Kipelov and/or Aria. Kipelov's The Best is a great album to start with or to add to your collection.

Happy listening!

title: What is This Book All About, Really?
text:
First off, the title should be something like "How The Study of Cell Biology Taught Me Things About the Human Condition - A Series of Lectures by Bruce H. Lipton, PhD". Or maybe "How Biological Processes at the Cellular Level Map to Multi-Cellular Beings Like Us.

What we have here is a lot of true basic science, mixed with rants about research that ignores possible quantum effects, sprinkled with a few old, but interesting and somewhat surprising human study results, packaged with some of the author's personal biography surrounding how he arrived at his positions.

This is not a textbook, but a majority of the volume is spent covering material that is most assuredly in textbooks; basic science that's likely not to raise an eyebrow on scientists of any stripe. In fact, early in the book, the author says something akin to that the reaction to the book by most scientists is "so what?" I'm not a scientist, but I'm a science news junkie. I've listened to about every T.E.D. talk and never stop reading layman science books and magazines. And my opinion is the same as Lipton's scientist reviewers: "So What?" If this was your first introduction into material of this nature, you might get something out of it, but for me, nothing new here.

Beyond the textbook science, another area which gets significant treatment is criticism of various sorts. Lipton airs concerns about how research science is not paying enough attention to how quantum mechanics might help explain more about the biology. I agree that scientists have a hard time abandoning an idea that has been the basis of their career, and we would be better off if that wasn't the case, but ranting about it isn't going to help. The author obviously doesn't like big pharma and doctors who see that as the only way either. No argument here, but again, preaching to the choir.

The style of the book is like a professor giving a lecture. There's the presentation of the material, plus wishes, hopes, rants, and experiences the professor. Some of the topics well correlated with the material, and some not so well correlated. But the professor only has you for a few lectures, and he wants to get his position on the world across to you before you leave. And for someone who claims to be a scientist, I'm surprised at how many points are "proven" using a single anecdote as "evidence".

So what's left in this book after we remove the rants directed at researcher community, after we remove the textbook science, and after we remove the autobiographical segments? There are a few references to older studies about human biology that might be interesting and surprising to some readers. There is an advertisement for his buddy's classes, that I consider shameful. But not much else. I didn't get anything about "Unleashing the Power of Consciousness, Matter & Miracles", but that was probably just the publisher anyway. The book title is deceptive. I can't believe this book sold as well as (I guess) it did. They must have one heck of a marketing department!

Dr. Lipton's writing technique is to set-up a flimsy straw-man and knock it down. For instance, a lot of the book is about the old nature/nurture question. Lipton sets up by saying "you are not your DNA". Ok, I knew that. I mean, we have alligator eggs that will change sex if incubated at different temperatures. We have human grandchildren that are affected by a sustained food shortage of their grandparents. He's preaching to the choir, and let me tell you, it's a long sermon if you don't need to be convinced!

Besides "Biology", the other word in the title that might be considered somewhat accurate would be "Belief", because he does talk about the placebo effect and related material. Again, the straw-man is "what/how you think does not matter to your biology." Huh? Who believes that?!?

Lipton mentions that the media takes liberties with causation, but I think he might look a little closer to home for examples. For instance he says that certain unexplained things "defy Newtonian biology." It is possible that there's some kind of quantum process going on in some "amazing feats of physical endurance" or with "the ability to walk across hot coals without getting burned", but maybe not. After all, Bill Nye the Science Guy walked across hot coals, no hocus pocus, just was trained by a fire walker and did it. It seems like anything the author finds that is not well explained, somehow ties back to quantum mechanics.

Sometimes the best biologists have been able to do is map-out a simplified version of how a process might work. When Lipton finds a process that is not well-understood, he leaps to the conclusion that there must be quantum effects going on. There very well may be non-Newtonian processes, but there's nothing he is saying that's even marginally convincing me. He tries, in one case, to say that because a protein is used for both sex determination as well as RNA synthesis that indicates non-Newtonian action. Well, I can use a screwdriver to drive a screw or as a pry tool, does that mean there's quantum effects there too?

This book was an easy read, and with the biographical references and professor's lecture style, was not totally unenjoyable to read. But the material is unconvincing and much of it is stale. The title of the book is deceptive, and having an undisclosed advertisement in the book for a paid class by his friend is stooping pretty low. title: Vivaldi for the nolstalgics of the 60s - but cheaper editions elsewhere
text:
This used to be the budget edition, from Vanguard Europe, Vanguard 08 6128 71, of a CD first published as 08 2006 71 in Europe, [[ASIN:B0000254LU Concertos for diverse Instruments]], and OVC 2006 in the US, [[ASIN:B0000023A8 Vivaldi: Concerti for Diverse Instruments]]. Well, no more budget on the marketplace, and at the time of writing the US edition is a much better bargain. There's also an edition licensed by the Musical Heritage Society, which currently sells even cheaper, [[ASIN:B000K2NFFA Antonio Vivaldi: Concertos for Diverse Instruments]].

They are the reissue of an LP published at the end of 1964, Vanguard/The Bach Guild BG 665 (mono) / Stereolab BGS (stereo) 70665, “Concertos for diverse instruments”, all performed by I Solisti di Zagreb under Antonio Janigro. Contents are:

- Concerto for 2 Mandolins RV 532 with Anton Ganocki and Ferdo Pavlinek
- Concerto for Flute “La Notte” op. 10-2 RV 104 with Julius Baker (flute) and Karl Hoffmann (bassoon)
- Concerto for strings RV 158
- Concerto for Bassoon RV 495 with Rudolf Klepack
- Concerto for Violin & double string orchestra “Per la Ss Assunzione di Maria Vergine” RV 581 with Jelka Stanic.

The Concertos weren’t attributed any catalog number back then, but the presence of the solo bassoon in “La Notte” makes it unmistably the Chamber Concerto version of that work, RV 104, and not the Concerto version, RV 439. Note that the continuo harpsichordist is Herbert Tachezi, better known as the harpsichordist of Harnoncourt and his Concentus Musicus Wien.

This is Vivaldi from the mid-1960s, then. Back then, in the realm of Vivaldi interpretation, reigned ensembles like I Musici, Renato Fasano's I Virtuosi di Roma, Angelo Ephrikian and his Orchestra della Scuola Veneziana. Many among the older generation of music lovers grew up with that, but in the 1970s new groups appeared who became great Vivaldi champions, like Claudio Scimone’s I Solisti Veneti and Neville Marriner and his Academy of St. Martin-in-the-Fields (and I Musici continued), and they were superseded by the first period instrument ensembles in the early 1980s, Trevor Pinnock’s English Concert, Christopher Hogwood’s Academy of Ancient Music, Nikolaus Harnoncourt’s Vienna Concentus Musicus, and even they were the springboard to new generations of Vivaldi interperters that emerged in the 1990s, many of them from Italy, like Il Giardino Armonico or Fabio Biondi’s L’Europa Galante.

So, other than the nostalgia effect on those older generations, how does Janigro’s Vivaldi hold up today? Well, what did you expect? It sounds like Vivaldi in the 1960s.

Heard on its own, without any references, this kind of Vivaldi playing may, at its best, seem convincing. After all the music is beautiful, sunny, buoyant, colorful. But as soon as you start comparing, it appears, even at its best, as a bit too thick, a bit too ponderous, a bit too proper and solemn and lacking true jubilation, a bit too overtly sentimental in the slow movements: and Concerto for strings RV 158 is very typical: there’s so much life and dynamism with Concerto Köln ([[ASIN:B000001WM0 Antonio Vivaldi: Concerti For Wind And Strings / Concerto Koln]]) (and Tachezi’s loud and clanging harpsichord doesn’t help either in the saccharine Andante). Julius Baker in “La Notte” (CD 1 tracks 4-7) is not to blame but - to limit myself to recordings of the chamber concerto version, RV 104 - Camerata Köln in 1988 ([[ASIN:B00000E6VA Vivaldi: Flute Concerti Op. 10 - Camerata Köln [Deutsche Harmonia Mundi]]]), and even more Il Giardino Armonico in 1990 ([[ASIN:B000000SEM Antonio Vivaldi: Concerti da Camera, Vol. 1 (Concerti, Op. 10) - Giovanni Antonini / Il Giardino Armonico]]) have brought so much more expression, imagination and drama in that work - and revealed how much the work gains being played one to a part: Vanguard’s La Notte is pretty, theirs takes my breath away (and don’t miss, on You Tube, flautist Sebastian Marq and Jean-Christophe Spinosi live on Mezzo in the "full concerto" version, RV 439, played one to a part: this is not “classical music” anymore, it’s rock & roll!). Compared to Klaus Thunemann with I Musici in 1994, [[ASIN:B00000133A Vivaldi: 7 Bassoon Concertos]], Rudolf Klepac and I Solisti di Zagreb sound positively trudging. Klepac’s tone is fine enough, but Thunemann ornaments profusely and imaginatively, and it sounds great.

The Concerto for 2 mandolins RV 532 (tracks 1-3) sounds again colorful, but pedestrian in the outer movements, too grand and heavy in its orchestral textures and too loud, verging dangerously on the solemn at the expense of the jubilant, Vivaldi in St. Marco rather than at Ospedale della Pietà. But the middle Andante – a beautiful “raindrop” movement – is still today entirely valid, despite the higher pitch and hence more crystalline sounds of the two mandolins compared to the one is accustomed of hearing now, and the Finale of the same concerto is taken with a drive and enthusiasm that leaves even modern period-instrument ensembles behind and that I’ve seen emulated only by Il Giardino Armonico. The two mandolinists, Anton Ganocki and Ferdo Pavlinek, are superb, and wouldn’t disgrace a period-instrument ensemble of today.

But sometimes, you don’t even need to compare to anything else to sense that something is wrong, as in the Violin Concerto with two antiphonal orchestras RV 581 (tracks 14-16): thick textures, heavy and trudging basses. This feels like, “ouch”. And go to Fabio Biondi – one of his first recordings, not with his Europa Galante ensemble but with counter-tenor Gerard Lesne’s Seminario Musicale, [[ASIN:B00000DNW5 Vivaldi - Salve Regina / Biondi · Il Seminario musical · Lesne]] – and hear not a big, juicy romantic tone like Jelka Stanic’s, much leaner, but hear also imaginative violin playing, going way beyond the written notes, adding wild improvisation at the cadential points in the first movement… and letting you fantasize what it might have been with Vivaldi himself played it. Giuliano Carmignola, [[ASIN:B0000245ZI Antonio Vivaldi Vivaldi: Violin Concertos / Concerto for Strings]], is much more score-bound than Biondi in the outer movements, but his violin playing is still way more interesting than Stanic’s; but his middle Largo is even wilder than Biondi, a long and ornate improvisation over Vivaldi’s melodic line. But, to be entirely fair, there is something to be said also in favor of Stanic’s simplicity there, just playing the notes as written. But the few individual moments or movements that still hold up today aren't enough to make this style of Vivaldi interpretation still valid today.

So, ultimately, who is this for? Nostalgics of the 1960s, people who grew up with that style of interpretation, learned their Vivaldi that way and want to stay there. But sometimes "before" is not better, and, in matters of Vivadli interpretation at least, I'm personnally glad to be "today".

title: An oustanding tour de force recording in the piano repertorire
text: In the history of recorded music, there are a small amount of performances that may be called over the top grand slams, much more than competent renditions. The MSR recording “Soul of Brazil,” matching the genius of composer Heitor Villa-Lobos with the insightful, skillful and talented pianism of Martha Marchena is among them. Marchena in a tour de force rendition of five Villa-Lobos pieces draws every bit of emotion, power, drama and poetry out of them in a bravura performance. Time stops while we succumb to the passion, fire, eloquence and grandeur expressed by Marchena while she reveals why Villa-Lobos, largely self-taught, became one of the greatest composers of the 20th century. As one of the truly creative souls of the past 100 years, no academic setting could contain Villa-Lobos, a man of natural talent, while he sought to express the depth and range of his native Brazil soul. The recording booklet contains two disarming portraits of Marchena, appearing demure and unassuming. But, when she engages the keyboard in “Rudepoema” or “Cicolio Brasileiro” in particular, she reveals who she really is while imparting every bit of what Villa-Lobos sought to express as a composer. The sound engineers also deserve credit for this outstanding recording in which they preserved its heavy bass clef aspects in balance with treble clef elements in Marchena’s full, unrestrained expression of the compositions.

title: This is almost certainly ATB’s best album. He is known for the two-disc format ...
text:
This is almost certainly ATB’s best album. He is known for the two-disc format with a dance-heavy disc followed by an ambient one. While at times I’ve prefered the latter (Two Worlds comes to mind), the first disc of ‘NeXt’ steals the show here. ATB has thoroughly updated his sound to match current sensibilities and trends, proving that he is not yet willing to fade into irrelevancy as he enters his 18th year as a recording musician. His last ‘best’ album “Justify” and very competent follow-up albums “Future Memories” and “Distant Earth” followed the typical format: strong singles and 4-5 showpieces, mostly clustered toward the beginning of the tracklist. But he seems to have broken the mold this time by presenting a cluster of 13 extremely strong songs that in isolation could each be considered masterpieces in their own right…any one of the 13 tracks could have been released as singles. Apart from the few instrumental tracks, his extensive use of guest vocals has perhaps created the unintended effect of making his album sound like a compilation disc of sorts. Yet all of the positives (strong beats, infectious vocals, gorgeous tunes) that inflect previous ATB albums are still evident here. I would go so far as to suggest that had this album been released in a vacuum (here meaning as his one and only album), it would be a serious contender for a Grammy.
As an added bonus (for me at least), upon receiving the CD, I opened up the album playbill and was hit with a wave of nostalgia when it opened to an aerial picture of Bangkok’s Sukhumvit Soi 11 district that appears to have been taken from the roof of the building adjacent to the very tower I lived in for 3 years (24th floor). That picture could have been taken from my former living room. Talk about (unintentional) targeted marketing!

title: Faithful recreations of the 1930s "Quintette" repertoire from a former member
text:
Dave Harris played tenor sax in the Raymond Scott Quintette in the late 1930s, and 20 years later, decided to re-record the band's music himself in high fidelity. There's not a whole lot to say about this album other than the fact that the music is very well played and faithfully recreates the Scott arrangements without attempting to improve or expand them. Scott himself was famously a control freak who did not encourage improvisation or group member input with the Quintette, and the compositions themselves are little clockwork masterpieces that deserve to be played as written. This was the first recreation of the music in the age of high fidelity recording. Amost 40 years later, during the 1990s Scott revival, these arrangements were recorded by the Dutch band The Beau Hunks, and 6 of them turned up on Don Byron's "Bug Music" album as well. To my ears, there are no clear losers--if you can afford to buy them all, do, because each has its strengths. The Beau Hunks recorded 33 small-group Scott tunes, so they win on breadth of material. Byron's recordings are very faithful to the originals, despite being played by a group of "downtown" NYC jazz wizards who mostly spent their time on more post-modern endeavors. If Byron had recorded 15 or 30 Quintette pieces with his Bug Music band, they'd probably be my main listening choice for modern recreations of the Quintette. But Byron only did 6 of the better-known tunes. Harris gives us 12 tunes with the right feel, and therefore a worthwhile album.

If I were going to introduce Scott's Quintette music to a young person (say a school-band music geek) who wasn't accustomed to the sound of 78-rpm recordings, I might actually send them to this album rather than Scott's original recordings. Otherwise, the first stop for anyone new to Raymond Scott should probably be the 1990s Sony/Columbia compilation "Reckless Nights and Turkish Twilights". It's got all the original versions of this timeless music.

title: Living Well Is the Best Revenge
text:
Although the Muffs were lumped into the "riot grrrl/kinderwhore" movement of the 1990s, Kim Shattuck's consistently masterful pop songwriting always lifted her trio to a higher status in my mind. And while Courtney Love's loud public antics have garnered more tabloid inches in the ensuing years, Shattuck has (somewhat quietly) given us better music.

Whoop Dee Woo (the band's first album in a decade) comes close to rivaling the Muffs' mid-90s masterstroke Blonder and Blonder, which is great news for us fans. Not just because the music is so damn good, but because it's terribly satisfying to see Kim rebound so gloriously from her short stint in the Pixies (which ended in a rather tactless termination notice via the band's manager). Living well is the best revenge, as they say, and Kim - plus bassist Ronnie Barnett and drummer Roy McDonald-Drums (both long-serving Muffs) kick off the event with "Weird Boy Next Door", which combines the band's patented garage-band snarl with Kim's absolutely ingenious melodic mastery.

As the album progresses, the rewards keep coming, even as the band never stray from the sonic template established decades ago. Their style is so well conceived, and the tunes so well executed, you just don't mind that the approach is somewhat formulaic. The fact is that very few bands can wrap almost labyrinthine but ultimately sing-song (scream-song?) melodies over thrashing garage-punk riffs like they do in "Where Did I Go Wrong". And there is a lighthearted, almost adolescent joyfulness to everything they do that is so endearing, it's almost impossible to reconcile the music with people in their 50s.

It's just wonderful to have the Muffs back.

title: The Red Letters Project ~ Electrifying!
text:
I received The Red Letters Project, a 3 CD set of the words of Christ from the Gospel of Matthew, for review from Tyndale. Produced by entertainment-industry legend Russ Regan, a committed Christian who envisions this as his legacy project, this set is a must hear!

The idea behind The Red Letters Project is to give the listener a unique experience in hearing the words of Jesus. While the words He spoke are read or sung, the listener also experiences amazing musical tracks (there are 40 in all) along with the narration/singing. This set is absolutely electric! I was blown away by the fast paced, at times hip-hop rocking music, that left me listening to the wise words of Jesus while tapping my feet or jamming out in the car in traffic. Who knew His words could be so thrillingly presented? I suspect The Red Letters Project is geared to the younger crowd because the music and tracks are at times hard thumping rhythm and fast moving vocals that really rev you up. I think this is an amazing way to get the word of God into your head in a way that hasn't been explored before.

I LOVED this CD set!!! I would highly recommend this set for anyone who loves their music a bit faster/harder and also yearns to have their mind filled with the words of Christ. This set would make a perfect gift for a teen or college student too. I was really amazed by how the music and singing/narration were put together so well, and I think this is the start of something wonderful if more books of the Gospel are done in this format. This is truly a new way to HEAR the words of Jesus! I not only recommend this set to any Christian who loves music, but I can't imagine any musical library comlete without it! Beautifully done!

Note: I received a free copy of The Red Letters Project for review from Tyndale House Publishing. I was asked for my honest opinion in the review and was not required or asked to give a favorable review.

title: The Best Darn Thing since 2004
text:
I fell in love with "Complicated" when I was 18 years old in the spring of 2002. I listened to samples of LET GO, the then-upcoming debut CD which the song was from, via the 'net and for some reason that I can't quite comprehend, felt the other songs weren't worth squat and figured it was one of those CDs where there was one good song with 10 songs that were recorded to give the album the appearance of having a reason for its $15 price tag when a CD single with a $5 price tag would have sufficed for the consumer. Then in the fall of that year I heard "Sk8er Boi" and liked it a lot, looked over the album again, online, and was like "my God, I need to buy this! What's wrong with me???!" I spent the rest of the fall listening to the CD extensively, and then, after enjoying the CD which I paid $17 for when you factor the taxman, sold it to the very store I bought it from for $1. I'm insane, OK? Let's not make a big deal of it.

So then a couple years later she's got UNDER MY SKIN. Good CD, doesn't capture the magic of my 18 year old self listening to LET GO in fall of 2002, but it ain't bad. "Take Me Away" and "Together" were the big highlights for me, the rest of the album was very listenable tho.

Her third CD kinda threw me off in the fact that it lacked all of the introspection of her first two CDs. I learned to appreciate it for what it is, but nowadays, I find the production to be too muffled. If the music itself weren't so shallow, it wouldn't be that big of a deal. The Get Up Kids' SOMETHING TO WRITE HOME ABOUT had bad production values, but was a very memorable experience b/c of the music. But THE BEST DAAA THING didn't have the best songwriting or expressionism, so the songs sounding like they were recorded from the inside of a cardboard box sitting in the midst of a busy street is not something I go back to listen to often at all.

Her follow up to that lackluster effort, titled GOODBYE LULLABY, was supposedly a deeper and more introspective Avril Lavigne, and I felt the songs were lacking in originality for one thing, and secondly, the songs were very somber, and, again, the production!: very muddy sounding. I swear I could hear this kind of "swoosh" in the background, like the album cover - featuring a piano stationed in a swamp w/ Avril sitting atop it - was not just an emotive image, but a warning: "this album sounds like swamp water!".

This song reminds me of LET GO, personally. It's got the hooks, it's got the emotion, it's got the live-like-u-were-dying attitude of THE BEST DAMN THING and the freshness that should have been found on GOODBYE LULLABY. It's a great song. I'm not a big fan of her first single from her upcoming full length, but it's not too shabby either. It too is better than the songs on GOODBYE LULLABY and the production is superior to that of THE BEST DAMN THING. I might pre-order her self titled upcoming full length. I'm like dirt poor so chances are I won't, but I'll just have to see where the wind blows my money (haha).

title: Some wonderful early Elgar
text:
The Dream of Gerontius was Elgar's first oratorio, though he had written cantatas earlier. The text is based on a poem by Cardinal John Henry Newman who was an English mid-19th century convert to Catholicism. This performance has tenor Anthony Rolfe-Johnson as Gerontius, mezzo-soprano Catherine Wyn-Rogers as the Angel and the bass Michael George as the Priest. The soloists are backed by the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Vernon Handley. Which version of `The Dream' you want to live with is very much an individual choice, usually depending on the soloists. I have lived happily with this version for a couple of decades. My second choice would be the version by Sir John Barbirolli wit the Halle Orchestra and Richard Lewis, Janet Baker and Kim Borg as soloists.

Elgar's Organ Sonata is an early work, composed even before the Enigma Variations: he was a competent organist himself and could also play several other instruments. I have heard this work too in its original form. Much as I like the sound of the organ, the texture, perhaps not surprisingly, sounds much more like the Elgar I know and love in this orchestrated arrangement by composer Gordon Jacob, who worked on the piece on the recommendation of Sir Adrian Boult. Indeed, it could be taken as Elgar's Zeroth Symphony, like Bruckner's. On the other hand, there are some more modern touches of orchestration so it sounds more like it could also be regarded as `Elgar's 3rd Symphony' were it not for the reconstructed version of the actual 3rd by Anthony Payne.

The orchestrated Organ Sonata received its first performance in 1947 by Boult with the BBC Symphony Orchestra. Here, this fine work is played on the CD in this original recording by the Royal Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Vernon Handley. For purists who object to this arrangement let us not forget that Elgar himself made orchestral transcriptions of several well-known works by Bach, Handel and Chopin. For those who know the organ sonata in its original form but have not heard this orchestrated version I would unreservedly recommend it.

title: For Boston
text:
Steely Dan live in Boston way back in 2009 when we were all much younger.
Fagen and Becker with whomever they are playing with are Steely Dan and with the homefield advantage they put on a great show. This radio broadcast finds our heroes in Boston on 22 July 2009 with an invited a special guest to play and sing with the band as well. With "Aja" and "The Royal Scam played in their entirety it was indeed a event for the Danfans.

This is a large band with Donald and Walter surrounded by plenty of support players to play the hits and the album tracks note perfect as you would expect them to sound. And (dig this!) sometimes the band extends a solo and pulls out a cover song ("Dirty Water") that makes it all bigger and better. This is one of the better bootlegs you are gonna find out there right now and for a broadcast show it sounds pretty good. With a equalizer you bring up everything from the flat middle where it was recorded at. There are 26 tracks and 140 minutes of fine ol' live Steely Dan on these two CD's and if you like these guys you will really enjoy this collection.

title: Great performance with Average Sonics
text:
The two stars are not for the performance, which is solidly majestic and no doubt well-known to Klemperer's many admirers. The two stars are for the sonics, which despite the claim to be "SACD" were - at least in the copy I received - a conventional Japanese CD pressing which sounded very similar and not superior to the EMI Great Performances pressing of the late 90's. I am told that a true SACD hybrid pressing with significantly improved sonics is now available, but advise interested buyers first contact the distributor to verify. All SACDs have the SONY trademark for "SACD DSD" on both the CD label and its cover.

addendum: I've just received and previewed the true SACD-hybrid DSD-transferred version of this performance. It is a noticeable if not to my ears quite a dramatic improvement over all past CD pressings of this performance I've heard. The improvements are most notable in an expanded sound "picture" of the chorus, along with more accurate timbers of the vocal artists and instrumental soloists (although more about below). It remains a dense sonic picture, however, with (again to my ears) weak projection of bass lines (cello, double base, horn) and also for some reason the bass soloist, Martti Tavela, who almost always comes across as under-miked. The vocal soloists also seem to be placed back too far into the orchestral and choral fabric and so don't seem to project as in other recordings of this wonderful work. Still, the SACD is likely to be the best this famous recording will ever sound..so if it shows up on Amazon..go for it. If not. try CD-Japan.com.

title: A lost treasure
text:
"Marinka" is based on the Mayerling incident (the 1889 murder-suicide -- if it /was/ a murder-suicide -- of Crown Prince Rudolph of Austria-Hungary and Baroness Mary Vetsera, his 17-year-old mistress), which you'd think would be unpromising material for a musical -- but Frank Wildhorn has a new show based on the same story, so who's to say? This 1945 version at least provides a happy ending; I don't know about Wildhorn's.

Emmerich Kálmán was probably the greatest operetta composer of the 20th century. He had his greatest hits in the teens and twenties, but might well have had more if he had not been a Jew living in Austria. As a celebrity, he was, unlike many other Jews, permitted entry into the United States, where he spent the forties. After his nearly finished "Miss Underground", a musical about the French Resistance, had to be abandoned when the lyricist, Lorenz Hart (yes, /that/ Lorenz Hart) died, he turned to "Marinka". The show had a respectable run, although some reviewers thought it was in bad taste to do a show about Austria so soon after the war.

There is no original cast album (something that in 1945 had only recently been invented). This recording, the first, apart from a few songs recorded separately, was made recently by the Operetta Foundation. Many roles are doubled, and the orchestra is replaced by two pianos. Some dialog is included, but not enough to follow the plot without the liner notes.

In some ways, this recording ended up as a trial run of the Ohio Light Opera production of summer, 2008. That version is expected to be released in a year or two on a DVD, but you might want to get this one, anyway. The OLO version had much of the book rewritten, and one song got a massive rewriting in the name of political correctness. On the other hand, the OLO has an orchestra. Anyway, at the time of writing, this CD is the only version available.

title: This release has received too much hype. Read before buying.
text:
I read several reviews about this release and since it was universally praised and I am such a Stevie Wonder fan, I looked and looked until I found it. Some reviewers even allege that some of the versions on this release are better than those sung by Mr. Wonder. Tall order, but I just think Stevie walks on water so I bit the bullet and all in all I am disappointed.
THE NOT SO GOOD: The disappointment comes not only from the hype but that for the most part the songs are either too loungy or, with some notable exceptions, combines it with sappy blaxploitation clichés that are stripped of Stevie's unique energy. I am all for reinterpretation of songs and listening to new things, but this is mediocre at best. The same reviews that praised this release go on to say that one of its positive attributes is that it shows one how influential and inspirational Stevie was to so many singers around him. Duh!!! No need to spend cash on an import release to learn this. Ray Barretto butchers Stevie's "Pastime Paradise" although it has a great piano riff that won't quit. The Supreme's version of "Bead Weather" starts a little too close for comfort to an Al Green song, and then degenerates into a bad sounding young Michael Jackson. No harmonies or anything that resembles the Supremes. Cedar Walton's "Another Star" sounds like the ultimate filler. The CD ends with Ramsey Lewis' jazzy but totally flaccid take on "Spring High."
THE ALMOST GOOD: I don't want to give the impression that this collection sucks in its entirety as Jose Feliciano does a GOOD job with "Golden Lady" and Sergio Mendes and Brasil '77 bring a soft touch to "Superstition" that totally changes the song into something aurally interesting. I also liked the instrumentals on Charles Earland's "I Was Made To Love Her" but without vocals the song loses its punch. Hugo Montenegro's "You Got It Bad Girl" is yet another instrumental but has some cool production work that somehow captures Stevie's essence and almost overcomes the lack of lyrics. Carl Anderson's "Buttercup" barely overcomes its quiet storm feel with some nice vocals but it still feels phoned in.
THE GOOD/GREAT: My favorite cut on the CD is Main Ingredient's "Don't You Worry About A Thing" as it takes the song at face value and although it's not Stevie, it does sound great. Gene Harris' version of "As" is quite good and almost sounds like Stevie (as does Norman Brown's "Too High"), but sounds a little derivative and not anywhere as good as the most recent cover by Mary J. Blige and George Michael, who really do it justice by bringing something new. First Choice's "Love Having You Around" at least brings some LIFE to the song and deserves to be congratulated for that versus others in this collection. I am a HUGE Minnie Riperton fan and I really wanted to like her take on "Stick Together," and it's actually surprisingly good as she makes it her own and she sounds so alive. The piano on this cut is awesome.
Any potential buyer should know that this package comes with two "versions" with the first cd mixing all the songs into a non-stop mix, while the second cd segregates the songs. I actually found mixed version marginally more appealing as it makes for good background music. It's very hard to give this release a rating as Stevie usually earns 5+ stars from me but this "celebration" gets a generous 2 from me.

Loved listening to this book on long drives -- felt like I had taken a trip into the past without having to endure the famines, floggings, or poor sanitation!
The speaker balances a palpable enthusiasm for the ancient world with plain speech about about its barbarity and prejudices, particularly the life of the disabled and poor.By focusing on the lives of the ordinary people he has stripped away much of the glamour that modern-day revisionists ascribe to ancient civilizations. For example, he discusses the great accomplishments of Greek culture while laying bare the deep-rooted misogyny and unreflecting reliance on slavery. He highlights the toughness, organization and civic-mindedness of the Romans without shrinking from their brutality.
This balance continues in every vignette, mixing affection and admiration with plain descriptions of misery and social caste and crippling tradition.
Perhaps my favorite chapters were on the Romans in Britain, where he juxtaposes the many achievements of the Romans (baths! roads! aqueducts!) with the lot of the Roman solider forced to serve in this outpost, and quotes from Auden's poem Roman Wall Blues.

title: Incomprehensible
text:
Bernd Alois Zimmermann was one of the greatest composers after the Second Viennese School. His masterpiece is rightly regarded to be "Die Soldaten," possibly the most complex opera ever produced. In fact, the work premièred in 1965 was the "simplified" version, the withdrawn original having been declared impossible to perform.
At first glace, Zimmermann, whose dodecaphonic scores erupt with horrifying Expressionistic fury, would have little in common with the elegant Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, but both, in effect, wrote their own Requiems. Zimmermann's last large-scale work was his "Requiem für einen jungen Dichter," a "Lingual" (linguistic piece) for massive forces, which incorporated texts from various sources, including Pope St John XXIII (an allocution to the German public, delivered in Latin on the last day of his life), James Joyce, Æschylus, and Adolf Hitler. The intellectual and artistic complexity of this work are staggering.
Musically, the apocalyptic score even incorporates a few seconds of a "pop" song by the Beatles (representing our anti-intellectual crass commercialism) and a few bars of jazz (representing our degradation), but in toto the effect is like that of a volcanic eruption, sweeping all before the fury of its cataclysm.
This 2005 "live" recording from The Netherlands is stupendous. Bernhard Kontarsky (who leads the definitive Teldec recording of "Die Soldaten," with Nancy Shade as Marie) conducts, proving his great talent with these difficult scores, the inestimable Claudia Barainsky and David Pittman-Jennings are the vocal soloists, with Jan Hage at the organ. The Dutch Catholic Radio Broadcasting Organisation (KRO) was involved in the production, which Cybele Records published in 2008. In 2019, Gramophone described this recording as, “An unsettling scream of an anti-war work.”
The "Requiem für einen jungen Dichter" was first performed in 1969, and the following year Zimmermann was, at the age of fifty-two, a victim of suicide while at work on his second opera, "Medea," après Hans Henny Jahnn. Requiescat in pace.

title: Like some prisoner’s last words
text:
“IT IS FINISHED,” John said as he fled to Prague, exhausted, spent.

Like some prisoner’s last words, this phrase rings in the collective cultural ether, an ephemeral epitaph on the tomb of a now-dead era. I could not be more thankful.

The passing of the Tape-beatles marks a final indignation, the last gasp of our society to preserve what it once fetishized as a privileged cultural activity, the making of “music.” Finally, we might let go of this deadening apportionment of our creative efforts. While its demise has been obvious for decades, it has taken the pitiful efforts of the frauds known as the Tape-beatles to generate the necessary outrage to accept the end of a precious, and ultimately duplicitous, endeavor.

Let us be clear: The Tape-beatles were not alone. They are the final step in a history of cultural treachery that spans the 20th century. From Stravinsky to Beck, we have been taken. There have been efforts to remedy this situation. This century is littered with names like Duchamp, Henri, Cage, Russolo, and The Sex Pistols. Some were genuinely radical, others merely brutal. Yet, all these individuals still desperately clung to the “idea” of music, as if some archetypal structure, some “Platonic Form,” guided their nearly unconscious endeavors. And it was, in the end, the Tape-beatles who wrote the final movement in what has become a prison, gilded by some of the most brilliant minds in our history.

In claiming to compose music with previously-constructed sounds, the Tape-beatles merely demonstrated the ultimate poverty of the modern Western musical lexicon. Why must it have been “music” that was made with “sound”? Such a question could never have been broached by these self-admitted cultural embezzlers. For it was not merely content they pilfered, but the whole of Western musical form. And this baroque crutch of musical history served them well. Able to pass off seemingly revolutionary notions such as Plagiarism®, guised in the sanitized, easily swallowed pill of musical structure, they arrived at a certain plateau of fame, experts in the intellectual currency of a clever elite. In this way they deflected any real criticism of their practice. The form, and even the content, were all part of a received language, constructed as a closed cultural syllogism which had already long since been discarded by anyone with aspirations to being genuinely radical.

But music is one of the greatest forms of artistic expression, you say. Listen to the Beethovens, the Mozarts, the Bachs. Western culture is rife with examples of such musical brilliance. How can we turn our backs on it now? What would be left? Yes, but what is left of music? Music can no longer serve as genuine expression in a society where its form has been so thoroughly co-opted in service of the market. When “The Revolution Will Not Be Televised” now advertises tennis shoes, when the once immediate, historically rich form of rap so completely pervades commercial media, when classical music can only pander to the classist sensibilities of a moneyed elite, and jazz sells luxury cars, what is left? Just the hollow carcass of a once socially important expression of collective and personal experience. To even attempt to reclaim music is only to force its decaying remains into a kind of empty nostalgia for a lost unity. This language has been devoured by spectacular consumption. Mourn it. Bid it farewell. But do not assert any radical intents by resurrecting its ghosts. The necrophiles of the Corporate Western Empire have beat you to its grave.

Yes, the Tape-beatles, at best, could only redigest the market-based sentiments, the corporate fantasies, of a popular media electronically extruded into our lives. They are consumers consuming the consumed, like a starving man forced to use his own body for food. What nurturing substance music may have once offered has been long since stripped away so it might serve as a convenient receptacle for a corporately-defined affect, an emotional identity apart from ourselves, we now desire to possess.

title: One of the really great 6th`s on record.
text:
Joseph Keilberth was a great conductor and a really great Bruckner interpreter.
He always was in particular connection with the 6th symphony, recording it three
times, at least. Here in Berlin he did a splendid and definitive performance of
the work. Keilberth is not as broad in his approach to the work as one might have hoped, especially in the slow movement, and the recording, though excellently clear, is rather on the dry side, but still enough satisfying than it seemed at first-beautifully brought off. The first movement, with a wonderful brass playing, is one of the best on record and the Scherzo and Finale are also splendidly delivered. I wonder why this recording isn`t more appreciated or mentioned by
so-called Bruckner specialists and reviewers, since it`s one of the best on
record and deserves a high place in the Pantheon of B6`s. An essential.
