title: Exquisite retrospective
text:
Subtitled 1982-2002, 20 Years of Acoustic Music, Harvey Reid's latest release is a magnificent overview of a life spent exploring plucked-string magic. The 40 selections on this two-disc set are precisely divided between instrumentals (disc 1) and songs (disc 2). Some tracks are compiled from earlier albums, while others are previously unreleased. Playing various combinations of 6- and 12-string guitar, slide, autoharp, bouzouki, mandolin, mandocello, 6-string banjo, and lap steel, Reid is captivating on three levels: First, his relaxed, yet articulate technique allows him to make even the most challenging pieces sound graceful and dynamic. Second, his tone is unfailingly ripe and ringing. Finally, his repertoire is vast: This album contains fiddle tunes, Civil War songs, gospel hymns and spirituals, ragtime fingerpicking, bluegrass flatpicking, traditional Appalachian and Celtic ballads, country blues, and even a Bach minuet.

Detail freaks will dig how Reid lists the instruments, tunings, and picking techniques he uses for each track, as well as when and where it was recorded. Best of all, there are numerous examples of Reid's partial capo innovations (including his multiple and "minus" capo techniques, which he explains in the liner notes). Exquisite sounds from a masterful picker.

title: Attempts at Third Stream with some elevator music thrown in for good (?) measure.
text:
This collection of musical oddities is a bit of a letdown, mostly on musical grounds, and partly because of the rather heavy remastering that I do not usually associate with productions from this source.
But first to the music. Incredibly, given his acidulous writing on Raymond Scott and John Kirby, renowned jazz writer Gunther Schuller calls the music on display here "delightful vignettes". Why he writes off Kirby, who at least swung most of the time and gave lots of room for improvisation, accusing him of redundancy, while he seems to forgive Wilder the same sin is beyond me. (Well, not quite: Schuller took part in one of the later recording sessions that make up part of CD 2 in the set....)
The titles are rhythmically clunky, melodically unmemorable and fail to engage at least this listener. There is hardly any jazz content, there are no improvisations. Sure, some of the harmonies are daring, the instrumentation is unique, and the music is well played, but soon redundancy sets in. The liner notes contain a telling quote from an unnamed contemporary Down Beat reviewer: "It's all very well for a while, but you wish along about the fifth tune that someone woul come in with a tailgate trombone and break things up." My sentiments exactly.
The second CD moves to 1945 with some semi-concert pieces that find Frank Sinatra at the helm of the Columbia Chamber Orchestra. They sound like Artie Shaw's Frenesi band without the beat. The same goes for the Percy Faith titles, which out-Mantovani Mantovani. Interestingly they feature record company executive Mitch Miller on oboe.
The octet sides are quite heavily noise-suppressed and, although not unlistenable, are a bit of a surprise coming from HEP.
Not an essential purchase, and to counter the two effusive reviews I'll give it two stars.

title: The weakest of the triology
text:
After the HT came up with a surprisingly cohesive and interesting release "Kill the King", what could they (or more likely "he") do next?

While there are some interesting moments in this release, the biggest flaw is that things move far too slowly. Sounds will continue unchanged literally for minutes and it's usually the least interesting ones that go on too long. There are also a few too many of the usual tricks that HT loves (sudden silence, sudden switches, slow deconstruction).

Since ambient recording often rely on surprise, I strongly recommend that if you intend to purchase this that you stop reading here since the following WILL CONTAIN SPOILERS.

The first cut "Bull Baiting" (and some other titles but no marks where they begin or end) starts off with a hum that will exercise your subwoofer. And it continues unchanged for almost two minutes! At last some swooshing sounds shoot past us along with a quick yet irritating electronic noise. Just as we hear some interesting distorted speech in the background, we also hear some high pitched whistles that are as irritating as the hum which go on for minutes. I found absolutely nothing interesting in this one.

After eleven long minutes of that I guess we're onto "Empty Rooms and Their Occupants" featuring a wonderful wall of swirling buzzing and what sounds like a room of hundreds of tuned percussive instruments lightly pounded. Barely audible sounds fade in and out and it sounds like certain instruments slowly dominate and recede. The buzzing stops and the barely audible sounds are clearer. It's a mix of percussive and sustained sounds. The percussive sounds fade but the sustained ones remain and a new more threatening distorted sound fades in. We then slowly flow through several unremarkable scenes which is more like trace music than ambient music -- nothing really stands out. It ends however with a great build up of what may be highly echoed voices mixed with long sustained notes... then HT's trick of pulling the plug. A moment of silence later we hear a field recording of voices quietly chanting in a strange language while slow drones rumble around them. It's great that HT was able to make a long piece that truly flowed together instead of a series of mismatched random scenes but it simply went on too long with no memorable moments.

Then the CD gets silly with no less than 32 untitled short parts lasting one to five seconds each. The series begins with some very creepy hurricane wind-like noise. "Untitled 17" changes the tone a little bit while the harsh grinding sounds of "Untitled 19" sets up the beginning of the final piece, "Untitled 33" which is more harsh noise.

Almost two minutes into "33" it gets quiet and we hear tones and hums in the foreground. In the background we hear something with a slight shreaking sound which sounds almost like strange creatures are talking or maybe laughing. It's strangely unsettling and one of the best moments. This continues with the voice-like sounds getting buried in louder distorted tones, then suddenly the tones vanish quickly followed by the voices.

"33" then has a field recording (very real human voices and car horns are audible as well as church bells). Some rustling suggests that we're moving. That ends and after a second of a siren, we hear several slowly rising and falling tones. Unfortunately it's no more interesting that that. Also two more times the recording cuts out which sounds more flaws in the master than an intended effect. While there are some quiet noises in the background, this was a waste.

Now we have another field recording and it's a mystery where we are. There's a low rumbling (probably not in the original recording) and possibly the sound of a large body of water. We are then attacked by what might be a subway train. The humming continues and we have a sound that would make an excellent ring tone (similar to the ring modulator effect on analog synthesizers). The humming fades and more ring tones appear.

It ends with what's unfortunately the most memorable cut. The only sound is a "laugh box", an old toy with a thin scratchy recording of an irritating belly laugh. It gets the HT treatment with a dozen overdubs at various speed until we have a chorus of annoying laughter. There's nothing subtle or clever about it.

title: great set
text:
I purchased this via Amazon France the price was cheapest at that moment or seemed to be, doesn't matter since the item appears isposted from Korea!

This box appears to be a set designed for the Korean market, Korean translations are everywhere but not visible so inot "weird".

I was initially critical of its presentation, the box was extremely tight at first, tight enough to be a problem. It has loosened up without tearing so that is good. Another review on Amazon Germany mentioned precisely the same problem!

The individual discs are stored in as-nice-as-can-be replicas of the original jackets. I cannot comment on how closely the discs parallel the original issues or the masters used. The sound in all cases sounds as fine as is possible, is all I can say.

Milstein is interesting, largely forgotten by the general public (all it remembers is "Heifetz"), but on the evidence of this box, he had with Heifetz and Perlman, the largest stable of successful recordings of any violinist. The only other large box set of a violinist is Menuhin's, which is a compendium of many sources not just studio recordings and not just successful ones from his artistic peak. There may have been a Stern set at one time but it is no longer available. There has been no set that includes all or most of Oistrakh's recordings though he cries out for one

In contrast, this box doesn't have any discernable "stage" showing decline or even development. Every recording is perfect from any perspective. Progressive recordings of various great works may improve in aspects of their engineering but Milstein's playing is consistently stunning, beyond stunning.

I PERSONALLY find Mistein to be the "anti-Heifetz", an Auer pupil who preserved a warmth and sense of style his fellow student Mischa Elman had, and which Heifetz seems to have consciously purged his playing of. I have heard many recordings of Milstein, the ones that first captured my attention were his Columbias of baroque pieces. His adoption of those pieces in his repertoire was a big deal at the time and I find the same emotional depth in them that I would expect from a student of Enescu (for example) like Haendel. They are not included in this set but his virtues didn't change or diminish.

If you accept my characterization of Milstein Heifetz and Perlman as the only violinists with large "name-brand" sets devoted to their work, Milstein's box is an easy and mandatory choice, especially for people like myself who can't take Heifetz.

Getting past the easy characterization of Milstein as "immortal", and drilling down to details, I was struck how beautifully he played different styles of music, even across the great concertos, Tchaikovsky, Brahms, Beethoven, etc. Each sounds so "right" to me there isn't a moment when I longed to hear another favorite player. The same goes for the second tier concertos like the Saint-Saens.

I have to say, I did not expect to enjoy this set as much as I did, I bought it because I thought it was "required listening". A lovely set. It probably will become with the Callas "red box" and Horowitz Original Jacket, one of my most treasured boxed sets.

title: Amazing score for a 60's horror film, complements Vincent Price perfectly
text:
When I first saw 'House of Usher' on TV in the early 80s, I must have been about 10-11 years old. After finding it on DVD and seeing it again my interest in this Vincent Price/Roger Corman masterpiece was rekindled, and with it the interest in Les Baxter's eerily romantic soundtrack.

The score is a solid one for a 60's horror movie; Baxter makes good use of several orchestral elements to create a creepy atmosphere that surrounds the House of Usher and its owner, Roderick Usher (Vincent Price). Themes for both Roderick Usher & his sister, Madeline (Myrna Fahey) are both presented here. Some tracks, such as 'House of Evil', 'Buried Alive', and the final track, 'Fall of the House of Usher' make great use of a choral element that seems to simulate creepy, wailing ghostly voices (certainly appropriate given the mansion's history & the events going on in the movie - Madeline had escaped her premature burial & attacked Roderick Usher).

Like Brent says, RUN - do not walk - to get this soundtrack. It's a very limited release so it is becoming difficult to get, however it's well worth it.

title: "Please Set the Transporter for the 1970s, Scotty!"
text:
I am an old-time musician and contemporary of many of the musicians in the original "Fat City String Band" (Berkeley) which evolved into the Highwoods String Band. Three albums were produced on the Rounder Label.

The announcement LIVE! brings back many memories for me. I would think that anyone who saw this band perform during its relatively short heyday will find magic here. Initially thought of as a revival of the Georgia twin-fiddle string bands of the 1920s and 1930s, the Highwoods Stringband (as written on the cover) was much more than that. The instrumentation was similar, but the aura and energy traveled far when Walt Koken and Bob Potts cranked up their fiddles. Koken is also known as a brilliant old-time clawhammer banjo virtuoso in his own right.

I have sought ANY film of this band in performance. If any reader knows of such a recording, please contact me through [ ... ] !

Watch the effect of this music on your children! Then, feel it yourself. There is nothing I've experienced that is closer to the joy of performing and interacting with the audience than this special group of musicians!

If you are looking for familiar tunes to jostle old memories, go elsewhere. These groups may be familiar, but the songs are not their old recordings. Here's the story:

In the mid 80s, Marty Pekar produced seven Doo Wop albums for Epic under a subsidiary name, Ambient Records. He rounded up the best, still-performing, vocal groups from the 50s and 60s and recorded new music in the exact style of their original hits. The goal was not to produce new hits, but to revitalize a musical style that was his personal favorite, and perhaps introduce a younger generation to this great genre.

The Capris, whose "There's a Moon Out Tonight" was a hit in 1958, actually charted with "Morse Code of Love" in 1983. The song was covered by the Manhattan Transfer in 1985. This song is so perfectly 50s, it's hard to believe it was recorded in the 80s.

For this CD, Marty picked 27 tracks from the original 84 on those seven vinyl albums.

title: Ozzy's Live....and He's Loud
text: There's no shortage of live Ozzy material, but that makes sense, as he's been known since the '70's to be one of the most entertaining singers that have ever hit the stage. This was the third official live CD, following "Speak of the Devil" and "Tribute." There was also a live "Ultimate Sin" home video and the "Just Say Ozzy" EP before "Live and Loud." This release came after the "No More Tears" album and tour, so it features five songs from that period- "I Don't Want to Change the World," "Desire," "Road to Nowhere," "No More Tears," "and "Mama, I'm Coming Home." It has the Sabbath tunes "Parnoid," "War Pigs," "Black Sabbath," and "Changes." "Black Sabbath" has all four original members of the band playing from Ozzy's farewell show (short-lived farewell that it was). From the Randy Rhoads era, you get "Mr. Crowley," "I Don't Know," "Flying High Again," "Suicide Solution," "Goodbye to Romance," and "Crazy Train." It has two Jake E. Lee songs, "Shot in the Dark" and "Bark at the Moon." And finally, there's one song from "No Rest for the Wicked," "Miracle Man." It also has a fantastic 24-page booklet full of pictures from the "No More Tours" trek and lengthy liner notes. This is a great collection of live performances from the glory years of Ozzy's time with Zakk Wylde, and on of the many great live albums from the Ozz-man. If you're especially a fan of the "No More Tears" period of Ozzy, you should love "Live and Loud."

title: Excellent Multi-Channel SACD Sound
text:
Of course any Guess Who fan already owns both of these albums and many if not most would consider them their two best as I do. The opportunity to hear a high resolution 4 channel quad mix was the impetus for me to buy this rather expensive 2'fer CD.

I remember back in the day owning a couple quad vinyl albums including one from the Guess Who. Since I didn't have a system that would actually play quad vinyl it was pretty useless at the time. Today I have a system that plays all SACD/DSD formats and am extremely happy to actually find a new worthwhile product to buy that utilizes that format.

This is my first purchase of a quad CD and I must say I'm very impressed. I was able to tweak my system to get a nice balanced quad sound that literally makes this music come alive for me like I've never heard before. Before playing this CD I was under the impression I might not be too impressed by the bass sound. I was wrong. Using my Yamaha receiver settings and my modest Yamaha 12 inch subwoofer, I was able to dial up a nice balance of bass with the 4 channel audio mix.

There are other quad CD's available including some additional Guess Who albums. Unfortunately, the pairing of the two albums on each CD is not quite as impressive as the pairing of the iconic American Woman and Share The Land albums. In most cases, the pairing includes one really good Guess Who CD with one not so good (at least in my opinion). That said, I might still explore some of the others as even getting one really good Guess Who album per CD might still be worth it to hear these quad mixes.

title: Very original epic, atmospheric metal with doom-ish moments, keys, flute and angelic background vox
text:
Released in 1989, TALES OF DARKNESS & LIGHT is the debut album of Montreal’s Thunder Rider. The album initially featured six songs running just shy of half an hour, which was actually longer than Slayer’s REIGN IN BLOOD (considered a “full-length” release). TALES OF DARKNESS & LIGHT was re-released in 1997 with two more tracks (“For Christ’s Sake” and “Preacher”), which upped the runtime to a more officially full-length 38:29.

The group only released one more album in 2002, TALES OF DARKNESS & LIGHT, CHAPTER II, which was tantamount to a double album, clocking in at a few minutes over an hour. Both albums are of similar quality content-wise, although – to be expected – CHAPTER II has slightly better production. Yet the production on this one is quite good, all things considered. It’s just that the vocals are a little too upfront in the mix and the guitars could be up a tad higher. Personally, I don’t have a problem with the production.

The band gets extra points for originality. Their style is epic, ethereal metal with doom-ish moments. Their singer has a nasally, almost monotone bellow, which fits well with the music, but he’s definitely an acquired taste. Solos could very well be by a flute or keyboard, as much as a guitar. They have elements of Jethro Tull, 70’s Deep Purple/Rainbow, Styx (think “Castle Walls”), Warlord, Lordian Guard, Cirith Ungol, Manilla Road, Manowar (but without the extra cheese), RUN TO THE LIGHT-era Trouble and Viking-era Bathory. The music’s moody and mid-paced to slow, so don’t expect much (if any) intense jamming. To be expected, their lyrical themes revolve around stories of good and evil with a biblical emphasis, but not always, e.g. the Native American tribute “Rain Dance.”

The best song IMHO is the 8-minute “Galaxy,” which is atmospheric and genuinely moving with moments of nigh-profound awe. “For Christ’s Sake” is just catchy, “Death to Death” is akin to ’87 Trouble, as noted above, but with a totally different vocal style. The quirky and offbeat “Preacher” is more dynamic than most of the other songs while the aforementioned “Rain Dance” stands out due to its notable Indian-ish ambiance.

GRADE: B+

title: Magical performances of J.S. Bach's violin sonatas.

In these recordings from 1979 and 1981, violinist Arthur Grumiaux and harpsichordist Christiane Jaccottet combine to play each of Johann Sebastian Bach's ten violin sonatas with incomparable artistry. Their musicianship exudes tremendous warmth and vitality, and the obviously special chemistry between them is in no way diminished by the addition of cellist Philippe Mermoud in Sonatas BWV 1021 and BWV 1023. "Bach: Complete Violin Sonatas" is one of the finest classical music recordings available. It was awarded a Rosette, and was also recognized as a Key Recording, in the "Penguin Guide to Recorded Classical Music 2009."  This is a very special listening experience. Most highly recommended.

title: When you have the Berlin strings, what's missing? Just small interpretive details
text:
"Serenades"? Not quite. If they were going to avoid Dvorak and include Elgar, Bychkov and Philips might have picked Elgar's Serenade rather than his Introduction and Allegro. And how about Britten's Serenade for soprano or tenor and strings? Barber's isn't a Serenade but the music is so beautiful we shall not be stopped by such petty concerns. And it was a nice idea to include the rarer Italian Serenade of Wolf, although it is not deep fare. Incidentally, this is the same program as the one recorded by Charles Munch with the Boston Symphony Orchestra in 1957 (and already in great stereo), except that Wolf's Serenade substitutes for Barber's Medea ([[ASIN:B00000E6PH String Serenades]]). The Berlin strings are superb, with a great silky tone, and with such an asset to start with, that Bychkov doesn't ultimately turn out great versions hangs on small interpretive details.

For instance the way he opens Tchaikovvsky's Serenade, with a big, solemn, stately "Andante non troppo" introduction in the manner of Karajan (in his second recording from 1980, [[ASIN:B000001G4G Tschaikowsky, Dvorák: Streicherserenaden - String Serenades - Serenades pour cordes]]), arguably more than is good for a serenade and certainly way under the score's metronome mark, although it didn't bother me as much as Karajan's - maybe just because I'm getting used to the approach, since objectively the differences between the two versions are here very slight (the sound is slightly thicker with Karajan though). The Allegro moderato proper unfolds at a leisurely pace and with great lyricism rather than the kind of zest and liveliness brought to it with a brisker tempo by Boult in 1937 ([[ASIN:B00008ERVG Boult's BBC Years (Tchaikovsky: Capriccio Italien Serenade in C; Beethoven: Symphony No. 8; Humperdinck: Hansel and Gretel Overture)]]), Munch or Karajan, but thankfully the light-footedness of the Berlin strings avoids any sense of plodding or dragging. Bychkov's Waltz is OK, if I want to be really nitpicking I could say that it is a bit characterless perhaps - I've heard nobody who grasped the agogics of Tchaikovsky here better than Barbirolli ([[ASIN:B00000DO90 Phoenixa Series- Tchaikovsky: Symphony no 5, Serenade]]), and Boult's brisker tempo again conveys an uncalculated freshness that nobody I've heard has quite equaled. Bychkov conducts a very slow Elegy, slower even than Barbirolli's, and he hardly even accelerates at the "poco più animato" at 1:27; consequently, it looses the movement's "Larghetto elegiaco" character, but it is quite effective nonetheless, wistful to passionately longing. After a hushed and tender intro, his Russian finale doesn't drag but it is far from dashing either and lacks a touch of robustness.

The same lack of robustness in the accents mellows down the introduction of Elgar's Introduction & Allegro and makes it a low-voltage experience - just go to Munch or Barbirolli ([[ASIN:B00003ZKRL Elgar / Vaughan Williams: String Orchestra Works]]) to hear what intensity is here. Bychkov also underplays the constant tempo changes of Elgar, his "a tempo" is taken at the same pace as the "largamente", and the "accel.", "più mosso" and "molto stringendo" hardly register, keeping it all in a steady moderato verging on the sentimental, which it doesn't need to be. The Allegro is fine, with a certain lack of beef in string tone (apparently, in order to allow for the solo string quartet to come out, the Philips engineers deprived the "continuo" string orchestra of some of its bloom) but with a biting fugue.

At 8:02, Bychkov leads a rather flowing Barber Adagio, which I hold in his favor, as it reverts to the earlier interpretive tradition of Munch and Ormandy ([[ASIN:B0000029WJ Bernstein: Candide; Barber: Adagio; other American masterpieces]]) in 1957 (7:40), before Schippers (9:01 in 1965, [[ASIN:B0000029V2 Samuel Barber / Thomas Schippers]]) and Bernstein (9:53 in 1971, [[ASIN:B0000CD5GJ Barber: Adagio for Strings; Violin Concerto / Schuman / Ives / Copland ~ Bernstein / Stern]]) established a more static model - indeed a very beautiful one, but Barber's Adagio doesn't need any milking either. Berlin's string tone is full and gorgeous, and the character is elegiac and longing rather than mourning, and a little short on intensity at the climax: in Barber's Adagio, a climax is intense when the microphones can't quite pick it up and it makes you eardrums vibrate: that is what happens with Toscanini in 1938 (now on [[ASIN:B004YNRHBO Historical Recordings]]), Stokowski in 1957 ([[ASIN:B000FPHFJE Leopold Stokowski Conducts Bartok, Barber, & Schoenberg]]), Schippers and Bernstein.

Playing Wolf's Italian Serenade with a string orchestra is a rarely exercised option, since the composer orchestrated himself his string quartet movement for full orchestra - and so imaginatively, adding a solo viola in the process, that it amounts to an entirely new composition. Bychkov takes a genial and amiable view of the string version; and it is a valid option, although I am not so happy with the way he further slows down the tempo when comes the second theme, at 1:18 - although this is only in conformity with modern interpretive usage. But there was an art of interpretation up until the late 1950s, that seems to have died away with the advent of stereo, by which performers knew that lyricism didn't need to be milked and underlined and made sentimental to fully unfold. Bychkov offers a genial Serenade, but for Italian Serenades full of zest and spirit, go to the old timers (in the orchestral version), like William Steinberg or Adrian Boult, both from 1957 (I'm now out of authorized product links, see comments section). In Philips' recording there's not quite enough stereo separation between first and second violins to differentiate them when they toss the same themes back and forth.

These are not the best versions of each composition that you can get, but again: it hangs on small details. The Berlin strings are gorgeous and the beauty of the music certainly comes through. You can find better, but nobody will be cheated even if they have only these versions in their collection.

title: High Tensions more pop-commercial album.
text:
High Tension is one of those lost '80s Rock/Metal bands you never heard of if you live in the US. Most of their output is some great Riff-Hook type Metal that is up there with some of the best of the '80s. They aren't the best band from that era but I wish they would have had more exposure. I hadn't heard of them until about a year ago. Would have been nice to discover them in the '80s when they first hit the scene. Better late than never I suppose.

Unfortunately '4' fails to hit the mark for High Tension and their original style of the past. '4' is an album that one might conjure up the phrase 'Sell Out Album'.
Though this was released in 1994 on the 'Musicolor' label it stills retains that '80s sound (as poppy as it is) and the band did not give in to the grunge music coming in.
So even though this is their weakest effort in my opinion at least they went the way of commercial '80s Rock and not try to ride the very short lived horrible grunge train that had weaseled it's way in just to sell records in that way.

Usually when a band goes from a Metal force to a poppy-commercial-air play band its due to pressure from the record company to put out something more viable to the general record buying public plus possibly get singles on the radio to enforce record sales even moreso.
Not sure what happened here, was it the band's decision or management, or both?

But whatever went down this is definitely not the High Tension that I'm used to hearing. On most of their earlier albums each song starts out with some killer guitar riff and then the song just makes you wanna bang your head and pump your fist in the air.

From the first notes of the opening cut 'Midnight In Tokyo' you know somethings changed right away.
Here High Tension add more keybords and lighter-poppier songs with the exception of 'Down 'n Proud' which is more the original style of HT's previous output.

'When Heaven Comes Down' really sounds like a reworked Billy Squier-'In The Dark' song a style which HT used a bit on their previous albums using other band's riffs here and there and reworking them into their own songs.
On '4' this is not so evident as in the past.

'Bad Dreams' and 'Always What U Want' add some saxophone solos from Ralf Vosseier which is a real surprise. Never heard saxophone on any of their early albums. This was a first for me.

The last four songs on the album: 'Waitin' 4 U', 'Always What U Want', 'Always The Same', & 'Best Thing Of My Live' (Yep! actually spelled 'Live')
sound alot like Bon Jovi tunes and would fit right at home on any '80s Bon Jovi album. This strikes me as odd as Bon Jovi had long surpassed their heyday by the time this album was released. I know that for a time in the '80s every Rock & lite Metal band were watching and emulating Bon Jovi trying to cash in on his band's success but trying that in '94 just seems out there.....

Tommy Diestein the guitar player still holds onto his 'whammy bar' style leads (when he's not being replaced by saxophone solos!) but its a little more subdued mostly due to the musical style change I suppose.

This album could stand on it's own as a typical '80s Pop-Rock style album even though it's from '94 but in my opinion wouldn't have made much of an impact even if it had been released in the mid '80s. It just sounds to typical of the style & era nothing stand-out special here. It's not a horrible attempt at '80s commercial Rock just not High Tension's style.

Strangely enough the album is dedicated to Tommy Diestein ?

So unless you are really into High Tension and are a 'completist' I would say avoid this album and stick to their '80s output and best efforts: 'Warrior', 'High Tension' aka'Leather Beauty', aka'Masters of Madness' , & 'Under Tension'.

So this was a disappointment compared to the early Rockin albums I got from them as I bought them in chronological order without even realizing it until I finally got '4'.

Looking forward at some point getting their 'Meanstreak' album from 2008 to see if they went back to their roots or not.

Be sure to check out my other reviews of High Tension albums!

MAD

title: A Fiasco!
text:
Please, leave opera to the professionals! I like Andrea Bocelli, but his voice does not sound good doing opera. The control, emotion and strength needed just are not there. The final scene is a perfect example of how unconvincing Bocelli is when he realizes Mimi has died, he sounds as if he just lost his pet cat not the love of his life. It's surprising because Botecelli himself talks about how important and emotional this opera is and that it has been a dream for him to perform, but he just does not deliver. Barbara Frittoli gives an OK performance of Mimi and Eva Mei a good Musetta and Mario Luperi a good Colline. Paolo Gavanelli as Marcello has an uneven vibrato. His voice sounds tired and his pitch goes flat at the end of phases. There is even a blatant wrong note from the brass section in the first act which the editors should have caught. The recording favors the singers and the orchestra sounds like background music instead of an integral part of the work except during forte passages.
Overall, it's a fiasco! I just could not warm up to any of these characters and FEEL this opera the way it should be felt, with great emotion. If you want to hear this opera the way it should be done get Bjorling and Beechem (EMI #67753 ASIN: B000063UM0 ) or the Domingo and Solti recording (RCA #39496 ASIN: B000009NIW ).

title: Worthless for hot summer watering, probably good in the north.
text: I live in Texas so in our summer weather, it gets really hot and lawns really need watering. I used the house once in cooler Spring weather and loved it, I didn't want a bunch of house cluttering up our sidewalk or damaging adjacent planting beds, so it was perfect for that. We even have had sporadic rains so we didn't need to water much.  However, the grass was getting crunchy so when we turned on the hose, the metal connector must have expanded and the inner waterproof hose popped out and now the water goes from the spigot to the fabric cover if the hose (not to the end of the hose) so it's worthless. If your summer temperatures don't hit 90+ (or at least when you water the hose is cooler than that) then it would be a great hose for you. If you need to water when it's hot, avoid expanding hoses. I guess I'm just going to have to live with meat hoses or put in extra effort to wrap up hoses when I'm done (no fun!).

title: major interpretations, worth the splash - but not in these pitiful transfers
text:
I tend to be sceptical about the cult around obscure and forgotten fiddlers, whose icon status seems directly dependent on the unavailability or rarity of their recordings - so that no one can actually check on the hear-say. When finally I get to hear them, I am often disappointed: was that all the splash was about? Not so with Julian Sitkovetzky (as spelled here). On the contrary, based on this CD, with him the hype seems not loud enough.

Julian (or Yulian) Sitkovetzky (more often written Sitkovetsky, but I've even seen it spelled Sitkovecky or Sitkoveckij -, the husband of pianist Bella Davidovitch and father of Dimitry Sitkovetsky, was a Russian-Ukrainian virtuoso born in 1925, whose career was tragically cut short when he died of cancer at the age of 33. Monopole's product info is shamefully wanting - other than a 10-line bio we are just told that the recordings date from 1953 and 1954 (but which we are not told) and the sources are not mentioned. From other releases of the same works it appears that Sibelius is from 1953 and Khachaturian 1954. I've reviewed the Khachaturian at length under one of those other releases, by Russian Disc ([[ASIN:B000001LPO Khachaturian Concerto for violin in Dm; Glazunov: Concerto for violin in Am]]. Note that it is NOT the same performance as the one issued by Artek, volume 5 of their [[ASIN:B000GQL8QS Art of Yulian Sitkovetsky]], which is a 1956 live recording conducted by the composer. The Russian Disc/Monopole performance is an interpretation of fabulous drive in the outer movements, and great lyrical intensity in the slow movement. In fact, the reading is very similar to the dedicatee and first performer's, David Oistrakh: his second studio recording, also made in 1954 with the composer leading the Philharmonia Orchestra in the first two movements ([[ASIN:B000002RTZ Composers in Person: Aram Khachaturian Conducts Masquerade / Gayaneh / Violin Concerto]]) and, in the finale, his live recording with Kubelik at the Prag Festival in 1947 (unfortunately in dismal sound, [[ASIN:B0000034DW Concertos - Liszt/Prokofiev/Khachaturian]]), which is even more dashing (in comparison Oistrakh in 1954 sounds gentle and meek). Sitkovetzky's digital virtuosity in that finale is awesome and, like Oistrakh, his incredible forward drive is never at the expense of tonal control. Worth noting is also the fact that he plays the first movement's cadenza complete - a decision rarely exercised, then (Oistrakh played his own concoction) and still now. It is a live recording, but other than various stage noises in the middle movement and the applause at the end, one has no clue - and certainly not in any finger slip or imprecision from Sitkovetzky. As for the orchestral support, if I had been told it was Leningrad under Mravinsky, I would have believed it: the Romanian Radio Orchestra under "Niyazi" (never heard of him. No first name? But Wikipedia does have an entry, showing that his complete name was Niyazi Zulfigar ogli Tagizade Hajibeyov - no wonder Monople, and maybe the conductor himself, dropped it) plays with tremendous drive, energy, precision and snap.

However, the horrendously shrill, harsh and cavernous acoustics of the Monopole transfer simply rule it out. The Russian Disc transfer is also harsh, but with none of the cavernous sonic perspective that sabotages the Monopole issue.

Interpretively, the Sibelius' Violin Concerto belongs to the same league. Although rarely exercised, the coupling of Sibelius' with Khachaturian's Violin Concerto seems to me a very appropriate choice stylistically, not only because of the sweeping lyricism shared by both compositions, but more to the point because of the Sibelian echoes in Khachaturian's finale. Again the source of this recording isn't indicated by Monopole. It is a studio recording that was first published on Supraphon Mono LPM418, reissued by the same company on CD on [[ASIN:B000024XNR Giants of the Violin]]. I don't have that specific reissue, nor the one published by Aulos/Melodiya ([[ASIN:B0009AHKSG Sibelius, Mozart, Saraste, Paganini - The art of Yulian Sitkovetsky Vol. 1]]), but, by an extraordinary stroke of luck, I've just found (and cheap, too!) a rarity reissue, a 1995 CD published by SYD Records, CYD 006, not listed here, no bar code, volume 6 of a series called "The Art of Yulian Sitkovetsky", which seems to be the source from which Artek licenced their own series - but, God knows why (and lamentably) stopping at volume 5. SYD vol. 6 is invaluable for pairing this Sibelius with the live recording of Sitkovetsky's performance of Tchaikovsky's Violin Concerto given during the final round of the 1955 Queen Elizabeth Competition in which he got 2nd Prize; a famous anecdote in Sitkovetsky's bio is that Menuhin and Oistrakh were among the jury, and Menuhin later claimed that Sitkovetsky should have received the first prize. That anecdote is recounted in every biography of Sitkovetsky, but nobody ever says who the hapless prize winner was: it was the American Berl Senovsky. Well... Sitkovetsky, Senovsky... maybe the secretary just made a typo. Anyway: collectors and fans of the violin, start posting permanent searches on eBay.

I'm bringing this up not just to have said collectors salivate in envy, but point out again at the botched transfer of Monopole. The SYD transfer is clearly direct from tape and sounds just fine. Monopole is from LP, with dim surface noise and harsh violin tone and saturation in the climaxes. The unavailability of this recording in a good transfer is to be lamented. As with Khachaturian, it is a performance of great urgency and considerable dramatic impact, one very close to the model established by Heifetz in his premiere recording with Beecham in 1935 ([[ASIN:B000009J15 Heifetz : Strauss, Sibelius & Prokofiev]] and reiterated by him in his 1959 stereo remake under Walter Hendl, [[ASIN:B0006PV5U8 Sibelius, Prokofiev, Glazunov: Violin Concertos [Hybrid SACD]]]. There is no enjoying the wide and calm Nordic vistas here, the Concerto is taken not as a panorama of haunting and evocative colors (as it has become in the interpretive tradition that developed from the 1960s onwards), but as a vehicle for violent drama (try the "allegro molto" section in the first movement starting at 4:38). Just to give an idea, Heifetz in 1935 took the first movement in 14:08, he was even faster in 1959 and established something of a record at 13:32. Sitkovetsky runs close second at 13:42 (but without the sense of rush sometimes elicited by Heifetz). Hilary Hahn, the most recent recording to have come my way, takes it in 17:10 ([[ASIN:B0011WMWUW Schoenberg Violin Concerto Op.36/Sibelius Violin Concerto Op.47]]). In the finale, Sitkovetzky is even FASTER than Heifetz in 1959 by four seconds - a feat I thought I'd never encounter - but he also has great rhythmic bounce, and although his double-stop scales followed by octave leaps are not entirely in-sync with the orchestra (and until Hahn, positively nobody's were, even Heifetz sounded scrambled here), his harmonic "whistling" at 4:28 is more assured than Heifetz', and perfect, really. Anossov conducts a powerful and urgent orchestral support (Czech Philharmonic).

If I had one (small) reservation, it is that, for all his fiery approach and incredible digital virtuosity, Sitkovetzky lacks perhaps the ultimate degree of expression, one that both Heifetz and Camilla Wicks ([[ASIN:B000HKDB5E Camilla Wicks (violin) plays Sibelius and Valen: Violin Concertos [Biddulph 80218-2]]]), in two widely contrasted approaches from those days, had in loads. Nonetheless this is, to me, one of the great recordings of Sibelius' Violin Concerto, still today.

The three encores with wife Bella Davidovitch and much better sound (source unknown) are not enough ground to purchase this disc, except maybe as a stopgap (even botched sound is better than nothing for interpretations of such magnitude), until you can find the Russian Disc for Khachaturian and any of the three indicated above for the Sibelius.

And a post-script: as I write, the Art vol. 6 Sibelius/Tchaikovsky is not just listed, but actually sold (and not for a huge amount, even with postage and exchange rate, nothing to deter the determined collector) on Amazon.fr and Amazon.uk, ASIN B000EHSK6K.

title: Deserves proper release (or does it?)
text:
I had never heard this album until before yesterday. The story is known of Columbia releasing this to spite Dylan for switching labels and when it came time to reissue his music (or even put it out on CD) Dylan requested this one not be among them. I recently got a new turntable and went vinyl hunting almost immediately for this album and found it.

The critics and Dylan hated this album. It got one star reviews from All Music Guide and Rolling Stone and I tend to think that's a pretty harsh review in itself. Yeah, it's a cover album basically but they all work in their own strange way. I mean I confess to being one of those "Dylan can do no wrong" folks. I liked pretty much every album he ever did and when I stumbled upon this one I felt no different. He brings his own style to these songs and it works. Even "Big Yellow Taxi" which is a song I have always disliked is given the Dylan treatment and I love it.

OK it's not "Blood on the Tracks" or "Blonde on Blonde" and you probably know that going into this one. But for what it is, it's enjoyable. I do however wonder, is the true reward finding it in a record shop over 40 years after it's release? Maybe it is an album that is best served being played on old vinyl instead of compact disc or MP3 download (which you can access on here). If it's an album that has interested you over the years, I recommend checking it out.

text: My wife likes this guy so, unfortunately, I felt compelled to listen to the CD since she insisted on buying it (even though I have a wall of Verdi operas from the true masters past and present). There is too much that is horrific about the singing on this CD that to enumerate them would be time-consuming and ultimately pointless since it is clear that his fans are hopelessly numb to any kind of critical thought.  I would just urge anyone toying with the idea of buying this CD to do themselves a favor.  Buy it if you must, but then also seek out a compilation of Verdi arias by Domingo (there are a couple of them extant) and compare.  The differences are not just technical.  You will find far more passion, heart, and intellect in a great Verdi performance than this meager disc offers.  Don't settle for mediocrity.  Sure, this is better singing than Michael Bolton, but let's set the bar a little higher, shall we?

text: If you're Irish (or not) and love upbeat Irish music, you'll love this!  The CD clocks in at 45 minutes, so for the price you are not getting cheated there.  The back cover shows as "Celtic Faire, by John Whelan".  I am not sure if John wrote some or all of these songs, but either way he and his ensemble deserve a lot of credit.  The instrumentation (and the music is all instrumental) is described as a Celtic ensemble with accordion, fiddle, guitar, bass, cittern, flutes, whistles, Uillean pipes, and mandolin, and has a very traditional sound.  Some songs have similar keys and structures, but overall the changes in pace make them all sound fresh.  I jokingly have said when my time is up and I'm still hearing this, I'll know I'm in the Right Place.  But seriously folks, if you want some great, energetic music to get you going, treat yourself and pick this one up!

title: Be Prepared to Have Your Mind Blown!
text: What we have hear are two completely instrumental Homer & Jethro albums on one CD, on which they play mostly Jazz and Popular standards (including some tunes by Johnny Mercer, Cole Porter and Duke Ellington) in the Country Swing Jazz style.  It is non-stop joy from start to finish.  Now, Homer and Jethro made a career out of doing cornball comedy, and I thought they were very good at it.  But if you are expecting to hear two goobers who are trying to reach way beyond their abilities, be prepared to have your mind blown!  These two men were virtuoso musicians on the guitar and mandolin, and this CD is a masterpiece.  The energy never lets up, their backup musicians blend in beautifully, the arrangements are very tasteful, and the music swings to holy heck. The recordings were produced by Chet Atkins, and are of audiophile quality, with clear and natural sound recorded in a good acoustic space with no gimmicks. This CD brings all of those qualities to life.  I love jazzy picking, and up until hearing this CD, my favorite acoustic instrumental recordings were those of Dave Grisman's jazzy bluegrass.  But this Homer & Jethro CD has become my new favorite.  Sadly, it is out of print, but if you love this type of music, you owe it to yourself to seek out a used copy.  You won't be sorry.

title: World Bore Z
text:
While I'll freely admit that it doesn't help to come to "World War Z" with an intense dislike for Max Brooks (something hard to avoid if you read any of his commentary), I don't think anything could have saved this thoroughly tepid story.

The book is just a rehash of every zombie movie you've ever seen, loosely organized around the idea of an 'oral history' - a hero investigator goes around the world and talks to survivors to get their stories. Brooks openly admits to getting the idea for an oral history from previous oral history books. So he uses two borrowed scenarios. The real pity is that he is completely incapable of making them exciting. It's just page after page of stilted dialog.

The audio book makes this worse, for two major reasons. First, it is recorded like video game audio (the participants in 'conversations' are clearly separately recorded, so exchanges that should sound spontaneous and natural have weird pauses as each person finishes what they were going to say, then stop abruptly as if someone were interrupting them, then there's a brief pause of silence, then the interrupting sentence picks up - the whole thing feels unnatural). Second, Max Brooks' tremendous ego wouldn't allow him to give the role of narrator to an actor. So you get decent readings from legends like Paul Sorvino interspersed with Brooks' flat readings.

If you like zombie stories, I'd recommend the Walking Dead books. There aren't a lot of new ideas in zombie land, but at least Frank Darabont writes interesting characters and situations.

title: Excellent Cowell recital by an outsider
text:
Considering the historical importance and the musical value of Henry Cowell's output for piano, it is saddening to see how rarely it is played and recorded, then and now. There was never much available on LP, although what there was, was of great value: namely the invaluable recording of a selection of 20 made by the composer himself on Folkways in 1963 and now reissued by Smithsonian ([[ASIN:B000001DM0 Henry Cowell plays his own Piano Music]]), and Sorrel Doris Hays' recording from 1977 on Finnadar, now on Townhall ([[ASIN:B00005T6H6 Sorrel Doris Hays Plays the Piano Music of Henry Cowell]]). The rest were limited selections included in miscellaneous collections (as with Shields 1975: [[ASIN:B000001K6M Piano Music in America 1900-1945]] and Miller 1976: [[ASIN:B0000030F0 Sound Forms for Piano]]). Sadly, not much has been added in the CD era: Anthony de Mare plays 11 pieces along with compositions of Ives and Lou Harrison on [[ASIN:B00004TKRZ Wizards & Wildmen]], Cheryl Seltzer and Joël Sachs from the Continuum Ensemble share ten on their Musical Heritage Society survey now reissued as two Naxos CDs [[ASIN:B00076SHHA Continuum Portrait 1]] and [[ASIN:B0007ACVMI Henry Cowell: Continuum Portrait 2]]. The recital on New Albion, [[ASIN:B000003TM6 New Music: Piano Compositions By Henry Cowell]], deriving from a series of concerts given in 1997 by four pianists (including Hays again), is flawed both sonically and interpretively (see my review), and I haven't yet heard the Cowell CD of Stacey Barelos, [[ASIN:B0088XQEAQ Cowell: Piano Music]]. So a warm welcome must be given to Chris Burn's collection, published in 1993 by the small and hard-to-find British label Acta: it certainly doesn't replace Cowell's invaluable but sonically flawed testimony nor Sorrel Hays contribution, but it provides a fine, modern complement to them, and is quite good in its own right.

The program is well-chosen, with most of the composer's most famous masterpieces, to which Burn adds some unpublished pieces, some of them real rarities: The Fairy Answer, The Sword of Oblivion, The Sleep Music of the Dagna, Sway Dance - for the last three, this is the only recording I am aware of. Burn's is also one of the only two versions I know of the (admittedly not essential) "Invention", and the only one of "The Fairy Bells", though the latter is as inventive and poetic as anything written by the composer, and the score easily accessible.

Apparently Burn is not a classical music pianist but one involved in free improvisation, which, according to the notes, "led him to a thorough and ongoing examination of piano technique. This resulted in the development of an extensive, personal vocabulary that frequently used sounds found from "inside" the piano", and this naturally led him to an interest for the music of Cowell.

Well, I can vouch that Burn's technique is impressive and entirely up to the particular demands of Cowell's piano writing - which also includes the digital fleetness associated for centuries with classical piano technique, but also much more. Witness his dazzling `Advertisement", in which he captures perfectly the piece's perky, cartoonesque, Katzenjammer humor and its dazzling bouce (in view of which it is unfortunate that he plays it without repeat). In "What's This" (the 1st Encore to Dynamic Motion) he is as dynamic and precise as Seltzer, though not as nuanced in his dynamic shadings. On the other hand in the "Invention" he takes a more moderate tempo and is less dazzling than Roger Shields.

He can be appropriately massive and pounding in pieces such as "Tiger" (although the rather mate recording robs it of some of its power), "Dynamic Motion" (but there, the recording doesn't allow for the resonances at the begining to be heard), "Amiable Conversation" (very dynamic, almost sprightly), "The Tides of Manaunaun" (solemn and weighty, but with great power), "The Voice of Lir" (great forward momentum and an impressive crescendo) although overall he doesn't quite command the same kind of massive pounding power and frenzy as the composer himself or Cheryl Seltzer and Joel Sachs, particularly so in "Amiable Conversation", "Anger Dance" (clean and precise, but not as angry as Cowell's) and the final pages of "Tiger".

But he displays a fine sense of color, as in "Sinister Resonance", "Aeolian Harp" or "The Banshee", maybe less "feminine" than Cowell's own but all the more terrifying. His Banshee is a monster, and you don't want to be around that night in the old, run-down mansion when it comes out to call.

He is precise, oftentimes more so than the composer himself ("Aeolian Harp", "The Snows of Fuji-Yama", where his first clusters sound off-pitch, probably due to ill-balance between both hands), and with a good sense of the Cowellian rubato - though nothing near the composer's unique hand at it. In "The Trumpet of Angus Og" he is faster and exudes more exuberant joy than Cowell's nostalgic solemnity - and it is, I find, an entirely valid alternative. On the other hand in "The Lilt of the Reel" his tempos are more contrasted than the composer's, more expansive in the first part and more exuberant in the faster passages, but again he has fine colors and good tempo flexibility. Burn is interesting also for following in some pieces the composer's recording rather than his score. For instance, in "Lilt of the Reel" again, he plays Cowell's apparently improvised coda/cadenza, and in "Aeolian Harp" he lets, like Cowell, the final chord resonate longer than notated.

With only 55 minutes on the disc, it is too bad Burn didn't add Exultation (a kind of boisterous barn-dance with left-hand clusters), Fabric (a superb study in polyrhythms), Piece for Piano (an impressive compendium of all of Cowell's special piano-playing techniques), Harp of Life (not easily accessible, not in the two -difficultly - available Schirmer/AMI collections of scores, but everybody including composer plays it), Antinomy and Time Table (the two last Encores to Dynamic Motion). It would have made it the indispensable modern Cowell piano collection. As it is, it is still an essential acquisition for anybody persuaded in the significance and beauty of that music, or wanting to find out.

text: When I first saw this I was excited to be able to acquire a version of the Rolling Stones “Their Satanic Majesties Request” LP with the original cover in a CD format. What I received was just what it said it was, a 3D version. Unfortunately that is not what the original cover is. The original cover is a lenticular, which similar to the 3D version also shows an illusion of depth, but adds to it by its ability to change as the image is viewed when you tilt the LP or change your sight line, in the case of the original a movement of the Rolling Stones heads changing directions along with a change in the angle and color of the flowers, and also most significantly the sudden appearance of the heads of all four Beatles camouflaged amidst the barrage of colors. The appearance of the Beatles was a major factor in the interest and popularity of the cover. In fact the 3D square mounted on the CD cover is actually truncated on the right and left sides, leaving off the sections where Paul & Ringo would have appeared along with the flowers that trimmed the original on the sides. title: the works of Richard Stoker are well worth a listen - and even a few re-listens
text:
Never heard of Richard Stoker (born 1938 and still alive as I write) before chancing on this CD, sold cheap by an eBay seller with whom I had purchased other stuff. I took my chance, more on the basis of the label, Priory, a small British indie mainly specialized in church and organ music, and the pianist, Eric Parkin, whom I've already heard on other CDs.

Well, good draw.

Stoker is a british composer, student of Lennox Berkeley and Nadia Boulanger, and later professor of composition at the Royal Acadmey of Music from 1963 to 1987. But ge is also much more than that: pianist, conductor, writer ("of lyrics, plays, novels, short stories, poetry and libretti"), painter/visual artist (the CD's cover reproduces one of his paintings) and even movie and TV actor ("he has appeared in over 100 films worldwide" claims his entry on Wikipedia, including a role in the recent Walt Disney "Maleficent"). My hunch is that this is exactly why Stoker is unknown in all those fields: it's an old rule that when you follow too many paths rather than doggedly plow a single furrow, you'll fail in all. There is an informative series of articles on Stoker on Musicweb International.

To be honest, not all of the piano music featured here is interesting. The opening cycle, Piano Serenade op. 17, from 1962, may sound inconspicuous enough, and did to me on first hearing, from gently wistful to insouciantly playful, something Poulenc might have composed, or any of the numerous very backward-looking composers who inhabited the British Isles in the 20th century before the tunnel was dug, protected from any outside influence, although, coming back to it in the light of some of the heavier stuff that follows, the introductory piece, Prelude, shows a whimsicality that goes beyond the merely decorative, and the very sparseness of the following Air, much of it a 2-part invention, is an intriguing feature. A Poet's Notebook op. 19 from 1969, another suite of six short pieces, continues in much the same (two) moods and very traditional language. Regency Suite op. 15, which gathers pieces composed between 1952 (Stoker was 13) and 1959, veers between Prokofiev's Visions Fugitives and, in the concluding Toccata, Debussy's Pour le Piano and Ravel's Tombeau de Couperin.

I first misread the track listing and thought I was listening to the Zodiac Variations, and wrote that it "sounds like lounge music improvised by The Pianist for inattentive patrons". Well, no: they were the "Two Jazz Preludes" op. 63 from 1980 (tracks 21 and 22). Well, the first one sounds like lounge music improvised by The Pianist for inattentive patrons", and the second like a lullaby to put baby asleep. There are a few more interesting moments and more pianistic invention in the series of very short variations that make up the Zodiac Variations op. 22 from 1965, like the ringing second to fourth variations Leo, Pisces and Aries, the terse and dramy two-part writing of variation 5 Gemini, the bouncing capriciousness of var. 7 Sagittarius: and the very shortness of these variations (the longest runs 45 seconds, the shortest 20) is one of those interesting and original features. There's nothing that breaks any new grounds here, but the music is not run-of-the-mill either and Stoker makes his expressive points eloquently.

But the First Sonata (1967) and the Variations opus 45 (1973) are two great pieces, serious, austere and grand, absolutely not "flashy", anchored in tonality but bordering on atonality, close to what other British composers, Tippett, Hoddinnott, Mathias, may have written in the same years. The Sonata's construction in two movements, Ritmico and Riposo, is inspired by Beethoven's op. 90 and op. 111, but it recalled the second Sonatas of Tippett or Mathias (although these are both couched in a single movement).

Parts of the second Sonata, written for Eric Parkin in 1992, are more overtly virtuosic and flashy, and especially its first movement, "Suonare" (in reference to the Italian sense of the word, "to sound" or "peal" as in bells ringing, but it's an equally serious affair and even, at times, thorny, jagged, dissonant and aggressive. The Sonata "reflects an interest in jazz writing and performance", but, despite very allusive references at the beginning of the Sonata, it's more in its processes than in it's melodic shape that Stoker took his inspiration from jazz, in that in movements two and four, called "Cantare" 1 and 2, "the parameters are not defined, much being left to the performer". The central movement, Scherzare, like the first movement and Finale a fast Toccata-type of movenent, sounds like Debussy on cocaine.

Those works of Richard Stoker are well worth a listen, and even re-listens and more performances. TT 79:39. The mikes have captured a soft traffic rumble in the background.

text:
This is 100% FAKE. Linkin Park have yet to release any official Greatest Hits compilation. There are tons of tell-tale signs that this "Greatest Hits" is bogus.

- The songs that will be "new" to some people (And One, No Roads Left, and QWERTY) are actually old b-sides and Linkin Park Underground-exclusive tracks from years past.

- There are a lot of songs on here really can't be considered "hits" since they were never released as singles. (No More Sorrow, In My Remains, Blackout, Don't Stay, Pushing Me Away, Hit the Floor, Valentine's Day, By Myself, Figure.09, Forgotten, In Pieces, In Between? Nope, never singles.)

- Foreword? It's a noise track that opens Meteora. IF it were included on a compilation as a lead-in for Don't Stay, it would, in all likelihood, be added onto the beginning of the same track as Don't Stay.

I'm sure this is a good quality burned CD. The art may pass as "official looking" to some, but it doesn't at all match the art direction LP stuff has taken in recent years, and it's made from easy-to-find band promo photos and graphics from the Living Things album cycle. If you don't mind buying a bootleg, go ahead. But if you're expecting a real, genuine LP "Greatest Hits", you're gonna have to keep waiting.

text: The record patiently awaits its turn among the large pile of music. Finally it is allowed to play, to shine, to sing, and to scream in its beautiful agony. It's like this: if you are a drooling mischievous apocalyptic follower of Godspeed You! Black Emperor or Mono, as well as Pelican, Neurosis, and Isis, then you absolutely _must_ get this album. One Starving Day is a group of Italian musicians, with a previous experience in some hardcore bands, but what they whip up on their debut album, Broken Wings Lead Arms to the Sun, is beyond metal, beyond screamo and post-nu-post-rock. It is a blend of very melodic and voluptuous swells of unfolding desperation which erupts into the mass of lava... flowing... slowly... All you can do is just stand there, agape, watching it helplessly wash over your ears, consuming everything in its path. Take the intimate lyrics on my favorite track on the album, Leave: "on these tears / lay down, and wait / for becoming / an abandon / to soothe / all your fears / a pure heart / to soothe / and leave". Into this deadly cocktail, throw in the spacey 70s synth sweeps, raw violin screeches, and explosive (excellent) drumming. And I did mention the screamed vocals, right? That may sound discouraging to some listeners (or readers), but it works _very_ well for One Starving Day, and is actually more than welcomed by yours truly (surprise!). The CD was released on Washington DC based Planaria Recordings, and then repressed on a colored 12" vinyl with two extra unreleased tracks on an accompanying 7" by KNVBI Records. Whether you're a collector or not, this record must be in your library for the likes of the above mentioned bands.

title: Mostly Complete Singles’ Collection
text:
This 5-CD box set claims to offer the buyer all of Dean’s Capitol singles between 1949 and 1961. For the most part, this is what you get. Short of purchasing the expensive Bear Family sets, this is one of the best collections of the songs that Capitol released in the U.S. in the 78 & 45 RPM “single” format. Many of these tracks are hard to find and should please the fan who doesn’t want to spend hundreds of dollars for the Bear Family boxes.

The buyer should be aware of what is missing prior to making a purchase. Since Dean signed with Capitol in 1948, the four singles from that year are not included. For some reason his first two singles of 1949 are not in this package. They are “Have A Little Sympathy” backed with “Johnny Get Your Girl” and “Dreamy Old New England Moon” backed with “Three Wishes”. Also, the producers elected to leave off all the duets he did. This means you don’t get the songs with Margaret Whiting, Helen O’Connell, Nat “King” Cole and Line Renaud. While it may not be important to most listeners, the songs are not grouped in pairs like the original singles. Disk number one does start with 1949 and 1961 is on disk five. I see from a review on Amazon’s U.K. site that the information with this release is all in French, so that doesn’t help much in the U.S.

You should know that I have not purchased this release since I already own all the songs. The main purpose of this review is to give you some additional information of what songs are here and which ones are not. Since I don’t own the set, I can not offer any information on the audio quality. I do own the 4-CD set “Young Dino” – a Proper Box release. It is outstanding with a wonderful booklet and fine sound. The only down side is that it only includes songs through 1955. You do get all twelve of his pre-Capitol releases which are really hard to find. There is no question that the Bear Family sets are the way to go if you have the budget.

title: Schnabel and Gould
text: We know that young Glenn so revered Artur Schnabel that the side breaks in his old 78rpm set were reference points for Gould’s own performances. What many listeners don’t know — though it seems clear to me — is that Gould also revered Beethoven, though he was loath to admit it, perhaps because that love didn’t jibe with more unorthodox loves, from Orlando Gibbons to Petula Clark. Consequently critics accuse Gould of playing Beethoven willfully, even disrespectfully. But to cite just one example for the defense: listen to the way Glenn Gould plays the adagio of Op. 2 No. 1. Yes, it’s slow, or as I would say, ruminative. Yes, the left hand plucks at the bass — or is it reminding us of Beethoven’s fortepiano? Gould contended that Beethoven from beginning to end fed off the tension between classical and romantic impulses. Now listen to the right hand melody and tell me Gould was not capable of heartfelt lyricism, that he did not love Beethoven. Is this a set for beginners? I say yes, because it will disturb and excite them. It spurs dialogue. It’s beautiful. We’ll always have Schnabel. But here and in the bracing concertos, make room for Gould.

title: Terrific jugalbandi of violin and sarod
text:
Great album of violin (South Indian) and sarod (North Indian) masters, in the jugalbandi style ("entwined twins" model of 2 lead instruments interacting with each other).

The album begins with a North India raga (Bhopali) followed by a South India raga (Malkauns). The violin and sarod players are accompanied on both tracks by tabla and mridangam, and these drummers have their own jugalbandi section at the end of both lengthy ragas.

The album concludes with 2 short solo pieces: first by the violin, and the last track by the sarod. I think the album was recorded in 1983.

The first 3 pieces are quite exciting; except for the alap section of the 2 main ragas, the last piece (the sarod solo) is the only one that is slow and meditative. All 4 tracks are played exceedingly well. I have 100+ albums of music from India, and this is one of my favorites.

This is a digital re-release of an LP. The CD has the 2 short solos which were not on the LP release. The CD has no liner notes, but the LP does. Search for the LP version on Amazon and you'll see a scan of the LP back cover which has information about the performers and the ragas.

title: Save Your LPs
text:
The music industry is now making big money selling "Digitally Remastered" CDs of pop albums to Baby-Boomers who desire improved CD versions of their old pop records. Most classical releases are also CD versions of recordings by famous old virtuosos. Unfortunately, the recordings here by longtime Ringling-Brothers-Barnum-&-Bailey bandmaster Merle Evans and the New England Conservatory Band, have not received the "Digitally Remastered" treatment. According to the liner notes, the transfer to CD was hampered by an "Inability to obtain the original tapes." (What? Somebody lost them? The owner of the tapes wanted a fortune to use them? What?)

So these CDs were made from someone's LPs, and it sounds like it. The sound is not terrible, but with circus music, you want a bass drum that will rattle the windows. You want shrieking high frequencies that will torment dogs. You want ferocious brass that will cause your neighbors to hide in the basement.

You get none of that with these CDs, because analog sound faces the same problem that an analogue photo does. If you make a copy of a photo, it will appear similar to the original, but if you make a copy of the copy, there is a noticeable difference from the original. These CDs are a copy of some LPs which were a copy of the original tapes, and as soon as I put the first CD on, I knew exactly what had happened. If you are elderly and are hanging on to your 1964 Maggotbox console, you might find the sound acceptable (it's amazing how lovers of classical music seem to actually >prefer< bad sound reproduction), but if you're into high-end audio, this set of CDs is not for you.

When these recordings were first released in 1970, they came as a five-LP set, and the collection was a national treasure. A landmark. America has always been known for its jazz, ragtime, dixieland, bluegrass, rock & roll, blues and Texas swing -- all of which came from the South and achieved world popularity. Here, however, was evidence that Northerners and caucasians were also capable of making exciting music! The factories hadn't turned us into soulless robots, and we too, could play music that would make your hair stand on end!

As a bonus, the fifth LP of the original set contained an interview with Merle Evans (who lived until 1987), and he has some great stories to tell. One is about some Holy Rollers (as Fundamentalist Christians were then called) who were gathered in a park near the circus camp one evening, expecting the Second Coming to occur that very night (this was before The Rapture was invented). So ol' Merle and another trumpet player sneak onto the railroad bridge with their horns and . . .

Well, with this CD set, you won't find out what happened. Too bad. So instead, buy the LP boxed set. Pay any price for it. It sounds better, and you'll get the complete recordings.

For those who are curious to dare listen to circus music, I recommend the superb-sounding, superbly-played [[ASIN:B000002SKA Under the Big Top: 100 Years of Circus Music]]. Practically every circus number ever written (and the practice of calling a song or piece a "number" originated with the big book of music that circus musicians played from; Evans would shout to the band what they'd play next by calling a number; as I recall, Karl L. King's "Barnum & Bailey's Favorite" was number 555 in the book) has been recorded by the [[ASIN:B000R00R5G South Shore Concert Band]]. Their earlier releases are a mite rough-around-the-edges (which may make them more authentic), but their conductor, Richard Whitmarsh, has whipped them into shape, and they now issue recordings better than this set.

As for whoever possesses the original master tapes to A Tribute to Merle Evans, if you have either allowed the tapes to deteriorate through neglect or refuse to share them, I place the most terrible of curses upon you. You shall be forced to listen to the music your teenage granddaughter likes for ALL ETERNITY!

title: this is one of the best folk music anthologies ever released
text: One of many Murray Hill box sets (There is also an edition of it on the Everest label), this is  one of the best folk music anthologies ever released. The 12 sides are reissues of one side each of 12 different albums originally released on the Tradition label. Side 1 presents 9 different folk artists with one song each (Judy Collins, Theodore Bikel, the Dillards, Ed McCurdy, Oscar Brand, Odetta, and others). The remainder of the box set devotes an entire side each to 11 other great folk artists. Carl Sandburg has a whole side of ballads that he collected, performed solo with his acoustic guitar (muddy sound quality on this side, but good once you adjust to it). The Woody Guthrie side consists of songs Woody recorded with Cisco Houston and Sonny Terry. The Josh White side has 4 songs by Josh accompanied by a small band. Lightnin' Hopkins, Leadbelly, and Big Bill Broonzy are each represented by entire sides of their bare bones self-accompanied early reordings (folk blues at its best). Brownie and Sonny's side is also both bluesy and folky. John Lee Hooker's side is a mixed bag of solo recordings (including a great live take of "Hobo Blues") and electric full band sessions. The side labeled "The Songs of Rod McKuen" consists of songs written by McKuen but actually sung by Barry McGuire with members of the New Christy Minstrels. The Glenn Yarbrough side is one side of his first album on Tradition, predating his tenure with the Limeliters. The Pete Seeger side is from a live concert. All of it is prime folk, widely varied, and well worth owning.

title: Warning - This Is NOT Quintet / Sextet with Milt Jackson
text:
There's a strange "Editorial Review" comment on the amazon.com site that says this is "the first time this LP has appeared on CD with it's original cover...". (The cover being Miles on the phone and a small boy in a doorway with a trumpet).

In fact the tracks on this disc are NOT those of Miles Davis and Milt Jackson "Quintet / Sextet". Please don't be confused into thinking this is the actual Prestige release from 1955, as I was.

The tracks on this compilation are in fact:

1-4 Little Melonae, Budo, Sweet Sue Just You, and Two Bass Hit - from " 'Round About Midnight".

5-8 On Green Dolphin Street, Fran-dance, Stella By Starlight, Love For Sale - from "Kind Of Blue"

9-11 On Green Dolphin Street, Bye Bye Blackbird, Bye Bye (Theme) - from "Friday Night at the Blackhawk".

Same musicians and exact session dates as those original releases.

No sign of Dr. Jackle, Bitty Ditty, Minor March, or Changes from the original Miles/Milt Jackson release, Quintet / Sextet.

Just the usual standard of record company ignorance? (in this case "Essential Jazz Classics") or an attempt to rack up some accidental sales? Either way, it looks like amazon in the UK will give me a refund.

title: Another Caveat Emptor
text:
The seller's reponse to those who have questions about the representations made for this CD:

"Seller Response: "Read the description. "These recordings were taken from the only known acetate record of the tapes, that were aquired some time ago. They are as they were recorded on Jan. 1, 1962."" Date: June 21, 2009

Actually, as another reviewer noted, Joe Pope offered these for sale during the 1970s-1980s as singles. He also offered them as an LP, which, having heard it, I noted was pristine in sound: no scratches, no pops, or other defects.

Apparently Joe Pope had a second "only known acetate record of the tapes," except that his was pristine.

Otherwise, to clarify as concerns the actual facts:

1. The audition was with Decca Records, not EMI. The producer there had the option of choosing one "guitar group," and the other auditioned was "Brian Poole and the Tremeloes". He chose the latter over "The Beatles" because they were in London, which was a convenience for the label, whereas "The Beatles" had yet to relocate from Liverpool to London.

2. The audition was not taped; it was recorded direct-to-disk. (See All You Need is Ears, by George Martin.)

3. As Decca Records still exists, or is part of the MCA group, it is not likely the sold these valuable recordings to EMI or anyone else. It is most probable that they contracted with EMI for use of some of them for the "Anthology" project, as they knew they would make a sizable profit from it.

It is one thing to make money from bootlegs -- keeping all 100 per cent of it for oneself -- but quite another to misrepresent, whether by commission or omission, the nature and quality of them in order to sell them.

title: Viva Umea!
text:
This is the Japanese import version of Cloudberry Jam's first full length album, "Blank Paycheck," with several bonus tracks. "Elevator," "Before Time," and "Kingfisher" come from "The Art of Being Cool" EP and "Scorch" is a b-side from the "Another Moment Follows" single. If you love Komeda or the Cardigans I can highly recommend this album. Superb pop craftsmanship.
I heard "Elevator" on a North By No South label compilation several years ago and it has always been one of my favortie Swede-pop songs. Only this month did I track down this CD (I happened across it at Shirokiya, a Japanese department store in Honolulu). After hearing an early Cloudberry Jam release ("La La La") that was disappointingly unremarkable I wasn't sure if this record would be worth buying. I was wrong, though, thankfully. "Cloudberry Jam" is a beautiful, energetic pop record, delighting with every creamy turn. Something magic happened in Umea, Sweden right around 1994. Pick up this great document of another fascinating chapter in pop history.

title: What’s “Old” is New And Beautiful Again!
text:
Imagine sitting in your living room and having John Batdorf play his music for you and maybe a few of your friends. He occasionally brings in a musical buddy to add some harmony or an extra bass line. You’ve asked John for a nice, long show which includes songs from his past and a story (now liner notes) about how they have inspired his present… And you are loving every moment of it! That’s how you will feel as you dive into this wonderful new CD, Me And My Guitar. John re-imagines many of his old songs in new and intimate ways. The first words I think of as I listen are “sincerity with purpose”. John is expressing his feelings in every song with strong voice and the wisdom of his now long career, and I think he wants us to really appreciate all the emotions he’s experienced in his decades of writing and recording. Think about it this way: if you could do something over again, with the of experience and the decisions you've made, would you be able to do it better? John has succeeded in this exercise.

If you are a fan of his duo days with Mark Rodney, James Lee Stanley and Michael McLean, or his catalog of solo discs, you’ll be so pleased to hear this variety of special songs painted in fresh ways. Listen to Poor Man’s Dream and hear John reflect about how grateful and lucky he STILL is for all the love he’s had and the career he’s experienced, with all its ups and downs. Enjoy the gentle beauty as he tells us again that “It’s Gonna Be Alright.” I especially love the new, acoustic versions of “You Are a Song” and “Is This Love,” as the third CD from B & R was so overproduced that the meaning of these tunes was almost lost in the noise. “Time to Say Goodnight” is the right ending to our living room show.

This is John Batdorf sharing his unforgettable songs in a new and engaging way, with pristine, you-are-in-the-room production. He's shown us once again how right we were when we fell in love with his music as teenagers, and we can still recognize and enjoy his greatness in his fifth decade of music-making.
