title: Is this remaster worth it?
text:
I've seen a lot of reviews about remastering the Hendrix cds.....I've bought so many remasters without really thinking about it. I saw a review of his first LP where someone said the vocal were lower in the mix on certain songs.....remastering is not remixing separate tracks! It's only equalizing the overall tones on the record, also compressing, and adjusting the loudness of it. I've heard remastered cd's where the loudness was emphasized but ended up more distorted....here's a note on mastering from wikipedia......

"Remastering music for CD or even digital distribution first starts from locating the original analog version.[1] The next step involves digitising the track or tracks so it can be edited using a computer. Then the track order is chosen. This is something engineers often worry about because if the track order is not right, it may seem sonically unbalanced.[1]

When the remastering starts, engineers use software tools such as a limiter, an equaliser, and a compressor. The compressor and limiters are ways of controlling the loudness of a track.[1] However, this is not to be confused with the volume of a track, which is controlled by the listener during playback.

The dynamic range of an audio track is measured by calculating the variation between the loudest and the quietest part of a track.[1] In recording studios the loudness is measured with negative decibels, zero designates the loudest recordable sound. A limiter works by having a certain cap on the loudest parts and if that cap is exceeded, it is automatically lowered by a ratio preset by the engineer.[1]
Criticism

Remastered audio has been the subject of criticism.[2][3] Many remastered CDs from the late 1990s onwards have been affected by the "loudness war", where the average volume of the recording is increased and dynamic range is compressed at the expense of clarity, making the remastered version sound louder at regular listening volume and more distorted than an uncompressed version.[2][3] Some have also criticized the overuse of noise reduction in the remastering process, as it affects not only the noise, but the signal too, and can leave audible artifacts.[4][5] Equalisation can change the character of a recording noticeably. As EQ decisions are a matter of taste to some degree, they are often the subject of criticism. Mastering engineers such as Steve Hoffman have noted that using flat EQ on a mastering allows listeners to adjust the EQ on their equipment to their own preference, but mastering a release with a certain EQ means that it may not be possible to get a recording to sound right on high-end equipment.[2][3] Additionally, from an artistic point of view, original mastering involved the original artist, remastering often not. Therefore, many times remasters result in a totally changed character of the music."

title: 'VOLTS' is actually Disc 4 in the Bonfire Box Set
text:
Volts is an album by AC/DC released as a part named "Disc Four" on the Bonfire box set. Released in November 1997, the album is a compilation of some alternate versions of songs recorded for the albums Let There Be Rock and Highway to Hell, and some songs previously released.

A hidden track containing various interviews appears after a short amount of silence following the last track. The album is the first rarity album by AC/DC, followed by Studio Rarities in 2009. Both albums are discs in rarity box sets (in Studio Rarities case, the box set is Backtracks).

TRACKLIST:
1. "Dirty Eyes" - 3:21
2. "Touch Too Much" - 6:34
3. "If You Want Blood (You've Got It)" - 4:28
4. "Back Seat Confidential" - 5:23
5. "Get It Hot" - 4:17
6. "Sin City" (live) - 4:58
7. "She's Got Balls" (live) - 7:57
8. "School Days" - 5:23
9. "It's a Long Way to the Top (If You Wanna Rock 'n' Roll)" - 5:14
10. "Ride On" - 10:03

-"Dirty Eyes" is an early recording, which later turned out as the song "Whole Lotta Rosie" which is found on both versions of Let There Be Rock.
-"Touch Too Much" is the same track found on Highway to Hell, but with different riffs and lyrics.
-"If You Want Blood (You've Got It)" is the same track found on Highway to Hell, but with different lyrics.
-"Back Seat Confidential" is an early recording, which turned into the song "Beating Around the Bush", which is found on Highway to Hell.
-"Get It Hot" is the same track found on Highway to Hell, but with different riffs and lyrics.
-"Sin City" was recorded live from Midnight Special on September 6, 1978.
-"Walk All Over You" & "T.N.T." were recorded live from Let There Be Rock: The Movie in the Australian version.
-"She's Got Balls" was recorded live from the Bondi Lifesaver, and is also found as a b-side to the single "You Shook Me All Night Long".
-"School Days" is from T.N.T., and was previously unreleased outside of Australia.
-"It's a Long Way to the Top (If You Wanna Rock 'n' Roll)" was previously released on T.N.T. a different version appears on the international version of High Voltage.
-"Ride On" was previously released on the Australian and international releases of Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap, and there are several hidden interview tracks after this song.

title: Good Concept, Bad Music
text:
So, to be fair, this music isn't TERRIBLE, but it's definitely not very good either. The songs aren't very melodic and seem to just trudge on through the lyrics. The songs are pedestrian and predictable, and while the cast (who all sound very much alike) makes their way through them well enough, they just aren't memorable or interesting. You just know there's going to be some brooding lyric that tries really hard to be poetic and dramatic, and then there's going to be some kind of build at the end and a really long high note at the end. Meh. There seem to be a lot of instances of the words "passion," "evil within," "gaze" rhyming with "blaze" and other such expected lyrics. It's just not great songwriting, and I really don't see it making its way to success on the Great White Way. It sounds like one long song cut into several short tracks, rather than a cohesive series of coherent and unique songs. The songs that actually stand out sound a little like rip-offs of other composers (see below).

Having recently been introduced to both this version as well as the concept recordings of Wildhorn's version, it's hard not to make comparisons. Wildhorn's music might sound a little more contemporary, but the story moves along better and there's more variety and better pacing to the score. To take something like Dracula and turn it into a musical seems like an ambitious and daunting (and unnecessary?) undertaking, and I believe it can be done, but this is not it.

title: beautiful record
text:
a good friend who has a knack for turning up the best things a thrift store has to offer found this somewhere--and I have no idea where--and gave it to a mutual friend of ours. I have listened to it twice, and can think of nothing to compare it to.

the most important thing to say about this record is that isla has a beautiful voice and a keen ear for interesting songs. the songs are either unaccompanied or only sparely ornamented, allowing the haunting melodies and unforgettable words to shine.

these are definitely rough gems--someone like joan baez will give you a much more polished feel, but this is the coveted "real thing" of folk music. isla listened to misremembered songs from already-aged people born before the turn of the 20th century, and tried to find the center of traditional songs from that.

I would definitely recommend this to someone interested in the history of folk music. I myself would love to have my own copy, and would even take a set of the mp3's of these songs, but the real lp has fascinating liner notes and is quite worth tracking down.

title: Jesus this album is boring...
text:
Granted, I found this band when searching for music similar to Faded Paper Figures. Such narrow searches are bound to come up a little short, and so this one did.

Originally I was able to find two songs by A Big yes and A Small No that I enjoyed enough to purchase the album. Those songs, however, are all this album seems to offer. Even they appear to wither in the context of this overtly poppy album. While typically I love true indie releases like this one, sometimes the reality is simply that there is a lot of music available these days and not all of it can be that exceptional. Basically, releasing an album (especially if you're from NYC) is no longer a sign that your band has that something special.

In the case of ABYAASN (really guys, what's with this name!?) it appears that they haven't quite gotten over their high school ska years. Or maybe they're still in high school, who knows. Not that there is anything wrong with ska undertones, and if that is your thing you very well may like this album more than I do. But it appears more that The Hippos and Belle & Sebastian spent one night of passion together and, nine months later, out came this average little album (emphasis on average).

All things considered, this album is not bad. The lyrics are somewhat silly but not nauseating, all band members appear to play their instruments adequately, recording quality is fine, packaging is neat, but the whole shebang just comes out as bland. Maybe you have to be friends with the guys to really get into their music, or have seen them live, or something. I just don't know. But if you are expecting more gems like "This Doesn't Feel Like Goodbye" or "I'm Always Manic", you may find this album sadly lacking.

title: Terrible re-mastering of a terrible album
text:
In 1969 after the Hassles broke up, keyboardist Billy Joel and drummer Jonathan Small started Attila. While the organ and percussion type instrumentation has worked with bands such as Hardin and York (both formerly of the Spencer Davis Group), it does not work all that well in this case, mainly because Attila is attempting to be a heavy metal band. Sure they' re certainly noisy, but I don't know if that is all that makes a metal band. Joel runs his organ through what sounds like distortion and wah-wah pedals to achieve what the original album's liner notes referred to as pure raunch. Joel also handles all the bass lines on the bass pedals of the organ.

While both Joel and Small have technical ability, the actual songwriting on this album is horrible. With lyrics like "Revenge is sweet, you can not kiss my feet and admit you were wrong" and instrumental numbers that sound like a psychedelic baseball game the only merit this album has is it's unintentional humor. The CD version listed here was issued several years ago by a small label out of Philadelphia (although they seem to have their discs mostly made in the Netherlands) called Creative Sounds Limited. As with most shoddy Creative Sound releases, this album was poorly mastered from a vinyl source. To make matters worse this recording is slightly off pitch either by someone not paying attention to the strobe on the turntable or attempted to slow it down slightly to make the younger Joel sound like the older Joel most people are familiar with. There is also a balance issue causing one channel to be slightly muffled which is really annoying since this stereo album is filled with panning effects.

As far as the confusing title goes, that was because early versions of this CD had about six odd tracks from an album from around 1980 called the "The Tough Boy" released by Billy Joel and the Hassels (yes, that is how they spelled it on the cover). This record was of questionable origin and while it obviously did not have any actual ties to Joel himself, I have not seen anything which states whether or not those tracks have any ties to the Hassles themselves. Either way it sounded every bit of 1980 and nothing like the actual band The Hassles from the late '60s (which you are not really missing much there either). I guess the folks at Creative Sound realized that those tracks had no actual Joel connection and yanked them off the cd, changed the layout of the tray card, but for some reason kept the same front cover. Anyway the two titles alluded to the fact you were getting two albums on one cd which really it equated to an album and an EP. I guess they thought putting a sticker that said single over the printing that said "double album" as good enough. Pretty much par for the course for Creative Sounds Ltd.

title: Ironically, this is the last album I bought of his
text:
This album has a lot of the original tracks from Live at Stubb's, and was released a year earlier. This was his first album, and it feels really authentic and full of real roots reggae. It is not an album that resembles anything he's done since. It is a very pure album, without all the bells and whistles of his latest albums. It shows why he has become so popular since then, because he had tremendous talent. I now know why some people said Youth was "overproduced." Compared to this first album, I'd have to agree, but I liked Youth, Light, and Spark Seeker, although Spark Seeker took me a little while to warm up to it.

This album has some really great tracks on it, starting strong with Chop Em Down, then going to some Jewish chant on the second track that you can hear on Live at Stubb's Vol. II, before he launches into Got No Water on both of those albums, which is such a great song. Then he goes to King Without a Crown, which is almost as good as the live version he did on his live album. The next track is Father in the Forest, and it has a nice, interesting sound to it. Then, Aish Tamid, which is another one of my favorites, is sung with almost complete accuracy to the live version. I haven't really listened to Short Nigun, because it seems to be a nonvocal, and I generally don't listen to those much. Candle is a little too long, but it's not a bad song. Close My Eyes is one of the best on this album, mostly because it also includes Heights from the live album. I guess he took that song apart for the live album. Either way, that song is one of the best. Then he sings Exaltation, which is also an amazing song on the live album, and on this one, it is also very good, nearly as good as his live version. Refuge is another great song, as it is similar to his live one, but with different lyrics at time. Finally, Warrior is such an amazing track, and is almost a carbon copy of his live version, although with a slightly different sound.

I'd say that this album has a very raw sound, and you can tell that this is a debut album, not because it is poorly produced, but because it is exactly what he wanted it to be. Many debut albums turn out to be an artist/band's best work, like The Dirty Heads (so far), and Sublime's 40 oz. to Freedom (although you could argue that their self-titled album was better). I'm sure most of the songs Matis wrote here before he was ever signed to a label. That is when creativity is usually higher IMO. This is where Matisyahu was born as an artist, and I have to say that it is one hell of a debut. So just sit back, close your eyes, take a ride inside, and let this music let you fly. ;)

title: A Very Good Collection for a Bargain Price
text:
A very nice set of this wonderful band. Has Silver Shoes which is a rarity, although this song does not sound remastered compared to some of the other tracks. My guess is that this 2-CD set contains a mixture of remastered and not-remastered tracks.

There are a few live versions but unfortunately there are no details of where and when the live versions were recorded. Instead the liner notes list the album that contains the the studio version of the song. The live version of "Rock N' Roll Widow" in this collection is exceptional. I have the first Live Dates album and judging from the introductory comments before the song, this version came from that 1973 recording.

Other live versions are Warrior (also from 1973's Live Dates I believe) and Living Proof. Both are excellent live tracks.

The rest of the songs seem to be full length studio versions, all from before 1970-1990. CD 1 is 74 minutes and CD 2 is 71 minutes. Not bad.

I would say this is not your basic starter set of "best of" for this band. For sure some classics are here (Blowing Free, Jail Bait, Warrior, etc.), but some of my very favorite songs are not included (Time Was; You Rescue Me; Lorelei; Outward Bound; F.U.B.B.; Rest In Peace; Goodbye Baby, Hello Friend; The Pilgrim; Doctor; Phoenix; Strange Affair). But it is worth it to get a few of the lesser known tunes I did not have.

title: True Beethoven in Alfred Brendel’s hands
text:
I think there are no other composers dearer to his heart and more suitable to his style than Beethoven and Schubert. Maybe Haydn's humorous subtexts or Mozart's floating cantabiles could appeal Brendel's musical interests at a comparable extent as - and come close to - his fondness of serving Beethoven and Schubert. However, these four giants of the Viennese Classicism have long been his four aces so that Brendel's reputation owes them its most consistent part. Therefore it is not a surprise that he recorded the complete cycle of Beethoven sonatas no less than three times, each at a different age, in a constantly ascendant development as a performing artist.

An always-elegant touch and a very subtle insight helped Brendel - during a longish career, spanning 60 years on stage - give benchmark renditions of those giants' masterpieces to be cherished by his large number of admirers. If one adds the flattering title of "thinker at the piano", earned from worldwide audiences and critics alike, this could explain the top position Alfred Brendel secured for himself among the contemporary pianists. His erudition overlapped his keen sensitivity and infallible musical intuitions, as to supply a seductively witty, serene, perfumed style of playing. So personal, though scrupulously rigorous with regard to the score.

This recorded cycle of complete Beethoven sonatas dates from Brendel's full maturity, being recorded and released in the first half of the 1990s, a period of great achievements in his artistic life. His legendary classical poise is nowhere better highlighted than here, in his last recorded traversal of Beethoven sonatas. Each of the 10 CD asserts for his conception. According to it a masterpiece should not be forced to mould the performer's obsessions or affinities - instead the performer has to find its essence and look for both the closest empathy with composer's intentions and the most natural re-thinking the score in its own terms. Otherwise, the masterpiece can well be considered betrayed. Any interpretation should remain within this ineffable contour and serve the truths of the piece. It is exactly what Brendel achieves here. In a magisterially refined manner!

Guided by Alfred Brendel, immersing in the all-embracing inner world of Beethoven becomes a pure delight!

title: Eye candy 'till you're diabetic
text:
Lucas, three words to you: "Less is more!"
CGI now permits a director to pack every screen with so much visual detail that you go into overload - to make dazzling CGI sets with nothing real in them at all. It *allows* the director to do that. George Lucas doesn't realise that it's one thing to have the capacity to do something, and it is quite another to actually do it. Again and again Lucas has said: "Special effects now allow us to do things that wouldn't even be possible back in the original films." Then why do the original films look so much more realistic?
Just because you *can* stuff a screen with photorealistic spaceships is no excuse to go around doing it. I mean, animated cartoons can display what they like too, and have been around for a lot longer. An animated movie would not be so tastelessly overdone as this!
By the way, the benefit of CGI is *not* that it makes special effects look *more real* than miniatures - it only allows you to do *new things*. It's capability, not degree. In this film, you can tell what's CGI and what's not - it's just blindingly obvious. If films are so blue-screened, they suffer. Those who think the new "digital Yoda" is "more real" than the puppet, have forgotten that Yoda never existed: only the puppet existed. SO essentially, making Yoda look *more real* than the puppet was utterly pointless.
Apart from "eye candy diabetes", there are major problems with the film. The storyline makes no sense, and has not the structural soundness of the earlier films. The script is awful. Lucas has said: "I rely on visuals, not dialogue". Yet the visuals and dialogue both fail.
Actually, this review has been 4/5 on visuals and 1/5 on everything else. That's a good match for the film!

title: El mejor CD de Juan Luis desde Fogaraté
text:
Por descuido de mi parte no había podido zambullirme en este nuevo CD de Juan Luis Guerra. ¡Cuánto lo lamento!

Tengo sentimientos mezclados al escucharlo, pero la mezcla de los mismos es un caldo de alegría, satisfacción... y lágrimas de felicidad. Creo que desde "Fogaraté" no me emocionaba tanto con un CD de Juan Luis. En esta ocasión, creo que la misión de Juan Luis ha sido la de volver a las letras románticas, a cantarle al amor, a sensibilizarnos con sus rimas sencillas e ingeniosas. Juan Luis logra inyectarnos el ritmo y la poesía de una manera muy parecida a los tiempos en que "La Bilirrubina" era un himno de alegría (aún lo es, sin dudas).

"Medicine for my soul" abre las puertas. Es la versión en inglés de "La Llave de mi corazón", y a mi juicio, hace más lógica escucharla en inglés que en español. Los versos "cuadran" mejor al ubicarse en un gringo de Lousiana enamorado de una "latin girl" de San Pedro de Macorís que un chico de Ciudad nueva. :) La nota beisbolística queda igual para ambas versiones, pues menciona a Sammy Sosa, quien se esfuerza por regresar a las Grandes Ligas. Supongo que el otrora "Bambino del Caribe" debe sentirse más motivado con este detalle. Pero volviendo al tema, es tremendamente pegajoso, y como siempre nos ha acostumbrado Juan Luis, un malabarismo de tonadas y arreglos. Empieza como un mambo que de inmediato nos recuerda a Pérez Prado, pero sin dejar de enriquecer la canción con la característica percusión salsera y los sonidos bachateros. Definitivamente, es tremendamente contagiosa.

"La Travesía" es un merengue con profunda percusión y moderadamente rápido (nada parecido a la agitación de "La Cosquillita" o "El Farolito"). La base lírica es sencilla: No hay nadie como tú en todo el mundo. Y es un tema didáctico, pues quien lo escuche debería sentirse motivado a investigar los lugares de los cuales habla en la canción. Debe ser excelente para bailarlo en cualquier fiesta.

"Te contarán" llega a ritmo de salsa, con un tumbao que no se me parece a nadie. Una salsa muy correcta, sin el dramatismo vocal de Marc Anthony, más bien cercana al ritmo pedagógico de Gilberto Santa Rosa. Pero Juan Luis es su propio imitador, y busca sus propias fronteras. "Te contarán" es también un canto al amor único, al amor insuperable. Te contarán que no hay un corazón que te ame igual que yo, es su premisa y sí que lo logra.

"Que me des tu cariño" es la primera bachata de este CD, y diría que la más hermosa desde que nos encandiló con sus letras de "Bachata Rosa". "Que me des tu cariño" es una excusa para cantar bajito al oído y enamorar a la enamorada. Suave tonada y delicado arreglo de metáforas.

"Como yo" resuena a ritmo de merengue y me recuerda bastante al "Niagara en Bicicleta", pero por supuesto sin el toque de protesta social sustituido por el canto al amor y la contemplación de la dicha.

"Si tú no bailas conmigo" es un compendio de metáforas que asombra, una tras otra va maravillando más que la anterior, y girando todo alrededor de una sencilla idea: la noche se conjura para bailar, pero si no bailas conmigo, prefiero no bailar. Es un merengue lento, casi acústico, ideal para abrir cualquier boda (y darle descanso a "Tú") o para que tu novia te enseñe a (por fin) dominar el baile de nuestra música. Esta es, por mucho, mi canción preferida de todo el CD.

"Sólo tengo ojos para ti" es una suave balada romántica. Demasiado romántica, si se puede pensar en que la belleza puede ser demasiado bella alguna vez. Juan Luis canta a la fidelidad, canta a la entrega, canta al compromiso que se renueva con cada verso que sale, con cada acorde que suena de su guitarra. Sencillamente, es una de las canciones más hermosas que he escuchado en mi vida.

"Amores" es un merengue como en los viejos tiempos, con una base rítmica muy diversa (a veces suena como los vallenatos de Carlos Vives, a veces le escuchas acordes de latin jazz). La letra es quizás la menos bonita de todo el CD, en el sentido de que no es tan asombrosa como cualquiera de las demás piezas.

"Cancioncita de amor" nos trae una salsa dividida en dos secciones, empieza lenta y suavemente, y se acelera un poco en el último minuto recordándome por un momento los coros de "A pedir su mano". Tiene una estructura muy fácil de seguir y muy bailable.

"Sabia manera" es un bolero abachateado que podría ser balada también. La única crítica que podría decir de este tema es que suena demasiado triste, cuando la letra es, nueva vez, un canto al amor. Siento que tiene acordes de despecho pero letras de esperanzada dulzura.

"La llave de mi corazón" es la canción que da título al CD completo, y tiene el mismo arreglo que "Medicine for my soul", que es la versión en inglés. Como expresé antes, es un mambo muy chévere, pero personalmente me gusta más el arreglo en inglés que en español.

"Something good" es una sorpresa. No me esperaba encontrar una pieza tan hermosa, en inglés, y a dúo con Chiara Civella, a quien confieso no conocer. La canción es en bachata y el saxo le da un toque de jazz tremendamente exótico. Y el ritmo... ¡es maravilloso! Es mi segunda favorita de todo el álbum.

"A la vera" es una balada que termina siendo merengue lento, y por las letras hay que ubicarse en tierra adentro. Es un tema que me recuerda el sentimiento de esperanza de "Ojalá que llueva café".

En mi opinión, este es el mejor CD de Juan Luis Guerra desde "Fogaraté". Sólo me encuentro mejor a "Bachata Rosa", "Ojalá que llueva café" y "Fogaraté". Pero sin dudas, este CD ganará muchos premios, es un producto tremendamente bien hecho, que le da de nuevo un aire positivo a la carrera de este artista del mundo.

Estoy feliz de haberlo adquirido. ¡FELIZ!

title: Essential Album From A Very Underrated Rock Band
text: Pittsburgh does not get its proper due as a city that produced some great bands. I attended Pitt in the '80s, and the scene was pretty amazing. You had Carsickness, The Five, the sadly short-lived Whereabouts, Norm Nardini & The Tigers, and the Houserockers, who were always on the verge of breaking out nationally. If you love anthemic bar band rock with astute lyrics, you will love "Have A Good Time...", and I'm happy to see a 40th anniversary reissue with bonus tracks. Not sure if this was remastered, but the sound is fine for me. Make sure to listen to the one-two punch of "Old Man Bar" and "Junior's Bar." Sorry for waxing nostalgic, but it takes me back to the Iron City-sticky floors of The Decade nightclub where the Houserockers often played. They were exponentially better live than they were recorded, but this is the album that best captures their magic. I can only hope that their follow-up "Blood on the Bricks" gets some anniversary love as well.

title: I am reminded of what made John Williams a household name
text:
This was one of those wild purchases I was unfamiliar with that I bought for 3 reasons:
I was looking for some Americana folk-type music
It's John Williams
I got it 33% off

If you would have asked me in the '90s who my favorite composer was, I would no doubt have said John Williams. Limited as my knowledge of soundtrack music was I knew one thing for sure -- this man's resume covered, by far, the majority of the film music that had an indelible effect on not only my appreciation of film score, but my musical tastes as a whole. Not that this is unique, but at the old age of 3 I was moved and exhilarated for the first time by the film music of Star Wars (1977). So, it is odd that between The Last Crusade (1989) and Phantom Menace (1999) there is a major gap that I call -- the '90s. I have the excellent collection John Williams Greatest Hits 1969-1999, but just don't find myself listening to the '90s music nearly as much as the older work.

I have always bought soundtracks, but would only recently consider myself an enthusiast, having discovered all the small labels that produce high quality expanded, "complete," and limited editions of film score within the last 4 years. One such label is La La Land Records who released this expanded version of Rosewood. I was reading peoples thoughts on this score for sometime, but since I didn't think much of the film at the time it was released didn't even consider buying it. Well, LLL had a buy 2 get one free sale and while narrowing down my choices and going back and forth on what I might buy at this price range I noticed Rosewood never left my list, so I gave a listen to the samples on their website and was quite intrigued by what I heard. Half of me was quite nervous as I've done this in the past with less than stellar results, but I went ahead and took the plunge...

This album is fantastic! This is one of the many cases where the music far exceeds the film in every way. It is at the very top with my favorite scores and very unique to anything else in my collection. The music is so rich, wonderfully orchestrated and beautifully played. The themes and motifs are quite beautiful with the hint of darkness that occasionally reappears. After the first listen I just sat and contemplated what I had just heard. I can't say that happens very often, even for other scores that I truly adore. The guitar, harp and woodwinds really draw me in. There are moments so gentle, fragile then streaks of despair start streaming through. Again, beautiful. The "southern action" work is quite invigorating. Then there are the tense "waiting" moments expertly crafted to keep you suspensefully on the edge of your seat. Regardless of the way I interpret it, just know that you get very high caliber music here. There are 2 brilliant gospel tracks that may (or may not) surprise Williams fans. In the very informative liner notes it is pointed out that John Singleton was apprehensive about hiring Williams for the authenticity of the black experience until the composer reminded the director that he had arranged and conducted for gospel singer Mahalia Jackson. I think many would agree that Williams succeeded with his gospel work here.

You get a wealth of material with the 78 minute score on disc 1 and the remastered 50 minute original soundtrack on disc 2. Some have complained about the 2 gospel songs that are not in sequential order in the score, but come on -- they aren't missing since the soundtrack is included. I think LLL did the right thing here for flow and spacial reasons. The packaging is very nice as usual from LLL with the aforementioned liner notes, film stills and track notes.

So happy I chose to go for this score.

title: VINTAGE SOUNDTRACK
text: For a long while, I was reluctant to buy this Monstrous Movie Music CD edition of the Rocketship X-M soundtrack mostly because of the negative reviews.  Let's set things straight.  The soundtrack is a nearly 80-year old recording made well before audio fidelity and stereo production methods were common place.  Like a number of other post-WWII B-movie soundtracks, the original was a "mono" recording and likely made with less than "A" quality recording equipment.  Compared to anything recorded after 1965 - it lacks audio quality and a left-right sound stage (channel separation) so yes it sounds flat and a little harsh at times.  But if you have to criticize, blame the source material that's available because the production values of the CD itself are first rate.  I have audition the CD three times now and all I hear is the music, there's no discernible background noise or transcription sounds as reported by others.  The only way this soundtrack could be made to sound any better would be a new recording of the music like what has been done with Creature From The Black Lagoon, The Bride of Frankenstein or the original King Kong.  (Here's my $100 to help initiate a new recording.)  The liner notes are extensive and quite thorough; the cover artwork is superb.  For soundtrack fans, this is the only way we can hear Ferde Grofe's evocative music outside of the film.  I'm very thankful the CD's producers elected to make this MMM edition available.  Recommended.

title: wonderful, first-rate music from a very obscure composer
text:
All the pieces on this CD have a somewhat 'exotic flavor' about them - the melodies, harmonies, indeed overall "sound". One can readily imagine scenes from more remote regions of SE Europe on hearing them. While there's no telling whether any other of Djabadary's works are anywhere near the equal of those on this CD, i would take a chance & immediately buy further recording(s) of his music.
A note about my musical tastes (as guidance to others): my interest spans from the Renaissance (Gabrieli) to even near mid-20th century (Bartok) in musical 'idiom', if you will. But my heart lies in the Romantic era, including its extension into the early 20th century ( this latter most notably perhaps in Richard Strauss' writing). Djabadary's 'idiom' lies within the later part of the Romantic era, but well within it. His music also reminds me of the work of two Romanian composers, whose names escape me @ moment.

title: A Cats fan Must-Have

I was then prompted to buy one of the cast albums, so I used a gift card I got for my birthday to get what I thought would be the original Broadway cast recording, but I instead got the London cast version. No problem. I would've gotten either of them. Anyway, I like the slipcase and libretto that comes with it, though the slipcase doesn't take long to get dented and smudged by anything that touches it. The printing is very nice and the pictures included are a nice touch. The CDs are remastered versions of the original recording and they sound amazing. It's cool to go from any later version of Cats and then listen to the very original version. The ways the musical has evolved and remained the same overtime is interesting. The cast is full of excellent voices that sound heavenly to listen to. The one downside about this album is that it doesn't include "The Awefull Battle of the Pekes and the Pollicles". While not a huge loss, it is an entertaining part of the musical that would've been nice to include. Overall, this is definitely a must-have for any Cats fan like me.

title: Remixed, Remastered and Resplendent
text:
There's a Christmas song containing the lyrics, "it's the time of year when the world falls in love..." Well, that tune is not on this CD. It's on the Sinatra Christmas album. But, the lyrics represent a feeling that the music on this cd embraces. I've listened to this album for many years and have always enjoyed the emotional warmth that is embodied in the arrangements and the voices of the children, as well as the almost ethereal qualities on a few of the cuts. These qualities stem from the delicate piano touch and light jazz phrasings of Vince Guaraldi. It's infectious. Guaraldi does a superb rendition of My Little Drum (actually,The Little Drummer Boy, a hit for the Harry Simeone Chorale in 1958). I never cared for the song, but the combination of the voices and the soft piano touch results in a relaxing work of beauty that I can now enjoy.

This is one of the few Christmas releases that I've never found tiring or tedious. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys Christmas and winter seasonal music. It is mostly jazzy, pleasant and soothing.

This 2006 release contains four alternate takes in addition to the full album. The sound quality is excellent and much improved over the 1988 CD release.

title: You Can Do This In You Own Time, Marv, But Not In Mine.
text: You may wonder why I'm reviewing this album so long after it was released. The answer is simple. When I first heard it I thought that it was a mess. I wanted to listen to it more and give it time to grow on me. It hasn't. If, like me, you're  a fan of Quarterflash, I fail to see how you can be enthusiastic about this album. Everything about it is wrong - the music, the production, even the cover. I loved the band's "reunion" album "Goodbye Uncle Buzz", which had beautiful songs and crystal clear production. It was Quarterflash for people who had, like the band, matured. What Marv and Rindy Ross are trying to do here is a mystery, but if they want to alienate their listeners, they have succeeded. I have listened with an open mind and with the idea that they wanted to create something different. What I hear is like a drunken Quarterflash fooling around at rehearsal. By the time the only decent tune, track 8 "Little Miracles" arrives, it's too late, and this is followed by "Rock On Little Brother", which is such a mess that I can't bear to listen to it all the way through. Marv Ross may want to stick two fingers up at me for this, but just as he's entitled to experiment, I'm entitled not to like it. And what's with the mushy production that gives little clarity to the vocals and instruments? This was co-produced by the drummer. Does he really want his kit to sound like cardboard boxes? I thought of being kind and giving this album two stars, but when my disappointment is so overwhelming, I just can't. Get a grip, Quarterflash.

title: Richard McNamee is a guitarist worth listening to
text:
A Groove Tune is a piece of music that hits in your hip and feet before your head. Booker T. recorded lots of them in Memphis, as did the Meters in New Orleans., Wes Montgomery etc. The music on this CD is clearly influenced by the greats of blues guitar.

From the CD sleeve ... "Testimony in the Church of last luscious loose groove, the gosple according to Stax, Mowtown and Chess. A soulasm abiding the funkalsitic principles laid down by he Saints: Cropper, Dunn, Jones, Jackson, Jamerson, Montgomery, Brown, Toussaint, King and Charles. Sunglasses recommended, seat belts required. ... Messages from a Soul dimension where there is grace under the grease of the groove ... let the good times blow... Going Grooving Gone".

This sounds like it all went down on tape, with no computers in sight, the music has a real genuine feel to it, as if you've entered the studio through an alley door next to the chicken place. "Grace of the Groove" was a concept put together by Seattle guitarist Richard McNamee. He wanted a contemporary project that would include his favorite musicians playing music written or selected with their strengths in mind. Including: vocalist Mark Dufresne (who was the lead singer for Roomful of Blues as well as on his own CD's), on blues harp; the great, Dick Powell who learned from James Cotton personally; and Dan Hannum , the R&B bass player from coastal Cali (long may he roll). Jerry Lee Davidsen from Chicago's enduring Walter Williams Band sings, as does Virginia Klemens (also a heavyweight from Chicago). The Living Daylights, a globe-trotting power jazz trio, supplied Arnie Livingston on a few bass tracks and the amazing Dale Fanning on drums. Cheri Adams is a Northwest institution as a solo artist and she graced the tracks with some delicious keyboard work. Jeremy Smithson had spent years as a Baptist Minister and church organist in Oakland, (can't get any deeper than that) played some keyboards as well. Another local favorite, Jim Plano, also played drums and told the best stories and there are many stories.

All in all this music is worth listening to again and again, and should be played loud!

title: Amazing debut album!
text:
Like many, I first heard the music from this album on the Weather Channel's Local On The 8s (surprise, surprise!). It was during high school, 10th to 11th grade to be precise, that I was first hearing songs like "Sunshine In The Rain", "Full Sail", and "Adoration" (my personal favorite from this album)... but I had no idea who or what I was listening to. I can even remember how, whenever I was watching the Weather Channel, and when it came time to display the good old Local On The 8s, I was crossing my fingers, hoping that the music would be the piece that I would later know to be "Adoration." If it was, then I'd be like, "Oh yes! Today's my lucky day!" However, soon thereafter, I would forget about worrying the name of this music or who made it, being too immersed in the college application process as I entered my senior year of high school.

Fast forward 14-15 years later... I was at the Museum of Science in Boston, MA (I am a lifelong Boston area local), and I went to see a show at the Charles Hayden Planetarium. It is in these places that they play all sorts of interesting "background music" as some folks with limited mindsets might call it, and the title track of Farish's "Life In Stereo" album happened to be playing in there. I can remember how much I loved it, yet didn't know who or what it was.... but this time, I was armed with my iPhone, and my SoundHound app, and so I whipped it out and had it listen. Sure enough, there it popped up - Life In Stereo, by Ryan Farish... so then I immediately navigated to iTunes, where I downloaded it. However, that isn't what this review is about, so I will save that for when I review that album.

So to get right into it, "Beautiful" is just that... it's absolutely BEAUTIFUL! When I still had my 2011 Jeep Grand Cherokee, this would be one of my top choices for driving music, especially for when I would drive out to the more suburban/semi-rural out-reaches in Eastern Massachusetts, just to observe the beautiful New England landscapes. Not only that, but the music itself, with all the soothing melodies and uplifting feeling made it all the more possible to avoid road rage. Aside from driving in the countryside, this is perfect for listening to on a Sunday morning, a time when everyone loves to kick back and relax. This is really all I can say, seeing as music like this is truly meant for the listener to digest upon actually listening to it.

All this being said, just buy it and listen to it so you can find out for yourself. Ryan is truly a genius of an artist, hands down, and there is no reason for even die-hard metalheads, such as myself, not to appreciate his amazing work. He'll always be light years ahead of all that over-commercialized junk that continues to pollute the airwaves on a daily basis.

Buy it and listen! You won't regret it! :)

title: "blended voices of the angels"
text:
Brian O'Donovan of WGBH in Boston has this to say about the group and the new album:

How do you describe the music of Navan? Yes, technical terms exist. Exquisite... acappella... harmony singing in all of the Celtic languages. But Navan is a classic case of the whole being greater than the sum of its parts. There is something about the blend of human voices without the burden or rhythm of instruments in accompaniment that affects us spiritually. This is the sound we popularly think of as that of angels.

In hearing the songs of Navan on this, their third CD, you will be transported to other places, other times. The sound is ancient, elemental. It is a continuum of experience for Celtic peoples through the ages seeking guidance and comfort in lives tied to the land but looking at the moon. The songs are food for the spirit, a warm drink on a cold night in front of a welcome fire; the smile of a stranger; the softness of a baby's cheek; the sadness of remembrance; and yes, the blended voice of the angels, wherever they may be.

text:
Velvety? Smooth? Smoky? (per another reviewer)

Those adjectives might apply to Karen Cargill in Les Nuits when she's singing softly. Once she lifts off above mezzo forte, her voice goes glassy. At high volume, it's in the peeling-paint-off-the-walls realm.

I don't hear much color or subtlety in her delivery. She seems to be trying to belt these songs out blues-singer style, all poetry driven out of circulation.

La Mort de Cleopatre is better, but I expect anyone who is interested in this disc is mainly looking for a new version of Les Nuits.

Linn recordings are usually top class, but in this case the orchestra is too recessed. Maybe conductor Robin Ticciati was keeping the players on tiptoe not to cover his soloist. He need not have worried. She could have been heard next to a jet engine.

I'm looking once again for a modern version of Berlioz's song cycle. Meanwhile I'll return with relief to Janet Baker.

title: Gorgeous
text:
I had the great luck of screening the US release of this film recently.
Before I list the good, I'll list my one and only complaint:
It is quite gory. If you have difficulty with gore, bring someone with you to the theater who can tell you when you can look up again. On video or DVD, there's always fast-forward.
Now on to everything else:
This movie is one of the most beautiful films I have ever seen. The cinematography is inventive, unique, and truly gorgeous. The use of odd camera angles and slowing of time (more subtle than The Matrix) make the simplest shots (i.e. feet landing in a puddle of mud) a thrill to watch.
Some of the most incredible fight sequences grace this movie, most starring cult-favorite Mark Dacascos. This is probably some of his most beautiful work, giving us a broad spectrum of his great skills. It's also quite obvious that the cuts used during his fight sequences are only there cinematic effect, and not for lack of ability or stamina. Some of his moves (all without wire-work) will leave you breathless.
See it in the theaters, and buy it when it comes out on video. You won't regret it.

title: who has just found out that her husband is exactly like his father and not only cheated on her
text: This is the second book in the new beginnings series and what a book it is! You have LeAnne, a society woman in her 60's, who has spent her entire marriage looking the other way as she was cheated on by her husband. Then you have Nicole, the daughter-in-law of LeAnne in her 30's, who has just found out that her husband is exactly like his father and not only cheated on her, but got his flavor of the day pregnant. Nicole wastes no time, she files for divorce and heads on to start over with her child. LeAnne, taking strength from Nicole, does the same. The story follows them as they find their place in the world and taking care of themselves as they find their way. The relationships they develop with each other and the people they come in contact with. This was a very well written story of starting over and finding a place in the world after losing the only life you have known. The character development was rich and robust. I listened to this book on CD and must say the readers did an excellent job of bringing the characters to life.

title: cover your ears
text:
Musically, this disc is a boon. As recorded sound, it's an assault on the ears. Unfortunately typical of Italian digital transfers from the 1990's, this CD is based on sound from the late 1930's that should be warm and agreeable--EXCEPT that many listeners have no appetite for the surface noise in the original recordings.This surface noise, as it happens, is the very air in which the antique sound swims. If you let the surface noise remain, you hear the full spectrum of sound. To eliminate the noise, you must cut out a great part of the atmosphere. In sonic terms, it's like looking at a ninety-year-old with multiple face-lifts--a parody of the original sound, just as the face-lifted human is a parody of the former self.

The net result is a disagreeably high-pitched sound that attacks the ears. Volume and treble have to be strictly controlled in order for the sound to become palatable. The music's original beauty is lost. The Pro Arte recordings of Haydn quartets, it seems, have never had fully successful transfers to compact disc. The listener would be well advised to look out for the LP's, or to find other digital transfers that are less offensive than the ones produced by this company. The ones by Allegro aren't bad: http://www.amazon.com/Haydn-String-Quartets-Vol-1/dp/B00005YHZA/ref=sr_1_5?s=music&ie=UTF8&qid=1440204628&sr=1-5&keywords=pro+arte+quartet+haydn

title: Interesting, but very misleading title
text:
I've started trying to learn all that I can on the subconscious mind in an attempt to live to my fullest potential. So far, I haven't found the "ah ha!" book that has done the trick for me. A few chapters into The Biology of Belief: Unleashing the Power of Consciousness, Matter, and Miracles, I really thought I had finally found "the" book!

The author has a very strong biology background and has made some interesting discoveries on how cells "think". He ties that in to how colonies of cells are more efficient than single cells and made good arguments in my opinion on how that resulted in the first multi-celled organisms many billions of years ago. I haven't dwelled on it TOO much, but I've always struggled mentally with how the shift from single celled organisms to a living breathing animal could have occurred... I mean what would have prompted a bunch of cells to band together and decide that they would be better off if some of them became a specialized tissue or an organ like a lung? :) This book lifted that fog for me, so I was really entrenched then.

I'm a "computer guy" by profession. In one section, the author started building up one of his eureka moments where he came up with a description of cellular structures that was identical to that of a microprocessor chip. I was very interested to see where this would lead.

Then he started throwing in the words "quantum physics". I love reading about quantum physics. I don't claim to understand much of it, but I am truly fascinated by it and I started setting myself up to hear the author's opinion on how cells might communicate with the subconscious via a quantum physics mechanism rather than being confined to those of classical Newtonian methods.

So at this point, I can't put the book down. I'm honestly not much of a reader (although I've been getting better about that lately), but I was going full speed on this book. I got to chapter 7, and I thought it was kind of a random tangent to the rest of the book. It was all about DNA selection/masking in the prenatal and early infant stages of life with an overtone of how to be a good parent during this time. It was interesting, but I'm not a parent so I was ready to get on to the parts that were relevant to me!

Chapter 7 was definitely a turning point in the book though, so I thought we were just starting to get into the "Unleashing" part that the subtitle promised. I purchased the Kindle version of this book for my iPhone, and if you're flipping through and focused on the book, you don't have any concept of how far along you are in the book as a whole. So I got to the end of chapter 7 and flipped to the next page, and....... That was the end of the book! @#%!@ I couldn't believe it!

There was no interesting connections made on his viewpoints of why a cell is like a microprocessor, the quantum physics never got any deeper than implying that biology and medicine today are still deeply entrenched in Newtonian physics, but most disappointing of all was that there was definitely no "Unleashing the Power of Consciousness, Matter, and Miracles". For that matter, there really wasn't any "Biology of Belief". It was truly an interesting and well written book on biology and how cells communicate. There really was nothing regarding the subconscious mind. The author made a point several times to show how he wasn't exactly mainstream in his biology field, so I was let down by the fact that he stopped so abruptly and didn't tie all of this together (even if it was a wild opinion on his part).

I was even more let down that there was no section whatsoever on his thoughts on how we can use anything in his book to make changes in our lives. I finally flipped a little further past the epilog and found an addendum where he comes right out and says that when he does lectures on this topic, his audience is pretty much left with the same feeling of "Ok, that was interesting, but where's the good stuff?! How do we do something about it!?" His answer is directing them to his partner Robert Williams who does seminars on his "PSYCH-K" technique. If you look that up, you'll see that they cross-reference one another and push each other's products. The author even touts PSYCH-K as a cure-all because that is what motivated him to finish this book. To me, that's an argument against it because I felt very strongly that this book was not finished and he just got tired of doing it and slapped an ending on it.

If you're looking for an interesting read on cellular biology, I have absolutely no problem recommending this book. If you are like me and were drawn here by the title that implies that you will gain useful self-help knowledge, keep shopping. Biology books don't sell as good as self-help books I'm guessing. :)

If any of you have suggestions on books that you think would have been more in line with what I was looking for, please comment!

title: excellent recital of Italian Renaissance music, impaired by the absence of texts
text:
Excellent recital of Italian Renaissance music, recorded in 1986 by IMP Classics, centered around Florence and music composed for the Carnival period (May 1 - June 14) in the days of Lorenzo de' Medici (1469 - 1492) and the Dutch composer established in Florence, Heinrich Isaac. Good and varied mixture of instrumental (lute & guitar, drum, recorder & shawn, sackbuts, cornett, viol) and vocal (always multiple voices, madrigal like), and, within the madrigals, of a cappella and accompanied, and good and varied mixture of the lively-playful and meditative-solemn. Other than the instruments, th booklet credits three (male) singers as comprising London Pro Musica, counter-tenor and two tenors, but I hear four including a basso, so I am supposing that conductor Bernard Thomas also sings. London Pro Muica was an ensemble specializing in Renaissance music, especially that of Italy, widely toured in Great Britain and continental Europe. There's still a London Pro Musica choir active today, but it is based in London... Ontario, Canada (!!!), and I doubt that it has anything to do with this earlier Renaissance ensemble. There's also a London Pro Musica publisher of ancient music, and this one based in London England, so maybe that is a distant offshoot of the performing ensemble, but I don't know.

All that is fine, except for the absence of texts and translations of the madrigals sung, which hampers enjoyment. As everyone with a taste for Italian madrigals will know, madrigals aren't just "pure" music, intertwining melodic lines meant to be vaguely listened to. No, they are setting of words, poetry, and if you can't follow closely the words, you just remain at the surface, you are condemned to listen only vaguely. Layer of disappointment, then, in a recital which could have been highly enjoyable.

IMP was an interesting English label, first set up by Pickwick in the early days of the CD, then passed on to Carlton Classics in the mid 1990s, and they disappeared around the end of that decade. Many of their installments sell for 1 penny and many more for less than a pound on the UK sister company. How can one resist. I've bought hundreds.

title: Too "Sunday school" to be cool
text:
Back when I purchased this CD, I had thought it was pretty good because it was one of the first contemporary Christian CDs to try and approach a real dance pop sound (she, Kim Boyce and Renee Garcia were some of the pioneers in the style). But listening to it now, I can see the "square peg/round hole" syndrome.

Angie Alan just was never really cut out for singing dance diva vocals...she almost never injects any real fire. And the tracks sound more 80s than 90s. La-la-la vocals give a Sunday school air to "Let's Get Busy". "Until We Meet Again" has a lovely arrangement, but Alan is shown up by it. Instead of soaring over it, you kind of wish they'd mix her out so you could hear the BGV's better. Nonetheless, two tracks here made the Christian radio charts: #12 "The Bottom Line" and #16 "Never Givin' Up".

HIGHLIGHTS:
The best cuts are probably the title track, love ballad "Heaven Sent" and "The Biggest Lie" (a song about temptation).

BOTTOM LINE (no pun intended):
Overall this CD is too forgettable for me to suggest it. If you're looking for a Christian dance pop CD of this era, I'd suggest Mad at the World's self-titled debut instead. It's synth heavy new wave a la Depeche Mode.

title: The Holy Grail for Beatles Completists
text:
The ANTHOLOGY series is definitely not for the casual fan. But for any true Beatles fan who grew up in the Sixties awaiting each new release, this first volume in the series presents a treasure trove of musical memorabilia from the Fab Four's genesis as the Quarry Men through 1964, when they spearheaded the British Invasion and forever changed popular music.

Disc 1 begins with the much ballyhooed "new" recording "Free As a Bird." It is a stunning track performed by Paul, George and Ringo recorded in 1994 using a 1977 John Lennon demo. Since the remaining tracks date from 1958 to 1964, this track seems out of place on ANTHOLOGY 1, but the advance hype of this song didn't allow for its delayed inclusion on ANTHOLOGY 3.

What makes this first volume special is the historical importance of many of these tracks. While the sound quality is marginal on some of these recordings, where else will you find anything by the pre-Beatles group the Quarry Men or any Beatles tracks with Stu Sutcliffe on bass or Pete Best on drums?

Most of the rarities are on Disc-1. Here are the previously unreleased highlights:

"That'll Be the Day" / "In Spite of All the Danger": A 1958 recording by the Quarry Men. [Note: The latter track was written by McCartney-Harrison.]

"Hallelujah, I Love Her So" / "You'll Be Mine" / "Cayenne": Home tapes featuring the only known recordings with Stu Sutcliffe on bass.

"Searchin'" / "Three Cool Cats" / "The Shiek of Araby" / "Like Dreamers Do" / Hello Little Girl": Five songs from their 1962 Decca audition. Pete Best is on drums. The latter two tracks were Lennon-McCartney originals that they never recorded after securing a contract with EMI.

"Besame Mucho" / "Love Me Do": From their initial 1962 EMI session produced by George Martin. Both tracks feature Pete Best on drums.

"How Do You Do It": Brought to the group by George Martin to be used for their first single. The session features Ringo on drums. The song was eventually scrapped in favor of "Love Me Do." [Note: But labelmates Gerry & The Pacemakers would have a hit with it.]

"One After 909": A 1963 attempt at a song that would not resurface until 1970's LET IT BE.

"Lend Me Your Comb": A 1963 BBC recording that was not included on 1994's LIVE AT THE BBC.

Disc-2 contains fewer unreleased rarities:

"Moonlight Bay": a comedic number performed in 1963 on "The Morecambe and Wise Show." The boys ham it up with the show's comedy duo.

"All My Loving": The live performance from the Beatles' historic first appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show" in 1964.

"Shout": A 1964 live performance of the Isley Brothers' song that never made onto another Beatles' recording.

"You Know What To Do": A demo of a George Harrison original from 1964. The song was never completed.

"Leave My Kitten Alone": Recorded for inclusion on BEATLES FOR SALE, Lennon provides the vocal on this cover of a Little Willie John number.

Technically, all of the tracks on this collection are previously unreleased; but the above tracks represent mostly songs that were never released in any form until the release of ANTHOLOGY 1. The rest of the tracks are either live recordings or alternate takes. None of these songs are presented in their original released studio versions. So if you're looking for the recordings you remember, you'll be disappointed. But if you're looking for a glimpse at the formation of the most popular band in pop music history, this is a must-have release. ESSENTIAL

title: THE edition to have
text:
You wouldn't know it based on Amazon's typically botched product information (I'm not blaming it on Amazon, but on the careless marketplace seller who created this listing) but the barcode, 3351472005718, spills the beans: this is Vanguard 08 2005 71, with Bach's Toccata & Fugue BWV 565, Fantasy & Fugue BWV 542, Prelude & Fugue BWV 548 & BWV 536, Passacaglia & Fuguee BWV 582, Fantasy BWV 572, by Anton Heiller. It is the European edition corresponding to Vanguard USA's OVC 2005, [[ASIN:B0000023A7 Bach: Organ Works]]. The history of Vanguard's CD reissues is a complicated matter and not the subject of this review. Suffice to say that in the 1990s, Vanguard founder Seymour Solomon had the distribution rights on this side of the Atlantic, and a Dutch Arcade company had those for Europe.

Reviewers of that US edition have complained about the botched sound of OVC 2005, and have forwarded instead to the later SACD edition, ATM-SC 1554, [[ASIN:B0002MPQQY Organ Works]], praising its great sonics. I'm not putting in doubt what they heard on OVC 2005. But I thought it was a real bummer the SACD edition came shorn of Toccata & Fugue BWV 565 and Fantasia and Fugue BWV 542: 20 minutes of music and not the most insignificant either. So I took my chances and bought this European edition.

I do not hear there what the reviewers of OVC 2005 are talking about. Yes, heard, very carefully, on headphones, there is a minuscule, one-second dropout in track 2 (Fantasia & Fugue BWV 542) at 0:21, and a vague patch of flutter around 9:19 to say, 9:34, and in track 5 (Passagaclia and Fugue BWV 582), there are three seconds of distinct dropout from 2:45 to 2:48. Other than that and small tape hiss in the softer passages, it sounds simply grandiose. Frankly, 3 or 10 seconds of minuscule sonic glitches weigh nothing in balance with the sonic splendor of that recording and transfer, and the addition of BWV 565 and BWV 542. I also bought the SACD reissue. Heard on a normal, non SACD system, it gains little if anything sonically, while it loses those two major works. With what I hear on 08 2005 71, I really need nothing more sonically.

I don't know what may have been the problem with the American edition, OVC 2005. Was it specific to the American transfers (but I always thought Omega/US and Arcade/Europe used the same) or maybe the CD "pressings" (I'm not sure CDs are "pressed", but you see what I mean), or only to some of the CDs that came out of the US production line? Anyway, if you don't want to take any chances, go for this European edition. It was also reissued by Arcade on their Everyman budget collection which at the time of writing sells very cheap on this website, [[ASIN:B0000257XU Bach;Famous Organ Works]].

Just for the record, this Heiller-Bach recital was first reissued on CD in the late 1980s, when the rights to the Vanguard catalog were owned by the Welk Music Group, on Vanguard VCD 72014, [[ASIN:B0028FZWT4 Great Bach Organ Works]], with a French release in 1990 by Carrère Vanguard 92523. Comment under the American release complains, but not very specifically, about the poor sound. The program was complemented by two Choral-Preludes not elsewhere reissued to the best of my knowledge, BWV 730 & 731.

title: SUBLIME!!!
text:
Drawing upon the old cliche, if I had only 10 albums that I could listen to for the rest of time, this would be one of them. For the other spots I would juggle contenders like DC Talk, Third Day, All Together Separate, Jimmie Black's "Darkness Into Light", Mercy Me, SonicFlood maybe or Delirious? perhaps, and maybe one or two others, but this one is a solid lock. Let's start with the fact that every single track on the album is a rock soild, tightly crafted piece of art. Two things stand out: first the voices in this brother-sister trio are clear, powerful, soulful, and inspiring...they interact and weave together in sheer beauty. Secondly, the production quality on this album is simply outstanding--at times it brings to mind Phil Spector's famous "wall of sound", but in ways that are even more spectacular, gripping, and emotionally captivating. Also, each song has its own clear personality and kick, drawing out a wide spectrum of musicality.

I suppose I should have said that there are three things that stand out, because as fabulous and enthralling as the two aforementioned characteristics are in tandem, they alone would not make it onto my top 10 list. These engaging and sweeping tunes are accompanied by unabashedly worshipful lyrics that are are creative, magnifying, humble, and always honoring. This album dares you not to sing along, every single word clearly enunciated and presented in explicit praise. But as I said, while you might often find yourself joyfully singing along with great gusto, you are as likely to just sit listening with your ears wide open, drinking in every single note, whether measured or driving. This album is incredibly well-balanced, each song presented having both complexity and simplicity. It's not uncommon for me to listen to this album two or three times each time I cue it up, even though I've listened to it dozens of times...it's that good.

Which brings me to my complaint--it is an absolute CRIME that this album didn't get more attention when it was released because the world was ROBBED of the second, third, and fourth albums by this impressive and incredibly talented trio. It was executive produced by Toby Mac & Bill Gaither, so I don't know why it didn't garner more attention. The thing that really surprises me is how far off the radar this album and this band have dropped--they have very little internet presence at all--nothing on Youtube that I could find...it's hard to even get a search engine hit.

In this case, I suppose, it is somewhat fitting, because the rarity associated with this disc isn't related to it being a diamond in the rough--instead, it is a gorgeous, magnificently cut 50-carat gem! You can be one of the lucky few to partake of the Joy!

Click buy and be blessed.

P.S.--I did find this one video of ThreeStrand on Youtube. This song, "Row Upon Row", is nice but I feel that all of the songs on "Famished" are better in quality. [...]

Amidst the terrible dialog ('Every day I die a little more.') and the terribly fake love scenes (see previous line), they finally threw some action in at the end. The last 30 mins of the movie was what we have come to love Star Wars for.
I hope that Lucas is smart enough to not have anything to do with the next movie except maybe to produce it. He really isn't all that good at directing or screenwriting. I really think that they have a possibility of resurrecting a good thing.

title: Recycled previous Capitol album tracks and hit singles
text:
SONNY JAMES, TRACES, Capitol ST 11108. This Lp dates from 1972, a package of 1963-71 recordings, bleeding off sales from Sonny's first Columbia Lp, WHEN THE SNOW IS ON THE ROSES, KC 31646, his new album after leaving Capitol.

Capitol released "Traces" on 45 single Capitol 3398, which competed with "When The Snow Is On The Roses" Columbia 4-45644 45 single on the C/W singles' charts ("When The Snow Is On The Roses" peaked at #1). "Traces" had previously been an Lp cut on Sonny's EMPTY ARMS, Capitol ST 734 album from 1971. The oldest track on this Lp is "Invisible Tears," from I'LL KEEP HOLDING ON Capitol ST 2317 album. Balance of the tracks are the obvious past Capitol country hits. The cover art on this Lp apes Neil Diamond's SHILO album, Bang BLP 221, with the connect-the-dots' theme.

Maybe about 1979, Capitol dumped the album to Pickwick Records, minus two tracks from this 1972 Capitol Lp.

title: Oh, daddy, you sure do swing!
text:
Recently, I happened across Wolfgang Parker on myspace.com -- and what a lucky find that was! I was raised on the classic swing tunes of the 1940s -- Dorsey, Goodman, Miller, etc. Thus I was thrilled when, from out of nowhere, a rocking swing revival cropped up about the time I graduated from college...suddenly, I wasn't some sort of weirdo living in the past, and I could lindy the night away every night of the week. Naturally, I got my hot little hands on all the albums of the fellows who were getting a lot of radio play on mainstream radio. (Well, alt-mainstream radio, anyhow...I don't do mainstream-mainstream.) I liked them. A lot. But, guess what? Mr. Parker is better than those other guys -- and you know who I mean. (It would be rude to name names.) His voice is better, the band is more rollicking and fun, and the lyrics are more original. In addition to toe-tapping, danceable tunes (there's not a single track on "Hep City Swing" I don't like), the format of the album -- that of a 1940s live radio broadcast -- is highly original, and quite a kick, with an announcer, and commercial breaks consisting of an endorsement of "Luxor Cigarettes" and a teaser for an upcoming mystery serial programme. It makes me smile every time I listen to it, imagining that I'm *actually* listening to a broadcast over my 1943 Westinghouse console radio (with the soft glow for ambient lighting whist listening in the dark, of course...is there any other way to listen to such things? I think not.) That is, I'm lying on the floor in front of the afore-mentioned glowing radio, chin in hands, *in* 1943, smokes, and a G&T close at hand. iPod-schmiPod. The album brilliantly blends a very modern version of swing for the 21st century, with a great deal of respect for the roots of this all-American form of music.

I wish I had known about The Talented Mr. Parker back when I was living closer to his home turf; I certainly would have liked to see him and his band play live -- I'm sure every show is a grand time. But, failing that, I think "Hep City Swing" is probably the closest thing you're going to find to a really great live swing concert. (One of those "Other Bands" has a (literally) live album, but this one is more fun.) It's certainly an album to take pride-of-place with your collection of those other swingy fellas in snappy pinstripe suits.

Bravo, Mr. Parker! I've been spreading the word to my other swing aficionados, and all are equally impressed. Oh, and PS, be sure to check out Wolfgang's latest, "Octoboure," on myspace and wolfgangparker.com Yet another treat!

title: Brendel and Vienna are experienced Beethovenians, but Rattle can seem a bit estranged
text:
Despite their differences in musical background, Sir Simon Rattle and Alfred Brendel developed a fondness for each other. This set of the complete Beethoven concerti documents their collaboration. The Vienna Phil, like Brendel, has had plenty of experience in Beethoven. The newcomer to Beethoven is our conductor, who had already made a big name for himself, just not in the German romantics. I believe that after his Berlin appointment Rattle went on to produce major successes in the German repertoire, particularly in Brahms, Schoenberg, Bruckner, and Strauss.

But that adjustment to the traditional repertoire hadn't taken place when this set was recorded. I consider Rattle a great conductor, meaning that he can nearly consistently add his own style to the music. That doesn't mean that his approach will be suitable, however. On most of this set, he's giving us Beethoven that sounds a bit like Mahler with HIP updating. Vienna is allowed to produce rich and full sounds, thankfully, but Rattle holds the reigns too tightly. The finale of the "Emperor", for instance, despite its fullness of tone, lacks brio. We can still witness wonderful playing, but expect mannerisms.

Brendel is fully within his comfort zone, and it sounds that way. Any complaint I would have about his playing would be nitpicking. He melds authority and sensitivity in such a way that has me on my knees. And his wit is present, this ability to speak of profound things with a sly face. I think it suits Beethoven perfectly, but then I'm sure others will disagree.

It's the performance of the 2nd and 3rd concerti where our interpreters mange to come together in a way that completely satisfies. The 2nd concerto becomes bright and youthful, just like it should. But it's in the 3rd concerto that I feel Rattle completely arrives. Suddenly he conducts with power, committed to the dark sound sphere of Beethoven's only minor concerto. Brendel is right with him. It's here that I feel that these two great musicians have been able to connect in a way that leaves a lasting memoriam of their kindred spirit.

In all, my opinion of this set is somewhat mixed, as Rattle seems out of sorts for most the disc only to deliver a stunning 3rd. Should you buy the single disc with the 2nd and 3rd? Perhaps, but for adventurous listeners, it's interesting to hear this collaboration in its entirety, even though it has its flaws.

title: The best, most diverse film in the Expendables series
text:
With action heroes who have Oscar nominations and wins to their resumes (Harrison Ford and Mel Gibson), actual comedic actors (Kelsey Grammer) and serious actors who show diversity in comedy and their usual seriousness (Antonio Banderas)—next to the big name action heroes of Sylvester Stallone, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Jason Statham, and many more who are marking their returns to The Expendables series—the third and new film offers the most diversity than any other film in the series.

This time around, we find the Expendables’ ringleader, Barney Ross (Stallone), coming face-to-face with the man—and TRAITOR—who he cofounded the Expendables with: Conrad Stonebanks (Gibson), long believed to have been dead but finally proving otherwise to his former partner after many years: during which Stonebanks was committing the most atrocious war crimes known to mankind. Stonebanks’ new target is now “his” Expendables, the leader of whom he fell out with for his (Stonebanks’) dealing of illegal weapons. The targets? A brand new team of Expendables: an ex-Marine named John Smilee (Kellan Lutz), a nightclub bouncer named Luna (Ronda Rousey), a computer expert named Thorn (Glen Powell), and a weapons expert named Mars (Victor Ortiz). The reason for the new, savvy-tech team of Expendables, meanwhile, is because Barney Ross wants a new, younger team and feels like he is putting the original team in danger by putting them up against Conrad Stonebanks: much to their chagrin, who unsuccessfully try to convince Barney otherwise.

However, long before they know it, they will indeed be in need and use for Barney Ross: the result of Conrad Stonebanks escaping from the justice Ross and his new team of Expendables brought him into and kidnapping all of the new Expendables, Ross himself a target of Stonebanks’ wrath. After letting his pride take him hostage, Barney Ross finally allows his old team of Expendables to help, with three brand new members for the audience and two for Ross: Doctor Death (Wesley Snipes), a brand new addition to the series but an old Expendable not introduced to audiences until now (a result of his character, like the actor portraying him, having just gotten out of prison, portrayed in a mockingly humorously light), both a fun Expendable and an Expendable who brings fear into the room, Galgo (Antonio Banderas), a Bosnian war veteran who offers up serious drama (with one particular scene) and outlandish comedy at the same exact time, and, saving the best for last, Max Drummer (Harrison Ford): a CIA field operations manager and pilot who picks up where Bruce Willis’ Mr. Church left off at in Expendables 2 and brings more credibility to The Expendables series than Willis could. The reason? It’s simple: Ford, in having essentially the same job as Willis, is doing Willis’ job with the authority of someone respected for being both an action star and a serious actor, not just an action star (remember this: Ford received an Oscar nomination for his performance in Witness; Willis lost a nomination for The Sixth Sense because of his history as an action star). As a result, Ford makes The Expendables 3 feel credible, and he brings his signature flying into the picture, just as he did with his roles as Han Solo and Indiana Jones! What dancing is to John Travolta, flying is to Harrison Ford, and it is great fun to have Ford doing his legendary onscreen and real-life work in The Expendables 3 with the likes of action heroes like Sylvester Stallone and Arnold Schwarzenegger. Mel Gibson is another credible addition to The Expendables 3 for the same reason Ford is, and he makes his Conrad Stonebanks villain a real psychopath who chills up the room and becomes more fun and chilling to watch by the second.

It’s not just Ford or Gibson, either. The Expendables 3 is packed with cheesy, witty, heart-filled comedy, courtesy of Kelsey Grammer and, in one of his most unique, diverse roles, Antonio Banderas. The action, of course, is in question by audiences, with The Expendables 3 being rated PG-13: did Sly and producers sell out the integrity of Expendables 3 for more money? I do know for a fact (see the article mentioned in comment of my review) that Sly wanted to reach a larger and broader audience this journey around. Some people will dismiss it as Sly having sold out; however; with Sly and director Patrick Hughes having included SCENES OF WAR, the PG-13 rating keeps things from getting a little too disturbing, don’t you agree? Besides, we all remember the sad age when we couldn’t see our childhood heroes’ new movie because it was rated-R; having empathy for kids who are the age we once were, isn’t it nice that Hollywood’s given us such a beautiful compromise for us and them?

Many people will disagree, but The Expendables 3 comes farther than any other film in the series did—a must-see.

title: Disappointing follow-up . . .
text:
I really enjoyed Seraiah's first outing, "Carnival World." Some people knocked it for being a clone of Motley Crue's later work, which maybe it is. Nevertheless, I love Jesus . . . and, I like the Crue's musical style (albeit, nothing else about the band impresses me) . . . so, I wasn't too disappointed by the CD. It's not my favorite in the world, but it does get a listen more times than not.

I can't say the same about this CD, "Seraiah." It's a disappointment. Whereas their previous work was clearly Glam/Slick Metal a la Crue (and, perhaps, Slaughter?), this seems to me to be a shift in a more "Hard Rock" direction. I ***HATE*** it when supposedly Metal bands go in the bluesy, crooner direction. But, then: Maybe, playing Heavy Metal for Christ was never in Seraiah's plan, anyways; maybe, they were just a Motley Crue clone following the trends in order to get a record deal. Unfortunately, there is nothing of distinction on this disk: The choruses are weak -- although, that could have been a production problem; the ballad at the end of the disk is saccharine and unmemorable. There's nothing on this disk that would make one want to bang his head or turn up the radio. Nothing.

I'll keep "Carnival World" as a memory of what was and could have been. But, I will be donating "Seraiah" to the local library.
