title: Awful recording
text:
This is a terrible performance of some wonderful music. Monteverdi published his 'Missa In illo tempore' along with the revolutionary Vespers of 1610, in order to silence critics who were in effect accusing him of adopting the 'stile moderno' because he wasn't smart enough to compose in the polyphonic 'stile antico' manner. The Mass is a parody on Nicolas Gombert's motet of the same name, resulting in a setting of exceptional sophistication and beauty.

Monteverdi made his point to stunning effect, but it all goes for nothing in this 1990 recording by the ORF (Austrian Radio) Choir directed by Gottfried Preinfalk. The choir is full of extremely wobbly voices, the polyphonic lines are entirely unclear, and that's even without the adverse effects of the muddy recording. Palestrina's Missa brevis fares just as badly. There's a certain sincerity about these performances, I suppose, but it's nowhere near enough to make up for the sheer awfulness of the choral sound.

There are some very fine recordings of the Monteverdi Mass available, including those from Philippe Herreweghe, Masaaki Suzuki and Roberto Gini – in the last two cases coupled with the 1610 Vespers. My own favourite, however, is the absolutely beautiful performance by Odhecaton directed by Paolo da Col. As for the present disc - forget it.

title: A seminal work of the off-Broadway renaissance of the 1970's, "Promenade" should be much better known today
text: This LP is an original cast recording of Promenade, book by Maria Irene Fornes and music by the Rev. Al Carmines, both winners of the Oscar of off-broadway theater, the Obie award. The show debuted in 1969 in the Promenade Theater, which was named for it.  The premise is rather like Candide:  Two prisoners escape and , in an attempt to worm their way into high society encounter all sorts of situations and characters , who appear in a variety of vignettes.  True to its period, the show presents quite a bit of social commentary through its exuberant, funny, and often heartwrenching songs.  Al's music draws on his early influences of gospel, vaudeville and opera, mainly, which he interprets in his own melodic, irrepressible  style.  The songs are all standouts, and the structure of the play enables each one to be enjoyed as an independent entity, making them work well as a recording.  "Capricious and Fickle", sung by the incomparable Alice Playten, is considered by many to be one of the best theater songs ever written .  Other standouts include the sardonic "Cigarette Song" with its distinctive take on life , the rollicking "Unrequited Love", and the searing self-knowledge of "I Saw a Man".  Though tremendously appealing, "Promenade" confronts its audience as well as entertaining it.  Along with the originality of words and music, it is this confrontational quality which insures its central place in the avant-garde theater that flourished in New York's Greenwich Village in the 1960's and 1970s.

title: Short, but with authority
text:
Kenneth Brian's follow-up EP to Welcome to Alabama shows that his debut was no fluke. It fully realizes the potential shown on that debut, while pulling out a few new tricks, even on such a short work.

Brian's debut album fit comfortably within an emerging subgenre that blends country with hard rock, and the presence of Jason Isbell on that debut album signaled the kind of fanbase likely to find an appeal in Brian's music, although Brian has more in common with Isbell's former bandmate, Patterson Hood. Not a virtuoso musician, he nevertheless plays with complete devotion, and makes you feel every note. Not a preternaturally gifted voice, he nevertheless sings the truth, and every harsh word of it. And everything with authority. Was that first album a fluke? No. Blackbird, though short, actually expands admirably on the sound of Welcome to Alabama by showing some influences that weren't as prominent on that debut.

Most notably, the Allman Brothers. There really is a palpable Allman feel in several places throughout, to the point that he is practically note-checking the band. That's not really Truckers territory, and while Patterson and Cooley wrote an album nominally devoted to Skynyrd, neither band really has a strong influence on the sound of the Truckers, nor much of the genre associated with them, except, ironically, Isbell. The punk-ish side of the genre just doesn't really go the Allman route. Here, though, Brian is getting in touch with not only the Truckers-esque side of twangy hard-rock, but with his Allman roots. Growth. We all like to see growth in an artist. Is Brian a Duane-level virtuoso, or a Derek-level virtuoso? No, but the point is his method of total commitment. He knows the fretboard, and that combined with total commitment and you will enjoy it. A new sound. What else can you really hope to hear?

title: I Solisti Veneti's earlier recording - of little more than archaeological interest
text:
This is another edition of a CD first published by Erato on its budget Bonsai collection, ECD 55013, [[ASIN:B00000E6IS Vivaldi : Mandolin Concertos : Concertos Pour Mandonines]], as of today selling much cheaper than this edition, and it is also the case with this next CD reissue: [[ASIN:B000009JYX Mandolin Concerti]] (but there's a botch with that latter entry, the review I posted there explains it).

Now, buyers, beware. What you need to know is that all these editions are NOT of Scimone and I Solisti Veneti's recording of Vivaldi's Mandolin Concertos made in 1983 with mandolinists Ugo Orlandi and Dorina Frati and first published on CD, here: [[ASIN:B0018KRYZA Vivaldi: Concertos for Mandolin]]. It is their earlier recording, from 1969, with Bonifacio Bianchi and Alessandro Pitrelli, first published on LP on Erato ERA 70545.

That recording - and, hence, the CD reissue - had only three of the four works performed in 1983: the Concerto for 2 Mandolins - back then referred to as P133, now as RV 532 -, the Concerto for mandolin RV425 / P 134, and the Concerto "for many instruments" (including two mandolins and two theorbos) RV 558 / P 16. Left out was the Chamber Concerto RV 93, and with some good reason: it isn't a work for mandolin, originally, but for lute and two violins.

But as a filler, back then and on the CD reissue as well, Erato added the Concerto RV 583 for scordatura violin and two antiphonal orchestras ("a due cori"), and to those four, the CD reissue adds again RV 581 "Per la Santissima Assuzione di Maria Vergine" for violin, and RV 552 "con violino principale con altro per eco in lontano" ("with a solo violin and a violin in distant echo"), for a generous TT of 73:22. The former is played by Piero Toso, the "historical" fiddler from I Solisti Veneti, and came out in 1976 on Erato ERA 70968 with three other “Solemn Concertos” (RV 212 "Fatto per la Solennità della S. Lingua di S. Antonio di Padua", 289 "Per la Solennità di S. Lorenzo", 579 "Funebre"); the latter, with both Toso and Giuliano Carmignola, was recorded in 1978/79 and first came out on Erato STU 71233 (with three concertos for flute performed by René Clemencic). At least (and at last), Erato has here corrected (most of) the botches of its previous editions, by which it did not give the now customary PV catalog numbers of the mandolin works, only their old Pincherle (P) catalog numbers, mislabled RV 552 into 522 (which would have made it "L'Estro Armonico" op. 3 No. 8) and didn't assign any catalog number, right or wrong, to RV 583. But you still won’t know, of the two mandolinists, who plays RV 425: it’s Bianchi. The original LP came with extensive liner notes by Scimone himself. All are gone from the CD reissues.

And with all that, and added to the fact that it's somewhat frustrating to have only tidbits from those two other LPs (the four "solemn concertos" have been reissued in Japan with one more from another LP, [[ASIN:B00005HI78 ヴィヴァルディ:教会暦にちなんだ協奏曲集]]), this is not the version of the Mandolin Concertos you should favor, and not even the version of the Mandolin Concertos by I Solisti Veneti.

I Solisti Veneti’s interpretation in 1969 may have been revolutionary in its time - in particular, Scimone boasted in his liner notes that it was the first time that Concerto P. 16 / RV 555 was heard in its original guise, with the so-called "violini in tromba marina" played by violins and not... trumpets, as (claimed Scimone) the previous editions and recordings had done, based on a mis-interpretation of Vivaldi's indication on the manuscript score. He's obviously referring to the Casella edition, which also substituted Heckelphones (!... a double-reed instrument of the oboe family, invented in 1904) to the salmoès (a simple-reed instrument and ancestor of the clarinet) and harps to theorboes, and for the recordings he may have had in mind those of Thomas Schippers with the Alessandro Scarlatti Orchestra of Naples, Schippers' first orchestral recording (said the ads), published on Columbia 33CX 1451 / Angel 35335 in 1956, and Bernstein's on Columbia ML 5459 / MS 6131 from 1958 (the latter reissued on [[ASIN:B0000062E5 Vivaldi: Four Seasons / Concerto for Diverse Instruments]]). But for the salmoès ("a wind instrument that doesn't exist anymore today"), Scimone used clarinets playing at the upper octave.

But independent of those considerations, Scimone's interpretation in 1969 is firmly anchored in the Vivaldi interpretive traditions of the 1960s and 1970s: a little too trudging, a little too thick, a little too solemn. By 1983 and with an almost entirely new personel (besides the conductor, only harpsichordist Edoardo Farina and flautist Clementine Hoodendoorn Scimone - Mrs Claudio - remain from 1969), they took on the interpretive lessons of the period-instrument ensembles that had emerged in the meanwhile, Harnoncourt’s Concentus Musicus Wien, Trevor Pinnock’s English Concert and Christopher Hogwood’s Academy of Ancient Music, or maybe it was only that they participated to the same stylistic trend towards leaner textures and more animated tempos. Their 1983 recording is better in all compartments, and it adds RV 93, originally a chamber concerto for two violins, lute and continuo, but played by them as a mandolin concerto. The slow movement of the Concerto for two mandolins RV 532 was very beautiful in 1969, but in 1983 the two new mandolinists add wonderful ornamentation in the repeats. There was a very nice touch in the slow movement of RV 558, where the mandolin trilled all his notes (played unisono with the violins) rather than simply plucking them, something not explicitly called for by Vivaldi but much more effective; but it’s there again in 1983. And then the 1969 Mandolin Concerto RV 425 was ruined by I Solisti Veneti’s choice NOT to follow Vivaldi’s advice that “the violins can all play pizzicato”. And you just need to compare that and the 1983 remake, where they do follow the advice, to realize how much more beautiful the pizzicato version is, turning an ordinary concerto into one of Vivaldi’s most sublime inventions.

So if it is the mandolin concertos that attracted you here, by all means, of the two, you should favor the remake. That is, if it is I Solisti Veneti’s version you want. Because in 1992 came Il Giardino Armonico, and they sent the interpretation of these works in another dimension, with more energy, more enthusiasm, more liveliness and joyfulness, more poetic imagination in the phrasings, more sonic presence, more everything, making all the previous versions, even those on period-instruments, more or less obsolete. About this, see my review, [[ASIN:B000V1V0XE Vivaldi: Ctos for Lute & Mandolin]].

For all those reasons, this one is of no more than archaeological interest.

title: A Fistful of Idiots or High Plains Moron?
text:
This film looks great and the acting is pretty good, but the story line is so dopey it ruins the film overall. The posse has got to be the dumbest bunch of fools to ever hit the trail.

WARNING: PLOT SPOILERS AHEAD (as if the plot wasn't already spoiled by the writers)

Previous reviewers have pointed out some of the more ridiculous gaffes, like a guy getting gut shot one day and riding around just fine the next. Here's a few more: Despite the villain getting away repeatedly, nobody in the posse ever thinks to put a blindfold over his eyes or a sack over his head. Nor do they ever tie a rope to leash him to someone or something. Then they head into Injun' territory with the bad guys hot on their trail. So what do they do? They stop and camp for the night (instead of pushing on) with a nice big fire so the Apaches can easily find them! When they get to town they decide to wait for the train by hiding at the hotel. Gee whiz, I bet them bad guys will never think to look at the hotel. Not! We later find out the hotel is half a mile from the station. Hmmm, not a real good location unless you want to give the baddies plenty of chances to blast you as you run for the train. They probably should have put the 14 year old kid in charge of the posse - he seems to be the only one with brains and initiative. I wanted to like this film but the implausibility is almost as bad as "High Noon." Apparently, if you believe this story, the West was won by cowards and fools.

title: The Long Lost Godzilla Review has finally arrived!
text:
* The Long Lost Godzilla Review has finally arrived!

This review was written in late 1998 or early 1999. I posted the review back when it was originally written but the review never appeared. This should have been one of the oldest, if not the oldest, review of this product on Amazon. It was issued on Amazon.co.uk on January 21, 2001. So, over a decade (twelve years in fact) after it was completed, here is my review of GODZILLA: THE SOUNDTRACK. It should be known that I have not heard this soundtrack since the late 1990s with the exception of "Come With Me" which is on my iPod. I have NEVER seen the movie. I remember "Undercover" being a somewhat funny, rather ridiculous song. I still stand by what I said in the original review though, even after over a decade of not having heard the album, that this was a soundtrack caculated slowly at reaching as many different type of markets as possible, and the record feels disjointed and does not flow. Very bad album, though the individual songs themselves (most of them) are actually pretty good.

Decmber 14-2011

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Godzilla: The Album Review
[There's a lot of great music out there with high integrity]...and this ain't it. Good album ... from the commercial standpoint. This album is pure product, nothing more. (Which, by the way, is what is ruined about Beatles for Sale). A few people have praised it for the variety of music contained therein. Sorry, on this record, not a strong point. It was just a blatant cash-in. Wallflower's cover of Heros costed $500,000. That is how much they paid the band. This was widely criticized in the recording industry. There was not a track put on here that the producers did not think would help them sell more of these LPs (still think in record terms). And they were right.

Actually, in terms of what they were trying to do (make pure product) this album is 5 stars because they succeed so well. In terms of artistic quality, like how the album will stand the test of time, - 5 stars. ; 0 ) It won't last at all.

Truthfully, I do like all of the music on this album. But the thing I don't like is everything on this has such a commercial feel. The movie (which I haven't seen...never appealed to me, although I am a big fan of SF/Fantasy movies) I have not seen, but have been told its just a special effects flick. It was supposed to be the big hit of the year. It did not go over as well as expected, though it did decently. That's how Godzilla: the album did.

Cine Come With Me, being (besides Heros) the most talked about track, is perhaps also one of the most disgusting. When you try to combine such different genres as rap and classic rock, it is bound to be hard to do successfully. Being a huge Zep fan, I couldn't believe they did that. And in the liner notes of the Zep Box Set, Page talks about how you have to be careful with tampering with music because it means so much to people. Here he was just rearranging the song sequences. Can we say...hypocrite? Although it is interesting, granted, it is truly a crime that they did that to Kashmir, one of the ultimate rock songs! That would be like taking the orchestra crescendos out of A Day in the Life. If Puff Daddy has to depend on established rock classics to sell his records, he is in very sad shape. Especially considering he did such a poor job. Page should be shot for allowing him to do that...even played on the damn track. Had I been Plant (who like the version) or JPJ, I would have torn into them. For Jones...he's been getting treated so crappy by his former bandmates.

(Interesting Factoid: John Paul Jones did the string arrangements for R.E.M.'s classic Automatic for the People. Now there's a real 90's album for ya!)

Bottom Line: If you want good rock, go get the real stuff. If you want commercialized tracks with no consideration for art; you've hit the mother lode.

There has to be a balance...everyone has to make a living. But there has to be some art to it too. This is entirely out of balance

The Ultimate Soundtrack of the 90s: Singles. Although it does not have Nirvana, it defines the grunge movement. That has art. It's the best sound track of the 90's I've heard. Don't waste yr money on this commercial crap! Go with Singles! Damn good album!

title: Adrian Younge is my hero
text:
I discovered Adrian Younge through his work on Black Dynamite, where he edited the film, compiled the outstanding collection of "Library Music" used to give the film a real "released in the 70s feel" but most importantly composed the original score for. The music is a character of the film as much as The-Militants-Who-Turn-Startled. Funny, expositive and endlessly replayable, the BD score (& accompanying sndtk) took me on a journey into the before time, in the long-long ago. What's more, is that he plays EVERY instrument on the album, with guest vocalists, playing old instruments & using vintage recording equipment (an interview said nothing was newer than about 1970). I looked forward to his next upcoming album, which was to be a reinterpretation of his first work, 2000's Venice Dawn.

Wax Poetics rereleased 5 songs from the album as a free digital EP as a prelude to Venice Dawn- Something About April (*****). The tracks, all recorded & produced by Younge, were a bit less dated than the intentionally anachronistic BD score & far less lush than SAA (hadn't built his magical mellotron/rhodes/awesome keyboard & hadn't learned all the instruments in the world yet, I guess). Copies of the original full length Venice Dawn album have been non-existant until recently on here.

After listening I can see why WP picked the 5 songs they did. They seem to be the most realized pieces on the album. They're all good to great (the vocals on trk 4 being the weakest part IMO), but its weird after 2+ years of listening to the 5-song, a truncated, abbreviated tour of the "suite". Fans will not be disappointed.

Adrian Younge's Venice Dawn was independently produced. The artwork on Amazon is from the Wax Poetics digital EP, while the disc i received has a hipster couple on the cover. Despite the track listing on the back and the instrument credits inside, there are in fact 14 tracks, not 12 as listed. Not that I'm disappointed but it seems to be a major oversight since one of those tracks is on Wax Poetics' rerelease and it is unlisted in both places. The layout seems kinda cheap, with pictures stretched funny but again this is an album with virtually no information about it online. I met Mr. Younge on tour recently, who indicated the album had "something like 15 songs on it". This is it, the unfortunate packaging being my only frowny face.

Compared to the rest of his work, I find it much more litenable than the recent Delfonics album, on par w/ his album w/ Ghostface Killah, but lacking the lush, haunting sexuality of Something About April. His Black Dynamite songs (both from the movie & cartoon) are his greatest triumphs. He is probably my favorite musician out there right now. This last month I saw Steel Panther, Opeth, Captured! By Robots and a half a dozen more bands but Adrian Younge's Venice Dawn (the band) opening and backing Ghostface was the BEST live band I've seen in years. They got down like magickists, w/ The Maestro bouncing back & forth b/w bass, guitar, The Selene, flute & clarinet as well as narrating & cheesing. He assembled a killer band (Venice Dawn was previously the Black Dynamite Soundtrack Orchestra) and I wonder how many of them were around for the original Venice Dawn (he does thank his touring band in the liner).

Check out the free EP and if you like it, try tracking down one of these rare albums (never saw it on torrent)

title: Cinematically-tinged symphonic choral music
text:
Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales seems ripe for musical interpolation, but alas, aside from a late 60’s musical theatre production, George Dyson’s symphonic choral work The Canterbury Pilgrims is all I am aware of. Each movement is a slice of life portrait of Chaucer’s observations on each character embarking on the pilgrimage, omitting the subsequent tales each tells on their travels. Much along the lines of Mussorgsky Pictures at the Exhibition, or more aptly Vaughan Williams’ 45-minute Five Tudor Portraits, each character study is 3-10 minutes long for chorus, soloists, and orchestra. Dyson cleans up much of the olde English, making the meaning of the texts more accessible to his 20th century audiences, although Canterbury is probably not best for casual listening, but thankfully Chandos provides texts for all of the music.

George Dyson shows stunning craftsmanship throughout, taking into account Chaucer’s saucy wit and sarcastic commentary to give full bloom to the dimensions of these characters. Dyson’s music mirrors Chaucer’s mind, where at once a character seems initially stereotypical to their vocation and miens, as Chaucer finds out more about the characters, the music changes gears with his mindset, giving stunning complexity to the depth of the texts.

Luckily, Dyson’s music is easy on the ears. There is a certain Romantic, cinematic quality to his music that keeps it from rambling on like Elgar’s, Delius’, or Holst’s longer symphonic choral works, and more in vein of Vaughan Williams or Hubert Parry with clear-eyed, colourful musical settings. At 90 minutes, the music has enough variety between the serious and wry, the raucous and serene, and chorus and soloist to easily hold attention throughout. Even at his most contemplative, Dyson never fails to inject a grand climax for variation for the listener, although the heartfelt epilogue never fails to bring a tear to the eye at the end, showing the exhaustive epic scale of Dyson’s setting, much along the lines of VW's Sea Symphony [[ASIN:B000000AJ7 on Chandos]].

It helps that this performance is stunning throughout. The London Symphony Orchestra is big and bold with the typical clarity from Chandos. The solo opening of flute, clarinet, and oboe is lovely, but it is the oft-called upon brass that really holds its weight in this recording alongside a solid string sound. If I had a want, a little more presence from the pipe organ is what I would ask for.

Equally, the London Symphony Chorus is hale and hearty here, with enough heft to sing against the upfront instrumentation, although the tiniest bit of juice might make the chorus’ texts a little crisper, a small niggle overall though. It is a boon to Dyson’s abilities that when the chorus rests for a movement or two, their presence is most a welcome return; the sinuously slimy opening of the clerk, the rambunctious swashbuckling in the Shipwright, the rugged merchant, and the hymnody of the Parson are so entertaining when the chorus arrives betwixt soloist musings.

The soloists are pretty good across the board. Yvonne Kenny has a bright, fizzy voice that sweeps along Dyson’s big climaxes such as the final third of The Prioress, although Dyson seems minimalist in orchestral contributions when the soprano sings in comparison to her male counterparts. Robert Tear’s tenor is full voiced, a bit breathless at first. Stephen Roberts has a slight adenoidal baritone quality that, while not off-putting, would not be my first choice. Each soloist is splendidly crisp with their diction, rolled r’s and all, and are put well in front of the sound for an excellent balance of soloist to orchestra and chorus.

The accompanying instrumental features, At the Tabard Inn Overture and In Honour of the City showcase Dyson’s cinematically-tinged orchestral contributions. Tabard Inn satisfyingly encapsulates the music of The Canterbury Pilgrims within 15 minutes, an outstanding standalone feature of that music. In Honour is a paean to London, another choral work with Medieval texts that, aside from the lyrical midsection that waxes on about the Thames River, heartily extols London’s virtues along the lines of Elgar’s Cockaigne Overture, but here with a choral focus.

There are no competing records to Hickox’s traversal of Canterbury. One can only hope that David Hill and The Bach Choir turn their attention to it, but Hickox did end up completing Dyson’s other oratorios before his death, Nebuchadnezzar [[ASIN:B000VPNK2Y on Chandos]] and Quo Vadis [[ASIN:B00008WQB2 also on Chandos]], as did Bournemouth [[ASIN:B075VVPN3R on Naxos]], as well as the Tabard Overture under Lloyd-Jones [[ASIN:B0008JEKEU also on Naxos]]. Chandos’ liner notes are top-of-the-line here though, with two comprehensive commentaries covering the works at hand.

I would characterize Dyson’s Canterbury Pilgrims as essential listening for symphonic choral lovers along with Vaughan Williams’ Tudor Portraits, again [[ASIN:B000000B24 on Chandos]]. I realize despite Dyson’s approachably colourful music for chorus and orchestra, this music is not particularly casual listening and so might not have broad appeal. Regardless of that, with excellent ensemble performances, big, clear sound, terrific solo singing, and captivating music, this recording easily comes Highly Recommended!

title: Gorr's Very Grand ORPHEE !
text:
Gluck's ORFEO is generally held to be the earliest opera in the standard repertoire, although two of Monteverdi's three surviving operas, Purcell's DIDO, and two or three Handel operas are now performed frequently enough to give it a run for its' money. It is also probably the simplest opera to realize on stage, and one of the most straightforward in terms of musical realization. Somehow, though, it has eluded a really first rate recording.
We have had, most frequently, mezzo-sopranos singing the title role, but there are also recordings by counter tenors, tenors, baritones and at least one recording in the original range, which was that of a soprano. This is not really the place to get into a lengthy discussion of Gluck's own two versions, for soprano and tenor respectively or the version by Berlioz, prepared in 1858 for the great mezzo Pauline Viardot. The Berlioz version remains the most frequently performed and recorded. The title role of that version has had some very impressive interpreters on disc, such as Kathleen Ferrier, Maureen Forrester, Rise Stevens, Shirley Verrett, Marilyn Horne, and Anne Sophie Von Otter, But in some ways this set of highlights with the great Rita Gorr is the best of all. Gorr was not a perfect vocalist. She sometimes sang just shy of pitch, However, the grandeur of utterance, the sincerity of phrasing are pretty hard to beat. This is a big all out emotional response to music and text that is very exciting.
The hour's worth of highlights center on Gorr and the chorus alone. Charles Bruck finds ideal tempi for all the pieces included. Apparently the rest of the performance had too many technical glitches to warrant release. (For the record the unheard Euridice and Amour were Nadine Sautereau and Edith Selig.)
The sound recording is clear but somewhat harsh.
There are notes in French, English and German, but texts in French only.

title: Derivative, with few interesting moments.
text:
Of all of the GS bands, I'm perhaps least impressed by the Carnabeats; their songs are usually provided by outside writers, their musicianship doesn't seem to be terribly spectacular, their chosen musical niche is the sing-song, over-melodramatic melody...seemingly pre-fab in every way shape and form.
This disc (their first album, padded out with quite a few bonus tracks, although--puzzlingly--their collaboration with Gary Walker of the Walker Brothers is absent) largely demonstrates the above. The songs aren't bad, exactly; they just aren't particularly interesting, and if they stick in your head, you're usually not the better for this (the odd, swooping "O.K." is particularly guilty of this). "Chu Chu Chu" and "Give Me Loving" show up on the far better (and far cheaper) compilation "G.S. I Love You, Too" and give the listener a pretty good idea as to what they're in for. There are a few highlights, though. "Sukisa Sukisa Sukisa," a cover of the Zombies song "I Love You," is particularly well performed, and call me crazy, but I really dig their version of the Walker Brothers' "Annabella," even though they completely mangle the lyrics.
Moving onto the extra-musical aspects, the packaging from Teichiku is excellent, as always, with heaps of information provided that I will never--barring a sudden ability to grasp Japanese--understand. The sound quality is typical Teichiku reissue quality, with good sources spoiled a bit by overzealous, "squishy" noise-reduction (there's an earlier Phillips edition of the disc without noise reduction, but that is mastered very bass-light).
The verdict? Avoid. The best tracks are availible on several compilations, anyway...although if you find the old Phillips "Carnabeats collections" discs, you might consider those to be a viable alternative.

title: Who needs Electricity?
text:
I recently heard a couple of goofballs on a Salt Lake City sports station wandering into the area of "Who is the best guitarist ever?" Of course, they went right into Hendrix v. Van Halen. Nothing against these two fine players, but I began thinking of all the guitarists that these two radio sports guys have prpbably never heard, guys like John McLaughlin, Buddy Guy, Duane Allman, Chet Atkins, Junior Brown, Wes Montgomery, Jim Hall,let alone some of the classical monsters. The reason I say monsters is because one of the best, Eliot Fisk, does things on guitar that not only can I NOT do, but I have no idea what the heck he's even doing. If I can't play a run by Van Halen, I at least know somewhat what's he's doing, just like when I see Mike Powell long jump--I know what his feet, legs and arms are doing; I just can't jump as far. With Fisk, you listen, and you think, how on earth did he do that? It's enough to make you blink in amazement.

What's more amazing is that Paganini, who was purportedly the second-best guitar player in Italy (but who said that the guitar was kept by himself only to spur musical ideas--in truth, Paganini was probably jealous of that best Italian guitarist), wrote these pieces for violin (Paganini was the best violinist in Italy, and one of the best ever). It was thought that these Capricci could not be rendered on guitar. The skeptics are wrong! Not only are they rendered, they come to a life that many traditional violinists could not give these pieces. The dynamics available on classical guitar give Paganini's work a new dimension that Paganini, with his "take no prisoners" approach to playing violin, had originally intended.

I will quote Ruggiero Ricci from the CD packet:

"Astounding. Even Paganini wouldn't have believed that it could be played on the guitar. An enormous accomplishment that will raise the level of guitar playing. Has to be heard to be believed."

title: A return to form by the most prominent Godzilla composer!
text: The soundtrack to 1991's Godzilla vs King Ghidorah is a return to form for the composer most identified with the Godzilla series, Akira Ifukube.  Apart from Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla (1993), this is one of my favorite soundtracks from the Hensei period of the Godzilla series.  With over 40 tracks, this CD includes a number of letimofs for both kaiju, as well as the main characters, with a number of a variations of each theme.  Tracks which are particularly nice includes the Introduction (Track 1), as well as the tracks when Godzilla first appears in Hokkaido.  Admittedly, much of the music towards the ending (the Shinjuku fight) is not included, but they are, for the most part, just versions of earlier tracks.  Also, the track "Get King Ghidorah" (originally created for 1959's Rodan) is included, but interestingly, it is the last track.  Toho actually released two versions of Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah's soundtrack in this single CD and a 2-CD set, which is interesting as this CD has much more music.  In any case, if you have a chance to pick up this CD, I would whole heartedly recommend it!

And I have to honestly say Beautiful Rainbow World by Daria is one of my son's favorites! It's usually the first one he chooses to play when he feels like listening to music (happily my son takes after my hubby in the music department!).

Plus, I love listing to the CD, too! The sounds are upbeat, with a world-music feel (hence the rest of the title of the CD, "World Music for Children By Daria"). The whole family can listen to this CD. It's a terrific blend of Caribbean, Latin American, African American, and many more including Hebrew and Arabic. Daria is a master at putting these sounds together in various songs with wonderful lyrics.

So if you are looking for something 'cultural' and upbeat, I highly recommend Daria's CD! We look forward to buying more of her CDs for family birthdays!

title: Sub-par, compared to Year Zero and Ghosts; it is free, though.
text:
The problem with The Slip is that there's almost nothing new about it. Even that aspect of it isn't new. NIN already have one "let's just rock out and have a good time" album, 2005's With Teeth. That album is also more fun to listen to than this one.

It's somewhat disappointing when you consider Trent Reznor's other recent work. Year Zero (2007) was a startling, original reinvention. At least, I personally would never have expected the voice of nineties teenage angst to become a visionary prophet of the apocalypse. Ghosts I-IV (2008) was uneven, but it was also an original move, possibly the only thing Reznor could have done at that point without repeating himself. And although it may have been too long, many of the tracks on it truly expanded Reznor's horizons as a composer.

But even the best songs on The Slip would have sounded more or less average on With Teeth. "Discipline" is a very catchy single, but it's practically a rewrite of "The Hand That Feeds," except the production leans more toward the electronic sound of Year Zero. And the drum track sounds like it comes from Blur's "Song 2." I'm sure it will sound great live, but it really shouldn't be an album's greatest draw.

The loud angry songs all sound very similar, and much more rudimentary than even the songs on With Teeth (which were already stripped-down). Songs like "1,000,000," "Letting You" and "Head Down" use almost identical two- and four-note guitar riffs. Of course, NIN albums were always more about Reznor's vocals than the music, but these songs don't have any particularly interesting vocal rhythms either.

And the lyrics, man, they're really phoned in. It almost seems like they're just mash-ups of typical NIN phrases: "when you crawl on your hands and your knees," "I feel a million miles away, I don't feel anything at all," "Believing your charade, begin to suffocate," "This is all a dream and none of you are real," "I'll give anything," "It keeps growing and I can feel it breathe," "Now I know what this is all about," "I will use my fist to destroy everything I can," etc. Even Year Zero suffered from this problem a little, but there Trent made a concerted (and successful) effort to tell a story about the world around him. Here, he's back to railing against "them" and describing his emotions.

The second half of the album changes gears completely and sounds more like Ghosts. But there, too, most of the music isn't as good as the best Ghosts tracks. "Lights In The Sky" is Reznor's least interesting piano ballad (if you want to hear one of his more interesting ones, try I-1 on Ghosts), and "Corona Radiata" is the kind of droning ambient loop that appears in a few Ghosts tracks, except here it's stretched out to seven and a half minutes to become the longest song on any NIN full-length. Yet it really doesn't have any more musical content than "999,999," the minute-long "Pinion"-like opener.

The one interesting exception is the instrumental "The Four Of Us Are Dying." In addition to an evocative title, it also has an excellent, deep bass line. Trent has never been the best guitarist, but he's become very good at writing bass lines -- all the good songs on With Teeth had bass and not guitar leads, Year Zero had a few of them too (especially "The Warning"), and so did a few of the best Ghosts tracks. Perhaps he's been secretly taking lessons from Peter Hook. Anyway, this bass line rumbles ominously with a softer keyboard rhythm laid over it, creating a cool dark-ambient vibe. Hopefully this is the kind of thing he'll be exploring on his next album.

Also, the one vocal track that grew on me with time was "Echoplex." It would have fit in well with the less aggressive bass-driven songs on With Teeth. The music largely consists of a bouncy drum rhythm and more of that deep bass, with little else of note. But despite the upbeat rhythm, the song itself sounds kind of murky and ambiguous. It never builds up to any kind of climax, instead there's a break in which Trent whispers in time with the beat. The odd tension makes it stand out.

I don't want to sound too critical...he did release the entire album for free, and it's still up for download on NIN's website. And critics liked it for once, so I might be in the minority. But I still feel that it falls below the standard Trent has set in the past two years. Perhaps one should view it as an EP and not a full-length album.

text: Cochise (the 70s version) were an oddity in a decade known for more than its share of the same: A British country-rock quintet known these days more for who was in the band than the music itself (including Mick Grabham - in between gigs for Jethro Tull and Procol Harum, respectively); Willie Weeks (soon to do better in Foreigner) and legendary UK steel player B.J. Cole). This was the first single from their sadly overlooked second album, SWALLOW TALES, and they came up with a memorable arrangement of the old Buddy Holly classic. The back and forth between the lead guitar and Cole's pedal steel is perfect. The label and sleeve are fun, too. The Sighs are all super-competent on their instruments (the drummer and lead guitarist, especially), the singing is fine, and the first 10 songs on this album are all good. But the last song is a live version of "Think About Soul" from their first album. "What Goes On," and it's terrific! I did, in fact, play it again as soon as it was finished; that's rare for me these days.
If you are thinking, "So, I should buy an album just for one song?" don't worry; if you like power pop, these guys are quite good at it. But, yeah; the last song is so good, it's worth buying the album for.

title: Not satisfying 3rd comeback CD
text:
This was the third CD this lady released after escaping the Ayatollahs. The previous two being Zartosh ( with lyrics by her ex husband, film director Kimiaii) and Manifest (written by the same team as this album).

I am posting the review I did of Manifest when it was originally released. Now that some time has gone by, in retrospect, I must add that the album is poorly mixed and engineered. It just doesnt sound powerful enough. Even though the album feauters a full orchestra, the arrangements are very poorly written. It makes a full orchestra sound worst than a keyboard. Now heres my review, which was published originally when the album came out:

1) Ay Mardom Mordam

This song is a CLASSIC and absolutely perfect. The melody and chorus, the part that says: "Ay mardom, mordam..." is absolutely brilliant, memorable, original and fit Googoosh's voice like a glove. The use of a real drummer gives the song the added strength that its lyrics demand! The lyrics are very important and up to date, in line with the realities of Iranian women today.

2) Nejaatam bedeh

This ballad starts with a beautiful string (violins) arrangement. Given that expensive string sections are usually not usually employed in making Iranian music abroad these days, it is great to hear strings in this production.

A beautiful vocal melody starts. The lyrics are again great and very important. I personally feel very close to the feeling of "wanting to be saved" which the lyrics talk about.

However, what could have been another classic, given the strong verse parts, doesn't quite become one, because it needs a strong chorus sung in high notes. The song writer does realize that such a part is needed and attempts with the part that has the lyrics going: "Nabaayad bezaarim setaareh..." Unfortunately this part is not measure up to the brilliance of the verse.

Still the verse and the lyrics are so great that they makes this a memorable song anyway.

3) Esgh Yani Hame Chiz

More string section here! Absolute brilliant. lyrics, saying "You are not alone. Who do you think all these stars in the sky belong to?" and "Thinking of freedom is living". Music wise, this song succeeds completely, as the strong verse leads to a surprising and unexpectedly fun and refreshing bridge/chorus that starts with the lyrics "nagoo maa dotaa kamim..."

Brilliant. and a classic!

4) Sangar bi Sang

Googoosh is able to save this song because she is able to sing low notes very well. This song is musically OK. The only memorable line "kaash bar migashtam" is too short to make up for the rest of the song.

5) Khoobe khoob

This is an embarrassment! The lyrics are absolutely horrible: "bas keh midoonam khoobe khoobee, khaabi khaabi, man keh bidaaram, cheghatdr khoobeh". It turns out that a similar song belongs to Shahriar. The music is dull.

6) Ghazal Shishehee ( Fragile Melody)

So far the album has offered slow songs. This one is the first upbeat song -- something the album desperately needs. This song has a disco beat, with the brilliant idea of contrasting the upbeat drum programming with a loud electric guitar playing the main arrangements. The vocal melody for the verse is great because the listener instantly feels like singing along with Googoosh.

The lyrics are clever and create great, educated images. The vocal melody has a climax that starts with the part: "Baa to zolaal mishavam...". The only problem is that the song needs a middle section that is as brilliant as the rest. The songwriter again knows a part is missing and attempts with the section that goes: "Dar ghafass-e abri..." but it's just not as memorable as it should be.

But anyway, the melody of the first verse is so beautiful that makes this song well worth it. Also, it is pleasant that they have taken some risks with this song. Googoosh sounds wild -- like she should! Her voice comes alive. It definitely sounds like no other record.

7) Aftabi

This one is also upbeat. It has a very marked "Mehrdad" quality to its melody. It runs smoothly and the lyrics "Aftaab hanooz ziaad miaad" is nice and tries to make the listener feel good. It has a short but sweet chorus with nice lyrics. It's a cool light song. In other words, it's pleasant but two years from now you are not going to be singing it. You may still be repeating: "Ay mardom mordam"!

8) Shenaasnaameye Man

This duet with Mehrdad starts with a rather dull arrangement. It is upbeat. "Vatan chieh, vatan kieh, laalaayee bacheghiyeh". Good lyrics. Unfortunately the music sounds a bit too generic Mehrdad. It doesn't suit Googoosh's voice either. Sounds better on Mehrdad. No chorus. This song seems to be what was supposed to be called "Khalij-e Fars". Still, great lyrics and the music is not too bad.

Packaging and jacket (0 out of 1 point)

The design and picture chosen for the front jacket are absolutely horrible. I don't know why Googoosh's jackets are always so lame. The same thing happened with her last two albums, "Zartosht" and "Akharin Khabar". The most boring picture has been chosen, then her name is repeated, which is annoying given that the album is a "Manifest" and trying to make a statement. Googoosh's name only appears in English text. An Iranian design should have been added. The white background is awful and doesn't match her clothes.

Also other big name artists in the Iranian market are starting to release their CDs with accompanying DVD of music videos, as an incentive for people to buy legal copies as opposed to downloading illegally from the net. It's a bit disappointing that they didn't do this with Googoosh. The rest of the CD package is not great either, with pictures from a single session taken indoors.

title: A jazzy album
text:
I originally heard Angie Aparo's version of Silent Night as it played in the background during a scene on the TV show Roswell. (You can listen to a 2 minute clip of it at [...]) Perfection comes close to describing the way he sings that song. As soon as I heard it, it struck such a chord in me that I immeiditately scoured the internet until I found out who sang it and where I could buy a copy of it. My quest finally led me here to this album. I didn't have a clue who Angie Aparo was (and still don't) but I bought this album just to hear him sing that song. Now I listen to this album because almost all of the songs are a joy to hear--with the exception of NSYNC's version of The First Noel. It sounds quite amatuerish. They are out of their league with the talented artists on this CD and should stick to singing teeny-bopper pop songs.

In addition to Aparo, a notable standout on this album is Santana's Posada. Wow!! I would have purchased this album just for that song too. I am adding it to my regular mood music playlist because it is exceptional. It has the exotic passion of an arabic instrumental. Very sensual and seductive.

Diana Krall doesn't disappoint either. Her breathy voice is a perfect match for a jazz lounge version of Have Yourself a Merry Christmas. I didn't want to like R. Kelly's song becuase I don't like him as a person but I can't deny the man can sing.

This album is more RB than your typical Christmas music so I caution those looking for traditional Christmas music that this may not be an album for you. However, if you want a different spin on the songs you grew up with, give this CD a try. You may find yourself enjoying this CD all year round. Not many copies of this album out there so snatch one up if you can.

title: a lovely, non radical reading on period instruments that should appeal even to HIP-bashers
text:
For all the popularity of Mozart's five Violin Concertos, his two true masterpieces in the genre are the Concertone - a Triple Concerto for two Violins and Oboe in all but name, at times turning into a Quadruple Concerto with the addition of an obligato cello - and the Sinfonia Concertante for Violin and Viola. The Concertone may be an early work of Mozart, written when he was 17 (all is relative of course - like Schubert's, all Mozart works are "early", and the Sinfonia Concertante, considered the "mature" work, was written at 22), and his first real Concerto (all the previous ones had been arrangements of Sonata movements from other composers), and it is still marked by the influence of the galant style in its middle movement and Finale, but it also teems with irresistible enthusiasm and wonderful melodies and smacks of the opera in its boisterous opening one.

These recordings by the Smithsonian Chamber Orchestra, with Jaap Schröder leading and playing first violin, made in 1986, are great versions on period instruments, likely to please even listeners adverse to historically-informed Performances (HIP), because there is nothing radical about them, they are played in a classic manner, lively and spirited in the outer movements (with the exception however of the Concertone's Minuetto-Finale, see further), and true to Mozart's "Andantino grazioso" in the middle movement of the Concertone. Anti HIPsters might object to their taking the middle movement of Sinfonia Concertante at a flowing pace, closer to the "Andante" written by Mozart than to the romanticized and solemn Adagio many (including, to an extent, Harnoncourt, [[ASIN:B008L450NO Mozart: Sinfonia Concertante, Violin Concerto, Kremer, Kashkashian]]) turn it into, but not only is it truer to Mozart's indication, I find that Schröder and McDonald show a touching restraint there, with neither flaunted pathos nor the emotional turbulence of Heifetz (a great reading, at an even brisker tempo, [[ASIN:B000003EQ9 Double Concerto]]), eliciting instead a mood of touching tenderness. There is the touch of acidity associated to period instruments but great timbral character from the strings, and oboes and horns in Sinfonia Concertante are covered just a little too much in the tutti in the first movement, but marvellously present in the finale. The two soloists, Jaap Schröder and Marilyn McDonald, play and blend well, McDonald's viola tone isn't big, but it is creamy.

The first movement of the Concertone teems with youthful jubilation, the sonic perspective of the orchestra is perfect, with the oboes and horns never covered by the strings and the strings never over-resonant and excessively symphonic, underlining the Serenade nature of the music. Schröder and McDonald blend beautifully, making them almost indistinguishable, and oboist Stephen Hammer must be lauded for his marvellous timbral character. Their take on Mozart's "Andantino grazioso" is exactly that: andantino and gracious, very catholic in its choice of tempo (it is virtually the same as Oistrakh's, [[ASIN:B00000DOJD Mozart: Sinfonia Concertante, KV 364 in E Flat Major, Concertone KV 190 in C Major, Adagio KV 261, Rondo KV 269]]), at times vaguely languorous, but with sombre hues when comes the passage in minor mode at 5:15. I would take exception only with their tempo in the Menuetto-Finale. There is a puzzling contradiction in Mozart's indications there: "Tempo di Menuetto", and you easily associate that with a somewhat pedestrian pacing - the menuetto was an elegant, aristocratic dance after all, not a rock-and-roll - but then Mozart adds "Vivace". A vivacious Menuetto, then. Clearly, Schröder favors the elegant aristocratic and vaguely stately dance. I find versions that take Mozart's "Vivace" at face value (as, recently, Yakov Kreizberg with Julia Fischer, [[ASIN:B000W043VA Mozart: Sinfonia Concertante [Hybrid SACD]]]) more convincing, and certainly more exciting.

But this very elegance of Schröder here is an additional factor likely to please even those adverse to the style associated to period instrument playing. The best offer at the time of writing is another budget reissue (with no liner notes): [[ASIN:B00000E6W9 Mozart Edition Vol. 1: Sinfonia Concertante K. 364 & Concertone K. 190]].

title: Walter Klien Plays Schubert -- 2
text:
When I was young, my love of classical music was formed by the many inexpensive recordings on Vox and on related labels. Among the performers on these recordings was the Austrian pianist Walter Klien (1928 -- 1991). Klien's extensive recordings included the complete piano concertos of Mozart, the piano works of Brahms, and the complete piano sonatas of Franz Schubert. Klien's Schubert recordings date from 1974. By that time Schubert's sonatas had emerged from a long period of obscurity but were still not well-known to many listeners. Schubert's sonatas are long, reflective, meandering, and full of song. They lack the careful formal structure and the drive of Beethoven's sonatas. I have loved Beethoven's sonatas for a long time and came to love the sonatas of Schubert somewhat later.

Schubert's sonatas are good to hear in private and they have been bringing me comfort lately in Klien's performances. With many wonderful recordings to choose from, Klien brings a lyrical, self-effacing character to his interpretations. His playing is light, simple, and clear without mannerism or the tendency to over-dramatize. The depths of Schubert's music comes through in the unforced lyricism of Klien's performance.

Klien performs six sonatas on this set, which includes two early works, in E major, D. 157 and C. major, D. 279, together with works written later in Schubert's short life, including the A major sonata, D. 664, the sonata in A minor, D. 784, the sonata in D major D. 850, "Gasteiner", and the posthumously published sonata in A major, D. 959. I was moved by the beauty of the music in Klien's performance.

I have played two of the sonatas on this recording for myself. The "little" A major, D. 664, is Schubert's best-known sonata and is filled with melody from its opening theme through its quicksilver, shifting finale. I have heard many readings of this work and was inspired to hear it through Klien. The A minor sonata, D. 784, is a darker, more difficult work to play that has many admirers. The work constrasts dramatic, foreboding opening themes with secondary themes of lyricism and hope. Unlike most sonatas, the second themes in the outer movements come to receive the most emphasis.

The A major sonata D. 859, is the middle work of Schubert's final three works in this form. Klien performs it with beautiful clarity and feeling. The highlights of the sonata include a sad, flowing slow movement with a dramatic middle section and a wonderfully extended and elevated rondo for the concluding movement, my favorite single movement of the sonatas.

I was taken with the "Gasteiner" sonata, D. 850, which I hadn't known as well as some of the others. The Gasteiner is a long, virtuosic, dramatic sonata, perhaps in its virtuosity resembling the "Wanderer" Fantasy. The work is much more in the manner of Beethoven than are most of the other sonatas. Both the sonata and Klien's performance have received mixed reactions. I read some of the reviews of D. 850, both of Klien's performance and of the performances of other artists. Although I have heard the work before, I don't remember loving and drawing inspiration from it as much as I did here. It was something almost new and the highlight of my listening.

I listened to these sonatas through streaming on Amazon Music. They brought back memories of the old days of LPs and of my love for music and for Schubert. Klien's performances brought me solace and inspiration during a difficult time.

Total Time: Two Hours and Thirty-Two Minutes

Robin Friedman

title: Worth the Effort
text:
As Soviet tanks crossed the Czech frontier in 1968, and as musicians of that nationality rushed home before the borders were sealed, some intrepid producer got on the phone so that the show, or recording session, could go on. Locals from Munich filled in the gaps; the hybrid ensemble that resulted is described on the album as "Large Symphony Orchestra."

From what I understand, this "Lohengrin" was planned as filler, a kind of bonus that would accompany four other opera recordings: The whole project was completed in just under a month. Predictably, things did get a little sloppy; for example, the King Henry vocalist is erroneously credited. I'll bet there are other gaffes, too. And why not?, given the chaotic and scary conditions prevailing.

Despite, or maybe because of the crisis atmosphere, this is an important document in the long, voluminous, and competitive history of recorded "Lohengrins." Locating a copy isn't easy in North America, but it is definitely worth the effort. Check out the raves on Amazon.de, mine included. While abridged in places, the Swarowksy interpretation successfully balances the dramatic and lyrical elements in ways you won't likely encounter elsewhere. There are no Big Names among the vocalists, but they are all superior, and some (Ortrud: Ruth Hesse) are extraordinary.

Go the extra mile and score a copy.

title: Mike Love released his debut solo album away from The Beach ...
text:
In 1970, George Harrison released his debut solo album away from The Beatles entitled ALL THINGS MUST PASS, in order to prove how talented he was from under the shadows of John Lennon and Paul McCartney.

It was a masterpiece.

In 1981, Mike Love released his debut solo album away from The Beach Boys entitled LOOKING BACK WITH LOVE, in order to prove how talented he was from under the shadow of Brian Wilson.

It was a PIECE of something, all right, but nothing masterful!

An entire collection of covers was his bold, brash, leading-himself-into-a-brave-new-future statement? It just shows how far his artistic sensibilities stretched: not very far at all. He actually thought the public would eat this stuff up in that it's-still-1963 "brain" of his.This disc is beyond the pale. Thank goodness record buyers didn't fall for it. Unfortunately, it meant he went right back to the safety net of The Beach Boys and continued to lead their descent into county fair-playing retro hacks (much to Carl Wilson and Al Jardine's chagrin), as if the progression of the early 70s meant nothing. (Let alone the artistic achievements of PET SOUNDS.)

The Beach Boys was the band that once challenged the mighty Beatles in terms of sonic superiority. There's not a hint of that in anything Mike Love does with the group, or - as evidenced from this waste of space of an album - on his own. This man was - and continues to be - a blight on music.

Do yourselves a favour and go get a copy of Dennis Wilson's masterful PACIFIC OCEAN BLUE if you want a REAL solo Beach Boy album from this period with some WEIGHT to it. And go see Brian Wilson tour while you still can. And just imagine this album - and Mike Love himself - doesn't exist.

title: Medieval audaciousness
text:
At 45 minutes, Ralph Vaughan Williams’ Five Tudor Portraits is probably the most digestible among 100’s of 20th Century English oratorios. Quite similar to Dyson’s Canterbury Pilgrim’s from a few years earlier, also found with Hickox [[ASIN:B000000B0Y on Chandos]], each movement is a slice of life portrait featuring verse by Medieval poet Skelton. His texts imbue Vaughan Williams’ music with course humour and cheeky wit, covering topics from drinking to death, ones rarely found in these dusty Victorian Society choral works. Similarly, VW’s music runs into Carmina Burana territory, especially the rhythmic 3rd movement for men’s chorus, the drunken solo in the first, and the boisterously jolly outer movements, of which, the opening movement is easily the jewel of the work.

The short, serene 2nd movement has some lovely choral work, a touchstone of Vaughan Williams, but the 20+ minute 4th movement, with women’s chorus and soloist, overstays its welcome. The elegy for a girl’s bird is heartfelt at first, but the religious overtones that include a bird Dies Irae, church incantations, and a parade of bird funereal personifications, all presented so earnestly, becomes almost laughable. Vaughan Williams, an animal lover, perhaps is more loving on this subject than I, however. All in all though, this work is a gas and a joyous delight.

The 10-minute Five Variants on Dives and Lazarus embodies the folk-song writing so closely associated with Vaughan Williams. Written for strings and harp, it is perhaps the loveliest thing to come off this disc.

The London Symphony Orchestra is excellent throughout this program, the unique moments with bassoons and brass come off particularly well. The string playing in Dives gets a little edgy in the violins, but nothing that churlishly hinders the performance, although one wonders what the Philadelphia Orchestra could have done with it in their day.

The choral and vocal singing is outstanding. There is some really characterful work from the London Symphony Chorus, particularly in the 1st and 3rd movements, that make this presentation so fun to listen to. Jean Rigby really sells her drunk solo with a throaty low register, and despite my feelings about the 4th movement, Rigby is lovely throughout. I really like John Shirley-Quirk as a baritone, but approaching 70 years old at the time of this recording, his instrument is not as facile as it could be; the 3rd movement shows slight wobbliness from him, not untoward though, and could demonstrate more tenderness, but listen to his high range in the 5th movement and all thoughts of age are gone. The Chandos sound is big and full, typical of these Hickox symphonic choral albums. The choral singing is mighty solid, but they could be given a little more juice over the orchestra, for the instrumentalists get a little head room above the singers.

As to recorded competition, there isn’t much: Steinberg with Pittsburgh [[ASIN:B007POCBJC on Albion]] is sounding scrappy, and while I would be interested to hear Boult [[ASIN:B00008F8AC on Intaglio]], I suspect it bears the same fate. I have never taken to Wetton’s Guilford Choral Society [[ASIN:B00000J7ZE on Hyperion]], who ride the line of amateur choral society, leaving me wanting in the chorus department, but usually employs outstanding English orchestras. Which leaves the great Sir David Willcocks [[ASIN:B00000DOCS on EMI]] from 1968 with Heather Harper, the New Philharmonia, and the Bach Choir. Their choral work isn’t as characterful as what is here on Chandos, but the 80’s remastering is good if not exhibiting quite the equal in fidelity to Chandos. Willcocks does offer the 15-minute Benedicte in addition to what Hickox offers, so if you don’t mind 80’s remastered stereo sound, EMI might be the one to head to for more music.

Regardless, I can easily recommend Hickox’s Tudor Portraits with characterful choral and vocal work, excellent instrumentals from the LSO, and fine solo singing from Rigby and Shirley-Quirk. It is all easy to listen to, a bit quirky in the lyrics department, ala Britten, but captured in big, detailed Chandos sound. Highly Recommended!

**This is an update of my original review of VW's Five Tudor Portraits under Hickox [[ASIN:B000000B24 found here]].

title: Real Good Feelings
text:
I can happily say that this CD is a Masterpiece. I listened to it last night for the first time and my ears are still smiling this morning!
The two things that struck me the most (other than the fantastic performances)were how great the sound quality is & also that the order of the songs is just right!
Opening with "Kansas City Queen", which pulls you in right away is a smart choice! The song features a wonderful guitar solo that sounds like pure classic Outlaws! Why this track wasn't on one of the first 2 records was a mystery to me?
The next 6 songs are a combination of familiar and new and they keep the energy moving in the right direction! The main differences between the versions we are familiar with and these versions are the tempos. Makes for a whole new way of hearing these songs!
"Take it anyway You want It" was never a favorite of mine, this version is BETTER than the official release and sounds great! Billy sounds more relaxed on this one!

title: The best worship sessions ever recorded
text:
I first began buying these (now 7) sets of praise songs in the 1980s on cassette, and have given a handful of sets out as gifts and often listen to them still while driving or mowing or doing other work. I love them because they are, in my experience/opinion, the only set of worship music that truly is encouraging and designed to lead you into worship along with the singers. All others seem to convey a strong tone of entertainment, which I see in many churches unfortunately. The voices are soft enough to not drown out the music or yourself, and yet clearly enunciated for the sole purpose of helping you to join in and sing out loud or in your heart. It's hard to not sing out, though.

The songs are a mix of choruses and traditional hymns, with minimal and meaningful comments between most of them, otherwise one songs leads right into the next. Even after listening to these 7 CDs/tapes for almost 30 years, just writing this review has made me want to worship with them again.

For listening in loud environments, I suggest using these: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00H27E6NQ and and loading these songs to your phone or other mp3 player.

title: Surprise!  Wrong Broadcast!
text:
This review is of Arkadia "the Golden Age" GA2008, of Gounod's FAUST, from a Metropolitan Opera broadcast with Jussi Björling and Cesare Siepi. It is a good performance, but it is NOT from the 1950 broadcast with Dorothy Kirsten and Frank Guarrera, as the cover would suggest, but from 19 December 1959, with Elisabeth Söderström and, the most obvious clue to the performance, Robert Merrill, in fine form as Valentin.

This was Björling's last Met broadcast, and while his voice was still in good shape, his aria, "Salut! demeure" is transposed down a half step; the final high note is a 'B' instead of the 'C' he sang in 1950. But otherwise the differences between his performances in the two broadcasts are not great. Siepi in 1959 is a more subtle Méphistophélès, and Merrill is an improvement over Guarrera in the earlier broadcast. There is little advantage with either of the Marguerites, nor is Jean Morel's conducting significantly better, or worse than Fausto Cleva's.

Arkadia was able to fit the whole thing on two CDs, since in 1959 the Met presented only fragments of the Walpurgis Night ballet, mostly those with vocal parts. The ballet was resurrected, somewhat abridged in 1950, having been absent at the Met since 1918, but it was cut back with the new production in 1953. The sound of Arkadia's edition is quite good, for a 1959-60 season broadcast, having only a few ill effects of the sonic experiments being done at the time. Occasionally the orchestra sounds a little thin with an echoy quality, though the frequency range is good, and the voices are still picked up well. At the start of the opera a few light "clicks" at a 33 1/3 RPM rate are heard, which might indicate the CD was "sourced" from an LP edition, or perhaps disc transcriptions were used in 1959 for rebroadcasts in countries where the English commentary would be replaced. No commentary is present, and at the ends of a couple acts, the applause goes on longer than I would expect without interruption by Milton Cross. A short jump is heard about a minute before the end of the second scene, which is probably where an hour-marker "beep" was spliced out, suggesting an off-the-air recording.

The 1950 broadcast was issued by Naxos, and can be found on Amazon by searching for ASIN: B0009JMEFG. It certainly has virtues of its own, though the sound quality is not as good as this one from 1959. While neither broadcast is an "ideal" representation of Gounod's opera, both are of interest to fans of Björling, especially since he did not make a studio recording of the role. For this purpose Arkadia's edition is fine, when found at a reasonable price, though I'll rate it down a "star" for the incorrect broadcast identification.

title: Terrible Chorus Lines
text: I'm guessing this is Nu metal or post Nu metal. All I know is that it reminds of bands such as Five finger death punch or We came as romans. Bands that play this style of metal start off with great heavy riffs, then this out of place, cheese ball, bad pop song, chorus line just comes out of nowhere and ruins everything that the song had going for it. Don't get me wrong, I love a good melodic chorus line to balance out the heaviness.  All types of different bands do this well.  [ Iron maiden, Mastadon, tool, Carcass, Wolftooth and Eternal champion just to name a few.]  This goes to show that a good chorus line can be done. The big problem is that these American Nu metal and post Nu metal bands actually believe that their bad pop song chorus lines sound better. This is another failed genre in American metal, but unlike glam rock or rap metal I think this post Nu metal movement can right the ship if they just fix those awful chorus lines. It's really frustrating to think about all the potentially great songs that have been created and then ruined by this type of Metal.

I wish the musicians on this collection had spent as much time thinking through the arrangements as I did between the time I ordered it and first heard it. A rich trove of very unique songs to be mined, and I could just imagine how bluegrass' rich vocabulary of sounds and feels might give them new life.
These are lame, lifeless reproductions. Not incompetant, not unpleasant. But some tunes seem to have been thrown together from memory or a single listen, and none really capture the elements that make the songs special. "Tribute"? Baloney. "Cash in."
After looking around a bit, it seems to me that this gang mass-produces this kind of stuff. It's January, time to do Pink Floyd. It's February, time for Jo Dee Messina... Zep, U2, you name it, they can cover it.
Save your money, listen to the original "See Emily Play," and use your imagination instead. You'll hear something sparkling inside your head.
Better yet, imagine Bela Fleck leading his Flecktones through the Floyd canon, or Yes' "Siberian Khatra" or ELP's "Tarkus" or Peter Gabriel or Kate Bush. Imagine... but stay away from this CD.

title: Under-appreciated, gone but never forgotten
text:
Tammi Terrell, Kim Weston, Chris Clark and The Velvelettes were all Motown artists who were more talented than they were lucky. Thanks to Amazon and UK spectrum the talents of these seemingly forgotten artists can now be appreciated once again - this time on cd.

Of course Tammi Terrell will always be remembered for her duets with Marvin Gaye. In referring to her as forgotten I am thinking of her solo work, recorded at Motown between 1965 and 1968. I vividly recall taking the bus and subway downtown to buy my soul singles during the mid sixties. There were two relatively large stores (by the limited standards of those days - no music "megastores" existed!) that stocked Motown, Atlantic and Stax-Volt. Often the stores would have to place special orders for me. Listening again, after all these years, to I Can't Believe You Love Me and Come On And See Me, I am bewildered, just as I was forty years ago, that they hardly made a dent in the charts.

This cd contains the two aforementioned singles along with sixteen other songs, several previously unreleased. The sound, instrumentation, lyrics and vocals are, generally speaking, reminiscent of Motown sound of 1960-65 than 66-68. Perhaps this explains Tammi Terrell's relative lack of singles success.

title: Karagöz ve Hacivat
text: 4/5. One may feel pessimistic about Haluk Levent's abilities as a recording artist after five long years of silence, but things are not so bad on Karagoz ve Hacivat. On this record there is remarkable shift from radio friendly Anatolian rock which retained the warm smell of Mediterranean summer nights, into the territory of more progressive, darker and somewhat stickier sound, he first began experimenting with on leyla.com album in 2000. Romance and hope give way to loneliness, thwarted love and despair, not to mention antimilitary messages and the doomy weary drag through 8 years of AKP in power. Musically, this is not Haluk Levent's best effort and most of the greatest tracks are slight and probably more mature renditions of what fans had already heard on previous records. To name a few repetitions, the chord progression and chorus part of otherwise moving song Filistin delivered entirely in Arabic in duet with Turkish female singer Lal has been taken from Anlasana (Mektup, 1997). The arrangement of solo part of the closing track Srebrenitsa written in memory of victims of the 11 July 1995 massacre during the Bosnian war is painfully reminiscent of the artist's Pamukkale nostalgia on Yine Ayrilik (1998). Another noticeable remake is the refrain part of Gürkan which has the same structure as Bu Sehirden Gidelim Artik (off Mektup, 1997).But luckily the political and social commentary is what makes it worth listening and more than compensates.  Using both metaphors (as in Kral Çiplak) and overly literal verbiage (Seni Görmem Lazim and O Kendini Biliyor) Haluk Levent portraits the country of coal smelling neighborhoods, devastated national resources, unresolved crimes, political oppression and state mafia clans. These and other songs create a brutally dark and impressionistic image of people fed with lies and ghostly echoes of the military past very much in the style of Yilmaz Güney movies.  Another highlight is Gürkan which has been written in memory of Gürkan Babutçu, a soldier who was permitted to go to hospital, but was found hanged with bruises and cigarette burns throughout the body just hours later. Gürkan's mother Gülsen Babutçu contributed her vocals to the song as narration of the meaninglessness of life after her son is gone. To make the picture even gloomier, Haluk Levent also refers to the Palestine war, the Kahramanmaras massacre of December 1978, human rights activist Engin Ceber who was tortured and killed in police custody, murder of socialist journalist Metin Göktepe, repressions among protesting students in Manisa among many other examples. With such profound historical and social background, the record in fact offers much more than music, but an insight into life in contemporary Turkey outside megapolises and beach resorts. With things still not too bright for this country, Haluk Levent  wraps up distinctive voice, jingling guitars and irresistible solos into a message that functions as both a romantic lament and cry for sociopolitical distress. And it really rocks.  --Sain Alizada

title: non-rhythmic, pleasant background music featuring 2 bansuri flute lines
text:
"Reiki (霊気) is a form of alternative medicine developed in 1922 by Mikao Usui. Since originating in Japan, reiki has been adapted into varying cultural traditions.." It reportedly began being taught in India around 1992.

This CD has 14 tracks, unnamed, averaging 4-5 minutes each. The musical focus is 2 (overdubbed) flute lines, with slight musical setting of keyboard and acoustic guitar. The music is all in free rhythm, and there is no drum or meter. One track flows into the next, and sometimes there is a different tonal center ('supporting chord').

The chief musician is Rakesh Chaurasia, the award-winning nephew of Hariprasad Chaurasia, the best and most famous bansuri player of this era.

The album could be simply new-age aural pablum; it's saved from that ignoble fate by the talent of Rakesh. Find his many other recordings to hear his great talent and what he's actually capable of.

It's not "music for listening" nor is it intended to be. It's marketed as music to be played in reiki healing; I'm guessing it will serve that purpose well. It would also work well at a low volume for going to sleep, adult or infant. It's purposefully non-exciting and does not draw attention to itself. It serves well as background music for various purposes.

title: Paul's Fatal Mistake
text:
The story goes that Paul decided to end the band after discovering that John had turned over the Let It Be tapes to Phil Spector behind his back, and muzaked his beloved Long and Winding Road. But truely the real end came with Paul's refusal to release the last song on this anthology.

Both John and Paul had a knack for tapping into the rapidly evolving zeitgeist of the 60's. All You Need is Love may seem a little precious at this far removed time, but it was the perfect world rally rant at the peak of the summer of love.

Similarly, the world's attention in early '68 was on the Beatles celebrated trip to India to study with the Mahariji. What secret had they learned that they could impart on us? Of all the songs written during that sabbatical, the one that would have satisfied the curiousity of of the current youth culture was John's vision of spiritual wonder and inner peace, Across the Universe. A beautifully tranquil mantra to allow the fans a couple of weeks to contemplate before moving on.

But the ever competetive Paul would not hear of it. He was working on his very catchy, paternal influenced Lady Madonna. Brian was no longer around to intervene with his wonderful sense of timing. John's moment to capitalize on world attention was shattered. A week later, during the very next session, Hey Bulldog, he brought into the studio for the very first time his new partner, Yoko.

There were plenty of songs written in India to fill up most of the white album, and John's sudden disdain for the group venture was not completely evident until that batch was used up.

So here it is, before it mangled by World Wildlife, Phil Spector and finally the naked Paul, John's last shot at global connection in all its shimmering glory. (68 was a year where a lot of potentially positive things ended up pretty downtrodden.)

"Life is very short, and there's no time for fussing and fighting my friend."

title: It was a very good aid to quitting smoking
text:
I was skeptical of the claims made by the creator of this CD, which was given to me by a friend. But I was desperate to quit my smoking habit of 40 years. Without any expectations I began listening to this CD while falling asleep at night (used an old-fashioned walkman with ear plugs) and found it soothing and actually pleasant to listen to. I listened to it almost every night for four months. One morning, to my surprise, I knew I was ready. I said "I'm done" and I was. This isn't a miracle cure and I definitely went through some pretty rough withdrawal symptoms, but I believe that listening to this CD nightly gave me the jump-start I needed to actually commit to quitting.

I still listen to the CD on occasion (always while falling asleep) and I believe it reinforces my decision to be smoke-free.
