title: slow-moving, ritualistic, bizarre: music for the admirers of Feldman, but maybe not the best introduction to Radulescu
text:
Horatiu (or Horatio as his first name is sometimes spelt) was an interesting and often fascinating composer in his willingness to explore un-chartered territories and try outlandish musical experiments. He was born in Bucarest in 1942 but established in France since 1969, acquiring French citizenship in 1974. He recently died, on September 25 2008. He was, of course, alive and kicking when this recording was made, in 1993, on the occasion of its premiere in Strasbourg (although it is not entirely clear that this is the recording OF the premiere, since that was given in open air, and there is no such ambience here. So presumably it was recorded shortly before or after).

Although not officially associated with the French school of "Musique Spectrale" whose main proponents are Gérard Grisey and Tristan Murail, he was one of the first composers, in the 1970s, to make music based on the spectral properties of sound, e.g. the physical property by which an acoustic tone will produce a spectre of overtones.

Inner Time II opus 42 is in fact a reworking of sorts of a piece originally composed in 1983 as the vis-à-vis of another piece from three years earlier, "Outer Time", bearing the same opus number. Says the composer: "Inner Time is a valley, Outer Time is a mountain. Inner goes from the highest register to the lowest to the highest, Outer from the lowest to the highest to the lowest". Outer Time exists in versions for 23 flutes, for 42 Thai gongs, for trio of alto-cello-double bass, for two concert grand pianos, for 8 brass. Inner Time was originally scored for solo clarinet, with subsequent versions for seven trios of flute-oboe-clarinet, and for solo clarinet and four accompanying clarinets. Did I say Radulescu was an experimentalist, and does that sound outlandish enough?

The present version is a new composition based on the same spectral material as the earlier composition(s). It is scored for 7 B-flat clarinets that, in live performance, are to be placed in a large circle around the audience. Radulescu (like Henry Brant) used these same-sounding instrumental ensembles to produce micro-clashes of micro-intervallic tones through which the spectral properties of sound might unfold. I won't enter the detail of the compositional processes - they are way over my head and I'm afraid to have smeared egg all over my face already.

From the listener's standpoint, what you get is a continuum of high-piercing clarinet sounds, sounding subtly "off-pitch" because written in micro-intervallic proximity, slowly moving and ritualistic, broadly descending in range but very slowly and not by much, then ascending again, over a span of 56 minutes. As the English liner notes recall, Radulescu claimed to compose "music of a special state of the soul, and not the music of action" and this is exactly what you get here. Although does elicit a certain fascination, this is not the most immediately seductive and appealing music I've heard from this composer. The clarinets are not playing in their most sensuous tonal range, not much happens in the first 30 minutes - and little more thereafter.

This is music for those who enjoy Morton Feldman. I've recently heard and reviewed a CD which I think is a better introduction to the art and unique personality of Radulescu: [[ASIN:B000KEG8P2 Intimate Rituals]] or [[ASIN:B000K7UGO8 Intimate Rituals]].

Different liner notes in French, German and English - and those in English are by far the most complete and precise, so much so that you need to be a composer or musicologist to get it all.

title: Bill Frisell, solo electric
text: In this installment of Solos: the Jazz Sessions, Bill Frisell plays seven of his standards. Frisell plays solo electric guitar and uses his arsenal of pedals and effect devices to achieve the atmospheric grandeur that is his signature sound. 'Keep Your Eyes Open,' is a strong and light-hearted opener. Courtesy of the close-up camera work, the home viewer can study how every note is played. 'Throughout' is as loose and open as the cavernous location, Toronto's Berkeley Church. 'Throughout' transitions into a gorgeous retelling of 'Ron Carter.' The beautiful song brings to mind a Frisellian redux of 'Ave Maria.' After a hazy avant-garde intro, 'Boubacar,' emerges as a thought-provoking Desert Blues piece. The Americana body of Frisell's work emerges with 'Shenandoah.' It is a lengthy piece that is packed with musical wanderings to forbidden places. After drifting around in the woods, the candle in the ol' homestead can finally be seen! Lightening the mood, 'Wildwood Flower' is perhaps the most recognizable song on the DVD. Bill Frisell does the Carter Family justice. "Poem for Eva" is a beautiful closer that summarizes the charm of a live Bill Frisell performance. The sound quality is excellent and the ecclesiastical background helps to emphasize the musician and his music. The DVD can be played in stereo and 5.1 surround sound. The viewer can choose to 'play all,' which will integrate the songs and short but insightful talks by the artist. Otherwise, the songs and interviews can be watched in separate blocks. The biggest potential mistake for the viewer is to skip the bonus songs. These covers are tons of fun! Bill plays Hank's 'I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry,' Dylan's 'Masters of War,' and Gershwin's 'My Man's Gone Now.' Frisellians that enjoyed albums like "[[ASIN:B00004NHIO Ghost Town]]" and "[[ASIN:B0029358HQ Disfarmer]]," are sure to appreciate "Solos." Since videos of this guitar player are far and few between, "Solos" offers a precious look at Bill Frisell.

title: Bitterly disappointing
text:
Fans of the original Star Wars trilogy hoping for a franchise revival with "Attack of the Clones" will be surprised to find a film that is, to be kind, badly written, badly acted and, shockingly, badly edited. Which is fine if you're watching the Star Wars Christmas Special, but not here.
Even for casual moviegoers who are looking to "just be entertained," the newest Star Wars film even fails to deliver on that task. Unlike the original three films, which put a simple story of good versus evil in a world formerly unseen by moviegoers, everyone involved with Attack of the Clones seems to have lost any sense that less is more. Why have two Jedis fighting when you can have 100? Why have one Jango Fett when you can have an army of them? Why have a simple good guy/bad guy story when you can create a plot much more needlessly complicated?
It's that mentality that hurts the film more than anything else. The film is overstuffed with effects sequences so long you feel like you're trapped watching someone else playing a videogame. In between are scenes of political dialogue so flat and dense it belongs on C-SPAN, and not in a fantasy film.
There are certain aspects to the film that are well done. Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan Kenobi is, at last, allowed to be an action hero, and McGregor gives his scenes a gravitas that melts away whenever he's off screen. A chase through an asteroid field is also extremely entertaining in its use of sound design. And we finally get a two-minute glimpse at the evil emperor (which prompts a question: Does George Lucas know that we all know the emperor's true identity, or does he plan on making this a plot twist of some kind?).
But all of the good parts are such a small part of Episode II that it doesn't make watching the rest of it worthwhile. Of particular agitation is the love story between Hayden Christiansen and Natalie Portman. Portman, who is the equal of Audrey Hepburn in looks only, looks like she'd rather be anywhere else but on screen reciting her lines. And, try as Christiansen might, he can't overcome dialogue so poorly written it reduces the audience to unintentional laughter. Is real teen romance this cheesy? Of course it sometimes is. That's why it's best left out of movies altogether. This is a romance that plays out like an extended version of the animal cracker scene in "Armageddon."
And even while those scenes have unquestionable camp value, the overlong action sequences in the film reduce the viewer more to boredom than anything else. Add in the return of Jar Jar Binks (who apparently learned Spanish while he was away), and a computerized Yoda, who now does his backwards-grammar thing every sentence to the point of annoyance, and the film's computer work ends up grating rather than gratifying.
Editing is also a problem. Because Episode II is basically an animated film with live actors, the challenge of the filmmakers is to have the two worlds blend seamlessly together. This is not the case here, as many scenes where people are computerized, and then are not, are handled clumsily. And for the viewer there's always a disconnect that won't allow you to get deeper into the story. There's no sense of danger, or urgency. And that's what ends up making the whole affair so dull.
Look, it's a tribute to the first three Star Wars films that fans continue to keep coming back to this series. They're looking for the magic, the excitement, they got when they saw those films the first time. But Episode II doesn't provide that, and neither will the trilogy's next installment, unless George Lucas hires a new screenwriter and a skilled director of actors. That likely won't happen. Still, Star Wars fans still have the original trilogy, and that's awfully tough to beat, as George Lucas should now be able to tell you.<P...

title: very appealing
text:
This was my first hearing of The Pearl Fishers, and I was pleasantly surprised by the appealing music of this lesser-known opera by Bizet. At times, the music sounds like that of his Symphony in C, although there is an "exotic" tinge to much of the orchestration and harmonies (in an attempt to create "Hindu-sounding" music). The music also reminds me of Gounod, especially Gounod's Romeo et Juliette. Although this opera is short on plot and drama, it is one of the few operas that I can listen to from beginning to end without getting bored or distracted. Bizet knew how to write appealing melodies and ensembles.

There are two negatives, however, that I should mention. First, the engineered sound is from the 50's, and this is most noticeable in the somewhat "screechy" sound of the soprano, Pierrette Alerie. I am reminded of Jeannette MacDonald singing in a 40's or 50's musical! (This is not meant as a criticism of Alerie's voice, which is actually very beautiful.) Secondly, there is no libretto in this CD set, so you will have to find one on the Internet, as I did. Unfortunately, I could not find an English translation. But, the French text is pretty basic, so it is not too difficult to understand if you have a basic reading skill in French.

As for the cast, I can find no fault, as all the leads perform admirably and have attractive voices. All in all, this is a performance and recording to treasure, despite its age (from 1954).

title: Hippie Classic
text:
Not as famous as The Beatles, 'Sgt. Pepper,' Love's 'Forever Changes' is, nevertheless, a terrific hippie album. Containing Latin rhythms and brass with some outstanding string accompaniment, the songs are simply marvelous. The interplay of acoustic and electric guitar bring the listener to sheer transcendence. Singer-songwriter, Arthur Lee, is a resourceful and succinct poet throughout. With anthem-like lyrics and haunting love songs, Lee brings his audience to another level. Certainly, it must be conceded that the venue is dated, like much of the music of their contemporaries, but this qualifier doesn't make the album any less worthwhile.

To start off, "Alone Again Or" is mesmerizing, alternating from a fast to a slow serenade. Then, "A House Is Not a Motel" kicks in with surreal images that tell a broken story of heightened awareness. Trippy, but partly nightmarish, "A House,..." reels in imagery, but refuses to totally commit to the confusion. The anthems take aim at the conventional world, but do it ably and concisely. "The Daily Planet" is nearly as brilliant as Dylan and as succinct as the Beatles. Before 'The Graduate,' Arthur Lee could sing, "There's plastic Nancy/With her children/Buys them toys/To keep in practice/Waiting on the war!" "The Red Telephone" also offers the contrast between the normal and new consciousness in a quieter, mournful way. However, the trajectory of "Live and Let Live" is really one of the album's highlights. Articulate and pulsating, Lee paints a landscape of Indians and bluebirds that are shot at simply because they're in the way. Beautiful touch. And, the lively "Between Clark and Hilldale" is about as footloose and fancy free as hippies got. Musically, the love songs really shine. "Bummer in the Summer" is shimmering folk, but "Andmoreagain" and "Old Man" are simply perfection! While it may be conceded that Lee, like many hippies of his era, could get corny, "Old Man" is an astonishing love song. Surely, you can't call the exquisite orchestrations of "Old Man" and "Andmoreagain" muzak to your ears! "You Set the Scene" is a finale that paints a rosy, optimistic send off with humor and encouragement laced throughout.

Some of the extras feel extraneous, but who can get enough? "Hummingbirds" and "Wonder People" are treasures that help the CD linger on. The rest of the alternate mixes and group interaction are interesting enough, but were never originally included for obvious reasons. You can always skip them afterall.

(Not to insult anyone's intelligence, but while I love drug induced music, I never recommend the use of dangerous mind-bending drugs. I'll take the vicarious listening experience at a safe [drug free] distance.)

title: At Home with Bob Ward, recorded in his living room in Monterey Park, California.  A private press organ Lp from 1961
text:
AT HOME WITH BOB WARD AT THE HAMMOND ORGAN, "MUSIC TO LIVE BY" Century Records V12980.

The 12" vinyl Lp is recorded as four extended medleys, two per side:

Side one:
(Jump Tempo)
When You're Smiling/When My Baby Smiles At Me/The Lady Is a Tramp/Beer Barrel Polka
(Slow Swing Tempo)
Sleepy Serenade/Slow Poke/Indian Love Call/Third Man Theme
Side two:
(Waltz Tempo)
Alice Blue Gown/Fascination Waltz/Melody of Love/Tennessee Waltz
(Bounce Tempo)
Swingin' Down the Lane/Sunny Side of the Street/Penthouse Serenade/Sentimental Journey

Sound is stereo; per the liner notes, Bob Metcalf of Century Records did a field recording in Bob Ward's house. Other than a worldless "vocal obbligato" by Martha Gilmour, or what sounds like deeply electronically echoed "humming" by "...Martha Gilmour whose voice is heard on many TV and radio programs...," the album is entirely Bob Ward's keyboard work. The Lp sounds like it was miked between two speakers on the organ and the stereo comes via how each part of the keyboard plays through which speaker side. Overall feeling is instrumental easy listening.

Bob Ward worked for the Alpha Beta grocery chain in Southern California and played for customers in his store; the price tag on this $4.98 Lp shows "price 2.79/Sales Tax .11/Total $2.90" from Alpha Beta (my copy; pressed on thick yellow wax). Pictured on the cover shot in Bob Ward's home living room are Bob, Darrow and Charlene Johnson, Carol Rugraff.

Bob Ward discography:

AT HOME WITH BOB WARD, Century Records V12890 (Century Records was a private/contract press custom pressing service)
AT HOME WITH BOB WARD, ENCORES, Continental Records V 12920 (pressed by Century Records)
MERRY CHRISTMAS, Continental Records V 13868 (pressed by Century Records) -- this 12" was also pressed on 7" EP
ORGAN FAVORITES, Continental Records 15548 (pressed by Century Records)

Century Records started as a private press service specializing in LDS/Mormon albums in 1956, then branched into custom small run albums mostly by middle schools, high schools, and college student concert recordings, as well as vanity/private press albums by recording artists making their own records to sell out of their homes, cars, or bookings. The label was based out of Saugus, California; Century pressed records showing sometimes a custom imprint, like Continental Records, numbered in the Century Records release series in the early '60s. I can definitely date a Three D's Mormon folk album, V17451, before May, 1964. Bob Ward's stereo albums date probably beginning in 1961, into 1962-3; stereo albums didn't become available until beginning about Christmas, 1958, generally. Bob Ward relocated about 1978 to Rexburg, Idaho.

title: An excellent audio-biography
text:
If you reading this page, you must know by now that Naxos has been issuing a series called Life and Works, audiobiographies of famous composers. Never shy of surprises, Naxos now gives us what I hope is the start of a new series, A Life in Words and Music. "Enrico Caruso" is now available on a 4-CD boxed set (8.558131-34) with a text and narration by British actor David Timson (the voice of the composers in the other series) and 30 original Caruso recordings to support and illuminate the text.
Caruso was a fascinating personality, prone to human weaknesses but seldom losing his sense of humor. Timson gives us all the pertinent facts about his incredible rise to stardom, his domestic problems, the Monkey House scandal, even the Black Hand's threats on his life, his continuing battle with throat problems. Unlike some other opera stars, he is a thoroughly lovable character and I found myself really getting to like and admire him as the story of his life spun out on these wonderful CDs.
By the way, each of the 30 recordings, dating from 1902 to 1920 (how sad he missed the age of electric recordings,) is played complete; so having this set can even be the start of a collection of all his recordings, all of which are available in 12 volumes in the Naxos Historical series.
The tracking list in the booklet can send you to any point in Caruso's career or to any one of the 30 recordings. All in all, a very worthwhile package from Naxos.

I love the music of Michael W. Smith. I think that he is an extremely talented artist, a likeable person, and a good Christian. I was introduced to his Christian music through his 2002 live album recorded in Canada...Worship. I love EVERY SONG on that album, every one of them. Several of them caused me to become emotional. As a result of that album I have ordered every Michael W. Smith DVD/CD combo album. That was a mistake.

I received the Sovereign DVD/CD combo today. I just finished watching the entire DVD. I kept listening to song after song, hoping that one of them would be half as good as those found on the Worship album. I reached the end of the DVD without liking one of the songs. The crowd, although respectful, was pretty much quiet throughout the entire show.

I will say that this DVD/CD is made to the same high quality standards as all of Michael W. Smith's products, but that's just about all that I have positive to say about "Sovereign." Michael said that Sovereign was basically an experimental album, and as far as I'm concerned it didn't live up to his previous efforts. If I had watched this show on YouTube prior to buying it, I wouldn't have bought this DVD/CD combo. Sorry, Michael.

title: review
text:
An eleven track compilation, 1972's "The Best of Crow" pulled together five out of the band's seven 1969-71 era singles. Missing in action were 1970's 'Slow Down' and 'Watching Can Waste Up Time'. Given the band's limited catalog (they'd only recorded three studio sets up to that point), a "best of" collection struck me as a bit premature, but with lead singer David Wagner having quit the previous year, I'm guessing Amaret wanted to capitalize on the band's audience while they still had a chance. And here's the really funny thing about this album - since the labelt got to "cherry pick" from the first three albums, on a song-for-song basis the results were surprisingly impressive. Yeah, Wagner's voice was an acquire taste (he frequently reminded me of a rock-oriented David Clayton-Thomas), and there wasn't a great deal of originality in these grooves, but looking back I find nine of the tracks score high with my ears (and that includes a couple with horn arrangements).

- Off their debut LP "Crow Music", 'Evil Woman' was their biggest and best hit (really their only hit). Driven by Larry Wiegand's pounding bass and some very daring lyrics (remember this was 1969), the song probably deserved to be a bigger hit than it was. Interestingly, the horns were added without the band's knowledge, or approval, giving the tune a Blood, Sweat & Tears-edge. rating: **** stars
- Their fifth single, 'Don't Try To Lay No Boogie Woogie On the (King of Rock and Roll)' was as horrendous as the title. A mindless slice of anonymous bar band moves, the song found lead singer Wagner trotting out his bluesiest voice to little effect. rating: ** stars
- Off of their second album, 1970's "Crow By Crow", 'Colors' opening with some Kink Middlemist church organ before unexpectedly exploding into one of the band's better rockers. Dick Wiegand acquitted himself with honors on the track and even Wagner's David Clayton-Thomas wannabe vocals were enjoyable on this one. rating: **** stars
- 'Gonna Leave a Mark' was another track off the debut LP. Driven by a crunching Dick Wiegand guitar riff, the song was actually pretty good and would have been even better had producer Bob Monaco restrained himself and dropped the needless horns which gave the song a dreaded BS&T feel. rating: *** stars
- Showcasing one of their better melodies and some of Dick Wiegand's best playing, 'I Stand To Blame" was a likeable country-rocker with a nifty nod to Elvis Presley. The song was also interesting for showcasing the band's seldom displayed harmony vocal skills and for Wagner's breezy delivery. Shame he did sing like this more often. rating: **** stars
- The band's debut single, 'Time To Make a Turn' has always reminded me of a Gary Puckett and the Union Gap song. Complete with punch horns, this one sounded like it had been penned for maximum radio play - hard to understand why it vanished without a trace. Elsewhere, Dick Wiegand turned in a tasty lead guitar solo. rating: **** stars
- A strange choice for a single (gawd only knows how it hit the top-100 charts), 'Cottage Cheese' was apparently written to spotlight drummer Dennis Craswell. Musically the song was little more than a brief jam session with each member, including Craswell), given a crack at a short solo. The song title was basically a place holder, but the band never came up with a better title. rating: ** stars
- Penned by bassist Larry Weigand, 'Busy Day' was built on a great rock riff (if I ever wanted to write a song, I'd steal it in a heartbeat). The only downside to this one was producer Monaco's needless studio effects. rating: **** stars
- Lifted from the band's third studio set (1971's "Mosaic"), 'Satisfied' was a bit different from the bulk of the group's standard bar band repertoire. Opening up with some attractive orchestration, including Craswell pounding away on kettle drums, the track didn't drift all that far from hardrock, but sounded considerably more self-assured than much of their earlier work. rating: **** stars
- Larry seemed to be the band's most commercial writer and that knack was aptly displayed on 'Keeps Me Runnin''. Nice pop-rock tune that again showcased the band's overlooked harmony vocals. rating: **** stars
- Three things save 'Yellow Dawg' from oblivion: 1.) Dick Wiegand's fuzz guitar (he also turned in a blazing solo), 2.) the title track chorus, and 3.) Middlemist's jumpy keyboard pattern which Dick and Larry follow a couple of times throughout the song. rating: **** stars

Darn, I guess I'm gonna have to go back and re-exam the studio albums.

title: Mo tells it like it is
text:
Yes, this album is very hard to find, but once you do, it was well worth the effort and the money. I found my copy upon its release over 20 years ago at the old Rose Records shop in Chicago, a couple of years after I finally heard the Velvet Underground and Nico for the first time (1987), and I love it to this day. Two tracks stand out: "Hey Mersh" and "Work". The former track opens with Mo yelling "Hey, Mersh, let's go to the mall", which was kind of scary considering my then-blossoming aversion to shopping malls. They were "the place to be" back in the late 70's and some time into the early 80's, but by the end of that decade, I had just about had it with them. "Work" is still as relevant now as it was then, with lyrics telling it like it is when it comes to long hours and low pay - this is leaps and bounds over anything Bruce Springsteen and Styx had to say on the subject. You do, of course, remember that horrible song, "Blue Collar Man". Tommy Shaw was a multimillionaire "rollin' in the dough" at the time the song was released. What in God's name did he know about struggle? Mo says it best, and it's set at a frenetic tempo with drums and guitars that sound as angry as the singer, and possibly as much as the record buyer listening to this track. She touches on such subjects as problems in the free-lunch program for public schools, rising utility bills and high deductions from paychecks: "My kids don't get a free lunch at the school they go...Gotta pay the lights - I GOTTA PAY THE PHONE!!!!!" The refrain, of course, says it all "WHEN I GET MY CHECK I KNOW SOMETHING'S WRONG...OH! SOMETHING'S WRONG!!!"

There are also nice covers of "Goodnight Irene" and Lou Reed's own "Pale Blue Eyes", and Mo actually wrote most of the other songs on the album, including "Mersh" and "Work".

Get this if you can - PLEASE!

Recorded with help from Reed, as well as Sonic Youth's Lee Renaldo, Kim Gordon and Thurston Moore, this is a true punk masterpiece.

title: So you wanna get into J-Rock or Visual Kei
text:
Its not often that I review singles (Matter of fact...this is THE first single I've reviewed on this site) so we are entering uncharted territory here.

The first time I heard the song "Fuyu Tokyo" it was in a video posted on Youtube from a LIVE that was done back in about 2006 and, at the time, I didn't know what the name of the song was because I'm not super proficient in reading Japanese yet. Anyways when I found that there was a PV for this song I ended up listening to it about 25-50 times on that day...no I'm not kidding!

The interesting part about the song is that the first part (and the first couple of lines in the chorus) are sung in ENGLISH! This isn't a TERRIBLY big deal but it kind of makes you wonder how the song would do if a band tried to cover it in English...on second thought...let's not!

When you listen to this single you immediately think (or at least I did) about a period in music that was more either "pop"-ish or maybe in some cases a bit of a jazz motif. I say this because of the fact there are clearly horns/trumpets being played and the first time I heard those I couldn't believe it to be honest but then again the lead singer of this group was/is part of a group which had a song that used a violin in it ("Amorphous" from the "JUBILEE" CD by Versailles if you were wondering) so it comes as little to no surprise there.

The second track on the single is "fiancailles" and if you haven't seen the PV for that song you are doing yourself a serious disservice by not seeing it! The video for the song is one of those that is borderline creepy and I could have sworn I had the ending scene of the PV in a dream of mine and to see the ending was surreal!

Anyways...

This version of Fiancailles is a "mix" version so its not the original version which is alright because I always love to hear other versions of songs I liked and this one didn't disappoint! Its about 9 minutes long but most of that is because there's some dead air and then a voice at the end which again speaks in English tells the listener something and its a heck of a way to end the song and the CD!

so the question we ask now is the same as the title of this review:

"So you wanna get into J-Rock/Visual Kei?"

If you do...there are very few singles I'll be reviewing on here that would be as good a starting point as this masterful single!

(Now if only I can find "Fiancailles"...)

title: Disappointing, a huge let down.

Even more painful is the lack of musical imagination that permeates the CD. Viktor is clearly more a sculptor than a musician. The improvisations are very linear and uneventful. The modal grooves are propelled by funky drums and bass but do not save you from utter boredom. So sadly, the instruments are spectacular visual promises than do not deliver musically in this CD. As a musician, I do believe you make can music within tight limitations, but a whole CD is a real challenge and would require a truly inventive, creative mind...So maybe the moot question here is "are those crippling limitations expressed in the CD coming from from the musician or the instruments? title: An excellent series
text:
"Great Operas at the Met" is a series of recordings, each highlighting a particular opera, published by The Metropolitan Opera in conjunction with RCA/BMG. Each boxed set has 2 CD's containing excerpts from the opera as sung by artists who sang the particular role at the Met. The first CD consists of older excerpts from the earlier part of the XXth century and the second CD has selections from more recent productions. There is also a small booklet of around 70 pages containing a short essay on the history of the opera as produced at the Met, very short synopses of the scenes, texts of the excerpts with translations, and around 50 photographs of the singers and sets from the productions.

I have posted an image of the back of the box, showing the selections and artists, on the "customer image" selection in the upper left hand corner. All of the selections are in good sound and the artists, representing the premier singers of their era, range from very good to great. Especially fine are the temple scene with Pinza and Martinelli, the nile scene with Rethberg, Lauri-Volpi and de Luca, and the tomb scene with Ponselle and Martinelli.

If you are familiar with historical opera singers, you do not need any recommendations for artists like Gadski, Caruso, Amato, Homer, Martinelli, Rethberg, Ponselle, Corelli, Warren, Tebaldi and Bergonzi. If you have not heard the earlier singers, this series is an excellent (and often inexpensive) introduction to them, and I recommend that you give it a hearing - you will not be disappointed.

title: All Stewart Copeland, all the time
text:
When Stewart Copeland's band The Police started to change out of the punk band they were into something else, it was mainly Sting's songwriting that emerged as the dominant force of the band by the time of their first album, much to the chagrin of founder Stewart, who had previously done most of the writing and playing. Enter Klark Kent, a pseudonym for Copeland, which allowed him to make music that he had complete control over. Indeed, Copeland plays every instrument on the record and sings all parts.

When I first found this record I found it easier to pick out aspects of The Police that were very much Stewart. That's because with the other two members of the band removed, what you get here is pure Stew. The odd rhythms taken from Stewart's roots in Beirut and Egypt mixed with his own eclectic sense of melody that you can hear in Police songs such as Any Other Day, It's Alright for You, Rehumanize Yourself and Does Everyone Stare are all well evident here. Stewart sings on 6 of the 8 songs but the 2 instrumentals are very strong and are favorites. All the songs are strong and really the weakest part is the singing. But all the humor and eccentricity of Stewart Copeland are here, along with the musical depth and excitement that one of rock's most diverse and talented composers can muster on such an early work.

The record is a 10", often clear and colored in green, and the sleeve is die-cut so watch out for damage. The Kollected Works, which contains these tracks and a few others, is near impossible to find so if you have a record player, pick up something not only physically unique, but musically as well.

title: Best of the Toni Martin era also the hardest to find
text: After Ozzy left a lot of people do not consider any of the Black Sabbath Albums to be true Black Sabbath albums, something that the band also agreed with.  Starting with the Dio Albums, the original band members tried to call the band Heaven and Hell, and again when all the members except Iommi left, Iommi tried to get Seventh Star released as a solo album that the record company intruded on.  I think some time after that Iommi realized that this was just part of the game and a way for him to get his music out there to the public.  For this part in his career I don't blame him, because Toni Iommi is the most influential guitar player in the history of hard rock and metal.  You do have to forgive him so very horrible albums by this point, Born Again and Seventh Star are among the worst albums in the history of the band, and even though Eternal Idol was a step in the right direction, it was not fully thought out.  Eternal Idol suffered from being high concept and having many different member changes in the middle of recording and the album did not sell to expectations as the band had cried wolf too many times and the fans were starting to leave.  Luckily all the discovery for Eternal Idol paid off here.  This is the best Toni Martin era album, and somewhere between Vol 4 and Sabbath Bloody Sabbath in my all time favorite Sabbath albums.  This album rocks.  The organ themes that the band had been playing around with for mood finally got toned down enough that they do not appear to just be filler.  This was done by a now defunct studio that even at the time did not have the money for sabbath to experiment and they just went with their instincts, and I think forced them to regain some confidence that would last in this line up through the mid 90's.  This is a very satanic and dark album, and for the blues and organ countering iommi's blistering guitar work martin is perfectly cast.  Stand out tracks would be Headless cross, When Death Calls, and Nightwing.  There are some slower songs on this album that make it more easy listening but the creative intensity mixed with lyrical content make it almost impossible bo ignore while listening.  Because it is no longer in print the price is steep, but if you loved Iommi, but can that it might not be formatted like Ozzy Sabbath, I recommend this album as being worth the money.  If you have any hesitations or lack of exposure to Martin Era Sabbath I suggest you check out Cross Purposes as it is also very good, but much cheaper to find, but still not as good as this.

title: A jambalya of simmering eclectic music from Merlefest 2005
text:
Playing Time - 45:00
Songs: Hayes Carll - Chickens, John Jorgenson - F.A.Swing, Caroline Herring - Trace, The Duhks - Dance Hall Girls, The Greencards - Love's A Word I Never Throw Around, The Wayfaring Strangers - Don't Put Off 'til Tomorrow, Knig Wilkie - Broke Down And Lonesome, Allison Moorer - I Ain't Giving Up On You, Gigi Dover - Back When We Were Young, Cathy Fink & Marcy Marxer - Hopelessly In Love, BR549 - Tangled In The Pines, Daybreak - Gone For Dreaming

Music lovers with eclectic tastes will delight in Merlefest's sampler of its "quality diversified American roots based musical experience." The festival's third Fresh Faces album samples tracks from featured performers at the annual Bluegrass and Americana event in Wilkesboro, N.C. which is a tribute to Doc Watson's late son, Eddy Merle Watson, who died as the result of tractor accident in 1985. The first Merlefest took place as a benefit concert in 1988. Fresh Faces 2005 is a fine sampling of styles and acts who will either make their debut in 2005 or who haven't performed there for some years. While some have already established their reputations, others are emerging, high potential artists who are garnering considerable high acclaim.

The challenge with any CD that presents such a variety is to organize the material so that the overall product provides a pleasing and entertaining aural journey. With such a disparate sampler, it can be a formidable task to produce a coherent flow from start to finish. That is my primary criticism. As an example, sandwiching Allison Moorer's and Gigi Dover's electric tracks between the acoustic King Wilkie and Cathy Fink/March Marxer songs can be problematic. Alternating these acoustic and electric offerings has the same effect as trying to mix oil and water.

The strength of Merlefest's 2005 Fresh Faces release, however, is that it is an effective promotional tool for the festival, as well as an interesting souvenir for fans and attendees. A person's limited time can be maximized with this exploration and discovery of twelve artist's music. One certainly has to appreciate the diverse nature of this music festival which doesn't operate within confined sideboards. They support many up-and-coming groups and performers that push the envelope within multiple genres of music. Merlefest clearly has a strong commitment to diversity, a good thing in a multicultural society with disparate musical preferences. The 45 minutes on this sampler includes a mix of blues, gypsy jazz, singer/songwriter, old-time, Celtic, bluegrass, folk, rock, country, rockabilly and honky-tonk influences. That's a heck of a lot. Imagine what you'll experience live at the festival!

Merlefest offers a little something for everyone. Focus on the unique character of each performer sampled, and try to broaden your own musical horizons. .f your musical preferences are very clearcut and confined, then you may only like a few tracks on this CD. If you're in the market for a jambalya of simmering music, check out Fresh Faces. There are other Fresh Faces and Live! albums on-line at Amazon and the Merlefest website store. (Joe Ross, NWBluegrass)

title: The gold standard of official McCartney releases
text:
This Netherlands only release is likely the gold standard of rare official McCartney releases. The album contains a full second disc of material. They are all b-sides to the Off The Ground singles. All but two are OTG session studio recordings. "Things We Said Today" and "Midnight Special" are both leftovers from the MTV Unplugged show.

Most of the songs are of equal or better songwriting quality than some of the OTG tracks. This is not only a personal opinion but one shared by the majority of McCartney reviews (I'm talking about you, Biker Like An Icon)! Most listeners will be pleasantly surprised by how varied and enjoyable this collection of b-sides are. There are many standout tracks, none being particularly weaker than the others.

If you are a value shopper, it will likely be more economical to hunt down all of the singles. Luckily I got this when it came out for a fraction of its going value now. Still listening to the second disc as a collection than the individual singles changes the feel of these songs as a body of work. It actually turns them into a body of work and makes an interesting compliment to the OTG studio album. This and a collector's desire to have an amazing piece in their posession are the main reasons to own this.

Having been a fairly big fan of Mr. Oldman (even having enjoyed his performance as Zorg in [[ASIN:B000QTD368 The Fifth Element]]), I've come to expect a certain level of entertainment from his film choices. Not so here.

Gary Oldman ([[ASIN:B000W45C70 Harry Potter]] films) stars as Paul, an Englishman on holiday in Spain's backwoods with his wife and another couple when they run afoul of the locals who are hiding a young girl away in what seems to be sickening conditions (they find her tied by the ankle in a dilapidated home drinking from a dog bowl). "Saving" the girl, they bring her back to their distant cabin and learn that some yocal-locals are looking for her ...and their carrying rifles.

Hiding her away, the English vacationers quickly learn that the nearby township will do whatever necessary to retrieve her ...including raping or shooting anyone who gets in their way.

Probably the biggest issue with this film is that it has no purpose, and flings about in uncertainty up to and beyond its horrible ending. It is never explained why the girl is tied up in the first place (she does act like an animal and the audience is left wondering if she were some sort of mentally handicapped kid or a hybrid human-canine, or even a werewolf ...but none of these are ever explored in any depth).

The acting is so over-the-top that I often wondered if the scenes were supposed to be taken seriously or were designed for laughs.

Regardless as to intentions, THE BACKWOODS should remain on the extreme "back shelf" of all DVD rental stores ...if stocked at all!

text: I really wanted to like this, I really did, especially since many billed it as an alternative to Maestro Bernstein's own disastrous operatic version with Te Kanawa and Carreras. Also, I really admired some of Schermerhorn's previous recordings, especially his complete Bachanias Brasileiros. But, this so doesn't work. To begin with, the tempi are often sluggish rather than vibrant. Listen to "I Feel Pretty" or, especially "A Boy Like That/ I Have a Love. The latter is particularly ruined by the pace, and the horribly off-key, unacceptably tremulous sound of the Anita. Plus, for some reason, the "Maria" cha-cha-cha which completes the Dance at the Gym sequence is completely missing. The "America" is the inferior film version featuring the Sharks boys and girls, with rewritten lyrics by Sondheim. The original for just the girls works so much better. Finally, the youthful cast is very variable in quality. The Riff sounds a bit fey in his dialogue break in "Jet Song", the Anita is definitely not up to the challenge. Best are the Maria and, especially, the Tony, who brings to mind the young Larry Kert, who originated the role in 1957. Which reminds me that the Goddard Lieberson OCR has never been matched in terms of freshness and authenticity. So, while some of these upstart versions may contain a little more music, the original has been reissued along with Bernstein's first and best recording of the brilliant "Symphonic Dances from West Side Story". For my money, that's the one and only disc to own.

It is said that from the age of eleven years, Guiseppe Verdi (1813-1901) wanted to write operas. Shortly thereafter he composed his first opera 'Oberto" which was so successful that his future seemed secure. However, the death of his wife and two babies some time later forced him into a state of depression. The impressario Mirelli gave him the book 'Nabucco' (Nebuchadnezzar) to read, and he immediately began to write music for it. Therewith he embarked on the career which eventually made him the "Grand Old Man" of Italian opera. In modern slang, he was a "natural".From "Oberto", written in his twenties, to "Falstaff", completed when he was eighty, his characteristic integrity and intensity persisted; as he wrote his 30 operas, his powers of expression broadened and deepened. By the time he wrote 'Aida', commissioned by the Khedive of Egypt, Verdi was 56. 'Aida' is often named as his greatest opera. The live elephants used in the production, the authentic costumes and musical instruments copied from ancient Egyptian tombs made an attractive picture, and his music made a "Celeste Aida" of the whole.

Lets face it; Bocelli is no Pavoratti, and perhaps it was not wise to choose some of the arias associated with the 'great' tenors, but Bocelli makes the best of his talents, which are considerable. title: Stunningly beautiful recording of English sacred music of the Tudor period
text:
The Tudor Choir's CD, "O Splendor Gloriae," is a stunningly beautiful recording that will greatly appeal to anyone interested in sacred music of the English Tudor period. The Choir, based in Seattle and under the direction of Doug Fullington, has nineteen singers: 6 sopranos, 5 altos, 4 tenors, and 4 basses. They sing this gorgeous music about as beautifully as anyone could wish.

Two versions of "Libera nos, salva nos" by early 16th Century composer John Sheppard serve as bookends for music by three eminent composers of the English renaissance period: John Taverner (c1490-1545), Thomas Tallis (c1505-85), and William Byrd (c1540-1623). There are four pieces by each of these musicians on the CD. Their musical styles, while having similarities, evolve over time.

Little is known about Taverner's life beyond the fact that he was organist and master of the choirs at Christ Church, Oxford, for five years. Nearly all of his compositions that we know of today were composed during that interval. An interesting aspect of his music on this CD is that each piece ends on a dominant major chord (for example, tonic e-minor ending on b-major). "Dum transisset Sabbatum" is an antiphonal work, with three chanted introits answered by choral "alleluias." The piece which gives the CD its name features solos and duets as well as extended choral passages.

Tallis served as the head musician of the Chapel Royal for four consecutive English monarchs, from Henry VIII to Elizabeth I. Though he remained a Catholic, he, like his student and successor Byrd, was protected by the Protestant rulers because of his musical capabilities, and he adjusted his style to suit the tastes of each monarch. His musical style is more inventive than that of Taverner. In places, use of unusual harmonization and quickly shifting keys resembles the music of Gesualdo (unknown to Tallis). Listen to the opening of "Susipe quaeso," where in relatively few bars the music modulated through a half-dozen keys.

Byrd was closely associated with Tallis, and they published a joint collection of sacred works under the auspices of Queen Elizabeth. Byrd's music reflects the influence of Tallis but sounds more structured and less polyphonic overall. His well-known "Ave verum corpus" is included on this recording. Byrd was a convert to Catholicism but served Elizabeth and James I in composing music for Protestant services as well as several Catholic masses.

In summary, this is one of the best recordings of brilliant a cappella singing that I know of. The Tudor Singers perform flawlessly and with feeling for music of this period. The Latin words are clearly pronounced, for the most part. The CD comes with a pamphlet that describes the musical selections and gives the Latin verses with English translation. This is a recording not to miss!

title: I grew up with the original Alley Cat album...and this isn't it
text:
When I was small, "Alley Cat" was one of my favorite songs. My grandmother owned the original 1962 "Alley Cat" album and gave it to me after I begged her for it. I loved the other songs on the record, as well as the lovely cover photo of a calico cat.

I was reminiscing about that album a few weeks ago and decided to see if it had ever been released on CD. Lo and behold, when I plugged in "Alley Cat", a picture of the original album popped up. It was quite expensive, some retailers were selling it for over $30.00 - mainly because it is out of print. I found a reasonable prince and bought it; boy was I disappointed! This recording is NOT the original 1962 Alley Cat album. The original one was issued in 1962 and featured Bent on piano with a drum and bull fiddle accompaniment (you can actually hear that version on You Tube in its 45 RPM release). No orchestra, no cheesy arrangements. The other tracks on that album were completely different from the ones offered on this CD.

This one sounds to me as though Bent is being accompanied by a synthesized band - to me even the piano sounds electronic (but that could be my stereo equipment). It is really nothing like the album I grew up with. In fact, the other tracks were not even on the original Alley Cat album and I don't recognize a single one of them. On the back of the jewel case, Elap says this is from "original recordings". If so, then it is from a totally different "original" album Bent Fabric must have done later on - because this isn't the album I remember. That smacks of falsehood, but again, how many people out there even recall the original Alley Cat, or even care? This makes me sad, though, because as a kid I loved that record. I may still have a dilapidated LP somewhere in my collection and if so, I'll get it out and play it once again.

title: Jade's 1st Symphony
text: "Bittersweet Symphony" is the first full length album from former Sweetbox lead singer Jade Valerie.  Jade is known for incorporating classical music into her dance/pop songs.  Also, I would have to agree with the previous reviewer's comments that the album is far better than "Out Of The Box", however "Out Of The Box" was essentially only an EP with 8 songs and possibly just an album to test the market as a solo artist.  Nevertheless, "Bittersweet Symphony" is a strong effort in my opinon.  The album for the most part is very upbeat and strong with the exception of songs such as "Empty Pages" and "Piece Of Love".  There were 3 songs on this album that I thought were the spotlight of the album.  "Like A Bird", Fast moving ballad with strong bass and subtle violins.  The song is mellow at the chorus but a strong verse leads into it.  "The Last", this song samples Christopher Cross's "Sailing", there was a song by Sweetbox that also sampled that song.  However, I like the incorporation of the song into this one as it has a very strong and singable chorus and the "Sailing" piece always brings me back.  Finally, the best track on the album in my opinion is "Undone", to some degree because it's an unexpectedly infectious dance song.  Strong Bass, Strong Vocals and then breaks into a synth dance rhythm.  The song bascially exemplifies what goes into a really great dance record.

title: Didn't Dig It
text:
I first heard Wayne Escoffery on Monty Alexander's super 2019 disc, "Wareika Hill", a reggae reimagining of tunes by the inimitable Thelonious Monk. Escoffery was great on that album, so I looked into checking out one of his discs as a leader, but hesitated because I didn't recognize the tunes on most of them.

This disc, veneration, seemed like a better bet, as it only features one original by Escoffery. The rest are described on the liner notes as under-recorded gems, or some similar wording. That was a clue, but I didn't realize it at the time. The tunes are under-recorded for the simple reason that they are not very memorable. This disc did nothing to make them so.

Further, the disc was recorded in 2007, when Escoffery was a long way from the robust, self-assured player I heard on "Wareika Hill". If that disc is any indication, then Escoffery has really grown into himself.

I like Escoffery's playing, but I don't like it on this disc, which to me is ordinary at best. It's already gone to Goodwill, where hopefully it will find a home with someone who likes it more than I did.

For example,the story "The Brook Hook" reads as follows: "A crook cast a hook into the brook. He hoped to hook a fish to cook. The fish took a look at the brook hook. The fish took a look above the brook and saw the crook. The crook would not cook a fish tonight."
I feel like I am reading Dr. Seuss' "Fox in Socks" (which is an excellent read, but too difficult for a beginning reader.) Phonics should be a tool for decoding and sounding out words for fluent reading WITH understanding.

title: They no longer sounded like they did back in 2001 and earlier
text:
I’ve been a fan of ‘Mist of Avalon’ since 1998 after I accidentally stumbled over the song ‘Lost In Feelings’ on their self-titled Mist of Avalon CD. They had a haunting distinctive sound with influences from The Sisters of Mercy and slight touches of the Ramones here and there. I live in the USA and at that time their music wasn’t available in the States so I contacted them in the year 2000 and Erik Sjölander, the guitarist, contacted me immediately. He helped me out big time, thank you Erik, and I ordered the 3 CD’s they had out at the time (Mist of Avalon, Sleepless, and Here And After). In 2001 they released the CD titled ‘Tears’. It is after this that things in the band changed drastically. It wasn’t until 2007 that another CD was put out titled ‘The Mist of Avalon Limited’. They no longer sounded like they did back in 2001 and earlier. Instead of the haunting vibe they morphed into a euro-pop rock sound.

The Dinya CD released in 2010 has all of the songs from The Mist of Avalon Limited CD plus 6 more songs. The CD isn’t bad, but the sound is so different from their previous work I personally feel they shouldn’t have used the Mist of Avalon band name when they released these last two CD’s. The best song on the Dinya CD is Negri. That is the only song I like on this CD, whereas on all the previous CD’s from 1998 to 2001 I like all of the songs. I attempted to contact Aram Yildiz the singer, but he did not respond. I’m guessing he no longer looks at their Mist of Avalon web page anymore and has moved on to other musical interests.

In any case Dinya is a good CD if you’re looking for a Euro-pop rock vibe, but if you’re looking for the classic Mist of Avalon sound I’d pass.

title: The Best Recordings of the Dvorak Trios
text: As a college student, I fell in love with the "Dumky" Trio by Dvorak because of the way the music, based on Czech funeral music, alternated between mournful introspection and a kind of frenzied grieving. The recording that I heard was this one by the Beaux Arts Trio. I assumed that all performances of the Trio would convey this magnetic contrast or emotional paradox. I've since learned that this is not always the case. Other performances by groups such as the Trio Fontenay, which plays beautifully with Wolfgang Holzmair on the Beethoven Scottish and Irish songs, have sounded almost coldly clinical. The Beaux Arts is for me the benchmark performance of these Dvorak trios. Strongly recommended.

title: French baroque flop
text:
Maybe it's just me, but I could not connect with this music at all. I love the French baroque – Lully, Delalande, the Couperins, Campra, Charpentier, Rameau, Leclair, Titelouze and assorted keyboard masters great and small. I have even heard some decent stuff by the present composer, Clérambault – notably some organ and harpsichord pieces – but the present collection of motets for three male voices with instruments does nothing for me.

Maybe it's the mannered, preciously melodramatic singing by countertenor, tenor and bass – especially from the second of these three – that puts me off, but one way or another I could not find anything to enjoy or appreciate here. The constant and copious vocal ornaments are distracting and sound forced. Instrumental support is all right, but there are no interesting passages or memorable melodies. Texts and translations are supplied; booklet notes are thorough, as well as eloquent in praise of the music.

An ordeal from start to finish. Any chance of getting my money back?

title: An often overlooked historically informed alternative
text:
I've owned the European pressings of this CBS recording for years and decided to add it my CD collection. First, don't be put off by the presence of La Grande Ecurie et Chambre du Roy, which scraped and sawed its way through several CBS issues of Handel's operas and the concerti grossi back in the 1970s. The orchestra sounds on its best behavior. The English choristers sing well and with substantial amplitude in the church acoustic. The soloists are a mix of native and non-native English speakers (Ulrik Cold) but there is no intrusive accent. Soprano Smith sounds refreshingly fuller voiced than many of her cohorts in the HIP competition. The use of a boy treble in the nativity narrative is one of those ideas that sounds good on paper but I don't care much for it in practice.

One of the attractions of the set, which the LPs proclaimed the 1741 Dublin version, is the use of alternative versions. The 1741 claim isn't absolutely accurate as two autograph version arias ("But who may abide," "Thou shalt break them") were replaced by secco recitatives now lost. McGegan's omnibus recording on Harmonia Mundi includes the "lost" recitatives presumably reconstructed. Otherwise, you get the 12/8 setting of "Rejoice greatly," the bass version of "Thou art gone up on high," and the autograph da capo aria version of "How beautiful are the feet" with "Their sound is gone out as the B section. Dublin heard a different version of the last to an alternate text as a duet for altos with chorus ("Break forth into joy"). Anyway, the set is an opportunity to hear alternates for those who aren't willing to go whole hog and get McGegan's version that includes all the variants (excepting simple transpositions).

This recording has been overshadowed from issuance by the competition (Hogwood, et al) and was only available in the US for years as a single disc of highlights. The Essential Classics issue shows up periodically at prices from dirt cheap to ridiculous. If the price is right, consider giving it a try.

title: Save your money
text:
I’d much rather see you but Elvis That’s The Way It Is or the other documentary, Elvis on Tour. Both stellar, and it’s what You really want.

As for Orion Ellis.......
Here you have a guy who spent his whole life “trying” to be Elvis, yet not admitting to it

He dyed his hair black, imitated Elvis mannerisms, wore a cape & jumpsuit, covered lots of Elvis material, and even wore a Mask over his face to give hope to Elvis fans that it was indeed Elvis

yet said he wasn’t trying to imitate nor sound like Elvis. Said he just naturally sounded like him. His speech pattern, his vocal inflections, things he said in between lyrics (play it son) etc all mimicked Elvis, as well as photos of him doing similar physical movements. It’s beyond clear he & his company were trying to copy Elvis without saying they were doing it

Signing onto Sun Records after Elvis died was another in a long line of footsteps he was tracing.

The “coincidental” book (Called Orion) that just happen to exist at the same time Elvis died, when he (Jimmy Ellis) took the name Orion was trying to break into the music business sure is a coincidence. The book is about a popular rock star who faked his death but comes back as a masked singer

Orion’s first album cover (which has been changed) was originally a drawing of a Dead rockstar laying in a coffin, with a masked man Holding a microphone being resurrected from the dead. Bad tAste

Later Orion took the mask off and tried to be a normal artist, but still using the Elvis voice he perfected over the years. He never made it big, and except some Elvis frantic fans Anxious to keep anything related to Elvis Alive, no one knows who Orion is.

However, after having said all this, Orion sings ballads well (Not as good with rock) and is among the better Elvis imitatators, albeit he tried not being called one

The material he covers of Elvis is unnecessary. We already have Elvis singing those songs

Ive heard some folks say Orion sang better, Which is rubbish......
but a few things to consider. Elvis had many voices, and sounded very different over his 24 yr career, such as:

Early hillbilly/rocking Elvis.......

smooth ballad Elvis from the early 60s.......

late 1960s & early 70s Elvis had a growl in his voice (if I can dream, high heel sneakers etc),

Mid to late 70s Elvis with a power nobody can match except an opera singer (hurt, trilogy, etc)

Orion was good with ballads, but nothing else. If you’ve heard Orion try to sing early Elvis (jailhouse Rock for example) it sounds lousy Compared to when 1950s Elvis sang it.

He did cover Can’t Help Falling In Love & Moody Blue, and it doesn’t measure up to Elvis versions, although they were both ballads You can catch him trying to sound like Elvis, vs actually sounding natural.

My point?

Elvis was the most flexible artist able to shape-shift to any genre, style, and vocal, whereas Orion was a 1-trick pony.

title: Complete letdown
text:
This CD is one of a series of early dance music programmes entitled « Dansez Renaissance », well documented and no doubt earnest in intent, played by Compagnie Outre Mesure directed by Robin Joly. One of its companion discs, [[ASIN:B00349F2Q6 Bal au Château de Chambord - Concert d'Alta]], is also still available but, sadly, the same criticisms I made of that disc apply equally to the present one. To cut a long story short, it is extremely disappointing. The usual names in the contents list seem promising enough - Susato, Praetorius, Gervaise, Arbeau, Phalèse - but the pieces are played without spirit, charm or any sense of spontaneity or enjoyment.

The dances are often moderately rhythmical in a crude sense, but none of them catches fire at any point. There is ample use of rather loud and insistent percussion, to the detriment of other instruments; also, while bagpipes have their uses, I find their unmelodious screeching most unwelcome in this repertory.

In short, this is as dull and disagreeable a programme of renaissance music as you can imagine, all the more disappointing because this genre has so many delights to offer to fans of early music. There are literally dozens of far better discs of this repertory available. I won't repeat myself any more, but if you do need to know the names of some decent early music groups and their recordings, please check the other review referred to above.

title: A great (and fun!) tribute to Frank and Tommy...
text:
[excerpted from a full review on VocalStandards.com]

... I find LET'S BE FRANK... to be somewhat unusual if not unique. The title clearly calls it as a concept album, but rarely do you see such a tight artist/material focus on a concept album ... Dorsey/Sinatra hits from 1940-1943 is about as thematically tight as you can get, and yet the breadth of emotion and style exhibited here is expansive and airy.

Also unusual on this LP was the front to back collaborative nature of the production. Peter deservedly receives top billing but Alan Copeland's deft hand with arrangements, baton and extensive lyrics work underpin one of the most collaborative vocal/musical efforts you will find today.

There is extensive and elegant interaction throughout the set list between Peter and The Dream Weavers. "Extensive" and "Elegant" are not hyperbole here ... the sheer volume of background lyrics -- all refreshed and rewritten with allusions to today -- and the constant weave, interaction and role reversals between Peter and Sally Stevens' "Weavers" is impressive (and exhausting!)

I expected Calabria Foti to dive in with a couple of duets, but Ms. Foti's wonderful vocals appear on virtually every number ... and she delivers full duet parts on four songs.

The collaboration extends to the musical performance as well with Copeland doing a masterful job displaying the rare talents of Alan Broadbent on piano and Bob McChesney's sexy smooth trombone throughout the production. At once folded into the wonderful orchestra and then out front soloing ... these guys are balanced perfectly and heard from beginning to end on this LP.

A Performance...

Concept albums can often benefit from an ordered play list flow. Whether intended or unintended playing them straight through, from beginning to end, sometimes enhances the thematic effect of the listening experience.

LET'S BE FRANK intentionally sets out to deliver a performance event feel. The LP kicks off with a cool intro medley ... leading out with the swinging title track written by Alan Copeland that flashes us back to the early 1940's and sets the stage for the "session" to come. The LP wraps with Peter thanking the team, closing out the "performance" and reminding you to ... "Put your dreams away for another day". Nice.

As always, the compete track list can be found below, and though this album is stellar from front to back I will hit on a handful of my favorite Let's Be Frank numbers.

Peter follows the title song in the intro medley track with a couple of sad separation/love songs "This Love Of Mine" and the 1940 chart topper "I'll Never Love Again" ... Peter's melodious, smooth baritone vocals emote the love, loneliness and longing these songs wonderfully express.

Alan C. and Peter pick up the tempo with a swing version of "All Or Nothing At All" that starts a run of superb tracks ... "It Started All Over Again" with Calabria Foti's initial duet landing in all it's sultriness and an awesome demonstration of the Peter/Dream Weavers interplay with a fun, Chesney trombone and Broadbent laden "The One I Love Belongs To Somebody Else".

As I re-listen to this recording...

I think could name each song in the set list as a favorite ... "Polkadots and Moonbeams" with Alan Copelands neat intro line "the best things happen while you're dancing" (!) ... the beautiful and atmospherically sad duet with Ms Foti "The Night We Called It A Day".

And the last three singing tracks are personal favorite numbers that Peter, Calabria, The Dream Weavers and the orchestra render in 40's big band period perfection ... Irving Berlin's "Be Careful It's My Heart", "Street Of Dreams" and the Tommy Dorsey classic "Sentimental Over You".

If you are a big band fan LET'S BE FRANK... is a fun fresh take on the early war years that you should have in the fold. If you're just starting to reach back to this amazing era of classic American standards music, do yourself a favor and give this album a listen ... I'm sure it won't be long before we see you at the fan club meetings!

BTW...

A couple of footnotes before the track list and VS ratings... first, LET'S BE FRANK... is not Peter's only 40's big band standards album. He released a 14 track LP called BOY SINGER in 2001 that I have only heard on the TheStandardsChannel.com and from snippets on Peter's website. What I have heard sounds great though, and I plan to snag BOY SINGER and offer a review around mid summer ... check back!

The last footnote is a follow-up well wish to Peter who very recently celebrated his 86th birthday. Peter was 85 when he performed and produced (along with Bob McChesney) this latest CD release ... I am completely taken with Peter's vitality, talent, commitment and sense of fun ... all of which are demonstrated in spades on LET'S BE FRANK. I only hope I wake up tomorrow -- at 55 -- with half the vimm and vigor Peter possesses!

LET'S BE FRANK... WITH A TOUCH OF TOMMY - Track list...

(VS_Guy ratings: "+++" pluses are good; "~" for meh to middling; "- - -" minuses are not good)

The point of mentioning (DR) is that the label advertised that full (DR) was maintained. However that is not the case compared to the original CD mastering as 20-30% of the (DR) is lost.

I have done a rather detailed compared between the original CD and the Rubellan Expanded Remaster and the sound on the original CD was more to my liking on every track that present on both CD's.

The bonus tracks on the Rubellan Expanded Remasters are nice to have.

My feeling is if this release had adhered to what they had advertised, it could have been audiophile. As 2020 masterings go it is very good but the sound quality for me personally is middle of the road; not good but it's also certainly not bad.

Seems to me this Rubellan remaster is not loud (DR lacking) enough to please those who love all LOUD all the time, nor does it preserve enough (DR) to make audiophiles happy. I really do not get what crowd this release was aimed at? But given the all LOUD crowd in 2020 tends not to purchase physical media, Rubellan should considered going all the way to make happy the largest Digital Physical media purchasing group that still remains and those are audiophiles/ quasi-audiophiles or those who like old school SQ

title: READ FINE PRINT:  Missing/shortened songs on two otherwise great albums
text:
Please note - this 2 star rating is NOT for either one of these albums. Both of these albums are in fact great. Read my reviews for Accept - Eat the Heat.

The fine print to this is the following:

1. UDO - Machine Man: Missing one song (it was a 45 second instrumental, but the fact still remains). Other songs have been obviously "shortened", and/or fade out too quickly - much different from how they are on the actual album.

2. Accept - Eat the Heat: Missing 2 songs (Break The Ice, and I Can't Believe In You). Both are very good songs, so right there alone you are missing a nice chunk of the actual album.

- Other songs are OBVIOUSLY SHORTENED, while many others have verses shortened or removed completely. If you know the album well, this is OBVIOUS while listening to this version. D-Train has been shortened by almost a minute (verses removed), while Mistreated has had over 3 MINUTES removed from the song. Prisoner fades out and ends almost 30 seconds shorter than the full album version, as does XTC.

To the very casual fan, they may not even know this. To the die-hard fan, this is kinda ridiculous and does take away from the actual albums as they were intended to be heard.

This was obviously done to fit both albums onto one 80 minute cd, but it sacrifices a lot in my opinion. Removing 3 songs collectively and significantly shortening or altering other songs was wrong. If anything, they could have released both albums together in their completeness as a 2-disc set.

I would only recommend this to a novice of both of these albums, or simply the casual fan who wants to check out the meat and potatoes of both of these OTHERWISE GREAT releases. For completists, or people wanting to hear either or both albums as they were intended, I would not recommend this, especially at this VERY HIGH PRICE. Buy the individual albums on Amazon or EBay.

So, this, the Euro Ed., has Locomotive Breath, but does not have Hymn 43 or Alive and Well and Living In, which was on the Am. version issued by BMG..  Both of which were on the orig. Am. LP, too.  But both the Am. and Euro. CD's are missing Teacher and Bouree, also on the LP version.  Besides these omissions, there are two songs that truly belonged on the original release, but were conspicuously absent.  The first of which is 17, which was the flip side of Sweet Dream.  The other is Sunshine Days, which was recorded around the same time.  So, (and this is my point!) it's high time Chrysalis releases this as a 2 CD set, and includes everything that has been released as Living.., on one edition or another, plus incl. bonus cuts that belonged on it in the first place!

title: Mechanical
text: Nice idea to try Bach's Cello Suites on a modern instrument but it isn't successful on this recording. The playing is very mechanical and sometimes so extremely rote that it sounds choppy. This give an unmusical impression unfortunately. The tone chosen by Mr. Patrick is not a pleasing choice either. He uses a phased effect which has an artificial quality to it. He also uses this effect on every track which adds up to an unpleasant listening environment. Perhaps varying the effect would help but personally, I would stay away from the phased sound. He even dials up some distortion later and this only adds to the generally unpleasant sound of the performance. The volume doesn't vary either, leaving out any sense of phrasing. I am sorry to say that Mr. Patrick needs to go back to the drawing board. It isn't enough just to play the notes Bach wrote. You have to do it with sensitivity, interpretation and musical intelligence. This performance unfortunately does not exhibit any of these in enough measure to bring a positive conclusion to the effort.

It would be like Barbra Streisand calling her next album "Barbra!"  Aside of this faux pas, I find much of the music here to be just average; nothing great/no big single.  In my opinion, it just falls flat, especially where it was supposed to be a comeback of sorts. title: Icecap Music
text:
I spent 2 summers on the Greenland Ice Cap in the early 90's at the abandon Dye II defense early warning site, 150 miles out on the ice, at 7000' elevation. Very remote, very flat, very white & blue, these being the predominant colors/shades.
I found a cassette of White Winds of the floor of the abandon mechanics shop, dropped it in the Walkman & have been a fan of Andreaus' music ever since. Called space, new age, earth music, whatever, his electric harp & choice of sounds, accompanying vocals & other instruments all contribute to a wonderful, peaceful, musical journey. It would seem to be a good fit for any situation needed a calming effect, meditation, yoga, birthing, winding down after a long day, and especially if you find yourself far from everything & everyone out on a ice cap, which are very white & very windy, trying to be one with your environment. This is the PERFECT fit.
I have several of his other releases and enjoy them all.

You'll hear tracks with comedy greats like Paul & Storm, Jim Gaffigan, Scott Dunn, Henry Phillips, Mike Birbiglia, Bob Zany, Tom Mabe, Sean Morey, Keywood Banks, and many others. You also get to hear the familiar Kenny Tarmac, Mr. Obvious, Jumbo the Elephant, Floyd Tucker, Donnie Baker, Sid and Bart, Larry King, Ernie Furglar, and many of your other favorites. The artwork of the cover and the CD faces is great, and the audio quality of each disk is very well done. You can purchase this collection right here on Amazon.com, or by going to the Bob & Tom Store: [...]

title: A Taste of Gold
text: As a life-long Beatles fan, I must temper my enthusiasm a bit here, folks, because some critics have said these 2 shows are outstanding in sound quality. The only totally satisfying live concert of the Beatles remains to be released(Live at the Hollywood Bowl). Thanks to Mal Evans, their late aid/handler, many bootlegs exist of Beatles sessions or live shows, and we owe tremendous thanks for him to leak these to us. I suspect he had a hand in these 2 shows as well. To us, any new showcase of their appealing harmonies and musicianship is thrilling. They are the only group I would forgive for flubbing lyrics or missing notes or singing off-pitch live. For a couple songs, the sound quality is good, but obviously secondarily taken from the console or dual microphone set-up. At worst, the microphone sounds from the back of the lads performing, which is not bad considering to be better than the sound flowing into he crowd. What is so compelling throughout is the banter between songs and the playful vocal flubs that are sometimes thrown in to get a reaction. The Fab Four are so humanly endearing here, playful and making majestic sounds in spite of small amps in huge stadii, that all is forgiven in quick order. It all comes back and all is forgiven just a few songs into the repertoire. We all know what follows but they do some songs here that were never performed on the Sullivan Shows so that is a plus. That said, that the sound quality varies, is far-outweighed by the harmonies made and notes played with bonhomie. I won't cover each one, but I will add the songs that make this a must to have nonetheless: "She's A Woman" and "Baby's in Black" from the Atlanta show and from the Vancouver show the under-rated "You Can't Do That," "Things We Said Today" and "If I Fell" where Paul or John intentionally goofs a note and then rejoins the song as if someone else erred. For me, having never seen them live, this is better than any balcony seat in those arenas. You are standing next to them, like Mal, here a chum enjoying the sidelines but a chum forever.

title: It's not the piano; therefore no tribute.
text: I must start by stating that I have not listened to the entire album. My review is based on the track samples. As with (some of) the other reviews, it sounds like a suitable relaxation background music while you are seated by the fireplace at a winter night. The sound of the musical instrument is nothing much to do with the real pianoforte; therefore, if anyone thinks of buying this album because s/he thinks that there will be a pianoforte sound, then this should not be any reason. Maybe it is a genuine Steinway or Yamaha or, even, the former Bösendorfer, but then the recording is so strange that only some of the mid-tones are heard and there are no bass and treble sounds. The arrangements, as far as I could understand from the samples, have no accompanying spirit and only too flat. One must not expect too much from the pianist on such albums, but there is nothing for virtuosity. If it were an elegant night club environment, then only in the background, this interpretation could be listened to. But if you expect something from Pink Floyd, or some other artistic interpretation, or the sound of a real pianoforte, then I believe this album is not a right choice.

title: A must have album!
text:
Sybreed is one of my favorite band. I found in them many elements that i search when looking to a strong outfit. Sybreed is groovy, catchy, technical, great composers, fun and original.

For me God is an Automaton is a great album, but not their best work to date. The reason why is because their is songs on it that for me lack greatness and are too average. Songs that I highlight are: 1) Red Nova Ignition for it's structure, various tempo, it's deathmetal feel. 2) Into the Blackest Light for it's heavyness and blackmetal feel. 3) Hightech Vs. Lowlife because it's different from their catalog. 4) No Wisdom Brings Solace for it's catchy chorus. The other songs lack originality, fun and catchyness. The Line of Least Resistance is good but the chorus don't fit that much in the song even in the album. Destruction and Bliss have potential, start really well but got too long and boring from the middle. Posthuman Manifesto, Downfall inc. and A Radiant Daybreak are just ok.

Overall, Ben the signer is solid and add some black/death feel to it's growls that bring something new on this record. The production is good, but maybe with a little to much bass in the mix. Use of death/black vibes are welcome. On the other side, they could have use more variety in the guitar tone. Guitar riffs are not that much addictive or groovy as it were on their past releases (aka. Slave Desing). The album is too homogenous. But, hey! It's still good material from one of my fav band. I just hope that on teir next record they will create a masterpiece with just highlights tunes that will surprise me by bringing more new elements on the table without compromise the Sybreed recipe.
