title: Horribly Edited Songs
text:
Anyone who's purchased K-tel's other early 70's 20-song compilations "20 Electrifying Hits", "20 Power Hits, vol. 2", or "20 Explosive Hits" will be in for a major disappointment with this record. Those other 3 albums had all complete full-length single versions. This record has the songs badly chopped up, sometimes salvagely so! How bad? Try just 59 SECONDS of "Turn, Turn, Turn"! Most of the songs start late, fade in late (yes, I said fade IN), fade out early, or a combo thereof. Also, you get only 50 minutes of music, as opposed to the over 60 in those other albums. The only untouched songs on this record are "Lady Willpower", "Persuasion", "Jesus is Just Alright", and "You Can Make it if You Try". Maybe the most senseless edit is "I've Got a Line on You" fading out just before the song ends anyway.

This is the second hits compilation from K-tel international, before the familiar round K symbol appears. The record label in the center is "Columbia Special Products". Much of the music represents the pro-peace movement of the late 60's/early 70's, and not necessarily top hits. This is especially true with the songs from the Byrds, Janis Joplin, Blood, Sweat, & Tears, Sly & the Family Stone, Santana, Mark Lindsay, Pacific Gas & Electric, Spirit, and the big peace anthem from It's a Beautiful Day. You do get a few hits with "I Want to Take You Higher", "Lady Willpower", "He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother", "Arizona", "More Today Than Yesterday", and "Cherry Hill Park".

Unfortunately, you get a preview of the typical 70's K-tel album with all those edits. It's too bad, because the music is very uplifting and inspirational. But you only get small snaphots of most of the songs.

title: Addio Andrea, senza rancor
text:
This La Boheme has Andrea Bocelli in a role that he has been marketed in, with amplification and operatic house acoustics to make those notes sound dramatic and loud and on pitch(at times). When you hear the recitative it shaky and small sounding..I don't know why they didn't pick up on them. Barbara Frittoli is as bad as she was as Liu with Mehta in Turandot in Beijing a few years ago. She does better with Jose Cura in Pagliacci, but she is third class at best, not worthy of this role, when you have Callas and Freni and Caballe and Scotto and Tebaldi and Te Kanawa et al. He voice is heavy and posseses unpleasant sounds in the high reaches, screams even. She sounds angry, like Tosca, and mostly uninvolved, which I must say cnnot be said for Bocelli, who is all emotion and tears..withjout the voice to carry it all. He is a pop singer..period, and has that Italian amplification all over him, which would make anyone with half a voice sound presentable..but it is false, like jean Hagen singing "Singin' In The Rain" with Debbie Reynolds behind the curtain doing the real job. In this case Mehta and High audio tech sub for Debbie.
Bocelli is being used of course, but this opera is selling like hot cakes and it may make other operas sell as well..after this Domingo and Pavarotti will sound great to the untrained listener..let us hope.
Bocelli is out there and he is going to sing, and so let him sing and be amplified, and let the dusty copies of Aida and la Forza and other worthy La Bohemes be bought, even if it is on his coat tails, coat tails that will be snipped in due time.

I discovered Anna Hutto at least 10-years ago. She came to our church in Lubbock for a concert. I'm not sure how that came to be, but was I amazed at her talent with words and loved to listen to her voice. At the time the only CD she had was Journey, which I bought at the concert.

I tried to find other recording by her over the years, but without success. A few years ago I heard she was producing a new recording, but I missed it. Fortunately, I discovered the recording, Welcome Here, a couple of weeks ago. I managed to capture a used copy from the Amazon Marketplace. It arrived this afternoon. It's already ripped and stored in my iTunes library and on my iPod. I listened this afternoon and was amazed that her voice sound more mature... a little richer.

Her talent with words is unabated as well. It will take me a few more listens to really get the work, but I already know this will be one of my favorite recordings, just like Journey before it.

All I can say is that I wish there was more of her work. It's good work.

title: a bootleg pirated album
text: This Lennie Tristano and Dave Brubeck double cd is a fake album in every way. It has nothing to do with Lennie's real album titled Intuition recorded in 1956; the tunes on this album all date from 1946 to 1949. The Brubeck disc is an interesting outing, not badly recorded, with son Chris on bass, but a hunt around the internet will tell you that this is one of THE most bootlegged pirated jazz albums and was originally released as a radio broadcast then stolen from there. The Jazz Piano Masters 2 disc cd set should probably not be for sale, but at the very least it should be identified for what it is. The album notes are of course, virtually none existent - especially for the Brubeck outing where there are several instrumentalists and only two are listed. I suppose that is something.

title: Anderson Does Simply Red, but with bad lyrics
text:
THIS IS BAD (except a couple of songs where the real Anderson comes through).

This is not soulful. This is disco pop of the late 1980s (when disco had evolved away from the Bee Gees and Donna Summer).

Released in 1988, this was recorded when Anderson left Yes for the second time. It is 47 minutes long. The original CD sound quality was OK (better than most of the Yes CDs released in the 1980s), but still not great. There is some harshness on the high end, which is a bad thing for someone who sings like Anderson. I have not heard the remastered version, but the original sure could use some fixing.

This is more of a producer's album than an artist's album. It was produced by Stewart Levine, who produced the jazz/soul/disco band Simply Red. Some are going to argue that Simply Red is not Disco, but that is what Disco had evolved into in the late 1980s until Grunge wiped it off the map. So, many of the songs have that kind of Simply Red feeling to them.

The lyrics on many of the songs were written by others, including Lamont Dozier of Holland-Dozier-Holland fame. He has written a number of classic songs, but his writing here is just horrible. Although we all complain about it, Anderson is better off just singing his spacy nonsensical lyrics than this pap.

There are a couple of good songs on this CD (Sundancing and Top of the World) where Anderson breaks away from the pop and sounds more like he does on his other solo albums.

To sum up:
-I like Jon Anderson
-I like Simply Red
-I don't like Jon Anderson doing Simply Red (it was like when Eric Clapton tried to do Phil Collins on August...another project involving Dozier)

title: monotonous dance club/rave music
text:
Many years ago I bought this album at random in the bargain bin of some hipster record store because I liked the dark, hand-painted artwork, and I wanted to take a chance on something new. The brooding alternative-graphic-novel cover had me expecting some kind of experimental rock music, something like a mix between Pink Floyd and Joy Division.

It turned out being like neither. It also happened to suck pretty bad. This isn't music as much as it is a collection of rambling and repetitive goth/industrial dirges that bump and clank on while some creepy French guy talks over it. It sounds like something you'd hear in a French goth-themed rave, one in a crappy part of town.

One track in particular, "le prommeur", was just plain annoying with its bass melody that repeated itself over and over again against the sound of distant washing machines fading in and out or something. That's actually the only track I remember, and it's because it was annoying. I was frustrated because I enjoyed the cover art more than the music. It was boring and uneventful, with a vaguely sinister subterranean/nautical feel. Like a tour of the bottom of the ocean where nothing happens, and you can't tell whether the creepy guy driving the little submarine with you is masturbating or not.

This is boring goth-dance-club music. There should have been a warning label. But dammit, the cover looked cool.

title: Among the very best
text: These have long been the standard for Tchaikovsky interpretations.  I didn't like Janson's #4 very much.  To my ears, Solti was much better.  That symphony is, really, just an old-fashioned, empty-headed sound wallow, the kind of thing Solti excelled at, but here the conductor and orchestra are superb.  The first rivals my previous favorite, Michael Tilson Thomas and the Boston Symphony in an interpretation that is remarkably similar, all light, fleeting, gossamer textures (to completely mix metaphors.)  The second and third are also beyond praise.  The music just sounds right.  Andrew Litton is also good in these early symphonies, but I prefer the recorded sound of Jansons/Oslo.  It looks like this was a re-issue of the original Chandos recordings for Musical Heritage Society.  I don't have the originals on hand for an a/b comparison, but this sounds great and better value than trying to gather up all of the recordings separately.

title: Poor Arrangements and Lethargic
text:
In a way I hate to write this mostly negative review, because I have numerous CDs with the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, and I normally enjoy hearing that fine group of musicians. Most of their recordings that I own are of classical pieces, but I also enjoy the several of theirs that I have of music from movies and musicals. However, "Classic Movie Themes I" I find to have poor arrangements and to be overall quite lethargic. Part of the reason that it's lethargic is that all the movie themes on here are slow, and often romantic, pieces to begin with. I would prefer a disc with more variety, some faster and some slower pieces, but some people enjoy discs of all slow pieces because they're relaxing. However, even considering the type of music these are, I still think they're unusually lethargic, partly the fault of the conductor for going too slow with some of them.

But much worse is that the arrangements are so bad that in most cases all the life of the music is drained, and they become insipid "elevator" music. For instance, I love the original recording of Lara's Theme from the film "Dr. Zhivago," and indeed I enjoy that whole soundtrack. But here even a lovely piece like that is rendered mostly lifeless and not like the original at all. In constrast, I very much enjoy the Royal Philharmonic's CD [[ASIN:B00000ICP2 James Bond Themes]], which is very vigorous and well-arranged, and I love their CD Leonard [[ASIN:B00000ICP0 Bernstein - Overtures to Candide, Symphonic Dances from West Side Story, Symphonic Suite from On The Waterfront]], so I wonder why there was a breakdown with "Classic Movie Themes I"? Oddly, no conductor is given on the packaging, which is very unusual for the Royal Philharmonic CDs, so perhaps that's a clue that this recording was not made with as much care as usual. This is a decent sounding digital recording using Super Bit Mapping, but I can't find a year on it. Also, I am pretty sure that all of this CD is re-recordings, and not from the original movie soundtracks, although the packaging does not address this. I have no problem with re-recordings if they're well done, but I do NOT recommend this CD.

I notice that the Amazon page for this does not list the tracks at all, so I'll briefly do that: 1.Tara's Theme (from "Gone With the Wind"), 2.Edelweiss ("The Sound of Music"), 3.Some Enchanted Evening ("South Pacific"), 4.Secret Love ("Calamity Jane"), 5.Over the Rainbow ("The Wizard of Oz"), 6.Summertime ("Porgy and Bess"), 7.Where Do I Begin? ("Love Story"), 8.Somewhere ("West Side Story"), 9.Lara's Theme ("Dr. Zhivago"), 10.Moon River ("Breakfast at Tiffany's"), 11.The Way We Were, 12.As Time Goes By ("Casablanca"), 13.Theme from "A Summer Place," 14.Blue Velvet, 15.True Love ("High Society"), 16.The Summer Knows ("The Summer of '42"), 17.When I Fall in Love ("One Minute to Zero"), 18.Hopelessly Devoted to You ("Grease"), 19.Arthur's Theme, 20.True Love Ways ("Buddy"), 21.Pachelbel Canon ("Ordinary People"), 22.The Sounds of Silence ("The Graduate"), 23.Someone to Watch Over Me, 24.People ("Funny Girl"), and 25.Evergreen ("A Star is Born").

title: Breezy personality, jazzy creativity and interpretive twists
text: Originally from Buenos Aires where she received a music education specializing in Argentine tango and folk music, flutist/artist/educator Carla Campopiano relocated to Chicago in 2013. Her connections to both locations have led to many music projects, including this album with fresh takes on songs from celebrated Latin American composers such as Astor Piazzolla, Gustavo Leguizamon and Julian Plaza. We hear various kinds of music for dances best described at milonga portena, zamba, tango, vals or nocturna. Campopiano’s arrangements are infused with the flutist’s breezy personality, jazzy creativity and interpretive twists. Percussionist Gustavo Cortiñas also contributed to the aesthetic vison built around sound colorings tinted with emotion and feeling. The album is dedicated to the late Argentine singer Alba Guerra who’s featured on two tracks, “Vieja Viola” and “La Pomena.” Guitarist Gabriel Datcu, guitarist Zac Selissen and bassist Kitt Lyles each appear on a few tracks. Campopiano’s self-penned “Lluvia” has a peppy, rhythmic quality in its sparse offering of just flute and percussion. This album is an expressive one that celebrates an authentic type of Argentinian roots music, a product of the country’s urban melting pot. Although the 8-song set is over all too quickly, the music’s magnetism draws you in due to the passion, sentiment and nostalgia it so splendidly conveys. (Joe Ross, Roots Music Report)

title: Horny Hitler on a Broken VHS
text:
This is bargain-bin anime that's gone through every process as cheaply as possible. A poorly produced 80's-era anime, entirely out of place in American culture (not that I pretend it was a shining perfect example of the East as well), that would've been hilariously awful if it had worked.

As such, the VHS transfer is literally so poor the tape runs out before the movie. I hope this is merely a physical fault in my copy, but I'm not about to spend more than another dollar to try and find out. I'll soon try and hunt down some of the other episodes to find out.

Otherwise, well... it's definitely in the level of "so bad it's good." Entire scenes made up of three scenes, totally six to eight frames of animation, shamefully mirrored to give the illusion of more action. Absolutely stock characters, caricatured over American translations. Ripoffs of every giant robot or fast-car style anime of the time. One of the three pilots of the robo formers, (a set of three flying vehicles who can become one of three different giant robots, depending on which car-and-pilot are "on top," as it were) is a fat coward I believe was named Tip, who--unlike his well-dressed compatriots--chose to fly into battle with an umpire's pad and mask. The others, a standard hero and a standard ninja-like Falco-esque cool guy, round out our heroes.

But the villains... you may have noticed on the cover that there appears to be a hitler with giant horns.

This character's name is Fuhrer.

So much time is spent shouting out plot points that one doesn't get to spend enough time with Horny Hitler here, but between the King of the Underworld (of which Fuhrer is a demon, however that works, Japan) that I wish there was more to enjoy in its rank awfulness. I recommend this to a a party of enthusiasts, somewhere between a screening of Monster a GoGo and a reading of The Eye of Argon.

title: Rollicking, harmonic Alt-Country from Billy Cowsill's Last Band
text:
The Blue Shadows were regrettably a short lived enterprise featuring Billy Cowsill of the Cowsills. The Cowsills were the all family band that were the model for television's "The Partridge Family." Vancouver, British Columbia, is where Billy Cowsill spent the last years of his life and it was there that the Blue Shadows formed. The Track listing of 1993's On The Floor of Heaven is as follows:

1. Coming On Strong (Cowsill; Hatcher)
2. The Fool Is The Last One To Know (Cowsill; Johnson; Ralph B.)
3. If I Were You (Cowsill; Hatcher)
4. Think Of It (Hatcher)
5. Deliver Me (Hatcher)
6. A Thousand Times (Cowsill; Irwin)
7. If It Ain't Rockin' (Cowsill; Hatcher)
8. On The Floor Of Heaven (Cowsill; Hatcher)
9. When Will The Heartache End (Cowsill; Hatcher)
10. The Embers (Cowsill; Hatcher)
11. I Believe (Hatcher)
12. Is Anybody Here (Cowsill; Hatcher)

Running Time: 43.22.

The Blue Shadows featured both Billy Cowsill and Jeffrey Hatcher on guitar and vocals, joined by Elmar Spanier on bass and J. B."Jay" Johnson on drums. Cowsill and Hatcher combine to create vocals and harmonies that bring to mind Don and Phil Everly at their prime. Standout tracks are "Coming On Strong", "Deliver Me" and "On The Floor of Heaven." Best described as rollicking alt-country the whole of On the Floor Of Heaven is a sonic revelation.

Unfortunately Spanier left after this album (replaced by Bill Muir) was released and though Lucky To Me, their second and last received critical approval they were no more by late 1995. A pity, but you can listen to their legacy best represented here with On The Floor Of Heaven. It may be hard to find but should you get the chance do not pass up the opportunity. Heavily recommended: **** 1/2 Stars.

title: Overdubs without Artist approval should be illegal
text:
Overdubs that are done after the death of an artist obviously never can have the approval of the creator of the music. I think they should be illegal. In all of music history, whether country music or any other style, time has proved all such overdubs to be gimmicks that destroy the original recordings. Whether simple demos or outtakes, the original recordings are always better and reflect what the artist intended. This set and all the sets on this label should be illegal and withdrawn from the market. The producers should be forced to surrender their profits to charity or the artists estate.

Anyone who has ever heard demos with no overdubs (such as Hank Williams, or the recent three CDs of Johnny Horton on Bear Family label) knows they are some of the purest expressions of a singer.

Give us undubbed Jim Reeves, and reject this artificial garbage that Jim Reeves had no control over

title: Once again Star Wars fails to deliver
text: I think even the most devout Star Wars fans entering the theatre weren't expecting to worship this film. So when we were challenged by stilted dialouge, bad acting, a convoluted plot and the most spiritless cliched romance I have ever seen, we took it all in stride. We were pleased by the conspicuously limited role of Jar Jar, pleasantly amused by the (for the most part) fun banter between C-3PO and R2D2, and awed by George Lucas' undiminished ability to create freshly beautiful alien landscapes. We didn't object when Lucas lifted scenes and dialogue from Gladiator, Blade Runner and the earlier Star Wars trilogy. We even cheered during Yoda's gravity-defying lightsaber battle at the end of the film. Still, leaving the theatre, I couldn't stave off a sense of regret. Count Dooku pales in comparison to the menacing presence of Darth Vader that gave depth and power to the Dark side. Anakin and Amidala's romance falls way short of the witty banter and magnetic chemistry that characterized Han and Leia's relationship. And most of all, the Force, which used to be a fascinating, mystical synthesis of Eastern religion and Western heroic tradition, has been reduced to a side-effect of some obscure microscopic parasitism (the Medichlorians?!?--in my mind they were indisputably George Lucas' worst science fiction creation ever). The legacy of original Star Wars, an innovative, fun, compelling film of epic proportions, has been reduced to a overly-commercialized special-effects fest.

title: An Import Gem

I ordered this CD because I was pretty sure it was an import..and owning everything Marshall Tucker has ever put out, I was impressed with the cover of the CD and the song list so, I gave it a go. Take note of the patch on Jerry Eubanks right pant leg at the bottom, it's the mushroom of The Allman Brothers Band.

This CD I have a feeling is going to be hard to find because I don't think it's authorized by the Marshall Tucker Band. So it makes it a bit of a collectors item. And it has all the markings of an unauthorized disc indeed. On the back where the songs are listed and the writer credits follow each song, a few of them have the writer, but most of them say "unknown". Now anyone who knows anything about this band knows who wrote most of the songs and if they just put Toy Caldwell on most of the unknown ones they would have been right, but the "unknown" is a flag. There are also all kinds of misspellings and some made me chuckle. It's too bad too, because this would be the one CD you would want to recommend to your friend who is just starting out listening to Marshall Tucker. After all the laughs, I'm glad I got my hands on this one. Thanks overseas bootleggers....

title: Umm... yeah... or something...
text:
I remember this one. I was a bit excited to see that some of the Top of the Pop's cd's had made their way towards the USA. But then after getting this and listening to it, I remembered that I never really liked Top of the Pop's cds even when I lived in England, and it was nothing but the familiarity that was endearing to me. A lesson learned too late! This is one of their 2000 releases, and it features, to its credit (or detriment), the same consistency as its predecessors.

And what is that consistency? Choppy, repetitive, annoyingly optimistic, cheesy and did I mention annoying? dance and pop tracks form the UK and USA circa the mid, second part of 2000. You have some real doozies here. But who can put a price on the memories? I can... and if you spend more than $10 for this, you've spent too much (its out of print and apparently people now use them for beer coasters at 50p - 5 pounds). Artists included that were popular at the time are Sisqo, All Saints, numerous boy bands from both sides of the ocean, Oasis, Blink 182, Artful Dodger, Moloko and whatever flavor of the month Trance star had a popular cut (in this case, Angelic and Sonique).

I have to admit, looking back, it is a real bringer of Nostalgia. Summer 2000... France edges Italy to win Euro 2000 (Boo!) & Alan Shearer (some say finally) retires, then a few months later we have the US presidency debacle, and in general the world was different than it is now some four years later which makes me sort of sad in a way. But the music - that cheesy poppy feel... at least for some it can conjure up innocent memories. Otherwise its one for the pre-teen/teen crowd of the time. If by some strange dark force, you happen to ENJOY the musicianship and singing (I use both terms lightly), then do check out several of the saturated UK compilation markets' unlimited rip-offs, including "Now That's What I Call Music" and... well... the cannibalistic "Top of the Pops 2000 v. 3" released all of 3 1/2 months later.

I listened to the whole set of recordings and found nothing new. If you're familiar with Law of Attraction teachings and techniques, you'll feel the same. The first 3 CDs are painfully repetitive with very little real content. That's over 3 hours of pure fluff before even the most basic concepts are discussed. I listened to all that in the hope of having the promised. If you read the classics like "Think and Grow Rich," "The Magic of Thinking Big," anything by Esther Hicks/Abraham, then watch the movie "The Secret" (original version with Hicks/Abraham,) learn EFT for free, read "Write it Down, Make it Happen," and focus on feeling good then you've got this collection. One CD is focused on selling the listener on joining up with his "Global Information Network" so that you can buy even more CDs (that all sound like CD sets already out there, such a real estate investing, Internet marketing, etc.) and be a part of his own private secret society for networking with others that sign up.

Interesting that there's so much focus on trusting your feelings throughout these recordings. I found myself questioning the existence of the lecture where these recordings were supposed to have been made. Throughout the audio one can hear background noise, such as car horns and sirens, yet when one of the lecture attendees asks a question they cannot be heard on the recording. Also, according to Trudeau, the lecture is taking place in some amazingly opulent home. Why would one be able to hear street noises in such a place? Doesn't seem to fit the image he was trying to put across. He refers to someone there is "king" and then jokes about how his real title is "royal highness" but since they're such great buds he calls him king. Maybe we have now found where Elvis is really hiding out. He repeatedly refers to his "colleagues" that are supposedly present there with him, amazingly wealthy and powerful people from all over the world, but yet none of them are ever heard to speak nor does he ever mention any of them by name. Ever. It's like the audio version of the emperor's new clothes.

title: A meta extraordinarily great pianist. There are ways in which he is ...
text:
Alexander Melnikov is out of this world, a meta extraordinarily great pianist. There are ways in which he is better than Rachmaninoff as a pianist. I have listened to so many performances of this concerto (and recordings) over the years and I always dreamed of hearing it nailed. The best I have heard before this one was Horowitz/Walter but the old recording quality has limitations.
Melnikov's approach has much deeper reach, depth, thoughtfulness, range and tenderness. Melnikov's piano solo is absolutely brilliant and turns one's soul inside out. The orchestra/conductor, sadly, are no Mravinsky. The orchestra fluctuates from average to poor, rolls off occasionally, and is not a good match for Melnikov. Not respectful of his interpretation, limiting him and the contrast is very painful. It's a miracle Melnikov did not loose his inspiration here. I wish Melnikov to play this with someone like Pletnev.
This is not a familiar or a conventional piano solo part that fits what one is used to... Melnikov's every note deserves nothing less than a completely full dedicated attention.

title: On a Hot Summer Day
text:
Mix the quirkiness of DEVO with the sunny surf of early Beach Boys, add a bit of Chris Isaak's musical flavor, and you begin to catch the drift of Drifting Sand. And unlike many surf bands, they aren't all instrumentals!

I admit I'm biased toward the smooth Strat guitar sound that Dana Point dishes out here, song after song, where so many surf guitars sound plinky. I mention Chris Isaak because it's his drummer you hear, Kenny Dale Johnson, keeping up the beat. But what really sets Drifting Sand apart is Surfer Spud's solid sense of pop fun, from the humorously church-like invocation to the kids shouting along on "Shark! Shark!".

In these days of grim irony, bland love songs, and howls of angst, too many bands have forgotten to be fun -- but not Surfer Spud & Drifting Sand. If you don't have a hot summer day where you are now, SURFPOP will provide one for you :)

Note: Arguably, this album deserves five stars -- but I don't trust lone five-star reviews & neither should you. Still: it's worth at least four in anybody's book

title: Baroque Masterpieces by Vice Kapellmeister Antonio Caldara
text:
These 12 Symphonies (Sinfonie in Italian) are the instrumental introductions to Oratorios written by Maestro Antonio Caldara while he was Vice-Kapellmeister in Vienna between the years of 1718 to 1735.
These Sinfonie are very short because they were meant to be a quick selah of the vocal part of the Oratorios, but nevertheless, sublime in nature; under normal instrumental compositions, these would be called Sonatas, and could not be more beautiful. Unfortunately there are no samples on this page, but if you know Caldara's calibre of masterpieces, go for it, get you a CD; you'll treasure it to the max; after all, we know that Gunar Letzbor and Ars Antiqua Austria are top notch.
The Sinfonie for the Oratories represented here are:
Il Martirio di S. Terenziano, 1718
Morte e Spultura di Christo, 1724
Il Battista, 1727
Naboth, 1729
La Passione di Gesù Signor Nostro, 1730
San Elena al Calvario, 1731
Sedecia, 1732
La Morte d'Abel, 1732
Gerusalemme Convertita, 1733

The DVD The Vegas Job and DVD/CD Live At The Albert Hall are better representations of that period, aside from being still in print and therefore much less expensive. The mix is pretty bad compared to the Albert Hall dvd. If you want to hear The Who 2000 at thier best, get Live At The Royal Albert Hall and The Concert For New York (worth it just for The Who, one of the best performances of thier career. These were all failures of the authorities of the opera world to control the kind of material being released into the market.  Bocelli cannot sing opera.  He doesn't have a powerful voice.  How amusing it is that people would describe round sounding voices to be powerful.  That is probably why the bar has been lowered- the people of pop have influenced the noble art of opera with their notions of "powerful voice" and such and so when they really can't fill an auditorium with their inferior instruments.  The same goes for Bocelli.  I would wonder why a conductor as respectable as Zubin Mehta would go as far as turning Bocelli into an ideal opera star of this century.  The good conductor should have considered other artists first before turning to this one.  Heck!  Even Juan Diego Florez could pull off dark-sounding Verdi even better than Bocelli could!  This CD is a mistake.  I do not urge you to buy it, even if you are a Bocelli fan.

title: Album Review by Dyan Garris, New Age CD
text:
“’Aerial Views’ is smooth, jazzy, light, free as a bird, feel-good music that we all need right now. Perfection.” – Dyan Garris

Who couldn’t use a different perspective right about now? Composer and award-winning guitarist, Todd Mosby, takes things higher with his new album, “Aerial Views.” The album is light, free as a bird, “feel good” music that we can welcome wholeheartedly into our lives and can take with us long after the music stops.
“Aerial Views” is the third in a series of concept albums that focus on highlighting natural elements, from composer and guitarist extraordinaire, Todd Mosby.

The other two albums in this series are “Earth Mountain,” a tribute to the Earth, and “Open Waters,” devoted to the oceans. This particular recording, “Aerial Views,” is 12 tracks, embracing the element of “air,” and evokes the emotions Todd had as a youngster co-piloting his father’s plane. For all, it’s an extraordinary, joyful, uplifting journey through and across and into the “wild blue yonder.”

“Aerial Views” is produced by Will Ackerman and Tom Eaton of Imaginary Roads Studio in Vermont and includes an impressive list of sterling guest artists. This is a first class, top-notch recording that is guaranteed to elevate your spirit from the very first notes.

The album opens with the melodic, free flowing “Gliding.” And here we are soaring high above all without a care in the world. This is a brilliant start to this album. Following is another uplifting track, “Across America.” This is “freedom.” I love the way we feel like we are gracefully flowing along with the air currents. The distinctive and unmistakable artistry of Charlie Bisharat on violin and Premik Tubbs on lapsteel (as well as Todd, of course, and the other completely wonderful guest artists), make this song really special. Just wonderful!

The gently flowing, slower, yet just as silky smooth, “Aether,” takes us into that quiet zone where there is nothing way up there except us and the magnificent sky. This is ultra-relaxing with both Todd and Will Ackerman performing on acoustic guitars. Premik Tubbs is outstanding here on soprano saxophone, as are Jeff Haynes on percussion and Michael Manring on bass. Gorgeous.

Another super-uplifting track is “Earth and Sky.” This is again melodic and features Todd on a variety of guitars, including one of his specialties, the Imrat guitar. Here he uses both the electric and acoustic Imrat guitar which gives the song a wonderful depth and breadth. The addition of Tony Levin on bass, Jerry Marotta on drums, and Jeff Haynes on percussion, give this piece even more texture, like a softly painted pastel sky. Lola Kristine adds Fender Rhodes electric keyboard rounding out the mix. Excellent.

From there, we almost float into the 6 minute “Into Starlight.” This is another one to love, and the ethereal wordless vocals of Lola Kristine are wonderful. Premik Tubbs on wind synth adds even more depth to a beautiful piece. The song moves and sparkles gently just like those softly twinkling stars we are graced with being able to see in our sky.

I find it impossible to choose a favorite on this album. Completely impossible. One really must get the entire thing. I am quite fond of the 6-1/2 minute “Sylphs,” however. I love the sensuous movement of the song, and the violin really speaks to the heart here. Well, it all does. But I found this completely soothing and calming to the soul. I love it.

If you’ve ever flown in a small plane – or perhaps any plane – you know there is a space in between clouds that seems somewhat magical. “Between The Clouds” is just like that. The piano adds another texture and dimension here. The guitars, bass, drums, percussion – ALL - is just right. This is a wonderful soundscape, perfectly evoking that sense of freedom being airborne can bring. And “ditto” for “Blue Horizons.”

“To The Sky” is gentle, quieter, with the acoustic guitar taking the lead. Tom Eaton on piano is simply wonderful. The etheric vocals of Lola Kristine add to the heavenly quality of this piece.

The title track is magical. Just magical. Everything here works in perfect harmony, just like the universe should. Again, Lola Kristine’s absolutely heavenly wordless vocals and that very special violin artistry of Charlie Bisharat, along with all else here, raise us up to new and soaring heights. I think if you get nothing else, be sure to get this.

“Solo Flight” perfectly captures that exhilarating feeling of one’s first flight. The wind synth is gorgeous here adding beautiful, uplifting textures to the rest of the instrumentation in the composition. It’s perfection.

The album – a total breath of smooth, jazzy fresh air – closes out with a lyric track. The vocals by Lola Kristine are again effortless and magnificent. The guitars – ALL ¬¬– again superbly superb. The song has kind of a gospel “choral” feel to it and is a perfect close to this outstanding, “must have” album. “…Now let it shine…shine true.”

Can’t go anywhere right now? “Aerial Views” is an easy, effortless trip you will want to take again and again. And CAN. Superb and masterful, through and through.

title: Whole lotta  crap
text:
LZ II is even worse than the first LP, which at least had a few good tracks.. The second shows no musical progress. It's not irony to say it crashes like a led zeppelin. It deserves greater condemnation if it really did give birth to heavy metal. "WHOLE LOTTA LOVE" is one of their worst songs, which they plagiarized from a Muddy Waters record, "YOU NEED LOVE". Willie Dixon wrote the song and sued the band. He wrote two songs the band covered on their debut-- and gave crefdt. They didn't give credit for the sequel, which was deplorable. The highlight is the HEARTBREAKER/LIVING LOVING MAID combination that radio always plays as one. But it is nothing special in the band's catalogue.; they didn't break new ground. The rest of the songs are rubbish. "MOBY DICK" may be the band's only instrumental and it's one of the worst in rock; it's as catastrophic as Ahab's quest. Robert Plant was a terrible singer. His voice was mostly a shriek or a squeal, and isn't really better on the tender "THANK YOU", which follows the predictable volley of going between soft and heavy , as does 'WHAT IS AND WHAT NEVER...'and "RAMBLE ON" It is a dynamic that they did better on other songs. "BRING IT ON HOME" is a throwaway, and not, unfortunately the same song as Sam Cooke's classic. "THE LEMON SONG" is ... a lemon. The whole album, really. But I'm not a hater of the band...

The band's fourth release is their only essential lp. The Beatles, Stones, Doors, Dylan, Hendrix, and Clapton ( multiple groups) had more great albums; so did the Band and Van Morrison((the first two for them both). The BEACH BOYS had PET SOUNDS and... well, they had Pet Sounds. I am an atheist on Velvet Undeground. A case could be made for Paul Simon (more definite if adding 'Troubled Water') or the Byrds having more than one classic too, but it doesn't hold for Pink Floyd or the Who, while Bowie is a toss up, CCR and SLY STONE are in the mix, and don't make me laugh by mentioning the Eagles(greatest hits don't count) or Elton John --unless the double lp Yellow Brick Road is the equivalent of two separate releases. Santana had some gems. Fleetwood Mac is a contender if you're weird enough to add TUSK with RUMOURS or, more weird, a pre Lindsay/Stevie choice. I am tempted to add Aretha & Stevie Wonder(for diversity), or Neil Young and Springsteen, but with the latter you may have to stretch a little far from the era of classic rock (60s & early 70s). Steely Dan are their own category. Jazz is better judged, likewise,against itself instead of rock; otherwise there wouldn't be enough space to list all of them(Miles & 'Trane, for starters).
LED ZEPPELIN II is not in the company of those artists' best. It may be among the band's best, but you'd have to redefine 'best' as not necessarily meaning 'good'. It's great... as a metal album, but it's less so as popular music. It illustrates well why metal is not truly popular music because something is usually good if it is popular, and metal does not usually equal good, as if it aspired to excellence. Led Zeppelin did not achieve that quality until the 'ruins' lp. Pass II up for that and listen tothe best off the debut and then you'll know what made the band truly great.

title: Caun Na Righ (Defend the King)
text: "Cuan Na Righ" was one of the old gaelic sayings that the Queen's Own Highlanders took as their regimental motto.  Formed in 1960 from an amalgamation of the Seaforth Highlanders and Cameron Highlanders the Queen's Own Highlanders were probably one of the most truly Highland regiments.  Their tartan was the old Cameron of Erracht which was the original Colonel who raised the early regiment that became known as the old 79th Highlanders.  The regimental pipe band of the Queen's Own was one of the finest in the British army in its day.  These recordings from the 1980s should easily support that claim.  Many fine tunes can be heard on this CD.  Many are lesser known compositions by Pipe Majors of the band. The regiment soldiers on today as The Highlanders (4th Bn. Royal Regiment of Scotland) after their latest amalagation with the Gordon Highlnaders in 1994.  Recommended for those who seek a great regimental pipe band which is sadly no more.

title: This is NOT Byzantine Chant--only a mimicry of it
text:
If you wish to listen to Byzantine Chant Hymns of the Nativity either in English or Greek or Arabic, do NOT get this album. This is not Byzantine music. It is a close approximation of Byzantine music, but no chanter worth his salt would say that this authentic classic Byzantine music. There is little evidence that the chanters are familiar with the nuances of the Byzantine music theory which is quite evident in the lack of execution of each of the modes, assuming that the pitch differences between notes are equal tempered (i.e what can be played on a piano) when they are not; also, the lack of aphikimata (intonations) except for the first hymn (which is not an established aphikima); the confusion of fourth mode legetos with fourth mode soft chromatic; the lack of established theseis (musical formulae) but rather something that sounds good; the lack of using music but insisting on "free chanting" which makes the chanting art look as if it is some sort of free-form composition coming from the sincerity of the individual chanter rather than what is considered good and proper execution from established compositions, etc.

If you want real Byzantine music for the season and the feast of the Nativity, I heartily recommend Sun of Justice by Proto (trilingual--ENglish, Greek, and Arabic), Byzantine Hymns of the Nativity by the School of Ecclesiastical Music (in Arabic) or upcoming releases from the Dynamis Ensemble. Avoid this CD at all costs. The canon, in particular, is extremely poor.

title: Mckenzie does it again
text:
There are two scores in this CD:

In from the Night
The opening theme is a winner, a lilting and wonderfully warm piece which would appeal to anyone fond of the romantic scores of Georges Delerue (or indeed Mark McKenzie). The main theme returns in all its glory towards the end of the score in the brief "We Are a Family", before the almost John Barry-like, heartwarming "Can I Still Come Home?" It's a short score, a shade under twenty minutes, but one which leaves an impression.

Siver Bells
Another one which calls for warm-hearted music, which is exactly what it gets. The ensemble is very similar to In From the Night- maybe just slightly larger - and on the whole the music is probably just slightly more restrained, not quite so full of the joys of spring (or Christmas). That said, there's another winning main theme, heard first in "Off to New York", which will bring a smile to anyone's face. "Shared Stories" introduces another theme, this time far more melancholy, with a hint of longing about it - another winner. "Christy Searching", with gentle flute solo accompanied by harp and strings is another heartbreaker. While occasionally there is something more urgent ("Intruder Chase" is great small-scale action music), overall it's unrelentingly gorgeous music.

title: 1982 vintage CD has some engineering issues...
text:
Since this is a vintage 1982 CD, I suppose we'll have to cut Varese Sarabande some slack, but you may want to know these issue up front. The sound seems to have been recorded a little lower than it should have. I had my small boom-box turned up to full volume, yet the CD seemed to be playing at mezzo-forte rather than blaring as one would expect. The other engineering issue is that all the music is listed as just 3 tracks, despite each of the works having multiple parts that could have been individual tracks. Nights in the Gardens of Spain is track 1, 3-Cornered Hat Part 1 is track 2, 3-Cornered Hat Part 2 is track 3. The only other time I've encountered this problem is a Marco Polo brand recording of Ippolitov-Ivanov's Caucasian Sketches.

As for the performances, the Nights in the Gardens of Spain is a good performance, the tempos and dynamics seem to be pretty standard. The hall in which the performances are recorded seems to have little or no reverb/echo, reminding me of the problem with a "dead" sound when the Phila. Orchestra tried making recordings in the Academy of Music in Philadelphia. In the Three Cornered Hat performance, where I got through Part 1 but only heard a little of the beginning of Part 2, there are a few times when Batiz inexplicably slows down the tempo so that the flow of the music seems noticeably interrupted. The old LP recording of this work with Artur Rodzinski (with the Royal Philharmonic?) conducting does not have this problem, and is excellent although his performance is just the 2 suites and not the complete ballet.

After listening to the Three Cornered Hat, Part 2, I was happy to find that the tempo problems I noted in Part 1 are not present. In fact, the tempos Batiz uses are quite brisk and move the work along splendidly, even a bit faster than the old Artur Rodzinsky performance I was used to.

Overall, not a bad CD, but a little lacking in how it was engineered.

title: Beware of misleading item info!  Disappointed.
text: I bought this Righteous Brothers cd; The Very Best Of, Unchained Melody, for two reasons.  First, I didn't have any Righteous Brothers music in my collection (other than a couple of hits on compilation albums with other artists) and second, after reading the product description it clearly said that this cd was released in Jan. 2020 on an "Import" label.  Well, by that I assumed that it being a recent release it no doubt had to be a remastered re-release.  That was the main reason why I choose to buy this specific Righteous Bros. cd.  Odd thing was, the next post underneath this one was for the exact same cd, which I also looked at, and it contained the same exact info; it was a duplicate posting of the same cd.  I did look at other Righteous Brothers cds posted, most of them being "best of" compilations, but their info stated that these cds were released years ago.  Anyway, I just clicked on the first post and bought the cd thinking it was a good choice based on the description info (the recent 2020 release date).  I got the cd the next day (I got Prime) and to my surprise when I read the info it said it was manufactured in 1990 and it was on the "Polydor" label.  I buy a lot of cds so I immediately knew what had happened.  The cd I bought was 32 years old.  It even looked old the way cds were manufactured back then.  When I played the cd it certainly sounded like a poorly mastered cd that was common in 1990 or any year around that time.  Now I certainly understand that a seller of recorded music has nothing to do with the quality or any other aspect of the music that is on a cd, vinyl record or tape other than the product itself being damaged in some way.  But in a case like this when the description of the product is so wrong and misrepresented than the seller should take responsibility.  So, I requested to return the cd explaining what had happened and I was granted a full refund.  Amazon was fair and protected the customer (me).  Being an experienced buyer of music (cds) I should have suspected something wasn't right with the way it was advertised but it can help in the future to watch out for these kinds of things.  And, fortunately, it all worked out with Amazon being a fair vendor.  But I would advise Amazon to either fix the incorrect information of this product (cd) or just delete it all together (including the duplicate posting).  Hope this info benefits other music buyers.

title: It's the Band -- It's Hot
text:
Some of the Band's finest studio work was done after they did the Last Waltz, finished their Capital contract, Robertson left the group. This album is a great example of The Band, sans Robbie, performing live. Excellent guitar from Jim Weider, and from the Cate Brothers (Btw, the Cate Brothers were in Ronnie Hawkins and the Hawks back when Levon joined the group before Robertson came on board.) Helm, Danko, Hudson and Manuel all come to the fore a little bit more, a bit less inhibited, than in the pre-Last Waltz days. Overall the music is infused with a little more rhythm and blues flavor, a bit closer to the style(s) of the Levon Helm Band as it performs nowadays. But there is plenty of the classic Band tunes here, given great presentations. Danko's bass is lively yet sophisticated. Levon was still practicing his busier drumming style back in 1983 -- just superb and both full of energy. And Levon's vocals are at their prime. Manuel's vocals are a bit more raw, but very emotional and expressive.

It would be ten years before The Band would produce the 3 post-Robbie studio albums -- some would argue they are among The Band's best along with Big Pink and the self-titled album. So the collection of tunes here are not new tunes (Band tunes and rock covers). If you don't mind Robbie's unique guitar work supplanted with lively organ and some other excellent guitar work Weider, Cate and Cate), and you can accept tunes by other composers in place of new tunes by Robertson, this is The Band performing live in full vigor and style.

The recording quality is reasonably good for a concert -- more echo and less "up-close" definition than a studio recording, so not as good as modern concert recordings can be but pretty good for 1983. So maybe you call it only 4 or 4 1/2 stars for that reason -- but no me; it's The Band, and they're smokin' on great covers and Band tunes. For The Band fans, lovers of roots rock, Americana music, good ol' rock 'n' roll, this something more is worth having.

title: Once Upon A Time....
text:
A young Jim Morrison once wanted to be more popular than the group of Love. Well, Morrison got his wish. The Doors eventually became more popular than the group Love, but this does not anyway, underestimate the Power of Love.

This is such a great recording. It's dripping in psychedelia. It's dripping with that 60s sentiment that Love really could change things. Of course, nowadays most people don't believe that it can, that's why it's often overlooked, but to those who secretly hold onto that belief...like me...we know that it will be Love and only Love that will change our lives and eventually, our world.

This is a very important collection of music and belongs on every audiophile's shelf. It's important not because it is a reflection of that time that once existed so long ago, but a time that could exist again if we let ourselves become hopeful, idealistic, and innocent enough to believe that "when the power of Love overcomes the Love of Power, the world will change"... a quote by the late, great Jimi Hendrix.

Yeah, you could say the music is dated and old and not too relevant or you could say, "Wow...this is refreshing...this is original...this is what raw creativity is supposed to sound like."

I love to listen to this recording when I'm feeling particularly groovy and I want to once again reclaim the truth that Love makes all things possible.

Discover the possibilities of Love.

title: ³³⁸ Magnificent Mylene
text: 4 years after the bland and detached "Desobeissance" (Mylene's only album that personally I feel indifferent towards), my expectations for "L'emprise" were not high. Not even the 2 great singles that were released prior to this made me think that she would present again songs with pure sentiment and that melancholy that runs through even the more uptempo ones. I am thrilled to say that with "L'emprise" she has found her muse again, as this is her best set of songs since "Interstellaires" (which in turn was a return to form after the cold "Bleu noir"). Excellently balancing ballads and dance tracks, Mylene on here shines again. Only 1 track has me think of skipping it, but even that is not bad. Rumoured to be her last offering before next year's - deemed to be farewell - concerts, this is a set worthy of her legacy, making any fan extra emotional just thinking that her heavenly presence and voice will be forever away. I urge you to listen to this, you will be more surprised than you think!

title: Star Wars:  Attack of the Clones
text: The Star Wars series is one of the few that will pull be out of my LazyBoy and put me into a theater seat.  In many respects, I was not disappointed by this latest installment in the Star Wars story.  The special effects, the non-stop action, and the all-around creativity of Lucas's characters are unsurpassed in the movie world.  You think you've seen it all when Lucas manages an even more fabulous landscape or grotesque character in a scene.  The threads of the previous 4 episodes are nicely brought together as we see Annekin's growing restlessness with the confines of the Jedi aprenticeship and his hatred of those who have wronged him.  We also see the background behind the bounty hunter Buba Fett's hatred of the Republic.  In general this was a well-done film and it sets us up nicely for the finale in Episode 3.  My main complaint is with the acting of the young lovers, who seem a bit uncomfortable with the wooden dialogue and the strange circumstances.  They do not "carry" the movie in the way that Harrison Ford and Carrie Fisher did in Episodes 4, 5, and 6.  It may be that they take themselves a little too seriously instead of having fun with the movie as the earlier characters did.

title: Promises equals the original material
text:
Promises is a selection of songs originally recorded by Herman van Veen, with lyrics translated by Lori Spee. It's only after you compare the original lyrics to the American ones that you see what a fine job Lori has done. She managed to stay very close to the original Dutch lyrics, which results in 11 very emotive songs. The entire production is synthesizer-driven, which is, in fact, quite a departure from the original recordings, and something I really had to get used to. But in the end, this CD really grew on me: Lori's voice is so warm and communicative, and very well suited to the material.
If you come across this record, don't hesitate, just buy it.

title: Ormandy's incomparable Richard Strauss
text:
In this and its companion 2-CD set, Sony Japan brings together all of Ormandy's stereo Strauss recordings for Columbia, in generally excellent sound.

Volume 1:
Till Eulenspiegel's Merry Pranks (1963)
Don Juan (1960)
Death and Transfiguration (1959)
Also sprach Zarathustra (1961)
Don Quixote (1963)

Volume 2:
Ein Heldenleben (1960)
Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme suite (1965)
Der Rosenkavalier suite (1964)
Dance of the Seven Veils from Salome (1962)
Burleske (1966)
Horn Concerto No. 1 (1966)

Many of these were available on "Essential Classics," but this is the first CD reissue of Ormandy's Till, Don Juan, and Death and Transfiguration (for those three works, Sony USA used the Szell performances in various couplings). As a prior review noted, and as you might expect, Ormandy's Till and Don Juan are more expansive than Szell's, and to good effect; only in Don Juan's mighty horn passages, which simply don't sound loud enough in this Sony Japan remastering, does the Philadelphia version seem a bit underpowered. Ormandy's Till is a merrier prankster than Szell's, and the cymbal crash as Till starts his romp through the marketplace is as fortissimo as I wish the Juan horns had been. As for Death and Transfiguration, this is an absolutely terrific performance, with the grim death struggle and soaring transfiguration both superbly characterized; this comparatively early recording, like Don Juan, had a different producer from the others, and the drier timpani sound is particularly effective here. Unfortunately, this 1959 recording also has audible tape hiss, very audible indeed in the quiet beginning, which Sony Japan seems sometimes able to eliminate, sometimes not. (In the 5-CD Beethoven set, the 1st Symphony's soft opening measures also have very audible hiss; yet that is a 1965 taping, later than some better-sounding recordings in the set.) Anyway, Ormandy's Death and Transfiguration is superb, tape hiss or no, as are Zarathustra and Don Quixote; the Heldenleben was always considered a stellar performance; the Rosenkavalier suite sounds as good as the "20th Century Classics" reissue (the only Strauss in that 12-CD box!); and the Bourgeois Gentilhomme is a great performance in great sound, with, by turns, sly humor, rich grandeur, chamber-like delicacy, and full-volume heft.

Sony Japan's Ormandy reissues seem uncommonly well chosen from the vast Columbia catalogue; important first reissues, besides the three Strauss tone poems, include a gorgeous Schubert 9th, Beethoven 1st-4th, Brahms 3rd, a 1959 Brahms 1st, and the 1968 Pines and Fountains. Other Sony Japan reissues, like the Mozart wind concertos (previously on Odyssey, in less than stellar CD sound) and both volumes of the Philadelphia "First Chair Encores," are available directly from Japan; and there are more on the way, for release next month. So far, the one lacuna seems to be Ormandy's Wagner, including knockout performances of the Meistersinger overture and Lohengrin prelude among many others. Still to come from Sony Japan? Or is Sony/BMG considering a Wagner box, which could include some of the pieces that Ormandy recorded only for RCA? It would be nice, too, if Sony Japan could post online English translations of what appear to be very interesting album notes, with reproductions of old Philadelphia concert programs and other memorabilia. But only a few years ago, we didn't have any of these Japanese reissues, and for them no thanks is too much.

title: If Phil Spector actually put any work into this, then its good he "retired" after ramones
text:
Given that the sides he cut with Starsailor in the early 2000s were pretty good and still displayed that Spector touch, and in spite of my reservations given the nepotistic nature of this project, and the dated feel of the cover art (get rich or die tryin meets hubba bubba bubblegum), I listened to this album with an open mind, hoping to once again hear that ineffable Spector quality reflected in the production, or the songwriting, or... anywhere. Unfortunately, I didn't hear that once, which, though disappointing, would be forgivable if the songs were any good and able to stand on their own; however neither case is proves true, and in fact, they're all quite bad - mostly mindless, generic, immediately dated electro-pop.

This album was a real slog to listen to, and having made it through, I find it has no redeeming qualities that I can think of. The "Produced by Phil Spector" stamp on the cover is either a lie, or he has totally, totally lost any ability to ascertain the quality of music, since I don't believe the man who made "River Deep" would put his name on this dreck if he knew how it sounded.

If you, like I, am a curious Spector fan, *please* save yourself the time and suffering and take my word for it: this album is beyond awful, and is not worth your attention (since it clearly wasn't given Phil's).

title: Give Him Up Marcia ... He Ain't All That!
text:
The film opens with Marcia (Joan Crawford) waiting for her date Sherry (Robert Montgomery) to pick her up for dinner. He was supposed to pick her up at 7:00. At 9:00 Marcia says To Hell with All This and crawls into bed. Of course, he eventually does show up. He bursts into her room (because people didn’t lock their bedroom doors in those days) and she tells him that it’s over and to get out!

Or at least that’s how it -should- have played … but that would make for a short movie.

Instead, he gets her out on the town for dining / drinking / dancing. We see that Sherry is a very popular person and something of a “ladies’ man”. He never sits still and wants to hit as many clubs / parties as he can each evening. He’s not the type to settle down!

He’s also not a man to trust around your wife. Marcia and Sherry run into Jim (Franchot Tone) while they are at the bar. Sherry woo’d Jim’s wife Diana at some point and she left Jim for him. Then Sherry grew tired of her and now she’s married to some British aristocrat. Jim hasn’t forgiven or forgotten.

That’s why it’s something of a surprise that Sherry kind of proposes to Marcia later that evening.

We don’t see the wedding, but we see Sherry working his magic with some nubile young woman he runs into at the beach on their honeymoon. See, a leopard just doesn’t change its spots.

Later, back in New York, Marcia has made plans to spend the weekend in the country. Grandmother Fanny (Edna May Oliver) and family friend / perpetual drunk Edgar (Charles Ruggles) joins them … but Sherry is distracted by someone who was supposed to be Edgar’s date – Theresa (Gail Patrick). Marcia, Fanny, and Edgar make the train. Sherry calls Marcia at their country house and lies to her about staying in town for the evening so he can take Theresa out for a spin. Marcia knows it’s a lie and confronts him the next day.

This is where Joan displays her talent for slapping!

Anyway, Marcia has a plan to get even with Sherry. She throws an impromptu party and invites women Sherry has had flings with and men who have been affected by those flings.

Wouldn’t you like to know how it goes?

This is a fairly pleasant film with some frustrating moments. I failed to see how Sherry is such a catch. He should have been thrown to the curb long ago; but I know it was a very different time back then. Adrian, Joan’s favorite gown designer, went a bit over-the top with Joan’s collars in this flick. In one scene her dress had a -square- collar, and in another she wears this big bizarre rigid bib/ funnel thing. It looks like she could’ve dumped her dinner on the flat part then held it up so it would slide down into her mouth. What was he thinking?

And on a random note … Does anyone in this silver screen universe -ever- finish a drink? The bartender pours a cocktail, the players touch the rim of the glass to their lips, then they’re off to the next thing.

Overall I’ll give this film a … *shrug*

title: Delightful Duet
text:
~ Some people may shy away from this album because of Archie Shepp's reputation as a fire breathing tenor sax man - a reputation he earned during the 1960's avant guard period in jazz. Others may turn to this CD seeking more of Archie's outside playing. Either of these potential buyers are in for a surprise. By 1978 when this album was recorded, Shepp had largely abandoned the ferocious attack and settled on more melodic flowing lines and a richer burnished tone as he drew inspiration and repertoire from modern standards and bluesy originals.
~ The pairing with South African pianist Abdullah Ibrahim (aka Dollar Brand) is perfect. Ibrahim's strong rhythmic playing is the perfect support for Shepp's hauntingly beautiful solos. The interaction between the two musicians in exemplary; one would assume they have played together for years.
~ The recorded sound is excellent on this 45 minute gem.
~ Highlights include the lovely Burrell/Brown composition "Fortunato" and Mal Waldron's "Left Alone". ~ Highly recommended for those looking for a relaxed, interesting journey. This disc will be of specific interest to those who enjoyed Shepp's mid-'70s dates for Arista/Freedom and Ibrahim's more subdued group efforts of the late '70s and early '80s. If you like this CD, you will love Ibrahim's solo effort "African Dawn".

YOUNG MORMONS SING BY JANEEN JACOBS BRADY, Composer of SONGS FOR A MORMON CHILD (Brite Records; no release number on cover nor record label. Lp dates 1978)

The vinyl album was available on Lp, cassette, and song booklet.

Track listing:
Side one--
Be A Friend/The Words You Speak/Daddy, Aren't You Glad (I'm a Mormon)/The "What If" Song/Maybe You Laughed/Little Steps to Heaven/Show A Little Love
Side two--
Opposites/Going to Sunday School/Mother Dear, I love You/A Little Seed/Someday I Will Be A Man/Eight Years Old/A Small Recorder/You can Be Anything

Running time on the Lp is approximately 13 minutes per side, total about 26 minutes for the album. There seems to be a mastering flaw (from tape to disc cutting?) on side two, "A Little Seed." The left channel drops out and distorts in places on that song. I've checked three copies (it's a common Lp at Utah thrift shops), all experience the same distortion.

Credits:
Executive Producers: Ted and Janeen Brady
Produced and Arranged: by Ron Simpson for Brite Enterprises
Arranging Assistance: by Clive Romney
Engineered & Mixed: by Jim Anglesey
Engineering Assistance: by Dave Hansford
Musicians: Dennis Nichols, keyboards; Clive Romney, guitar, bass; Bob Macart, drums; Craig Turley & Alan Weight, trumpets; Bryan Hofheins, Trombone; Daron Bradford, sax, flute, oboe; Ron Simpson, ARP strings, bells
Recorded at Sound Column Productions, Salt Lake City, Utah

Vocals/Vocal Group: Michelle Nicolo, Kenneth Jackson, Patrick Brady, Katie Miner, Todd Russell, Kirsten Brady, Wendy Brady, Sue Anne Turley. (Michelle Nicolo is referenced as being age 11 years in the back cover b&w photo; apparently the other children are likewise in the same age group.)

Todd Russell, Wendy Brady, and Dennis Nichols were previously listed in the credits for the 1976 Lp, SONGS FOR A MORMON CHILD. The producer (pictured in the back cover b&w photos), Ron Simpson, is currently (2013) the label head for Tantara Records, the BYU Music Dept.'s recording label. Clive Romney's arranging credits also appear on a 2008 Tantara Records CD release, THE NEW AMERICAN SONGBOOK by the Young Ambassadors.

Best tracks on this kitsch Lp are "The `What If' Song" (a proselytizing/mission theme to other neighborhood children) and "A Small Recorder" (which purports that a tape deck is "...spinning `round and `round inside my brain...I wish I could erase....")

text:

title: Some Hot, Some Lukewarm
text:
This summer, 1978 release represented a change in K-tel policy. Instead of cramming 18-22 songs on one record, this one spreads 18 songs over two records. This format lasted for only one more release (Starburst), before going back to one record. So what you get here are 18 complete songs with 17 single edits and one album cut (The Name of the Game).

With the movie "Saturday Night Fever" a big hit months before this release, you get a large taste of the movie's soundtrack, without the Bee Gees. "If I Can't Have You", "Disco Inferno", and "Boogie Shoes" are the tunes from that movie found here. There are more dance tracks from Parliament, the Michael Zager Band, and the Emotions. Other recent hits are from ARS, Dave Mason, Dan Hill, ABBA, and Jay Ferguson's forgotten island gem. There's quite a bit of soft rock here (Gene Cotton, Dan Hill, England Dan & John Ford Coley, Player, BJ Thomas) and a little too much filler-ish material to warrant a 5-star rating. But it's still a good buy.

title: Taras Bulba hits the bargain basement
text:
I've acquired the key elements of this excellent Waxman score on several compilation albums recorded within the past 20 years, the longest of which is a 10+ minute suite; all of these little suites are performed beautifully and in magnificent sound.
THIS recording may be the original but it is in mono (they DID have Stereo in 1962) and if Hallmark (a/k/a Pickwick) didn't bother to get the stereo masters and lifted it off a mono LP or tape, either way, it's hardly acceptable. There was nothing done to remaster or improve the flat, mono sound. It has no resonance. The artwork is redundant (front, back, inlay) and it's a no frills affair redeemed only by the magnificent music of Waxman. Based on this release and some lackluster vintage pop releases from Hallmark with similar sound issues, I will avoid the label. I can't believe the other reviewers of Taras had no bone to pick about the sound, unless they're listening to it on an alarm clock CD player. This is a sound-stage orchestra, not a trio. Let someone re-issue classic soundtracks who cares and knows how. FYI...there was a newly recorded complete score of Taras issued recently, but I was the fool who saved a couple of bucks because I preferred to have the original. There's a lot of good things to be said about score re-recordings.

title: I Solisti Veneti's earlier recording and of little more than archaeological interest
text:
Buyers in search of I Solisti Veneti's recording of Vivaldi's Mandolin Concertos, beware. This is a budget reissue, on Erato's early budget series Bonsaï, NOT of Scimone and I Solisti Veneti's 1983 recording with mandolinists Ugo Orlandi and Dorina Frati, first published on CD, here: [[ASIN:B0018KRYZA Vivaldi: Concertos for Mandolin]]. It is their earlier recording, from 1969, with Bonifacio Bianchi and Alessandro Pitrelli, originally issued on LP on Erato ERA 70545.

That recording - and, hence, the CD reissue - had only three of the four works performed in 1983: the Concerto for 2 Mandolins - back then referred to as P133, now as RV 532 -, the Concerto for mandolin RV425 / P 134, and the Concerto "for many instruments" (including two mandolins and two theorbos) RV 558 / P 16. Left out was the Chamber Concerto RV 93, and with some good reason: it isn't a work for mandolin, originally, but for lute and two violins.

But as a filler, back then and on the CD reissue as well, Erato added the Concerto RV 583 for scordatura violin and two antiphonal orchestras ("a due cori"), and to those four, the CD reissue adds again RV 581 "Per la Santissima Assuzione di Maria Vergine" for violin, and RV 552 "con violino principale con altro per eco in lontano" ("with a solo violin and a violin in distant echo"), for a generous TT of 73:22. The former is played by Piero Toso, the "historical" fiddler from I Solisti Veneti, and came out in 1976 on Erato ERA 70968 with three other “Solemn Concertos” (RV 212 "Fatto per la Solennità della S. Lingua di S. Antonio di Padua", 289 "Per la Solennità di S. Lorenzo", 579 "Funebre"); the latter, with both Toso and Giuliano Carmignola, was recorded in 1978/79 and first came out on Erato STU 71233 (with three concertos for flute performed by René Clemencic). There are various botches in Erato's cheap edition: they mislabel RV 552 into 522 (which would have made it "L'Estro Armonico" Op. 3 No. 8), they give, for the mandolin concertos, the old Pincherle catalog numbers (P) instead of the now customary Ryom references (RV), they fail to give any such catalog number, right or wrong, to RV 583, and finally don't tell you which mandolinist plays RV 425: it's Bianchi. The original LP had lengthy line notes contributed by Claudio Scimone himself: the CD reissue has none.

With all that, and added to the fact that it's somewhat frustrating to have only tidbits from those two other LPs (the four "solemn concertos" have been reissued in Japan with one more from another LP, [[ASIN:B00005HI78 ''''''':'''''''''''']]), this is not the version of the Mandolin Concertos you should favor, and not even the version of the Mandolin Concertos by I Solisti Veneti.

I Solisti Veneti’s interpretation in 1969 may have been revolutionary in its time - in particular, Scimone boasted in his liner notes that it was the first time that Concerto P. 16 / RV 555 was heard in its original guise, with the so-called "violini in tromba marina" played by violins and not... trumpets, as (claimed Scimone) the previous editions and recordings had done, based on a mis-interpretation of Vivaldi's indication on the manuscript score. He's obviously referring to the Casella edition, which also substituted Heckelphones (!... a double-reed instrument of the oboe family, invented in 1904) to the salmoès (a simple-reed instrument and ancestor of the clarinet) and harps to theorboes, and for the recordings he may have had in mind those of Thomas Schippers with the Alessandro Scarlatti Orchestra of Naples, Schippers' first orchestral recording (said the ads), published on Columbia 33CX 1451 / Angel 35335 in 1956, and Bernstein's on Columbia ML 5459 / MS 6131 from 1958 (the latter reissued on [[ASIN:B0000062E5 Vivaldi: Four Seasons / Concerto for Diverse Instruments]]). But for the salmoès ("a wind instrument that doesn't exist anymore today"), Scimone used clarinets playing at the upper octave.

But independent of those considerations, Scimone's interpretation in 1969 is firmly anchored in the Vivaldi interpretive traditions of the 1960s and 1970s: a little too trudging, a little too thick, a little too solemn. By 1983 and with an almost entirely new personel (besides the conductor, only harpsichordist Edoardo Farina and flautist Clementine Hoodendoorn Scimone - Mrs Claudio - remain from 1969), they took on the interpretive lessons of the period-instrument ensembles that had emerged in the meanwhile, Harnoncourt’s Concentus Musicus Wien, Trevor Pinnock’s English Concert and Christopher Hogwood’s Academy of Ancient Music, or maybe it was only that they participated to the same stylistic trend towards leaner textures and more animated tempos. Their 1983 recording is better in all compartments, and it adds RV 93, originally a chamber concerto for two violins, lute and continuo, but played by them as a mandolin concerto. The slow movement of the Concerto for two mandolins RV 532 was very beautiful in 1969, but in 1983 the two new mandolinists add wonderful ornamentation in the repeats. There was a very nice touch in the slow movement of RV 558, where the mandolin trilled all his notes (played unisono with the violins) rather than simply plucking them, something not explicitly called for by Vivaldi but much more effective; but it’s there again in 1983. And then the 1969 Mandolin Concerto RV 425 was ruined by I Solisti Veneti’s choice NOT to follow Vivaldi’s advice that “the violins can all play pizzicato”. And you just need to compare that and the 1983 remake, where they do follow the advice, to realize how much more beautiful the pizzicato version is, turning an ordinary concerto into one of Vivaldi’s most sublime inventions.

So if it is the mandolin concertos that attracted you here, by all means, of the two, you should favor the remake. That is, if it is I Solisti Veneti’s version you want. Because in 1992 came Il Giardino Armonico, and they sent the interpretation of these works in another dimension, with more energy, more enthusiasm, more liveliness and joyfulness, more poetic imagination in the phrasings, more sonic presence, more everything, making all the previous versions, even those on period-instruments, more or less obsolete. About this, see my review, [[ASIN:B000V1V0XE Vivaldi: Ctos for Lute & Mandolin]].

For all those reasons, this one is of no more than archaeological interest.

- Owner Of A Lonely Heart (Edited Version)

Just a single mix of the album version. It's about a minute shorter than the album version and feels a bit stunted because of it. Although I admit it does hit all the important marks, but you miss some cool instrumentation.

If you are a major Yes fan and need all the mixes (including the bad ones) then I suppose you will find value in this 12". Everybody else just pass it up.

title: A Cheerful Earful!
text:
Take a pinch of Douglas Fairbanks’ swashbucklers, add a dash of Richard Lester’s Musketeer movies, season with the fantasy films of Ray Harryhausen, and you have SINBAD AND THE PIRATE PRINCESS! It’s simply that much fun!

Writer/producer/director Mark Redfield, an accomplished actor of both stage and screen, is the new Sinbad; a hero who has his hands full as he pits his wits against those of Juna the pirate princess (Munro) and the sorceress queen Badra (Beswicke). This feature-length, larger-than-life audio adventure is an absolute treasure you’ll want to revisit again and again.

title: Not very well-done. Inconsistent and amateurish.
text:
I enjoy falling asleep to the sounds of the ocean. I have several CD's of this type. This one is the worst in my collection.

First, I have to say, you do get what is in the description of the product. This is indeed a CD of sounds of the sea, in an acceptable quality.

The problem is in the mix. It's basically a sound bed of the ocean, with effects thrown on top, and not very artfully.

For example - a few seconds into the recording, you'll hear a ship's bell. But the bell gets clipped at the end, ruining the immersion. This happens every time the ship's bell effect is heard. Other ship's horns go off far too often and far too "close" to the listener. They repeat, and there is no sense of distance gained or lost. You'll hear the creaking of a wooden ship, then suddenly the putt-putt of diesels.

It's just not immersive, consistent, or well-done. Too many effects are used too often and with no art to the mix. You are very aware that you are not listening to a continuous recording, but rather a pile of SFX over the background of the ocean. I was too aware of the incongruities to fall asleep. I was distracted rather than relaxed.

In my opinion, a CD like this should be subtle. It should sound like the recorder went aboard a ship and just rolled on the natural sounds for an hour. I understand that this is probably not how these recordings get made, but they should SOUND like they were made that way, and this one doesn't at all. It wasn't for me.

text: Flat out, Episode II is not great. In fact, it's not even that good. There is NO action for the first hour and a half except for a brief chase scene in the beginning of the film. As Homer Simpson would say: SOOOOOOOO BORING. Don't get me wrong, I am a huge Star Wars fan who grew up on the original franchise which makes Attack of the Clones even more of a disappointment. Besides the aforementioned lack of action, the acting especially Hayden Christiansen is terrible. Yoda who was touted as having an expanded role in Episode II is scattered throughout the film at best. Although easily the best scene in Episode II is seeing Yoda get some swordplay against a rogue jedi, the scene only lasts about five minutes. The last hour of Clones does pick up in intensity, fighting, and action but it still can't save the film. The fighting, while entertaining leads to no ultimate payoff. Leaving the theater I felt no satisfaction whatsoever and I can honestly say that I enjoyed Episode I: The Phantom Menace much more. The FX are amazing in Clones but the story is too much to fit into a 2 1/2 hour film. Which leads to Episode III and as Yoda would say: "Clouded this films future is, indeed." Lucas has lost the pulse of the Star Wars films.
