title: for Busoni, don't look here
text:
Ronald Stevenson is the legendary - well, all is relative: legendary, I guess, among a minuscule circle of pianists and music lovers - Scottish pianist and composer who fell in the music of Busoni when still a music student at the end of the 1940s, and never got out of it, composing extremely elaborate and complex Passacaglias and Fugues modeled after Busoni's Fantasia Contrapuntistica ([[ASIN:B000003IYF Ronald Stevenson: Passacaglia on DSCH / Recitative & Air, for Dmitri Shostakovich / Prelude, Fugue & Fantasy, on Themes from Busoni's "Doktor Faust"]]), and Piano Concertos that sound like Busoni's 2nd and 3rd ([[ASIN:B000003W7T Stevenson: Piano Concertos No. 1 & 2]]).

But this here isn't quite of the same ilk. These are compositions by Ronald Stevenson the Scottish pianist and composer - stress on Scottish. They are only harmonized Scottish folk melodies, played on violin and piano. The music is sentimental, wistful, merry, and inconsequential. The harmonizations are more or less elaborate - as Stevenson writes, he's interested in the two styles of harmonizations, the one used by Kodaly in which the harmony is derived from the tune's melody, or the freer approach preferred by Percy Grainger. But there's no Busoni in the piano part, that's for sure, and Stevenson doesn't treat the folk tunes as Busoni treated the great Bach organ pieces or Violin Chaconne when he transcribed them for piano. May I add: too bad.

The CD ends with two original compositions of Stevenson, a little more demanding, the slow and meditative Recitative and Air, composed with Shostakovich in mind and sounding like it, and a Nocturne, dedicated to the memory of John Field and going from sentimental salon-music to lusher atmospheres reminiscent of French music at the turn of the 20th Century or some of Ernest Bloch's Violin and Piano compositions without the Jewishness.

The violin is played by Stevenson's grand-daughter. The recording pickup is a little too close for the full beauty of the violin tone to fully unfold, but it is okay - and this isn't Bach after all. TT is 41:04. Not that I wished for more, but it is pretty stingy. If it is Scottish folk music that attracted you here, you might want to explore this, too: [[ASIN:B000003IY1 Salute to Scotland]]. But it is the Busoni-influenced Stevenson you are interested in, better go to his piano music - or to the source itself, Busoni (which Stevenson has recorded, too, [[ASIN:B000003IY2 Toccata]]).

title: Another must-have for Elvis completists!
text:
This collector CD on the Famous Groove label gives us the (nearly) complete October 15-16th, 1961 recording session in which Elvis recorded five titles: Night Rider, Anything That's Part of You, I Met Her Today, Good Luck Charm, and For the Millionth and the Last Time. All of the session outtakes are included, the greatest number being for the three ballads, Anything..., I Met Her Today, and For the Millionth... The latter two titles were first released on the Elvis For Everyone LP in 1965; Night Rider was released the following year on the Pot Luck LP (despite another attempt at re-recording during the Pot Luck sessions); and Good Luck Charm was paired with Anything That's Part of You as a single release, also in 1962.

Many of these outtakes sound just fine to the listener, but Elvis being the perfectionist continued with additional takes until the final one. Due to lack of space on the CD, the five master takes are not included, but this doesn't really affect the quality of the CD as they are readily available elsewhere. The two takes for Night Rider and the three for Good Luck Charm are presented consecutively, while the many takes for the three other titles are presented in segments of on average one to three in a row, which makes it perhaps a more tolerable listening experience. Audio fidelity is ideal studio quality, and Elvis is at his early sixties zenith as a recording artist.

title: An excellent Debussy ballet Jeux by Baudo and the Czech Phil
text:
This is a compilation disk, but I want to single out Serge Baudo's recording of the ballet Jeux, concerning a flirtatious trio of a man and two young women on a tennis court at evening.. This ballet was performed shortly before The Rite of Spring in Paris so its fall into relative obscurity was not that surprising. However Debussy's score was as original as Stravinsky's albeit in a more subtle elusive way. The absence of conventional themes or song melodies have often led to conductors aimlessly plowing through the score. While there are few awful performances there are almost no great performances. Baudo however turns in one of the best ever here with fine attention to phrasing. He also did a fine performance of Jeux with the London Philharmonic.

Jeux despite its lack of obvious themes does have structure but quite different from the sonata/rondo or atonal forte dynamics based structure that conductors usually lean on. With Jeux, Debussy takes about 20 different accompaniment motives and endlessly varies them. They are organized typically in 2-measure groups that are extended sometimes out to 4 or 6 measures. Within these brief groups of measures there is more repetition of the motives. The longer 6 measure groups function in lieu of cadences.

title: This One Gives Bootlegs A Bad Name!
text:
This two disc set contains 50 tracks spread over two CD's and as I should've known better I am so tired of waiting for an official release of the Hollywood Bowl LP from 1978 to appear on compact disc I made the move and picked this up. The package looks good and also of note is a professional recording produced for British TV that is found here from an: 04-11-65 show at the Empire Pool in Wembley that is a good sample of the Spring 65 show. The sound from Wembley isn't bad with the vocals mixed way above the instruments and there is no Ringo for the first few numbers but by the fourth song "Ticket To Ride" Ringo does appear in the mix and he rides the cymbals (to be heard?) on every beat. This snippet from Wembley is a good find.

Things take a bad turn at track eight where this collection becomes unlistenable with a very bad audience tape from Italy (June 1965) and as I hoped things would improve with other shows featured at the end of disc one it continues to become a mess of audience noise and talking with what sounds like a Beatles record being played at the wrong speed way down the road.

Disc two is a piece of sonic crap from start to finish with a Circus Krone show from Munich being the only thing you are going to be able to listen to and as this 06-24-66 show isn't The Beatles best performance the audio is way below the board tapes from Wembley found on the first disc so again you can play these first eight tracks from disc two but it isn't much fun to do so when there are excellent tapes of this era still sitting in the vaults for nobody to enjoy. After Munich there is nothing of the remaining seventeen tracks to waste your time upon as the sonics rate below zero quality as worthless and the radio voice-overs are about people in audience needing medical assistance and it's amazing that anyone would keep recordings such as this and believe they are of any value.

This is as bad as it gets and for everyone's enjoyment there is a five-star review of this collection found here and I do think we have found one of the bootleggers that manufactured this mess of a set. Go to your nearest donut shop and tell a cop about this guy before he re-releases this garbage yet again!

Nothing has yet been solved as there really is a market for live Beatles music and the Hollywood Bowl show (or Shea Stadium or Japan or anything decent!) needs to be released on compact disc but until it does indeed really happen the market will continue to be flooded with crap like this and that's a huge shame.
One Star (and it deserves ZERO stars!)

Another installment in the budget-priced Jive Bunny series, "Summer Holiday" is yet another example of an album full of good intentions that fails to deliver. It's not as bad as it's predecessor, in fact, it does grow on you after a while. Still, considering what's on offer in way of quality, even the budget price seems a bit steep in places. What "Summer Holiday" does do is it gives you that 'feeling' of summer (I'm listening to this CD on a cold spring day in March...and it's snowing!).But I can't imagine this keeping me entertained during the summer months.
The word is Jive Bunny's current record label are planning a third 'summer' album. Let's hope they compile a CD full of genuine 'summer' classics (a la "Lovely Day", "Summer Breeze", "Long Hot Summer" etc), and forget about these silly novelty albums that, quite frankly, are terrible.
Jon.

title: Best Kept Hidden New Age Gem!
text:
Garry Hughes(NOT to be confused with British hard rocker musician and singer, Gary Hughes) first came to my attention about 10 years ago. I was on a wild search spelunking through huge aisles of used vinyl record albums at my local music store.As I frantically flipped through the "New Age" section, I was skeptical but kept searching for maybe one or two New Age albums at random whose cover artwork might just catch my eye; As an avid record collector, sometimes there is NO logical rhyme or reason for looking for records and searching for that next vinyl fix(Is it because one is looking for a particular artist? Is it because the artwork or photography on a particular album catches the eye as a striking art piece suitable for framing?Or, just looking for any album on a spontaneous whim without knowing zilch about the music or artist---as such was the case with Garry Hughes' "Ancient Evenings"). Skeptical for two reasons: One, most New Age music over the years has received such a bad rap for sounding,well,like a parody of said genre. Two,when it came to ANY New Age music, all I ever listened to and knew about were just the big names: Vangelis,Kitaro,Tangerine Dream, and Jean Michel Jarre!...It was time to take a gamble and find out just what Garry Hughes had to offer.

10 years later, and I still own and listen to "Ancient Evenings" on both the vinyl and cd formats(on the Audion record label/co.). I listen to it at least once or twice a week! This is NOT spacey-"New Age"-generic electronica fodder by any means. Hughes sonically paints exotic locations and places,ancient temples and city bazaars or open market places for one's mind's eye and imagination to take flight and travel to! Despite the album being released in 1988, I can say that Garry Hughes was ahead of his time with "Ancient Evenings"...His use of all synthesizers and available digital technology of the time was used in such a way that to this day, it holds up pretty well without sounding dated. A gamut of 80's "New Age" recordings from other artists have not held up well over the decades and ultimately just sound like an electronic cliche of the times.In fact, his was the first album in which even the Audion blue record label with glowing analog audio tube still fascinates me;It's the sheer beauty that went into creating records---such an art form in and of itself! It was the first Audion record label I had ever seen.Since then, I have collected other Audion label New Age artists' works.

Hughes infuses a strong Middle Eastern,World-Music influence(an "ethnic vibe")throughout with highly atmospheric,dream-like, artistic machinations; He's a truly gifted alchemist of the synth-sound that would prove to help in his progression with other projects in the future of his career decades later.The music can be sparse at times, yet,intricate---less is more---it allows the mind to absorb the music much better rather than be distracted by synth-electronic gimmicks and gadgets. Wonderful and warm organic textures that absolutely counteract any thoughts one would have that it's just another cold and campy new age release.This was before this type of said genre of music would sometimes be called "chill out" or "ambient lounge" music.It is also certainly not club-dance music by any stretch of the imagination; It is in essence an escape for the mind!Guaranteed that no coma will be induced; You'll want to LISTEN to the cd/album in its enticing entirety.It is intelligent sounding. "Ancient Evenings" is a fantastic foray into another realm and not droning drivel into dullness.

The first track's intro solo key notes (title cut, "Ancient Evenings"), are highly reminiscent of a lullaby melody.You will ask yourself, "Where have I heard this before?", as it is in a similar vein as the musical notes used in the film "Close Encounters of the Third Kind" when trying to communicate with the aliens. However,this intro-lullaby is for the adult mind,not that of a child's or alien's.The song does eventually soothe into a finely crafted and multi-layered relaxing instrumental. The track, "Alexandria" evokes pure mystery as well as a wailing male(or female?) vocal-chant(real human voice or synthesized?). I will often listen to this album at night before falling asleep...There is something intoxicating about the whole title track and album! All songs evoke visions of mystical journeys to foreign desert lands,Middle Eastern, U.S. Southwest or otherwise, whether ancient or not...Not quite or necessarily taken to an oasis but yet one can visualize and see the beauty of the terrain and desert as well as what time of day or night(especially, the evening) the tracks accompany, or, on other tracks, allude to.At the end of the entire mind-journey, Hughes even incorporates in a tongue-in-cheek manner (and probably an inside joke that only he knows why he did it)a bit of movie dialogue from a male actor--- from the era of the Golden Age of Hollywood perhaps?...it makes for great side trivia as to what film the dialogue comes from---the source.As odd as that piece of spoken dialogue may seem, it actually works! "Ancient Evenings", in my humble opinion, is one of the BEST New Age albums to capture the desert and Middle Eastern lands vividly through Hughes' ingenious musical talent and visionary skill.

Garry Hughes has since been involved with many projects throughout his career and is currently with The Bombay Dub Orchestra. An ensemble that creates intriguing world ambiance and clu-dub lounge chill music or "grooves"! It is truly a befitting and wonderful progression and evolution from his early days and work("Ancient Evenings") as a solo new age artist decades ago!

title: The worst Star Wars yet!
text:
This movie was horrible!
Is there more I could say? Yes. Does it deserve more? No, not really. A more thorough review would begin with...
I tried not to get my hopes up for this one, but I was at least expecting a better movie than "Scorpion King." Boy was I wrong. Then all the reviewers said this was a lot better than Episode 1....boy were they wrong too. Episode 1 was far more exciting, fun, suspenseful, better paced, better acted, and even better animated. Now that last one might seem surprising. "Better animated? Are you crazy?" you might say. I will concede that the animation itself in Episode 2 is better than Episode 1, however it's alignment with the real actors, sets, and props is far worse than Episode 1. I don't know if Amidala or Yoda (or both) need their eyes checked, but they sure weren't looking at each other as they spoke together. And it seemed that half of the time, the Jedi in the arena scene were swinging their light sabers around defending and attacking against thin air. And the battle scenes at the end seemed ill paced, ill directed, and ill conceived.
Sure there are some good scenes. Anakin, the partly evil jedi, was the best part of the movie. The best sequence was Anakin finding his mother and going medieval, but this scene, which should have been a central part of the movie, was far too short and almost seemed like an after thought.
The light saber dueling at the end was also disappointedly short, and almost seemed like it was a spoof of itself. The factory scene was, by contrast, FAR too long and completely needless. Oh, but it is fitting that Jar Jar is used as a patsy to destroy the Republic. That was cool.
And I always assumed there were, like, a LOT of Jedi. This movie implies that there are about 20 active Jedi. In fact, you have to be a pretty lame Jedi to be active and NOT be a member of the Council. After this movie, I guess the "Great Jedi Purge" will only involve killing about 5-10 Jedi.
Overall, I was never felt "invested" in the story or any of the characters. I never felt excited, happy, or sad. I was only rarely and briefly entertained. And it is not the case that I had read spoilers before seeing it, because I knew about the same amount about Episode 1; and heck, I read the entire novel for Return of the Jedi before seeing that movie, and those movies still connected to me on an emotional level that this movie never reached. title: Plymouth takes you to a place of free jazz and avant-garde improvisation
text:
The name Plymouth evokes discovery and freedom. In American history, Plymouth Colony was established by Pilgrims fleeing religious persecution in England, and was one of the earliest successful colonies founded in North America by English-speaking settlers. Plymouth is also an explorative and nonconformist ensemble which spins out extensive avant-garde, free-jazz improvisations. Keyboardist Jamie Saft (whose résumé includes Bobby Previte and John Zorn) and versatile guitarist Joe Morris collaborated on Plymouth’s 2013 Slobber Pup project, and this year the two friends have reunited for yet another heady and challenging offering, a self-titled effort which features Salt on organs, Echoplex piano and Fender Rhodes; Morris on electric guitar; and three guests: electric bassist Chris Lightcap (who has worked with Anthony Braxton, Cecil Taylor and Archie Shepp), drummer Gerald Cleaver (who has been active with Roscoe Mitchell, David Torn and more), and up-and-coming electric guitarist Mary Halvorson. Cleaver and Lightcap previously performed in Morris’ quartet, while Halvorson is Morris’ former student. Thus, the group’s interaction and communication is formidable.

The hour-long album contains three aural excursions which vary from meditative to nightmare-like ferocity, characterized by musically associative leaps which defy categorization or traditional musical structures. None of the three extended pieces are commonplace or tidily self-determined. The twenty-minute opener, “Manomet,” (named after a seaside village of Plymouth, Massachusetts) is a smoldering mixture of free jazz and noise-rock. The sprawling track agitates around Saft’s aggressive B-3 organ, and Morris and Halvorson’s disorientating and often distorted guitars. Lightcap and Cleaver’s rhythms don’t present any semblance of relief. The drums and bass skitter and spike as much as the other instruments. The amount of digitized fuzz accelerates at the conclusion, as Lightcap runs his hollow-body electric bass through a fuzz pedal; Salt increases his organ’s warped sonic sound; and the dueling guitars become lathered in a dense auditory disfigurement.

The pressure temporarily ratchets down on the 13-minute “Plimouth,” where the intensity isn’t quite so unrelenting. At the onset, the quintet develops textures and pocket-sized digressions into recognizable melodic themes. By the end, “Plimouth” enters heavy-metal territory, with guitars, organs, piano and drums clashing out a voracious quality closer to Metallica than, for instance, Miles Davis in his electric years.

The final, 29-minute epic, “Standish,” (presumably titled after famed Plymouth Colony administrator Myles Standish) is a fearless, flexible foray. “Standish” combines quieter moments of ambient landscaping alongside deafening outbursts. Saft puts forward note-bending exercises in response to Halvorson’s coiled coloring. Lightcap keeps the bottom end fluid with drifting bass lines which bounce away from Cleaver’s drum fills, cymbal smacks and tom-tom eruptions. The B-3 organ swells up as both guitarists solo together as one unit.

This kind of extreme, spontaneous rock-jazz is not for everyone. It stands halfway between Cecil Taylor’s chiseled pianistic concentration and Frank Zappa’s incendiary rock-based solo guitar sorties. That’s not a comfortable space for some listeners, but if one is inclined to such unconventional terrain, Plymouth is a great place to visit.

title: Good work, some problems
text: George Clooney's black and white feature is about journalist Edward R. Murrow's effort to challenge the methods of Senator Joseph McCarthy during the 1950's when he actively investigated and indicted members of the entertainment, media, and military industries for communist sympathies and Soviet membership. The film is decent and well acted, David Strathairn plays a very convincing Murrow, and Clooney's directing is competent. However, the film takes an entirely too simplistic moral view of its subject, it fails to acknowledge the paranoia of the period and has the benefit of hindsight. Additionally, the film makes CBS and Murrow's efforts more heroic then they actually were, Senator McCarthy certainly didn't have as much power as the entire CBS Corporation, and the journalists who brought him down weren't really risking as much as the film implies. Furthermore, McCarthy was not attacked until he investigated individuals with real power like high ranking officials in the military; the film fails to make this clear. An average work on the whole, but worth seeing none the less.

title: Searching for the Healing Spring
text: According to her website, 2010's "Ever Since You Never Heard of Me" is Melanie's newest CD.  The folk-popper who captured so many fans with her hit "Brand New Key," her appearance at the legendary Woodstock concert and her early recordings on Buddha has continued to work as an independent artist.  This set is another strong offering produced by her son Beau Jarred Schekeryk and her husband-producer Peter.  "There is a thread that joins each to the other, brother to the sister, sister to the brother, and it's almost like being in love," Melanie sings on her opening anthem "Angel Watching."  "A Kiss from the Heart" slows the pace with a lovely melody and a sentimental treatise on love.  "I Tried to Die Young" is a wry look back on the vagaries of youth, "My heart kept on breaking in the cracks of the edge where the hand of a shadow grabbed the hand in my head; There were demons I know there & they still come back, but we've become friends, my demons and I."  Beth Nielsen Chapman joins a chorus of background vocals on the African-folk-flavored "Motherhood of Love," "Are we all on our own island struggling with our broken dream, searching for the healing spring?"  "Hushabye" is an emotional heartbreaker about a military widow comforting her son.  "Deserts of Blue" is a gorgeous instrumental composed by Beau Jarred.  "Big Big Bear" is a silly two-minute track that that puts a smile on your face.  The set concludes with the electric rocker "My Surprise," "It's my love & I'll do what I want when I want to with it; It's my love & I'll wear it like a flag."  This is a delightful set by one of our master musicians, well worth the search!  Enjoy!

title: Milnes at His Recital Best
text:
[[ASIN:B01K8MWNP4 Sherrill Milnes in Recital, Vol.2 [IMPORT] (1997-10-02)]] This CD is a compilation of some of Sherrill Milnes' best recital work from the years 1980 to 1990. The American baritone, in his prime in the 1960's and 1970's, had a vocal-chord issue in 1981 (when he was forty-six) that led to a relatively early vocal decline. However, only tracks #3 and #18 really reflect this decline; and those tracks both show, if not the most beautiful tone, then the superb legato that always was a hallmark of Milnes' style.

"Nemico della patria" from ANDREA CHENIER is the only operatic aria on the disc, the remainder being comprised mostly of French art songs and Milnes' beloved oratorio repertoire; the comically Handelian song "Old Mother Hubbard," written by Victor Hely Hutchinson in the twentieth century, is also present. Though the two Baroque oratorio selections that open the disc find Milnes in wonderful voice (these were recorded in 1980), the clear highlight of the CD is the set of four Serious Songs by Johannes Brahms. Captured in 1984 or 1985, they show Milnes at his peak: serious vocal decline had not yet set in, and his artistry was fully mature. Most impressive is the fourth of the songs, "Wenn ich mitt Menschen," which sounds almost as though it could have been written expressly for Milnes' voice. But to hear a side of Milnes that was not frequently apparent in opera, go to track #19, "Old Mother Hubbard," and delight in the droll (and agile!) performance that draws laughter from the enthusiastic, Carnegie Hall audience.

Milnes' friend and regular accompanist, Jon Spong, provides adept piano support in all of the tracks. THERE BUT FOR YOU GO I is a valuable document of the non-operatic, later-career Sherrill Milnes. If you are a fan of his, then you need this CD.

title: Incredible cd from down under
text:
In a day when such untalented and unoriginal bands like Kittie, Orgy, Kid Rock, Methods of Mayhem, and Limp Bizkit are ruling radio airplay and mtv by producing music for the mass market rather than the fans, leaves me disappointed when a band as talented as Superheist will probably never be heard by the general public. I do not know if it is because they are from Australia or if they are labeled as just another copycat band, but whatever the reasons, this band definitely deserves some recogniton. While this cd may only contain 8 tracks, "8 Miles High" easily puts to shame all of the combined efforts of the aforementioned bands.
Superheist's music is a meltingpot of rock, rap, funk, alternative and metal creating a sound that is not only incredibly cool, but also fresh. The guitars, bass, and drums all feature excellent workmanship that flows extremely well together accompanied by keyboards and scratching that really adds to their music. Each song features different genres of music at times sounding like Coal Chamber and then shifting into a Foo Fighters type flow, followed by some techno and pop rock influences. Very intelligent and mature song structures.
The vocals are another well defined aspect of Superheist's music. The lead singer and backing vocals can either rap or sing with melody effortlessly. Not the greatest vocalists in the world, but definitley better than most with a confident and distinct style. The vocalists easily accentuate the music with memorable choruses and lyrics that are simple but at least intelligent.
As far as I know Superheist has had six eps put out with "8 Miles High" their lastest and by far most accomplished cd. Starting out with "Pulse" which is an incredible rapcore song on the heavy side featuring Coal Chamber type riffs and a fast beat, rap-laden lyrics and a cool melodic chorus. "Karma" and "Two Faced (Check Your Head)" are two of their older songs which the listener can tell since they are weaker than the other songs but very cool nonetheless. The latter features a very cool and memorable chorus with a kind of techno/dance flow. "Have Your Way" is the best song on the cd with very little rap and is more of an alternative rock song with a very cool melodic chorus that reminds me of Foo Fighters. "1.4.U" is more of a harder rock song with some rap and dark melodic choruses interspersed. "Detonate" is another very cool harder-edged rapcore song with some Coal Chamber overtones and a melodic chorus underlined by a rap-laden attack from the backing vocals. "The Hollow Blue" goes back to that Foo Fighters alternative rock vein with more of a melodic edge chased down with some hardcore screams and Coal Chamber type riffs during the chorus. The cd comes to an end with "Beachview" which has more of a pop/alternative feel and a beautiful chorus where the backing vocalist is rapping while the lead vocalist is singing a melodic overture. Thus, the end to a great cd.
Superheist is a band with a lot of talent and have already exhibited extreme growth within their music. Given time and the right kind of marketing, I see this band blowing up, if the states give them a chance. If not, then the rest of the world can have the benefit of enjoying their music. This is not a high-risk commitment people, Superheist is one of the more talented and up-and-coming bands out there today. Check them out, I highly recommend Superheist. Other unheard of bands that I have had the pleasure of being introduced to: Linea 77, Shovel, 40 Below Summer, Star Island, Tenfold, Hybrid Theory, CrawlBlind, Dolly Trauma, Fear the Clown and Half Gauge.

title: Avoid this one, even Duke Ellington Fans
text: In 1963 some folks had the idea of turning the source material of the film The Blue Angel into a musical.  From here everything went wrong.  They reset the thing in New Orleans, they brought in Duke Ellington to do the music (he had no background in musical theater) Marshall Baerer to the lyrics (not bad on paper, he had done Once Upon a Matress a few years earlier), Lilo (she of Can Can 10 years earlier) and Theodore Bikel who while a fine performer had only had a minor personal success in the mega hit The Sound of Music as the leads.  None of this came together and the thing limped into New York for 3 forgettable performances.  I don't even hear a lot of the older theater mavens claiming to have seen this train wreck as they do Carrie and Kelley.  But with songs by Duke Ellington people kept wanting to hear the score and Ellis Larkins put this package together with Marshall Baerer and Barbara Lea sharing the vocal chores.  I am unable to tell if the songs are dull or the fault lies with the singers, neither of whome brings any real sparkle to the task.  Larkins at least does a competant job, but the whole package is deadly.  I can't even imagine playing through the whole thing again, not one song jumped out at me, and I am a huge fan of the Ellington ouvre.  Dull, Dull, Dull.

title: Avoid! Uncomfortable and toxic mattress and terrible customer service!
text:
I purchased a Novosbed mattress directly from the company but had such a bad experience I wanted to post here as well. I’ve also heard that negative reviews don’t get published on the Novosbed site, which is appalling on its own, but all the more reason to spread the word in other venues.

I had two concerns about my mattress that I approached Novosbed customer service about. The first is that Novosbed claims to not use any harmful chemicals in their mattresses. I naively believed this when purchasing the mattress but later came across a Novosbed page that said their mattresses have a fire retardant cover. I asked Novosbed about this and they said the cover is made of Alessandra fabric which they said is non-toxic. With some more research, I realized that Alessandra fabric contains modacrylic fiber, which contains antimony oxide (a carcinogen) and melamine resin, which contains formaldehyde (another carcinogen).

My second concern was that the gray bottom portion of the mattress is shorter in one area of the bed than other parts of the bed. In all parts of the bed except one, that portion of the mattress is 8.5 inches high. However, at one end of the bed, that section is only 7.5 inches high, which just doesn’t seem right naturally.

When I contacted Novosbed about these issues, they were less than helpful. They told me that yes, the mattress cover contains modacrylic fiber, but that the toxicity is “subjective” – so in other words (and she actually said this) if it’s something you’re worried about, it will concern you and if it’s not something you’re worried about , it’s not going to concern you. Very disturbing doublespeak going on and not much customer service. None of that makes sense to me but the customer service rep talked me in circles and was pretty aggressively rude about her stance and so it was impossible to argue my point. I asked why the contents of the cover were not disclosed on the Novosbed website and the response was that if I had asked, they would have gladly told me. It never would have occurred to me to ask about this since their website claims they don’t use harmful chemicals. I only realized how inaccurate this was when I did my own research. And of course anyone could ask. How about being upfront and transparent about your business practices instead of putting that burden on the consumer?

Regarding the height issue of certain parts of the mattress, I was told this is normal. OK? How so? Well, they say it’s because the cover moves around. Well, how would that affect the height of the gray base part of the mattress in any way? It’s had the varying heights since I received it. Well, just deal with it is their effective response.

If you find the mattress uncomfortable, which you inevitably will, you will need to keep the mattress for an astounding 60 days before you can even consider returning it. They will give you the spiel that after 30 days you can order the Comfort+ kit and that you can walk on your mattress every day to try to make it more comfortable. Even when you are FINALLY able to return it, they tell me you must take numerous pictures of the mattress.

Above all, I found that the customer service at Novosbed was the most upsetting part of the process. The customer service rep I dealt with, Caitlin, was incredibly rude and condescending, both over email and on the phone. And she was so by the book and clearly annoyed at having to deal with customers and just going by rote of what has been said to poor hapless customers in the past.

Honestly, purchasing a mattress can be an agonizing and stressful situation. You don’t want to add to this by having a bad experience with a mattress company. I have dealt with other mattress companies in the past and they were always very helpful and friendly. Novosbed’s customer service was shocking in contrast and I’m not sure how they think they will stay in business with this customer service model.

If you have any issues or concerns with your mattress, be prepared to suck it up and suffer because there will be no help forthcoming from Novosbed customer service. I wish there were more honest reviews of mattresses, especially this mattress, as I would have appreciated the heads up to avoid this one.

title: sentimentalizing and belittling Chopin
text:
I'm a great fan of transcriptions. They offer a great way to listen to the old warhorses in a new light, and they can be not only hugely entertaining, but sometimes also revelatory... but this pushes my tolerance a little too far. I'm sorry I can't be more positive about this disc, the concept WAS appealing: it is a collection of arrangements of Chopin's piano music made between... 1904 (track 18, "Nocturno" after Chopin's Nocturne op. 9-2, possibly an arrangement of Pauline Viardot, sung here - in Russian - by Maria Michailowa, soprano from the Imperial Opera of Saint Petersburg) and 1947 (track 3, Carmen Carvallaro's Polonaise Fox Trot after the Military Polonaise). There is even a (modern) recording of a music box Minute-Waltz built in Switzerland around 1885 (track 19). So the first half of the last century seems to have been when these transcriptions were in vogue. Then the vogue must have abated.

The first ones are in Jazz style - Clement Doucet's Chopiniana from 1927, track 1, after the Military Polonaise and Waltz in C sharp Minor, Hazel Scott's scurrying Waltz in C sharp minor from 1946 - and they are fun, because they are played at the solo piano and retain the leanness of the originals. John Kirby's jazz orchestra and its dizzying rendition of the Minute Waltz (1939) is still fun and even funny (track 4), but bombast and kitsch start setting in with Carmen Carvallaro's Military Polonaise in 1947 (track 3).

There is, I guess, a certain kitsch charm - the charm of faded, sepia photographs - to Chopin's nocturne with wailing cello sung by a Russian Imperial soprano in 1904, or to Amélita Galli Curci (misspelled Gurci in the liner notes) turning the Minute-Waltz op. 64 into a Rossini aria in 1909, track 17 (none of them is entirely pitch-right in the upper reaches). But it's really when Chopin's themes are used for easy-listening arrangements and crooning singing that I start cringing. And the main bulk of the CD is made of such arrangements: "A Song to Remember" (from the soundtrack of the 1945 King Vidor film, a biopic of Chopin), by Freddie Martin and his orchestra, with Artie Wayne crooning, track 5, Ninon Vallin's coying sentimentalizing of Etude op. 10-3 (appropriately called "intimacy"), track 16, the two arrangements by André Kostelanetz imitating Glazunov, turning Chopin's music into music fit for the New Years ball in Vienna or Saint Petersburg (tracks 6 & 7) and, most egregious of all, the arrangements (by Polish émigré Bronislaw Kaper (misspelled Kasper in the liner notes) used in the Broadway show Polonaise, supposedly very successful in 1945 and 1946 (tracks 8 to 15). Maybe there can be a nostalgia effect on generations old enough to remember what it was to listen to the radio in the 1940s, but it doesn't work on me. All I can say is that it is fascinating to see how arrangers have gone for plunder of the melodies of Chopin (always the same: the Minute-Waltz, the Military and Heroic Polonaises), only to sentimentalize and dwarf his music. The concluding music-box is fascinatingly ghostly - secretly expressing maybe that all these arrangements were meant to dissipate and turn to dust with the passing of time and fashions, while the original music of Chopin will eternally remain.

The label by the way is Frémeaux & Associés, a French label specialized in Jazz reissues and spoken material, and I suppose PID is the American importer. Fine liner notes, but despite a little leaflet inserted in the liner notes boasting a "quality charter" with the claim that "all recordings are transferred and mastered with extreme care, using the most up-to-date technology", the transfers are more than mediocre, with the typical (and unbearable) desiccated quality brought by excess and careless filtering.

title: sacred chants of popular tradition in Italy
text:
Sacred songs both traditional and 'popular' (ie, folk tunes apart from the formal church liturgy) from Emiliano, Italy, performed by the instrumental group Pivari Trio and vocalists from Compagnia del Maggio di Frassinoro (The May Ensemble from Frassinoro).

Musicians:
Fabio Bonvicini: flauti, organetto, baghèt, ciaramella, canto
Mario Nobile: violoncello, organetto, ciaramella, canto
Renzo Ruggiero: ghironda, nyckelharpa, mandoloncello, canto

Listen to the mp3 page for this album to see song titles and hear song samples - very professional!

from liner notes:
The work presented in this CD by the Pivari Trio and by the soloists of the May Ensemble of Frassinoro takes its origin from a research on the sacred chants of popular tradition commissioned to Fabio Bonvicini and Mario Nobile by the Cultural Department of the municipality of Nonantola (Modena). The research developed on two main levels: on one hand a field enquiry, which availed itself of some recordings of still existing rites and of the direct testimony of elderly informers who sang and narrated their musical memories; on the other hand – well aware we were in quest of a treasure definitively and inexorably fading away – the close study of researches carried forward by previous scholars at a time when this musical tradition, choked nowadays by imported cultures, was still alive.

Once the enquiry stage was ended, the problem arose of how to elaborate and repropose the rich and evocative material we had collected: thanksgiving chants, songs coming from the liturgy, Passion chants, purely popular melodies played on holy days. The first necessity for the Pivari Trio, in comparison with their previous work on the songs and dances of the Frignano area entitled "Passa e ripassa", was to find voices that still bore upon them the mark of an ancient musical history, common to the repertoire and to the cultures in question. At this point came the meeting with Marco Piacentini and the May Ensemble of Frassinoro, who immediately agreed to the project of working together to the elaboration and reproposal of the repertoire we had assembled in the course of our research. The selection, the arrangements, the instruments, the voices, the project organization, everything was formulated and discussed together, to get to the result which is now presented by the Pivari Trio and by the May Ensemble of Frassinoro.

The order of the songs follows the course of the solar year: from the Epiphany to Christmas. The choice of the instruments and of the arrangements – mainly directed by Marco Piacentini – has been organized according to two main themes: we could call the first one a liturgical one, based on absorbed and intimate sounds, more apt to narrate the events of the Passion and to perform the tunes of more strictly liturgical origin; the second one, which we could define as festive, gathers together, in a more joyful and abounding style, the church songs linked to the celebration of holy days and popular traditions, where the Christian message mingles with ancient pagan festivities such as the Befana (an old fairy bringing toys to children) or with extra-religious musical traditions such as the dramatic May. What hasn't been touched at all but reproposed, on the contrary, in all its transparent authenticity, is the colour, the accent, the vocal expression of the May singers. Like the faces of "The Gospel according to St. Matthew" by Pasolini, or the language of "Funny Mystery" by Dario Fo, the ancient voices of the May singers bring a message from another culture, from a world which today can only be found in the folds, in the salvation oases of a musical landscape too often flattened and reduced to a single, monotonous, deafening colour. - Fabio Bonvicini

title: Two, not Two
text:
Peter Brotzmann, now seventy-two, is a leading free jazz reed man from Germany, who has been on the scene since the mid 1960s. He is a titan with dozens and dozens of recordings from around the world with all manner of musicians as well as numerous solo recordings. His son, Casper, is an electric guitarist who specializes in distortion and special effects, not (say) legato runs or intricate song structures.

Taken together, this father-son team is a bit of an odd coupling--although both have played together in larger ensembles. On this CD, there are no supporting players; in fact, the Brotzmann's were not in the studio at the same time. The "togetherness" was wrought through the overdub. The effect is less than majestic, although hard-core Peter Brotzmann listeners will want it simply for his nonpareil playing.

title: I'd skip this one...
text:
I was sent this version of Carmen by mistake -- I had ordered a different set, and apparently the seller didn't know the difference. There are different versions of Carmen available with Bumbry, Vickers and Freni, so beware which one you're ordering. This one is the Von Karajan version, a live performance from the Salzburg Festival. I gave it a good listen before sending it back, and it is far from a good recording.

To start, this sounds like an archival recording that was never intended for commercial sale. The sound is monophonic and low-fidelity, almost sounding like an old 78 rpm record -- except it was recorded in 1966. The stage mics that were used to record this were placed in such a way that they picked up a great deal of noise, such as footsteps. Imagine listening to live opera on an AM transistor radio and you'll get some idea of how this one sounds.

This recording is saved from a one-star rating by some excellent singing. Not all the singing is perfect, and the chorus is sometimes quite ragged-sounding, but the principals are all very good. However, the poor quality of the audio in general makes listening to it a less-than-enjoyable experience.

I would suggest that, if you're looking for a good 1960s-era Carmen, you go with a different one. Unless you're specifically wanting this performance, there are quite a few others that are significantly better.

title: The sad last gasp of what was once the greatest.
text:
With some simple hand gesturing and going through the motions, the band known as 10cc died with the release of this album.

This album was created out of contractual agreements, bad producing decisions and the least amount of contribution by one of it's original members since Sir Anthony Hopkins' 16 minute Oscar work for "Silence of The Lambs."

Listening to this album, which clocks in at a quick 54 minutes and 10 tracks, reminds me of a bit of Sting's 90's solo efforts with a touch of Phil Collins and a dash of Peter Gabriel. A few of the songs are a bit introspective, subtle, rich and will be a treat for your ears. The rest are horrible abortive projects that should have stayed in someone's writing satchel.

The shame of it is why the album was created and the what the results were.

Kevin Godley and Lol Creme had a contractual agreement with Polydor for one last album and they decided that they didn't need the albatross tied around their necks any longer. After contacting Eric Stewart and Graham Gouldman, the album was begun in earnest in late 1991.

Sadly, a combination of the "band"'s usage of a new producer and utilizing many other artists to help create the sound for their album shows it's lack of cohesiveness.

Here's 10 songs, and here's my 10 second review of them:

1. "Woman in Love" - Six minutes of light radio filler - who decided this would be a hit of any sort? Even for 1992 this sounds overproduced.
2. "Wonderland" - A bit of light fun, once again a total 1992 experience, which says something here - ugh, I really did not like this song - it's like overcranked Jimmy Buffett lyrics and lite jazz flavored ice cream. Bleah.
3. "Fill Her Up" - A kind of rocker - still, it's so syrupy lite I'm getting a toothache!
4. "Something Special" - Despite the wonderful piano of Dr. John, it's boring, the lyrics right out of some amateur's songbook. There's no life in this song at all... yet it segues right into...
5. "Welcome to Paradise" - one of the stronger songs of the album, and it has a cool reggae-scented sound, and is one of the only songs I listened to a second time to be sure I liked it as much as I did when I heard it the first time - yup, it's decent.
6. "The Stars Didn't Show" - Kevin Godley has even publically noted that his vocals here (and backing tracks on two other songs) were the only contribution to this entire album, and sadly it shows... and I liked this song a bit, and I wonder who the mystery "man in black" is here they're crooning about, but it's a short balld of sorts that doesn't go beyond repeating the chorus more than the lyrics...
7. "Green Eyed Monster" - this is the closest that 10cc sounds like the 10cc of old - staccato harmoious lyrics firing over decent music... too bad too sad for them, though.
8. "Charity Begins at Home" - another small glimpse of 10cc breaks through the endless echoes and layering of music, but once again, too little too late.
9. "Shine a Light in the Dark" - The harmonies are wonderful, but what they're singing is stinky, and the music is dull and uninspiring, and it sounds EXACTLY like Chicago's late 80's/early 90's sound, with their middle of the road boring music so hypnotizing you could play it for your 18 month old child and they'd get a good nap in.
10. "Don't Break the Promises" - here's a interesting bit of trivia: this song was written by Paul McCartney & Eric Stewart (he'd been working with him for several years prior to this) and I think this was tacked on to appease Stewart and give the album a bit of A-list credibility - Graham Gouldman was also given a bit of writing credit, too - but it falls apart under the crushing weight of overproduction and moderate to extremely dull song performance - it's a shame, too, because I think this might have had a chance, somewhere.

So I listened to 10cc's album, and immediately gave it away to a friend. I'm just hopeful my friend doesn't hate me for giving them such painfully underperformed straight-from-the-songbook-by-the-numbers material.

I have to give it two stars only because I really don't want to give them one, yet this really shows me that the power of money can kill creativity in a heartbeat. I feel bad for these four guys, because they created one of the greatest songs ever off one of the great albums ever, but this?

This is an exercise in what not to do, especially when you all haven't been in a room together for the last 10 years and then decide to try and cohesively create something again that probably will never return once they left the room.

The result - like this album - will be sloppy overly-created garbage.

Do yourself a favor and pass on this one.

Please check out my other reviews of less painful music. Thanks for reading!

title: Waste of Time
text:
This review is for the Warner Archive DVD release (Amazon currently has it mis-categorized as "Audio CD"), which is a very excellent transfer of "No Time for Comedy." I think the very best classic films are in the time period of 1935--1944, with exceptions, of course, but films of those years have a certain atmosphere, and give viewers a certain feeling, like Hollywood really knew what it was doing and turned out some excellent work. This film, however, from 1940, is a waste of two great stars, James Stewart and Rosalind Russell.

The first 20 minutes or so are wonderful, light and funny, but then it's as if another director takes over and throws everything in reverse; the whole thing goes toward dark drama with Jimmy, the country boy from Minnesota who was head over clogs in love with Rosie, suddenly (and for no apparent reason), seeing another woman on the sly ... and it's so unbelievable that the whole picture loses steam---and your interest. The viewer is left with no sympathy for his character, and Russell's character folds into an unsympathetic travesty of mawkish, fake hope, saying she wants to keep her husband, but do we really believe her?

It's hard to believe this was scripted by the same authors who would later create "Casablanca," and is from a play produced by Katharine Cornell.

Save your money and time and watch these two great stars in their other great films of 1940: James Stewart in "The Philadelphia Story " or "The Shop around the Corner," and Rosalind Russell in "His Girl Friday."

There have been plenty of BBC sessions released since the millennium that are fine, but as the century progresses, the sound quality gets worse and worse. The bootleggers do a better job, then, now and in the future I’m sure.

The problem with this is it contains high midrange distortion that should not be there. The original sound of these recording has been altered thru bad mastering. Some of these have been released in decent quality, like on the Raven issues and as bonus tracks on the Mono Animalism CD.

I use an equalizer. I can improve these tracks somewhat and make them less annoying to the ears, but it’s gone too far to eliminate the noise completely. This isn’t quite as bad as the Rolling Stones On Air, but it’s getting close, hence the 2 stars and not the one.

I write a lot about sound quality. It seems a large portion of the CD listening public is either hard of hearing, have no idea what proper sound is, or are using such horrible sound systems like Bluetooth computer speakers, that they can’t actually hear sound quality at all.

The one positive: it’s good to know this much more material exists in the archive that needs a proper release. There’s a lot here I’ve never heard.

The negative: Too bad it’s in the wrong hands to release it properly. Eric released some himself, he should release it all again in the same sound as on the Raven issues…

Frankly, I’m getting tired of the epidemic of bad sound.

title: The reissue of another superb rediscovery by Concerto Köln - early romantic music of great sweep
text: This is one of the numerous entries (and, as I write, not the cheapest either!) for the reissue by Brilliant Classics, the "other" very-budget label (Naxos being the first one) from the Netherlands, of a CD first published by Archiv Produktion in 2004, listed here and still selling very cheap at the time of writing: [[ASIN:B00016OYNW Johann Wilhelm Wilms: Symphonien Nos. 6 & 7]]. I've posted a detailed review thereunder. Johann Wilhelm Wilms was born in 1772 near Cologne - which makes him Beethoven's junior by two years - but (like Bonn-born Beethoven with Vienna) at the age of 19 took the bold decision to establish in Amsterdam, where he spent the rest of his life. He died in 1847, which makes him a near-contemporary by death of Mendelssohn (1809-1847) and Chopin (1810-1849). In other words, he witnessed the advent and blossoming of the early romantic style in music, and his two last symphonies bear witness of it. Composed respectively in 1820 and 1837 (which dates the latter seven years after Berlioz' Fantastique and Mendelssohn's Reformation, four years after the Italian), they are milestones on the path leading from Spohr to Schumann, really, works of great sweep, melodic invention, orchestral splendor, representative perhaps of a time of stylistic transition (of which Spohr, Raff and maybe even Schumann in his symphonies would be other champions) but no less appealing because of that. Endless gratitude to Concerto Köln for offering this invaluable discovery.

title: Too much Schneeweiß, not enough Weiss
text:
I share the view of Sean Kasabuske and Moreton. Silvius Leopold Weiss is occasionally audible on this CD, but it's almost entirely covered up by Schneeweiß. This CD sounds more like Augustin Barrios or 1960s Spanish soft jazz for guitar than like Weiss. This is more like a heavy metal or rap arrangement of Cole Porter--maybe you can still hear the tune and the words, but you'd never listen for the same purposes or the same way, right? That's what this feels like. On the other hand, many guitar arrangements of lute music are very successful--that's what this doesn't feel like.

Weiss' compositions are like the best French croissant—delightful buttery lightness. Schneeweiß is like smothering it with a can of Hershey's Chocolate Syrup. Nice enough for some purposes, but not the baroque music I like to use to help organize my mind when I'm thinking hard and writing. Stephen Muires notes "it sounds as if it was written yesterday." In my view, that's exactly the problem. The pieces have been entirely recomposed—the harmonies are 1960s, not 1730s-1740s.

[[ASIN:B00QG15MQO Michael Cardin's recording of Weiss' complete London manuscript]] is very very nice. [[ASIN:B00000E2NX Göran Söllscher's arrangements of Bach for guitar]] (or [[ASIN:B0000B09Z2 here]]) are also among my favorites.

But an "arrangement" is usually thought of as minimal change to adapt to a different instrument, to bring out colors that are faithful to the composer. "Arrangement" is not the right word for heavy-handed mutilation. The Schneeweiß box went into the pile for resale without me even finishing listening to it.

The cliche-ridden lyrics encapsule half-baked ideas for songs.  In the title track, Holbrook says to his erstwhile significant other: we're both drowning; I have no help to give; save yourself. title: Get a dictionary
text:
I've got a problem with two words used to describe this album. They are Rock and Masterpiece. First, to be called a Rock album an album actually has to rock. This one doesn't. Even the Doors, surely a psychodelic rock band - not a favorite of mine, by the way - rocked - listen to 'light my fire', or 'break on through to the other side' or several of their other well known singles. They show a drive and a passion, and generally encourage the listener to go nod 'yeah yeah' with his head, as all good rock should. Think of big rock bands today, even those you don't particularly like - Beatles, Queen, U2, Led Zeppelin, you name it. Regardless of how much you (dis)respect them, they all know how to rock. Love doesn't.
As for the masterpiece bit - what makes a masterpiece? Well, several things. First of all, a unique sound, a sound that tells you, "hey, you're listening to [insert favorite band name here]". This album lacks it - it sounds like many other uninspired folk rock album out there. Second of all, timelessness - several tracks on this album have aged considerably. Third, brilliant catchy melodies, such as on Beatles albums or other good 60s albums - but not here. Fourth, excellent lyrics, as in Bob Dylan's or Tom Wait's albums - while some of the lyrics are good, some are plain dumb, especially those about snot (a sublime metaphor indeed). And fifth - intelligent arrangements. Some songs on this albums include a trumpet or strings, but that doesn't qualify them as being any good. They often just sound cheesy.
I'm not saying this is a "bad" album. Hey, music is subjective. I don't like Celine Dion, but tens of millions do, so who am I to judge them? What I'm trying to say is this: just because some dumb music critics - and some music critics are known not to be the brightest people in the world (I'm talking about people who, e.g., praised The Strokes) - have put this album on their top 100 list, don't be tempted to buy it. Nor should you let the glowing 5 star reviews on Amazon pesuade you to. If you want good proof of the uselessness of most Amazon.com reviews, just try reading the glowing 5-star reviews on various albums YOU can't stand. Then you'll understand what I mean. And remember, always trust your OWN musical taste, not that of critics or the masses.

title: The Best of Rohn's Recordings
text:
Often people overwork their material and end up ruining it. Stephen Covey's later 7 Habits audio material isn't as good as the early '90's versions.I always thought this was the best Jim Rohn program out there. It was early on, so it's tightly presented and stays on track. But the material is superior here - outlined precisely. His presentation is compelling.

In later live recordings, he's very flippant and tries too hard to entertain. The routine can get tiresome and downright trying at times; particularly when, to stress a word, he knowingly uses that trick of emphasizing the wrong syllable and then whining the word out like a screeching magpie. And the later live work is poorly organized, compared to this.

Rohn empathizes here. In later work he seems to ridicule and rub his success in people's faces; a smart-aleck, put-down approach. When people are in pain, they don't want to be scolded. Here the tone is measured, proper.

I met Rohn once, in the late 1990s. He was smug, almost imperious. I'll just bet he was more approachable and friendly around the time this was recorded. Who knows...

title: of very specialized interest
text:
Kurt Schwaen (1909-2007) was an East-German composer, a collaborator of Bertold Brecht at the Berliner Ensemsble in the 1950s and an “official” of East-German music: “Schwaen has held numerous honorary positions, e.g. in the Association of Composers and Musicologists and in the Academy of Arts, to which he was named official member in 1961. His compositional output, which spans seven and a half decades, contains more than 600 works in every genre, from song and chanson to choral music, piano works, chamber music and orchestral works, and includes opera and works for the ballet.” There’s a website for Schwaen.

He said, quoted in the liner notes, that he enjoyed “writing music to folk poetry more than any other genre”. The cycle “Komm wieder zur künftgen Nacht” (tracks 1-8) on 16th century texts is subtitled “Deutsche Volksdichtung” (German folksongs), and that’s how they sound indeed.: folk music, maybe a sophisticated arrangement of folk-music, but not sophisticated modern or contemporary music. Perfect for an amateur choir. “Ein Zicklein” subtitled again “Volksdichtung” (track 10), is slightly more sophisticated, sounding something like one of Orff’s “pedagogical” choruses, but without the distinctive personality. “Schlaf mein Kind” (12), a lullaby, is sweet and mellifluous, very pretty in a Christmas Carol style. “Wenn du zu mir kommst” (track 11) and “Schlafe wohl zur nacht” (track 26) sound like simple lullabies or folksongs that Brahms could have written or harmonized.

Psalm, track 9, (not a psalm, it is the title of a poem of Brecht) and the cycle “Nimm an die Weisheit” (13-19), on proverbs of King Salomon), the cycle “In den stolzen Städten” on poems by Günter Kunert (22-24), “Sie sind nicht tot” (they are not dead) on a poem of Pablo Neruda, and the cycle of four “folk poems” (Volksdichtungen) “Untern Himmel, under Sternen” (tracks 27-30) are harmonically more daring and grating, but they don’t go far beyond Hindemith or Karl-Amadeus Hartmann. The one that sounds most advanced in its harmonic language is Gagarin, track 21, sounding (appropriately to its text about, indeed, the Astronaut, a poem by Günter Kunert) very “Ligeti-space” with the mysterious softness but without the violence, and it comes as no surprise that it the one composition of Schwaen here that starts being interesting.

TT 59 minutres, texts of songs given in their original German, no translations. This is of very specialized interest: collectors of music from East-Germany perhaps, or those looking for compositions suitable for amateur choirs. Megadisc was an interesting label, established in the early 1990s, that brought to the listener’s attention little-exposed Belgian composers and composers from the ex-Soviet area, starting with Shostakovich’s maverick student Galina Ustvolskaya. A new management took over a short time ago and obviously they don’t have the intention of keeping this one in their catalog: they’ve attributed the same catalog number, MDC 7795, to another release, Christian Zanesi's Paysage électronique avec train (2015), not listed here, barcode 9780201379655. Can’t entirely blame them.

title: Five Julian Bream commissions and classics of 20th century British guitar, in outstanding interpretations
text:
A quasi-perfect program, gathering five big and small classical masterpieces of 20th century British guitar: Britten's Nocturnal (1963), Tippett's The Blue Guitar (1983), Walton's Five Bagatelles (1972), Berkeley's Sonatina (1957) and Richard Rodney Bennnett's Five Impromptus (1968) - and all Julian Bream commissions. There are more of those, of course, even limiting myself to the solo pieces: by Reginald Smith Brindle, Malcolm Arnold, Alan Rawsthorne, Humphrey Searle, Giles Swayne, Peter Maxwell Davies (Hill Runes), Michael Berkeley and a Sonata by Bennett from 1983, but, with a recital here already clocking 71:34 it is doubtful that any would have fit on the CD.

And outstanding interpretations as well. Craig Ogden's Tippett The Blue Guitar is both precise and very atmospheric, beautifully pensive and dreamy in the opening "Transforming" and in the closing "Dreaming", and with great drive in the scherzando 2nd movement "Juggling", but never, as can be the case with Norbert Kraft on Chandos, at the expense of clarity and rhythmic precision ([[ASIN:B000000AJL Michael Tippett: The Blue Guitar, Sonata for Solo Guitar / Benjamin Britten: Nocturnal, after John Dowland, Op. 70 / R. Murray Schafer: Le Cri de Merlin - Norbert Kraft, Guitar]]), and yet with more flexibility than the atmospheric but very strict David Tanenbaum on New Albion ([[ASIN:B000000R2S Acoustic Counterpoint]]). This will now serve as my version of reference for The Blue Guitar.

Score in hand, Ogden's reading of Britten's Nocturnal is as precise rhythmically and as imaginative interpretively as his Tippett. The Blue Guitar is a masterpiece of 20th century guitar... and Nocturnal is even more, or at least an even more immediately accessible one. In each of the piece's 8 short movements Britten explores a new idea and each time, truly, a fantastic one, not just in the sense "great", but also, nocturnal, nightmarish, evoking the wildest fantasies of the imagination, all the way to its concluding Passacaglia, with the obsessive return of the ground motto, as if it were ever stifling any attempt of the music to escape off... the ground, but ultimately giving way to the despondent but soothing Dowland air on which it is all based, "Come, heavy Sleep, the image of true Death". Nocturnal is echt and unmistakable Britten - listeners familiar with his output will easily recognize twists and turns-of-phrases already encountered, especially in the Cello-Piano Sonata and the Three Cello Suites, of which Nocturnal could almost pass for a transcription for guitar. Julian Bream, recorded in September 1966 ([[ASIN:B000003FG1 Music For Voice & Guitar (Julian Bream Edition, Volume 18)]]), may have been a touch more eloquent than Ogden, but not nearly as precise (and in fact often surprisingly imprecise) in his rendition of the rhythms and articulation marks of the score (I haven't heard Bream's remake from 1993, [[ASIN:B000002RTP Nocturnal]]).

I don't have the scores of the others so I'll pass interpretive comment for the moment, but I have no reason to doubt that Ogden there is as precise and imaginative as in the Tippett and Britten. Very thorough and informative liner notes by Geraint Lewis, although they are mistaken in their claim that this is the first recording of Tippett's The Blue Guitar in the order of movements as originally conceived by the composer, e.g. with the fast movement, "Juggling", in the middle rather than, as published and as Julian Bream had performed it, at the end. Ogden's recordings were made in March and September 1994, but the Blue Guitar had been been recorded in its original order already by David Tanenbaum on New Albion in 1990 (see link above).

title: Some marginal recordings, some not hits
text:
I was surprised that this two-CD set wasn't stronger. I ripped none of the tracks for my music collection which I occasionally use as a deejay. I generally focus on the Billboard top 100 singles charts, but I also include favorites from top albums.

Disc 1 is centered on Artie Shaw although Helen Forrest sings on some tracks. What is most disappointing is that the tracks appear to be mostly live with some background noise and announcer commentary.

One track sounds like it is a studio recording: "Oh! Lady Be Good", Artie Shaw with Count Basie. It sounds very good, but, as best I could tell, this version was not a hit single. I'm not sure where it might have appeared in some other album.

Disc 2 is centered on Helen Forrest. If you just want to hear Helen's voice on good recordings, this would be for you. Unfortunately for me, most of the songs are dated 1969-71, well after the big band era. Three are dated 1949-50, and one seemed to be dated about 1946 or so. As best I could tell, none of the tracks were Billboard singles hits.

I have found it difficult to find a list of Helen Forrest's hits. She had only one solo hit on the Billboard 100: "Time Waits for No One" in 1944. I found eight joint hits with Dick Haymes. But the songs she did with big bands seem to be credited to just the bands. That means that one must go through the hits of big bands when she was with them: Artie Shaw (1938-9), Benny Goodman (1939-41), and Harry James (1941-3).

As far as packaging goes, the two CDs are somewhat clumsily packed in a 4-CD case with a folded strip of liner notes laying loose inside. The strip unfolds to eight small "pages". Not a very classy arrangement.

One more disappointment: There are errors in the track lists that show up on your computer when you go to rip tunes. Disc 1 is worst. None of the tracks are properly identified. You must change this before ripping. Disc 2 correctly identifies the tracks but incorrectly credits Artie Shaw as an artist on all of them.

Unlike most who have reviewed this recording of Bruckner 6 from Josef Keilberth, I'm not a fan. (Nor am I a fan of his B9.) I find this to be an unperceptive reading which just kind of rides roughshod over the work. When I purchased it, it did not impress me. So I never listened to it again at that time. Flash forward many years, and on a recent long-distance car trip, I grabbed this CD off the shelf and said, let's listen to it with fresh ears, maybe you were just having a bad day. Nope, that wasn't it--this just is not that good, in my opinion.

What's wrong with it? It just seems to be running on automatic pilot without any particular attention to what's going on in the music. At no point in the performance did I feel I was listening to someone who is truly inside Bruckner's music. It just feels surfical and lacking in...well, everything. I'm struggling to find something positive to say about this. And I'm just failing to do so. Truth be told, I threw the CD away at a rest stop after listening to this performance for the 2nd and final time while on said car trip.

The 2 1/2 stars are for the playing of the Berlin Philharmonic, although I would also add that I've heard them sounding far better than in this performance. They don't sound particularly involved in it either.

It's not. It's as if they're trying to be dark and tortured, but not TOO MUCH so as to appeal to a wide, popular-music audience. And the creativity standard is in the toilet. I mean, what went through their minds in the studio? Something like, I imagine, "We need to give this song some more edge. Where's that button that makes a sound like an evil typewriter? Let's throw *that* in a few times! *Then* this song will *really* be creative and dark!" Yes, I'm being really mean. But I expect more from Reznor, again, especially in light of the two aforementioned soundtracks that I really enjoy.

I downloaded this EP free, legally, from the band's website. I'm really glad I did this first. I suggest you do the same, if you still can, before wasting your money.

title: A Surprisingly Strong Album
text:
This CD has held up reasonably well over the decade-plus since its release. It is an all-too-rare occasion when Brother Norman releases an album that is composed entirely of new material, and much of this is quite well written. The production (and probably most if not all of the arrangement work) can be attributed to the musical maturing of Norman's little brother Charly, whose "signature" feels heavily present throughout the album. But that, thankfully, is a good thing -- because, in all honesty (and this from an admirer of Larry Norman's music), big brother Larry's fount of inspiration appears to have been barely trickling for a good three decades now.
It is difficult to speculate precisely regarding the sudden cessation of the kind of music that Norman proved capable of writing and performing in the late 60s and early 70s. He has not been hesitant to offer his own (often quite varied -- and hackneyed) explanations over the years, in print, for his dramatic falloff in the mid-70s after "Upon This Rock" (still a very fun late 60s "period piece"), "Only Visiting This Planet" (oh my goodness -- classic, truly classic early 70s "Jesus Rock" that addresses the gamut of social issues with sanctified-but-cynical wit), and "So Long Ago the Garden" (crafty songwriting and some great blues).
In fact, Norman has offered more "spins" on his tailspin than one could possibly keep straight: often it's those nasty music companies who keep screwing him over one way or another(i.e., "The Man"); or else he spent so many long and thankless years selflessly producing other people's albums (i.e., "my so-called 'friends' stabbed me in the back"); or else he was emotionally spent by a ruined marriage (though in fact much of his best work appears to have been animated by lost love); or else it was that really serious head injury in a plane accident . . . and many more. Come on, Larry -- you were just getting old! (I should know; I'm creakin' along not far behind.)
I know I've strayed from the issue, which is to review "Stranded in Babylon." Forgive the venting . . . and suffice it to say that this album certainly stands up reasonably well alongside Norman's finest work. His lyrics can still be biting and prophetic (especially in the excellent rant "Step into the Madness," where he warns against "a kinder, gentler World War Three" and proclaims America to be the "land of the free [where] everyone gets liberty -- if you've got the money").
For the most part, though, the kind of truly wicked (in the best sense of the word) humor that once characterized Norman's writing has almost entirely vanished, at least on this album. (I have yet to hear his most recent, and possibly his final, studio album, "Tourniquet," but I have heard good things about it.) And "Stranded" also provides evidence aplenty that his capacity for crafting a tune that is actually attractive and catchy has diminished considerably.
If I could, I'd probably have actually given this 3 and 1/2 stars, rather than 4. (I'd have reserved 4 stars for "So Long Ago the Garden" and, I suppose, "In Another Land.") Nonetheless, the album is / was a solid effort by the single most important figure in the history of Christian rock music -- at a time when few could really have expected something so fresh and alive from an aging-before-his-time, apparently burned-out musician.

title: Disappointing recording of Portuguese polyphony
text:
This is a programme of Portuguese late-renaissance lamentation and other sacred music, built around a Mass setting by Duarte Lobo together with works by a few other composers including Cardoso, Morago, Fernandez and De Brito. In his booklet essay, the Marian Consort’s director Rory McCleery sees the works as an expression of Portuguese nationalism in reaction to the dominance of the ruling Habsburg emperors.

The programme is introduced by Cardoso’s Lamentations for Maundy Thursday, with the remainder framed by the movements of Duarte Lobo’s parody Mass on Palestrina’s motet ‘Veni Domine’. Among the better interspersed pieces are Lobo’s ‘Pater peccavi’ (track 7) and Estevao de Brito’s ‘Heu Domine’ (9).

Unfortunately I do not find the works offered here especially interesting, at least in this recording. The problem is exacerbated by the quality of the performance and the sound balance. The vocal blend of the Marian Consort’s six voices is far too top-heavy for my liking, with little lower-voice weight in evidence to balance the texture; their six voices consist of two sopranos, alto, countertenor, tenor and bass. One of the sopranos also applies too much vibrato for my taste. The recording balance does nothing to compensate for the vocal balance, with the result that the works scarcely sound the way renaissance sacred music should. Altogether I find this a very disappointing recording, which compares poorly with other Iberian renaissance programmes from the likes of the Tallis Scholars, Gabrieli Consort or Ensemble Gilles Binchois.

As a footnote, readers should also beware of occasional fake reviews of recordings by the present ensemble, often giving themselves away by obvious unfamiliarity with the recording they purport to review, or else by an apparent ignorance of musical matters. Such five-star but one-word reviews (or sometimes stretching to two words, to give them due credit) can result in an unjustifiably high overall score out of five at the top of the product page. I should add that there are also perfectly sound reviews by knowledgeable writers (you know who you are!).

title: No drama, no exitment
text:
Villa-Lobos is the only Brazilian “classic” composer that ever made to the mainstream. Besides soccer players and retired or dead F1- racers, Brazilians don’t have a lot of cultural or national heroes. They hear a lot about Villa-Lobos, as if he was the ultimate genius that “shown Brazil to the world”. Brazilians are very sensitive about their own image and enjoy to be noticed by the rest of the world, something that barely happens. The nationalism propaganda in Brazil turned Villa-Lobos into a cultural giant that amazed the whole world, promoting Brazilian ingenuity. Villa-Lobos made - and still makes - Brazilians proud of their country even if they hardly know his music.

Villa-Lobos is popular with classic guitar players because of his collection of Prelude and Etudes. These compositions are often compared to Chopin’s homonymous compositions for the piano.

The Bachianas Brasileiras are great compositions. The #5 is by far Villa-Lobos’ most famous work.

“Floresta do Amazonas” is a true masterpiece. Unfortunately, it is seldom performed. It reminds me of Respighi. Although, it is better than Respighi. But you wouldn’t know this from this Neshling performance.

I discovered this music when I listened to it on the radio in Rio about 35 years ago. The recording that played on the radio was probably the only one at that time. It is a recording conducted by the composer in the early days of the stereo era. I could not believe when I saw the CD of this recording at Future Shop in Canada about 20 years ago. For what I see, it has been out of print.

I read or heard a while ago that Villa-Lobos was a great composer but a lousy conductor. This Neschling recording made me realize how great conductor Villa-Lobos was. All the excitement and drama from the Villa-Lobos recording are nowhere to find in Neschling’s. Neshcling is also slower. On the hypothetical plus side, Neschling brought the complete score. It is only now that I realize that Villa-Lobos’ recording had cuts. But I dispute the quality of this extra music. I wonder whether Villa-Lobos was fond of this music and decided to take them out from his recording. Or maybe the reason was that his recording was intended to fit in only one LP. The truth is that the final product in Villa-Lobos’ recording, with the cuts, is preferable than this complete score. Villa-Lobos knew better.

On the Villa-Lobos recording we also had Bidu Sayao in great shape. To fully appreciate Villa-Lobos genius, you have to find his recording (it is on youtube, btw). After you listen to that one a few times and get familiar with the music, give Neschling a try.

Two stars because the sound recording is pretty good.

title: You Can Have Only So Many Death Stars
text:
Perhaps in fairness to George Lucas, the Star Wars saga is played out, and it is difficult to continue to milk it. After all, you can have only so many death stars.
As for this movie, I challenge anyone to describe to me the basic story. There is no story, no characters and cetainly no clever or snappy dialouge. The original Star Wars saga was good, sometimes great because: (i) the story-line was clear and easy to follow; and (ii) it presented simply and effectively a myth-like, romantic confict between good and evil; and (iii) the script and dialogue were well done and at times clever and funny; and (iv) the foundation of the movie was not special effects but, rather, a solid story-line and good characterization. The special effects were great but not the foundation of the whole saga. Lucas seems devoted entirely to special effects and creating pointless (and stupid) alien characters to demonstrate his special effects prowess.
I will not go see another Star Wars movie, and I am ashamed of myself for going to see this last one.
