title: Original Roots-Reggae Music from Saginaw Michigan IS a Thing!
text:
TL;DR: This is absolutely amazing music and you need it in your life!

Back in my day as a local Flint punk rock singer, I heard tales of David Asher. In whispered hushes, local music fans told me about this mysterious wildman from Saginaw who played in a band called The Process. “Go see them,” they said. “You won’t be disappointed.” Well, the stars never aligned to allow such a thing to happen. Years later, I came across a release by the David Asher Band (DAB). upon confirming that this was the same neo-mystical David Asher I’d heard about, I bought a copy. I’m damn glad that I did because this is GREAT stuff!

Okay. Full disclosure, I’m writing liner notes here. I’ll sum up DAB as such: An amazing collective of talented Michigan musicians who’ve come together to deliver some memorable songs. I plan to focus on these songs with this review. Let’s start with the three cover tunes on the album:

1. "Keep On Moving" by Bob Marley
2. "Give A Hand" by Gregory Isaacs
3. "Knockin' On Heaven's Door" by Bob Dylan

In short, DAB masterfully aces all of these cover songs. And in doing so, they achieve what few local bands do in this regard. That’s striking the balance between honoring the spirit of the original tune while also making these songs their own. Bravo to David and the band! You’ve masterfully pulled off what many bands can only aspire to.

Now, I’m excited to change gears to what really attracted me to this release: the band’s original music. Let’s take a look at this body of work track by track:

1. "47 Shots (The Ballad Of Milton Hall)" - Reggae wouldn’t be reggae without a protest song. And this number is DAB’s protest song. In it, Asher shares his take on the tragic case of Milton Hall, a man killed by Saginaw police. Like the title of the song suggests, Mr. Hall was shot 47 times. DAB channels their fury over this incident into a tune that manages to move and groove with a funk all its own. The band’s razor-sharp musicianship and Asher’s soulful vocals are all on display here.

2. "Keep A Little Faith" - It’s no secret that the world can grind us down. We all could use a little musical pick-me-up, and DAB delivers. This upbeat number shares an inspirational kinship with Bob Marley’s “Three Little Birds.” That said, this tune maintains its own originality throughout. Who needs a guru when you have DAB? I trust that each note of this number can easily lead us to the promised land of positivity.

3. "Deputy Dawg And The Marshall" - I don’t know the story behind this song but I’m sure it’s an interesting one. What I can say is that all of DAB’s strengths are on display here. Excellent storytelling and singing combined with a sound that’s a warm and rich as honey dripping from the jar. The most interesting highlights include a background vocal arrangement, rap monologue, and humorous tribute to “The Good the Bad and the Ugly.” DAB pulls these elements together to forge a song that’s as fun as it is catchy.

4. "There's A Fire" - I’m a lyricist at heart, so it came as a shock that this one was such as standout for me. I say that because “There’s a Fire” is not lyrically complex, but that’s NOT a bad thing. The fire Asher sings about in this one is his burning passion for his music. He says exactly what needs to be said about that inferno within the confines of this catchy number. Furthermore, this song is a dance number and a damn fine one at that. If you don’t get out on the dance floor while this tune is playing, you don’t have a pulse. It’s as simple as that.

5. "Donkey Jawbone" - This song makes a great showpiece for Asher’s powerful vocals. I almost feel guilty for saying it because it could appear that I’m slighting the other hardworking members of DAB. Rest assured, the entire band is on point here. And the inspirational message encouraging the small to stand up to the mighty is not missed on me. DAB’s signature hypnotic trance state flow is on full display as its ability to rise above the current it creates to showcase some excellent workmanship. Musically, this number manages to cover a lot of ground while remaining rooted in something exceptional is on full display. Sit back and enjoy!

6. "Love Ballad" - David is joined on this one by Miss Mikki Sound. It’s a great example of the magic that’s created when two soulful vocalists come together on a great jam with a top backing band. This track is as smooth as silk, and every bit as evocative of any of the great soulful love duets of the 70s. Perhaps even better. In fact, if this song isn’t used in a future movie or TV series, a great injustice has been done to music fans (And DAB) the world over.

7. "Donkey Dub" - I’m no reggae purist. I am a lover of great music and THIS is it! Based upon a solid melody, the song’s horn section flawlessly melds with its slinky bassline, steady drums, Caribbean poly-rhythmic percussion, and echoing guitar and clavichord effects. The end result is a jam that is both powerful and hypnotic. If you’re looking to travel off somewhere deep in your inner space while your body sways and moves to the beat, this is it. Highly recommended!

8. "Love Ballad Instrumental" - This is the same song without David and Mikki’s vocals. The instrumental version is everything you’d expect it to be and more. Imagine a sunset stroll down the beach in Montego Bay, hand-in-hand with your lover. All is well and right in your world and there’s nothing more than that moment. These are the vibes captured in this song.

All in all, this is a great album. If you’re still reading this, you should know this by now. Normally, I would tell you to “support your local artist,” and buy this release. But I’m not going to that here. Why? Because too many reviewers fall back on the local angle to help sell sub-standard art. DAB’s great work here is FAR from that. This music has national appeal. Get it because it’s absolutely amazing. Like I said above, you need it in your life!

title: Sincere Homage to the Great British Tradition ...
text:
... of cathedral and university choirs, especially of boys' choirs, from which have emerged many of the most artful ensemble singers of the "Early Music". Even the OVPP ensembles -- The Hilliard Ensemble, The Orlando Consort and others, the antithesis of choir performance -- include graduates of the English boys' choruses. This true, of course, of German ensembles also; Andreas Scholl was a boy soprano before he became a man soprano.

The Westminster Cathedral Choir usually includes roughly twenty boys and ten adult males. They are tightly rehearsed, probably with piano, and tightly conducted, but such a choir of semi-professional, not-fully-trained voices can't possibly manage the complex polyphony of the 16th Century. Add to their overly broad timbres the sounds of "His Majestys Sagbutts and Cornetts" and what you get is a vast whooshy sound in which it's impossible to sort and hear the various lines of polyphony. Try to record that whooshy sound and flush it through a couple of speakers in somebody's parlor, and the whoosh turns to a tinny white noise with only a hint of human timbres left. The tuning of such a large choir of modestly skilled singers will inevitably be "tuning by committee". On this CD, everything sounds "in tune" because nothing really is. The cross relations, suspensions, dissonances of every piquant sort sound exactly the same as the cadences and consonances; "more or less in tune" is no better than blatantly out of tune. This performance might have been impressive for parents and friends in some resonant cathedral ambience, but as a CD it's unlistenable.

title: Perhaps El'Zabar's best post-bop album, but still not his real strength
text:
Jitterbug Junction, recorded in 1997, is an interesting album to compare to Kahil El’Zabar’s What It Is. Both Ritual Trio albums are somewhat anomalous in El’Zabar’s discography for their adherence to a more mid to late 60s, Coltrane-esque post-bop style rather than the African trance thing that characterizes much of El’Zabar’s music, whether with the RItual Trio, the Ethnic Heritage Ensemble, or various other projects. On these recordings, Kahil works with his root players, Ari Brown and the late Malachi Favors, who helped him form his sound, and one can hear the refinement of Kahil’s approach to music on the early Ritual Trio albums with these two artists, combining influence from Coltrane and others with an African percussion kit that he plays in a way that owes less to any specific African tradition than to what he takes from the instrument itself. Yet he never loses the 60s post-bop root, which explains his capacity to play with artists like David Murray, or the late Hamiet Bluiett.

On 2013’s What It Is, there was a little more of a pedagogic feel to the exercise. Everything was well played, to be sure, but it did feel more like an exercise rather than where Kahil’s soul was. As much of modern jazz can feel like rote exercise, El’Zabar’s 2013 album was something like showing the kids how it is done, and that he did. It was a fine album, easily standing alongside the tradition Kahil so deeply respects, yet there is something different when Kahil steps behind the standard drum kit rather than his African setup.

On this earlier album, recorded in 1997, Kahil did much the same. By this point, one can hear either from the Ritual Trio or the Ethnic Heritage Ensemble that El’Zabar had found his sound. In the same year, he released The Continuum with the Ethnic Heritage Ensemble, as an exemplar of what that project can do, and Love Outside Of Dreams. Kahil knew what he was doing. Yet in the same year, he steps behind a standard drum kit (on all but one track) with Ari and Malachi to record a more traditional set, and it works more effectively. Why? Compared to What It Is, there are just those subtle tricks of rhythm. Consider the excursion, The Sweet Nectar of Cacophony, which may be the better tribute to Coltrane than “One For John” because rather than trying to think like Coltrane, the players weave in and out of conventional time in a way that Coltrane would have loved, as Kahil sets a rhythm that flows without actually being in any way cacophonous. Coltrane circa ’65 wouldn’t have played it, but rather, he would have heard it and been inspired. Then told Elvin, hey, check out that drummer! Play to your heroes, not from them.

Nevertheless, will Jitterbug Junction be considered central to El’Zabar’s discography? Given that it is not his core sound, nor what he does best— that trance groove thing— it is important more as a demonstration that at his best, he can do 60’s post-bop as well as or better than anyone, particularly accompanied by his most sympathetic collaborators, who allowed him to bring in the subtle rhythmic twists behind the more experimental Ritual Trio recordings. El’Zabar’s best? No, but a very fine album.

text:
I caught Tom last summer when he and his outlaw band showed up in Philadelphia, and recorded the show from the Worst Seat In The House. Point being, during a conversation with Tom after the show, I pulled out my copy of Rolling Stone where he talked about his upcoming tour, saying not to expect the tried and true oldies, that he was gonna concentrate on his new release Mojo ... which he didn't, playing all the old stuff, and leaving this genuinely terrific album standing in the wings, with only a few of the tracks to see the spotlights. When I asked him about it, he rubbed his face from chin to his forehead with one hand, in one continuous motion, leaving a tight lipped smile, and said, "Yeah?"

While this album doesn't contain all of the material from Mojo, he certainly pulls out some of the best tracks, tracks which were delivered smokin' and red hot. This vinyl release is a very limited production [5000 numbered copies] and contains a digital download card, just so you never have to play it. The track "Sweet William" had previously only been a B-Side from the single "Room At The Top." Me [?], I'll download those songs and then rock back with my best air guitar as warm analog notes filter through my speakers.

title: The new BEST choice for the Conan soundtrack
text:
Until recently, fans seeking the amazing Conan the Barbarian movie soundtrack had only to chose between the widely available (Milan) edition and the Varese edition that is 18 minutes longer, but out-of-print. Now this newly recorded 2-disc COMPLETE score provides a third option that you should strongly consider. Here are three reasons why this new version is a must-have:

1. It is the complete score, 100 minutes of music, so there is significantly more material than the previous recordings (33 minutes more than Varese, and 51 minutes more than the Milan edition). It also features a few alternate versions of tracks and one track from Conan the Destroyer.

2. It is performed by a larger orchestra (96-piece orchestra and a 100-voice chorus) with more instruments, as Basil Poledouris originally intended.

3. While the Milan and Varese editions sound somewhat dated due to the early 1980s recording quality, this brand new digital recording sounds AMAZING!

To be clear, this new recording is not going to sound exactly like what you heard in the movie. I think this version sounds BETTER! If you really want the exact movie sound, get either the Milan or Varese editions, but get this new version too, or you're going to miss out on great sound and more music.

Currently, the new recording is only available on Amazon through third-party Screen Archives Entertainment. For some reason, that option isn't offered on this page, but Amazon has another page for the same 2-cd set with a different cover picture of Conan. That's the same album I'm describing here, and that picture is actually from the back cover of the cd. By the way, don't be deterred by the low-quality of that painting; the music is absolutely first-rate.

title: John Denver's LIVE Recordings are the BEST!!!!!
text:
This collection is a wonderful, five-star addition to John Denver's legacy. If you are a Denver fan at all, BUY IT!

The casual fan might look at it and say, "I've got live (or studio) versions of most of these songs on other CDs." But as a couple of the other reviewers noted, this collection offers many of the songs in different arrangements and settings than live recordings that have been released previously.

To hear the "Foxfire Suite" performed with a symphony orchestra _ WOW!
For this collection, Denver fans owe a big THANK-YOU to STUART RUBIN, who chose the songs, and KRIS O'CONNOR, who produced it. This fan also would like to thank HAL THAU, MILTON OKUN, JOAN CANDEE and anybody else that had a hand in making this package possible! Not to mention Denver himself _ John, I hope you're reading this somewhere out there! _ and the many extremely talented musicians he worked with on all of these recordings.

There is no doubt in my mind that Denver was at his best when he performed live because he brought such joy and enthusiasm to the stage. And he always had those terrific supporting musicians and singers. The audience responded to that. And even when it was just him and his guitar, the enjoyment he got from singing to people was very evident.

There are three very minor quibbles with this collection. The third one, which I will elaborate on in a moment, also was mentioned by a couple of the other reviewers.

The first quibble is the fact that although the first disc is a full 74-plus minutes, the second and third discs are each around 60 minutes. It's a shame the latter two discs weren't filled to the brim as well. There must be plenty of additional live material that could have been used for that purpose.

That's because Denver apparently was recorded live quite often, both when he was with RCA and later on his own Windstar label. There must be additional songs from the seven concerts represented in this collection that could have been included. Or additional unreleased songs from "Live at the Sydney Opera House (1977)," the "Wildlife Concert (1995)," "Sing Australia (1994)" and "Live in London (1976)" shows, which have been previously released, to name a few. The fact that there are other concert and live TV appearances posted on YouTube just shows that the surface probably has only been scratched regarding what is stored in the vaults.

BUT ALL OF THIS MEANS THAT A VOLUME II OF "IN CONCERT" IS POSSIBLE! Hint, Hint!

The second quibble I have is related to the first. For some reason, two versions of the song "Is It Love?" were included in the set. It would have been preferable to me if another live song from the vaults had been included instead.

The third minor quibble I have with this set is the liner notes, which leave it to the listener to figure out which concerts 41 of the 45 songs are taken from. But as another reviewer stated, that is not too hard in most cases.

Considering the timeframes of when the songs were originally released on studio albums, the instruments and/or orchestra that can be heard, and Denver's occasional between-songs comments, here is my list of where I believe the songs were recorded (for reference I have included the track list below).

With the exception of one song, Disc I is taken entirely from the show at Wolftrap in Virginia, where Denver performed with the Washington National Symphony in June 1995. The lone exception is Track 7, "Old English Folk Song," which, as noted in the liner notes, comes from the show in Harrogate, England, five years earlier. Track 13 on Disc II, "Calypso," also comes from the Wolftrap show.

Tracks 1-3, 5-9 and 11-12 on Disc II come from the Ames, Iowa, show in December 1987. On those songs, Denver is solo with his guitar, except on Track 12, "Flying for Me." When he did that song in concert in the mid-1980s as his tribute to the Challenger astronauts, I recall he played his guitar and sang live while accompanied by the studio recording of the orchestra he used on the "One World" album. According to the liner notes, he also used a piano string quartet at the Ames show, and that might be what the listener hears on this recording. I'm not sure.

Tracks 4 and 10 on Disc II, along with Tracks 1-10 and 13 on Disc III, are from the show at the Saratoga Springs (N.Y.) Performing Arts Center in June of 1980. In that show, Denver had ace backup from James Burton, Hal Blaine, Glen D. Hardin, Jim Horn, Herb Pedersen, Danny Wheetman, Rene Armand-Horn and Chuck Fiori.

Track 14 on Disc II and Tracks 14-15 on Disc III are from the Star Lake (Pa.) show in June of 1995. The liner notes for that show say Denver was backed by Chris Nole, Alan Deremo, Michito Sanchez and Pete Huttlinger. That is most of the backing group he used for the "Wildlife Concert" the same year.

The four songs from the venues in Britain are covered in the liner notes. I feel reasonably confident about the rest of this listing, although others may disagree.

title: Sadly, a letdown.
text:
I wanted SO BADLY for this CD to be wonderful. I have been a fan of of the VoiceMasters releases since day one, and have enjoyed them all with very few exceptions. I truly love all of the early releases because while they were new overdubs, they stayed true to the style of Jim Reeves, with beautiful orchestration, while still making his magnificent voice the focal point.
Unfortunately, this cd does not do that. The musicians are certainly extremely talented, and top notch. I feel the intention is true and hopefully honorable…but almost every song feels like the musicians are ahead of Reeves, as if they are trying to speed up a stilled voice. There are flaws in the vocal edits, which make Reeves sound choppy in places…”Almost”, “We Could”, and “You Belong to Me” for example. The music is wonderful, but just doesn’t fit the singing style.
The duets are cool, but the “harmonies” on “That’s My Desire” make Patsy Cline sound strange…almost draggy.
The bright spot on this release is the acapella version of “Losing Your Love”. It’s beautiful, and really does showcase the voice of this fantastic vocalist.

title: Decent cover album, some misses, but some great stuff too
text:
Wow, this CD's been out for 7 years and not a single review on Amazon?! OK, I'll bite...Kerrang is a heavy metal magazine that, in 2006, thought they'd pay tribute to Metallica's Master of Puppets album by getting a bunch of musicians together and having each and every song from the album re-recorded by different musicians. The result is worth getting, in my opinion. Here's a breakdown:

1. Battery by Machine Head- Decent cover. They put it in drop D, which sounds cool for the opening acoustic and opening distorted riff, but once it kicks into the faster tempo the lower tuning makes the guitar strings sound a little floppy and flabby. Still, good vocal performance and tight drumming.

2. Master of Puppets by Trivium- BETTER THAN THE ORIGINAL. Yes, I said it. Yes, I've seen Metallica perform this live, twice, and I grew up listening to Metallica's Master of Puppets. I've heard the song countless times. Trivium outperforms the original in every sense. Whereas Machine Head's downtuning didn't service Battery, Trivium's same drop-D approach really fits Master of Puppets. The guitar work is tight and focused, the drumming is fantastic, and the vocals surpass Hetfield's, and I know that's saying quite a bit. The clean channel interlude in the middle has more artistry to it and has more emotional impact. This recording is the best interpretation of Master of Puppets I've ever heard, almost like they understood the song better than Metallica. Sorry if you don't like reading that, Metallica fanboys, but that's my take.

3. The Thing That Should Not Be by Mendeed- Ugh. At least it's in the original key, a first for this cover album so far, but the scratchy vocals and added blast beats ruin it. These guys didn't understand the song works best as a simple groove metal riff; adding power metal blast beats kills the vibe. Skip this one, and if you want to hear a cover of The Thing That Should Not Be done well, check out the album "A Tribute to Metallica" that has Jason Bonham on drums NAILING this song, with a great vocalist to boot. Shame that cover didn't end up on this Kerrang album.

4. Welcome Home (Sanitarium) by Bullet For My Valentine- Overall this is decent, albeit there's a few things that bother me about it. They don't quite play the first 22 seconds of the clean intro like the original; instead they add in that weird harmonic Kirk Hammet's been playing live that doesn't sound as good as the original recording, but Bullet For My Valentine does play the intro distorted solo better than Kirk's recorded performance. Bullet's lead singer has a little bit too much whiny emo tone for my taste, but at least he's singing pitches and is in tune. There's a part in the middle where they switch up the groove from the original and it's a good interpretation of their own thing. I listen to this over the original from time to time.

5. Disposable Hereos by Chimaira- ah, the first "filler" song of the album. This was never a great song, and Chimaira nails the guitar, bass, and drums. Unfortunately the singer goes for a scratchy, growly approach instead of Hetfield's much better vocals. Not terrible though.

6. Leper Messiah by Fightstar- and now the second filler song. The riff is too plodding to be interesting, but that's not Fightstar's fault; they do a great job with the "short straw" song they were tasked with covering.

7. Orion by Mastodon- ANOTHER DROP D TUNED SONG? What's wrong with the standard tuning that created so many great songs in the 80s? Anyways, Mastodon does a fine job recreating Cliff Burton's fuzzy bass in the intro and the rest of the song too, and the riffing and drumming is solid. There's a few musical elements here and there that they change that makes it "Mastodon" without ruining the feel of the song, so nice job. The slower middle part with the bending harmonized guitar parts get a tad out of tune at times but the song never crashes.

8. Damage, Inc. by Funeral for a Friend- the swelling guitar intro lacks the reverb and delay effects the original had that gave it atmosphere, and the fast riff that crashes in is way too high-gain to even tell what the bottom note of the riff is. And the vocals ruin it.

All in all, I ripped this CD onto my hard drive and I kept tracks 1-2, and 4-7; I erased tracks 3 and 8 and don't regret it. But hey, 6 out of 8 ain't bad.

title: not the hit recordings that you probably want
text:
The Beach Boys tracks here are ones that the group recorded BEFORE they signed with Capitol Records in 1962. NONE of them were hits; in fact, half of them weren't originally released at all. The ones that were released are "Surfin'," "Luau," "Barbie," and "What Is A Young Girl Made Of." The former two tracks were released as the group's first single; the latter two were released under the name of "Kenny And The Cadets." "Surfin'" was included on the group's first album, but was sped up for some reason. The group later re-recorded "Surfin' Safari" and "Surfer Girl," and those remakes were the versions that were hits for the group.
Most of the Jan & Dean tracks are NOT the hit recordings; they are re-recordings that were made in the late '70s without Jan. They can't compare to the hit versions. In fact, although J&D had recorded "Little Deuce Coupe" in the '60s, it wasn't a hit even then. "Heart And Soul" is the only hit J&D recording here --- not only that, but it's also the only hit recording on this whole CD.
Not really a terrible CD, I guess, but don't get it looking to find the hits.

title: Excellent non-traditional cross-cultural album featuring bansuri flute and tabla drums with piano
text:
This is a very nice cross-cultural music album from a trio: the pianist and bansuri flautist are Belgian, and the well-known tabla player is from India.

They bill the music as "modern music based on north indian tradition, introducing piano's harmony." That's an apt description. Each of the 9 songs is set in a particular tala (rhythm cycle), and the name and count of the tala for each song is written on the back. So, the rhythmic framework for each song is set firmly in the age-old tala tradition of India - 6 beats, 8 beats 10 beats, 12 beats, or 16 beats in a repeating musical cycle (tala).

The melodies, on the other hand, are intentionally not set within the 'raga' system. And there's no drone instrument. Instead, the melodies - and western harmonies - unfold through the jazzy interplay of bansuri (bamboo) flute and piano. 'Jugalbandi' means "entwined twins." On this album, this doesn't work exactly the way that 'jugalbandi' music traditionally is played in India, where you have 2 different melody instruments interacting with each other on equal footing, neither being a 'support' instrument. On this recording, since the piano is playing chords and there is no drone, it is by nature supporting some musical lines of the bansuri flute. So I think that the trio's name only sorta-kinda fits the actual music in the technical sense. Note that the trio's other album is all based in the raga system of classical Indian music, so if that's what you're looking for, get that album. If you want more of a jazz feel, get this one.

But, you're asking by now, what does it actually sound like? Ahh ... it's terrific! Some of it has an ECM vibe, some is like a slow ballad, some has fast pairing of the flute and piano lines, a little of it passes the melody between the flute and the tabla. It goes between improvisation and composed musical portions (as does more traditional musics of India in the raga system). I find it very pleasant as lower-volume background music, and very rewarding as louder-volume foreground music. It's not too new-agey, it's not musical fluff, it's certainly not 'smooth jazz,' and I like that it's grounded in rhythmic cycles of India, played by a master musician.

By the way, I found the bio of the tabla player (Suman Sarkar) online, and his resume is quite impressive. He's been playing professionally in India since the 1980s, and working in Europe since the 1990s. He is is one of the visiting Tabla teachers at the Sangit School of Indian Music in Brussels, where presumably he met the two Belgians who lead this trio.

I love jazz piano, I love classical Indian musics, I love contemporary global fusion musics, and I love the bansuri flute. Put all these elements together and you get this satisfying album. I have dozens of recordings of the bansuri played in many contexts, and I go searching for it being used in non-traditional as well as traditional contexts. This is one of the better non-traditional cross-cultural albums that features the bansuri, and it is a rich listening experience which I enjoy greatly.

title: Academic and expressive
text: Alfred Brendel is probably the most knowledgeable Beethoven interpreter that we have seen in the past half century along with Richard Goode. It also helps that he is a phenomenal pianist and chamber musician. When listening to these performances I got a sense of a warmer more intimate ideal for the works, not everywhere, it was as soloistic as these need to be, but the connection between melody and accompaniment was very well balanced right on par with Fleisher and Szell. Levine gives the music everything it needs and the Chicago Symphony plays wonderfully. The live recording gives these works a wonderful atmosphere and the audience is reverently silent. If you want to seek out individual performances of these concertos by all means do it but for a box set of them all I would recommend this as well as his more recent with Rattle, as well as Fleisher and Arrau. All of them are wonderful however this is by far the best live recording of these works. Highly recommended

title: Oh, Yeh!
text:
Jennifer Brown of Sweden, Franziska Kleinert of Germany, Pauline Ester of France, Dido of England, Anna Vissi of Greece, Aimee Mann of the U.S., Chantal Kreviazuk of Canada and not least, Abby Dobson of Leonardo's Bride of Australia! She may be counted among the best female vocalists in the world. Abby's impassioned, nuanced and singular voice, inspired and inspiring, invokes the mystique of Edith Piaf, the warmth and vocal range of Sandy Denny, as well as the pure joy of Clara Nunes' singing.
Picture John Lennon's, George Harrison's, Richard Thompson's and Aimee Mann's songwriting skills rolled up in one, and you've a slight sense of what you're missing in not having heard Dean Manning's songs performed. How I envy you the experience of hearing Leonardos Bride's "Open Sesame" or "Angel Blood" for the first time. Dean, Abby, Pat and Howlen performing as a group, is proof that the sum of four individual extraordinary talents, is greater than the parts.
Dean is one of the best writers of love songs and ballads in the world today. From the introspective "Everybody Wants to Take You Home," to "Alaska," a gem of a love song, on to the pure desire found and expressed in the lines of "Let Me Come Over," it just doesn't stop. You've got to hear the acoustic version of "That Boy," on the "Open Seasame" single! Sweet and unpretentious, just perfect. "Even When I'm Sleeping" from "Angel Blood" is pure magic, the best love song of the 1990s, period.
My favorite song on Open Sesame is "Oh, Yeh." And don't forget folks, that's an Australian Yeh! You'll get the point once you've heard the song. Incisive. Oh, Yeh.

title: invaluable Honegger rarities
text:
Honegger was mainly an orchestral composer - he does have a catalog of piano pieces, which nicely fills one CD, of songs and chamber works, from solo violin sonata to three string quartets, but they are not the most essential and significant part of his oeuvre, and, by his great biographer Harry Halbreich's admission, past 1923 (which is early in Honegger's compositional career), "chamber music occupies only a marginal place in his output, and his last years are entirely devoid of it".

His orchestral output seems a well-know quantity: five symphonies, a number of symphonic poems (among which Pacific 231, Rugby, Mouvement symphonique No. 3 and Pastorale d'été are the most famous, but there are a number of others and highly valuable ones), the great oratorios (from King David to A Christmas Cantata), operas and operettas. Honegger was also a prolific film composer, and the CD era has seen the publication, mainly through the ministry of Swiss conductor Adriano and Naxos, of many symphonic suites derived from them.

But reading Halbreich's biography and its year-by-year accounts ([[ASIN:1574670417 Arthur Honegger]]), the abundance of Honegger's compositional activities is breathtaking, and they yielded many works that are today entirely forgotten, many of which never even published, and some even lost. It seems close to unthinkable that a composer should be so casual about what comes out of his pen that he wouldn't carefully keep a copy in his archive, even with no immediate prospect of being published, but then, we also tend to forget that copying wasn't so easy before invention of the Xerox machine. It is mainly in the realm of ballet that Honegger's works are forgotten. Halbreich lists 19 of them. They disappeared not so much because the music would have been inferior Honegger, but because, for various and extra-musical reasons, they didn't meet any success when they were premiered. Of those 19, Halbreich mentions that the scores of three are lost, and three more retained only in fragmentary form. The only ones to have some currency on disc are "Le Dit des Jeux du Monde", one of Honegger's earliest compositions (1918) and the one that established him as a major young composer on the French scene, and "Horace victorieux" from 1921 (because, from the start, it had a career as a concert piece). "Skating Rink", Honegger's fourth ballet, from 1922, has also been recorded ([[ASIN:B000004A3T Skating Rink Choreographic Symphony L'idee]]).

This CD, together with its companions on Timpani, with more of these forgotten ballets ([[ASIN:B000001YNH Honegger: Amphion / L'Imperatrice aux Rochers]] and [[ASIN:B00003NHC0 Le Dit Des Jeux Du Monde / Cto Da Camera]]), was masterminded by Halbreich, and eternal gratitude to him. It gathers premiere recordings of pieces that were salvaged from oblivion thanks to Halbreich's cataloging work made for the publisher Salabert. The main dish is the Ballet-Pantomime Semiramis, fifth commission from Honegger by patroness, dancer and actress Ida Rubinstein, Amphion being the fourth written like Semiramis on a book by French writer Paul Valéry, and Paul Claudel's Joan at the Stake the sixth and last. The first three were the incidental music to L'Impératrice aux rochers and to D'Annunzio's Phaedre (recorded by Rozhdestvenksy, [[ASIN:B0002I692I A.Honegger - Symphony No.2, Phedre: Suite for the Tragedy by d'Annunzio, Three extracts from film 'Napoleon']]), and Les Noces d'Amour et de Psyche, a ballet made of an orchestration of various English and French Suites of Bach. Semiramis flopped on its premiere at the Paris Opera on 11 May 1934, one of the reasons being that Valéry had inserted, near the end, a long, 15-minute monologue with no music, in which (based on the testimony of Hermann Scherchen, recounted by Halbreich in his biography), Rubinstein "meowed interminably , always on the same lachrymose and monotonous tone". The score was never published and Honegger's widow even banned any performance during her lifetime, who knows why. The first modern revival took place in November 1992, immediately after this recording (which seamlessly cuts out the monologue, although its text is provided in the booklet). Running nearly 39 minutes, it is great Honegger. The instrumentation is very original, heavily based on woodwinds, brass and percussion (which can bring to mind some pieces of Stravinsky, like his Symphony for Winds) and with apparently the first use ever of the Ondes Martenot (and two of them) in an orchestral piece. There is also a chorus and soprano, but they sing only occasionally. The musical result is stark, often aggressively pounding and "tonally dissonant" as Honegger often was (at least for ears untrained to Bartok, Varèse or Schoenberg), often very lyrical in Honegger's unmistakable type of lyricism, always ear-catching and intriguing. The great and imposing quasi-funeral march on track 9 is entirely the sonic universe of Symphonie Liturgique or the Fifth Symphony.

The rest are fascinating scraps, like the short Largo for strings that Honegger initially composed when responding to the commission of wealthy patron and conductor Paul Sacher that ultimately yielded the Second Symphony, but then discarded, or excerpts from the incidental music to Shakespeare's Tempest, of which only the extraordinary powerful and violent Overture from 1923 had been hitherto known and recorded (and the rest, which was composed off and on until 1929, for a production delayed many times, isn't as powerful and striking, but it is always agreeable and has a few catching orchestral moments). Some of the early pieces, like the interlude for the uncompleted chamber opera "The Death of Saint Anthelme" that Honegger briefly worked on in 1918 before the project was abandoned for lack of funding, are surprisingly romantic (Halbreich hears Debussy in them, but if so it is the early Debussy of Damoiselle Elue), and the ensuing Vivace, which Halbreich tentatively ascribes also to 1918, sounds almost like Tchaikovsky, but peppered with the light-hearted and cheerful spirit of Les Six. It is entirely the spirit of Les Six that is at play in Fantasio (tracks 14-16), a "Skit in Three Pictures" (rather than "Sketch in three scenes" as the translation has it) composed in 1922 for a famous mime, and apparently never performed. It could have been written by Sauguet (not a member of Les Six) or Auric. Interesting to note: of course Honegger was a member of Les Six, but that was more by dint of journalist Henri Collet's famous article in Comoedia and Cocteau's ensuing publicity stunts, Honegger never followed the Cocteau-ish party-line, never professing a great admiration for Satie but always an admirer of Debussy and Wagner, and his music was always more beefy and dramatic than the typical Les Six fluff. Only in the 1924 Piano Concertino and 1930 Cello Concerto did he really show off his lighter side, which culminated in his operettas. But the scraps gathered by Timpani reveal that it was there before. The two short orchestral pieces on tracks 22 and 23 are excerpted from a radio play that Honegger composed near the end of his life, in 1951, and are among the last he composed. Despite the crippling heart-attack that had struck him in 1947 and that would ultimately claim his life in 1955, it shows a composer of undiminished powers, but also one whose "serious" music and film music cannot be dissociated. Although his compositional processes could be very elaborate, Honegger always aimed for the big effect and the basic emotions. Much of his "serious" music sounds like (superior) film music, which is probably what accounts for Honegger's lack of popularity today: too dissonant for the lay listener, too popular and smacking of film for the high-brow amateur or critic.

Not a disc for the casual and occasional Honegger listener - he should go first to the symphonies and symphonic poems - but, with its two Timpani companions, an indispensable one for the Honeggerite. Liner notes by Halbreich, TT 78 minutes, you can't ask for more.

Check the disc's other entries for price, [[ASIN:B0000285FB Semiramis]] and [[ASIN:B0009N5L5W Honegger: Semiramis - Unpublished Orchestral Pieces]].

title: Outstanding version of a great baroque masterpiece
text:
The listings are not short of fine recordings of Heinrich Schütz's beautiful Mass for the Dead. The present disc has been around since 1998, and it is still one of the truly outstanding versions. Françoise Lasserre directs her regular Akademia ensemble of fourteen lovely, pure voices (with female sopranos and male altos) and a medium-sized instrumental band including the excellent La Fenice wind ensemble and familiar names such as Jean Tubéry (cornetto), Christina Pluhar (harp and theorbo) and Laurent Stewart (organ).

The Requiem itself is preceded by a very well judged selection representing the composer's major collections such as Geistliche Chormusik, Symphoniae Sacrae and Kleine geistliche Konzerte, interspersed with a handful of instrumental pieces by Scheidt and Gabrieli. These are all given beautiful performances and the arrangement works better, in my view, than placing the Musicalishe Exequien first and then following it with other pieces as fillers.

The performance of the main work differs from some other fine recordings, the best of which tend toward the small-scale and intimate; these include outstanding versions directed by Meunier, Cordes and Haller. The present performance applies larger forces (but certainly not too large) and richer textures, bringing ample colour and drama to the work. Passages such as 'Er sprach zu seinem lieben Sohn' are delivered superbly, with the contrast between soli and cappella powerfully expressed. In the final section, 'Herr nun lässest du deinen Diener', the chorus line is again clearly delineated in texture and perfectly captured by the recorded sound; the effect - both musical and emotional - is beautiful.

Lasserre's recording conveys a powerful unity and a grand overall vision of Schütz's great work, representing a superb counterpart to the more intimate performances available – which, in case it's not already clear, I also greatly admire. Recorded sound and ambience are outstanding, booklet notes are excellent, and texts and translations are included.

title: You need this set
text: If you liked Sony’s Bernstein sets, getting this set is a no-brainer. It provides the answers to the question “What would Bernstein have done with (fill in the blank) had he ever recorded it?”  Previn fills those gaps in a way that is completely satisfying, making his set a perfect compliment to LB’s. But it is, of course, much more than that.  I have often thought that Previn’s greatest gift was bringing previously overlooked works into the classical mainstream. Nobody was paying much attention to the Rachmaninov symphonies or Walton’s first symphony until his recordings came out. After that everyone was recording them, but Previn’s originals set benchmarks that still stand to this day.  His Vaughan Williams recordings are also treasurable and have stood the test of time as well. Add to them the various chamber and solo piano recordings and you have a voyage of exploration that is well worth the effort. Finally, I find the recording quality to be excellent. I assume that the recordings have been remastered from earlier attempts; I had a previous incarnation of VW’s 3rd and was disappointed when the sound quality was nothing like the vinyl recording I had grown up with. Now the lush richness is back and I am eternally grateful. Enjoy!

title: Heavy and hard lyrics, but the music could be better
text:
Let me start saying that I am a big Marillion fan - from both Fish and Hogarth's periods. But even being so, I can't help to recognize when they produce a weak album. And, unfortunately, this has happened already, more than once.

Well, let me get straight to the point: FEAR seems to me like one of those albums were the lyrics are way more important than the music. Not that the music is bad, but it sounds to me... irrelevant, uninspired. The whole album seems like a huge leftist-anticapitalist-against system-against modern world protest, and the prevailing tone is a VERY depressing and dark one. But - and THAT's the important thing here - the music isn't, by any means, memorable or interesting - except maybe one or two tracks.

Musically speaking, I liked "White Paper" - it has a beautiful tune and harmony - and, to some extent, "The New Kings". The rest is, well... really boring. I know that Marillion's music is not easy at all - well, being a fan of them, I'm more than used to the fact that their albums start to get good after, at least, three listenings. But, in the case of FEAR, I listened to it more than ten times and really tried to like it - honest. But about the music... I found it uninteresting. "Sounds that can't be made" was a way better album, in my opinion.

I know that the prevailing opinion here and in the media is that this (FEAR) was a "great" album, "one of their best", but unfortunately, I have to disagree. I think people are judging this album much more based in its lyrics and political/social message than by its music. And, well... even politically speaking, I do not agree with Hogarth's apocalyptical view of today's world. Not that I'm a "naive" person that thinks that we are living in a "wonderful world" (far from that), but I tend to see our reality in a much more complex way - with all its subtleties. I know, it is easier to simply adhere to a "against everything" position, but for me, that'd be much more like an adolescent's view of things - not a mature view of reality.

And, just to finish this review, I'd like to say that the prevailing mood in this album is so depressing that, whenever the CD finishes, I always have the impression that the singer will kill himself after the last song. I know that today's world isn't an easy thing to cope to, but... here comes a word of advice (in case anybody wants it, hahah): you'll not turn this world into a better place by turning yourself into a HUGE depressing mental state. Did you hear that, Hogarth? Heheheh!!

title: Techno/industrial and soft jazz
text:
Released in 2003, this is something like Jan Akkerman's 19th solo album, depending upon how you are counting. It is over 60 minutes long and the sound quality is very good, but punchy and booming to match the musical style.

It actually starts out good with the first track and has one other good track on it. It is kind of a blend of electronica, jazz and progressive rock with lots of Akkerman's guitar playing.

I don't like the rest....it is either boring, tedious repetitious or head ache inducing or sometimes all four at once.

Most of the tracks are techno or industrial. I am not a fan of most techno. There is some I really like but most I don't. Most of it is tape loops and just a bunch of pounding repetitive notes. It is why an album like this is so long....the same chords get repeated over and over again. It is sometimes OK in a disco but not for home listening or anywhere else. If you like techno, you might enjoy this.

There are a few tracks of Akkerman style soft jazz on this album....which in a way is a precursor to this foray into techno. Much of his soft jazz can be repetitive and tedious. He has some great numbers, but others not so great.

title: HAS MOMENTS BUT DISAPPOINTING

I've followed Moby Grape (of which Peter Lewis was an important

Peter Lewis' songs were the most thought -provoking in the Grape's
songbook, and his fingerpicking guitar style was a good complement to Jerry's blues licks and Skip's slash and burn chords. But this album is a casualty of over-done and mis-guided
production; the goofy synth effects and sugary male backround vocals really sink this disc. the songs are pleasant enough. And

not 80's style glistening Eagles-style pop sheeny new-agey dross.
It's a case where even though i really wanted to like this album,
especially at the import price, i truly felt disappointed in the end. this one is only for the diehard Moby Grape fans, who have to own everything connected to the band.

title: Heads up: this is a French release from the early 90s
text:
When I stumbled onto this listing, and saw the price for this hip-hop classic, from a group who’s albums can sell for $100+ due to sampling disputes, I figured it had to be a some kinda catch. Bootleg? Clean version? I know the decades-long fight for a re-issue was finally settled, and one was due soon, but this listing was too old for that, so what was it?

I received the tape very quickly, and STILL SEALED, which kinda stopped me in my tracks. I hated to open it, but also had to listen to it and see what I had gotten, if not cheated.

Turns out, it’s an original press from France, and it doesn’t disappoint. All of the original samples are in place unlike the re-issues, but the tracks are very slightly altered. There are different versions of a few songs, which are just the Euro release versions, and arguably better than the US version.

Personally, I love hearing this album in a very slightly different way. It’s not altered enough to feel like the experienced is ruined, and as someone who didn’t own a physical copy until now, I don’t feel like I need to hunt down a U.S. copy to fill a void left by this version. If you don’t own a copy, I personally would suggest this over the re-issue, as the re-issues, while well done, have some significant changes made where sampling is concerned. If you’re a purist like me, you’ll be more satisfied with this version.

RIP Trugoy

title: Great trip down memory lane!
text:
Came across the cassette version of this album this morning and played it on my stereo. Brought back memories from the summer of 1990. Kenny Maclean was the last member to join Platinum Blonde in the mid-80s at the height of their success. Remember their album "Alien Shores"? That was the smash follow-up to their debut album "Standing In The Dark" and Alien Shores marked the start of Kenny's career with the group.

His solo album "Don't Look Back" marked a clear departure from the high-energy pseudo punk sound of Platinum Blonde. This album leans more towards the Adult Contemporary/Soft Rock side and it actually works. There are a few rockers on the album ("One Night", "State of Mind", "Hot Pink") but the rest of the album is slightly more mellow.

Kenny harmonizes well with fellow Toronto singer Molly Johnson on the vocals. And his ballads (one of my favourites - "I Can't Resist") capture the listener with their honest and emotional lyrics. I don't think this album is available anymore unless you can get your hands on a used copy but it is certainly worth the hunt if you recall the title track being played incessantly on the airwaves. It was definitely one of the biggest summer hits back in '90.

title: American Country with a Russian Flavor
text: Larissa Tormey is a classically-trained Russian emigre living in Ireland and singing American country music with a thick Russian accent.  So you're thinking, "Can this work?"  And of course the answer is "No, it can't."  It's tempting to give two stars to Ms. Tormey for the old college try.  She has a warm, pleasant alto and is clearly courageous--there's nothing she's not willing to tackle.  The first song on the album is an adapted version of John Denver's "Thank God, I'm a Country Boy," which Ms. Tormey changes to "Thank God, I'm a Country Girl."  As this song unfurls, the listener starts to marvel.  Is this for real?  Then comes the sobering realization that it is.  Way down on the end of the song list, Ms. Tormey launches into "Danny Boy," which is strangely out of place on a country record.  After the first verse in English, Ms. Tormey sings the next several verses in emphatic Russian.  It's a bit of a jar for the listener.  This album sounds like Eva Gabor from "Green Acres" somehow escaped the farm and cut a country record.  It's definitely for the fans of the unusual.

title: Besta Polka Youbetcha
text:
Released as an in-store special for Sam Goody and Musicland stores (I got my copy at the Staten Island Mall for a whopping 99 cents back in the day), this party-starter of a polka disc is as much a tribute to the king of Cleveland Style, Frankie Yankovic. He'd just released an album of duets with fellow accordionists and folks influenced by his style and four of this disc's eight tracks come from that release.

There's not a bum track in the lot! "Weird Al" Yankovic and band polkacize Queen with "Bohemian Polka", Jimmy Sturr takes on Smokie's "Living Next Door to Alice" (cleaning up British fans' chants accompanying the original), and Frank meets with Eddie Blazonczyk ("In Heaven There Is No Beer"), Weird Al ("Whole Stole the Keeshka"), and norteno legend Little Joe Hernandez ("Just Because Polka").

A bit of indie cred comes from Brave Combo's "Flying Saucer".

Far too short, this comp of "happy snappy" tunes is sure to liven up any gathering, and belongs in any self-respecting polka hall's jukebox.

title: Great book, well performed... but the worst-edited audio book in history
text:
Make no mistake: John Lennon, A Life" is a fantastic book -- well researched, with intricate detail and plenty of new information about Lennon's life, starting with his grandparents. Author Norman pulls no punches about Lennon's foibles, from the way he mistreated (and once threatened the life of) his father to his almost pathological cheating on his first wife and earlier girlfriends.

The problem -- the unforgivable problem -- with this CD set is the way it's been abridged. Although the cover doesn't warn listeners of this, whole sections have been excised from this version of the book. After all, the book is 864 pages -- there's no way to fit that in 10 CDs. But instead of skipping some of the minute details of Lennon's grandparents, for instance, or sections where the author explains the British class system or how the music business of the 1960s worked, the editors have seen fit to edit out whole sections of the book. Glaringly.

The first part isn't too bad -- we skip the Beatles' first rise at The Cavern, and find ourselves on the way to Hamburg where the five-person band (then with Pete Best and Stuart Sutcliff) will learn their chops. We never learn how the Beatles' name was created, but that's not the worst thing. The next cuts are ruinous.

The first one takes us from the Beatles recording their very first album for Geffen in 1962 straight to 1965, when the Beatles are already a world phenomenon. Ignored is their first trip to the U.S., their Ed Sullivan appearance, their introduction to pot by Bob Dylan, the rise of the whole Beatlemania thing. Now they've got a half-dozen albums under their belt and are about to release Rubber Soul.

By the time we recover from this huge jump in time, we get another insufferable loss. After we see Lennon first being introduced to Yoko Ono, the editors again skip the section showing how Lennon fell in love with her and left his wife for her. They don't discuss the impact this had on the group, or the Beatles' break-up at all. Next time we join them Yono is six months pregnant and the Beatles are no more.

Just to stress: the book included all this info. The audio CD edited it all away. There are other cuts during the next 10 years of Lennon's life, but at that point it hardly matters. This CD is a crime. I assume the performer who read this book out loud read the whole thing somewhere -- they should release it in a much larger collection, or at least a better-edited one. Anybody truly interested in the whole story of John Lennon will find this CD too infuriating to enjoy.

title: Yes - A Must Buy for Any Deftones Fan
text:
Deftones have left an indelible mark on alternative rock, moving silently through shifts and changes in the heavy rock industry for the past 20 years, yet have remained a unique, evocative, heavy and beautiful band to listen to. Following Deftones from their debut when I heard "7 words" on MTV, Adrenaline quickly became a novelty for me. I was captivated by the excellent Around the Fur. White Pony dropped and The Deftones suddenly tasted more widespread success. The following self-titled and then Saturday Night Wrist, to me, were slightly weaker records. I had almost lost interest in the band until Diamond Eyes blew me away. An incredibly tightly written and dynamically well-executed album, it will be one of my favourites for years to come.

So, what can I say about this compilation? I was pleasantly surprised by a 2-disc CD set containing ALL of the best Deftones songs from all the albums. I was so surprised that I wanted to buy a second copy of this just for collectors-sake. It does not appear on shelves anywhere and I have never encountered a Deftones 'Best-Of' before, but whoever created this tracklist was obviously concerned about the wellbeing of Deftones fans. This is not a cash-in, and you will truly taste everything Deftones have to offer, with an excellent mixture of everything, including difficult to find tracks: If Only Tonight We Could, Back to School, No Ordinary Love, Savory, Crenshaw & Wax & Wane, which don't appear on the standard versions of other albums. The addition of these makes buying the compilation worth it, for fans who already have the original discs. For those of you new to Deftones, well, you only need to buy this Greatest Hits compilation as an introduction and representation of the band as a whole.

I have to say that there I have 2 regrets. One, is the inclusion of 'If Only Tonight...', which is the only live-track on the album. It offers nothing but an interlude which disrupts the flow of the 2 discs, it doesn't sound spectacular. I feel that this track really should have been replaced with the excellent demo 'Like Linus'. I can only guess that it wasn't because Like Linus may not have had the best recording quality and might have also sounded out of place.

My second regret is the exclusion of the iTunes only Diamond Eyes bonus track 'Do You Believe', which could have replaced the much weaker song 'Wax & Wane'. 'Do You Believe' is such a good Deftones song that it surprised me it's not available in CD format, whereas 'Wax & Wane' doesn't actually sound very much like Deftones. Regardless, to critisise this collection of songs, of which there are 38 in total, would be silly.

This is the perfect compilation of everything great about the Deftones, for new and old fans alike. Just buy it and ride the wave.

title: Vivaldi for Queen Marie-Antoinette, hello, goodbye
text:
I was happy when I found this CD at an affordable price, Vivaldi’s “complete works with lute” played by Michel Amoric and an instrumental ensemble led by violinist Jean Estournet, a release from the French label Ades dating from the early years of the CD (released in 1986 – the recording itself is from 1981) and, for that reason, hard to find, because not even listed on most Amazons, and hardly anywhere else.

It was well-received back then by the Vivaldi critics that I read and, in 1981, it was considered by some to be “state-of-the art” in interpretation. Although the back-cover credits mention “string instruments from the 18th century”, I’m not sure they are period strings, but it’s a small ensemble nonetheless with five solo strings and woodwinds. Yet, at one point while listening to the CD, I started wondering : “why is the music so unexciting?”. I mean, it’s Vivaldi, his wonderful works for lute – Concerto RV 558 (with in addition to lutes has mandolins, and much more), RV 540, RV 93, Trios RV 82 and 85 – it should be colorful, playful, touching, exciting, no? But here it sounded so… proper (as in “Victorian proprieties”), elegant, stately, music sounding serious rather than having fun.

So I pulled out of my shelves Il Giardino Armonico’s recording of [[ASIN:B000000SK4 Concerti per Liuto e Mandolino]], which shares the three concertos and two trios offered by the Adès disc and adds two more concertos (the two marvelous RV 425 for Mandolin and 532 for 2 Mandolins) and and the one by The Parley of Instruments, [[ASIN:B000002ZI4 Music for Lute & Mandolin]], with the two trios and Concertos RV 93 and RV 540 (+ the same two Mandolin Concertos). And, oh, wow.

Going from Amoric-Estournet to Il Giardino Armonico in the first movement of RV 558 (which opens both discs) is like from going from your old, puffing sedan to a Formula 1 – or going down the roller-coaster as opposed to going up. Fasten seat-belt, stiffen your neck for the acceleration and be ready for your hair to fly! At first, I had thought that Amoric and friends’ cautious tempi might have something to do with the limitations of the plucked instruments, whether mandolins, lutes or theorbos: after all, there’s just a number of strings you can pluck within a second. But if such technical limitations, they clearly don’t apply to the performers of Il Giardino Armonico! RV 588 a fabulous work, a late concerto of Vivaldi and one of his best (among many great ones), and, as it’s original title rightly puts it, it is not so much a concerto “for” mandolins as a concerto WITH two flutes, two theorbos, two mandolins, two chalumeaux (salmoè), two marine trumpets (actually a string instrument of the violin family) and a cello, all getting their share of the limelight, a “concerto for orchestra” ahead of time. But that greatness you will immediately perceive listening to Il Giardino Armonico, not so with Amoric & friends, if even you perceive it at all. I don’t want to be unfair to them: to their credit, I love the sound of their chalumeaux, sounding less like clarinets than like the sound you imagine would come out of one of those big-sized sea-shells or “conch”. There’s also a nice touch in the andante: it is scored for violins and mandolins playing in unison, and frankly the mandolins, even in Il Giardino’s version, can hardly be heard, just soft punctuations under the violin line. So the Adès players repeat part of the movement with mandolins playing alone: not prescribed by Vivaldi, but very welcome. Still, it’s not enough to offset the rest, and if I had a sense of lack of excitement hearing them the first time around, it is true boredom after Il Giardino.

Difference in choice of tempo isn’t as pronounced in the Concerto for Viola d’amore and lute RV 540 – the march-like outer movements rely more on energy than speed - but even there, as soon as the first movement, Il Giardino Armonico scores, because its basic tempo IS slightly more animated, because its strings phrase with more muscularity and because its two solo instruments sound fuller. And their Finale sounds like a Finale, e.g. more animated than the first movement, where Amoric & friends adopt exactly the same beat, wich is not only wrong but makes the music sound stately and unexciting. Very typical is also the way the respective viola player phrases the chords indicated as “arpeggio” in the score (at 2:30 on Adès): two eighth-notes per beat for Adès’ Jean-Philippe Vasseur, vs dazzling spiccato arpeggios (and remember: at a faster tempo) for Giardino’s Enrico Onofri (at 2:10). Paul O’Dette and The Parley of Instruments are also preferable though not as convincing as Il Giardino, with an apparently more reduced ensemble and a more astringent tone. They too adopt the same beat in first and last movements, but that’s because their first movement tempo is faster. And I like their fastish and unsentimental approach to the Largo. Amoric and friends take it the slowest of all, but it’s okay, the music here can take a variety of approaches.

But if sometimes it’s not so bad, sometimes it’s even worse. Going from Il Giardino, and even The Parley of Instruments, to Amoric in the Chamber Concerto RV 93, my jaws drop with a big boink! I was braced for the worst, but it’s even worse than that, they stroll at such a trudging tempo in the first movement that this wonderfully lively composition is deprived of any life. If I stretch my understanding abitilites to their maximum, I guess there is a certain nonchalant elegance to the approach, one that would make Vivaldi suitable for young maidens of the nobility in galant 18th century France - when under surveillance of their duegna, I mean. No wonder I was bored on first hearing! I have nothing against their flowing tempo in the middle Largo, but there’s so much more imagination in the ornamentation of Il Giardino’s Luca Pianca. To Amoric’s credit, though, the improvised cadenza at the end of that Largo, and the Finale is fine, not as animated as Il Giardino’s and with Amoric’s instrument sounding more metallic and less virtuosic, but not inferior to the Parley’s. Would this have been the rule and not the exception! Same with Larghetto and Finale of the Trio RV 82, or with the complete Trio RV 85 (with there too a very flowing Larghetto, and, for once, a nicely racing Finale): despite Amoric’s somewhat metallic tone, they compare well to The Parley’s; but in tonal luster, technical ease and interpretive imagination, Il Giardino is in another dimension, and nowhere more than in the middle Larghetto of RV 82, where they turn a very pretty Larghetto into one of Vivaldi’s most sublime inventions (see my review for more details on this).

Il Giardino is Vivaldi for the Venetian tavern, a Vivaldi of blood, sweat and tears. Amoric & friends is Vivaldi transplanted in France and played at the Versailles salon of Queen Marie Antoinette, surrounded by her infamous sheep: prim, proper, elegant, Vivaldi for the ladies of the court – and their duegnas! Nothing to lose your head about. Despite the CD’s rarity value and the few nice touches of interpretation, this one is not staying in my collection, hello, goodbye.

title: One of the two BEST WORST country ...AT THE HAMMOND ORGAN instrumental albums ever made
text:
The Fabulous Hank Turner, THE GOLDEN COUNTRY & WESTERN HITS, Columbia CL 1958 (mono)/CS 8758 (stereo)

The Lp dates mid-late March, 1963.

Song list on CL 1958/CS 8758:
side one--
San Antonio Rose/I Fall to Pieces/Sentimental Me/He'll Have to Go/Cold, Cold Heart/I Can't Stop Loving You
side two--
Moon River/I Can't Help It (If I'm Still In Love with You)/Please Help Me I'm Falling/Rose Are Red (My Love)/Tennessee Waltz/I Walk the Line

Playing time for this album is about 31:30.

Small combo group, just incredibly basic lead instrumental work, played like background muzak for a roller skating rink. The style is utterly dreadful, the blandest imaginable, sophomoric, lousy. No swing, no groove, just whitebread, child's simplistic white pop. Note that the album includes some not-country pop songs: "Sentimental Me," "Moon River," and "Roses Are Red" (I'm sure you get the Andy Williams-Bobby Vinton theme on two out of three; out of place on a country record).

Taking a look at the credits, here's the explanation for the overall sound: Arranged, Conducted, and Produced by early '60s middle-of-the-road boring pop guy, Robert Mersey. If this were a country album for Columbia, the credits would run through the great Don Law & Frank Jones (Ray Price, Little Jimmy Dickens, the good stuff). This ain't an album for honky-tonk fans. Frankly, I think it's Columbia's pop A&R's all-out April Fool's 1963 joke album on country fans: there's no other Hank Turner records extant, only this and the 1968 chopped up Harmony repackage (HL 7435 mono/HS 11235 stereo, dates June, 1968, missing "I Can't Stop Loving You" and "I Walk The Line" cut off the 1963 full list Lp.).

It's inexplicable that the marketing guys at Columbia thought enough of this dreadful album to put out the mid-'68 Harmony junker Lp, then some time in the early '70s (?), put it out again on a Columbia Special Products budget reissue as CRSP 8758. If there was a marketing reason for this album, it may have been as closer music when radio stations need a generic instrumental to close/fade out a music program segue into news or other programming (Starday Records made a ton of money with that marketing niche). -???

If you're a fan of really, really HORRIBLE easy listening "...at the Hammond organ" muzak and the deliciously perverted C&W song choices, this is a real treasure. In my searches for music this BAD, I've only found one other country "...at the Hammond organ" album that makes me both spastically cringe and laugh so hard that tears run down my cheeks: JIMMY RHODES GOES COUNTRY. If you can ever find that album (has a classic cheap private press Lp "headstone" front cover art), grab it!

title: Takin' care of your insanity...
text: Having come relatively late to the BOA party, I had never heard the original single live LP of ‘Raunch N’ Roll’ but I know how important it was to their career. Never a huge band by any definition, Black Oak Arkansas definitely filled a niche as slightly avant garde Southern rock band (probably not the correct term but I don’t know how else to describe their music). Like many classic 70’s bands who put out live albums, ‘Raunch N’ Roll’ would be the band’s most consistent seller and I still feel it contains the best songs from their often freaky catalog. ‘The Complete Raunch N’ Roll’ may seem like overkill, as one reviewer intimated but it is probably the best version of this record available. All of the aspects that made BOA memorable and kind of a cult favorite are featured here and most descriptions of this band pretty much begin and end with frontman Jim Dandy and while not a great singer by any means, he is entertaining as hell! He was also perfect for these songs in addition to playing a killer washboard (hard to write this with a straight face!) Highlights include “Hot n’ Nasty”, “Mutants of the Monster”, “Uncle Lijah”, “Hot Rod” and “When Electricity Came to Arkansas”. What made the original LP fairly unique was that while being the band’s fourth release and only containing seven songs, four of which had not been on any of the previous three records, including “Hot Rod”. “Up”, one of the aforementioned tunes to make its LP debut features a monstrous drum solo from future Ozzy Osbourne and Whitesnake drummer Tommy Aldridge, considered one of the best in the business. In the double CD reissue you get double the “Up” along with the mock orgasmic “Movin” and many of the previously commented on classics. You may want to seek out the original single LP on CD unless you want BOA overkill and the sound quality may not be as much of an upgrade (opener “Gettin’ Kinda Cocky” really buries Dandy’s vocals) but if you really want to experience this band in all of their tokin’ (ahem) glory, ‘The Complete Raunch N’ Roll Live’ will give you all the Black Oak Arkansas you’ll ever need. Misfits of mankind indeed...

text: Oh man I hated this.  I read a lot of reviews for other Christmas "compilations" and all were discouraging, and when I came upon this I thought it was great based on all the reviews, and saw that it was not one but THREE CDs, and since I was having a party in four days and in a hurry, I bought it (wished I'd shopped around earlier!  Lesson learned).  The first CD seemed "legit" as it started right off with "Jingle Bell Rock," and led into other great, familiar Christmas standards, but then I put on the second CD and third CDs, and it was embarrassingly bad, I kept hoping it would get better, but no - a lot of really bottom of the barrel songs, literally the first time I had ever heard them, yet done by "real" vocalists - there was "Baby's First Christmas (?)," "Santa Clause got stuck in my Chimney," "I'm Gonna Lasso Santa Claus," "Dig that Crazy Santa Claus," "I'm Gonna be Warm this Winter," "Lonely Pup in a Christmas shop (?!)," and plenty more that baffled my guests and I.  I have the distinct feeling these were added as "filler," because unless I've been living under a rock for 59 years, not ONE of those rang a Christmas Bell in MY memory.  If they trimmed the fat and made it a two CD set, maybe it would be okay, for as I said, many more recognizable, memorable songs are on this set, AND in good tonal quality, I was impressed by that, but that's about it.  Stay away from this set!  Too, they cleverly print the playlists SO SO SO tiny on the back that you practically need a jeweler's eye to read it.  Intentional?  Who knows...

title: Good book but not good for listening to in car
text:
Memo to self: books I listen to in the car should not have
- a complex plot (because if I miss something I'm out of luck)
- a wealth of detail (because it makes the book just too slow-moving)
Unfortunately, this book has both, which drastically limited my appreciation of it. It didn't help, either, that Muller reads with a fast, low, conspiratorial tone, which is appropriate to the book but makes it very hard to hear when driving at the speed limit on I-95.
That being said, LeCarré does a great job of giving one an inside feel of the espionage trade, and he has well-drawn characters. But I think to do the book justice I'd have to read the text rather than having it read to me. Too many times I just didn't understand what was going on or else I let my mind wander as someone's facial expression was described in excruciating detail.

text: Buying this collection (which you can find at Japan's HMV) is the only way that I know of to get the stereo 4th (1957) and 6th (1961) currently, which I think are worth the price of this collection.  Everything else here is available elsewhere in equivalent (or, for the mono 7th, better) sound.  The 5th (1957) sounds the same here as on the Gala (Sony Germany) coupling with the Classical (both of which are better on Gala than in the Essential Classics versions).  The Classical (1961) sounds here like it does on the 2012 "Ormandy Conducts 20th Century Classics" -- closer up than either Gala or Essential Classics.  Kije (1962) and Oranges (1963) are available on that still-available Odyssey disc, coupled with the Classical.  The 7th (1953), only available mono (since EO never re-recorded it), is simply not in as good sound in this collection as in the Ormandy mono box.  It got better remastering in the Ormandy mono box than Sony Japan affords here. Philadelphia and Prokofiev were made for one another, and Ormandy’s touch shows both off to their best advantage.  As Harold Schonberg, music critic for the New York Times, said of a Carnegie Hall concert in February of 1976 featuring the Classical and the 6th:  "Mr. Ormandy through the years has had more than his share of Prokofiev premieres, and there is something in the Russian composer's music—the dash, the virtuosity, the rhythmic ebullience—that inspires the Philadelphia Orchestra to make a special effort."

title: A movie trying to be what it isn't.
text:
I decided to watch this movie because the trailer looked very interesting. The first few minutes into the movie were very well done and were really scary. The sound was crisp, the cinematography was luscious, and the first murder scene was very suspenseful and brutal.
But then, things kind of went downhill from there.
My impression is that the movie was trying to be something that it wasn't -- a Crouching Tiger / Matrix / Angels and Insects / Titanic / Plot-Twisting epic. It just took pieces from different kinds of movies and put them all together.
You know how in some Hong Kong / Bruce Lee martial arts movies, the good guy gets surrounded by all these goons who get their... kicked because they attacked him one at a time? There's about half a dozen of those scenes in the movie.
The effects were also not very good. The fast-slow motion effect was very gratuitous and pointless in certain scenes (and that is really the ONLY "The Matrix" link to the movie). Even the effects for the movement of The Beast was cheap. It was very choppy and it made me think of bad computer animation.
As for the plot, it didn't even twist. It was just a conglomerate of different ideas that hardly had anything to do with one another since there wasn't enough storyline or character development. It tried to be complex but the lack of creativity actually made things predictable.
Lastly, the movie was so damn long - about two and a half excrutiating hours. I really considered leaving earlier (like some of the viewers) because it just keept going on and on.
I suggest you wait for the video or watch a cheaper matinee in the afternoon. This movie was hyped up as if it was really good because in reality, it's quite bad.

title: Add Cathedral Bellringers to Your Christmas Collection
text:
In the 1970s I attended the Cathedral of St. Phillip in Atlanta, home of the Cathedral Bellringers. Christmas eve performances by the Bellringers had by that time become a tradition, so I took the experience for granted. In 2009 I ran across this album at eBay by chance. I bought the album and had it professionally coded to DVD and sent a copy to the Cathedral. I had not realized how much the Bellringers added to my life, until I was able to hear the music again all these years later. Since, the music has richly enhanced the Christmas experience for my entire extended family.

This is a very unusual compilation of Christmas music to be treasured, and the actual performance of the young Bellringers is astonishingly sharp given the pressure that must have been on them for the session. Some of the Bellringers were as young as five or six years old. The tracks were recorded live without audience in the Cathedral's main worship hall, accounting for the excellent acoustics of the recording.

The Bellringers were first assembled in the early 1950s and achieved their greatest notoriety in the late 1950s and 1960s even performing for President Dwight Eisenhower on the White House front lawn during the ceremony of the lightning of the Christmas tree. The group traveled in the U.S. and abroad fairly extensively performing mostly in small and medium sized churches.

The Bellringers program was finally disbanded in the 1980s.

Over the years, I have kept many various recordings of Christmas music, but track for track, this is the best Christmas collection I have ever run across. If you purchase this album in good enough condition to transfer to DVD, pay a professional to have the job done right. The music will bless your life.
