title: Inexpensive but Flawed
text:
A company called "Real Gone Jazz" released four volumes of Les Baxter music (32 complete albums) and the sound quality ranged from terrible to very good. By terrible, I mean that some of the albums had skips and surface noise as you would find on a worn record.

This company, the "Documents" label, seems to be using many of the same sources, as the occasional static splotch or record skip occurs at the same exact moments on the same exact tracks. At first glance, a one-to-one comparison between the "Real Gone Jazz" release and this "Documents" release may give the sound edge to the "Documents" Milestone collection, as the recording is louder, and it gives the impression of being brighter and less compressed. But this may be part illusion. In many cases, if you just turn up the speaker volume on the "Real Gone Jazz" release, you would get sound close to the "Documents" release sold here. Additionally, this release seems to accentuate flaws, and any defects in the source album are highlighted. Finally, this release is too shrill in places, bringing out distortion in denser passages.

Note: If you are mainly interested in Baxter's Africa/South America/etc. exotica sound, by all means find a copy of the out-of-print "Exotic Moods of Les Baxter" collection. I's a sampler of many of Baxter's albums, but sound is very good and there are no obvious flaws like record skips.

The "Documents" Milestone collection pairs 2 complete albums on 10 CDs for a total of 20 albums. Each CD is in a cardboard sleeve, and it is difficult to remove a CD without getting fingerprints on it. The 10 sleeves fit in a cardboard box. There is no documentation beyond a few paragraphs on the back of the cardboard box.

Sound varies, so see below:

CD1: The absolute classic "Ritual of the Savage" has good sound overall, but the tracks "Quiet Village", "Coronation", and "Love Dance" have 1 or 2 minor defects each. (These are the same exact glitches on the Real Gone Jazz set, but other productions have found sources without these flaws.) These defects are typically a "micro-skip," like a quarter-second skip ahead. They are noticeable if you know the music or are just paying attention, but they might slip by if it's just on in the background. The other album is "Festival of the Gnomes." It may be conducted by Baxter, but it is otherwise classical ballet-like music written by Prince Di Candriano. Not what Baxter is known for, and my least favorite album in this collection. Sound is mainly fair, but bright.

CD2: "Thinking of You" is easy listening, though the arrangements are often creative. The sound is good with no flawed tracks. It is paired with "The Passions", an album that has to be heard to be believed. Vocalist Bas Sheva sings, grunts, and screams thoughout. The last track, "Joy", is worth the price of admission. Sound is good, but can get too bright or shrill.

CD3: "Kaleidoscope" is more easy listening than exotica. Sound is generally OK to good. Only "April in Portugal" had 2 minor defects, but some album dust is apparent now and again on other tracks, but nothing that would distract a typical listener. The other album is "Caribbean Moonlight". Defects, such as micro-skips, can be heard on "Taboo", "The Breeze and I", and "Nightingale". No deal-breakers, just momentary irritations. The record source seems obvious.

CD4: "La Femme" is easy-listening composed by Baxter. Relaxing enough to guide you to sleep. The terrible, muddy sound on the Real Gone Jazz set is improved upon here to a fair sound, but this is achieved with the introduction of significant hiss. Unfortunately, the other album "Round the World" (just as on the Real Gone Jazz set) is repeatedly mangled with micro-skips and record pops. Only the last three tracks, I believe, come out unscathed. This is the low point of the set.

CD 5: "Skins" is a concept album. It is entirely percussion music, mostly all of it composed by Baxter. No melody, just ambiance, but that's OK. Sound is pretty good except for a layer of hiss that might become more apparent at louder playing levels. The album it is paired with, "Midnight on the Cliffs" is problematic. Several tracks are marred with volume drops, moderate clunks from a scratch as a record spins around, record dust, and/or flat-out skips. "Take My Love", "Unchained Melody", "Suddenly", and "When You're in Love" had significant problems.

CD6: The first album is the famous "Space Escapade" with its futuristic exotica. The recording is a bit bright, with an occasional shrillness in the violins. "South Pacific" follows and is a step down. There's more intrusive album noise including some buzzing on a few tracks, album dust, one track with a warble, and one sudden spitting static sound.

CD7: The easy-listening "Love is a Fabulous Thing" starts out roughly, with an oscillation to the sound volume which might indicate a warped record source. The first track is the worst and then it gets better over the next 3 tracks or so. Otherwise, there is album dust sound and some distortion. The fantastic "African Jazz" album is quite enjoyable, but you'll notice a buzzing distortion at times in louder and denser passages. This is Baxter at his best.

CD8: The first album is "Wild Guitars" and is made up of creative covers. The sound is pretty good, except that distortion can be heard here and there - nothing serious, but a layer of buzz at times during denser passages. The film score "Goliath and the Barbarians" follows. The brightness helps at times, but again, there is just a bit of distortion that occurs every so often. Not noticeable unless you're really listening. This type of audio issue is certainly more preferable to the album dust and skips we were hearing earlier in the set.

CD9: "Teen Drums" starts us off. As you might expect, there is lots of percussion, but other instruments are featured throughout. It may be the best sounding recording on the entire set. It is paired with "Young Pops" which is definitely in the easy-listening category. The record source is evident now and again, and there is some distortion. The only flaw which might really bother you, though, is a glitch on "Summer Place" which sounds like a skip. (Again, it's the same skip on the "Real Gone Jazz" release.)

CD10: The delightful record "Jewels of the Sea" start off us, and this is a relaxing and melodic album. The record source is obvious and there is hiss and a few light pops. There's a sort of oscillating reverb that is more obvious on some tracks than others, but this might be part of the original concept. The film score "Master of the World" ends the collection. Sound is bright, but can get harsh and start to distort at times. No flaws like skips, though.

title: 25 years later, who is this music for?
text:
This 1996 recording of Metropolis Symphony was the first of a series of three Michael Daugherty albums released by Argo, thrusting him into the spotlight. It didn’t hurt that David Zinman and the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra were fully supporting his own brand of music-making either. However, it took until the mid-2000’s for Daugherty’s orchestral music to be regularly released, with a particular stranglehold of recordings from Naxos. Fortunately with advocates such as Neeme Jarvi, Marin Alsop, David Alan Miller, and a host of decent college wind ensembles, his music has spread rapidly.

Daugherty’s orchestral music is defined by a regular programmatic subject: pop-culture kitsch. That said, I don’t consider his music cinematic at all, so I think his music easily stands on its own two legs in the classical music world in terms of complexity. His music is not melodic in a traditional sense, although the outer movements have quality thematic material. Instead he seems to rely on rhythm, colour, and atmosphere moreso than tunes. In this vein, I would set Daugherty’s music next to Stravinsky and Philip Glass, the former for rhythm and chamber-like orchestrations at times, and the latter for his use of percussion and rhythmic cells. In this way the other reviewer is correct in that Daugherty’s orchestral music doesn’t develop in a classical structure relying on repetition instead. There is also a wit to his music that never becomes cloying or invasive, but the pop-culture references make eye-winks throughout the music.

The Metropolis Symphony is obviously indebted to Superman comics, with movement titles taking the characters from the superhero’s stories, although its composition comes before the advent of the Marvel movies. Daugherty makes full use of orchestral effects: string glissandi, synthesizer outbursts, plenty of concertante-style instrument features and virtuoso spotlights, and odd percussion and effects instruments (I’m looking at you flexatone). Daugherty doesn’t rely on obvious predicated musical structure or exoticisms either, with the exception of the Red Cape Tango which heartily gives into the titular dance style alongside the Dies Irae chant to guide his music; otherwise his music seems to be completely original.

The companion piece for winds and percussion, Bizarro, is an apt pairing and very much a sister composition to Metropolis. Again, motor rhythm and percussion seem to guide his music, the harmonies gently glide between approachable and dissonance for punchy effect, and the brass and winds seem to evoke a jazzy element in the music. I really enjoy this music for its kitschy fun, and I am glad that it will have a wide appeal for its subject matter. I don’t know, however, if the casual listener will be pleased with the lack of cinematic musical style nor the serious music listener for its lack of spirituality and structure.

David Zinman and the Baltimore SO obviously have fun premiering this music on record and attack it all head on. The percussion and brass get a little too much spotlight in the soundscape, with the strings taking a back seat, but the sound is big and clear if not a bit boomy in their empty hall. If you don’t care for the infusion of pop culture into the classical music scene, obviously stay far away, but this is good clean fun in music that doesn’t slavishly appeal towards easy listening. In that respect, I am not sure who this music is for; this music would be challenging for the average comic fanboi and too on-the-nose for classical music aficionados, so I guess I ride the middle road here. Regardless, despite a second outing of Metropolis Symphony [[ASIN:B002JIBC80 on Naxos]] with the Nashville SO from 2009, this original 1996 recording comes Highly Recommended!

title: Preussens Gloria
text:
So muss es wohl geklungen haben, als Österreich von Alten Fritz buchstäblich der Marsch geblasen wurde. Haydn wird mit schweren Stiefeln traktiert und auf Linie gebracht. Nichts ist von der Eleganz geblieben, die uns Eugen Jochum, Georg Solti und Adam Fischer (um nur ein paar zu nennen) vermittelt hat. Die vertopfte Aufnahmetechnik unterstreicht die preussische Verzopftheit, mit der man in - nun ja - Berlin - Haydn begegnet ist. Bei Schubert ist es nur wenig besser, nicht ganz so verzopft. Wer sowohl Haydn als auch Schubert so hören will, wie sie klingen sollen, ist mit George Szell und seinem Cleveland Orchestra musterexemplarisch besser bedient.
This must have been the sound when Frideric the Great tried to bring Austria in line with his Silesian wars. Heavy Prussian boots stomp out any elegance which which has been communicated to us by (for example) Eugen Jochum, Georg Solti, and Adam Fischer. The dated bathtub recording technique underlines Prussia’s approach (surprise, surprise, Berlin alas!). Schubert fares hardly better. If you want to hear both Haydn and Schubert as they are supposed to sound, go to Cleveland. Here, George Szell has set standards which have yet to be met.

text:
I bought this album during a time when I was relatively new to metal (I wasn't allowed to listen to secular or hard music as a kid) after hearing the cut "Ungrateful" on G-ROCK and loving it to death. What I ended up with when I got home from the store was what I knew even then to be a shoddily-produced album filled with what were obviously prototypical ideas. If you like blandish garage metal (that sounds like it was recorded in said garage) with blunt and goofy lyrics about being a sinner and... well that's the lyrical gist of the entire album, then you will probably enjoy "Indecision". I didn't, and still don't, so to me this was one of the bigger disappointments of my early music purchasing career. During a period when I was also coming across Christian bands like P.O.D., Project 86, and Five Iron Frenzy, this album found itself way at the bottom of the pile, under even Jars of Clay. Quite frankly, all of these reviews gushing heaps of praise for this sonically accursed thing strike me as probably all having been posted by two or three people using different accounts, because any other explanation just seems completely out of sync with any semblance of possibility.

HOWEVER...

If you surf the Interwebs, you will find cuts from a self-titled Gryp album that must have been released some time after "Indecision". On it are redone versions of tracks from this album that are a DRASTIC improvement over what is on display here, so evidently Gryp did find time to become a decent band, pretty damn good even. Information being scant, pack some luck in a duffel and look for that disc instead. Because despite the probable and unseemly circlejerk going on here, "Indecision" is not the Gryp you're looking for.

title: Not Available on CD for a Reason
text:
A number of reissue labels have had a go at the Capitol recordings of The Four Freshmen. All of them are or have been available on CD save the ones on this LP, and that's not likely to change.* For you completist collectors, please thank me for spending $11 to find out (and inform you) that your Four Freshmen Capitol collection is complete WITHOUT this embarrassment. While listening to the just-received LP, I visualized the Freshmen singing these songs at gunpoint, with arranger and conductor Shorty Rogers among the hostages. The initial tip-off is the back-of-the-jacket headline "You've never heard them like this! Here's the new 'Top 40' sound of The Four Freshmen." Here's the track list:

Baby Won't You Please Come Home, Hold Me, When the Feeling Hits you, Ja-da, Looking Over My Shoulder, Just A-sittin' and A-rockin', Mississippi Mud, Summertime, Walk Right In, I Gotta Right to Sing the Blues, Do You Really Love Me, Basin Street Blues.

The song selection is a mixture of blues, folk, rock, and pop songs dating back to the 1920s. But the whitebread rock-ish and country-ish arrangements (sorry, Shorty) don't - in fact can't - take advantage of the trademark jazz harmonies of the Freshmen. The majority of the lyrics were sung in unison, and what vocal harmonies there were could have been handled by a trio or even a duo. The performances do not have the usual Freshmen precision and occasionally sound a little flat. But let's be fair. The Freshmen had a lot of fellow travelers. During the mid-sixties almost all standards-toting pop singers were recording unsuitable songs with dumbed-down arrangements. We can't blame them for not putting their hearts into such dross.

The one positive I can point out is the killer trumpet section. Trumpeter Shorty Rogers led small jazz groups in the 1950s, so it is no surprise that arranger and conductor Shorty Rogers highlighted the trumpet section.

Definitely not recommended. To paraphrase Jeff Foxworthy, if you still want this album after reading my review, you're probably a masochist.

*The recording of "Do You Really Love Me" was reissued on the LP "Funny How Time Slips Away" and subsequently reissued on a Collectors' Choice CD.

title: Liszt's Lieder: wonderfully chosen, beautifully sung, excellently recorded
text:
It would be as idle to pretend that Liszt's Lieder are on par with Schubert's as that the Wanderer-Fantasie is on par with the B minor Sonata. However, this does not in the least mean that Schubert's magnificent piano work or Liszt's remarkably multifarious songs are without a great deal of intrinsic value. Indeed, they ARE true masterpieces, if on a slightly smaller scale than the greatest ones in the genre. Despite the fact that many eminent Lisztians have clearly expressed their admiration for Liszt's Lieder - and these include names like Alan Walker, Humphrey Searle, Harold Schonberg and Sacheverell Sitwell - this is one of the most neglected areas from Liszt's enormous output, rivalled in this sad contest only by his choral works perhaps. There are very few recordings of Liszt's Lieder and almost all of them are of just few pieces, usually coupled with other composers. Only in 2010 did a complete recording project start (on SACD, mind you), but only two volumes (about half of Liszt's songs, not counting any revisions) have been released so far.

So far as I know this box set is the only one more or less extensive selection of Liszt's Lieder recorded by a single singer. We are indeed fortunate that this singer is Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau himself, the man who is arguably the finest exponent of Schubert's Lieder from the last century. Even though he was a little past his prime in 1979 and 1981, when these recordings were made, his voice had lost none of this formidable expressive qualities. Occasionally, the inherent lack of power may become a little annoying in passages which require certain vocal excess, but this was always the case with Fischer-Dieskau. Even in his prime, his voice was small and ill-suited to many operatic roles; yet without this very limitation, one may speculate, he would never have achieved his superb diction and his performances would have lacked their trademark subtlety and sensitivity. Daniel Barenboim on the piano is far more dispensable but still excellent in these recordings. DG, for once, have done a great job with the sound. Both pianist and singer are splendidly recorded, with excellent balance between them, outstanding clarity of detail and exemplary dynamic range. If there are any Lieder in which the piano should be equal to the voice, these must be the ones composed by Franz Liszt, reportedly the greatest virtuoso and one of the most imaginative composers for the instrument who ever lived.

Unfortunately, but expectedly, the original edition of this box set from 1981 is hopelessly out of print. But since at the time this recording won the Gramophone Solo Vocal Award, it was more recently (2004) re-issued by DG in their so called ''Awards Collection''. This recent release is the one that is being reviewed here; so far as can be ascertained, it is identical with the original one in terms of sound and presentation. Very unfortunately, and rather UNexpectedly, the re-issue is perfectly out-of-print as well, and second-hand copies are offered at exorbitant prices. I can only say that for ardent Lisztians, Lieder lovers or fans of Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, the box set is worth every cent.

Before pointing out some highlights, it is useful to have a kind of playlist. The three CDs have timings 65:20, 42:18 and 62:47, respectively, and contain exactly 44 Lieder, that is more than a half of all (about 70) that Liszt composed. Poets and catalogue numbers are omitted for the sake of clarity.

If the first thing one looks for are the originals of some of Liszt's most famous piano pieces - ''Liebesträume'' and ''Tre sonetti di Petrarca'' - one is in for quite a few surprises.

Those who are familiar with the Petrarch Sonnets only in their final versions for solo piano in the ''second year'' of ''Annees de Pelerinage'', cannot but be surprised how different they are as songs. To begin with, the first two pieces are in reverse order: ''Pace non trovo'' is the famous 104th sonnet which appears second in the aforementioned set of piano pieces. But the really astonishing thing is that the works for solo piano are no mere transcriptions of the songs. They are indeed strikingly different: for Liszt, as always, the act of transcription, even when it comes to his own works, is an act of composition as well. It must be added, though, that the versions recorded here are the early ones, composed in 1839 during Liszt's sojourns in Italy; these were accompanied with solo piano pieces (again in the same reverse order) which are naturally closer to the Lieder originals. Later, during his Weimar years in the 1850s, Liszt thoroughly revised both the piano pieces, for inclusion in ''Annees de Pelerinage'', and the songs for separate publication. So in this particular case it is truer to say that for Liszt the act of revision was in fact an act of composition.

The case with the ''Liebesträume'' is even more complicated. Regarding the piano versions, even though the third piece is far more famous than the other two, they ARE a set and so were they first published in 1850, if seldom performed since. Apparently the songs appeared at roughly the same time as the piano pieces and thus should be considered as a set also. Strangely, they are not so recorded here, but all of them ARE here nonetheless: tracks 1, 9 and 10 on CD 1. The famous third piece (almost always mistakenly referred to as ''Liebestraum'') takes for its song title the first line of Ferdinand Freiligrath's poem: ''O lieb, so lang du lieben kanst''. The first two pieces are settings of poems by Ludwig Uhland; no. 1 is usually known as ''Hohe Liebe'', whereas no. 2 appears alternatively as ''Seliger Tod'' or ''Gestorben war ich'' (the first line of the poem, usually used only for the song version). These titles, the first two at any rate, are often used for the piano pieces as well, at least when these are played at all.

It is astonishing to compare the piano pieces from the cycle titled ''Liebesträume: 3 Notturnos für das Pianoforte'' with the songs, all the more so since both versions, apparently, were published at the same time. The first two songs are mere two minutes long each, hardly having anything to do with more than twice longer and much more elaborate piano versions. The main material is recognisably the same, but the treatment is so completely different that these are for all purposes different works. The famous third piano piece is of comparable length with the song and somewhat more similar to it, but it is not very easy to recognise immediately the latter, especially considering the overwhelming popularity of the former. The song utilises only the first two verse of Freiligrath's much longer poem and Liszt's treatment of the text - or Fischer-Dieskau's perhaps, for that matter - is not always as sensitive as in the incomparable piano version.

For the rest of the songs all I can say is that they appear to have been excellently selected insofar as they finely represent Liszt's impressive versatility. The aforementioned sets of songs are sufficient testimony that Liszt was a supreme melodist, though nowhere near Schubert's class in this respect. Another fine examples for that are some of Liszt's most popular (if that is the right word) songs, such as ''Angiolin dal biondo crin'', ''Es muß ein Wunderbares sein'', ''Kling leise, mein Lied'' and ''Ich möchte hingehn''. The last one of these is the famous song in which Wagner's ''Tristan chord'' appears almost identical; it has long been considered - wrongly - to be one of those instances when Liszt stole from the music of the future, but we now know that the notorious chord was an afterthought from the time when Liszt already knew ''Tristan und Isolde'' and it is more probably that it actually was a quotation from Wagner. Which is not to say that Liszt did not anticipate daring harmonic inventions before Wagner, as evident from ''Loreley'', a fine setting of Heine's powerful poem. Another, more tangible for the layman, source of fascination is comparison of Liszt's settings of some famous poems with those of Schubert, such as in the case of Goethe's ''Über allen Gipfeln ist Ruh'' and ''Der du von dem Himmel bist''. In contrast to such quiet and lyrical songs, there are long narrative ballads with many dramatic verses, such as Hugo's ''Gastilbelza'' and Lenau's ''Der traurige Mönch''. The latter, indeed, is no song at all but a melodrama for voice and piano in which text is spoken, rather than sung - and which is one of the earliest compositions in music history entirely based on the whole-tone scale. Quite an advanced composition for 1860!

Last but not least, few words about the sumptuous presentation. The booklet contains an excellent essay by Wolfgang Dömling (in English only, but translated from German) in which he has a number of fascinating things to say about Liszt's stature as a Lieder composer or his numerous revisions. The booklet also contains all texts in original language (German, French, Italian) with English translations. In addition to the names of the poets, there is a great deal of useful information such as which version or setting was used for this recording and the year of publication and/or composition (the latter only when it can be ascertained with some degree of accuracy and is significantly different than the former). Of course for all songs the number in the Searle catalogue is given as well.

title: Just One Lad's Opinion, Nothing More
text:
Knowing that this book is about James Bond, and knowing that it’s called “The Man with the Golden Touch,” you might think it’s a biography of Ian Fleming. Wrong. You might next think it’s a biography of the fictional character of James Bond. Wrong again. Given the subtitle (“How the Bond Films Conquered the World”) you might think it’s a history of the making of the James Bond films. Close, but still wrong. It is in fact just one journalist’s opinions of each movie in the series. Which ones he liked, which ones he thought were bad, and why.

His opinions – and that’s all they are – are backed up by no more than the “lads” he hung out with when he watched the films in the cinemas. There are frequent mentions of a “close friend” who holds the same opinion as himself, thus validating it (ahem). He acknowledges growing up with the Moore Bond, so those tend to be held in higher regard than those that came before and after. For example, “Thunderball” is slow and boring, so it’s crap. “You Only Live Twice”? That was awful too. And you know what? So were the Dalton films. Oh, and some of the Brosnan stuff was “naff” too, just look at the silly plots of “Tomorrow Never Dies” and the awful “Die Another Day.” Moore doesn’t get away unscathed, however. “Man with the Golden Gun” is dismissed as rubbish also. You could almost slap a different cover on this book and use it to argue why the Bond films are NOT worthy of praise.

All boat chases are dull. All underwater sequences are boring. The “naff” double entendres are pointed out. The “For Your Eyes Only” song is awful. The “View to a Kill” lyrics are awful. (The author's actual reaction is: “What? I mean, what?”) The lyrics of “Living Daylights” are awful as well. (And he repeats the reaction: “What? I mean, what?”) Villains are referred to as “wrong ’uns.” Not exactly an esteemed journalistic analysis.

For the author is a journalist, although I must use that term loosely. He continually refers to female members of the Bond audience as “sisters” and “laydeez.” Yes, ladies is spelled l-a-y-d-e-e-z. Condescending and not very professional, and quite ironic considering that the author acknowledges that, yes, the Bond films could at times be racist and/or sexist. Based on the dates and ages referenced in the text, the author is apparently in his forties, which is why it is surprising to find he appears to have an eight year-old’s mentality regarding how women should be referred to.

The author is also in love with the word “insouciance.” It crops up several times in almost every chapter. On the plus side, this book did send me to the dictionary to find out what “insouciance” means. But no thanks, Mr. McKay, I’ll stick to the word “indifference.” The book argues an excellent point that although Bond is perceived as being a Cold War hero fighting Russians, he in fact does nothing of the sort; the Bond villains are always rogue psychopaths who are never directly affiliated with the Soviet government, and this was by design, since the creators knew the Cold War wouldn’t go on forever. The book also spells out the differences between Fleming’s novels and their equivalent filmed versions, but out of the hundreds of other books about the Bond phenomenon, I’m sure others cover this equally as well, if not better.

So, if you want to know what a small group of “lads” in the UK (i.e. the author and his “mates”) thought about how “naff” the Bond films can be (even though they’re great, honestly) then this is the book for you. But I think your time and money could be better spent watching the Bond films for yourself and forming your own opinions. They’re just as valid as McKay’s. He just happened to be the one to get the cushy book deal, not you.

title: Poor live recording of Dvorak’s 8th that’s better avoided
text: This live recording of Dvorak’s 8th is a somewhat slipshod affair, with thin strings and brass and the parts and rhythms barely cohering. Even the memorable melodies in the inner movements are botched. This sounds like a student orchestra more than the renowned Vienna Phil, or a Vienna Phil that was listlessly resisting the lead of Ozawa, a maestro who can usually be relied upon to deliver performances with rhythmic sure-footedness and at least a beautiful surface sheen. Not so here. This sounds more like a bad rehearsal take and should never have been released. The coupler of “The Noon Witch” is much closer to the mark, with Vienna’s typical woody sonority and a nice sense of atmospherics, but it’s too little too late.

title: Wow...
text:
I've been an avid fan of this band since I saw them on MTV's "120 Minutes" in 1987 with the video "Faith Healer", so the release of this album (their first since 1990) was a major event for me. I was prepared to be disappointed, but I'm happy to say the exact opposite is the case. As much as I worship "Heavens" and "Craps" as two of the best albums of all time, "Crashes on the Platinum Planet" is at least as good, if not better. All of the songs are great, and there has been much justified buzz about Gary Waleik's compulsively catchy composition, "Robert Pollard". But the best songs on the album are, in my opinion, the beautiful, sad "Happy New Year" by Bill Goffrier, and what I consider to be Gary Waleik's masterpiece, "Sarah and Monica". It is one of the most beautiful, hook-filled songs I've heard in a very long time. The "C" section of this song is absolutely Beatles, and it sends shivers down my spine like any preternaturally gorgeous bit of music should.

The Goffrier/Waleik song "New Machine" rocks just like the good old days (with biting lyrics). And it is great to see drummer Jeff Oliphant's song writing develop with "Princess Warrior" (an inspiring song about fighting breast cancer), and especially his elegiac song with Bill, "Forget the Chef".

This band's musical ingenuity has always been incredible. The added element of maturity makes them all the more must hear. And you must hear. Buy it now.

title: ... but there's finally a Jimi Hendrix album I don't like. This is almost unlistenable
text:
I didn't think it was possible but there's finally a Jimi Hendrix album I don't like. This is almost unlistenable. Taped to two track by Jimi himself the sound quality is excellent, however what is being played is not. This isn't Jimi jamming in the studio, playing amazing guitar solos. This is just a few guys on acid (I assume) noodling around at home. There's no "lost classics" here.
The cd lists the players in addition to Jimi as:
Juma Sultan flute/percussion
Jerry Velez percussion
Mike Ephron keyboards
Billy Cox bass
Mitch Mitchell drums

First of all, there's no bass or drums anywhere on here. Billy Cox and Mitch Mitchell DO NOT play on this.
Disc 1 is literally just Jimi strumming what appear to be random chords while Juma and Jerry play with some bongos. 70 minutes of that. Occasionally an out of tune keyboard can be heard. Only the last track is even remotely interesting, a very very loose version of Stepping Stone. But again, no bass, no drums, and Jimi's amp is set to the clean setting.
Disc two is slightly better. At least there's some recognizable riffs. The early home demo of Isabella is mildly interesting, I guess.
I got so bored listening to this I lost track of the song titles, but I'm pretty sure the track list on the back of the CD doesn't quite match up with what's on the disc itself.
If you're a Hendrix nerd like me you're probably going to buy this anyways no matter how horrible it is. I did. I don't regret it (other sites have it for sale much cheaper than here. Check auction sites) but I'll never listen to it again.
Two stars just for Jimi's presence but he'd be totally embarrassed if he knew people were listening to this.

title: Finger at the ready?
text:
Well... here's a problem: an indispensable late 60's album that is regularly rated in industry polls as amongst the best of all time for good reasons, one of which is that the original record just flowed from start to finish. So, now we have an excellent digital re-mastering that enhances the original tracks by fully revealing their extraordinary intricacies - particularly the group's use of multiple acoustic guitars - but which also includes seven bonus tracks that range from the intriguing to the essential.
The problem?... well, a key feature of the original LP was its sequencing with side two building-up to the final ecstatic fade out on it's last cut - "You Set the Scene" - leaving the listener, quite deliberately, to reflect in the silence that followed. On this version there's not much time for reflection before being jarred back into reality by bonus tracks that weren't on the original because they weren't good enough, weren't recorded yet or didn't fit. And, while there's nothing wrong with "Laughing Stock" and the fabulous "Your Mind And We Belong Together" and, for Love fans, real interest in the other alternate mixes and unreleased workouts that have been added to this version, the truth is that they shouldn't be there! Subtle but important stuff when dealing with a carefully crafted masterpiece. The solution?... pretty simple really: program your CD player to stop after track 11, but it's a pain to remember and, for first time recruits, an unlikely event.
Here's an idea: with "classic" records that deserve this kind of meticulous re-mastering (and which have usually been elevated to such high status precisely because they worked so well as a unified whole) why not put the bonus tracks on a separate disk - the cost can't be that great and the benefits would be enormous. In the meantime have your programming finger at the ready to savour the full impact of this magnificent slice of musical genius.

title: Crushing Disappointment!
text:
Verdi's Requiem is my all time favorite piece of music and I was thrilled by the promise of hearing it as recorded by these stars. But it really is poor. I blame Gergiev. Overall, the soloists do not deliver the passion this music deserves - and the passion is what makes this work so wonderful. Perhaps Gergiev feels that a quieter interpretation is somehow more reverent - I disagree. The only place where the stops are pulled out are in Fleming's Libera Me, and not with a good effect. I love her and I know she could have delivered this music better than anyone ever has before, but she seems to be sputtering with anger instead of trembling in awe and fear.
Good points are the chorus, which is really exceptional, and the incredible beauty of vocal tone by both Fleming and Borodina.
Is this recording worth owning? Of course! But if you are only going to have one recording of the Requiem you might want to try the '64 Ormandy (my personal favorite) with Tucker and London, or the wonderful Toscanini or Giulini.

title: a voice teacher and early music fan
text:
QUEEN MARY SAID: 'LET'S CELEBRATE; SO HENRY YOU COOPERATE' THO HE FOUND IT DEMEANING TO COMPLY, IT REALLY WAS 'DO OR DIE'!
Henry Purcell (1659-1695) looked like a Florentine prince, was hail-fellow-well-met in tavern and taproom, wrote for the church and also for the stage and salon, was in fact a most likeable young man, as well as a "very great Master of Musick." Except for his appointment as organist at the Chapel Royal and other churches, his compositions were the chief events of his life. Henry Purcell invented the English celebratory style in music.

His odes were often written for various groups and annual celebrations. Purcell's ode 'Welcome to all the Pleasures' was composed for an inaugural celebration in 1683 for a group of musicians that made up a so-called "Musical Society".

'Of old, when heroes thought it base', the so-called 'Yorkshire Feast Song',was composed in 1690 for the otherwise obscure annual London gathering of York nobility.

'Come, ye sons of art, away' was the ode for what was to be Queen Mary's last birthday-April 30 1694. It is the least ostentatious of the birthday odes. This ode is a countertenor's dream, for Purcell favours this voice as the soloist throughout. The famous duet recorded by many countertenors "Sound the Trumpet" is in this ode. It is my personal favorite, though I like them all.

You really couldn't have a better performance of this music than is on this disc. The Choir of the English Consort and the English Concert all put together by Trevor Pinnock. The soloists are the best, my favorite being countertenor: Michael Chance with his lovely voice and intelligent delivery of the music AND tenor John Mark Ainsley And bass Michael George who are experts at interpreting the music of Purcell. All other soloists are very good indeed. Such an entertaining disc!!!!!

His albums may seem high-priced, but when you become hooked, you will understand that they are worth it.

title: "When a woman has strong gifts that can be used against you, it's a really bad idea to threaten those she loves"
text:
Riley Poe and her vampire guardian fiancé, Eli Dupre, have traveled to Scotland, along with a few other vampires to help Worldwide Unexplained Phenomenon (WUP), an elite team they have agreed to help. Each member of the small team has unique gifts that will help the task force. The current mission is to bring down the Black Fallen, a group of fallen angels that have been overcome by the darkest of magic and now use it to get whatever they want and they want is the source of power that could make them unstoppable.

Riley and Eli are training hard with the rest of the team when it becomes apparent that at least one of the members of the Black Fallen has become aware of them. During what should have been a simple and semi relaxing training run between Riley and Eli turns deadly and at the end, only Riley returns to the team's headquarters. Riley knows that Eli is out there and not dead and that only defeating the Black Fallen will give her the keys to find her fiancé. Now it's a deadly Riley who seeks out the fallen angels determined to destroy all of them and the power they want so badly. A fierce battle incurs between Riley and the rest of the WUP team and the Black Fallen. When the dust settles who will still be standing strong and will Riley find the way to rescue Eli and bring him home safe?

When a woman has strong gifts that can be used against you, it's a really bad idea to threaten those she loves. In Black Fallen, Riley learns just how strong and deadly her gifts can be when her lover, guardian and fiancé, Eli, is taken by the very group of fallen angels they and the rest of their team are hunting. I knew that Riley was still learning just what she was now with the help of Eli and other vampires, but I think when Eli was taken, a deadly flame was lit in Riley and now anyone behind keeping her from Eli is at risk. The love between Riley and Eli is very apparent to anyone observing them, so I wasn't surprised when Riley fought even harder when that battle happened. Now I'm waiting for the next book so I can, hopefully, see the loving reunion of Riley and Eli. I'm also keeping an eye out for a couple of other vampires that might be jumping a bit too fast and could be burned for it. Black Fallen is dark and full of fast paced action, but with a touch of true love that exists between Riley and Eli. A definite keeper for any paranormal library.

Here he is very Holden Caulfield-like where despite being self-centered and manipulative, he somehow eventually elicits pity and understanding from the viewer.

title: Attack of the CG
text:
A long time ago in Hollywood CA...A young, considerabley brilliant writer/director named George Lucas had a vision of creating a universe all his own. Well the rest is history. His brainchild spawned arguable the greatest trilogy ever made. Now fast forward to the "new" Star Wars trilogy, what happened? Where is the magic, where is that brilliance, where is Han Solo? They're not around anymore, they were abandoned in the early 80's for a career in computer technology. The new Star Wars trilogy is less a man expanding his mythical legacy and more an excuse for him to display his innovations in computer graphic effects. Case in point: Episode II, Attack of the Clones.
Anyone who is reading this review has no doubt seen the film so there is no reason to plot summarize, instead, a few observations. First, this film is a joke as far as the acting is conserned. Ask any good director, casting is 90% of an effective performance. Hayden Christensen? He whines, he cries, he can't deliver the diologue (which was terrible, but hold on). As in Episode I, Anakin is not sympathetic. Aren't we suppose to care that this young man will subcome to the dark side and a life of evil? At this point it will be a relief when he becomes Darth Vader, Anakin is not interesting, as say, Luke was. Other priciples, particularly Portman, are also aweful. The relationship between Padme and Anakin is laughable. If they did not say they were in love out loud, no one would believe it, she looks repulsed by him, not seduced by him. The script, what is this? The story is there, but the screenplay is horrible. Who is Jonathan whats-his-name? One can only imagine how bad the script was before he pollished it with lines like, "I don't like sand it's rough and coarse, but you're smooth." Ahhhhhhhh! Where have you gone Lawerence Kasden, our galaxy turns it's desparate eyes to you.
And on another note is the computer graphics. George Lucas has made amazing strides in the industry with ILM, they are the Jedi of special effects, but come on! This looks more like a cartoon than live action. In Return of the Jedi, the dog fight between the Rebelion and the Empire looks so real, how did they do it? In Attack of the Clones (and in Episode I) it's just computer graphics and it looks as such. Did Yota have to be CG? How are the actors suppose to perform against characters and settings that aren't there? Instead they stand against a green screen, and a director who could not care less about their performances, describes to them what will be around them. It's enough to make a grown man cry.
Steven Spielberg and Francis Ford Coppola are suppose to be two of Lucas's good friends. What kind of friends are they being by letting Lucas take everything out of what made Star Wars great? At least tell him he needs to turn it over to another director like he did before. Give him some advice, please, there is still time to save Episode III.
Star Wars was great because it was creative, exciting, and we cared about the characters. I wonder when years from now, when there are six completed films, how many people watching them for the first time, in chronological order, starting with Episode I, will actually make to Star Wars (Episode IV). Unless Episode III is amazing, I wouldn't. Shame on Lucas.

title: What A Waste...
text:
This seems like Ty Tabor's most creative and refreshing solo album of all... and I'm stating that after having heard only the samples!

Sadly I can't stand listening to more than those couple 30 seconds... Why? Because of the quite unrealistic programmed fake drums. Every time there is a drum fill, it makes me cringe like hell. Unrealistic dynamics with no human feel and a clangy triggered snare sound makes it really hard for me! It's kind of OK during the grooves... but for instance, in Everything Changed, in the (or one of the) guitar solo(s), the drum fill going into the solo, and one of the fills in the 3rd and 4th measure... UGH! it hurts my drummer ears... it's like somebody spilled coffee in the keyboard, with the "drumkit" patch on... I don't know if you guys who gave 5 stars noticed that, or are agressed by that... It's always a small bit insulting for a drummer to hear super smooth and funky guitars with "programmed-always-the-same-velocity" snare and kick drums. I know this lowers the production time and costs for Ty, but there is nothing like real warm Jerry-Gaskill-banged drumshells. The music on this CD right here DESERVES real drums... it.... COMMANDS real drums.

To sum it up : I'm a huge fan of great guitar-playing, but to much of an acoustic drummer to endure programmed drums.... and it's a sad waste, 'cause otherwise I would have spinned that CD for a year, rockin' to my buddy Ty...

title: The Definitive Varese
text:
This album has been, for me, the definitive performance of Varese since I bought it 40 years ago (though I like the more recent Chailly "Complete Works" as well). Simonovich and the Paris Contemporary Music Ensemble offer a languid pace, rich tonality, lots of ambience (something Varese liked), thunderous percussion, and a passionate approach that may be, in the minds of some, a bit excessive for music as abstract as Varese's. For instance, it stands in pronounced contrast to the more intellectualized approach taken by Boulez. But I think Simonovich's approach is consistent with the drama and lyricism one hears in the tape interpolations on "Deserts", which presumably represent as close a reading of Varese's intentions as we can get. It's a powerful performance, one that's alternately meditative and robust, but one that does not sacrifice precision for power.

This album hasn't been reissued on CD. I was thrilled to find a "Used--Like New" copy of the vinyl on Amazon, which is the best I'll manage for something to replace my worn-out original vinyl LP.

title: Real organ literature on a fake organ!
text: As a youth in the 60's, I absorbed every organ record I could, and there were a fair number in my local St. Louis suburban library. This was one of them. Mario Salvador was known in St. Louis as the longtime organist at the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Louis, containing a large Kilgen instrument (renovated and rebuilt in the 80's and also more recently), a decent musician with training in Rome. The organ sound is awful, but lots of cathedral reverb makes up for it to a small degree. The only piece I can remember with any clarity is "Naiades" (Water Nymphs) from Vierne's 24 Pieces de fantaisie, a fast-flowing quiet piece which takes a fair bit of technique. Interesting musical curio for an organ lover!

title: Big disappointment
text: I'm a big fan of Dmitri Hvorostovsky's singing and had viewed some songs from the Deja Vu album on youtube.  I was looking forward to playing my own album and interested to hear more of his crossover music which had been highly praised.  But the disc was a huge let-down, mainly because of its unbalanced mix - all the songs overpowered by a thumping bass and facile orchestration.  His voice is still beautiful and his diction - in three languages - is excellent, but he would have done better to sing a cappella, the mix was so bad.  And then - to add insult to injury - the DVD of Toi et Moi !!!  What on earth induced him to introduce chains, whips and a woman screaming in .... pleasure? Anguish? Who knows?  Who cares?  Whatever it was, it was ludicrous, cliches stacked on top of cliches in a package that would have been offensive if it wasn't so laughable.  I think I'm still a fan of Hvorostovsky - singing opera and Russian folk songs - but this album does nothing to enhance his reputation and I won't be playing it again. Each of these records are more cohesive than her KAPP/MCA days (with the exception of DARK LADY which is actually a fantastic record that needs a remastered box set! - well - all of her albums do! --- AND this is BELIEVE's 20th anniversary so we should get a vinyl box!)

title: "A Truly Phenomenal Experience"
text: "The stars quite simply align in this stupendous 2012 recording by Moldovan violinist Patricia Kopatchinskaja with Ensemble Modern and Peter Eotvos - the ensemble and conductor who had premiered the five-movement Violin Concerto in 1992...Kopatchinskaja takes things into altogether new dimensions conjuring a performance that feels wrought from her very nerves and sinew...she and the ensemble...manage to convey the sense of spontaneity and risk inherent in a score full of startling gestures and unusual sounds...the result is a kind of transitional space in which technical brilliance and playful theatricality exist to serve mercurial, deeply felt emotions...this underlines the distinctly eastern European sensibility from which the concerto springs...where folk traditions are not just part of history, but a lived reality...most astonishing is how every contradictory aspect of Ligeti's invention is gathered into the final 'Appassionato'. The cadenza is Kopatchinskaja's own, an outpouring of unbridled virtuosity that celebrates like no other this passionately enigmatic work." (Steph Power BBC Music January 2020)

title: Young Brendel
text: Back when I was in college, learning to love classical music, there were no better values on vinyl than the many cheap treasures offered by Vox and Turnabout. I bought them by the dozen from a mail order place called Publishers Central Bureau, for a mere buck apiece. Many of them were recordings by the young Austrian pianist, Alfred Brendel—mostly Beethoven, Mozart, & Schubert. I've owned his Beethoven cycle 3 times—LPs, CDs in the '90s (which I foolishly sold), and in this set. A friend gifted me with it and I'm happy to have Brendel's lively, agile, and intelligent performances back in my musical life. This box is a treasure trove and, despite the variable sound quality, well worth owning. P.S. I'm writing this exactly a year after the review above and this set is selling for $500. Yikes. I like Brendel a lot, but that's a lot to pay for a pile of old records.

title: forgettable then, forgettable now
text: I bought this album not long after its original release on vinyl.  My own opinion:  Arthur Lee didn't have much of a voice, his lyrics had all the subtlety and poetry of a jackhammer, David Angel's arrangements are some of the cheesiest ever recorded, and The Red Telephone and You Set the Scene are among the most embarrassingly awful songs in rock history.  I'll never understand why many people now think this is a great album.  It was undeniably creative in places but also hopelessly heavy-handed, and most of it literally makes me cringe.  Other than Alone Again Or, I really *never* want to hear any of these songs again.  To put this on the same footing with the best of Tim Buckley and Nick Drake is laughable in my view, let alone the Beatles and Dylan.

title: A Must have re-issue of two great LPs on one CD for the first time.
text: I'm pleasantly surprised at how good this CD sounds.  I thought that being released by a company called Tone Arm Records that it would be mastered from vinyl, but it isn't.  I bought both these albums on vinyl when they came out in 1980 and 1983 respectively, and always liked them.  I was at a record store in Ann Arbor, MI, in 1980 and they were giving a way a Gus 7” single that had ‘One More Border to Cross’ on one side, and ‘Sweet Delight’ on the other.  That’s what introduced me to Gus, and buying the first album.  Tunes such as 'I'm not Finished' and the cold war classic 'The Russians are Coming' (fitting in a cyberspace way at the end of 2016!) are fantastic, and the reggae influenced 'Southern Most Part of my Soul' sounds better than ever.  Also, who else ever wrote a song criticizing the Japanese government for ‘busting’ Paul McCartney for marijuana possession?  The low end on the Convicted! mastering is stunning, with bass and drums loud and clear.  I would love to hear an album mixed like this right now, but it's amazing that this is 36 years old!  I write this review after listening to it on CD for the first time last night at full volume driving through the desert at night in Arizona, from Tucson to Phoenix, and was blown away at how good it sounds.  It’s too bad it’s out of print and so expensive here.  I found it on the other auction sight for ten, so I feel lucky.  Hopefully it will be re-issued soon…

title: Mercury U.S. Lp from early '65 with a MONSTER hit single that went around the world; four rechanneled tracks on the stereo Lp
text:
One U.S. Lp release, February, 1965:

JULIE ROGERS, Mercury MG 20981 (mono)/SR 60981 (stereo)

Songs on this Lp:
side one--
The Wedding (rechanneled)
The Love of a Boy (rechanneled)
Young and Foolish
Friendly Persuasion
A House Is Not a Home
Love Letters
side two--
Like a Child (rechanneled)
Without Your Love (rechanneled)
In The Blue of the Evening
How Soon
I'll Be Around
Hawaiian Wedding Song

You know the Lp cuts (filler) as songs/hits identified with Pat Boone ("Friendly Persuasion"), Elvis Presley ("Love Letters"), and Andy Williams ("Hawaiian Wedding Song"). The first two tracks on each side of the vinyl Lp are rechanneled--mono track balanced over to the left, right channel has some faint bleed-off echo added. Obviously, U.S. Mercury took about half of the UK album tracks (THE SOUND OF JULIE, Mercury UK 20048) and cut in her two UK 45 singles' tracks (see below: MF 809 and MF 820 UK singles' four sides) on this U.S. Lp. The balance of the album is otherwise is decently balanced with-orchestra very middle-of-the-road stereo. Julie Rogers is in FINE voice on these songs, a voice that strongly suggests the kind of pipes, power, and beauty that makes me think of early '60s' Eydie Gorme', but without all the Columbia pop deep echo.

Mercury 45 singles:

72332 The Wedding/Without Your Love (Oct. 1964)
72380 Like A Child/The Love of A Boy
72426 Hawaiian Wedding Song/Turn Around Look at Me (May, 1965)
72535 Another Year, Another Love, Another Heartache/Don't Waste Your Young Years On Him
72646 While the Angelus Was Ringing/Climb Ev'ry Mountain (Dec. 1966)

Note: the first U.S. version of her world-wide hit was by Anita Bryant on Columbia 4-42148 45 single, "The Wedding"/"Seven Kinds of Lonesome" (September, 1961--it barely charted on Cash Box's LOOKING FORWARD bottom 100-150 "almost a hit" chart for six weeks); Tony Martin did a cover on Randy Woods's Dot Records, December, 1961, Dot 45-16313, "The Bride"/"Horizons of Joy" (thanks to Amazon reviewer Bill Busse for the tip!). Keely Smith also put out the song on her Reprise 0313 45 single, "The Wedding"/"Turn Around Look At Me" in late '64.

In 1969-72, Julie Rogers recorded for Jeffrey Kruger's UK Ember Records, and here in the U.S., Mega Records (C&W label known for Sammi Smith's huge "Help Me Make It Through the Night" hit) licensed some of Ember's UK recordings and issued a 10-song abridged version Lp on a similar UK title.

(45RPM single)--
Mega 0075 Where Do You Go/Almost Close to You (May, 1972)

(Lp--U.S.)--
JULIE ROGERS...WITH FEELING, Mega M31-1013

The Mega Lp was the U.S. version of UK Lp, Ember NR 5050, JULIE ROGERS ONCE MORE WITH FEELING, which featured 14 tracks (7 per Lp side) versus the U.S. version on Mega Records with only 10 tracks. Two of the songs, "Once More With Feeling," and "Where Do You Go," were published through Glen Campbell's publishing companies from GC's TRY A LITTLE KINDNESS Capitol SW 389 Lp, and both Rogers' Lps, the UK Ember and US Mega, have liner notes credited written by Glen Campbell. Glen Campbell's 1968-70 UK records were released on Ember, and Jeffrey Kruger's organization booked his UK tours into the 1980s.

title: Two old favorites...
text: I saw the movies "La Violetera" and "Carmen la de Ronda" when they came out in the 1950s. I bought the  records for both immediately, and missed listening to them, so it has been a joy to listen to them in CD format. La Violetera is a movie about a Spanish music hall singer (fictional) and practically all the songs are old "cuplés," many of which were favorites of my parents' and grandparents' generations, Sarita Montiel brought them back into fashion and gave them a new lease on life. "Carmen la de Ronda" is a variant of the Carmen legend, in which Carmen lives during the Napoleonic invasion, and has both a French soldier and a Spanish "guerrillero" in love with her, and is torn between the two; the triangle of course ends in tragedy. In this movie many of the songs are from the Andalusian folk tradition (including a wonderful scene in which the resistance fighter is hiding in an inn where Carmen is entertaining, and a French platoon comes searching for him. Carmen leaps on the tablado and begins to sing a well known (and fiery) Flamenco tune, improvising the words so that he guerrillero will understand that his presence been discovered and must flee... even warning him that a certain road is not safe!  The songs are beautiful in themselves, and she interprets them with a lovely voice and feeling.

title: Sudanese-centered, with blues, jazz, funk and Afrobeat
text:
Western listeners of African music have mostly been exposed to the sounds of a few countries. Thanks to its direct connection to the blues, Mali and a few adjacent countries have often been the focus of attention, and these days, desert blues is big. South Africa got its spotlight thanks to that popular 1980s album from a 60s folkie, although there is far more to explore. East Africa, though, has a wide variety of musical traditions that do not receive nearly as much attention. Tarig Abubakar moved from Sudan to Canada, and formed the Afronubians to play a set of styles rooted in Eastern African styles, but more diverse than merely traditional styles. His band consisted of artists who moved to Canada from various African countries, and that allowed Abubakar to lead a group that blended styles in a way that centered around Sudanese, while still showcasing the interconnections as well as how African music had, obviously, been influenced by rock, funk and jazz in the 20th century. One hears the Ethiopian/reggae connection, the central African/funk connection (see: Fela Kuti and Afrobeat more generally), bits of blues guitar, creative horn and percussion arrangements, and styles that will feel vaguely familiar to those who listen to styles from across Africa without necessarily being able to place any particular rhythm or melody. The band is top notch, and includes participants from the African Guitar Summit as well— Pa Joe and Adam Solomon, both of whom are strong instrumentalists, although this is not a guitar-led group. Rather, one hears horns, guitars, percussion and vocals trade lines as Abubakar allows the group to travel from Sudan to Kenya to Ethiopia to Mali, Guinea and further. Sudan, though, is at the center, and it is fascinating to hear Abubakar explain to the crowd on these live performances how each country treats the styles, and the relationships between them. All around, interesting and valuable recordings.

Further listening: Ndala Kasheba, from Tanzania.

title: Interesting mix of songs & well worth the price
text: I love train songs. I grew up hearing them on the radio & listening to my dad & uncles playing them on harmonica during long trips or on piano, guitar or banjo at their homes or ours. I admit there are some missing from this collection -- no Orange Blossom Special or New River Train, or City of New Orleans or The L&N Don't Stop Here Anymore, but, by & large, it is an impressive collection. Ten CDs, each with 20 tracks. Each CD is in a separate cardboard slipcover with the contents of that CD listed on the back. Each list includes the name of the person or group performing, name of the song, name of the writer, & original release date of the specific recording. The 10 CDs, in their slipcases, are all in a nice box. The CDs average 50 minutes each, so it's a set you could listen to all day while you build that new deck or put together that special meal for the homecoming veteran. You might want to remember that the collection was put together by a German company, which may explain the inclusion of Mule Train (the Frankie Laine version & the Tennessee Ernie Ford version) as well as Marty Robbins' wonderful (but not train related) Big Iron. There are several songs performed by more than one artist so technically there are not 200 different songs -- but there are more than you will find in any other album. There are 2 versions of The Rock Island Line, 3 of Choo Choo Ch'Boogie, 2 of Wabash Cannonball, 3 of This Train, 2 of Chattanooga Choo Choo, 2 of The Golden Rocket, 3 of Mystery Train, & 2 each of Folsom Prison Blues, Pan American, Hobo Bill's Last Ride & Wreck of the Old 97. I think that covers all the repeats but I wouldn't swear to it -- & since the various versions are done by different performers, they are not exactly "repeats". I am enjoying this collection and I suspect anyone who is  a train song nut would enjoy it as well. Sure, it isn't absolutely perfect, but what is? It is an interesting mix of songs and it is well worth the price.

title: A wholly absorbing sound ....that will easily engross your attention
text:
A blue moon is a second full moon in the same calendar month, and it's been a few years since the last one happened on November 30, 2001. However, for a lively Tennessee-based group called Blue Moon Rising, the month of July, 2004 should be especially memorable for that's when a blue moon will rise again. By then, you'll have heard of these guys who actually received the inspiration for their band name from the famous Bill Monroe song, "Blue Moon of Kentucky." In their relatively short four years together, they have played a number of noteworthy festivals and venues. BMR is Chris West (guitar), Keith Garrett (mandolin), Justin Moses (banjo, fiddle) and Tim Tipton (bass). Guest dobro-player Rob Ickes also joins in. Keith and Chris share the lead vocal duties, with Justin typically singing tenor.

"Where Wood Meets Steel" has twelve originals, eight of which were written by band members.
Chris West composed the right hot and snappy opener, "Dead Man on the Run." I also enjoyed "My Turn," written in the brother duet style reminiscent of groups like the Delmore Brothers in the 1930s. Garrett and West are more low and forlorn than they are high and lonesome, but the song still works for them. I was left pondering how the song would've turned out with high, soaring vocals, however. "I Don't Want to Hear it" has a nice hook and reminds me of Jim Lauderdale's songsmithing. Tragedy songs are fairly common in bluegrassdom, and "When the Mountain Fell Down" tells the story a fictional miner named Billy Joe and his death at the Fraterville Mine disaster in Tennessee. The event occurred in 1902, and 214 miners died as a result of an explosion inside the mine. West's understanding of the thematic stylings of this genre may best be captured on the "Highway of Despair" where the "highway's paved with agony, and every exit leads you into misery." Keith Garrett's best songwriting is demonstrated in "Moonshine Hard Times," about a moral churchgoing man who would make and sell moonshine but not drink it. Moses' fiery instrumental "Locust Hill" moves right along in high-stepping allegro fashion.

Keith, Chris and Tim are only in their early thirties. Keith Garrett has performed with The County Boys (that played Dollywood for six years), in a duo with Jay Clark, Browder Hollow, and Kentucky Wind. Chris West is a former member of Coal Creek, The Pitney Seibers Family, One Way Track, and Roscoe Morgan and Lonely Train. The youngest band member at only 22 years old, Justin Moses can pick any bluegrass instrument and still plays in his family's band, The Moses Family. Tim Tipton has played with Kentucky Wind and Clear Creek. Since the release of this album, I understand that the band has added
Lou Wamp on Scheerhorn resonator guitar and twin fiddle.

You hear many disparate influences in the music of Blue Moon Rising. Their traditional consciousness indicates a full understanding of Bill Monroe's and the Stanley Brothers'music. Yet, at the same time,
it's apparent that this group of young technicians have heard more recent innovative bluegrass ground-breakers like Tony Rice, Knoxville Grass, Boone Creek, Del McCroury, IIIrd Tyme Out, Lonesome River Band, Lou Reid, New Grass Revival, and Ricky Skaggs. With continued growth, strong support, plenty of hard work, and a little luck thrown in, we might be one day adding Blue Moon Rising to this list of seminal bluegrass influences. BMR has a wholly absorbing sound, one that will easily engross most listeners' attention. Always creative and entertaining, this up-and-coming band's signature sound is novel and immediately appealing. title: Completely different from anything else he's made.
text:
I really don't get why people talk so much smack about this album. Sure, it lacks the experimental quality of Ram, but it truely sounds like a band's first album. In that respect, a seasoned professional like Paul McCartney really succeeds. Wings Wild Life is intimate, unpolished, and maybe even a little crude.
On "Mumbo," Paul manages to put together a throat-shredding yet lyricless piece which is shocking (I can't imagine what his fans must have thought upon hearing this for the first time back in 1971!) but rather interesting. Yeah, "Bip Bop" IS pretty queer lyrically, but the vocal effect and guitar riff are nevertheless entrancing. The over 6 1/2-minute "Wild Life" is a song that Paul wrote after (as the lyrics clearly describe) walking through an African park and seeing a sign which read, "Remember: the animals have the right of way." I find it to be an incredible piece of music. Paul screams his lungs out, "WILD LIFE," as the band harmonizes beautifully, "whatever happened to?"--a nice clash of sound. The lyrical and instrumental buildup on this song is amazing. On "Some People Never Know," a sweet love song and another long one, Paul & Linda do a near-duet. The result is actually very nice. Linda handles most of the lead vocals on "I Am Your Singer" competently. A lot of people made fun of her vocal capabilities, but no one ever seemed to realize that her voice matched Paul's perfectly...despite the fact that he obviously overshadowed her skill-wise. The piano-based "Dear Friend" has the eeriest sound of any record Paul has ever made. Desolate & beautiful.
Bonus Tracks: Of all the bonus tracks to be included on the CD reissues of Paul's albums, the collection of these four is the best. You've got to admire a guy who has the stones to release a song such as "Mary Had A Little Lamb" as a single just to thumb his nose at the people who banned "Give Ireland Back To The Irish." "Little Woman Love" is a quick one that could sound right at home musically on the Beatles' Rubber Soul album. Then, of course, there's the beautifully melodic "Mama's Little Girl," a soft number which went unissued officially until 1990!

title: A wonderful set of jam-packed, long-running, cover-the-waterfront, cross-the-decades discs
text:
*** Note: Read the final sentence in this description. It is important. *** A superb set at a bargain price (sometimes listed as low as around a dollar fifty a disk). The facts: The first 12 disks are from the 1950s. The remaining 43 are from the 1960s through the early 2000s. All are of top-notch sound quality for the era in which they are recorded (and 1960s and later high-speed multi-track tape recording is at least as good as current digital recording--in fact many would say better). Equally impressive, Decca has jam-packed each disk to overflowing. Each disk not only includes a complete earlier album (a previously released vinyl LP for the disks before 1980 and a previously released CD for the later ones), but an added half-hour or more (sometimes much more) of "bonus" song material by the same performer or performers. Many of the 55 disks have a running time in the 70-minute range and a few push into the mid-80s. (I didn't even know you could fit 85-minutes of uncompressed music on a CD, but you clearly can, since they have!)

So much for the facts about the release. The performers and performances are, almost without exception, as good as studio recordings of whatever year get. Since they are studio recordings, there is not the danger and adrenaline rush of a live performance, of course, but in compensation there is the perfection of something performed and recorded over and over again in a studio until it is perfect. The names of the performers and the pieces speak for themselves. This is a series of opera All-Star games. Decca had the money and the commitment and found a way to sign most of the superstars of opera during this 60-year period. So that's who you will hear, performing the greatest arias, duets, and trios of the classical opera and, more rarely, the operetta repertory. What's not to like?

No librettos are included, and none are available on line to support the set as far as I can tell. But I mention the absence of lyrics in the accompanying booklet simply to find something negative to say. You can find most of the texts if you search the internet, and if you simply listen carefully enough to the tones, feelings, keys, and modulations, you don't really need a libretto, even if you don't speak Italian, French, or German. It's operatic love-, hate-, hope-, devotion-, fear-, and self-sacrifice-singing, after all; it's not math or physics. For anyone capable of being moved by music and the extraordinary expressive power and infinite emotional range of the human voice, this set is unequalled in the quality--and quantity--of the singing. Highly recommended from someone who is not easily pleased.

A postscript added a week or two later: My view of this set is unaltered, but it occurs to me that for opera babies, opera newbies, this may be too much of a good thing--too long, too demanding, too expensive, just too too much. If that is the case, I wanted to give you an alternative. Search, on Amazon, for "Opera Gold - 100 Great Tracks," a six-CD set released by the same company (Decca) more or less simultaneously with this one (and that remarkably enough does not overlap with it). It is shorter, and slightly easier, if you want to start in the shallow end of the pool and be sure you don't drown--or, to change the metaphor--bite off more than you can chew. I highly recommend it if you want or need a more manageable opera highlights listening project. It is just as wonderful as this set, but much shorter, and a bit more "war-horsey," with more of the most famous pieces--but just as superbly performed and recorded. Take your pick: the high-dive into the deep end (this set) or the wading pool that will let you work your way out more gradually and safely (the "Opera Gold" set). Or buy both, as I did, and don't regret doing. *** P.S. I am posting these facts on this page to describe this set accurately. But be sure to purchase the set not on this listing page but on the other Amazon page where the price is not totally wacky and out of line, as the one on this page is -- at least as of the date that I am making this posting. The other page is the right one to check out the price and make the oder from. ***

title: Awaiting My Destination in Time.
text:
This is the very first album that introduced me to ELT. And I must say: it made me an immediate fan.

The music that was displayed here was exceptationly beautiful. I noticed all sorts of unique instruments--like that heavy emphasis on the electric guitar. It made the album sound so much more distant in my opinion. Like how music was like in the 1980's--a time I didn't exist yet I might add. *Laughs*

Even if you don't understand/speak Japanese, the melodies, vocals and varied arrangement within the songs are enough to make you fall in love with this album. Believe me, not knowing the language shouldn't restrain you from listening to this amazing album.

I never expected to hear peaceful, yet heartfelt messages within these songs. The album itself seems to thrive on the concepts of the ups and downs of everyday relationship until it eventually leads to an end of that particular romance. The song "Time goes by", heavily emphasizes the theme of that sad fact:

"過ぎた日に背をむけずに
ゆっくり時間(とき)を感じて
いつかまた笑って
会えるといいね
Time goes by..."

"Unable to turn our backs on the days that had passed
I hope that someday
We can meet agin with a smile
Time goes by..."

"Time to destination" is one of those perfect albums where every track is as good as the last. I can easily see how this album became the 10th best-selling album in Japanese music history with 3,520,300 copies sold. The themes that are showcased within this album are so honest and real that it will never become boring--even after hundreds of listens! I can't think of one flaw that this album has--the music, the singing, the album art and the lyrics of the album all blend together and form a complete masterpiece that should be listened to by anybody that has even the slightest interest in 80s/90s pop music.

I have four superman soundtrack editions. The original 1987 cd release by warner, the 2 cd remaster released in 2000 by Rhino, The 8 CD Film Score Monthly version, and this 40th anniversary edition.

In this 40th anniversary remaster, the stereo image of the original recording is practically completely destroyed, as compared to any of the other versions.

To quantify the difference: In al the other versions, I can literally point to each instrument in the orchestra within the stereo image, tell you what instrument it is, and where it is compared to the other instruments in the orchestra. This is important especially in orchestral music, since composers commonly play instruments against each other. Hearing each instrument independently (string section, horn section, wind section, etc.) increases the drama of the music considerably.

But in this 40th anniversary remaster, I am presented with a "wall of sound", with all the instruments blended together and almost no delineation between them at all. Imagine what it's like to listen to music in headphones (everything sounds like it's a ball inside your head) and move that outside your head between the two speakers. That is what this soundtrack reminds me of. Absolutely, absolutely, terrible.

What an incredible shame.....

title: What a Monumental Waste of Talent
text:
"Bombastic" is not a word I would normally associate with Gershwin's "Porgy and Bess", but it's the word that came to my mind about four bars into the opening cut, "Summertime". I then immediately recalled the advice dispensed by Lester Young to jazz musicians when playing ballads: Know and understand the lyrics. Only then can you improvise inside the song. "Summertime" on this album is a runaway train, a real barn burner, and in my view totally loses the jazz soul of this wonderful opera.

What else can I say? For me, none of it gets better, and all of it makes me wish this wonderful music had been rearranged by someone more attuned to it, such as Ellington and/or Strayhorn.

Sure, there's some pretty playing, but not nearly enough to make up for the overbearing arrangements. Bill Evans at piano has virtually nothing to do, and for me, the "Jazz Soul of Porgy and Bess" is nowhere to be heard. I'd have given it one star, but added a second just because of the wonderful musicians on the band.

This review is not at all objective but is based on my taste and listening experience.

title: Fun Irish Film Music
text:

This was the perfectly peppy solution to midwinter blues.
It is true that my quest to obtain this elusive cd was fraught with heartbreak and misery. It is out of print and therefore incredibly rare and horrendously expensive. Do I regret paying nearly fifty dollars for this cd? Yes and no. Yes, my pride was hurt. It is hard to admit to spending so much on one soundtrack. But who could regret the hours of enjoyment and improved spirits one experiences from listening to such wonderful music?

title: Technically poor recording
text: Klara Wurtz’s playing of the complete Mozart piano sonatas, when compared to those recorded by Friedrich Gulda (with a Boesendorfer Imperial) in 1982 on audio tape and then restored to a certain level by Deutsche Grammophone, can be deemed very good; however, the work done by the recording engineer on these CDs is only poor and degrades that very good performance of Ms. Wurtz. This could also be due to the place (a café in Utrecht) where the sonatas were recorded. Recording solo piano is one of the most demanding jobs in the world, these CDs sound like they are recorded on cassette tapes, lacking any clarity and details, and the enormous reverberation effects due to the recording place also gives the sound a foggy nature. I would like to direct the classical piano lovers to an example on how solo piano can be recorded in a superb way:  “Pianist: Dubravka Tomsic, A Liszt Recital, IPO Recordings, Inc.” Please be warned that after you have a chance to hear (of course “not” listening to it with a handheld electronic gadget or through a computer) how actually the classical piano must be recorded as exemplified by the above CD, you may never go back and listen to your once favorite piano CDs, because 99.9% of those solo piano CDs we purchase with high hopes only came out to be recorded in a mediocre manner, by using sub par microphones and microphone placement techniques. To my opinion, Klara Wurtz should sit once again and record the complete sonatas with a more professional recording engineer in a professionally-checked hall; the world is in need of hearing such excellent pianists through better recorded CDs.

A wonder mix of power pop, "Americana" roots rock and alt-country from four of the original-era Cowsills (Bob, Paul, John and Susan) recorded circa 1993 but not released until 1998. Siblings Bill and Barry did not participate and mom Barbara passed away in 1985. They are joined by bassist Robby Sharf and occasional others.

The musicianship and production are outstanding and the vocal harmonies are great as always. At times, I'm reminded a bit of the Traveling Wilburys' albums, though the Cowsills are undeniably superior vocalists. In particular, Susan's lead vocals on several tracks shine as they subsequently would with the Continental Drifters and on her solo albums.

As with so much of the Cowsills' post-1971 work, this one seems to have flown under the commercial success radar. It's worth your attention.
