title: Besta Polka Youbetcha
text:
Released as an in-store special for Sam Goody and Musicland stores (I got my copy at the Staten Island Mall for a whopping 99 cents back in the day), this party-starter of a polka disc is as much a tribute to the king of Cleveland Style, Frankie Yankovic. He'd just released an album of duets with fellow accordionists and folks influenced by his style and four of this disc's eight tracks come from that release.

There's not a bum track in the lot! "Weird Al" Yankovic and band polkacize Queen with "Bohemian Polka", Jimmy Sturr takes on Smokie's "Living Next Door to Alice" (cleaning up British fans' chants accompanying the original), and Frank meets with Eddie Blazonczyk ("In Heaven There Is No Beer"), Weird Al ("Whole Stole the Keeshka"), and norteno legend Little Joe Hernandez ("Just Because Polka").

A bit of indie cred comes from Brave Combo's "Flying Saucer".

Far too short, this comp of "happy snappy" tunes is sure to liven up any gathering, and belongs in any self-respecting polka hall's jukebox.

title: HIGH QUALITY lp VERSION OF RHIESE BEAUTIFUL WORKS
text: I HEARD WHAT I THINK was one of the first performances od Ode to the West Wind  at the Albert Hall in London in 1964. Performed by Janos Strarker and The London Symphony. I was smitten by the beauty of the Work and the playing. The richness of the orchestration, the lyricism of the Cello lines are amazing. The other work on this LP is the violin Concerto by Henze also: It predates the Cello work by five years and therefore is one of the first works for solo inhstrument and orchestra in his oeuvre. It also predates his serial period. One word about these labels : "serial", "dodecaphonic" which are indiscriminately applied to such varied composers as Schonberg, Berg, Webern and even Stravinsky... One may find the serial compositions of Schonberg difficult to appreciate, but also fall in love with works of Berg, his violin concerto, in particular and be seduced by certain works of Webern and Stravinsky after his  serial period began. The same can be said of Henze who, for the major part of his career remained within the bounds of "tonal"  music. His works may be experimental, but never painful to hear: the richness of his orchestration is always admirable and the energy of his music always amazing. A twentieth Century composer to be discovered by most twentyfirst century listeners: his works are rarely heard in our concert halls. Discover them on recordings: Deutsche Gramophon has published a complete set of their recordings of this major composer!

title: The Late Loren Maazel Knew How to Draw Optimum Dramatic Effect from Beethoven's Opera to Thrilling Impact
text:
Many critics, and the listeners whom they influence, downgrade the worth of this supremely exciting recording of Beethoven's "Fidelio" (in the usual final version of the score). Well, they are wrong! It is true that Otto Klemperer's recording is very beautiful, and it features the incomparable Jon Vickers as Florestan among the well cast soloists, but even Klemperer's recording reeks too much of the overly-devout, oratorio-like quality of far too many performances (whether recorded in the studio or in the theatre) of this work. "Fidelio" is an OPERA (even if there is some spoken dialogue), a real music drama, NOT an oratorio or cantata!

Loren Maazel really digs into the music, driving the music forward relentlessly to thrillingly theatrical effect! There is no doubting, under Maazel's baton, that indeed this is a stage work, one as fervently dramatic as any in the standard repertoire. Bergit Nilsson's voice, singing Leonore, rings out with blazingly heroic impact; she is heard in some live recordings of "Fidelio", under other conductors' direction, interpreting her part at higher levels of histrionic intensity than in this studio recording under Maazel's direction, but most buyers will prefer Maazel's excitingly conducted recording with her in the role in stereo sound that so vividly has more sonic "presence". Her partner, tenor James McCracken, in subsequent recordings that he made seldom sounded so good as he does here; as Florestan he powerfully rises to the considerable challenge of partnering a soprano of so clarion a voice as Nilsson.

Yes, Klemperer, and some other conductors too, have shaped the score's orchestral detail more exquisitely, but nearly always in musical performance contexts that vitiate the dramatic impact which Beethoven surely intended. Maazel, on the other hand, while perhaps at times driving rough-shod over some minutiae of orchestral detail (at least compared to "Dr. Klemps"), ignites the thrilling drama that so imbues this great music. Okay, get the Klemperer recording too (which has many beauties and is sung by a superb cast of vocal soloists), but buy Maazel's recording first!

title: Very special - for all the wrong reasons
text:
I was over my mom's this evening and her radio was turned on to the local classical music station. Right after a Mozart Piano concerto ended (which turned out to be #8), immediately I heard the notes to Wagner's Prelude to Act I of Die Meistersinger von Nurnberg. It didn't take long before I was completely transfixed...because while I recognized all the notes, there was nothing else recognizable about this performance. In the place of the exuberance we're all used to hearing, it offered neutrality. In the place of the energy that pervades this Prelude/Overture, it offered routine. At times it sounded as if the orchestra was playing the music together for the first time (and collectively marveling that it all came together). No collective spirit enveloped the musicians.

It totally captured my attention and I could not stop listening. As it limped to the finish line, I had to know who was responsible for this, so I anxiously stood close to the radio to hear the announcer tell us whose performance this was. I said to my mom and husband, "This is not coming from any of the K-conductors (Karajan, Kempe, Knappertsbusch, Klemperer, Keilberth, Kurtwangler, etc.), nor a German orchestra the way they're playing this. I have no idea who this is."

The announcer intoned, "That was Wagner's Prelude to Die Meistersinger von Nurnberg, performed by the Minnesota Orchestra conducted by Neville Marriner."

I can't say this is in Florence Foster Jenkins territory. But it's not far from it either.

title: Valuable historical recording with terrible sound quality
text:
I hope you never hear a recording with worse sound quality than this performance, conducted by Toscanini at Salzburg in 1937. It has nearly every flaw imaginable: hiss, flutter, wow, cracks, pops, assorted coughs, an extraordinarily limited frequency range, and a muddy texture. None the less, this is the only recording we have of Toscanini conducting a Mozart opera, and we are fortunate to have it.

Music lovers born in the latter part of the 20th century probably don't realize the fame and popularity of Toscanini in the popular culture of the early and middle part of the century. Can you imagine a major television network today hiring a classical music conductor for millions of dollars, paying for him to have his own symphony orchestra, and making his concerts an integral part of their prime time programming? Was Toscanini great enough to warrant such fame? That depends on "matters of taste", which can not be argued in a logical manner. In my opinion: if you enjoy Verdi, you need to have every recording Toscanini made of Verdi's music to know what it should sound like (in spite of his penchant for imperfect and pedestrian soloists). If Beethoven is your primary interest, stick with Mengleberg, Furtwangler, v. Karajan, Weingartner, Bernstein, Kempe, et al, as your taste dictates.

If you can listen through the terrible sound quality, his conducting on this recording is interesting to consider. It has Toscanini's hallmark characteristics: it is vigorous, precise and has great integrity. I think a little more charm and humor (not characteristics that he was known for) would have made this a better performance.

Unfortunately, the soloists (with the exception of Kipnis and Domgraf-Fassbaender) are neither interesting nor pleasant. Helge Rosvaenge (Tamino) was never an elegant singer. In Verdi and in verismo roles, he could sing with vigor and elan. Here he sounds awkward and un-princely. Julie Osvath is probably the worst Queen of the Night recorded. She does all right in the slow parts, but when you get to the coloratura, the train goes off the tracks (Florence Foster Jenkins anyone?). Jarmila Novotna was a well regarded singer (primarily in late 19th and early 20th century works) in the `30s & 40's. As Pamina she sings well enough, but seems uninvolved.

Willi Domgraf-Fassbaender, as Papageno, has a light, pleasant voice, which he uses to excellent effect. One of the very best bird catchers (as nearly as I can tell). The great Ukranian bass, Alexander Kipnis, uses his deep and sonorous voice to give us a great Sarastro in spite of the slowest tempo I have ever heard for "Isis und Osiris". (If you want to hear just how good the famous bass arias of opera can sound, listen to the recordings made by Kipnis in 1930/31.)

The bottom line? This is a recording which you will study with interest rather than listen to with pleasure.

Been fascinated by Ray and Peter for ages ever since I first heard the original "Shut up Little Man" single disk. Had high hopes for this set and was fortunate enough to be given the box set as a gift recently. Have to say I really wish the person had saved their (large amount of) money, this was a complete disappointment.

Not sure what a previous reviewer found exceptional about the sound quality - I think it's pretty poor and not comparable to the original at all.

Unless you are interested in hearing hours of the traffic around the apartment, background noise and occasional commentary by the folks doing the recording, there is NOTHING here that warrants the outlay of cash being asked for this set.

Even the interview of Peter and Tony - which was one of the most compelling reasons for buying the set - is a complete snooze. The pair clearly had long since passed their capacity for providing anything interesting, mostly it's a conversation about their dogs, and their dogs, and - oh yes - their dogs. Some stuff about Ray and a few other things but sadly nothing terribly remarkable.

The packaging is DIY for the most part - not even a box for the "Box Set" at least in my case, which for the price is pretty ridiculous.

Finally - $70 bucks for this set????? Give me a break. The production costs were virtually nothing, the product and it's packaging are bargain basement at best, and the seller didn't even have anything to do with the performance. Anyway you get the point, IMO the price is insane.

So in conclusion - if you love the original "Shut up Little Man" stick with it - you've pretty much got what you are going to get, plus you'll save yourself quite a bit of money.

text:
I had a lot of trouble with this. Enjoying it, that is. And considering that I am quite a fan of Brahms' music, and in particular his chamber pieces, this is surprising. I am not such the expert, as other commentators on Amazon, but my impression of this CD, it's key problem, was that it was a poorly recorded, or transferred. The microphones seemed to be in the wrong places; the instruments, especially the piano, sounded too strong, and out of place very frequently. There is no problem with the purity of the sound itself, though.

Another problem here was the music itself. I don't think that these three pieces are among the finest of Brahms' chamber work. Actually, I think they are among the weakest. I enjoyed the third, opus 60 the best, although opus 26, the second was interesting. And I am trying to interpret these works *through* this recording, my only of these three Piano Quartets, not simply with their aid. (Which makes it more difficult.) Nonetheless, I know Brahms can be cool and astringent sometimes, aloof, but here I thought at times he was more than melancholic, to the point of being sullen, even mordant.

There may be an issue with the interpretation by the Borodin Trio [with help on the viola]... but I am unable to decipher any, though it may exist. My complaint is, in conclusion, is, minimally, with the recording/transfer, and then..._the works themselves._
If interested, I would try another Quartet, possibly another recording studio, unfortunately.

title: historically significant but musically and sonically sub-par Bartok
text:
This recording of Bartok's Violin Concerto by Max Rostal and Sir Malcolm Sargent conducting the LSO has an unquestionable historical significance. Released in 1951 on Decca, it was the first version to be published on LP, and, if my information is correct, only the second recording ever, after the recording premiere of Menuhin and Dorati conducting the Dallas SO in 1946, now on [[ASIN:B00000E6PB Violin Concerto 2]] (the invaluable live recording of the premiere performance, in March 1939, by Zoltan Szekely and Willem Mengelberg, resurfaced publicly only in 1970, from Szekely's private archive, [[ASIN:B00008FJJ4 Bartok: Violin Concerto No. 2]]). Retrospective has their dates wrong, though: they give the recording date as October 1951, which is impossible, since the LP was reviewed in the Gramophone issue of June. There is somewhere on the net a stupendous discography in .pdf form of the London Symphony Orchestra which I've downloaded, and the info is there, plus more: producer Peter Olof, engineer Kenneth Wilkinson, recorded in Kingsway Hall 30-31 October 1950.

Unfortunately, the recording's interpretive and sonic values are not up to its historical significance. In fact, it must rank as the - shall I say "worst"? let's settle for "least recommendable" version I've ever heard. Sonically, one good point: these are not dubs from LPs, but officially licensed transfers from whatever tapes Decca provided: no surface noise, and no obtrusive tape hiss. It is, unfortunately, the original sonics that are badly flawed, with a close up violin (which is fine) and an orchestra that seems to be playing in the next room, or caught from an poor air-check from the early 1950s, or again pre-recorded and played-back on a poor loudspeaker in a rustic attempt at overdubbing. Some instruments are artificially spotlighted - the opening harps in the first movement, celesta in the second, triangle and snare drum in the finale - while the rest sounds, at best, ghostly distant, and at worst, inaudible - with no perceptible logic as to when one and when the other. This is the next worst thing after music minus one - only here it is solo minus an orchestra.

Interpretively, although Rostal was closely associated in those years with Bartok's Concerto, being its introducer to the UK and playing it numerous times, he has very much an "old-school" approach to it, a view that from day one was entirely out-of-situation in this work, as magnificently demonstrated by Szekely and Mengelberg, and even (though to a lesser extent) by Menuhin and Dorati. You can hear constant adumbrations of the old-fashioned portamento. You'd think you were hearing Misha Elman. But worst than that are the tempos in the outer movements, so deliberate, reined in and cautious as to sound impossibly sluggish. And that this is no mere subjective impression is shown by the timings: it takes Rostal 17:30 to get through the first movement, which turns the movement's lyricism into a mood that verges on the plangent. Bartok's VC, plangent? Now something surely is wrong here. Compare to Szekely's fiery 14:33 (and Gitlis in circa 1954 was as fiery, in 14:40, [[ASIN:B000001KC1 The Art of Ivry Gitlis]]) and Menuhin's more leisurely but still acceptable 15:34. On the positive side, this approach at least doesn't "sectionalize" the Concerto as Menuhin does with his large tempo variances; Rostal's slower sections don't register as abruptly slower than the faster ones. Still, this is Bartok for the old people in the retirement home. The finale? Szekely a hair-raising 10:21, Gitlis a hair-raising 10:49, Menuhin a comparatively more restrained but still energetic enough 11:33 - and Rostal a perfunctory 12:18, despite some fine expressive points in the "grazioso" passages. From what the sonics let you hear, Sargent whips the orchestra to fine snap sometimes - but not always either, and rarely enough to offset the impression of sluggishness born of those all-too cautious tempos. Some wrong entries were also left unedited in the finale (9:33). Rostal is tonally and technically OK, although he isn't a first-class virtuoso: his harmonics at 10:47 in the finale are off-pitch and his first-movement cadenza very fussy - whether it is by musical choice or just from trying to conceal some technical limitations behind exaggerated "expression" is hard to tell, and I would incline for the latter.

Rostal is best in the middle "andante", where Bartok's gossamer orchestration is less dis-served by Decca's sonics, and where the fiddler is relatively free of sentimental exaggerations. All this might have provided an interesting, if quite wrong-headed "alternative interpretive view" of the Concerto (interesting for the completists, that is), hadn't the orchestral sonics been so poor.

Beethoven's Kreutzer is much better, sonically (despite some stranges splices)and interpretively. My only qualm would be an excessively slow statement of the theme in the middle movement. Rostal made a series of recordings, with his partner Franz Osborn, of Beethoven's Violin and Piano Sonatas, for Decca, in the late-forties and -78rmp years and early fifties. I don't know if they recorded the complete ten. I am happy to have been able to hear Rostal's Bartok because of its historical significance and I am grateful to Retrospective (although nowhere indicated on the CD, it is a historical sub-label from the Dutch budget label Brilliant Classics) for making it available, although this is a highly specialized kind of gratitude that I doubt can extend to many other music lovers. In truth, Rostal's memory would have been better served if Retrospective had reissued more of the Beethoven, along with the Brahms Scherzo, an earlier recording from 1949, transferred from the 78rpm, with good instrumental definition and a fair amount of surface noise.

title: jazzman
text:
Beautiful, gorgeous interpretations of some of the great Antonio Carlos Jobim's
best known (and not so well known) songs with arranging and accompaniment by
his son and grandson, Paulo and Daniel, that wonderfully complement Lisa Ono's
voice and style. Had never heard of Ono before this, but am a fan now. She re-
minded me many times on this recording of the late, great Brazilian songbird Elis
Regina ("The Hurricane" as they called her in Brazil), who was also a magnificent
interpreter (and frequent collaborator with Jobim) of his music and art before her
tragic death. Ono does a sublime version of a lesser known Jobim tune called "A
Correnteza" (The Stream), which I first heard on his fabulous "Urubu" album from
1976. The great Brazilian singer Miucha also contributes her voice on this track,
as well as on "Samba do Aviao" - first became aware of Miucha from the previously
mentioned "Urubu" album with her duet with Jobim on the classic tune "Boto" (Por-
poise). "Two Kites", which I had only heard before on Jobim's staggeringly romantic
"Tera Brasilis" album from 1980, is included as well, this time with the lead vocal
by Daniel Jobim. "Sabia" (Song of the Sabia), "Falando de Amor" (Speaking of Love),
and "Samba de Uma Nota So" (One Note Samba), all three included on "Tera Brasilis"
as well, are all here in beautiful versions by Ono. My all time favorite Jobim piece,
"Fotographia" (Photograph), is here and sung flawlessly by Ono, along with eight
other Jobim masterpieces, all sung to brilliant perfection in the original Portuguese
lyrics. With stellar backing by piano, bass, drums, flute, clarinet, trombone, guitar,
and cellos, this is a marvelous work of art from beginning to end. After this most
pleasant introduction to Lisa Ono and her bossa nova style, I will be adding more
of her cd's to my collection. Bravo!

title: What a Major Disappointment
text:
As someone who has been a Willie Nile fan since the release of his first album, I anxiously look forward to hearing anything he puts out.His last two releases have been excellent and probably some of his best work ever.

Live at the Turning Point is something else entirely. Its a poorly recorded, amateurish release that no one except completists should shell out $15 or more for. I was stunned when I listened to this by the awful sound. Its as if someone with a 1970's tape recorder and a single microphone walked into the club and placed it on a table in front of the band and hit 'play'. The percussion sound (are those drums or garbage cans the guy is hitting?) is hideous, the between song banter often obscured by crowd noise, and the performance itself just fair. I've seen Willie many times, including 3 times last year at SXSW and any of those shows were far better than this allegedly 'legendary' performance.

I don't like when artists do large amounts of overdubs to make live albums sound better, but when the other end of the spectrum is just to release something 'as is' with no effort made at all to make the listening experience more enjoyable, its even worse. Willie should be ashamed of himself for letting something like this get released. Its an insult to his fans and a complete rip off.

I am relatively confident that fans could source better live shows from the 'Streets of New York' shows on the internet without having to pay good money. I am all for supporting artists, especially ones who are as woefully overlooked as Willie Nile, but even that has its limits, and 'Live at the Turning Point' is not worth buying.

title: Great album, horrid remastering, irrelevant bonus tracks
text:
Those pop culture curators and preservationists over at Rhino usually do a fantastic job of remastering and repackaging old classics for the new century (see, for example, the excellent reissues of The Stooges, Gram Parsons, The Cure, etc.). Unfortunately, they completely and totally butchered the sound on this otherwise fantastic folk-psychedelic gem.

I am not an audiophile so forgive my non-technical description but basically they cranked up the bass which muddies and overwhelms the vocals, guitars, horns, and strings--essentially all other sounds. Further diminishing the sound is their unnecessary separation of said instuments: you have the acoustic guitars isolated to, and hence, coming out of only the left speaker, the horns coming out the right one, etc. This has the effect of providing neither good mono nor good stereo but some sort of crappy offspring of both.

Given the fact that the bonus tracks are ho-hum at best, you'd do best to seek out the now out-of-print original issue. It's cheaper and the sound quality is better by some distance. (I'll give the Rhino folks one mulligan or two, but please don't ever ruin one of my favorite albums like this again!)

text:
JOHN DAVIDSON CLOSE UP, Accord SN 7202 junk Lp reissue

Uh, this is one of those so bad it's good easy listening contemporary turkey albums. The thing looked horrible (c. September, 1982), not-right song selection, but probably a vanity/private press album of a lounge lizard pop sold after the artist's ("artist" qualified) gig in a casino bar's gift shop. The tuxedo drawing also hinted at dated middle-of-the-road out-of-touch sheer awfulness contained in the vinyl grooves.

Nope, but almost there; it's an oldie that is packaged to look like a new-ie title, with two tracks lopped off.

Song selection:
side one--
Hey, Good Lookin'
More
Once in a Lifetime
Love Me Forever
Blame It On My Youth
side two--
I'll Take Romance
I Wish You Love
Then I'll Be Tired of You ("tired" is misspelled "tried" on the back cover song listings)
Run To Him
I Want to Be With You

I figured either this was a new Bad music contemporary album by a fading star, but a couple songs jumped out at me that suggested it was dated ...for 1982: "Run To Him," a Bobby Vee (November, 1961) song, "I Wish You Love" on one of my 1959-ish Keely Smith Capitol albums, and that lounge lizard "More" song. Ditto: reissue.

This Lp is a 10 track abbreviated (missing "Two Sleepy People" and "Snowbound") repackage of John Davidson's THE WARM SOUND OF JOHN DAVIDSON Lp on Colpix CP-485 Lp vinyl album, from October, 1964 [[ASIN:B004MKBCME John Davidson: The Young Warm Sound Of John Davidson [VINYL LP] [STEREO]]]. And the back cover liner notes make no mention you're buying another churning of old CBS Pictures/TV spinoff Colpix "for-youth" pop back catalog from 18 years past. While the music contained is excruciating, the sound reproduction, pressing quality, is GORGEOUS for a budget bin reissue.

I'd give a budget bin masquerading as a "new" album preying on unsuspecting fans like this a one-star normally, but I'm taken by how HORRIFICALLY AWFUL the over-cooked music, the sheer rottenness of overly bright and unsubtle the arrangements, performances, and Davidson's studied caterwauling are on this turkey.

title: Revealing Beethoven!
text:
Bruno Walter at the front of the NYP achieved during the first years of the Fifties, a notable conductorial shift. His Brahms Second ( my desert island choice of this Opus) and Fourth symphonies are crucial evidences or the historical Mozart cycle (available in Sony France) talk by themselves about his galvanic intensity and powerful expressiveness.

The Second finds him in good shape. Vibrating and lyrical; despite it has not the ferociousness of Toscanini with the NBC or the authoritarian reading of Reiner with the Pittsburgh, B.W. gets to manage the balance between the Dyonisian breadth and the Apollinean flow.

The Fourth, is specially interesting. Walter depicts with admirable eloquence the inner tension of the beginning of the first movement. The rest of the work is displayed with sumptuous grandness and flamboyant atmosphere.

P.D. I'd like to remark with emphasis this fact because I don't buy his approach about the Fifth, Seventh and Eighth Symphonies. I think his best reading of the Sixth was made with the Philadelphia during the late forties and respect the Ninth he achieved a special peak with the notorious live perfomance from 1947 with the LPO.

title: The Revolution betrayed by the Red Army and Paris Opera choruses
text:
Revolutions and ideological concerns rarely produce good music - or maybe it is just because it is badly played. This Adda CD bears no copyright year, the recording must have been made on the occasion of the concert mentioned in the liner notes on July 2, 1989, and the CD was reviewed in the French Diapason issue of May 1991, which points to a belated release by Adda. It uses the combined forces of the Paris Opera and the Red Army Choruses (and remember, the latter were still Soviet back then - the former probably still are today), and the Wind Band of the City of Le Havre. It offers a selection of military marches, overtures and symphonies for Wind Band and of revolutionary hymns - three by Gossec, "Chant du 14 Juillet", composed for the first anniversary of Bastille Day, "Peuple, Eveille-toi !" (People, Awake!) written for the translation of the remains of Voltaire to the Pantheon Church on 11 July 1791, and what is announced as his orchestration of the Marseillaise, and Méhul's "Chant du depart", composed in July 1794 for the celebration of the decisive victory of the Republican army at the battle of Fleurus. With only four numbers for chorus, the disc's title, "Revolution in the Choir", is something of a misnomer. The minimal liner notes just give short biographical info on the Le Havre band and two choruses, but say absolutely nothing of the works, and don't even give the first names of the composers, just initials. But after all we are not dealing with W.A. Mozart or L.v. Beethoven. How many music lovers will know off-the-cuff that C.S. Catel is Charles-Simon, F.J. Gossec François-Joseph, E.N. Méhul Etienne-Nicolas, L.E. Jadin Louis-Etienne (not to be confused with his brother Hyacinthe), and add the even more obscure Michel-Joseph Gebauer and Frédéric Duvernoy?

Likewise, the credits show that all these pieces are played in modern orchestrations, but nothing is said of their nature. Most are credited to Désiré Dondeyne, the longtime conductor of the Wind Band of the Paris Police. Sometimes he is credited as arranger, sometimes as orchestrator, and sometimes even both (Gossec's "Chant du 14 juillet"), and in the case of the "Pas de Manoeuvre" (Marching Drill) of Duvernoy and Gebauer and the Military March and Symphony of Catel tracks 2-4 and 6, he appears both as arranger and under the cryptic designation of "reconstitution", but we are not told what exactly was reconstituted. Two of the arrangements, of Louis Jadin's Symphony (track 5) and Gossec's Symphony (track 10), are by a J. Molenaar. And in the case of Chant du Départ and Marseillaise, conductor Philippe Langlet added his own layer of cream by further adapting Dondeyne's arrangements for Mixed and Men's Chorus.

No information being given about them, I wondered where these symphonies and overtures came from, and what those modern orchestrations were about. Had they set for wind band works originally written for full symphony orchestra? Did the overtures come from operas, and in which case, which ones? Likewise, I wondered about Gossec's Marseillaise. Gossec is often referred to for his orchestration of Rouget de Lisle's song, the most famous one before Berlioz'. But I wondered why the Adda CD played Dondeyne's orchestration of Gossec's orchestration of Rouget's song, and not Gossec's. It is also the case with another CD with a very similar program, [[ASIN:B000009IGC Les Grands Hymnes Revolutionnaires (Erato)]], the compilation of 19 revolutionary hymns and military marches with the Wind Band of the Paris Police (Orchestre d'Harmonie des Gardiens de la Paix de Paris) under Claude Pichaureau, published by Erato in 1989, which shares the four choral pieces that are on Adda, as well as the two Pas de Manoeuvre of Duvernoy and Gebauer. But, researching on that, I had been puzzled not to find any trace of a publication, recent or not, of Gossec's original score. So what exactly was Dondeyne's orchestration in relation to Gossec's original?

These might seem to be very petty details, and they are if you just want to hear the music for what it offers, without any concern about sources and authenticity. But sometimes you start pulling on a minuscule thread of wool that's sticking out and sweater shirt and pants start unraveling in your hands.

I'll refer the reader interested in those matters to the review - rather, a lengthy essay on the sources of the Marseillaise and other revolutionary songs - that I published under the Erato CD. But to make this long story short(er), it turns out that what Dondeyne did was simply to orchestrate a piano reduction of Gossec's score, made by an archivist of the Paris Conservatoire, Constant Pierre, at the end of the 19th Century. This admirable man spent years locating all the original sources of all the revolutionary hymns and band music played at the official ceremonies in the 1790 decade, researching in the various libraries of France, even pushing his investigations to the British Library and Royal Library in Berlin. Most of this sheet music remained in the form of scores for voice only or voice and keyboard, some of them as instrumental parts, a few in the composer's original autograph or manuscript scores. Pierre published the scores in 1899, but, for reasons of practicality, with piano reductions of the orchestral or band accompaniment (when scores or parts existed). In a complementary volume published in 1904 he listed all the locations of the original material.

So Dondeyne could have gone to Bibliothèque nationale or the Library of the Conservatoire to consult the original sources (in which case his "orchestration" would have been limited to rescoring for modern tuba the instrument then known as the "serpent", whose role was to double and reinforce the bassoons and that was replaced by the Ophicléide in the 1820s - this will ring a bell with fans of Berlioz played on period instruments - before the invention of the tuba in the mid-1830s). But evidently, he didn't, and this is clearly shown by his orchestration of precisely The Marseillaise.

When Rouget de Lisle wrote his song, then known as the "War Song for the Army of the Rhine", in April 1792, its success was so blazing that within a few weeks it shot to Marseilles, and from there to Paris, now called indifferently the Song, Air, Hymn or March of the Marseillais, and where everybody sung it and wanted to hear it. As was the custom back then, Gossec turned it, with a few other revolutionary songs, into a lyric scene called first "Hymne à la liberté" then "Offrande à la liberté", and first played at the Paris Opera on 2 October 1792. THAT is Gossec's original orchestration, and it is NOT for wind band but for symphony orchestra.

A year later, for the Celebration of the first anniversary of the King's emprisonment on 10 August 1793 (they sure did have a sense of the occasion in those days), Gossec wrote a second orchestration of Rouget's song, now for wind band and for outdoor performance. Curiously, it was set to other words than Rouget's original stanzas, written for the occasion by a "citizen Varon" whose first name seems to have been lost by History. That orchestration (with Rouget's original words) became the official version of the song (made to the national anthem of France in 1795), the one that was played at the official ceremonies, and would be as "authentic" as the first one, even with the stanzas of Rouget reattributed to it.

Then in 1798, another Gossec version was printed, an arrangement for wind band of the 1792 operatic version, limited to three out of Rouget's six stanzas. The original parts, apparently once in the possession of Constant Pierre, are now kept at the Music and Theatre Library of Sweden. But Constant Pierre having published a piano reduction, THAT apparently is what Dondeyne re-orchestrated, using an instrumentation way more lavish and abundant than Gossec’s.

Most listeners will probably have little interest for these arcane matters of "authenticity", and will only want to know if the compositions, whatever the authenticity of their orchestration, and Langlet's interpretations of them, are enjoyable. Not always.

The worst is Méhul's "Chant du départ". Whatever Dondeyne's orchestration, Langlet's arrangement of it gives a badly corrupt and distorted idea of the original work and the composer's intent. Chant du départ was an important revolutionary hymn, as successful if not more than Rouget's Marseillaise, and it almost made it as France's national anthem. The original hymn has 7 stanzas all followed by the refrain sung by chorus, but the interesting point is that each stanza and ensuing chorus is ascribed to a specific and different character: "a representative of the people" and chorus of warriors, a mother and chorus of mothers, two elderly men and chorus, a child and chorus, a wife-chorus, maiden, and three warriors followed by general chorus. So, evidently, Méhul intended each stanza and refrain to be sung by different soloists and sections of the chorus, including children.

But Langlet doesn't do that. The song duly starts with the tenor, Leonid Pchenitchni, but, presumably because he needed to employ his two choirs, Russian and French, Langlet attributes the solo lines before the refrain to the Russians, and the refrain to mixed chorus (but the women are so overpowered by the men that they are hardly audible anyway). Then he has the verse of the mother sung not by a female solo but by full woman's chorus, the last line before refrain again by the Russians and again the refrain by mixed chorus. Then, instead of seguing directly into the next stanza, he repeats the long orchestral intro, and tenor Pchenitchni sings again a last verse, but in truth I can't say which one, because he's singing it... in Russian! I guess you can call it a hymn to people's fraternity, but what a hopeless jumble. If you want even an approximation of Méhul's original conception for Chant du départ, Pichaureau is better but still unsatisfactory, as he cuts three of the stanzas and divides the rest between only male and female soloist, the latter suitably matronly for the wive but much too much for the child. It is Plasson, despite using a modern orchestration for full romantic symphony orchestra, who gives you a much more faithful idea ([[ASIN:B00000DQY2 Revolution Francaise / Music of The French Revolution / Michel Plasson (EMI)]]).

And to that, add the interpretation. That the orchestra and chorus should be so grandiloquent, OK, I can accept it, it is not entirely out-of-sync with the meaning of the words and music. But tenor Pchenitchni! He's awful. Suitably stentorian and somewhat nasal, and I'm sure his Russian accent is perfect, but his French accent is comical. He should have sung it all in Russian.

The Marseillaise is not much better. Well, at least, we don't have to suffer Pchenitchni, since Langlet has it all sung by the chorus, which is a permissible option (Gossec's 1793 version for wind band, to the words of citizen Varon, was scored for three-part men's chorus, and even the 1792 version left the option of having the solo line sung by unissono chorus), although a much less appealing one than with solo verse and chorus refrain. But Langlet's version (reduced, as all the 1798 Gossec version and Dondeyne-derived versions that I've heard, to three stanzas) wouldn't have been as offensive had his choral forces not been so bad. The liner notes rhetorically ask "how do you squeeze two hundred and seventy musicians into a rehearsal hall in Le Havre"? Well, not very effectively I am afraid. The choruses are loud, tonally unrefined, poor in ensemble, thick and lacking transparency, making the words often incomprehensible (and the Soviets are given the first stanza of the Marseillaise, and they sing it with Russian accents), and the women sound tremulous and old, the worst of the French choral tradition. Sure, in a revolutionaly and war context, that's exactly what you expect and want a chorus to be: guts and brawn, not elegance and refinement. But again, as a purely musical experience, this is very unrewarding.

In "Chant du 14 juillet" Langlet and his forces sing only three verses out of the hymn's six - and thank God, because the 7:44 minutes it takes them, at Langlet's funeral tempo, are already way too long. In the Marseillaise and Chant du 14 juillet, Pichaureau on Erato is much preferable. Strangely, it is the other way around in "Peuple, éveille-toi", because there it is Pichaureau who takes it at an impossibly funeral tempo (it isn't a funeral march, it is a call to revolt!) and Langlet who, despite his choruses' untidiness, is true to the song's enthusiastic and martial accents. That said, I defy anybody to understand what they are singing, except for a few words here and there ("liberté!" comes out clearly, so you get the gist of it). No texts are provided.

Ultimately, if the hymns are your main interest, this is not the place where to stop. Pichaureau offers much more and, with the exception of "Peuple...", much better played. Langlet makes the music sound terribly grandiloquent, more than it needs to be. His program of overtures, marches and symphonies for winds is slightly better, if only because we are now rid of the impossible singers, and also because it offers the opportunity to hear rarely played works from that era. It turns out that all those symphonies and overtures were indeed origially scored for wind band. As the hymns, they were written for the official ceremonies and were published with them in regular collections, documented by Constant Pierre who also provides the scores with piano reductions. What the track listing simply calls Gossec's "Symphonie" is in fact his "Symphonie militaire", in three movements. Despite their title, those of Catel and Jadin are no more than Overtures. It's not great music - the two "Pas de manoeuvre" and the "Military March" are exactly suited to their purpose, music to whip up the troups and get them marching in time - but some of it is fun. In fact, other than the brassy orchestration, some don't even sound specifically military. Catel's Symphony and Overture in C are especially felicitous, and wouldn't be out of place in a Rossini opera. They are all the more valuable as very little of Catel is represented on CD.

That said, Langlet can be taken only as a stopgap. In the Marches, he is acceptable. Duvernoy's Marching Drill is slightly more lively with Pichaureau than with him but not decisively so, and Gebauer's is played more playfully by Pichaureau (music for an equestrian parade of prancing horses by the Republican Guard), more militarily by Langlet, and both approaches are legitimate. But that's the smaller fare. Without any competition it is always harder to judge an interpretation, but I am in no doubt that there is space for far more animation than Langlet brings to Catel's indication "très animé" at the top of his Sympony, and more vivacity in the "allegro vivace" of the Overture. By the same token, I didn't need to go the the competing version of Gossec's Military Symphony by John Wallace ([[ASIN:B0000037CU Berlioz: Grande symphonie funèbre et triomphale]]) to detect that Langlet's "larghetto" seemed terribly slumbering - surely a "larghetto" at the end of the 18th century shouldn't be played as a largo - and that he played the finale as a moderato parading march, which doesn't sound totally absurd but is certainly contradictory with Gossec's "Allegro" indication. Wallace resoundingly confirmed the impression, and proved how much more lively and exciting Gossec sounds played at the right tempi. I can accept that Langlet's very solemn tempo in the first movement conforms better to Gossec's "Allegro maestoso" than Wallace's vivacious and lightfooted one, but the music sounds so much better with Wallace, and his less brassy, more woodwindy orchestration (not by Dondeyne) is also far more characterful.

So I'll be keeping this disc in my collection mainly for the Catel Overture and Symphony and the Jadin Symphony. That's about 18 minutes of music out of the CD's none-too-generous 58.

title: Generally excellent
text:
I didn't listen yet to all the 20 CDs (I would never have written a review of this box if I had to). yet, for what I've heard this is a generally excellent recording, with a very healthy tendency towards directness and no nonsense (The Well-Tempered Klavier, the French Overture (by the way, if you don't know András Schiff's 1978 recording of the French Overture and you love this work, it is really the one with the most flexibility, joy and drive), some Preludes and Fugues, the Art of the Fugue, the Toccatas, are exceptional) but (for lack of a better transition), somehow one can fell where Ivo Janssen absolutely loves what he plays, where he does not have the same level of intimacy with the works as Schiff, and where he is perhaps less convinced and less convincing, where he relies perhaps slightly more on the score probably in front of him.

For example, the Fantasy BWV 921 is a bit more interesting if perhaps less impressive in the fingers of Cyprien Katsaris and Elizabeth Sombart and the BWV 922 as well, in the fingers of the same Ms.Sombart and Alfred Brendel. Also, while absolutely irreproachable and in the same quality category as Murray Perahia, Glenn Gould, Richard Goode or Schiff on ECM, his Partitas are played with very little ornementation (where he ventures into it he is the most inspired: this is where intimacy shows) and Schiff on Decca is still the stellar benchmark in this respect. Individual renditions of some partitas are more interesting in the fingers of others: The 1st by Katsaris, Anderszewski, Wild, the 2nd by Martha Argerich (who else?), the 4th by Jeffrey Kahane.

His Goldberg Variations are again perfect but I still prefer above all Maria Tipo for her pianistic qualities (her colours are second to none), András Schiff (Decca again) for his boldness in ornementation, Gould or Koroliov for their vigor and who are a bit more characterized.

His French Suites are again in the same vein in terms of sheer excellence but they have yet to dethrone others in my pantheon: The six Suites by Gould, the 4th by Andrei Gavrilov (EMI), the 5th by Schiff (1978) or Gavrilov (EMI), the sixth by Fasil Say ...

Same for the English suites where I'd put him near the top with Perahia and mostly ahead of Schiff (do my ears detect a slight textual difference in Janssen's Bourrées in the first?) but the other Ivo (P) is still at the top of the 2nd and 3rd, with Anne-Marie McDermott.

The Concertos after Vivaldi and others are perfect in Janssen's hands! The 972 reminds me of the old Sylvia Marlowe of yore, the 979 after Torelli (the Andante!), incomparably more interesting than Alexandre Tharaud's (who plays only the Andante), the Alessandro Marcello absolutely moving in its simplicity and the others that I've heard by Janssen are as affectionate.

What else? Of course, the beautiful BWV 998 Prelude, Allegro and Fugue which nobody to my knowledge plays at the piano (there are some problematic pinched notes but to hear them, you'll have to hear the exceptional Wanda Landowska or a few guitarists or lutenists) the Aria variata alla maniera italiana BWV 989 (where I think I prefer Tamara Stefanovitch who probably plays the first variation too fast but the way I like) and many largely unheard of works, Sonatas and Suites which complete this marvellous voyage.

And while this excellent, beautifully recorded set is an obvious bargain, buy it without thinking about the money. You'll be getting some of the best (in my opinion the best), most difficult to play music ever written, and perfectly played too. It is now in my phone's memory and always with me.

I now hope that Ivo Janssen will do some organ works (the Fugue BWV 578 which could have been included) and some transcriptions by Busoni, Kempff and others. Anathema to some I know ...

title: Very mannered and jumpy, where's the legato?
text:
Starting from the hyper-kinetic overture, Currentzis is bent on bringing attention to himself and cannot let Mozart's music alone. Not one bar or phrase is spared of his bizarre accent or willful manipulation, such that the gentle breezes in the Act 1 Trio "Soave il Vento" startle rather than caress... The rest of the reading is full of jumpy phrases and oddly-placed accents, devoid of dramatic context and disrupting Mozart's sublime legato lines. All too often one is made painfully aware of the puppeteer's strings rather than flesh-and-blood characters drawn up by Mozart and Da Ponte.

His "Marriage of Figaro" fares little better.

I honestly am appalled by all the hype and superlatives surrounding Currentzis, as well as the $985 price on Amazon; I wouldn't pay $9.85 for this travesty.

title: Outrageously Swinging Band in the Kaempfert Manner...
text:
Wow... just wow.. this band swings like h....!!!

For starters, let's talk about the choice of tunes... "Woodchopper's Ball," "One O'Clock Jump," "Two O'Clock Jump," "Intermission Riff," etc., all borrowed from the masters of the Swing Era. There's no doubt that Kaempfert puts the usual touch with the strings and chorus that came to be his hallmarks but don't let that deter you from the fact that this rhythm section drives these hard swinging tunes like a well-oiled machine. The brass cuts through like a razor sharp knife and the reeds are every bit as impressive.

It's a great album, well-recorded and executed the way a big band recording ought to be. The only weak link in the chain are the original tunes towards the end, which, in my opinion, lack the spark that Kaempfert's tip-o-the-hat to his American big band idols possess. Even so, it's an enjoyable trip back in time and you'll be smiling ear to ear.... or rolling up the rug for an extended jitterbug session.

In short, love it!

title: Choppy
text:
This was recorded live at Koenji 20000V on August 31, 1997, the band jamming with the master (he does a fair bit of this - around the same time Haino Keiji also did a recording with Coa, and he has worked on album projects with KK Null, Merzbow, and many others). Haino's concerts tend to go on for hours and hours, and this CD only contains 72 minutes of excerpts from a much longer whole (that, I suppose, must exist somewhere in its complete form... and with better sound quality, I'd expect). All of the titles are very long. First track "A Rise, A Moment Before Something Unexpected Is On The Verge Of Starting" has a long drone, with meditative moaning interspersed with the occasional spurt of insane bellowing. Drums come in, the droning swells, as does the insane bellowing. The song ambles along, eventually petering out with a bit of drum. At over 15 minutes before it fades out (all songs either fade out or are cut of abruptly), it is the longest song on the release. "Not Knowing If It Will Be Agony Or Comfort For Us" starts off with cool drum blasts, wicked shouting, and a real Boris jam. "Wonder What Colour Would Be Suitable For The Dwelling" is mainly about caterwauling and tooth gnashing, although there's also a fair bit of manic drum madness and guitar squeal with wild bass zooms. "The Decision Of A Dream Which Will Never Be Completely Red" slows things down a bit, while keeping the insanity fresh, and "It Should Be Watched, Not To Fail To Notice These Flashes Of An Accusation From Inside" indulges in wild, wild drums and screams. and strange long wild musical meanderings. The song is chopped quite suddently. "Offer It All Up, Our Madness That Will Be Crushed On This Land That Has Come To Be Called Chaos Unzipped" starts up with amplifier buzz, then goes into some sort of plaintive camel bellow/whale song that is probably created by a guitar. Or maybe it's a snake charmer's pungi. "From The Distance, With Their Own Gentle Eyes Always Fixed On Us, They Are Affectionately Gazing At The Black_Implication Flooding" is somewhat musical, in a dissonant way, and the song hoots and hollers, growing slowly into a great, clattering crescendo of noise power! "Don't Be Cheated By The Oozing Silt From Both Of The Accuser And The Accused Which Is Always There, Saying `Something Has To Be Done'" is all about smashing drums, the slow buildup of guitar, and then a big rock bash-in. "The Person Who, What Is S/He Like, The One Who Has Been Determined And Prepared" is probably the best fun on the release, starting with weird Godzilla sounds, the song starts off in a scary, echoing industrial world, with wombat attacks erupting constantly, roiling and rolling, a tiger worm struggling to blast itself away from its existence. But nothing ever really happens after that.

Unfortunately, the release would have been better if the mix weren't quite so awful - the recording sounds like crap.

"Mystic Mixes" is a bootleg. The mixes are all mis-labelled on the packaging. Here's the actual official names for the tracks, along with where they come from:

1. TNT For The Brain (Midnight Man Remix) - this is the version on Love Sensuality Devotion.
2. Sadeness (Violent US Remix) - this is on the companion remix ep for Love Sensuality Devotion.
3. Mea Culpa (Catholic Mix) - this is the radio edit of the song, and you can find it on Love Sensuality Devotion.
4. The Eyes of Truth (The Twilight Of The Gods Remix) - from the remix single for The Eyes of Truth.
5. Gravity of Love (Dark Vocal Club Mix) - from the remix single for Gravity of Love, which is now available for download.
6. Light Of Your Smile - this is the regular version, not a remix. It's a b-side from the "Beyond the Invisible" single.
7. Modern Crusaders - on Love Sensuality Devotion, and originally from The Screen Behind the Mirror.
8. Gravity of Love (Judgment Day Club Mix) - on the remix ep for Love Sensuality Devotion.
9. Mea Culpa (Fading Shades Remix) - yup, you guessed it... it's another from the remix ep.
10. Endless Quest - not a remix, but the original track from the album The Screen Behind the Mirror.
11. The Eyes of Truth (The Twilight of the Gods Dub) - also on the Eyes of Truth remix single.
12. Sadeness - album version from MCMXC A.D.

Hope this helps for those debating on whether to get this or not. There's no new stuff here. You're better off getting the new repackaging of [[ASIN:B0027DP4TK Love Sensuality Devotion: Greatest Hits & Remixes [2CD, 2016 Edition] - European Release]].

I only gave "Mystic Mixes" two stars because it's Enigma, and the remixes are genuinely good in their original format. But, like I said, it's a bootleg and the production quality of the printing is crap. Support the mastermind behind Enigma (producer Michael Cretu) by buying his official releases, and don't give your money to the bootleggers responsible for this half-assed collection.

title: DEGENERATE opera for DEGENERATE audiences !
text:
This is by far the stupidest and ugliest opera that I have ever listened to & I've been going to the Opera for years... The story is incomprehensible, the music subtle to the point of inaudibility and the libretto - totally GROTESQUE! The medieval-modern mix - either in the plot itself or in the sets or the costumes - makes NO SENSE whatsoever and proves utterly inefficient, since we don't even know what the opera is about...

How could anybody in his right mind give this wiling, creepy, condescending piece of CRAP more than one star (even that is too high a score!) is beyond my understanding : not only the protagonists are vilely removed from plausibility (which straight husband would reject his wife's advances on the pretext of their being puerile?!), but women are presented as solely sensual creatures, whose purpose in life is to ensnarl even angels...

This opera's plot is a distasteful rewrite of the biblical story of Adam & Eve, with the ostensible pretension of empowering women by supporting the view that sexuality is divine & the driving force behind all that's good in the world... Now, that's a feeble message : what about LOVE (which surpasses sexual desire, in my humble opinion), morality, loyalty, pity, compassion for the weak, the helpless, the unfortunate? The Group proved very popular in the U.S in truth having greater success than here in the U.K...........the group disbanded 1970.

text:
This review is for 461 Ocean Boulevard Deluxe Edition (I am explaining that here because Amazon tends to mix the reviews of different versions of an album).

I was a huge fan of this original album and I think most of the extra material is even worse.

On CD1 there are 5 bonus tracks that are outtakes from the recording sessions. There is only one track, the last one that is very interesting. The rest don't appear to be remastered or remixed. Three of the tracks sound mostly like a rhythm track with the main song way in the background. You just get mostly drums and some bass.

On these bonus tracks, Clapton sings in an affected way, like he trying to be soulful. He makes these moaning sounds that are really creepy, like he is in the bathroom doing who knows what but trying to stifle the sound.

The second CD consists of 72 minutes of live tracks taken at the end of his 1974 tour. The sound quality is OK but the mix is off. You can't hear the singers most of the time. It is really bad on Tell the Truth where it is difficult to make out Marcy Levy' soulful vocals.

The performance is not that great, compared to what it will be like in later years with this band. It was like the band had not played together long enough and were still finding their way. There are some good songs on this CD but I would just get Crossroads 2 and skip this.

title: Very amusing, lots of fun!
text:
Until very recently, this album contained the only known recordings of the Popeye radio shows of the 1930s.

These shows have been dismissed by critics as being purely juvenile and off-putting for its use of other actors (excluding the legendary Jack Mercer-the most famous of Popeye voices), a kid named Matey in place of the infant Swee Pea (which made sense for radio since Swee Pea couldn't talk), and the substitution of a forgotten breakfast cereal called "Wheatena" (apparently similar to Cream of Wheat and the sponsor of the show) for spinach.

In spite of these facts, I enjoyed these shows. The actors, musicians, writers, and sound effects folks do an excellent job of creating entertaining adventure tales where our man saves the day with spin-OOPS! I mean Wheatena. The stories always close with Popeye giving Matey some kind of moral, which is ok since these are preceded by some pretty amusing adventures (the one involving Popeye and the runaway train is particularly suspenseful). The actors who play Olive Oyl and Wimpy in particular give good adaptations of the characters, albeit different from what the cartoon fans are accustomed. The Wimpy character in particular is even more comical than in the cartoons, spouting snappy lines that provide good humor for adults.

If you enjoy the radio adaptations of Superman, the Lone Ranger, the Green Hornet, et. al, you should also have a field day with these radio Popeyes. I read recently where 16 other recordings of episodes have been found. I hope they will also be available to the public soon.

title: Brass Quintet...where's the tape?
text:
This LP was purchased in 2011 as new old stock: a sealed lp from 1972. I remember hearing this LP at the local public library as a junior high student and wanting to buy it. 30 years later I have it and it's not all that great. The LP pressing is noisy and the levels exceed the dynamic range of the LP, so the sound is distorted. Furthermore, the Partita for Brass Quintet and Tape is all brass and no tape... they actually didn't perform it with the tape accompaniment (unless Lazarof recorded other brass players for playback). I don't think that it is his best work, either. In summary, I recommend avoiding this LP, which turns up online from time to time as an overpriced item. Instead...

Readers of this review should sample the amazing Naxos CD of Tableaux/Symphony #2/Violin concerto. Lazarof writes great music. The quality of the recording is top-notch, too. For that reason, if his music is to your tastes, I would forgo the MP3 format and buy the CD.

title: Ancient, live Arturo Toscanini recordings.
text: These are live recordings of  Arturo Toscanini and the NBC Symphony on the Arkadia label.  I don't know where they were recorded. It doesn't sound like Studio 8 H and so maybe it was Carnegie Hall or some unknown house in an unknown country while on tour.  There are no program notes.  The two orchestral excerpts from Psyche were recorded in 1939, Les Eolides, 1940, The inescapable Franck Symphony in D (actually, I love the work - but I have duplicates on top of my duplicates) was recorded in 1940.  "Redemption" was recorded in 1947.  The tapes have been cleaned up and so the sound isn't nearly as bad as it should be, considering....  There are no bangs, coughs, rustling sounds and weird perspectives; so the recordings probably aren't bootlegs.  Neither is there noticeable tape hiss or the snap, crackle and pop associated with old 78 records - but it's a far cry from the clean mono of the 1950s, and an even further cry from early stereo -- not to mention digital.  On the plus side: it IS Toscanini and even when he's not at his best in repertory we usually don't associate with him, he's worth a listen.  There was no cover art and no product description.  I should have known better.  Maybe they should have put a great big question mark in the product description and labeled it "classical grab bag."  LIve and learn.

title: Ehrling's great Nielsen 3rd!
text: Sixten Ehrling's recording of the Nielsen 3rd symphony belongs in every self-respecting Nielsen collection. I heard Ehrling perform the 3rd Symphony in Detroit in the mid 1960s. At the time I had hoped he would record it with the Detroit Symphony, but no such recording was made. This later performance with the Danish National Orchestra is truly 1st class, although the DSO certainly was a better orchestra (and probably still is!). Ehrling probes the very depths of the 3rd symphony, and his two soloists are quite good. I have heard nearly every recording of the Nielsen 3rd symphony and probably own most of them, but none comes close to this wonderful Ehrling reading. It is sad that Ehrling never did a complete cycle of the Nielsen symphonies (and equally unfortunate that he did not re-record his Sibelius cycle). This 3rd is a souvenir of what we might have had!

title: This CD goes against the wishes of Elvis. The producer's comments on the reviews ruin what little enjoyment the CD gives
text:
There is a blurb on all the websites advertising this CD that finally they have complied with Elvis's wishes and brought his vocals out in the forefront. However, this is completely wrong. The producer, Larry Jordan, will probably start arguing about this with me now (EDIT--just as I predicted, he has) in the comments to my review. (EDIT--now he has started asking Amazon to delete any and all comments on the reviews that make the CD look bad, see below. He is also personally attacking the taste and credibility of every single person who has posted a negative review on this site, in the review comments). If you read Guralnick's acclaimed Elvis biographies, you will see that Elvis complained repeatedly that Col. Parker tampered with his recordings to bring his voice out more. So, on the original albums Elvis thought his voice was too loud and he wanted to hear the backup singers more. On the New Recordings, Elvis would not be happy that his voice is now three times as loud as he thought it should be and the backup singers are even quieter.

The main thing that is wrong with this CD is that the versions are too close to the originals. I had no problem with "Viva Elvis," for instance, because they were doing different things with the songs. Here, they add just a few instruments here and there in the empty spaces, which ends up in most cases making the songs feel just a bit too cluttered. When you go back and hear the original albums, you begin to "hear" the New Recordings versions in your mind and ask "where is that corny saxophone? Isn't it supposed to play here?"

There are a handful of arrangements that ruined some of the songs that just should not have been tampered with. I am no purist. If something is different and it works, I like it. The worst part of this CD is the jazz saxophones that are just "doing their thing" all over the songs, sometimes even while Elvis is singing. It's a bit too much and it's like, "will you please stop?" Also, I thought the strings were fake, but I was wrong. There are actual string musicians. The string arrangements sometimes seem intrusive or badly placed.

(EDIT) Here is a more detailed breakdown of which songs don't work for me:

First, the "sax offenders":

So Glad You're Mine: The sax on this song is very out of tune (flat sounding) and annoying.
Stuck On You: An example of that busy sax just "doing it all over it."
I Gotta Know: Busy sax doing it even more and even worse this time.
Soldier Boy: More of the same..another busy sax doing its annoying thing all over the song.
Fame and Fortune: Not quite as bad as the others, but this "smooth jazz" sax sound is annoying.

And on to the rest:

Love Me Tender: A bad country duet with a woman.
Good Luck Charm: The guitar doesn't quite work.
Home Is Where The Heart Is: The flute doesn't belong here.
Can't Help Falling In Love: The string arrangement is cliche.
Anything That's Part of You: More cliche strings.
In My Way: The strings here are too busy and ruin the intimacy of the song.

I like the album even less after seeing all of the remarks from the album's producer and friends on all of these Amazon reviews. There is definitely a "campaign" at work here.

title: 5-plus stars for artistry, negative one for nonartistic considerations
text:
Any new recording from Emma Kirkby, whose elocution knotted to a sweet and clear tone distinguishes her from most singers, is in itself an event. I had high hopes for a new recital of Franz Josef Haydn's English canzonettas and other solo vocal music from the reigning queen of early music performance. While Kirkby and her accompanist didn't disapoint, my hopes for an unqualified success were dashed in the opening tune.

The main shorcoming of the Brilliant Classics' production, recorded in Switzerland in 2009 and copyrighted in 2011, is a boomy and reverberant recording acoustic, a brief recital (57:26 -- less than an hour), production that did little to amend the first shortcoming, and something less than a blast off opening. Haydn's songs, while lacking the dramatic tension and literary variety of Schubert lieder, nevertheless are different enough so a concert can be programmed sufficient that one item after another does not essentially sould alike. But that's what happened in the beginning until an overexcited version of Fidelity broke the monotony after three mellow songs.

Beginning with the fourth item, Fidelity, Kirkby proves she's still a fabulous singer with her own ideas about the music -- like her octave leaps after one stanza in the aforementioned Fidelity mated to a ringing top -- that keep your attention. Her fiery Italian in Adrianna a Naxos is also a winner, as is her prose and passion in A Pastoral Song. While the aural disappointments are insufficient to deter lovers of Kirkby's soprano, the poor sound of this album could sink your enthusiasm.

The culprit is an audio fog (maybe mud is a better word for it) that shrouds the the soundstage rendering the singer's English unintelligible and blemishing the substantial contributions of fortepianist Marcia Hadjimarkos and her delicious-sounding instrument. I can't tell if it's the recording venue (Salle Charratmuise, Charrat, Switzerland) or the engineering from Jiri Heger -- or both -- that's responsible for this travesty. Anytime you can't understand Emma Kirkby's enunciation of English language songs, something is very wrong. I turned my treble adjustment on my tuner up as far as it would go (+10 on the readout) and turned the bass up +6 and it was much better. This shouldn't be necessary in 2012, even on a discount recording.

On the plus side, this inexpensive disk comes with complete English texts, a discussion about the keyboard used (a Christopher Clarke copy of a 1795 Anton Walter), three pages of notes on the songs, and brief bios of both performers. Ironically, while engineering is definitely a problem, this recital is recorded with an extremely wide and deep soundstage.

This will doubtless thrill Kirkby's fans and song conneiseurs may find her Arianna a Naxos up there with the version I know by [[ASIN:B000003GJH Andrea Folen]] on a concert with some of Haydn's equally remarkable German language songs. Kirkby's selection from Battle of the Nile, while heady, frothy and heroic with Hadjimarkos' equally dynamic accompaniment, lacks the Haydnesque subtlety and humor of [[ASIN:B00005COYC soprano Ann Monoyios's]] from a remarkable collection with the Four Nations Ensemble.

It's a memorable collection if you can either adjust your equipment or live with the engineering faults. For those that cannot, I might recommend soprano [[ASIN:B00008F6HV Adrienne Csengery's]] lower voltage but still effective collection of the 14 canzonettas, ably accompanied by fortepianist Malcolm Bilson, as an alternative with a couple caveats: Csengery is more mezzo than coloratura soprano, her collection has only 50 minutes of music, there is a noticable balance issue in the recording, and Csengery's English (she was born German and works in Hungary), while good, requires some help from the booklet to understand all the words. All the texts are included. But she and Bilson make quite a team.

title: Not to my tastes
text:
Boy oh boy, I wished I liked this more. Going off all the "lost prog classic" accolades it gets, never mind a "mellotron classic" (my favorite instrument) I was really primed for something exceptional. Well, let's start with positives . . . . it's EARNEST. You can tell the musicians are putting their all into it. The musicianship is good. It's a good sounding and well mixed recording. That's it for the positives. The negatives - I just finished listening to it and there's not one track I have the slightest interest in hearing again. Some are downright annoying (not a fan of the vocalist). And it's really anemic melodically. It's chock full of proggy "fiddley bits" but they don't coalesce into anything or build to a climax or resolution. Comparisons to Genesis I don't see at all, and while there's some echoes of Yes they don't have the compositional moxie of that band. As for mellotron, well yeah, it's there but not in great heaping amounts and played in a fairly conventional and uninspired way.

I'm glad it has it's fans and wish the band well. Just not my stripe of prog.

title: A good collection worth getting
text:
The Heart Of Classic Rock is a collection of hit rock songs mostly from the 70’s, with a few songs from the 60’s and 80’s. Some of these are the short radio versions, but others are the longer album version. It has a total of 144 songs on 10 CDs, totaling 9 hours and 30 minutes.

The people at Time Life did a good job of choosing songs to include in this collection. But the problem is that the songs are sometimes placed in a random order, where two songs of widely differing styles are next to each other, such as Bread next to Foghat. They could have put songs in a more logical order.

This collection does not have everything. There are no songs from artists like Paul McCartney, Eric Clapton, Crosby, Stills & Nash, Creedence Clearwater Revival, the Rolling Stones, and the Who. But this might fill what you’re missing in the one-hit wonders and lesser-known artists.

Aside from all this, this is a way to buy songs from many artists in one package. You should shop around to get the best price for this set. You might get a better price if you look elsewhere on the internet. Some of the CD’s are also available individually if you don’t want the whole set.

One more thing.--When I ripped these CD’s to my computer, some of them were filed as “Heart Of Classic Rock,” and some were filed as “The Heart Of Classic Rock.” This meant the files were not all together where I expected. Then I figured it out and corrected the names manually. I am just telling you this so you won’t be caught surprised.

Some of us were lucky to be living during the time when this music was popular and these artists were active.

title: Takes You Back Disney Memory Lane
text:
Compared to other Disney CD's out there (both OOP and new), this particular set is the most comprehensive. In addition to the traditional "Tiki Tiki Room", "Pirates of the Caribbean", and "Haunted Mansion" tracks from the Magic Kingdom, this set includes rare tracks from vintage EPCOT such as "Universe Of Energy" (not the Ellen version), "Spaceship Earth" (Tomorrow's Child), "Listen To The Land" (not the new "Living With The Land" boat tour that no longer has a human guide), "Test Track" (not the new theme from the refurbished pavilion that opened this month), and "Canada" (the mesmerizing duet, not the reboot single).

If you look at the track listing provided by another review, you'll also notice this includes attractions that have closed, including Horizons and World Of Motion. There's also the enchanting "Magic Journeys" that I remember hearing as a kid while watching the first 3D movie that showed in the Imagination pavilion back in the early 80's.

I bump this one down a star to 4 stars only because visibly missing is the Main Street Electrical Parade and Fantasmic, although there is a CD available you can get separately that contains just those two.

These kinds of CD's are expensive because they were exclusive to the Disney theme parks, and this particular one is Out Of Print (OOP). If you love Disney World like I do, shell out the money for this one!

title: Superb jazz and classical performance
text:
Very few artists are equally proficient and comfortable performing both jazz and classical, especially in front of a full orchestra. Eddie Daniels and Wynton Marsalis come to mind, and this album demonstrates that Bill Watrous is also a member of this elite group.
From popular tunes to Debussy to the breathtaking Patrick Williams composition that opens the album ("La Fuerza"), this 1986 collection displays a broad stylistic range. Six of the eight tracks are full orchestra arrangements; the other two ("No More Blues" and "There Is No Greater Love") are Watrous plus rhythm section. "No More Blues" is actually a bonus track, though it's not identified as such - it was not included in the original LP release.
In addition to "La Fuerza," other notable orchestra tracks include: "Come Rain or Come Shine," rendered so beautifully it'll make you weep; "Suite Memories," a Patrick Williams arrangement that juxtaposes "I'm Getting Sentimental Over You" with Jerome Kern's "Yesterdays" in a very different, very tasteful treatment; and the two classical selections, "Adieu Mon Petite Table" and "A Tribute to Debussy." Neither of the classical pieces contains material originally written for solo trombone, but once you hear them, you'll be convinced that they should have been.
It's a shame that this great album is "currently unavailable" on Amazon, and as of this writing, they offer little hope that they'll restock it. It's a masterpiece featuring a master musician, and it belongs in every classical and jazz library.

title: The Clash of Civilizations
text:
This may well be the movie of the year. Helen Mirren, as just about everybody has rightly noted, turns in another wonderful performance, this time as the restrained "duty first, self second" monarch. Her particular trial here is having to face a clash of civilizations, not between nations as during World War Two, but now within her own country. A culture of heroes, of maintaining a stiff upper lip during crises and of "good show, flying colors" as the behavioral ideal, has slowly eroded and been replaced by one of vulgar celebrity and "letting it all hang out." In the middle of this clash stands Tony Blair. He must induce the noble yet now unintentionally comic, because isolated, queen into an awareness of how her society has been "Oprahfied," an insight that would not naturally occur to her since she sees Diana's death as calling for little more than royal privacy and a family removal to Balmoral. Herein lies the movie's subtlety. The high-minded, stoic queen, for all her wit, nonetheless values brute animals more easily, apparently, than she does people. She quickly sees, for example, the beauty of a glorious stag pursued by royal hunters, but has little sympathy for the beautiful Diana pursued by equally murderous reporters.

As regards Tony Blair, we have equivalent complexity. For all the film reveals of his political opportunism and readiness to take advantage of changed circumstances, for all the emphasis on generational differences between him and the queen, he is allowed by the well-written script to genuinely recognize the queen's essential fineness. His awareness here leads him in an emotionally charged scene to berate some of his own staff in private after they openly express their shameless glee at the queen's discomfort. At the same time as he recognizes that the "duty' agenda of the queen will allow him to talk her into doing what has become in present circumstances "the right thing," he also reveals to us his clear awareness that something fine has been compromised in the process.

title: So bad that I'm angry it exists
text:
This is clearly a third party, bootleg cash-in.

If you're a psychotic completist or were actually at the show, it may be of historical interest, but don't bother listening to it more than once, it's atrocious. Instead of buying it, just look at the setlist, think to yourself, "Oh, wow, they played Surfin' Bird for the first time in a few years," then move on with your life. It's the Ramones, it's not like Johnny was doing some mind-bending extended jam solo on We're a Happy Family that is only available from this concert. They play everything exactly the same as they did on the other 150 dates on that tour.

Other than a few late-era songs (mostly covers from Acid Eaters) that aren't available live elsewhere, there's nothing interesting about the performances from this concert. The audio itself sounds primitive, and there's very little care taken with the levels in the mix - It's a straight soundboard recording for an FM radio broadcast. Oh yeah, and as others mentioned, it has plenty of gaps that kill the flow and criminally step on CJ's "1-2-3-4..."

If you want to hear basically this same setlist from the same tour, just get "We're Outta Here." If you want to hear them at their most musically exciting with a broad setlist that spans the prime of their career, go for "Loco Live." And if you want to hear that original line-up at the peak of their powers, grab the classic "It's Alive." They all sound better than this, you can hear separation between the instruments, you can hear crowd noise, you can hear... excitement.

But whatever you do, do not buy this, it's awful.
