title: Two thirds of the way there
text:
Since going on hiatus in 2003, the members of Great3 were plenty busy. Akito Katayose put out a solo record and cut several with his wife, Chocolat. Drummer Kenichi Shirane showed up on everyone else's album, as well as releasing the fantastic "Manmancer." And Kiyoshi Takakuwa, as Curly Giraffe, embarked on an apparently-quite-successful solo career. So news of a Great3 reunion--an un-hiatusing--was quite welcome.

Unfortunately, despite playing with Kenichi Shirane on the Beatniks tour, Takakuwa elected to opt out of the reformation. On "Great3," the first Great3 album in almost a decade, he's replaced by an interesting, elvin creature named "Jan," whom a) is simply too precious to have a last name, and b) was born in, wait for it, 1990, making him 22 years younger than the other two. Well, then.

"Great3" is a mixed bag, but mostly in a good way. It bears remembering that "Climax," the group's 2003 album, was an odd beast in and of itself, representing the single most eccentric collection of songs yet. By comparison, "Great3" is far more normal, abandoning some of the John McEntireisms of the group's later catalog for a more straightforward approach; "Higan" approaches power-ballad territory, even.

The good: "Emotion," "Lady," the fantastic "Red Room" (which reminds me somewhat of YMO's "Neue Tanz"), "Walking a tightrope," the aforementioned "Higan."

The indifferent: Jan will take some getting used to. Apart from being an excellent songwriter, Takakuwa contributed a wonderful low counterpoint to Katayose's higher register. Someone apes his part on "Higan," but his presence is otherwise missed. Although Jan seems to be a perfectly serviceable bassist, his two vocal contributions--acoustic, whispy, and thinly adorned--sound like they belong on another album entirely. Unfortunately, the album's remake of Shirane's excellent "Explosion No. 1" isn't as good as his solo take; it's a pity they abandoned the superior arrangement.

Verdict: An encouraging sign of a band finding its footing after a long break. It's a shame that Takakuwa isn't back, but Jan might grow into his role. "Great3" isn't as *interesting* as most of the group's post-Romance output, but it seems fair to give them time to ramp back up to speed.

If you google Richard Bennett and find his website, take a moment to look over his discography. As he states, it's not complete, making it all the more mind-boggling. His talents have obviously been in demand for well over 30 years as a first-rate session man, and as witnessed on this CD: no wonder.

For this, his own release, he has taken well known genres and made them sound fresh with ear-catching melodic twists and hauntingly beautiful guitar work. If you're into guitar tone - not some over-processed and distorted mess - but pure, warm, rich, vintage electric TONE, then you have to add this to your collection.

I bought this, listened once or twice, then put it away for about a year thinking "very nice - I'll come back to that someday". Thankfully that "someday" came again recently. Since then, this disc has rarely been far way from my player. I can't get enough - and if you give it a chance I'll bet you'll feel the same.

title: A Great Presentation of the UKs " Embassy Records "
text:
From the mid 50's to the mid 60's the Embassy ( UK ) record label was created and existed for Woolworth Department Stores in the UK, afectionaly often referred to as " Woolies ". These were " Sound Alike " otherwise known as " Cover Records " imitating the chart hit versions by the artists that made the songs famous. The objective of Embassy Records were to offer Woolworth Customers a more affordable budget priced alternative as Embassy Records sold at about half the price of the charted Hit Version on the major record labels of the day. Embassy Records featured a Hit Song on each side of the record adding even more value to some of these lower priced gems. By no means were Embassy Records something obscure, they sold thousands of copies of each of the many records they made during the approximate 10 year life of Embassy.

The CD being offered here are " Cover Versions " of hit Beatles Singles as performed by Embassys own version of the Beatles, " The Typhoons ". The CD itself is of first class replicated ( not home made or individually burned ) quality. The liner notes include a brief but fairly comprehensive history of Embassy Records, the individual 4 primary members of " The Typhoons " , well written descriptions and session information on the individual tracks featured on this CD.

The audio quality is excellent on this CD if you consider that the material used for the creation of this CD may or may not be from original Master recordings but quite possibly from well preserved, pristine 45's. My ears tell me that the audio quality on this CD is representative of the audio found on UK manufactured 45's of the era. With many CD re-issues of material from the analog recording era, when it is so called " Digitally Re-Mastered " often times the sound will be altered or played with such as redistributing the sound to make original mono recordings sound like stereo as well as changes to the original audio levels and EQ . Personally I don't care for this and I am very happy that it sounds like No Tampering of the original sound was done on this CD, and many thanks to the production crew of this CD for " keeping it original ". I have not heard any sounds of scratch, hiss from record wear and only a very very slight tracking error wear near the end of a couple of tracks but it is so slight it could be my imagination. title: The thunder god of Beethoven Eighths, a brilliant First, highlight Suitner's magic
text:
Conductor Otmar Suitner was a product of the old German conducting school and is respected as a masterful interpreter. But given that most of his career was spent on the "other" side of the Iron Curtain, his impressive recorded legacy (including some of the finest Beethoven, Brahms, Mahler, Schumann, etc. available) is not top of mind. Make the effort and you will find performances that compete with the best of all time. This Beethoven Eighth is a magnificent example.

Here is an Eighth brimming with edgy power and high spirit, reckless exuberance, and Central European warmth. The first movement, which contains some of the biggest moments in all of Beethoven, is a house on fire under Suitner's baton, crackling with explosiveness and energy. It brings to mind the kinetics of George Szell's and the robustness of Gunter Wand's versions, but Suitner surpasses them on both counts. Szell's is leaner and more nervous. Wand's strong take, the closest to Suitner's, lacks Sutiner's sensitivity. This is the most aggressive and thrilling recording of this movement that there is, and ever will be.

The second movement, Beethoven humor at its finest, is bawdy, raucous, and witty, and the Staatskapelle plays brilliantly. Suitner treats the third movement, the minuet, as a slower movement, more romantic than most, an approach that I prefer. It is fragrant, gracious, and evocative, characteristic of Suitner's wonderful touch on Austro-German fare. Finally, Suitner ends this perfect Eighth with a fourth movement that combines the wildness of the first movement with radiance and joy.

The Eighth, a condensed encapsulation of the very best Beethoven, is sadly ignored among Beethoven's symphonies, Beethoven himself favored it. Here is a performance that does it very proud.

Suitner's Beethoven First is also a brilliant performance. It is one that bears a resemblance to the version by George Szell and the Cleveland Orchestra, but fuller and warmer under Suitner.

Not only do I highly recommend this disc, but the entire Otmar Suitner Beethoven set. It is not easy to find, but as good as any cycle, and better than the majority of famous big name productions.

This is one of the great motion picture scores of all time. Composer Alex North, who was director Wise's original choice, opted out citing the film's (at that time excess) "violence" among other reasons. He recommended his protoge', a young Jerry Goldsmith, whom SAND PEBBLES would be his fourth or fifth film. (Goldsmith had also cut his teeth on Serling's legendary TWILIGHT ZONE.) Sadly, Mr. Goldsmith would not be recognized with an Academy Award for another ten years although he did receive a nomination for SAND PEBBLES.

Goldsmith tackled the job like a veteran, giving us one of the most beautiful and haunting scores--and one of the lengthiest for a non-musical, not only of the 60s, but of all time. The melancholy strings will remain with you long after you remove the disc or the film's final fade out. Perhaps the only criticism that can possibly be leveled at Goldsmith is that he should have made more and better use of traditional Chinese music, which I understand, is written radically different than Western music.

The present edition includes previously unreleased tracks plus some period or "source" music which is heard in the film. The liner notes are very informative.

title: There's better competition out there
text:
Pros:
- Nothing

Cons:
- Sloppy playing by the Philharmonia Orchestra; late and early entrances one after another and muddy sonics ruin the performance. It seems like Michael Tilson Thomas was in a big rush and had very little time to rehearse the piece.

Additional comments: Somehow I expected more from Michael Tilsom Thomas and the Philharmonia Orchestra; they really don't offer anything new to the table. For outstanding performances, look for Fritz Reiner's 1960 recording of the excerpts with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Antal Dorati's recording with the Concertgebouworkest, and Gergiev's recording with the Kirov Orchestra (now the Mariinsky Theater Symphony Orchestra). But keep in mind that Reiner's reading is approached as symphonic concert, so expect quick an quirky tempos. On the other hand, Dorati's reading is a lot more sterile and steady. All in all, Reiner and Dorati's readings are performed with such precision it makes Tilson Thomas's recording sound like a High School Band. It's a pity, because Tilson Thomas has some magnificent recordings out there (Beethoven's Late Choral Works with the London Symphony Orchestra), but this just isn't one of them.

If you're looking for a more recent recording, I strongly suggest Sir Simon Rattle's recording with the Berlin Philharmonic. All in all, avoid Tilson Thomas's recording, there's just way more and better competition out there by better orchestras.

title: A superbly told, exquisite story from a talented author
text:
When I picked this up I was expecting a light hearted, easy read. What I got was a heart warming tale of second chances. And I loved it.
The Coffee Club is the best coffee place for miles around, run by Noah and Elle. When Jennys marriage to Zak, the owner of a local fashion house, falls apart after some shocking revelations from the man himself, Jenny finds herself and her 10 yr old daughter April sharing a cottage with the Coffee Club owners. What appears at first glance to be a total comedown complete with public humiliation at leaving a multi millionaire and an 8 bed house to move into a loft conversion where Jenny and April share a room turns into a starting point for a new life, after hitting rock bottom.
This is a story of not only starting over, but finding yourself again. Whether you are a 30 something adult or a 10 yr old child, it's never to late.
We are introduced to such an amazing cast of characters. The author has given them all such depth and are completely relatable. I'd like to say I loved them all, but as with any community, there are some that will grate on you, we can't like everyone, right? And this is testament to the skill of the writer that she can evoke these feelings in the reader and it just makes it all the more believable.
I have to say that I'm finding myself hoping the author has plans to write more stories set in this village. There are a lot of the supporting /fringe characters that I feel I'd like to get to know better. And I'd like to revisit this little group to see how their stories progress further down the line. All in all, a superb read with some profound storylines tackling some hard hitting issues. Dealt with in a sympathetic manner and a book that has clearly been well researched. I highly recommend this to everyone.

It's hard not to love the dirty, debaucherous sound of the Morning 40's, even if their first three albums cover a lot of the same ground. For those new to the 40's, it has been described as "burlesque" and "sleazy", but it is a straight-up New Orleans vernacular hybrid; a heavy, moody horn section trades prominence with blistering guitar over dark, hilarious lyrics.

While You My Brother has many of the same songs from their self-titled release in 2004, it is a stronger album. Sure, the recording may not have been as state-of-the-art, and it certainly wasn't promoted as well, but the few songs that didn't make it to the later recording, like the title track, more than make up for it. Get this album.

title: A Jolly Good Time
text:
There are only seven known live recordings of Egg, the great polyrhythmic English trio who gigged extensively between 1969-1972, and this disc collects the best tracks from all but one of them. Some of these recordings are quite decent (BBC Top Gear and Sounds of the Seventies) and others are either audience recordings or something like them. All have been cleaned up and digitally enhanced to sound better (much better!) than any of the bootlegged versions which have been circulating among fans for years.

Couple that with a beautiful package containing copious notes from Dave, Clive & Mont and their longtime roadie Alf Gascoine, and you have a real treat. Egg were outrageously influential for such a short lifespan, so any documentation of their legacy is important -- plus as a band they had a lot more fun on stage than in the studio. Their rehearsal-intensive "serious" music is offset here by some seriously twisted and wild improvisations.

title: This is what good rock should sound like
text:
Unlike so many of the post early 90's rockers that have just resorted to incomprehensible lyrics and outright mayhem, this band returns moody rock to days gone by.
Post-Bikini Kill, I was worried what I would listen to because it seemed like all my favorite grrrl bands were splitting or going mainstream to the point of watering down their trademark assertiveness. Then I found Slumber Party and instantly became a fan.
The quartet of Detroit girls pens and writes lyrics that would make the late great Kurt Cobain immensely proud. Their self-titled debut album (a previous six inch was released through the Kill Rock Stars "Mail order Freaks" club) sent shivers up the spines of cowards everywhere as they scrambled for a way to describe this dynamic force to be reckoned with.
As with every truly alternative CD, the band is uncategorizable. They are there and they are unique and that is about it. This tradition is completely consistent with independent music, and the band must be applauded for being themselves and waking up the world.
Although the music is incredibly mellow, potential listeners should not buy it expecting to hear something gentle, soft and radio friendly. While there is no doubt that some forward thinking college station could play this album (hey, it practically screams brooding!) it is unlikely it will even make some of major city alternative stations (some of whom have turned into little more than a top 40 rock and roll station) that in turn cater to suburbia.
As much respect as I have for the women in music who do perform such music, I think it unfairly delineates a manufactured concept of what "Male" and "Female" music is really supposed to sound like, and undoes (unintentionally of course) much of the work that pioneering acts such as Patty Smyth and the Raincoats did in the 1970's and 1980's.
Slumber Party revives women's rock music into the next century and tells the remaining few nay Sayers that we are here to stay. Turn it on; crank it up, because women in rock are here to stay for good.

title: Big Joni Mitchell Fan--Until Now
text:
I've listened to, and sung with, Joni Mitchell forever.
From the early stuff of angelic highs, gorgeous poetry and idealistic love songs, to later, when her range and her voice was roughened by cigarettes and booze, I sang along, the eternal fan. I sat at the feet of her musical and poetic genius like an acolyte, ever seeking inspiration.
My best friend had this album in the 90's; she has a great ear, and our tastes are frequently similar.
So, I bought it, only to find that I hate it.

title: The bass sounds like it could have been lifted off a Mastadon album
text: This is a preview of the 50th anniversary remixed edition of "Sgt. Pepper," and all I can say is, oh, hell no. Giles Martin, the son of fabled Beatles producer George Martin - judging only by this single - doesn't understand the music. "Strawberry Fields" sounds full-bodied and extremely bass heavy. When you apply that to approach to "Penny Lane" you are bludgeoning a skipping-light classic. The bass sounds like it could have been lifted off a Mastadon album. It is not even tight and tuneful bass, it is bloated and dominant. When the "Love" album came out, I was struck by the modern, vivid, spacious production, but that was largely pastiche, not the actual Beatles. Yes, after 50 years I am used to the album's true sound, so a new sound is startling, but what I am saying is that it is not only different, it is not good. It might work for some of the heavier songs, but not the lighter and is not in any way true to how McCartney's playing ever sounds. I hope the remix and 50th anniversary doesn't replace what's available publicly, what was a George Martin masterpiece with the work of his son. That would be a travesty. If just "Penny Lane" is an example, this is a MUST to avoid.

title: A no-brainer purchase
text:
I bought this Limited Edition set on Amazon’s UK site and the cost is far less even with overseas shipping included.

The video is in B/W, included only 12 of 31 songs performed live, and the quality is poor. It was probably shot with a consumer video camera onto tape, but it adds tremendously to the experience when one can relate to the environment and the atmosphere.

The DVD is advertised as in PAL format, not the NTSC format used in US and Canada, but I had no trouble playing it on my Oppo BDP-105 player that feeds a Panasonic VT60 TV. The disk is “region free”. So it can be played on any player. Many players, like the Oppo, can handle analog videos of different frame rates and resolutions, convert them to digital and output through an HDMI cable to the digital HDTV set. On my system, the disk played with no fuss whatsoever. In case it didn’t, I do have an older region free DVD player that I use to play foreign DVDs. These players can play both formats and output analog component videos. As a last resort, it could be played on a computer. I’m glad that option #1 worked just fine. Others will find one of the 3 options work for them.

The DVD was the first disk I played. The audio was handled by a Yamaha RX-A3010 receiver and Energy RC-70 main speakers. I was immediately taken by how much better the sound quality was compared to other Eva Cassidy CDs, all of which I bought 10-15 years ago. I then played the CDs, feeding the stereo output to my vintage stereo system which has better amps and speakers, confirmed that these CDs are also far better sounding than all the old ones. The voice and instruments have excellent clarity and tonal balance. The recordings captured the club ambiance quite well. In other words, there is now finally a CD set with audio quality that does justice to the superb vocal.

The artistry of Eva Cassidy should require no introduction or description than what has been said countless times. Suffice to note that there are a total of 32 songs. 31 of them live recordings from one session, 12 of which previously unreleased, and 8 of those are new songs. Why it has taken 20 years to release the complete concert recording is hard to comprehend, but thank God that we can finally hear it, and see it too. After just one pass of listening, it's safe to say that this is my favorite EC recordings by a wide margin. I could not have bought myself a better Christmas present!

It never sounds dull or old. Always refreshing to hear as is it different than most anything I have heard. Jackson Heights went through some personnel changes with each release until Lee Jackson recruited Patrick Moraz to join up. That became "Refugee" and the rest is history. "King Progress" is the bands first album (1970) and the other releases are hard to find indeed. But now , through the wonders of the "re-issue" - this album can be had by anybody who wants to hear something new, from a long time ago.

title: The Lost "13" Tracks Unearthed At Last!
text:
This "sold at concert venues ONLY" CD is quite the gem to the Black Sabbath fanatic like myself. When the reunited Sabbath (minus original drummer Bill Ward) got back together after Ronnie James Dio's passing and the end of Sabbath's Mark II's "[[ASIN:B001UREJWM Heaven & Hell]]", they could have put the phone book to music and we'd all come a runnin'. The resulting album 2013's "[[ASIN:B00BTHWFBK 13]]" was an amazing album considering that they hadn't been recording together for over twenty years and guitarist Tony Iommi's lymphoma illness. Though Bill Ward's absence was definitely felt, the songs truly tried to capture the spirit of the band's first four albums. Some songs even sounded like remakes of classic tunes like Black Sabbath, Planet Caravan, and War Pigs. However, when the album came out it was released in different versions, some with only eight tracks with deluxe versions had a total of 11 and 12. It was rumored that Ozzy, Geezer and Tony actually completed a total of sixteen songs for the record, and this CD prove that.

The first four tracks on the CD are the final four that never made it to any other version of "13" before it. Surprisingly, each of the tracks sound as mastered and completed as anything on "13" (even sounding better than the Best Buy only track "Naïveté In Black" which to me sounds demo-ish and somewhat incomplete). What's surprising is like the song "Methademic", a song that was on 13's bonus disc yet made it into their live set, the first track "Season Of The Dead" could have been one of Sabbath's next singles it's so good. The other three: Cry All Night, Take Me Home, and Isolated Man each have a uniqueness that have merit being on the final product as well, almost as if they planned for this release for the live shows, to leave four great tracks to sell as new a few years later. These songs are not throwaway to any Sabbath fan & must own to sit next to your copy of 13.

As if those tracks weren't enough, you get four live songs, all with incredible clarity and performance. To anyone else like me who has a copy of the live album/DVD "[[ASIN:B00FKIB3XA Live...Gathered In Their Masses]]", you already have a live version of Tracks 5 & 7, but the live tracks "Under The Sun" and "Age Of Reason" are brand new to the audio front. Under The Sun (originally on [[ASIN:B01H2ROWDE Volume 4]]) is special because I have never heard of them playing this live before (correct me if I'm wrong), nor at least it appearing on a bootleg. Age Of Reason didn't make "Masses" set either, so bonus points for that too. Make no mistake, even after all these years, nobody jams live like Sabbath, and these four tunes proves that.

In the end (pun), this is a great treat for Sabbheads. I would be fooling myself if somewhere down the road, these songs as well as all 16 tracks with the live ones, end up on some deluxe version a few years from now, but for now this is the only way to have a hard copy of them. Not to be ignored if you're either an Ozzy freak or Sabbath die-hard, this rare CD is quite the treat. Thanks for reading & thanks for Sabbath!

text: Raven usually produces excellent and interesting organ cd's, but this one is a major exception.  The playing itself lacks energy and movement (not to be confused with fast) particularly the Finale/fugue of the Theme, Variations. and Fugue.  The organ, one of Aeolian-skinner-Harrison's masterpieces, sounds so turgid that there is an oppressive block of sound with no hint of transparency in the larger pieces.  I have heard this organ, and it is a magnificent  instrument,  but this recording belies that.  (There is also some slight background noise throughout, which may be the result of poor engineering or a bad pressing, but these are not the cause of the mediocre playing.)  Try to find--easily available from ebay--the Ellsasser LP "Yankee Organ Music,"  in which the piece and the sound of the mongrel Hammond Castle  organ are both superb.

title: Gorgeous and unusual repertoire; some wonderful singing
text:
I'm tempted to begin with my one main objection concerning this recording, but I'll focus on what is good first.

François le Roux is an astonishing singer - a baritone with a warm and sympathetic voice whose timbre is intimate and full of profound depths. I may as well admit it - I love his voice. And he phrases so beautifully - you can hear this very clearly in the first few lines of the Lalo duet "Au fond des halliers". As he sings "Mignonne...", it's hard not to melt.

The repertoire is stunning - some very unusual French duets which don't seem to have been recorded by any other artists. Admittedly there were a couple of duets here that I thought were perhaps mistakes, given the vocal forces here, but all in all, what a delight.

The pronunciation of the French - oh, glory, what a pleasure when French songs or duets are sung by French singers! One hears all too often the praise "he/she has very good French", but if we think about this for a moment, we can understand that what is NOT being said is "he/she sounds French". I must be candid - the only singer I've heard whose sung English and sung French were perfectly indistinguishable from native singers of those languages was Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau. Not even the divine Elly Ameling, the superb Schwarzkopf, the splendid Domingo, etc., were able to eradicate all trace of their own native language from their singing in other languages (particularly noticeable in English). - Very well - I look then for phonetic particularity, and it does make a difference (often very slight when the voice is ravishing and the understanding deep) to how much enjoyment I have when listening to singers essay art songs in particular.

The playing is terrific. Jeff Cohen does a splendid job and it's no surprise he's accompanied some of the best French singers in the business. He shapes phrases with sensitivity, he plunges right in with robustness when it's needed, and he supports the singers beautifully. (I particularly liked his playing in the fiendishly difficult piano part for the Duparc duet.) The only piece in which I didn't entirely like what he did was "Au fond des halliers", and that's not his fault - it became a jauntier accompaniment because of the speed at which the duet was taken. I have every confidence he would have been sublime if the tempo had been more languorous to befit the poem.

Now the not-so-good elements...

The recording quality is not entirely awful, but it's not the best. The sound seems slightly dead - boxy, I think, is the best way to describe it. Yet this is not as important to me as it may be to others, because for me the performance is virtually everything...

The second - and most important - reason for my not giving this recording 5 stars is the singing of Collette Alliot-Lugaz. Her voice is too prosaic in comparison with le Roux's. It's a pleasant lyric voice, but I feel it's not a deeply sympathetic one, and she doesn't phrase anywhere near as intelligently as her baritone partner in this recording. Some of the top notes were definitely lacking fineness although overall it's quite a nice voice. But she does not colour it. That's the major flaw in my opinion - it hasn't the sensitivity and the ability to convey mood and meaning that I wanted. (However, she sings beautifully in the Poulenc "Colloquy", and the duet work between her and le Roux in "Par une belle nuit" is sublime.)

The worst of the duets is a drastically lowered "Chanson espagnole" by Debussy. Admittedly we all pull keys around to suit our voices, but here it seems to have altered the entire colour of the duet! However, I have got to admit that repeated listening (by which I mean listening the 20th time) makes me less inclined to mind this change, even though I still consider that duet not really suitable for these singers. (And neither is "Tarantelle" by Fauré - originally written for two sopranos, it goes at a cracking pace and really needs that light bright touch which the use of a baritone as one of the voices cannot give.)

The other duets are much better choices - I adored "Les fleurs", the Poulenc, the Massenet "Horace et Lydia" and so on. Le Roux is always wonderful to listen to, and most of the time Alliot-Lugaz is quite nice if not of the same standard as le Roux.

If you love French vocal music, this is highly recommended for you. Had a soprano with more ability to put shades of meaning into her voice been used, I'd have had no hesitation in giving this five stars. Even as it is, it's got many lovely things to recommend it.

title: Excellent Mosaic Set
text:
Unbelievable that the only reviews for this are one star (and one of those apparently due to an easily corrected mistake). Of course everyone is entitled to their opinion, but it seems to me the arrangements and music included in this 3 CD set are far and away more deserving of higher regard.

Included in this set are Music Inc.'s self titled release from '71 on Strata-East, which in addition to Tolliver on trumpet include Cecil McBee on bass, Jimmy Hopps on drums, Stanley Cowell on piano and wind/reed players like Clifford Jordan, Bobby Brown, Jimmy Heath and Wilbur Brown. There's not a bad track here. The second disc contains music from Impact, released on the Strata-East label in '76. Strings are included in this set, tastefully done I might add. The last disc is a previously unissued set recorded in '79 in Germany, covering many of the tracks included on the first two sets.

I find the music lively and spirited; the solos creative and melodic. The liner notes tell of Tolliver's desire to form and sustain a big band (which wasn't easy to do) and provide some background information on what he was attempting at the time. Seek out samples online and listen for yourself. These excavated offerings Mosaic included here are highly recommended.

title: It's a bluegrass gem
text: Many know Kenny Smith from his rock solid guitar work with the Lonesome River Band from 1995-2001 which led to his twice winning the IBMA's  "Guitar Player of the Year" award. Smith's solo project, "Studebaker," had us take note of his songwriting abilities and also introduced us to his lovely and talented wife of six years, Amanda, whose soulful singing makes us sit up and listen closely. When the couple decided to embark on this latest project, "Slowly But Surely," they assembled a band of tasteful musicians to give their debut album a unique, original sound. Ronald Inscore (mandolin), Jason Moore (bass), Steve Huber (banjo), and Ron Stewart (fiddle) do just that by ably contributing some tight picking with drive to the Smiths' arrangements of contemporary bluegrass and Gospel. Sonny Smith plays banjo on one track (River of Regret), and Ronnie "Buck" Freeland offers light percussion on "Nancy Jane." The songs include a nice mix of original material, as well as some old, but reworked, classics from the bluegrass, country and western swing repertoire. This album has many strengths - beautiful vocals, expert picking, solid arrangements, excellent repertoire, and a high recording quality.  Simply put, it's a bluegrass gem. We'll be hearing more from Kenny and Amanda Smith, and I hope that they'll be touring with a band as fine as the one put together for this recording project. (Joe Ross, Roseburg, Or.)

A suitable segue from the soundscapes of Pharoah Sanders and the LSO would be the new release, Mercenary Blues, from Svobodi- Phil Hunger, Davi Priest, Brian Seyler, and Bennington, just out on the latter’s ThatSwan! imprint. It is an enveloping sonic experience drawing from the imagined birth of civilizations.
Darker and moodier than ‘Floating Worlds’ with Pharoah Sanders, the titles for the sonic suite are suggestive: “The Whore from Larsa” (an epic 17 minute excursion) and “Blues in the Key of Ur.” The opener “Cicada Song Forum” (highly topical) like much of the album, is pervaded by an ominous sonic throb, Bennington’s simmering cymbals, Priest’s arco bass - a giant murmuring in sleep - Seyler’s tenor, emerging as if from cocoon. Phil Hunger adroitly controls synth swathes with intense intent, bordering on evil. The gingerly awakening rumble encircles and then parts for chaste solo Seyler, who subsequently forages around the lunchtable legs of the aforementioned sleeping giant, scouring for scraps. The title piece embarks with Bennington’s tolling martial low-jungle-drum beats around (sampled) hyena yelps and Hunger’s phantom-of-the-opera organ heralds. The jungle is periodically visited by extra terrestrials.
It’s unsettling but absorbing music, enveloping even; perfectly paced; it’ll surprise those unfamiliar with Svobodni's 1st release, “Out in the Taiga at Night.” My suggestion to Jimmy lovers today: Rather than send him an emojii, why not download or, preferably, order a CD?Svobodni are intriguing and they’ll take you to ancient places, some even as ancient as the birthday boy himself!
- Michael Jackson (of DownBeat Magazine), May 22, 2021

title: A very happy US Navy Veteran.
text:
The year: 1977
The location: Bremerton WA, on board the USS Ranger CV-61
One thing that should be understood is that as far as personal music technology, there were really only a couple of viable options. Vinyl records, which would scratch, jump, and hiss because you looked at them. Or cassette tapes, which just loved to get caught in the spindles needed to play the tape. Unfortunately most of the time by the time you realized something was wrong, the tape itself was usually so badly tangled in the player, that the only remedy was to cut the tape out. Which of course destroyed the tape.
Anyway I became friends with a shipmate, named Mark. For reasons I don't remember why any more, he was the only enlisted man that had a private stateroom in officers country.
We spent a lot of time listening to his cassette player.
One day I knocked on his door, and he didn't answer. It turned out that his enlistment was done. So I got my player out, and I was going listen to some Simon, and Garfunkel. Except I couldn't find the tape, anywhere.
But sitting in my collection was this tape by some group called Kraftwerk, whom I had never heard of. So I listened to it, and immediately liked it.
Fast forward to my college years, I somehow lost the tape.
It has taken me until now to find it again.
Which brings me to a very interesting Amazon practice which in my opinion boarders on...let's just say I don't understand it. "Only one (1)left order now." Yet there always seems to be just one more.
If you like Kraftwerk, you must have this CD, as a foundation of what the group became.

title: Gardiner or Shaw: A difficult choice
text:
Verdi's mass for the dead is one of my favorite pieces in the western canon, so I've collected a few over the years. You can read the other reviews for poetic waxing on the themes and scope of this work, but I will concern this review with the musical and performance merits of two specific recordings: the best period performance (Gardiner's, albeit the only one) and arguably the best modern performance (recorded by the regrettably late Robert Shaw, and there are some other moderns in close contention).
I won't make you read the entire review to get my take: I prefer the Gardiner/ORR recording to the Shaw/ASO for the simple reason that there is more fire, drive, dynamic, or other related adjective involved in this performance than any other.
Gardiner's players are absolutely deadly - you need look no further than tracks two and three for evidence of that! The tempi, while quite brisk, do not daunt this remarkable ensemble, and they play with an astounding precision. 50 percent of that credit is due, however, to Gardiner's outstanding conducting (most/all of his recordings with just about any group are staggeringly precise - check out The Planets with the Philharmonia!).
The choir, being the Monteverdi Choir, sings an incredible performance, but using far more vibrato than is normally heard from them - consistent with the style of the work. Their technique and facility equal that of the orchestra: a combination that is difficult to beat.
The tempi, taken as literally from the score as possible, are faster than we normally hear (by lesser ensembles) so, some listeners may feel that the music is not given enough time to breathe, or that it is too fast to comprehend. Enter Dr. Shaw...
Robert Shaw's outstanding account of this requiem has an incredible asset: phrasing unparalleled in any other recording. Under the guidance of the best choral conductor of his time, the Atlanta Symphony Chorus responds to their director's brilliant musicality with aplomb. His superb vocal phrasing transfers well to the strings too. Every phrase has a top and bottom, and he exposes many textures that other conductors do not.
But, Shaw's larger, less agile, and more-distantly miked ensemble do not capture the immediacy that Gardiner's does. Compounded with a slower performance, Shaw's - while breathtakingly beautiful - does not have Gardiner's impact.
So here's my recommendation: purchase Gardiner for the recording quality, tempo, orchestra, perferable choir, and effect. Purchase Shaw for the contemplative setting, outstanding choral phrasing/conducting, and superior soloists. Really, purchase both when you can.
But to feel the true power and effect of Verdi's opera for church, Gardiner's is the one to get.

title: This is not Arrau, this is Beethoven himself
text:
First of all I would like to say, I have to disagree with a reviewer that says Arrau plays "too slow" this I can handle although I consider his speed is fine... but mostly when he says something like "he gives a romantic touch to these sonatas that were dedicated to men".

That is a huge blasphemy and here's why: Beethoven was a passionate man, I guess every Beethoven fan and student knows that, and if you still don't believe it just listen to his piano, violin and cello trios to see how much passion and romance there is involved. So it doesn't matter if he dedicated these sonatar (or any of his works) to a woman, a man or an alien, it is quite clear that whoever it was intended to, Beethoven would have probably execute it with passion and romance.

The execution of the Appassionata sonata is the ultimate execution. I need more words from other universe to describe how you can easly breeze into the composer's mind and actually feel what he felt and thought when he composed this piece. The 3rd movement is to me the best around and the best I've heard (from dozens of dozens), especially the last two minutes when it's clear the composer went drive mad. With other performers you will see that in these two minutes (when the piece reachis its climax) they will normally slow down which obviously a clear mistake and not what Beethoven intended). The last two minutes are to be played with madness, more madness, anger, more anger and all the passion you can put into those 88 keys. You can't slow down the climax of the piece ! That's why it is called Appassionata ! Such a beautiful piece.

The moonlight execution is the best I've heard too (with the exception of the 1st movement). Each one of the three movements take you to a mind state where you can feel how and what Beethoven felt about countess Giuletta Giucardi: love, joy and then hate, respectively. Just like the appasionata, the 3rd movement's performance is stunning. By the time you reach half of it, your mind will think you're listening to Beethoven.

Patetique is a good execution. I haven't really heard a notable performance, probably due to the fact of being one of Beethoven's earlier -more Mozartian/classisist- works. Still it is very good, and the movement that impresses me the most is the second.

Do your self a favor and get this CD. You will trash any other Beethoven Piano sonatas CD, and you will eventually look forward to buy the 32 piano sonata box set by Claudio Arrau -to listen to the man himself playing all his works-, which I proudly own and just like this disc, it is worth every single penny.

text:
The TV show and its soundtrack have been overplayed, exploited and rehashed through the meat grinder for the last decade, even ABC reduced the whole package into a rap tune for one of its promos. Yet, despite the onslaught from commercialization Lucy originally hinted at in the special, Charles Shultz’s holiday tome remains steady classic, thanks mainly to the simple level of sincerity.

The soundtrack has become a staple that doesn’t wear out its welcome with syrupy sentimentality that, say, Johnny Mathis and Michael Bublet (or however you spell his last name) are known for. I’ve heard the opening track, the jazz coolness of O Tannanbuam, so many times and yet, I don’t feel sluggish or overwhelmed; it’s calm, breezy and, like the show, intimate. It doesn’t force itself down your throat and easily puts you in the holiday mood.

Sure, the merchandising behind the show and album is annoying as hell, but once you carve this crust off the edges and throw it away, it reminds you of a philosophy and time when, as Lewis Black once ranted, Santa wasn’t “sticking his ass” into the economy. title: Left to drift...
text:
It’s fair to say that I’m a huge Michael Knott fan. I have most of his many (and incredibly diverse) albums, I traveled over a couple of western States to see him in concert, and I’ve decided to write detailed reviews of all of his proper releases (not comp or live albums or mixed albums). This guy deserves no less. His songs and artistry have been an inspiration and encouragement to me, wearing his heart and faults on his sleeve, challenging my assumptions, and declaring the beauty of his Lord and Savior often in the midst of pain and trauma and confusion. He also does a great job of sympathizing with people in general and tells some funny, heartbreaking, and engaging stories about a variety of true characters he’s encountered but he never turns them into caricatures. All of this is to say that I’m not blind to what works and what doesn’t, or that I love everything he puts out. I don’t. Case in point: “Dogfish Jones”. No matter how many times I’ve listened to it I can’t get into it. For me it is one of if not my least favorite Knott release. Why? Some possible/probable reasons are that the tempo of many of the songs and thus the overall album is simply slow, especially over the first half. This sets an expectation and while the second half’s tempo picks up the proverbial wind is already out of the sails. Another BIG reason is that there’s a lot of organ music spread throughout and I’ve never been a big fan of most of the Hammond organ sounds incorporated into songs. If you like those sounds then by all means give this disc a spin, you’ll likely enjoy it. Perhaps another reason is that this is a concept album (Dogfish Jones travels over the seas/ navigates the trials of life—is Jones a reference to Michael’s father? To himself? To both?) but it’s not the fact that it is a concept album, it’s that the concept is an allegory and not clearly conveyed. It’s hard to care for the character without some more specifics, or a tighter story. Lastly, there’s just so much repetition. Knott has always been one to repeat. It’s been part and parcel of his structure. But on this release there is so much repetition! It wears out welcomes to several songs.

So is there anything I like about this album? Knott comes up with some nice melodies. Though this is way overused of so much music it’s also nonetheless true but there’s a Beatles influence that bleeds through. That’s something I’ve never heard on any other Knott project. The sheer variety and amount of music, “Dogfish Jones” included, continues to awe me. So there’s that, and a couple of songs I like okay. But it’s not enough. I’m sad to give this a 2.5 rating, but I must. I always come back and listen to it every few years, hoping that I’ll like it more, but never do. I never enjoy this listening experience.

1) Dogfish Jones ~ Lots of repetition (lyric and melody) and a chorus that is a little like nails on a chalkboard.
2) Storm At Sea ~ A sea shanty!!! Sung by Michael’s father, Howard Knott. Is it me or do all sea shanties sound Irish?
3) Let Me Out ~ Gene Eugene supplies the boppy B3 Organ heard on this track. One of the stronger tracks on the album. Doesn’t go all over the map but goes different places than one would expect.
4) Barnacle Bob ~ There are layered, harmony vocals that makes this sound unnecessarily busy shooting right out of the gate, also heavy on the drums and especially percussion. After a minute or so it transforms into a more typical Knott tune complete with some spoken word storytelling.
5) Down ~ Gene Eugene shows up again with the Organ grinding again. The song, appropriate to its title, is downtuned with this being felt especially on the second half of the song. It almost feels like two songs. Again suffers from too much repetition. Drags on way too long. That Hammond B3 Organ music has never been my favorite and there’s a lot of it on this track, so…not my favorite.
6) Greensea Island ~ The previous song ended on a downtuned note. This song goes further. It’s ponderous, slow tempo feels not like you’re exploring a lush green sea island but that you are stuck in the seaweed slowly moving. Heavy use of the organ again. Knott’s vocals are clear at least, and not multi-tracked.
7) Hated Souls ~ Another slow moving tune with an underbed of organ music. The guitar, thankfully, is more prominent at least and there’s a simple melodic sweep and obvious chorus. Not a great song by any stretch but it breaks us out of the trudge of tracks 5 & 6.
8) Tell of the Well ~ A playful song, more in Michael’s wheelhouse. Lots of layered vocals on this, a buzzy background guitar, and a little funkiness. Great rolling rhythms provided by the drums (thanks Mr. Chuck Cummings).
9) Mercy Maid ~ One of the more memorable songs. Lots of repetition.
10) Magical Rainbow Door ~ A dancing organ, very lively, shows up and helps to give this song a Beatles-esque flavor. Mixing metaphors “dead man’s curve” and racing are added to the seafaring allegory. Allegedly written with his daughter.
11) Seashell Sally ~ Organ. Repetition. Multiple vocal tracks/layering. Also memorable, with a moderate tempo and again overstays its welcome.
12) Edge ~ The most driving and guitar-centered track. It’s a rock tune. Not hard. Not even heavy. But satisfying. Finally, after eleven tracks. It’s also the track that boasts the most non-repetitive lyrics.
13) Shanghai Overdrive ~ The guitar celebrates its feature…but it’s buried a little too deeply at times especially under all of the repetitious vocal melodies.
14) The Boyos ~ Another shanty, sung in round. You just want to take a pint and jig it over your head mindless of the slosh. The most memorable song on the album.

A couple of closing comments. One reviewer mentioned this release as ….“Christian” music that surpasses all other Christian music, and most secular music…”. As far as the music goes that’s always a personal/preferential issue but these songs are hardly Knott’s best and I think that one has to take the criticism of repetition seriously. As to the “Christian” label it is well known that Michael Knott is a Christian and he’s done some work, such as praise and worship offerings, and has incorporated his faith in obvious ways in a variety of his band and solo projects. This may be true too of “Dogfish Jones” but you’d have to dig, deep, to discover it. It’s not just not obvious, it’s that if it’s there it’s allegorical (sorry, that’s a lot of “its”). To anyone thinking they were going to get an obviously “Christian” music CD they’d be way, way, way off. And for anyone scared off by that label, they simply needn’t be. This concept is more along the lines of an allegory, like Plato’s “The Cave”, though there seems to be a lot of Knott history steeped in the story. If you’re looking at this release for a buy but haven’t heard Michael Knott’s other concept albums “Grace Shaker” and “Fluid” then I’d direct you to either of those releases. They’re great.

title: Caustic, unlistenable noise with an oasis of Haydn
text:
The Spektral Quartet, the ensemble-in-residence at the University of Chicago, is an envelope-pushing ensemble that thrives on introducing the newest and often edgiest music to audiences outside of the daring modern art enclaves that live on the strangest, most difficult and most shocking grist. This album is a perfect example.

The group explains in its notes that it is an exploration of humor through the lens of classical music, but it is “not a funny album”. This is music that “might be a little uncomfortable” but “rings through in its truth”, the works “brilliant and clever, and unequivocally worth entering the cave for”.

“Uncomfortable” is, in my opinion, putting it mildly. This particular "cave" is a torture chamber.

There are three pure avant-garde works, each evil-sounding, dissonant, bizarre. Sky Macklay’s “Many Many Cadences” is eight minutes’ worth of nasty stabs and squeaks. David Reminick’s “The Ancestral Mousetrap” is an ugly punk piece in which the quartet “sings” about such things as “bringing dead people back to life”, “an old woman’s breakfast” and other absurd non-sequitors, in between screeching and squealing. Chris Fischer-Lochhead’s “Hack” makes ugly noises out of the cadences of the routines of various famous stand-up comedians. If one were unaware of the goal or the program, it is nothing but, well, even more squeaking and squealing.

It takes a lot of intellectual gymnastics to justify and tolerate these affronts to the ears. Just because the ideas behind the works are mean-spirited and absurd doesn't make the works funny. At all.

But in the very middle of all of this aural violence is an oasis of sunlight, brilliance and sanity: an outstanding Haydn op.33 no 2 string quartet (“The Joke”). Interestingly, the Spektral not only plays this time-honored if obvious example of musical humor straight and sober, but they do it very seriously, perfectly phrased throughout and at a moderate tempo, with a touch of darkness---as if to suggest that Haydn’s musical “funny" that is not exactly ha-ha funny. (In fact, the inner movements are quite sober.) I suppose that is in keeping with the entire album.

The ugliness and noise resumes after the Haydn.

The question is whether this little Haydn respite (which comes across as starkly out of place) (strange that they chose the Haydn instead of, say, a Shostakovich or Prokofiev quartet) enough by itself to get you to pay for and suffer through the rest.

It would seem that many lovers of this brand of modern performance "art' disagree with my issues. This album was nominated for Grammy award in 2017 for best chamber/small ensemble performance. Fine. I don’t get it. Good luck if you can.

This doesn't even qualify as bad bootleg, but I suppose if the audio was better, it might be interesting hearing Gram explore his first album material, along with some covers. title: History in the Making
text:
This first Anthology CD has lots of treasures, including the earliest recordings The Beatles made.
The spoken word segments are interesting, I think. It is helpful that they have been assigned a track each, so that you don't have to listen to them every time you play the CD.
A lot of the material was previously released on expensive bootleg recordings. These LPs, tapes and CDs were often marketed at about twice the price of commercial recodings, and were often only 15 minutes long.
The sound quality of the Anthology is vastly superior and much much cheaper than those now superseded pirate recordings. Even if the Anthology series had not been produced, it would still be hard to sell those bootlegs in our peer-to-peer on-line environment.
Some of my favourite tracks:
Free As A Bird It is great to hear The Beatles together, even if one member was not able to appear personally. Real Love is a better song, but FAAB was a great introduction to the Anthology set, I think.
Three Cool Cats and The Sheik of Araby are great fun. I love the "not 'arf!" in Sheik.
How Do You Do It It is interesting to hear how The Beatles, however reluctantly, performed this song, later recorded by Gerry and The Pacemakers[who, some say, are now geriatrics *with* pacemakers].
One After 909 The alternative versions made available in this set are interesting and this one is a real gem.
Leave My Kitten Alone is one of the best songs recorded, but not released by The Beatles.
I'll Be Back is one several songs on the Anthology series which let us listen to The Beatles creating their masterpieces. It is great to hear this version with a different metre and feel, and The Beatles evaluation of their experiments.
Not the best of the 3 sets, but well worth owning and listening to every once in a while.

title: Classic new age piano-based instrumentals from a clever creator!
text:
Before I sat down to take in Ronald Van Deurzen’s recording from 2012 Imaginations I had to take a look at the album’s one sheet. Also, the reason I am covering it now is that it was just released on Bandcamp.

This is what was said about the album: The songs have been composed throughout the years of Ron's journey exploring the nature of Sweden. A country of vast forests, ice, snow, and ethereal sunrises. An environment that inspires thought, reflection, and creativity. Imaginations tries to simplify and communicate the beauty that can be experienced in this far northern area of the world. It speaks to the listener in images of the imagination.

I think it helps the listening experience to glean some information like that. It most certainly works for me prolifically at times. Ronald is from the Netherlands and he is a pianist, composer, and teacher. For the listener, this is a lesson for an all-encompassing musical experience. This is realized after knowing how this music was created of course. Although each listener is an individual with their perceptions of colors, light, and sounds, the basic premise holds for us all. Music is the universal language that speaks to everyone. Ronald especially does that through his music while creating an ongoing script or movie in the mind’s eye.

The one track that reached me instantly was “Moon Flower,” in fact I felt it should be placed on my NAMR Spotify Playlist. Every track is excellent but there are always one or two you happen to connect with better than all the others and this was the one for me. Ronald’s classically influenced new age journeys are created and enjoyed in different platforms such as music soundtracks, movies, and most of all for the pleasure of you, the listener, who stands to gain the most benefit from listening and letting this music whisk you away to another frame of mind or space that allows for healing and simply quality listening enjoyment.

“Momentum Figures” is the longest track clocking in at 7:22 and it is an eclectic composition with varying paces and emotions weaved through it like a musical patchwork quilt. I can see why it took up that much time and the various layers of music and instruments that come into play make it a real treat for senses. It is serene, exciting, and joyous. All of that is pieced together in segments for you to feel and absorb. For my ears, it was a delightful trip from one end of the musical spectrum to another. It is the most complex work on the recording.

“Midsommar Känsla" is Swedish for "midsummer feeling." It is a gorgeous melody and as picturesque as one could imagine. This was another track that moved me and touched my inner spirituality. That is the spirituality that we keep captive at times buried deep down so nobody can break the barrier and come in. With all your defenses down and no triggers of negativity, you have nothing to lose and everything to completely enjoy and feel without someone talking to you, arguing a point, or just making you feel uncomfortable. This is the reality of our days and life on this planet at times and we must find healthy outlets that demonstrate something that turns that switch on to bring about our true selves and a one-way line to our higher self or higher power.

That is what this kind of music helps me to accomplish while I am writing about it, I cannot explain it fully but the music inspires me and brings out these thoughts and images that I feel compelled to put in words. This is much like the process of making the actual music and it is my role to provide an interpretation of the sounds I am hearing. It is my honor to do so, every single time I do this.

Imaginations is the most appropriate title for this recording and if you have not had the pleasure of hearing it now is the time to go sample it at Bandcamp or listen right here and now as I have provided the media player as well. Don’t miss out on a chance to hear some classic new age piano-based instrumentals from a clever creator.

Keith “MuzikMan” Hannaleck-New Age Music Reviews
July 7, 2020

title: Still The Best Version Of This Tricky Symphony
text:
I have owned a version of this recording since I found it on LP years ago. It was my introduction to Bruckner's Sixth Symphony, which was not played very often anywhere at the time. It is still something of a stepchild at the concert hall. It was a revelation then to discover this great piece of music, so uncharacteristically upbeat and triumphant. I have always regarded it as Bruckner's Eroica. It may be the most personal of all Bruckner's works. I often think that one day he got up and out of the opposite side of the bed and had great positive feelings that left him later on.
There is basically only one edition of the Sixth, so you don't need to worry about versions.
Joseph Keilberth was a German conductor during WWII. He survived to 1965 when he died conducting on the podium. His career was mostly in Europe. The recording of his Ring Cycle at Bayreuth was unearthed and highly praised long after his death. I gather he was no glamor guy like von Karajan. More importantly, Keilberth plays this symphony naturally and energetically, like he had lived with it for a long time and loved it. That helps. No phrase is taken for granted or played on autopilot. The sound has held up remarkably well. It is true early stereo, and the Berlin Philharmonic plays like the great orchestra it was then.
After hearing the many, many other renditions (25 plus) that have followed, and concert performances that have followed (Salonen gave a splendid one at Disney Hall in 2007 when this review was first written,) I still go back to the Keilberth as the benchmark. Others have their advocates, but this is still the yardstick for me. Yes, it is a symphonic boa constrictor as Brahms dubbed Bruckner's symphonies, but a very nice one that does not play itself. Many, like Klemperer and Jochum and Haitink and Blomstedt, come very close, but it is surprising in how many hands the needed inspiration can flag and sag. I have heard the Bernstein NYP live performance recording and surprise, surprise it was not bad. Sorry he did not make a studio recording. Some Brucknerians like Van Beinum, Giulini, and others steered clear of it. Several others should have. You cannot just beat time through the 6th. There is something going on in Bruckner's symphonies that is difficult to define and more challenging to bring off. More modern conductors get Mahler "right" than Bruckner. Why is that? The sixth for some reason is more of a challenge than say 3,4,7, and 9.

I was driving halfway across Kansas, listening to college radio, when I heard a hauntingly beautiful song called "Only Gold" -- it was one of those mystical moments that only happen on personal road trips. This album has a little of everything you'd expect from a multi-instrumentalist singer-songwriter -- the love stuff, the social commentary, the seeking for meaning, and several straight ahead rockers. At times he sounds like a mix of Bruce Springsteen and Billy Joel, with the entire palette of expression they both bring.

I for one am sad that he didn't get the exposure he obviously deserved. I am a fan.

title: Jansen, Barbieri and Karn - Need I Say More?
text:
[JANSEN / BARBIERI / KARN - BEGINNING TO MELT (1993) - Produced by JBK] This was the first of 15 Medium cd's to be released featuring the various projects of Steve Jansen, Mick Karn (RIP) and Richard Barbieri, all originally of Japan (the group, not the country). It reflects that rare occurrence when a democracy actually works in music, or anywhere else, for that matter. All of the players excel on all tracks, but in light of Mick Karn's passing away in January, 2011, it's a reflective testament to the mans undeniable genius on the fretless bass. His contributions to this instrument are in sore need of re-evaluation by all. Barbieri's textures on synths are nothing short of otherworldly and wraithlike, and Jansen's percussive ethnomusicology and programs are always a hypnotic, meditative treat to come home to. Together, they become a Zen garden of musical enlightenment.

Supporting players include David Torn on guitar loops and solos, Steve Wilson on processed acoustic guitar, Suzanne Barbieri on vocals on the second track (totally unnecessary, IMO), Robbie Aceto on vocals and guitar on track four, and even an appearance by Japan's original guitarist, Rob Dean.

In spite of the additional input supplied, the cd manages to maintain an air of homogenous continuity, like a further melding of Porcupine Tree, Japan and other JBK releases. Personally, I could care less about the vocals, as the strengths and nuances of these players dictate constant attention and the vocals become an unnecessary distraction anyway. While not as strong as 'ISM' or 'SEED', the four of seven standout tracks indicate all loyalists are required to have this one in possession without exception.

"Call The Shots" isn't my favourite Girls Aloud single. I'm a huge fan of the girls, but I find CTS a little bit bland. But it has been a huge hit for them and for that I am glad.

Here is my rundown of the tracks:

01. Call The Shots [Main Version]
The radio edit of CTS. Like I said, not my fave GA single, but it's still a good song. This is chilled out, quite relaxed, which is a new thing for the girls. The best part of this song is the middle 8 which Nicola sings She sounds amazing! I love listening to this song just for that part. Overall though, this is a good, if yet a bit bland song. (3/5)

02. Blow Your Cover
This is the high point of the single in my opinion. Get this CD just for this song. It's another one of GA's brilliant b-sides (of which they have many!). This song is VERY reminiscent of "Love Machine" - one of GA's previous (and best) singles. The tune is mostly the same, but it's not a complete copy. Nadine and Cheryl lead this bouncy upbeat track, which isn't really about anything but is loads of fun to sing along to. Great. (5/5)

I'm glad Xenomania are remixing GA's songs themselves, because Tony Lamezma was getting tiresome. But this is a quite good remix, it's clubby and speeds up CTS a lot. Rather good. (4/5)

04. Call The Shots [Enhanced Video]
Of course this single has the video. The video to CTS is gorgeous - it was filmed in Santa Monica and features the girls on the beach at night in beautiful purple outfits, singing the song. Simple, but it works with the relaxed nature of the song. (5/5)

Despite me not liking CTS so much, this single still receives 5 stars because of "Blow Your Cover" and the video. You need this if you're a GA fan. 5 stars!

title: really fine performance, good recording, forgettable composition
text:
Well-composed music finds a balance between repetition/familiarity vs. evolution/surprise (for one of the best explanations, read Marvin Minsky, Music, Mind, and Meaning, Computer Music Journal, Fall 1981, Vol. 5, Number 3).

Furtwangler's first two symphonies lack the repetition side. There are no memorable melodies, and thus no identifiable "themes" or "development" or "recapitulation" that carry through to tie the work together. These two symphonies have lots of interesting individual measures, lots of melodies pop in and out, but no one of the melodies sticks around long enough to provide any coherency or coalescence. The movements have a shape -- the first and last movements culminate in lovely orchestral climaxes, but the climaxes don't have anything to do with anything that came before, so there's no sense of "arrival."

(To my ear, this is the opposite of Bruckner and Tchaikovsky -- those two are too much repetition, not enough variation. I think Bach, Beethoven, Brahms, Mahler, Rachmaninov's best compositions hit the balance just right.)

Furtwangler's harmonic language and use of the orchestra is very similar to Mahler. If you like this late Romantic style, you might like one or two hearings. The recordings capture the lush orchestral playing.

This same Albrecht/Weimar recording from 2003 is available as a [[ASIN:B0007PLKWK 2007 release]], as a [[ASIN:B000666QSI 2013 release in Japan]], and as a [[ASIN:B01K8LWEYK 2017 release]]. [[B000067DO3 Barenboim and Chicago also recorded Symphony Nr. 2]]. Albrecht and the Staatskapelle Weimar recorded all three of Furtwangler's symphonies, [[ASIN:B00004VX6T Symphony No. 1]] (which I also reviewed), and [[ASIN:B00003W7YJ Symphony Nr. 3]] (also [[ASIN:B000BO0KYQ here]] (which I haven't listened to).

title: Selling her talents for the consolations of fame
text:
Anna Ternheim's debut and her second album touched me deeply: I felt her sensitive lyrics and natural, fragile vocal style spoke directly to me as I wandered around Berlin. This was all the more so on the first album which was more acoustic and less bombastic than the second one. But already on [[ASIN:B000WC2US6 Separation Road]] you could sense that Ternheim wanted to become a pop star. When [[ASIN:B002DBG0JY Leaving on a Mayday]] dropped in November 2008, there was no more doubt: gone were a good deal of the shyness, the deep introversion of the lyrics and unpretentious guitar playing to be replaced by overblown production and diffuse, increasingly banal lyrics.

So I wasn't waiting for The Night Visitor with bated breath. On German radio I happened to hear her play one track live - Lorelei-Marie - and found it awful. What's with the naive sentimentality and the oh-so-pretty vocals? Even Heather Nova or Sarah MacLachlan would be embarrassed to put that kind of oh-so-pretty triteness on one of their albums. And then came all the promotion - the website promising great things to come, the story of the album's genesis (being born during a power-cut, etc.) trying to - literally - spark interest in what is a thoroughly unimaginative album. The depth of feeling and emotional sincerity found on [[ASIN:B000CSUWPI Somebody Outside]] seems like a distant dream now.

Goodbye Anna! It's a shame it didn't last.

text:
The rating is reduced to four stars due to the recorded sound. It's not as bad as that in Sardinia a week later, but this one in Spain is not real good. The disc says "digital" but it is one channel, monophonic. The fidelity is mediocre, being somewhat boxy, cavernous, and shrill in the tuttis. This was 1999, but it sounds more like 1949. Amazon reviewers debate whether
the Sardinia recording was a 'pirate' (surreptitiously recorded by someone in the audience). There, as here, that would explain how a 1999 recording could be so poor.

As always with Kleiber conducting, the performances are exciting and propulsive. Beethoven's 7th symphony was something of a specialty for him, he giving us a few recordings of it over the years. He showed the ultimate in both approaches to it. The '76 VPO and '82 Bavarian St. Orch. performances are very dramatic and hard driven. On the other hand, his '83 Concertgebouw performance (DVD) is very lyrical with great joy, lilt and sparkle. Which way would he go at the end of his career in this performance with the Bavarian Radio Orch. in Spain? Well, something in the middle. There is the dramatic symphonic thrust, but there is also some lyricism. It is certainly an exciting and enjoyable performance despite the poor recorded sound.

Much the same could be said about this performance of Beethoven's 4th symphony. It has some of both the dramatic, hard charging '82 Bavarian performance and the lyrical, sparkling '83 Concertgebouw performance (DVD). It is certainly lively and exciting, again despite the poor recorded sound.

So, these Beethoven symphony performances, exciting and enjoyable as they are, are a fitting end to an amazing career for Kleiber. It is disappointing that the poor recorded sound is not befitting of a career's end.

title: 2 classic Beatles' Apple albums on 1 great CD!
text:
During the final stage of the career of The Beatles, they still had what it takes to create great music, even if tensions among the band members were too much for them to cope with. These 2 albums, "Abbey Road" and "Hey Jude", were originally released on the group's own Apple label only a few months apart from each other, with "Abbey Road" in September 1969 and "Hey Jude" in May 1970. What these 2 classic releases provided us with was a brilliant selection of music that proved the lads could still create some stellar music moments and memories.

"Abbey Road" was the final album recorded by The Beatles (although "Let It Be" was actually the last one released). This masterpiece creation is comprised of 17 individual tracks, all arranged together into a fabulous and cohesive unit. Opening the proceedings is the Lennon rocker "Come Together" followed by the Harrison ballad "Something". These 2 songs were also issued together as a double A-sided single with both sides reaching number one simultaneously. Paul's sense of humor shines through with "Maxwell's Silver Hammer". McCartney gives us another great song with "Oh! Darling", which has an otherwise nostalgic feel to it. Ringo Starr shines with his composition, "Octopus's Garden". This is followed by the album's longest track, "I Want You (She's So Heavy)". Harrison delivers another winner in "Here Comes The Sun" which is considered by many fans to be the best song that they ever recorded. The beautiful three-part harmonies of Lennon, Harrison and McCartney stand out in the song "Because". Opening the Long Medley is "You Never Give Me Your Money". After this song fades out into the sound of chirping crickets, it then segues into another showcase of harmonies on "Sun King", which ends with Italian and Latin lyrics; followed by "Polythene Pam" which also features a refrain of "Yeah, Yeah, Yeah" which is reminiscent to that of "She Loves You"; and winding up this part of the medley is "She Came In Through The Bathroom Window". After a brief pause, the next medley begins with the song "Golden Slumbers" which almost sounds like a lullabye; after this is the song "Carry That Weight" which has the distinction of being the only Beatles song to feature 4-part unified singing from all 4 members together along with a brief bit that sounds like an unused verse in "You Never Give Me Your Money"; all this concludes with the track "The End", which is highlighted by Ringo's drum solo followed by Harrison, Lennon and McCartney each taking turns on the guitar solos before the song's conclusion. After a lengthy 17-second moment of silence, is the track "Her Majesty", the shortest song ever released by the group with a running time of only 23 seconds.

The 1970 release "Hey Jude" was not actually recorded by the band as an album proper. Instead, it is comprised of 10 recordings that had never previously been included on a Beatles album released by Capitol records in the United States. The original running order of the songs on this album were presented somewhat chronologically. The first 2 songs were "Can't Buy Me Love" and "I Should Have Known Better"; they were also featured in the 1964 motion picture "A Hard Day's Night". Both songs were issued as singles on the Capitol label and on the United Artists soundtrack album. Here, they made their debut on a Capitol label Beatles album. Following these songs are "Paperback Writer" and "Rain", the respective A and B sides of their hit single from May 1966. Up next is the piano-driven R&B-style rocker "Lady Madonna", a top 5 hit single from March 1968. The next 2 selections were issued as the group's first single on their newly-formed Apple label; "Revolution" and "Hey Jude". The album's only George Harrison song is "Old Brown Shoe", which was released as the B-side of a single from June 1969. This is followed by the Lennon ballad "Don't Let Me Down", another B-side - this time, from April 1969. Closing the album is "The Ballad Of John And Yoko", the A-side of the "Old Brown Shoe" single.

For unkonwn reasons, the "Hey Jude" tracks do not appear in their original album order on this CD. They are presented in this sequence : "Hey Jude", "Revolution", "Paperback Writer", "I Should Have Known Better", "Lady Madonna", "Can't Buy Me Love", "Don't Let Me Down", "The Ballad Of John And Yoko", "Rain", "Old Brown Shoe".

Nonetheless, what you have here is a prime and perfect example of what happens when 2 favorite Beatles albums are presented together onto a single-disc CD. The result is remarkable. 40 years later, these 2 classic releases sound just as good now as they did the first time around.

It's people like Mr. Sumner that aided in Elvis' decline and eventually his death by enabling and caretaking. Not that Elvis doesn't share the blame. Addiction and alcoholism have at their roots selfishness and self-centeredness and he was told by more than one person to clean up and because of his delusional state, refused to clean up. I suppose it's difficult for someone to hit bottom when he has a host of "friends" who aren't willing to tell the truth to him and when you make $100,000 for an appearance that certainly doesn't seem like someone who has hit bottom.

title: Beware, incorrect product description.
text: This cd edition of The Stones album "It's Only Rock 'n' Roll" (the album originally released 1974) has incorrect information in the product description.  Specifically, the cd release date and what that would logically imply.  The release date shown is the year 2020 which, would suggest that this is an updated remastered version of some kind of this album on cd.  At least that's what I thought.  I already had the 2009 release of this album on cd so I figured it had now been upgraded in some fashion (the whole Stones catalog was remastered in 2009 and is still, in general, the best versions of their albums on cd).  The main reason that I assumed this was that The Stones previous album, "Goat's Head Soup" (originally released 1973) was re-released in 2020 with a major remastering job that I was quite impressed with comparing it to the 2009 cd release which I also had.  Well, based on that logic, I bought this new version (the 2020) of It's Only R n R and to my amazement it is an exact duplicate of the 2009 cd release!  No change in remastering as with eq's, volume levels or anything that one would expect with a remastering (I checked it out on my digital audio editing software).  There is not even any expanded info in the inner cover as one might expect, it's exactly the same as the 2009 version.  I then noticed on the bottom of the back cover in small print (needing a magnifying glass) that the release date was, in fact, shown as 2020.  On the cd itself 2020 is printed (in the circular small print around the outer edge of the cd).  I then got out my 2009 cd version and compared it to the 2020 version.  The only difference between the two is that this 2020 version lists areas of the world, other countries, that this cd was previously not available, mostly South American countries and a few in Southeast Asia (again, needing a magnifying glass to discover all of the foreign legal licensing mumbo-jumbo only a lawyer would understand).  But the 2020 product description on Amazon doesn't tell you that!  I don't live in Argentina or Cambodia!  So, in the end, I paid est. $18.00 for a cd advertised as being released in 2020 that had already been released in 2009 that was identical in sound and packaging.  By the way, the 2009 version is still posted on Amazon for about half that price (and the product description for that version is correct showing 2009 as the release date).  So, buyers beware, this version of It's Only Rock 'n' Roll is NOT what it is advertised as.  It is only a duplicate of the 2009 version but now is available in other foreign markets.  There is, however, another Japanese version of this album also released in 2020 that is posted on Amazon.  That one looks as if it is a genuine remastering with specific notes citing extra tracks and different packaging.  It goes for about $27.00 (I'm holding off on that one just yet).  I returned the bogus 2020 version that I received and got my refund.  Although it was kind of difficult explaining all this in the limited characters space that is available to explain why I was returning it.  You can fit only about 20 words in it!  By the way, the one star rating I posted is for the bogus advertising, whether it be a mistake or intentional on the manufacturer's part.  It has nothing to do with the music of this album which is a Stones classic.  Additionally, I would like to point out that this is not the first time I have run into this problem of false product descriptions of cds, specifically the inaccurate release dates and the confusion it creates whether it be because of an error or intentional.  I know it must be difficult to screen all product descriptions for mistakes but with music one can be easily misguided over seemingly simple errors as with release dates and other simple information.  So, my advice to music lovers who want to get what they are paying for, read the product info and compare it to other similar or identical posts of the same product before clicking "Buy".  Even with being careful one can still wind up with a bogus product, like I did.  Fortunately, Amazon is very good with their customer relations, and they always fix the problem (financially) with their customers.  Now, having said that, I would think that it is Amazon's responsibility to either correct or remove bogus product posts because of deceptive product descriptions, especially concerning music products, after the false product descriptions, such as this, have been called to their attention.
