title: McBain Has At Tricky Dick, Reader Suffers
text:
Ed McBain gets metaphorical in this 1973 edition of his 87th Precinct crime series, taking on then-President Nixon in the person of Randy M. Nesbitt, leader of a gang on a killing spree.

As a time capsule, "Hail To The Chief" is a sometimes interesting read. As a police procedural, it's weak. The leader of the "Yankee Rebels" (one of many symbolic nods to Nixon perfidy) Nesbitt is presented to us as a guy elected to his second term in office, fighting a war he inherited without much enthusiasm but that he is intends to finish because, as he piously insists, he is a man of peace. "I pray to God every night that I'll always do the right thing," Nesbitt insists.

McBain has at Nixon both in terms of Watergate, then blowing up but still a year away from its final resolution with Nixon's resignation, and particularly with U.S. troops in Vietnam, just then being brought back home. The opening scene, of men, women, and an infant lying in a ditch, deliberately conjures up the My Lai massacre and similar atrocities which Nixon was seen by many to be complicit in, even though My Lai took place during the previous administration. You keep waiting for Nesbitt to tell someone he is not a crook. He doesn't, but that's about the only button McBain misses.

Subtlety is not his goal here, nor is humor. Both are missed. While McBain criminals can be quite deep and multi-faceted (more than the cops often) it quickly becomes clear to anyone reading this novel that Nesbitt is a knuckle-dragging moral leper, a boil on the face of humanity, unable to see beyond his own colossal egotism. When he condemns his fellow gang member's girlfriend (a character named Midge, based on the wife of John Mitchell who talked to reporters during the height of the Watergate investigation) to what becomes her doom, he insists that there is no blood on his hands. He only gave the orders. [Cue the Nazi marching music here.]

As a polemic, McBain offers meat to chew on. But "Hail To The Chief" is a police procedural featuring the 87th Precinct, and it's an ill-fit seeing the familiar environs of Isola playing host to a doctrinaire political parable. McBain had been writing about gang violence since the first 87th Precinct novel two decades before, and before that, under his real name Evan Hunter in the classic "Blackboard Jungle." Maybe he wanted to jazz up the old formula. But the Yankee Rebels can't work as satire if they don't work in the reader's mind as a real gang, and they don't. For example, how Nesbitt, a pious, paranoid blowhard with a marked aversion to obscenities, sex, and drugs, got to command a street gang is never explained.

It's sometimes fun to pick up on the Nixon references. Nesbitt has a bug installed in one of his rivals' headquarters, known as "Gateside" rather than "Watergate." His chief negotiator is called "Doc," (i.e. Dr. Kissinger) and he works on a policy of triangulation against two rival gangs much like China and the Soviet Union. In the end, Nesbitt is done in by his own paranoia, and it's something of a credit to McBain he seems to beat Woodward and Bernstein to Watergate's conclusion.

But the book just doesn't work as crime fiction. There is no mystery to solve here, just dead bodies lying around and a gang too drunk on bloodletting to cover its tracks. By the time Nesbitt explains how his "second term as president" was his mandate for seeking peace through strength, we got the point long ago. One good thing about Nixon resigning the next year - it meant McBain had to go back to writing about real crime.

title: This Album Is A Preview Of Later Video Game Soundtracks
text:
Most people who recognize Spencer Nilsen's name remember his work with Sega Genesis in the 1990s, specifically the video game music from the "Sonic The Hedgehog" CD, "Ecco The Dolphin", and "Ecco 2: The Tides Of Time". (The first of the latter two titles reflects an ambient direction, continued to some extent in the second "Ecco" game, however, blended with a good dose of World and Tribal music.)

With "Architects Of Change", listeners are treated to a preview of what would evolve into the sound of the "Sonic The Hedgehog" soundtrack (available on the U.S. version of the game). The same textures and electronic sounds are all present. In fact, the same overall tone and feel were laid down in this earlier work. For the most part, the music is bright, cheerful, and cleverly showing the way to the future, as does really good Tangerine Dream music. Clearly, this album was paving the way for Spencer's best remembered music.

Whereas the "Sonic The Hedgehog" music was constructed and designed for video game looping, "Architects Of Change" retains more soul in that, the music is constructed like a song, and reflects much more than music played repeatedly in a video game. This album has more to offer in feeling and sonic quality (no pun intended).

If you happen to like Spencer Nilsen's work, be sure to track down this album to see his artistry unfolding a few years prior to his best remembered body of work. The architect was already laying his foundations.

title: Poor sound quality and very little new or exciting
text:
This comes from the Catfish Rising tour. It is a little over 50 minutes long and the sound quality is marginal.

The sound quality of this CD is borderline. I think it is just bad enough that I don't want to listen to it. It is supposed to be a BBC concert master tape. The BBC concerts have had varying sound quality. Some have been very good (like Caravan) and others have been very bad (like Yes). This sounds like a bootleg audience recording. There is no high end. The drums and bass are booming as if recorded from the echos on the wall. The vocals and guitars have no dynamic range. However, the sound is clear and there is no static or hiss. But, it has a strange quality that is pleasant for repeated listenings.

I have many, many Jethro Tull albums, including the 25 and 30 year anniversary boxsets. I have lots of live recordings from those and other sources. Most of the songs on this CD are available live from other concert CDs. Almost nothing is done in a new or interesting way, so you just get reruns with bad sound quality. I certainly don't need to hear another 7 minute Thick as a Brick. The one exception is a nice blues jam I haven't heard before..

title: No heart; no soul
text: I heard the Spring Festival Overture programmed at a Lunar New Years concert under Carl St. Clair, which sent me looking for it, leading me to this disc.  SFO [5 minutes] is fine, stirring and melodic – works compositionally because it doesn’t throw the baby out with its culturally ancient and rich bathwater.  The other two works on the disk, White-Haired Girl Suite [22 minutes - 15 too many] and Heroes Monument [19 minutes - 19 too many] are just so much dreck.  Eastern European post romanticism on roid rage w/no cultural informant.  Uninspired, thick, noisy, bombastic, dull and unrelentingly devoid of melody.  Patriotism/propaganda by the numbers – infuriatingly cold and clumsy.  SFO is nice to hear, but this CD was expensive and completely out of proportion to its content.  Sound good, playing good, engineering good.  Anything over $10 -max- including shipping and I think you’re going to be sad.  Not recommended unless you’re researching Chinese agitprop.

title: What a great album!
text:
The recording of "My Bonnie" is crystal clear and rocking! The first 21 recordings are beautifully reproduced and as fresh as the day they were recorded. This is high-energy, feel-good, rock-n-roll! The material with Tony Sheridan features great piano and saxophone accompaniment. Sheridan sounds as if he could've come from the Sun Records / Memphis, Tennessee crowd. With tinges of swing and jazz, the Sheridan / Beat Brothers combination is delightfully eclectic. The versions of "Dream Baby", "Memphis Tennessee", "Please Mr. Postman" and several other tracks are live recordings. They're important for their historical value, but the quality of the recordings is quite rough compared to the tracks that precede them.
The same is true for disc 2: the studio recordings are of good to high quality, while the live recordings are a bit shaky (revealing the limitations of the equipment of the time).

title: Barrel Bottoms and Lost Years
text: Even the immense talent of Danny Gatton are not enough to make me want to sit through third rate warblers.  That's what you get here, folks.  Poore, Seaton and Anderson may have had their strong points as singers, producers, whatever, but they're not found within these four discs.  Maybe you'll think that the instrumental pieces on disc four are worth the price of admission.  Maybe you just want to complete your Humbler collection.  If both apply to you, look for the Live 1977 disc.  The sound quality is comparable and it's cheaper.  Sonic qualities rarely count for much when the recordings are rare and historic, but here, they are annoying.  Even the instrumental cuts feature shameless spoken intros by Seaton that must've had D.G. squirming in his boots.  What I'm really trying to say is that even the widest of attention spans will struggle to get through one of these discs-Gatton fanatic or no.  I bought it used for 45 bucks.  I sold it only slightly more used for 44.  I don't miss it.

title: An Act of Faith Rewarded
text:
In the old days, we bought albums, not songs. As hard as it is for our impatient moderns to imagine, there was a time when owning a song which you already loved meant exposing your ears to a half-dozen other tracks that you had probably never heard of, much less heard. The great virtue of this ancient state was that it more or less forced you to listen to music you didn't already know: You had bought it all, so you at least tried it all, feeling bound by your purchase to give all the tracks a play. And for me - very, very often, actually - I found over time that some of the tracks I'd never heard before became the ones I valued most.

When, through YouTube, I tracked down the album which contained "No Time To Lose," I bought the disc to get that track, which could have been practically the theme song for a girl I know born in the same year as this album. I was following again my oft-rewarded philosophy: Buy the whole mine for the gem you can see, and find others hidden inside. These are happy accidents originating in acts of faith.

But not in every case! The perfect miracle of "No Time to Lose" was evidently never granted again to the Tarney/Spencer outfit - and I say "evidently" because there are thirteen other opportunities on this disc, and they all land me in one or another forgettable poppy-place. I've tried hard, and patiently, to find other glimmers of immortality here, but I finally have to summarize the experience in this way: The rest of these are tunes that could have been playing in the background at parties your parents would have approved of. Feh.

I envy the other reviewers here who found 53 minutes of delight. I'm the poorer, you're the richer, and this may well be because your ears are more open than mine. But do understand, I'm not disappointed in the purchase. I have a full-fidelity track of one flawless gem from 1979, ready at any time to remind me of another.

title: Buy these splendid performances in decent transfers, not this garbage
text:
The performances themselves on this disc are classics. Toscanini was actually a fine Gershwin conductor, perhaps not as fluent in the jazz idiom as some others but with a firm grasp of the composer's internal logic and structure. I doubt you will find a better or more coherent performance of American in Paris, and in all of these pieces the conductor's attention to detail and meticulous phrasing and dynamics serve the music well. And even Toscanini's legendary swift tempi are a match to the composer's own performances. Earl Wilde is his usual magnetic self in the Rhapsody, and Oscar Levant gives a highly-charged and (to me) convincing reading of the Concerto.

So why two stars? Because these transfers are pretty bad. They appear to have been made from old LPs, with little or no filtering or adjustment for dynamics or pitch (or even editing for glitches in the source material). The result is strident strings, obvious surface noise, dynamic overload in loud passages and, in several cases, skips in the music (like what you'd get if you had a scratch or a small particle stuck to the grooves of an LP).

There are better transfers of the Rhapsody and Concerto and I encourage you to buy those instead. As for American in Paris, this is the only CD copy of the live 1943 performance I know of that's currently available. Toscanini did record the piece again in the studio in 1945 and that recording is still available on an RCA CD. Like most Toscanini studio performances I've been able to compare to live ones, the studio version is a bit stiff, but the performances are essentially the same, the sound is better, and it remains my favorite.

Go elsewhere.

title: A Not Fully Cooked and Behind the Times Country Corn Album.  It's a miss, except for the out-of-date Beatles' novelty song
text:
Don Bowman, FUNNY WAY TO MAKE AN ALBUM, RCA/Victor LPM 3495 mono/LSP 3495 stereo. Lp dates about January, 1966.

Track list:
side one--
Dear Harlan Howard/The Other Ringo/I Get the Feeling We're Through/Dear Sister/That's Show Biz/Little Diesel Drivin' Devil
side two--
Things Are Looking Up/More than Me/Kansas City Star/Freddy Four Toes/Boll Weevil Air Lines/Freda on the Freeway

Well, how shall I say this? If Don Bowman were playing baseball at bat, he had one decent at bat ("...Ringo"), maybe two close call fouls ("More Than Me" and "Boll Weevil Air Lines"), and fanned out on his other nine tries.

"The Other Ringo" -- this is a minor gem. This song is a reference or mashup dig at the Beatles, referencing or spoofing "She Loves You" (early '64 Beatlemania, so it's 18 months out-of-date when released; the mostly female chorus breaks into "Yeah Yeah Yeah"s throughout the song), Ringo Starr fandom and country digs at Beatle haircuts, and parodying Lorne Greene's "Ringo" hit for the tune.

"More Than Me" -- his wife has left him and her hairspray cans have blown up and splattered his place with all her makeup. Lipstick containers as bullets pocking the walls and his refrigerator.

"Boll Weevil Air LInes" -- the references/parody is built around Bobby Bare's "Detroit City" as a talky recitation about flying on a seat-of-the-pants outback country hick airline.

"Freddy Four Toes" -- a song about "The Foot Grabber" lawn mower. (Deadpan here:) ha. ha. ha.
"Things Are Looking Up" -- a not done, not well done, actually pretty lousy reworking of Ferlin Husky's "The Drunken Driver" (Capitol) '50s song done so much better/worse years before.
"Freda on the Freeway" -- lost on a freeway cloverleaf. (Deadpan here:) ha. ha. ha.
Roger Miller's "Kansas City Star" is given a straight cover reading.

Bowman is clearly borrowing --and toning down for sedate semi-suburban mid-'60s audiences here-- Ferlin Husky's great hillbilly clown alter ego, Simon Crum. Bowman apes Crum's cartoonish clown accent, stretching out one-syllable words like "that" as "tha...yat," "they-yay," and "there" as "there-yer," but he does it in a voice that suggests Wink Martindale having burnt out his pipes cigarette chain-smoking four packs of Camels a day. Backing instruments on this are an electric guitar, I think Hank Cochran's or Chet Atkin's, his producer on this, dobro, restrained drum kit (brushes), an ANNOYING deliberately badly played (comic) piano, and a soft-voiced male-female chorus (less pizzazz than the Anita Kerr Singers; very restrained). Liner notes on back by Jethro Burns, of Homer & Jethro fame/infamy.

This album is a "talky" recitation reading done in a more musical manner than Telly Savalas, Lorne Greene, Everett McKinley Dirksen, Red Sovine, and/or Wink Martindale, done over the sedate Nashville sound. Think a more suburban, very campy but dull version of Simon Crum laid over backing for Jim Reeves easy listening "country" pops. The album charted a bit. He had hits. Hearing this, I wonder why???

title: Forgotten album from an underrated songwriter!
text:
I'm an 80s pop junkie, for me the production values of the time had never been, and will never be better when it comes to pop music. There was a great blend of new technology, but no "Bedroom producers" like today, so good songwriting was rewarded, you couldn't come out with nonsense like Rebecca Black's Friday and have it hit the Billboard 100. And Michael Sembello was a great songwriter. Known best for his #1 hit Maniac from the Flashdance soundtrack, and his Top 40 hit Automatic Man from his first album Bossa Nova Hotel, Sembello wrote songs for Michael Jackson, Stevie Wonder, Sergio Mendes, Diana Ross, George Duke, and many others. But he had a great voice in his own right, and while his pop career never really took off, he did cut a few great albums, and Without Walls is one of them. If you like 80s Kenny Loggins, Lee Ritenour, Mr. Mister, or Journey, you'll like this album. Sembello blends together the West Coast production values of the time with some really catchy hooks, and his voice is actually quite nice. He's got a great range, and the songs on the album benefit from it. I really like the opener "What You Really Want", the ballad "Wonder Where You Are", and the darker rocker "The Picture." And Sembello got some great artists to perform on this album with him, including Bobby Caldwell, Steve Porcaro of Toto, drummer Carlos Vega, and Stevie Wonder.

Overall, great album. Shame the CD re-release is Japan-only and very rare, as this album is very good. Definitely give it a listen if you like 80s Pop!

title: 2 1/2 Stars: Howling Wolf
text:
"Cry_Wolf" is director Jeff Wadlow's first film and it many ways it shows: an over-eager sensibility permeates the simple story of a murderer on the loose at a ritzy boarding school. Like many novice directors, Bauman is eager to show us all that he has learned his entire life about making films and this is especially apparent in the frenzied editing and lack of focus of the screenplay: several of the key scenes lack forward propulsion because the words stop them dead in their tracks.

One thing that Bauman has right, though is the production, all phases of which: camera, lighting, mood are right spot on. This film is gorgeous with Bauman favoring the deep dark rich colors over pastels which perfectly set and hold the scenes and the action that unfolds.

Also, though we've seen the plot of this film many times, Wadlow and writer Beau Bauman manage to come up with a few good plot twists though the big surprise ending would have had more effect if the editing had been tighter.

The acting is okay to good with the veterans like Anna Deavere Smith (in too brief a performance) and Gary Cole coming off best.

"Cry_Wolf" is a good film but it could have been better. Wadlow is talented and has got the basics of production down. Next time though, he needs to pay closer attention to the finer details of the screenplay.

title: A very nice and melancholy bit of well-arranged psychedelic rock/pop
text:
This was a random purchase I made as part of my exploration of psychedelic music released during the late 1960's. Happily, this turned out to be one of the nicer listening experiences I have had as of late and was generally impressed with the lush arrangements, acoustic textures, and melancholy mood. Although sounding partly like a product of its time (November 1967), this album is pretty sophisticated musically, with themes of paranoia and death commingling with at least a few cheerier themes. In spite of the fact that this record is largely unsung, it apparently influenced a few other musicians, as I can hear bits and pieces of this album on The Soft Parade (The Doors, 1969) and Twelve Dreams of Dr. Sardonicus (Spirit, 1970). The English folk/prog group Strawbs has also acknowledged the influence of Love on their From The Witchwood album of 1971.

The musicians on Forever Changes include bandleader Arthur Lee (vocals, acoustic and electric guitars); John Ecols (lead electric guitar); Bryan Maclean (rhythm guitar and vocals - lead vocal on Alone Again and Old Man); Ken Forssi (electric bass guitar); and Michael Stuart (drums and percussion). In addition to the key band members there is an additional bassist, guitarist, drummer, and a pianist along with string and brass ensembles. The string ensemble is used a lot throughout and very effectively. I guess it's worth noting that the liner notes indicate that Arthur felt that the band did not possess the technical ability of a Cream or a Jimi Hendrix Experience and channeled his efforts into arrangement. As such, Forever Changes features layers and layers of instruments, excellent orchestration, rich vocal harmonies, nice melodies, acoustic textures, great production, and gloomy atmospheres. As a progressive rock fan I certainly appreciate virtuosity but appreciate good arrangements a whole lot more - I really enjoyed this album a lot in fact.

The eleven pieces (2'20" - 6'49") largely consist of strummed acoustic guitars and the occasional electric guitar solo atop a solid foundation of electric bass and drums. Skillfully woven into the overall "psychedelic rock sound" are trumpet and string parts that range from classical to big band (just like Chicago used their brass section, although Herb Alpert's Tijuana Brass sound does creep in there too). The trumpets really add a distinctive touch, while the strings make an unavoidable Beatles connection. Although I have described this music as melancholy and gloomy, there are occasionally bouncy and cheery sections that provide a nice balance.

Rhino did a great job remastering this album and there are extensive liner notes and photos of the band. The bonus tracks do not add too much, although they certainly are of historical value to fans of the band.

This is a great album that should prove to be of interest to those folks that like the proto-progressive British bands such as The Moody Blues ([[ASIN:B000002GQG In Search of the Lost Chord]], 1968) and Procul Harum ([[ASIN:B000006ZZ6 A Salty Dog]], 1969) along with other American west coast psychedelic acts like Jefferson Airplane ([[ASIN:B0000A0DRX After Bathing at Baxter's]], 1967), Spirit ([[ASIN:B000002AF2 Twelve Dreams of Dr. Sardonicus]], 1970) and The Doors ([[ASIN:B000MCIBB6 Waiting for the Sun]], 1968). I can honestly say that as a huge progressive rock fan who is exploring the psychedelic roots of the genre, this is a great album and is definitely worth adding to the psychedelic/progressive rock collection.

text: Ok, I'm tired of people taking weak shots at Lucas.  Everyone goes into the theaters with the highest expectations that absolutely no one can match, not even Lucas.  You can't expect the prequels to surpass the origianl trilogy, that's utterly impossible.  So my advice is to have an open mind about the prequels and be receptive to new ideas... aka STOP LIVING IN THE PAST.  i think the acting was very good... Hayden Christensen played a very good Anakin - people say his dialogue was broken and poor.. i disagree.  He plays his role right - confused, angered, and head over heals in love all at the same time.  His mind is a whirlwind and it shows through Christensen's acting.  Natalie Portman did very well also, not letting feelings for Anakin get in the way until the very end when her heart overcomes her brain, and it shows.  McGregor did excellent as well, portraying a more mature and well balanced Obi-Wan than in Episode I.  Christopher Lee did excellent as well, one can almost see regret in his eyes for all he has done.  The critical, unspoken attributes of all the actors come through if you watch the movie with a critical eye.  So instead of seeing it once and rejecting it, watch it again and the unspoken acting shines through.  The film filled in critical gaps in the storyline, and did it well.  I almost view Lucas as a modern Shakespeare, in which Shakespeare was famous for his ability to tie together every lose end at the conclusion of his works.  The computer graphics were astounding, flat out.  Many don't agree, but I view it this way.  This film was during a time where there were huge armies and giant wars, unlike during the original trilogy where the Rebellion was striving to survive on any older ship they could find to fight the Empire.  Lastly, if any of the above hasn't convinced you, listen to the soundtrack.  John Williams uses his musical magic yet again and no can argue that, flat out.  Mr. Lucas, you're right on track, don't let anyone tell you otherwise.  Can't wait for Episode III!

title: A highlight of early prime Caballe (1974)
text:
This is the second volume on CD of recordings made by Spanish Columbia (released later on DeccaLP) and even more difficult to find than the first. But the rewards are immense as this was made at the zenith of the Caballe's power (1974) before her enormous expansion of roles in the lyrico-spinto repertoire at the greatest houses on three continents. As such, the purity and flexibility of the 60s is evident, but also the incipient power and dramatic qualities of her later career.

Noteworthy are arias in three roles in she did not appear in on stage: Gilda, Suor Angelica, and Amina (Sonnambula) --- and they are sung to perfection with ideal accompaniment by Gianfranco Masini (who conducted some superb live recordings of Caballe in this period, all imperative listening). Arias from concurrent stage roles include the Trovatore Leonora, Amelia, and the two striking arias of Vepres Siciliennes.

Although there is considerable overlap with other aria albums of this period (EMI, RCA etc), the Suor Angelica lament is truly special.

title: Technical Detail: I do not believe this is a 1962 recording.
text:
The notes to this RussianDVD recording say that it was "recorded in 1962." However, I do not believe this is a 1962 recording for the following reasons.

First of all, we know there were only two performances in 1962, the world premier on December 18, 1962, and the second performance two days later, December 20, 1962.

The out-of-print RussianDisc recording is of the December 20, 1962 performance, the first known recording available here: www.amazon.com/Shostakovich-Symphony-No-Babi-Yar/dp/B000001LP5/ref=sr_1_4?ie=UTF8&s=music&qid=1239515052&sr=1-4 . (Text will wrap, but the CD and reviews are available at Amazon.com).

I have that December 20 recording, and the text and liner notes include the Russian text and English translation of Yevtushenko's poem, "Babi Yar":

Mne kazhetsya seichas -- ya judei.
Vot ya bredu po drevnemu Egiptu.
A vot ya, na kreste raspyaty, gibnu,
I do sikh por sledy gvozdei na mne.
Mne kazhetsya, shto Dreifus -- eto ya.
Meshchanstvo -- moi donoschik i sudya.
Ya za reshotkoi. Ya pola v koltso,
Zatravlennyi, oplyovannyi, obolgannyi.
I damochki s brusselskimi oborkami,
Vizzha, zontami tychut mne v listo
Mne kazhetsya, ya -- malchik v Belostoke.

English translation:
Now I imagine that I'm a Jew.
Here I wander through ancient Egypt.
And here, on the cross, crucified, I perish,
And still I have on me the marks of the nails.
I imagine myself to be Dreyfus.
The Philistine -- my informer and judge.
I am behind bars. I am surrounded,
Persecuted, spat on, slandered.
And dainty ladies in Brussels frills,
Squealing, poke their parasols into my face.
I imagine myself the boy from Belostok.

After the December 20, 1962, performance, Shostakovich's 13th Symphony "was banned unless Yevtushenko would make alterations in his verses, which he finally did, adding lines to "Babi Yar" to indicate that not only Jews were slaughtered there (at Babi Yar) and that the Russian people fought the Nazi beast with solidarity during the war" (identical text from both the liner notes of the RussianDISC CD and the cover notes of the Everest 3181 LP, November 20, 1965, performance in Moscow).

The earliest known performance of the Symphony with Yevtushenko's revised text was on February 10, 1963 (from the Everest LP cover notes above).

Because the RussianDVD.com recording contains the revised text, not the original text, it could not be of a 1962 performance because the words to that performance were not written yet (in 1962).

Don't confuse this RussianDVD.com recording with the original and out-of-print RussianDISK recording; they are not the same.

title: Worth a listen for Eden Brent fans
text:
Eden Brent should be one of the towering giants on the blues scene. While she has a following, she isn't quite the superstar she should be, and she hasn't recorded nearly enough for my tastes. What she has recorded, we can treasure. Those fans she has may go in search of more, and find themselves here, with The Brent Sisters, and Party Dress. Here, Eden is joined by... do I have to finish it? Her sisters are Bronwynne and Jessica, and Party Dress is a set of songs by their mother, Carole Lamb Brent. There are a few more musicians accompanying, all talented.

The material is good, and diverse. It ranges from blues, to country to some old, jazzy type material, and you get the sense that if not Carole herself, then the Brent family is in many ways as musically omnivorous as Eden herself. Eden didn't come from nowhere. The album is quite short, at just over 22 minutes, though, and from the perspective of an Eden Brent fan, there isn't all that much of Eden cutting loose on the piano, nor showcasing the power of her voice. If you are looking for something like Mississippi Number 1, this isn't it. She is, of course, sharing the stage with some other talented musicians. This is a talented family, but the affair as a whole is more laid back in its entirely than an Eden Brent album, which would also take some turns towards the rollicking. This is more of a homey album, as you might expect. Good? Yes. Comforting? Yes. Revelatory? No.

If you are looking for the lost Eden Brent album, this isn't quite it. But, it is a good album, and if you can't get enough of Eden, pick up a copy, if you can. You'll enjoy it.

title: The worst CD I've ever heard. Abysmal performances. Appaling recorded sound.
text:
This is undoubtedly the worst CD I have ever heard in my 30+ years of collecting them. Sigh....where to begin?

I'll cut straight to the chase - this reading of the Borodin 2nd Symphony is abysmal. Anshel Brusilow adopts thick, heavy textures, and does not keep a constant tempo for more than a bar or two before slamming on the brakes and bringing everything to a halt. This occurs throughout all 4 movements and becomes so overwhelmingly irritating one can hardly force oneself to continue listening. Never have I heard the 1st movement distorted so badly out of any semblance of musical purpose. Its tempos are stretched and pulled in every direction to the point of exhaustion and complete destruction of musical structure. Even in the Scherzo, which starts promisingly as a true Prestissimo, a few bars into it Brusilow again slams on the brakes, halting all sense of momentum. The 3rd movement, Andante, is taken Grave. Good grief, it crawls on for over 10 minutes (!), nearly 4 minutes longer than Martinon or Ansermet. By the time the Finale gets here, the listener has nodded off into a coma and hardly notices it is afflicted with the same egregious tempo violations. The strings play everything on-the-string, long bow, adding to the mush and lack of momentum. This is as far removed from sounding like a Russian symphony as one can imagine.

One wonders why Brusilow is such a horrible conductor. According to his book, "Shoot the Conductor" (which I just recently read), he was assistant concertmaster under Szell for many years and went on to be Ormandy's concertmaster for a few years. I'm pretty sure he didn't learn this complete disregard for the printed score from Szell! And I doubt Ormandy would have approved either. I also doubt he was allowed to play his violin for either conductor in the manner in which he demands from the Bournemouth strings in this recording.

Incidentally, I read that he was the Dallas Symphony Orchestra's conductor in the early 70s - for just 3 years before they fired him. After listening to this disc, I can certainly understand why. I also found it amusing that Mr. Brusilow regards himself quite highly as a conductor (and even singles out this Borodin recording as one of his "accomplishments"). Seriously, he should have stuck to playing the violin.

So then, abysmal performance aside, this is also one of EMI's worst-sounding recordings - at least in this remastering. This is a 1989 release in their mid-priced "Studio" line (the attractive series with the red trays). The sound is edgie and harsh, with an overwhelming, glassy glare to the bloated body of sound. And in fortissimos, the sound turns so raw and unrefined, it is practically unlistenable.

I'd like to make perfectly clear that the abysmal attempt at music-making heard on this disc is not for a moment the fault of the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra. They do not sound disinterested, or bored, or unprofessional. And I highly doubt their brass players could sound this unrefined and unmusical if they tried. They are simply trying to be responsive to the preposterous directions coming from the figure on the podium and EMI rewards the entire affair with the worst imaginable recorded sound.

Put it all together and you have what is, without doubt, the worst CD ever.

title: One of the best songs omitted - what was he thinking?
text:
EMERGING, by the Phil Keaggy band, is basically Keaggy's third solo album. It stands up fairly well among his other early albums, even though it doesn't contain any of his best-known songs.

The main problem with the sole (and now very rare) CD reissue called RE-EMERGING is the unexplained omission of the final track, "Gentle Eyes," which was easily the second best song on the original LP. (The best was definitely "Struck By The Love," written and sung by keyboardist Phil Madeira rather than Keaggy.) Why was this song omitted, while some lesser tracks (like the lyrically unfortunate "Sorry") remain? I've heard something about "licensing issues" being involved, but one would think these should have been resolved before the CD was released. The worst part is that the omission seems to have been glossed over, as if listeners were somehow not supposed to notice it.

There are four bonus tracks, newly recorded by the temporarily reunited band. Each of these gives a lead vocal spotlight to one of the band members, including the two who didn't sing at all on the original album, but oddly excluding Lynn Nichols (guitar & backing vocals).

"My Auburn Lady" has Keaggy celebrating his wife, and her hair color. Cute but inessential.

"Mighty Lord" is by Phil Madeira, and has sort of a Billy Preston vibe. Besides being the best song among the bonus tracks, it's also the most "valid" in that it was intended for the original LP (but left off because the record company didn't want there to be too many non-Keaggy songs).

Drummer Terry Anderson co-writes "You're My Hero" and gives it a shaky but sincere "Ringo" vocal (as Keaggy calls it).

Bassist Dan Cunningham sings the countrified cover tune "Amelea Earhart's Last Flight." He's not a great singer but the song suits him perfectly.

If you're a Keaggy fan and can find this CD for anything like a reasonable price, go for it. But see if you can get "Gentle Eyes" put to digital form as well.

title: Available at Long Last!
text:
Everyone is familiar with the triple-LP, double-CD, Live Europe 72 from the Grateful Dead. The songs selected for this collection represented a mere fraction from their 1972 European Tour. The tour covered twenty venues.

Rhino Records released the complete recordings from this tour, in seventy-three CDs, in 2011, in a limited edition suitcase, and later as an ordinary box set. These collections instantly became a collector’s items, and if one is lucky enough to find one online, the collector’s suitcase edition alone will run almost one thousand dollars. Rhino released individual concerts on CD, but even these are becoming difficult to find. Finally, these concerts are now available for download.

The previous occasion the band played this venue was a bit rocky, with the band apparently perplexed at a lackadaisical audience. Perhaps to liven the set the band played a tune infrequently included in concerts, let alone used as an opening number, Cold Rain and Snow. This first number was typical of their first step. Lively, upbeat performances without drama. Their first set closed with Black-Throated Wind” to a more enthusiastic applause.

The second set began with Casey Jones. In the same way, the band’s rendition of tunes such as Sugaree and Playin in the Band were performed with verve. A novelty in this second set was that the band buried a song they usually reserve for an encore number, One More Saturday Night. The band was apparently more at ease this time around in Tivoli, and it showed in the audience’s response. After they played El Paso in this second set, the audience gave the band an especially long and appreciative applause.

In general, these and the other songs in this concert were done more or less in a straightforward manner, with no great guitar flourishes or melodious cascades up and down the bass fret. The band could be forgiven for this straight up performance, considering their previous concert at Aarhus University saw them play with single-unit abandon.

Weir wearily said the band was going to “take a short break” at the end of their second set. When they returned to their third set, they employed an incredible intro before getting into their Dark Star medley. It started with JC’s guitar dueting with the piano keyboards, Lesh’s bass entering soon thereafter. Weir and Kreutzman on the drums contribute subtle, understated flourishes here and there, and for the next half hour the four instruments communicate with each other, one playing off the other. Really, it is one of the best Dark Stars in this tour. After traveling the reaches of outer space, the band returned back to earth with peppy Sugar Magnolia. The band segues into an improvised bit of jamming called Caution (Do Not Stop on the Tracks). Things must have been going well with the crowd, because they ended with Johnny B. Good, the only time they played this song in the tour.

All in all, it was a good concert and I wish I could have been there.

Next stop is Germany for a change of pace.

title: Original Fortunes Decca Recordings
text: THE FORTUNES are possibly one of the most neglected artists whose career are not represented very well on CD. The group's most successful recordings could be divided into decades and labels. From 1963 to 1966, they were on Decca in the UK, and Press in the US. From 1967 through the mid-70's they were on various EMI labels - United Artists, World Pacific and finally Capitol where HERE COMES THAT RAINY DAY FEELING AGAIN was their biggest hit. That period is covered expertly on the Taragon label CD -THE VERY BEST OF THE FORTUNES 1967-1972. This CD covers their Decca recordings, and was not even released in the US. That makes it hard to find. But it is worth seeking out, as it includes their biggest hits from this period, and some hard to find singles not on other CD collections. YOU'VE GOT YOUR TROUBLES remains a staple of the British Invasion era that is still played today. HERE IT COMES AGAIN and THIS GOLDEN RING were the other big hits they had. Their sound included harmonies that vie with The Hollies, but with more orchestration. Rod Allen was the main lead singer, and Glen Dale and Barry Pritchard sang as well. It was a sound that major solo artists from the UK usually had - a powerful vocalist backed up with lush, and sometimes bombastic orchestration. The Fortunes have this accompaniment on many of the songs here, and recorded songs by the major British songwriters of the day such as Greenaway-Cook, and Reed-Mason. They also wrote their own material, which are more Beat group sounding. This CD includes some excellent rockers such as THINGS I SHOULD HAVE KNOWN, GONE FROM MY MIND, and YOU GAVE ME SOMEBODY TO LOVE. Equally compelling songs include SILENT STREET and AM I LOSING MY TOUCH, plus B-sides like I'VE GOT TO GO, I LOVE HER STILL, and I LIKE THE LOOK OF YOU, among many others on this 20 track CD. Tagged at the end are 2 LIVE cover versions of SHE'S SURE THE GIRL I LOVE  and YOU'VE REALLY GOT A HOLD ON ME that were released on a various artists Live at the Cavern Club album. The booklet also includes excellent liner notes and a discography/session list of their Decca recordings. Released on the Dream label in the 90's, it offers up the best amount of songs from this period of the band. With the market saturated with countless re-recordings on various budget labels by later incarnations of the group , usually still with Rod Allen, it is hard to find the original recordings. Seek this one out and you won't be disappointed.

title: Such a wasted opportunity!
text: I have just listened to this recording on the radio. I had not heard the announcer say which recording it was, so my impressions are based solely on the recording itself, with no preconceptions based on my knowledge of the performers (though I was sure that I had never heard this particular recording before). (Verdi's Requiem is one of my two favorite musical works, along with his Otello; I have sung it four times and heard it several times with major orchestras and first-rate soloists.) From the soloists' first entrance, I was blown away by the soprano, impressed with the mezzo, and appalled by the tenor! The bass seemed fine, though a bit light and dry in timbre. I found the conducting idiosyncratic, running to extremes of tempo -- in particular, often very slow, yet without intensity, and sometimes very brisk, yet lacking excitement. My impression was of a conductor who knew and loved the work, but was self-indulgently trying for effects he couldn't quite achieve. The audio quality was excellent, with good detail and balance, though the chorus could have been more present. I was very puzzled by the discrepancy in quality among the soloists. I especially wondered how a recording came to be made that paired an obviously world-class soprano at the peak of her powers with a travesty of a tenor! My first thought was that he was an elderly, well-respected tenor way past his peak AND having a bad day. But it soon became apparent from his phrasing that he could never have been a first-rank opera singer. What on earth was he doing on this otherwise fairly accomplished recording? Well, when I checked the radio program listings, all became clear! Such a wasted opportunity! With a different tenor, this could have been a fine, interesting recording, even if not a contender for the short list. I'm giving it two stars as a compromise; Bocelli deserves no stars at all, but I would give the rest of the recording three. My favorite recording of the Requiem, despite its limitations in audio quality, remains the Giulini, with Schwarzkopf (no, I don't agree that the soprano needs to be an Aida; a great interpreter of Strauss fits the part perfectly), Ludwig, Gedda (who named this as his favorite among his own recordings), and Ghiaurov (my all-time favorite Verdi bass).

title: METICULOUS SUPPLEMENTS TO THE ABBADO RAVEL CYCLE
text:
Four very fastidious artistes—Abbado, Accardo, Margaret Price and Ravel himself—are convened here, in clinically clear, modernist performances. They’re in the Pierre Boulez mode but given heart and warmth by soloists Price, Accardo and the LSO in tiptop form at All Saints’ (Tooting) and Watford Town Hall. The DG digital engineering, by Klaus Hiemann and Hans-Rudolf Müller, is appropriately sumptuous throughout. The Ida Rubinstein ballet and TOMBEAU are from Abbado’s complete Ravel orchestral cycle, while the addenda (not otherwise reissued) are the highlights here, TZIGANE and the exotic, louche SHÉHÉRAZADE, made originally as a standalone supplement in November 1987.

We ordinarily want a French conductor for Ravel (Monteux, Martinon or Manuel Rosenthal), but Abbado and Ravel both were notoriously fastidious and this A/R choice works interestingly for me. The playful formality of TOMBEAU exactly suits Abbado’s style (the quaint suite sounds more cohesive, less frivolous under the Abbado baton), and BOLÉRO similarly benefits from the unvarying but inflected beat laid down by this dirigent, coaxing fine solos from the LSO first chairs and an unleashed Watford gong at the final iteration of the faux-Moorish tune.

Abbado’s countryman Accardo, forwardly recorded, is assertive but not aggressive in TZIGANE, trading cheeky raspberries with the symphonic band in the neatly disciplined climax. The late great Margaret Price (Carlos Kleiber’s inspired choice for his Isolde) is typically impressive in the two concluding chansons of SHÉHÉRAZADE, given Liederlike artistry, depth and (Welsh) warmth, although for the fully exotic coloration and languour of “Asie” the classic versions by Maggie Teyte and Régine Crespin (Barbara Hendricks too) remain unsurpassed. Klingsor’s texts for the cycle are not included in this budget set (which is unique in its couplings), but Price’s French enunciation (her instrument recorded just slightly veiled) is magnetically alluring, as in her (electronically assisted) Isolde. Unlike Crespin, operatically huge of voice and demonstrative, Dame Margaret sings SHÉHÉRAZADE as the introspective French song cycle that it is.

title: Fascinating docudrama...
text: This is a fascinating and educational film, but viewers looking for an ordinary movie-going experience might be disappointed.  The movie is a docudrama - it is just a re-enactment of the backstage drama that went on when Edward R. Murrow, Fred Friedly, and the people at CBS News took on Senator McCarthy.  There are some references made to the personal lives of these people (there is a sub-plot about a secret marriage) but not much.  We do not follow Murrow home and Joe McCarthy appears in newsreel footage as himself.  Still, it is an intriguing look inside the world of TV journalism and of a time when television was a much simpler thing - no special effects, and Murrow reads from a script.  Of course, the obvious message is to see how our war on terror is driving us again into a state of McCarthyism, but - since none of this movie happens in the present - that remains subtext and the movie does not become overly preachy.

title: A Marvelously Musical -- and Dramatic -- St. John Passion
text:
Just before the HIPP movement began to hit its stride in the early 1970s Wolfgang Gonnenwein recorded both Bach Passion settings in Munich for EMI's German affiliate, Electrola. At that time (and yes, I was around back then) they attracted, at best, lukewarm critical reactions in the USA. In fact, only Gonnenwein's St. Matthew Passion received a release on EMI's US affiliate, Angel Records; I had to buy this recording of the St. John Passion as an expensive German LP import. Competing against widely admired Passion LP recordings by Karl Richter (DGG) and Karl Munchinger (Decca/London), Gonnenwein's recordings disappeared from record store shelvesalmost as soon as they were released.

Well, with the passage of time Karl Richter's recordings in particular have suffered eclipse at the hands of contemporary scholarship about Baroque performance practice. Indeed, the current plethora of Bach Passion recordings could seem to pass definitive judgment about Bach performed anyway other than those proclaimed by the Gospel of HIPP.

Except ... many of us who love this music continue to go back to the likes of Richter and Munchinger -- and even Klemperer & Furtwaengler -- for their insights into Bach's great choral music. Most of us don't dismiss the particular excellences offered by conductors like Brueggen, Gardiner, Herreweghe, McCreesh and Suzuki, but we still feel an affinity for conductors who experienced Bach as part of their grounding in an age-long musical culture and tradition.

This is all by way of saying that, to my mind, Gonnenwein's Bach recordings are remarkably satisfying. On the one hand, they convey the spirit of Bach with deep emotion as felt by generations of performers who took seriously the music's religious 'message'. On the other hand, both Gonnenwein's St. Matthew and St. John Passion recordings present the music lucidly and without leaden heaviness.

Gonnenwein's soloists are a distinguished lot, including Elly Ameling, Brigitte Fassbaender, Franz Crass and Kurt Moll. His primary chorus in both recordings is the South German Madrigal Choir and it delivers choral textures with a satisfying transparency. Ditto the chamber orchestra contribution provided by Gonnenwein's excellent instrumentalists.

To sum up, clarity and transparency are marvelously combined with rich musical coloring and real spiritual feeling in Gonnenwein's recordings. I return to them regularly and with real pleasure.

EMI/Electrola's analog stereo sound quality is first-rate for the period. The particular recording of the St. John Passion reviewed here is a Musical Heritage Society CD set leased from EMI/Electrola. I can report that the CDs impressively convey the warmth of the LPs plus that additional clarity delivered by high quality digital remastering.

Wolfgang Gonnenwein's Bach recordings might be little-remembered 'dark horse' contenders in today's ever-so-saturated market of recorded Bach Passions. But IMHO Gonnenwein continues to provide a compelling, spiritually nourishing musical experience.

title: Better than TPM but not as good as the classic trilogy!
text:
SOME MINOR SPOILERS!
While the classic Star Wars films (episodes IV-VI) felt exciting and full of energy, the SW prequels (epidodes I-III) are so far a huge letdown. What is missing in these prequels are humanity and humor, which has been replaced in the prequels by better special effects, but these effects completely take over the story, instead of enhancing them.
After The Phantom Menace, which is rightfully regarded not only as the WORST Star Wars film, and one of the most ridiculous science fiction films ever made, George Lucas followed up TPM with Attack of the Clones which has a better story, but one that still disappoints.
The "romantic" element in AOTC, between Anakin and Padme feels forced and right out of a soap opera. Not only that, but the teenage Anakin is more of a brat and feels nothing like the feared future Dark Lord of the Sith. I'm sorry, but no sane person could ever picture young Darth Vader running around grassy knowles along with his girlfriend. As for Padme, she is possibly one of the most boring written characters ever conceived, while everyone knows that she will be the mother to both Luke and Leia of the classic trilogy, Padme, has none of the qualities of her feisty and stubborn daughter. She is simply window dressing that will most likely be killed (possibly by Anakin/Darth Vader) in the final episode of the six-part saga, Episode III.
The ending felt like it was ripped out of Gladiator, with Jedis battling all sorts of droids and C-3PO making a complete fool out of himself!
Obi-Wan Kenobi is the only interesting character in both The Phantom Menace and in Attack of the Clones, and I liked his personal investigation into the assassination attempts on Padme's life along with his fight scenes with villian Jango Fett.
The real villian of the piece is Christopher Lee, who did a terrific job, with a lackluster script, as Count Dooku, a former Jedi knight who succumbs to the dark side. His lightsaber battle with Yoda is the highlight of the whole movie.
Overall, the first half of the film consists of a boring and cliched romance between Anakin and Padme, (Just to show who the parents of Luke and Leia are!) along with a few cool fight scenes, and ONE outer space battle in the entire film in an asteroid field! The last thirty minutes are non stop action that becomes repetitive very quickly!
All in all, Attack of the Clones is another overall disappointment in the SW "prequel" trilogy with some redeeming qualities....Here's HOPING that George Lucas can please young and old fans alike with the tragic final episode in the six-part Star Wars saga, (Sorry fans, Episode III is the final chapter) with Star Wars Episode III, due in theaters summer 2005!

title: Long Time Band mates Make More Music
text:
Mr. Brotzmann and Bennink starting playing together in the middle 1960s, as pioneers of European free jazz. They have continued to play together off-and-on for about forty years.

This set finds them in fine mettle, surging through an number of duets. Mr. Bennink sticks pretty close to his drum kit without indulging himself in exotic (and often irritating) percussion noises, as he does on other recordings. He keeps his yelling down as well. A few good yelps are fine. When he possesses the standard drum kit, he is masterful, displaying a deep resonance with Brotzmann's now fierce, not tender playing. He not only hits the cymbals and drums, but plays rims and the sticks themselves in unique and fitting ways.

Much of free jazz is without a set beat, working more in pulsations or waves than a standard time signature. This is true for some of this recording, but not all. Bennink can capture a rhythm profoundly.

As usual, Mr. Brotzmann is endlessly creative, intense, and mesmerizing on this reed instruments. If he is on a recording, I will try to find it.

title: Boring for the most part and similarly recorded
text:
This is an SACD compilation of 12 short works for organ, brass and timpani and arrangements of works for such ensembles. It is unique in two ways. First, the selections are not just blockbusters but also serious music. Second, you might assume that an SACD of Organ, Brass, and Timpani would be an astonishing disc. It is not.

The Strauss work with which the album begins is not widely known but is nonetheless a work of art. Some of the selections are well-known but primarily among classical music lovers such as the Baroque period Overture from Handel's Royal Fireworks Music. Gabrieli, another Baroque composer, is well represented by several of his sensational Canzons. Bach selections include music from three of his Cantatas. Even an arrangement of Mussorgsky's The Great Gate of Kiev from his Pictures at an Exhibition is included to bring the final curtain down on the disc and the two people who bought it. In fact, I may be the only one!

This disc suffers from selections that are not the most popular and sound that is good at best. I have heard few organs more poorly recorded. The organ is as unexciting as is most of the disc. If you are looking for spectacular sonics or selections fairly well-known outside serious classical music circles, look elsewhere. Two stars may be generous - and I'm a classical music lover.

title: Snap this CD up if you can get it
text: I recently found this CD used on Amazon after literally six years of searching for it. All I can say is, this is hands-down the best recording I have ever heard of either of these concerti. Serkin's pianism is dynamic and assured with no "dead spots"; he's clearly given thought to each note and phrase and is taking no sections of the music for granted. Schneider and the ECO back him up with a solid, sure orchestral accompaniment, really digging in and projecting the notes - not reducing these two concerti to "charming rococo pieces" the way so many others do. What really seals this recording's worth for me is the connection the performers draw between these works and Mozart's operas, and the palpable sense of fun they bring to the whole proceeding. Listen to the dramatic slow movements, their piano line given an almost bel canto style in Serkin's capable hands. Listen to the finale of the 14th concerto and Serkin's daringly relaxed tempo for the final 6/8 variation - one that brings out the jaunty insouciance of the main theme. And listen to the finale of the 15th concerto, where everyone involved is obviously enjoying the heck out of the piece and playing for the joy of it. I've never heard the spirit of Mozart come across as well in any other recording of these works. If you're at all a fan of these concertos or of Mozart in general, buy this CD wherever and whenever you can get your hands on it. It's that good.

title: Audience recording...poor sound.  Not a great performance but some really interesting stuff.
text:
This is an audience recording. The sound is just barely passable in spots and unlistenable in others.

This was recorded on July 6, 1972 after Duane died but while Barry Oakley was still alive. It does not have Les Dudek, who played with the Allman Brothers in concert for a short period of time.

Johnny Winter plays on the two encores, but this is where the sound quality is the worst. You cannot hear the vocals and the guitar work is very audible. Dust My Broom is pretty interesting but Johnny B. Goode is nothing special.

Other than the encores, this concert is basically the same set the group had been playing for 3 years. Only each night a song may be switched out or one song would get a long jam. Here, You Don't Love Me is only 7 minutes as is Elizabeth Reed. Whippin Post is 17 minutes.

The only thing really intersting about this concert is how Oakley comes more upfront and some of his solos blast off the speakers. This might be the best version of Statesboro Blues, if the sound qualiy wasn't so bad. There is an interesting jazzy 6 minute secion in Whippin Post that I have never hear before from any other concert recording.

This is really 1 star CD and I wouldn't buy it if I had known. I bump up to two stars becaus of the few musical moments I haven't heard before.
